notes.text: The sentence uses the infinitive absolute to strengthen the idea.

15.text: But if he should nullify them after he has heard them, then he will bear her iniquity.”

notes.text: In other words, he will pay the penalty for making her break her vows if he makes her stop what she vowed. It will not be her responsibility.

16.text: These are the statutes that the Lord commanded Moses, relating to a man and his wife, and a father and his young daughter who is still living in her father’s house.

notes.text: Heb “between.”

1.text: The Lord spoke to Moses:

notes.text: This lengthy chapter records the mobilization of the troops (vv. 1-5), the war itself (vv. 6-13), the death of the captive women (vv. 14-18), the purification of the nations (vv. 19-24), and the distribution of the spoils (vv. 25-54). For more detail, see G. W. Coats, “Moses in Midian,” JBL 92 (1973): 3-10; and W. J. Dumbrell, “Midian—a Land or a League?” VT 25 (1975): 323-37.

2.text: “Exact vengeance for the Israelites from the Midianites —after that you will be gathered to your people.”

notes.text: The imperative is followed by its cognate accusative to stress this vengeance. The Midianites had attempted to destroy Israel with their corrupt pagan practices, and now will be judged. The accounts indicate that the effort by Midian was calculated and evil.

The war was commanded by the Lord and was to be divine vengeance on the Midianites. So it was holy war. No Israelites then could take spoils in this—it was not a time for plunder and aggrandizement. It was part of the judgment of God upon those who would destroy or pervert his plan and his people.
This would be the last major enterprise that Moses would have to undertake. He would soon die and “be gathered to his people” as Aaron was.

3.text: So Moses spoke to the people: “Arm men from among you for the war, to attack the Midianites and to execute the Lord’s vengeance on Midian.

notes.text: The Niphal imperative, literally “arm yourselves,” is the call to mobilize the nation for war. It is followed by the jussive, “and they will be,” which would then be subordinated to say “that they may be.” The versions changed the verb to a Hiphil, but that is unnecessary: “arm some of yourselves.”
Heb “give.”

4.text: You must send to the battle 1,000 men from every tribe throughout all the tribes of Israel.”

notes.text: Some commentators argue that given the size of the nation (which they reject) the small number for the army is a sign of the unrealistic character of the story. The number is a round number, but it is also a holy war, and God would give them the victory. They are beginning to learn here, and at Jericho, and later against these Midianites under Gideon, that God does not want or need a large army in order to obtain victory.

5.text: So 1,000 from every tribe, 12,000 armed for battle in all, were provided out of the thousands of Israel.

6.text: So Moses sent them to the war, 1,000 from every tribe, with Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest, who was in charge of the holy articles and the signal trumpets.

notes.text: The Hebrew text uses the idiom that these “were in his hand,” meaning that he had the responsibility over them.
It is not clear what articles from the sanctuary were included. Tg. Ps.-J. adds (interpretively) “the Urim and Thummim.”

7.text: They fought against the Midianites, as the Lord commanded Moses, and they killed every male.

notes.text: Many modern biblical scholars assume that this passage is fictitious. The text says that they killed every male, but Judges accounts for the Midianites. The texts can be harmonized rather simply—they killed every Midianite who was in the battle. Midianite tribes and cities dotted the whole region, but that does not mean Israel went and killed every single one of them. There apparently was a core of Midianites whom Balaam had influenced to pervert Israel.

8.text: They killed the kings of Midian in addition to those slain—Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba—five Midianite kings. They also killed Balaam son of Beor with the sword.

notes.text: Here again we see that there was no unified empire, but Midianite tribal groups.

And what was Balaam doing among the Midianites? The implication is strong. This pagan diviner had to submit to the revealed will of God in the oracles, but he nonetheless could be hired. He had been a part of the attempt to destroy Israel that failed; he then apparently became part of the plan, if not the adviser, to destroy them with sexual immorality and pagan ritual.

9.text: The Israelites took the women of Midian captive along with their little ones, and took all their herds, all their flocks, and all their goods as plunder.

10.text: They burned all their towns where they lived and all their encampments.

notes.text: Heb “burned with fire.”
The ban applied to the encampments and forts of this group of Midianite tribes living in the region of Moab.

11.text: They took all the plunder and all the spoils, both people and animals.

12.text: They brought the captives and the spoils and the plunder to Moses, to Eleazar the priest, and to the Israelite community, to the camp on the rift valley plains of Moab, along the Jordan River across from Jericho.

notes.text: This is the area of the rift valley basin to the north of the Dead Sea and east of the Jordan. See the note at Num 21:1.
The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
Again this expression, “the Jordan of Jericho,” is used. It describes the intended location along the Jordan River, the Jordan next to or across from Jericho.

13.text: Moses, Eleazar the priest, and all the leaders of the community went out to meet them outside the camp.

14.text: But Moses was furious with the officers of the army, the commanders over thousands and commanders over hundreds, who had come from service in the war.

15.text: Moses said to them, “Have you allowed all the women to live?

notes.text: The verb is the Piel perfect of the word ‏חָיָה‎ (khayah, “to live”). In the Piel stem it must here mean “preserve alive,” or “allow to live,” rather than make alive.

16.text: Look, these people through the counsel of Balaam caused the Israelites to act treacherously against the Lord in the matter of Peor—which resulted in the plague among the community of the Lord!

17.text: Now therefore kill every boy, and kill every woman who has been intimate with a man in bed.

notes.text: Heb “every male among the little ones.”

The command in holy war to kill women and children seems in modern times a terrible thing to do (and it was), and something they ought not to have done. But this criticism fails to understand the situation in the ancient world. The entire life of the ancient world was tribal warfare. God’s judgment is poured out on whole groups of people who act with moral abandonment and in sinful pursuits. See E. J. Young, My Servants, the Prophets, 24; and J. W. Wenham, The Enigma of Evil.
Heb “every woman, who is a knower of a man by the bed of a male.”

18.text: But all the young women who have not experienced a man’s bed will be yours.

notes.text: Or “girls.” The Hebrew indicates they would be female children, making the selection easy.
Heb “who have not known a man’s bed.” The verb ‏יָדָע‎ (yadaʿ) “to know,” “be intimate with,” is used as a euphemism for sexual relations.

Many contemporary scholars see this story as fictitious, composed by the Jews during the captivity. According to this interpretation, the spoils of war here indicate the wealth of the Jews in captivity, which was to be given to the Levites and priests for the restoration of the sanctuary in Jerusalem. The conclusion drawn from this interpretation is that returning Jews had the same problem as the earlier ones: to gain a foothold in the land. Against this interpretation of the account is a lack of hard evidence, a lack which makes this interpretation appear contrived and subjective. If this was the intent of a later writer, he surely could have stated this more clearly than by making up such a story.

19.text: “Any of you who has killed anyone or touched any of the dead, remain outside the camp for seven days; purify yourselves and your captives on the third day, and on the seventh day.

20.text: You must purify each garment and everything that is made of skin, everything made of goats’ hair, and everything made of wood.”

notes.text: These verses are a reminder that taking a life, even if justified through holy war, still separates one from the holiness of God. It is part of the violation of the fallen world, and only through the ritual of purification can one be once again made fit for the presence of the Lord.

21.text: Then Eleazar the priest said to the men of war who had gone into the battle, “This is the ordinance of the law that the Lord commanded Moses:

22.text: ‘Only the gold, the silver, the bronze, the iron, the tin, and the lead,

23.text: everything that may stand the fire, you are to pass through the fire, and it will be ceremonially clean, but it must still be purified with the water of purification. Anything that cannot withstand the fire you must pass through the water.

notes.text: Purification by fire is unique to this event. Making these metallic objects “pass through the fire” was not only a way of purifying (burning off impurities), but it seems to be a dedicatory rite as well to the Lord and his people. The aspect of passing through the fire is one used by these pagans for child sacrifice.

24.text: You must wash your clothes on the seventh day, and you will be ceremonially clean, and afterward you may enter the camp.’”

25.text: Then the Lord spoke to Moses:

26.text: “You and Eleazar the priest, and all the family leaders of the community, take the sum of the plunder that was captured, both people and animals.

notes.text: The idiom here is “take up the head,” meaning take a census, or count the totals.

27.text: Divide the plunder into two parts, one for those who took part in the war—who went out to battle—and the other for all the community.

28.text: “You must exact a tribute for the Lord from the fighting men who went out to battle: one life out of 500, from the people, the cattle, and from the donkeys and the sheep.

notes.text: The verb is the Hiphil, “you shall cause to be taken up.” The perfect with vav (‏ו‎) continues the sequence of the instructions. This raised offering was to be a tax of one-fifth of one percent for the Lord.

29.text: You are to take it from their half share and give it to Eleazar the priest for a raised offering to the Lord.

30.text: From the Israelites’ half share you are to take one portion out of fifty of the people, the cattle, the donkeys, and the sheep—from every kind of animal—and you are to give them to the Levites, who are responsible for the care of the Lord’s tabernacle.”

31.text: So Moses and Eleazar the priest did as the Lord commanded Moses.

32.text: The spoil that remained of the plunder that the fighting men had gathered was 675,000 sheep,

notes.text: Heb “people.”
Heb “had plundered.”

33.text: 72,000 cattle,

34.text: 61,000 donkeys,

35.text: and 32,000 young women who had not experienced a man’s bed.

notes.text: Here again we encounter one of the difficulties of the book, the use of the large numbers. Only 12,000 soldiers fought the Midianites, but they brought back this amount of plunder, including 32,000 girls. Until a solution for numbers in the book can be found, or the current translation confirmed, one must remain cautious in interpretation.
Heb “who have not known a man’s bed.” The verb ‏יָדָע‎ (yadaʿ) “to know,” “be intimate with,” is used as a euphemism for sexual relations.

36.text: The half portion of those who went to war numbered 337,500 sheep;

37.text: the Lord’s tribute from the sheep was 675.

38.text: The cattle numbered 36,000; the Lord’s tribute was 72.

notes.text: The word “numbered” has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

39.text: The donkeys were 30,500, of which the Lord’s tribute was 61.

40.text: The people were 16,000, of which the Lord’s tribute was 32 people.

notes.text: Heb “soul.”

41.text: So Moses gave the tribute, which was the Lord’s raised offering, to Eleazar the priest, as the Lord commanded Moses.

42.text: From the Israelites’ half share that Moses had separated from the fighting men,

notes.text: Heb “the men who were fighting.”

43.text: there were 337,500 sheep from the portion belonging to the community,

44.text: 36,000 cattle,

45.text: 30,500 donkeys,

46.text: and 16,000 people.

47.text: From the Israelites’ share Moses took one of every fifty people and animals and gave them to the Levites who were responsible for the care of the Lord’s tabernacle, just as the Lord commanded Moses.

48.text: Then the officers who were over the thousands of the army, the commanders over thousands and the commanders over hundreds, approached Moses

49.text: and said to him, “Your servants have taken a count of the men who were in the battle, who were under our authority, and not one is missing.

notes.text: Heb “to Moses”; the proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“him”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “lifted up the head.”
Heb “in our hand.”

50.text: So we have brought as an offering for the Lord what each man found: gold ornaments, armlets, bracelets, signet rings, earrings, and necklaces, to make atonement for ourselves before the Lord.”

notes.text: Heb “our souls.”
The expression here may include the idea of finding protection from divine wrath, which is so common to Leviticus, but it may also be a thank offering for the fact that their lives had been spared.

51.text: Moses and Eleazar the priest took the gold from them, all of it in the form of ornaments.

52.text: All the gold of the offering they offered up to the Lord from the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds weighed 16,750 shekels.

notes.text: Or about 420 imperial pounds.

53.text: Each soldier had taken plunder for himself.

54.text: So Moses and Eleazar the priest received the gold from the commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds and brought it into the tent of meeting as a memorial for the Israelites before the Lord.

notes.text: The Hebrew text does not repeat the word “commanders” here, but it is implied.
The purpose of the offering was to remind the Lord to remember Israel. But it would also be an encouragement for Israel as they remembered the great victory.

1.text: Now the Reubenites and the Gadites possessed a very large number of cattle. When they saw that the lands of Jazer and Gilead were ideal for cattle,

notes.text: While the tribes are on the other side of Jordan, the matter of which tribes would settle there has to be discussed. This chapter begins the settlement of Israel into the tribal territories, something to be continued in Joshua. The chapter has the petitions (vv. 1-5), the response by Moses (vv. 6-15), the proposal (vv. 16-27), and the conclusion of the matter (vv. 28-42). For literature on this subject, both critical and conservative, see S. E. Loewenstein, “The Relation of the Settlement of Gad and Reuben in Numbers 32:1-38, Its Background and Its Composition,” Tarbiz 42 (1972): 12-26; J. Mauchline, “Gilead and Gilgal, Some Reflections on the Israelite Occupation of Palestine,” VT 6 (1956): 19-33; and A. Bergmann, “The Israelite Tribe of Half-Manasseh,” JPOS 16 (1936): 224-54.
Heb “the place was a place of/for cattle.”

2.text: the Gadites and the Reubenites came and addressed Moses, Eleazar the priest, and the leaders of the community. They said,

3.text: “Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo, and Beon,

notes.text: Smr and the LXX have Sibmah. Cf. v. 38.
Cf. Baal Meon in v. 38.

4.text: the land that the Lord subdued before the community of Israel, is ideal for cattle, and your servants have cattle.”

notes.text: The verb is the Hiphil perfect of ‏נָכָה‎ (nakhah), a term that can mean “smite, strike, attack, destroy.”

5.text: So they said, “If we have found favor in your sight, let this land be given to your servants for our inheritance. Do not have us cross the Jordan River.”

notes.text: Heb “eyes.”

The verb is the Hiphil jussive from ‏עָבַר‎ (ʿavar, “to cross over”). The idea of “cause to cross” or “make us cross” might be too harsh, but “take across” with the rest of the nation is what they are trying to avoid.
The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

6.text: Moses said to the Gadites and the Reubenites, “Must your brothers go to war while you remain here?

notes.text: The vav (‏ו‎) is a vav disjunctive prefixed to the pronoun; it fits best here as a circumstantial clause, “while you stay here.”

7.text: Why do you frustrate the intent of the Israelites to cross over into the land that the Lord has given them?

notes.text: Heb “heart.” So also in v. 9.

8.text: Your fathers did the same thing when I sent them from Kadesh Barnea to see the land.

9.text: When they went up to the Eshcol Valley and saw the land, they frustrated the intent of the Israelites so that they did not enter the land that the Lord had given them.

notes.text: The preterite with vav (‏ו‎) consecutive is here subordinated to the parallel yet chronologically later verb in the next clause.
The infinitive construct here with ‏ל‎ (lamed) is functioning as a result clause.
The Lord had not given it yet, but was going to give it. Hence, the perfect should be classified as a perfect of resolve.

10.text: So the anger of the Lord was kindled that day, and he swore,

11.text: ‘Because they have not followed me wholeheartedly, not one of the men twenty years old and upward who came from Egypt will see the land that I swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,

notes.text: The clause is difficult; it means essentially that “they have not made full [their coming] after” the Lord.

The sentence begins with “if they see….” This is the normal way for Hebrew to express a negative oath—“they will by no means see….” The sentence is elliptical; it is saying something like “[May God do so to me] if they see,” meaning they won’t see. Of course here God is taking the oath, which is an anthropomorphic act. He does not need to take an oath, and certainly could not swear by anyone greater, but it communicates to people his resolve.
The LXX adds “those knowing bad and good.”
The words “to give” are not in the Hebrew text but have been supplied in the translation for clarity.

12.text: except Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite, and Joshua son of Nun, for they followed the Lord wholeheartedly.’

13.text: So the Lord’s anger was kindled against the Israelites, and he made them wander in the wilderness for forty years, until all that generation that had done wickedly before the Lord was finished.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”
The verb is difficult to translate, since it has the idea of “complete, finish” (‏תָּמָם‎, tamam). It could be translated “consumed” in this passage (so KJV, ASV); NASB “was destroyed.”

14.text: Now look, you are standing in your fathers’ place, a brood of sinners, to increase still further the fierce wrath of the Lord against the Israelites.

15.text: For if you turn away from following him, he will once again abandon them in the wilderness, and you will be the reason for their destruction.”

notes.text: The construction uses a verbal hendiadys with the verb “to add” serving to modify the main verb.
Heb “and you will destroy all this people.”

16.text: Then they came very close to him and said, “We will build sheep folds here for our flocks and cities for our families,

notes.text: Heb “our little ones.”

17.text: but we will maintain ourselves in armed readiness and go before the Israelites until whenever we have brought them to their place. Our descendants will be living in fortified towns as a protection against the inhabitants of the land.

notes.text: The MT has ‏חֻשִׁים‎ (khushim); the verbal root is ‏חוּשׁ‎ (khush, “to make haste” or “hurry”). But in light of the Greek and Latin Vulgate the Hebrew should probably be emended to ‏חֲמֻשִׁים‎ (hamushim), a qal passive participle meaning “in battle array.” See further BDB 301 s.v. I ‏חוּשׁ‎, BDB 332 s.v. ‏חֲמֻשִׁים‎; HALOT 300 s.v. I ‏חושׁ‎, ‏חישׁ‎; HALOT 331 s.v. I ‏חמשׁ‎.
Heb “from before.”

18.text: We will not return to our homes until every Israelite has his inheritance.

19.text: For we will not accept any inheritance on the other side of the Jordan River and beyond, because our inheritance has come to us on this eastern side of the Jordan.”

notes.text: The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

20.text: Then Moses replied, “If you will do this thing, and if you will arm yourselves for battle before the Lord,

notes.text: Heb “said to them.”

21.text: and if all your armed men cross the Jordan before the Lord until he drives out his enemies from his presence

22.text: and the land is subdued before the Lord, then afterward you may return and be free of your obligation to the Lord and to Israel. This land will then be your possession in the Lord’s sight.

23.text: “But if you do not do this, then look, you will have sinned against the Lord. And know that your sin will find you out.

notes.text: The nuance of the perfect tense here has to be the future perfect.

24.text: So build cities for your descendants and pens for your sheep, but do what you have said you would do.”

notes.text: Heb “that which goes out/has gone out of your mouth.”

25.text: So the Gadites and the Reubenites replied to Moses, “Your servants will do as my lord commands.

26.text: Our children, our wives, our flocks, and all our livestock will be there in the cities of Gilead,

27.text: but your servants will cross over, every man armed for war, to do battle in the Lord’s presence, just as my lord says.”

28.text: So Moses gave orders about them to Eleazar the priest, to Joshua son of Nun, and to the heads of the families of the Israelite tribes.

29.text: Moses said to them: “If the Gadites and the Reubenites cross the Jordan with you, each one equipped for battle in the Lord’s presence, and you conquer the land, then you must allot them the territory of Gilead as their possession.

notes.text: Heb “and the land is subdued before you.”

30.text: But if they do not cross over with you armed, they must receive possessions among you in Canaan.”

31.text: Then the Gadites and the Reubenites answered, “Your servants will do what the Lord has spoken.

notes.text: Heb “that which the Lord has spoken to your servants, thus we will do.”

32.text: We will cross armed in the Lord’s presence into the land of Canaan, and then the possession of our inheritance that we inherit will be ours on this side of the Jordan River.”

notes.text: The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

33.text: So Moses gave to the Gadites, the Reubenites, and to half the tribe of Manasseh son of Joseph the realm of King Sihon of the Amorites, and the realm of King Og of Bashan, the entire land with its cities and the territory surrounding them.

notes.text: Heb “the land with its cities in the borders of the cities of the land all around.”

34.text: The Gadites rebuilt Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer,

35.text: Atroth Shophan, Jazer, Jogbehah,

36.text: Beth Nimrah, and Beth Haran as fortified cities, and constructed pens for their flocks.

37.text: The Reubenites rebuilt Heshbon, Elealeh, Kiriathaim,

38.text: Nebo, Baal Meon (with a change of name), and Sibmah. They renamed the cities they built.

notes.text: Heb “called names.”

39.text: The descendants of Machir son of Manasseh went to Gilead, took it, and dispossessed the Amorites who were in it.

40.text: So Moses gave Gilead to Machir, son of Manasseh, and he lived there.

notes.text: Heb “in it.”

41.text: Now Jair son of Manasseh went and captured their small towns and named them Havvoth Jair.

notes.text: Havvoth Jair. The Hebrew name means “villages of Jair.”

42.text: Then Nobah went and captured Kenath and its villages and called it Nobah after his own name.

1.text: These are the journeys of the Israelites, who went out of the land of Egypt by their divisions under the authority of Moses and Aaron.

notes.text: This material can be arranged into four sections: from Egypt to Sinai (vv. 1-15), the wilderness wanderings (vv. 16-36), from Kadesh to Moab (vv. 37-49), and final orders for Canaan (vv. 50-56).
Heb “hand.”

2.text: Moses recorded their departures according to their journeys, by the commandment of the Lord; now these are their journeys according to their departures.

notes.text: Heb “their goings out.”
Heb “mouth.”

3.text: They departed from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month; on the day after the Passover the Israelites went out defiantly in plain sight of all the Egyptians.

notes.text: Heb “morrow.”

Heb “with a high hand”; the expression means “defiantly; boldly” or “with confidence.” The phrase is usually used for arrogant sin and pride, the defiant fist, as it were. The image of the high hand can also mean the hand raised to deliver the blow (Job 38:15).
Heb “in the eyes.”

4.text: Now the Egyptians were burying all their firstborn, whom the Lord had killed among them; the Lord also executed judgments on their gods.

5.text: The Israelites traveled from Rameses and camped in Sukkoth.

6.text: They traveled from Sukkoth, and camped in Etham, which is on the edge of the desert.

7.text: They traveled from Etham, and turned again to Pi Hahiroth, which is before Baal Zephon; and they camped before Migdal.

8.text: They traveled from Pi Hahiroth, and passed through the middle of the sea into the wilderness, and went three days’ journey in the wilderness of Etham, and camped in Marah.

notes.text: So many medieval Hebrew manuscripts, Smr, Syriac, and Latin Vulgate. Other witnesses have “from before Hahiroth.”

9.text: They traveled from Marah and came to Elim; in Elim there are twelve fountains of water and seventy palm trees, so they camped there.

10.text: They traveled from Elim, and camped by the Red Sea.

11.text: They traveled from the Red Sea and camped in the wilderness of Sin.

12.text: They traveled from the wilderness of Sin and camped in Dophkah.

13.text: And they traveled from Dophkah, and camped in Alush.

14.text: They traveled from Alush and camped at Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink.

15.text: They traveled from Rephidim and camped in the desert of Sinai.

16.text: They traveled from the desert of Sinai and camped at Kibroth Hattaavah.

17.text: They traveled from Kibroth Hattaavah and camped at Hazeroth.

18.text: They traveled from Hazeroth and camped in Rithmah.

19.text: They traveled from Rithmah and camped at Rimmon Perez.

20.text: They traveled from Rimmon Perez and camped in Libnah.

21.text: They traveled from Libnah and camped at Rissah.

22.text: They traveled from Rissah and camped in Kehelathah.

23.text: They traveled from Kehelathah and camped at Mount Shepher.

24.text: They traveled from Mount Shepher and camped in Haradah.

25.text: They traveled from Haradah and camped in Makheloth.

26.text: They traveled from Makheloth and camped at Tahath.

27.text: They traveled from Tahath and camped at Terah.

28.text: They traveled from Terah and camped in Mithcah.

29.text: They traveled from Mithcah and camped in Hashmonah.

30.text: They traveled from Hashmonah and camped in Moseroth.

31.text: They traveled from Moseroth and camped in Bene Jaakan.

32.text: They traveled from Bene Jaakan and camped at Hor Haggidgad.

33.text: They traveled from Hor Haggidgad and camped in Jotbathah.

34.text: They traveled from Jotbathah and camped in Abronah.

35.text: They traveled from Abronah and camped at Ezion Geber.

36.text: They traveled from Ezion Geber and camped in the wilderness of Zin, that is, Kadesh.

37.text: They traveled from Kadesh and camped at Mount Hor at the edge of the land of Edom.

38.text: Aaron the priest ascended Mount Hor at the command of the Lord, and he died there in the fortieth year after the Israelites had come out of the land of Egypt on the first day of the fifth month.

notes.text: Heb “mouth.”

39.text: Now Aaron was 123 years old when he died on Mount Hor.

40.text: The king of Arad, the Canaanite king who lived in the south of the land of Canaan, heard about the approach of the Israelites.

41.text: They traveled from Mount Hor and camped in Zalmonah.

42.text: They traveled from Zalmonah and camped in Punon.

43.text: They traveled from Punon and camped in Oboth.

44.text: They traveled from Oboth and camped in Iye Abarim, on the border of Moab.

45.text: They traveled from Iim and camped in Dibon Gad.

notes.text: Iim is a shortened form of the name Iye-abarim mentioned in v. 44.

46.text: They traveled from Dibon Gad and camped in Almon Diblathaim.

47.text: They traveled from Almon Diblathaim and camped in the mountains of Abarim before Nebo.

48.text: They traveled from the mountains of Abarim and camped in the rift valley plains by Moab along the Jordan River across from Jericho.

notes.text: This is the area of the rift valley basin to the north of the Dead Sea and east of the Jordan. See the note at Num 21:1.
The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarity.

49.text: They camped by the Jordan, from Beth Jeshimoth as far as Abel Shittim in the rift valley plains of Moab.

50.text: The Lord spoke to Moses in the rift valley plains of Moab along the Jordan, across from Jericho. He said:

51.text: “Speak to the Israelites and tell them, ‘When you have crossed the Jordan into the land of Canaan,

52.text: you must drive out all the inhabitants of the land before you. Destroy all their carved images, all their molten images, and demolish their high places.

notes.text: The Hebrew text repeats the verb “you will destroy.”

53.text: You must dispossess the inhabitants of the land and live in it, for I have given you the land to possess it.

54.text: You must divide the land by lot for an inheritance among your families. To a larger group you must give a larger inheritance, and to a smaller group you must give a smaller inheritance. Everyone’s inheritance must be in the place where his lot falls. You must inherit according to your ancestral tribes.

notes.text: Heb “of your fathers.”

55.text: But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land before you, then those whom you allow to remain will be irritants in your eyes and thorns in your side, and will cause you trouble in the land where you will be living.

56.text: And what I intended to do to them I will do to you.’”

1.text: Then the Lord spoke to Moses:

notes.text: This chapter falls into several sections: the south (vv. 1-5), the west (v. 6), the north (vv. 7-9), the east (vv. 10-15), and then a list of appointed officials (vv. 16-29).

2.text: “Give these instructions to the Israelites, and tell them: ‘When you enter Canaan, the land that has been assigned to you as an inheritance, the land of Canaan with its borders,

notes.text: Or “command.”
Heb “this is the land that will fall to you as an inheritance.”

3.text: your southern border will extend from the wilderness of Zin along the Edomite border, and your southern border will run eastward to the extremity of the Salt Sea,

notes.text: The expression refers to the corner or extremity of the Negev, the South.

4.text: and then the border will turn from the south to the Scorpion Ascent, continue to Zin, and then its direction will be from the south to Kadesh Barnea. Then it will go to Hazar Addar and pass over to Azmon.

notes.text: Or “the Ascent of Scorpions” (‏עַקְרַבִּים‎ [ʿaqrabbim] means “scorpions” in Hebrew).
Heb “its going forth,” or the way it runs.

5.text: There the border will turn from Azmon to the Stream of Egypt, and then its direction is to the sea.

notes.text: That is, the Mediterranean.

6.text: “‘And for a western border you will have the Great Sea. This will be your western border.

notes.text: The word for west is simply “sea,” because the sea is west of Israel.
That is, the Mediterranean Sea (also in the following verse).

7.text: “‘And this will be your northern border: From the Great Sea you will draw a line to Mount Hor;

8.text: from Mount Hor you will draw a line to Lebo Hamath, and the direction of the border will be to Zedad.

notes.text: Or “to the entrance to Hamath.”

9.text: The border will continue to Ziphron, and its direction will be to Hazar Enan. This will be your northern border.

10.text: “‘For your eastern border you will draw a line from Hazar Enan to Shepham.

11.text: The border will run down from Shepham to Riblah, on the east side of Ain, and the border will descend and reach the eastern side of the Sea of Kinnereth.

notes.text: Or “the Sea of Galilee” (so NLT); NCV, TEV, CEV “Lake Galilee.”
The word means “harp.” The lake (or sea) of Galilee was so named because it is shaped somewhat like a harp.

12.text: Then the border will continue down the Jordan River and its direction will be to the Salt Sea. This will be your land by its borders that surround it.’”

notes.text: The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

13.text: Then Moses commanded the Israelites: “This is the land that you will inherit by lot, which the Lord has commanded to be given to the nine-and-a-half tribes,

notes.text: The infinitive forms the direct object of what the Lord commanded. It actually means “to give,” but without an expressed subject may be made passive.

14.text: because the tribe of the Reubenites by their families, the tribe of the Gadites by their families, and the half-tribe of Manasseh have received their inheritance.

notes.text: Heb “the house of their fathers.” So also a little later in this verse.

15.text: The two-and-a-half tribes have received their inheritance on this side of the Jordan, east of Jericho, toward the sunrise.”

16.text: The Lord said to Moses:

17.text: “These are the names of the men who are to allocate the land to you as an inheritance: Eleazar the priest and Joshua son of Nun.

notes.text: The verb can be translated simply as “divide,” but it has more the idea of allocate as an inheritance, the related noun being “inheritance.”

18.text: You must take one leader from every tribe to assist in allocating the land as an inheritance.

notes.text: This sense is created by repetition: “one leader, one leader from the tribe.”

The sentence simply uses ‏לִנְחֹל‎ (linkhol, “to divide, apportion”). It has been taken already to mean “allocate as an inheritance.” Here “assist” may be added since Joshua and Eleazar had the primary work.

19.text: These are the names of the men: from the tribe of Judah, Caleb son of Jephunneh;

20.text: from the tribe of the Simeonites, Shemuel son of Ammihud;

21.text: from the tribe of Benjamin, Elidad son of Kislon;

22.text: and from the tribe of the Danites, a leader, Bukki son of Jogli.

23.text: From the Josephites, Hanniel son of Ephod, a leader from the tribe of Manasseh;

24.text: from the tribe of the Ephraimites, a leader, Kemuel son of Shiphtan;

25.text: from the tribe of the Zebulunites, a leader, Elizaphan son of Parnach;

26.text: from the tribe of the Issacharites, a leader, Paltiel son of Azzan;

27.text: from the tribe of the Asherites, a leader, Ahihud son of Shelomi;

28.text: and from the tribe of the Naphtalites, a leader, Pedahel son of Ammihud.”

29.text: These are the ones whom the Lord commanded to divide up the inheritance among the Israelites in the land of Canaan.

1.text: Then the Lord spoke to Moses in the rift valley plains of Moab along the Jordan near Jericho. He said:

notes.text: This section has two main parts, the Levitical cities (vv. 1-8) and the Cities of Refuge (vv. 9-34).
This is the area of the rift valley basin to the north of the Dead Sea and east of the Jordan. See the note at Num 21:1.

2.text: “Instruct the Israelites to give the Levites towns to live in from the inheritance the Israelites will possess. You must also give the Levites grazing land around the towns.

notes.text: The verb is the perfect tense with vav (‏ו‎) consecutive: “command…and they will give,” or “that they give.”
Heb “they”; the referent (the Israelites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

3.text: Thus they will have towns in which to live, and their grazing lands will be for their cattle, for their possessions, and for all their animals.

4.text: The grazing lands around the towns that you will give to the Levites must extend to a distance of 500 yards from the town wall.

notes.text: Heb “1,000 cubits.” The standard cubit in the OT is assumed by most authorities to be about 18 inches (45 cm) in length, so this would be a distance of 1,500 feet or 500 yards (457.2 meters).

5.text: “You must measure from outside the wall of the town on the east 1,000 yards, and on the south side 1,000 yards, and on the west side 1,000 yards, and on the north side 1,000 yards, with the town in the middle. This territory must belong to them as grazing land for the towns.

notes.text: The verb is the Qal perfect of ‏מָדַד‎ (madad, “to measure”). With its vav (‏ו‎) consecutive it carries the same instructional force as the imperfect.
Heb “2,000 cubits” (also three more times in this verse). This would be a distance of 3,000 feet or 1,000 yards (914.4 meters).

The precise nature of the layout described here is not altogether clear. V. 4 speaks of the distance from the wall as being 500 yards; v. 5, however, describes measurements of 1,000 yards. Various proposals have been made in order to harmonize vv. 4 and 5. P. J. Budd, Numbers (WBC), 376, makes the following suggestion: “It may be best to assume that the cubits of the Levitical pasture lands are cubit frontages of land—in other words on each side of the city there was a block of land with a frontage of 2,000 cubits (v 5), and a depth of 1000 cubits (v 4).”

6.text: Now from these towns that you will give to the Levites you must select six towns of refuge to which a person who has killed someone may flee. And you must give them forty-two other towns.

notes.text: The “manslayer” is the verb “to kill” in a participial form, providing the subject of the clause. The verb means “to kill”; it can mean accidental killing, premeditated killing, or capital punishment. The clause uses the infinitive to express purpose or result: “to flee there the manslayer,” means “so that the manslayer may flee there.”

7.text: “So the total of the towns you will give the Levites is forty-eight. You must give these together with their grazing lands.

8.text: The towns you will give must be from the possession of the Israelites. From the larger tribes you must give more; and from the smaller tribes fewer. Each must contribute some of its own towns to the Levites in proportion to the inheritance allocated to each.

9.text: Then the Lord spoke to Moses:

10.text: “Speak to the Israelites and tell them, ‘When you cross over the Jordan River into the land of Canaan,

notes.text: The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

11.text: you must then designate some towns as towns of refuge for you, to which a person who has killed someone unintentionally may flee.

12.text: And they must stand as your towns of refuge from the avenger in order that the killer may not die until he has stood trial before the community.

13.text: These towns that you must give shall be your six towns for refuge.

14.text: “‘You must give three towns on this side of the Jordan, and you must give three towns in the land of Canaan; they must be towns of refuge.

15.text: These six towns will be places of refuge for the Israelites, and for the resident foreigner, and for the settler among them, so that anyone who kills any person accidentally may flee there.

16.text: “‘But if he hits someone with an iron tool so that he dies, he is a murderer. The murderer must surely be put to death.

notes.text: the verb is the preterite of “die.” The sentence has: “if…he strikes him and he dies.” The vav (‏ו‎) consecutive is showing the natural result of the blow.

17.text: If he strikes him by throwing a stone large enough that he could die, and he dies, he is a murderer. The murderer must surely be put to death.

18.text: Or if he strikes him with a wooden hand weapon so that he could die, and he dies, he is a murderer. The murderer must surely be put to death.

19.text: The avenger of blood himself must kill the murderer; when he meets him, he must kill him.

notes.text: The participle ‏גֹּאֵל‎ (goʾel) is the one who protects the family by seeking vengeance for a crime. This is the same verb used for levirate marriages and other related customs.

20.text: “‘But if he strikes him out of hatred or throws something at him intentionally so that he dies,

notes.text: The Hebrew text is more vivid: “by lying in wait.”

21.text: or with enmity he strikes him with his hand and he dies, the one who struck him must surely be put to death, for he is a murderer. The avenger of blood must kill the murderer when he meets him.

22.text: “But if he strikes him suddenly, without enmity, or throws anything at him unintentionally,

23.text: or with any stone large enough that a man could die, without seeing him, and throws it at him, and he dies, even though he was not his enemy nor sought his harm,

24.text: then the community must judge between the slayer and the avenger of blood according to these decisions.

25.text: The community must deliver the slayer out of the hand of the avenger of blood, and the community must restore him to the town of refuge to which he fled, and he must live there until the death of the high priest, who was anointed with the consecrated oil.

notes.text: Heb “in it.”

26.text: But if the slayer at any time goes outside the boundary of the town to which he had fled,

27.text: and the avenger of blood finds him outside the borders of the town of refuge, and the avenger of blood kills the slayer, he will not be guilty of blood,

28.text: because the slayer should have stayed in his town of refuge until the death of the high priest. But after the death of the high priest, the slayer may return to the land of his possessions.

notes.text: Heb “he.”

29.text: So these things must be a statutory ordinance for you throughout your generations, in all the places where you live.

notes.text: Heb “a statute of judgment” (so KJV).

30.text: “Whoever kills any person, the murderer must be put to death by the testimony of witnesses, but one witness cannot testify against any person to cause him to be put to death.

notes.text: Heb “at the mouth of”; the metonymy stresses it is at their report.
The verb should be given the nuance of imperfect of potentiality.

31.text: Moreover, you must not accept a ransom for the life of a murderer who is guilty of death; he must surely be put to death.

32.text: And you must not accept a ransom for anyone who has fled to a town of refuge, to allow him to return home and live on his own land before the death of the high priest.

notes.text: Heb “the priest.” The Greek and the Syriac have “high priest.” The present translation, along with many English versions, uses “high priest” as a clarification.

33.text: “‘You must not pollute the land where you live, for blood defiles the land, and the land cannot be cleansed of the blood that is shed there, except by the blood of the person who shed it.

34.text: Therefore do not defile the land that you will inhabit, in which I live, for I the Lord live among the Israelites.’”

1.text: Then the heads of the family groups of the Gileadites, the descendant of Machir, the descendant of Manasseh, who were from the Josephite families, approached and spoke before Moses and the leaders who were the heads of the Israelite families.

notes.text: The expression is “the heads of the fathers by the family of the Gileadites.”
The Greek and the Syriac add “and before Eleazar the priest.”
Heb “heads of the fathers.”

2.text: They said, “The Lord commanded my lord to give the land as an inheritance by lot to the Israelites; and my lord was commanded by the Lord to give the inheritance of our brother Zelophehad to his daughters.

notes.text: The infinitive construct “to give” serves here as the complement or object of the verb, answering what the Lord had commanded Moses.

3.text: Now if they should be married to one of the men from another Israelite tribe, their inheritance would be taken from the inheritance of our fathers and added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry. As a result, it will be taken from the lot of our inheritance.

notes.text: “Men” is understood; it says “to one from the sons of the tribes of the Israelites for a wife,” or if he has her for a wife.
Heb “which they will be to them,” meaning, to those who have them, i.e., the marriages.

4.text: And when the Jubilee of the Israelites is to take place, their inheritance will be added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry. So their inheritance will be taken away from the inheritance of our ancestral tribe.”

notes.text: The verb ‏הָיָה‎ (hayah) is most often translated “to be,” but it can also mean “to happen, to take place, to come to pass,” etc.
Heb “the tribe of our fathers.”

5.text: Then Moses gave a ruling to the Israelites by the word of the Lord: “What the tribe of the Josephites is saying is right.

notes.text: Heb “commanded.”
Heb “mouth.”

6.text: This is what the Lord has commanded for Zelophehad’s daughters: ‘Let them marry whomever they think best, only they must marry within the family of their father’s tribe.

notes.text: Heb “the word that.”
The idiom again is “let them be for wives for….”
Heb “to the one who is good in their eyes.”

7.text: In this way the inheritance of the Israelites will not be transferred from tribe to tribe. But every one of the Israelites must retain the ancestral heritage.

notes.text: Heb “turned aside.”

8.text: And every daughter who possesses an inheritance from any of the tribes of the Israelites must become the wife of a man from any family in her father’s tribe, so that every Israelite may retain the inheritance of his fathers.

notes.text: The subject is “Israelites” and the verb is plural to agree with it, but the idea is collective as the word for “man” indicates: “so that the Israelites may possess—[each] man the inheritance of his fathers.”

9.text: No inheritance may pass from tribe to tribe. But every one of the tribes of the Israelites must retain its inheritance.’”

10.text: As the Lord had commanded Moses, so the daughters of Zelophehad did.

11.text: For the daughters of Zelophehad—Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah—were married to the sons of their uncles.

notes.text: They married in the family as they were instructed. But the meaning of ‏דּוֹד‎ (dod) is not necessarily restricted to “uncle.”

12.text: They were married into the families of the Manassehites, the descendants of Joseph, and their inheritance remained in the tribe of their father’s family.

13.text: These are the commandments and the decisions that the Lord commanded the Israelites through the authority of Moses, in the rift valley plains by Moab along the Jordan River opposite Jericho.

notes.text: Heb “by the hand.”
This is the area of the rift valley basin to the north of the Dead Sea and east of the Jordan. See the note at Num 21:1.
The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

1.text: This is what Moses said to all of Israel in the Transjordanian wilderness, the arid rift valley opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Di Zahab.

notes.text: Heb “These are the words.”

Heb “on the other side of the Jordan.” This would appear to favor authorship by someone living on the west side of the Jordan, that is, in Canaan, whereas the biblical tradition locates Moses on the east side (cf. v. 5). However the Hebrew phrase ‏בְּעֵבֶר הַיַּרְדֵּן‎ (beʿever hayyarden) is a frozen form meaning “Transjordan,” a name appropriate from any geographical vantage point. To this day, one standing east of the Jordan can describe himself as being in Transjordan.
The Hebrew term ‏מוֹל‎ (mol) may also mean “in front of” or “near” (cf. NCV, TEV, CEV, NLT).
This place is otherwise unattested and its location is unknown. Perhaps it is Khirbet Sufah, 4 mi (6 km) SSE of Madaba, Jordan.
The Hebrew term ‏בֵּין‎ (ben) may suggest “in the area of.”
Paran is the well-known desert area between Mount Sinai and Kadesh Barnea (cf. Num 10:12; 12:16).
Tophel refers possibly to eṭ-Ṭafîleh, 15 mi (25 km) SE of the Dead Sea, or to Dâbîlu, another name for Paran. See H. Cazelles, “Tophel (Deut. 1:1),” VT 9 (1959): 412-15.
Laban. Perhaps this refers to Libnah (Num 33:20).
Hazeroth. This probably refers to ʿAin Khadra. See Y. Aharoni, The Land of the Bible, 199-200.
Di Zahab. Perhaps this refers to Mina al-Dhahab on the eastern Sinai coast.

2.text: Now it is ordinarily an eleven-day journey from Horeb to Kadesh Barnea by way of Mount Seir.

notes.text: An eleven-day journey was about 140 mi (233 km).
Horeb is another name for Sinai. “Horeb” occurs 9 times in the Book of Deuteronomy and “Sinai” only once (33:2). “Sinai” occurs 13 times in the Book of Exodus and “Horeb” only 3 times.

Kadesh Barnea. Possibly this refers to ʿAin Qudeis, about 50 mi (80 km) southwest of Beer Sheba, but more likely to ʿAin Qudeirat, 5 mi (8 km) NW of ʿAin Qudeis. See R. Cohen, “Did I Excavate Kadesh Barnea?” BAR 7 (1981): 20-33.
Mount Seir is synonymous with Edom. “By way of Mount Seir” refers to the route from Horeb that ended up in Edom Cf. CEV “by way of the Mount Seir Road”; TEV “by way of the hill country of Edom.”

3.text: However, it was not until the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year that Moses addressed the Israelites just as the Lord had instructed him to do.

notes.text: Heb “in” or “on.” Here there is a contrast between the ordinary time of eleven days (v. 2) and the actual time of forty years, so “not until” brings out that vast disparity.
The eleventh month is Shebat in the Hebrew calendar, January/February in the modern (Gregorian) calendar.
The fortieth year would be 1406 b.c. according to the “early” date of the exodus. See E. H. Merrill, Kingdom of Priests, 66-75.
Heb “according to all which.”

4.text: This took place after the defeat of King Sihon of the Amorites, whose capital was in Heshbon, and King Og of Bashan, whose capital was in Ashtaroth, specifically in Edrei.

notes.text: Heb “when he struck [or “smote”].”
See Deut 2:26-3:22.
Heb “who lived.”
Heshbon is probably modern Tell Hesban, about 7.5 mi (12 km) south southwest of Amman, Jordan.
Heb “who lived.”
Ashtaroth is probably Tell ʿAshtarah, about 22 mi (35 km) due east of the Sea of Galilee.
Edrei is probably modern Derʿa, 60 mi (95 km) south of Damascus (see Num 21:33; Josh 12:4; 13:12, 31).

5.text: So it was in the Transjordan, in Moab, that Moses began to deliver these words:

notes.text: Heb “this instruction”; KJV, NIV, NRSV “this law”; TEV “God’s laws and teachings.” The Hebrew noun ‏תּוֹרָה‎ (torah) is derived from the verb ‏יָרָה‎ (yarah, “to teach”) and here it refers to the Book of Deuteronomy, not the Pentateuch as a whole.

6.text: The Lord our God spoke to us at Horeb and said, “You have stayed in the area of this mountain long enough.

notes.text: Heb “lived”; “dwelled.”

7.text: Head out and resume your journey. Enter the Amorite hill country, and all its neighboring areas, including the rift valley, the hill country, the foothills, the Negev, and the coastal plain—all of Canaan and Lebanon as far as the Great River, that is, the Euphrates.

notes.text: Heb “turn”; NAB “Leave here”; NIV, TEV “Break camp.”

As a geographic feature the rift valley (‏עֲרָבָה‎, ʿaravah) extends from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba. The reference here probably includes the Jordan Valley and continues to the wider part of the rift valley below the Dead Sea. Some versions transliterate the name as Arabah (ASV, NAB, NIV, NRSV).

The ‏שְׁפֵלָה‎ (shephelah) is the geographical region between the Mediterranean coastal plain and the hill country, sometimes called the “western foothills” (NIV, CEV, NLT), “Judean foothills” (Holman), “lowland” (NASB, ESV), or by the Hebrew “Shephelah” (NRSV).

The Negev is the area of central, southern Judah, south of the hill country and Beer Sheba and west of the rift valley. As a geographic feature it is a depression extending south to the gulf of Aqaba, but the reference here is probably to the northern portion of the region.

8.text: Look! I have already given the land to you. Go, occupy the territory that I, the Lord, promised to give to your ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to their descendants.”

notes.text: Heb “I have placed before you the land.”
Heb “the Lord.” Since the Lord is speaking, it is preferable for clarity to supply the first person pronoun in the translation.
Heb “swore” (so NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT). This refers to God’s promise, made by solemn oath, to give the patriarchs the land.
Heb “fathers” (also in vv. 11, 21, 35).
Heb “their seed after them.”

9.text: I also said to you at that time, “I am no longer able to sustain you by myself.

10.text: The Lord your God has increased your population to the point that you are now as numerous as the very stars of the sky.

notes.text: Heb “multiplied you.”
Or “heavens.” The Hebrew term ‏שָׁמַיִם‎ (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.

11.text: Indeed, may the Lord, the God of your ancestors, make you a thousand times more numerous than you are now, blessing you just as he said he would!

notes.text: Heb “may he bless you.”

12.text: But how can I alone bear up under the burden of your hardship and strife?

13.text: Select wise and practical men, those known among your tribes, whom I may appoint as your leaders.”

notes.text: The Hebrew verb ‏נְבֹנִים‎ (nevonim, from ‏בִּין‎ [bin]) is a Niphal referring to skill or intelligence (see T. Fretheim, NIDOTTE 1:652-53).

14.text: You replied to me that what I had said to you was good.

15.text: So I chose as your tribal leaders wise and well-known men, placing them over you as administrators of groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, and also as other tribal officials.

notes.text: Or “selected”; Heb “took.”

16.text: I furthermore admonished your judges at that time that they should pay attention to issues among your fellow citizens and judge fairly, whether between one person and a native Israelite or a resident foreigner.

notes.text: Or “you.” A number of English versions treat the remainder of this verse and v. 17 as direct discourse rather than indirect discourse (cf. KJV, NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).
Heb “brothers.” The term “brothers” could, in English, be understood to refer to siblings, so “fellow citizens” has been used in the translation.

The Hebrew word ‏צֶדֶק‎ (tsedeq, “fairly”) carries the basic idea of conformity to a norm of expected behavior or character, one established by God himself. Fair judgment adheres strictly to that norm or standard (see D. Reimer, NIDOTTE 3:750).

Heb “between a man and his brother.” The first use of “brother” in this verse refers broadly to fellow citizens. This second use is narrower, being in opposition to the “resident foreigner.” The ‏גֵּר‎ (ger) “resident foreigner” was not simply a foreigner (Hebrew ‏נֵכָר‎; nekar) but was essentially a naturalized citizen and had equal protection under the law. This is one of the verses designed to ensure that equal treatment (see also Deut 10:16-19; 16:18-20; Exod 12:49; Num 15:16, 29).
On the Hebrew ger (‏גֵּר‎) “resident foreigner,” see notes at Exod 12:19 and Deut 29:11.

17.text: They must not discriminate in judgment, but hear the lowly and the great alike. Nor should they be intimidated by human beings, for judgment belongs to God. If the matter being adjudicated is too difficult for them, they should bring it before me for a hearing.

notes.text: Heb “you,” and throughout the verse (cf. NASB, NRSV).
Heb “the small,” but referring to social status, not physical stature.

18.text: So I instructed you at that time regarding everything you should do.

19.text: Then we left Horeb and passed through all that immense, forbidding wilderness that you saw on the way to the Amorite hill country as the Lord our God had commanded us to do, finally arriving at Kadesh Barnea.

20.text: Then I said to you, “You have come to the Amorite hill country, which the Lord our God is about to give us.

notes.text: The Hebrew participle has an imminent future sense here, although many English versions treat it as a present tense (“is giving us,” NAB, NIV, NRSV) or a predictive future (“will give us,” NCV).

21.text: Look, he has placed the land in front of you! Go up, take possession of it, just as the Lord, the God of your ancestors, said to do. Do not be afraid or discouraged!”

notes.text: Heb “the Lord your God.” The pronoun (“he”) has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons, to avoid repetition.
Or “has given you the land” (cf. NAB, NIV, NRSV).

22.text: So all of you approached me and said, “Let’s send some men ahead of us to scout out the land and bring us back word as to how we should attack it and what the cities are like there.”

23.text: I thought this was a good idea, so I sent twelve men from among you, one from each tribe.

notes.text: Heb “the thing was good in my eyes.”
Or “selected” (so NIV, NRSV, TEV); Heb “took.”

24.text: They left and went up to the hill country, coming to the Eshcol Valley, which they scouted out.

notes.text: Or “the Wadi Eshcol” (so NAB).
The Eshcol Valley is a verdant valley near Hebron, still famous for its viticulture (cf. Num 13:22-23). The Hebrew name “Eshcol” means “trestle,” that is, the frame on which grape vines grow.

25.text: Then they took some of the produce of the land and carried it back down to us. They also brought a report to us, saying, “The land that the Lord our God is about to give us is good.”

notes.text: The Hebrew text includes “in their hand,” which is unnecessary and somewhat redundant in English style.

26.text: You were not willing to go up, however, but instead rebelled against the Lord your God.

notes.text: Heb “the mouth of the Lord your God.” To include “the mouth” would make for odd English style. The mouth stands by metonymy for the Lord’s command, which in turn represents the Lord himself.

27.text: You complained among yourselves privately and said, “Because the Lord hates us he brought us from Egypt to deliver us over to the Amorites so they could destroy us!

notes.text: Heb “in your tents,” that is, privately.

28.text: What is going to happen to us? Our brothers have drained away our courage by describing people who are more numerous and taller than we are, and great cities whose defenses appear to be as high as heaven itself! Moreover, they said they saw Anakites there.”

notes.text: Heb “have caused our hearts to melt.”
Heb “greater.” Many English versions understand this to refer to physical size or strength rather than numbers (cf. “stronger,” NAB, NIV, NRSV; “bigger,” NASB).
Or “as the sky.” The Hebrew term ‏שָׁמַיִם‎ (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.
Heb “we have seen.”
Heb “the sons of the Anakim.”
Anakites were giant people (Num 13:33; Deut 2:10, 21; 9:2) descended from a certain Anak whose own forefather Arba founded the city of Kiriath Arba, i.e., Hebron (Josh 21:11).

29.text: So I responded to you, “Do not be terrified of them!

notes.text: Heb “do not tremble and do not be afraid.” Two synonymous commands are combined for emphasis.

30.text: The Lord your God is about to go ahead of you; he will fight for you, just as you saw him do in Egypt

notes.text: The Hebrew participle indicates imminent future action here, though some English versions treat it as a predictive future (“will go ahead of you,” NCV; cf. also TEV, CEV).
Heb “according to all which he did for you in Egypt before your eyes.”

31.text: and in the wilderness, where you saw him carrying you along like a man carries his son. This he did everywhere you went until you came to this very place.”

notes.text: Heb “the Lord your God.” The pronoun (“him”) has been employed in the translation for stylistic reasons.

32.text: However, through all this you did not have confidence in the Lord your God,

33.text: who would go before you on the way to find places for you to camp, appearing in a fire at night and in a cloud by day to show you the way you ought to go.

34.text: When the Lord heard you, he became angry and made this vow:

notes.text: Heb “and swore,” i.e., made an oath or vow.

35.text: “Not a single person of this evil generation will see the good land that I promised to give to your ancestors!

notes.text: Heb “Not a man among these men.”

36.text: The exception is Caleb son of Jephunneh; he will see it and I will give him and his descendants the territory on which he has walked, because he has wholeheartedly followed me.”

notes.text: Caleb had, with Joshua, brought back to Israel a minority report from Canaan urging a conquest of the land, for he was confident of the Lord’s power (Num 13:6, 8, 16, 30; 14:30, 38).
Heb “the Lord.” The pronoun (“me”) has been employed in the translation, since it sounds strange to an English reader for the Lord to speak about himself in third person.

37.text: As for me, the Lord was also angry with me on your account. He said, “You also will not be able to go there.

38.text: However, Joshua son of Nun, your assistant, will go. Encourage him, because he will enable Israel to inherit the land.

notes.text: Heb “the one who stands before you”; NAB “your aide”; TEV “your helper.”
Heb “it”; the referent (the land) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

39.text: Also, your infants, who you thought would die on the way, and your children, who as yet do not know good from bad, will go there; I will give them the land and they will possess it.

notes.text: Heb “would be a prey.”

Do not know good from bad. This is a figure of speech called a merism (suggesting a whole by referring to its extreme opposites). Other examples are the tree of “the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen 2:9), the boy who knows enough “to reject the wrong and choose the right” (Isa 7:16; 8:4), and those who “cannot tell their right hand from their left” (Jonah 4:11). A young child is characterized by lack of knowledge.

40.text: But as for you, turn back and head for the wilderness by the way to the Red Sea.”

notes.text: The Hebrew pronoun is plural, as are the following verbs, indicating that Moses and the people are addressed (note v. 41).

Heb “the Reed Sea.” “Reed” is a better translation of the Hebrew ‏סוּף‎ (suf), traditionally rendered “red.” The name “Red Sea” is based on the LXX which referred to it as ἐρυθρᾶς θαλάσσης (eruthras thalassēs, “red sea”). Nevertheless, because the body of water in question is known in modern times as the Red Sea, this term was used in the translation. The part of the Red Sea in view here is not the one crossed in the exodus but its eastern arm, now known as the Gulf of Eilat or Gulf of Aqaba.

41.text: Then you responded to me and admitted, “We have sinned against the Lord. We will now go up and fight as the Lord our God has told us to do.” So you each put on your battle gear and prepared to go up to the hill country.

42.text: But the Lord told me: “Tell them this: ‘Do not go up and fight, because I will not be with you and you will be defeated by your enemies.’”

43.text: I spoke to you, but you did not listen. Instead you rebelled against the Lord and recklessly went up to the hill country.

notes.text: Heb “the mouth of the Lord.” See note at 1:26.

44.text: The Amorite inhabitants of that area confronted you and chased you like a swarm of bees, striking you down from Seir as far as Hormah.

notes.text: Heb “in that hill country,” repeating the end of v. 43.
Heb “came out to meet.”
Hormah is probably Khirbet el-Meshash, 5.5 mi (9 km) west of Arad and 7.5 mi (12 km) SE of Beer Sheba. Its name is a derivative of the verb ‏חָרָם‎ (kharam, “to ban; to exterminate”). See Num 21:3.

45.text: Then you came back and wept before the Lord, but he paid no attention to you whatsoever.

notes.text: Heb “the Lord.” The pronoun (“he”) has been employed in the translation here for stylistic reasons, to avoid redundancy.
Heb “did not hear your voice and did not turn an ear to you.”

46.text: Therefore, you remained at Kadesh for a long time—indeed, for the full time.

notes.text: Heb “like the days which you lived.” This refers to the rest of the forty-year period in the desert before Israel arrived in Moab.

1.text: Then we turned and set out toward the wilderness on the way to the Red Sea just as the Lord told me to do, detouring around Mount Seir for a long time.

notes.text: Heb “Reed Sea.” See note on the term “Red Sea” in Deut 1:40.

2.text: At this point the Lord said to me,

3.text: “You have circled around this mountain long enough; now turn north.

4.text: Instruct these people as follows: ‘You are about to cross the border of your relatives the descendants of Esau, who inhabit Seir. They will be afraid of you, so watch yourselves carefully.

notes.text: Heb “command” (so KJV, NASB); NRSV “charge the people as follows.”
Heb “brothers”; NAB “your kinsmen.”

The descendants of Esau (Heb “sons of Esau”; the phrase also occurs in 2:8, 12, 22, 29). These are the inhabitants of the land otherwise known as Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea. Jacob’s brother Esau had settled there after his bitter strife with Jacob (Gen 36:1-8). “Edom” means “reddish,” probably because of the red sandstone of the region, but also by popular etymology because Esau, at birth, was reddish (Gen 25:25).

5.text: Do not be hostile toward them, because I am not giving you any of their land, not even a footprint, for I have given Mount Seir as an inheritance for Esau.

notes.text: Mount Seir is synonymous with Edom.

6.text: You may purchase food to eat and water to drink from them.

notes.text: Heb includes “with silver.”

7.text: All along the way I, the Lord your God, have blessed your every effort. I have been attentive to your travels through this great wilderness. These forty years I have been with you; you have lacked nothing.’”

notes.text: The Hebrew text does not have the first person pronoun; it has been supplied for purposes of English style (the Lord is speaking here).
Heb “all the work of your hands.”
Heb “he has.” This has been converted to first person in the translation in keeping with English style.
Heb “known” (so ASV, NASB); NAB “been concerned about.”
Heb “the Lord your God has.” This has been replaced in the translation by the first person pronoun (“I”) in keeping with English style.

8.text: So we turned away from our relatives the descendants of Esau, the inhabitants of Seir, turning from the route of the rift valley which comes up from Elat and Ezion Geber, and traveling the way of the wilderness of Moab.

notes.text: Or “brothers”; NRSV “our kin.”

As a geographic feature the rift valley (‏עֲרָבָה‎, ʿaravah) extends from the Gulf of Aqaba to Galilee. Traveling up the middle of the rift valley probably would have been the easiest path, at least up to the Dead Sea.
Heb “from.”

Elat was a port city at the head of the eastern arm of the Red Sea, that is, the Gulf of Aqaba (or Gulf of Eilat). Solomon (1 Kgs 9:28), Uzziah (2 Kgs 14:22), and Ahaz (2 Kgs 16:5-6) used it as a port but eventually it became permanently part of Edom. It may be what is known today as Tell el-Kheleifeh. Modern Eilat is located farther west along the northern coast. See G. Pratico, “Nelson Glueck’s 1938-1940 Excavations at Tell el-Kheleifeh: A Reappraisal,” BASOR 259 (1985): 1-32.

Ezion Geber. A place near the Gulf of Aqaba, Ezion-geber must be distinguished from Elat (cf. 1 Kgs 9:26-28; 2 Chr 8:17-18). It was, however, also a port city (1 Kgs 22:48-49). It may be the same as the modern site Gezirat al-Fauran, 15 mi (24 km) south-southwest from Tell el-Kheleifah.

9.text: Then the Lord said to me, “Do not harass Moab and provoke them to war, for I will not give you any of their land as your territory. This is because I have given Ar to the descendants of Lot as their possession.

notes.text: Ar was a Moabite city on the Arnon River east of the Dead Sea. It is mentioned elsewhere in the “Book of the Wars of Yahweh” (Num 21:15; cf. 21:28; Isa 15:1). Here it is synonymous with the whole land of Moab.

The descendants of Lot. Following the destruction of the cities of the plain, Sodom and Gomorrah, as God’s judgment, Lot fathered two sons by his two daughters, namely, Moab and Ammon (Gen 19:30-38). Thus, these descendants of Lot in and around Ar were the Moabites.

10.text: (The Emites used to live there, a people as powerful, numerous, and tall as the Anakites.

notes.text: Emites. These giant people, like the Anakites (Deut 1:28), were also known as Rephaites (v. 11). They appear elsewhere in the narrative of the invasion of the kings of the east where they are said to have lived around Shaveh Kiriathaim, perhaps 9 to 11 mi (15 to 18 km) east of the north end of the Dead Sea (Gen 14:5).

11.text: These people, as well as the Anakites, are also considered Rephaites; the Moabites call them Emites.

notes.text: Rephaites. The earliest reference to this infamous giant race is, again, in the story of the invasion of the eastern kings (Gen 14:5). They lived around Ashteroth Karnaim, probably modern Tel Ashtarah (cf. Deut 1:4), in the Bashan plateau east of the Sea of Galilee. Og, king of Bashan, was a Rephaite (Deut 3:11; Josh 12:4; 13:12). Other texts speak of them or their kinfolk in both Transjordan (Deut 2:20; 3:13) and Canaan (Josh 11:21-22; 14:12, 15; 15:13-14; Judg 1:20; 1 Sam 17:4; 1 Chr 20:4-8). They also appear in extra-biblical literature, especially in connection with the city state of Ugarit. See C. L’Heureux, “Ugaritic and Biblical Rephaim,” HTR 67 (1974): 265-74.

12.text: Previously the Horites lived in Seir, but the descendants of Esau dispossessed and destroyed them and settled in their place, just as Israel did to the land it came to possess, the land the Lord gave them.)

notes.text: Horites. Most likely these are the same as the well-known people of ancient Near Eastern texts described as Hurrians. They were geographically widespread and probably non-Semitic. Genesis speaks of them as the indigenous peoples of Edom that Esau expelled (Gen 36:8-19, 31-43) and also as among those who confronted the kings of the east (Gen 14:6).
Most modern English versions, beginning with the ASV (1901), regard vv. 10-12 as parenthetical to the narrative.

13.text: Now, get up and cross the Wadi Zered.” So we did so.

notes.text: Wadi Zered. Now known as Wadi el-Ḥesa, this valley marked the boundary between Moab to the north and Edom to the south.
Heb “we crossed the Wadi Zered.” This has been translated as “we did so” for stylistic reasons, to avoid redundancy.

14.text: Now the length of time it took for us to go from Kadesh Barnea to the crossing of Wadi Zered was thirty-eight years, time for all the military men of that generation to die, just as the Lord had vowed to them.

15.text: Indeed, it was the very hand of the Lord that eliminated them from within the camp until they were all gone.

notes.text: Heb “from the middle of.” Although many recent English versions leave this expression untranslated, the point seems to be that these soldiers did not die in battle but “within the camp.”

16.text: So it was that after all the military men had been eliminated from the community,

notes.text: Heb “and it was when they were eliminated, all the men of war, to die from the midst of the people.”

17.text: the Lord said to me,

18.text: “Today you are going to cross the border of Moab, that is, of Ar.

notes.text: Ar. See note on this word in Deut 2:9.

19.text: But when you come close to the Ammonites, do not harass or provoke them because I am not giving you any of the Ammonites’ land as your possession; I have already given it to Lot’s descendants as their possession.”

notes.text: Lot’s descendants. See note on this phrase in Deut 2:9.

20.text: (That also is considered to be a land of the Rephaites. The Rephaites lived there originally; the Ammonites call them Zamzummites.

notes.text: Rephaites. See note on this word in Deut 2:11.
Zamzummites. Just as the Moabites called Rephaites by the name Emites, the Ammonites called them Zamzummites (or Zazites; Gen 14:5).

21.text: They are a people as powerful, numerous, and tall as the Anakites. But the Lord destroyed the Rephaites in advance of the Ammonites, so they dispossessed them and settled down in their place.

notes.text: Heb “them”; the referent (the Rephaites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “them”; the referent (the Ammonites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

22.text: This is exactly what he did for the descendants of Esau who lived in Seir when he destroyed the Horites before them so that they could dispossess them and settle in their area to this very day.

23.text: As for the Avvites who lived in settlements as far west as Gaza, Caphtorites who came from Crete destroyed them and settled down in their place.)

notes.text: Avvites. Otherwise unknown, these people were probably also Anakite (or Rephaite) giants who lived in the lower Mediterranean coastal plain until they were expelled by the Caphtorites.

Caphtorites. These peoples are familiar from both the OT (Gen 10:14; 1 Chr 1:12; Jer 47:4; Amos 9:7) and ancient Near Eastern texts (Miriam Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature, 2:37-38; ANET 138). They originated in Crete (OT “Caphtor”) and are identified as the ancestors of the Philistines (Gen 10:14; Jer 47:4).
Heb “Caphtor”; the modern name of the island of Crete is used in the translation for clarity (cf. NCV, TEV, NLT).

24.text: “Get up, make your way across Wadi Arnon. Look, I have already delivered over to you Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land. Go ahead—take it! Engage him in war!

notes.text: Heshbon is the name of a prominent site (now Tel Hesbān, about 7.5 mi [12 km] south southwest of Amman, Jordan). Sihon made it his capital after having driven Moab from the area and forced them south to the Arnon (Num 21:26-30). Heshbon is also mentioned in Deut 1:4.

25.text: This very day I will begin to fill all the people of the earth with dread and to terrify them when they hear about you. They will shiver and shake in anticipation of your approach.”

notes.text: Heb “under heaven” (so NIV, NRSV).
Heb “from before you.”

26.text: Then I sent messengers from the Kedemoth wilderness to King Sihon of Heshbon with an offer of peace:

notes.text: Kedemoth. This is probably Aleiyan, about 8 mi (13 km) north of the Arnon and between Dibon and Mattanah.

27.text: “Let me pass through your land; I will keep strictly to the roadway. I will not turn aside to the right or the left.

notes.text: Heb “in the way in the way” (‏בַּדֶּרֶךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ‎, badderekh badderekh). The repetition lays great stress on the idea of resolute determination to stick to the path. IBHS 116 §7.2.3c.

28.text: Sell me food for cash so that I can eat and sell me water to drink. Just allow me to go through on foot,

notes.text: Heb “silver.”
Heb “and water for silver give to me so that I may drink.”

29.text: just as the descendants of Esau who live at Seir and the Moabites who live in Ar did for me, until I cross the Jordan to the land the Lord our God is giving us.”

30.text: But King Sihon of Heshbon was unwilling to allow us to pass near him because the Lord our God had made him obstinate and stubborn so that he might deliver him over to you this very day.

notes.text: The translation follows the LXX in reading the first person pronoun. The MT, followed by many English versions, has a second person masculine singular pronoun, “your.”
Heb “hardened his spirit” (so KJV, NASB, NRSV); NIV “made his spirit stubborn.”
Heb “made his heart obstinate” (so KJV, NASB); NRSV “made his heart defiant.”
Heb “into your hand.”

31.text: The Lord said to me, “Look! I have already begun to give over Sihon and his land to you. Start right now to take his land as your possession.”

32.text: When Sihon and all his troops emerged to encounter us in battle at Jahaz,

notes.text: Heb “people.”
Jahaz. This is probably Khirbet el-Medeiyineh. See J. Dearman, “The Levitical Cities of Reuben and Moabite Toponymy,” BASOR 276 (1984): 55-57.

33.text: the Lord our God delivered him over to us and we struck him down, along with his sons and everyone else.

notes.text: The translation follows the Qere or marginal reading; the Kethib (consonantal text) has the singular, “his son.”
Heb “all his people.”

34.text: At that time we seized all his cities and put every one of them under divine judgment, including even the women and children; we left no survivors.

notes.text: Heb “every city of men.” This apparently identifies the cities as inhabited.

Heb “under the ban” (‏נַחֲרֵם‎, nakharem). The verb employed is ‏חָרַם‎ (kharam, usually in the Hiphil) and the associated noun is ‏חֵרֶם‎ (kherem). See J. Naudé, NIDOTTE, 2:276-77, and, for a more thorough discussion, Susan Niditch, War in the Hebrew Bible, 28-77.

Divine judgment refers to God’s designation of certain persons, places, and things as objects of his special wrath and judgment because, in his omniscience, he knows them to be impure and hopelessly unrepentant.

35.text: We kept only the livestock and plunder from the cities for ourselves.

36.text: From Aroer, which is at the edge of Wadi Arnon (it is the city in the wadi), all the way to Gilead there was not a town able to resist us—the Lord our God gave them all to us.

notes.text: Aroer. Now known as ʿAraʾir on the northern edge of the Arnon river, Aroer marked the southern limit of Moab and, later, of the allotment of the tribe of Reuben (Josh 13:9, 16).

Heb “the city in the wadi.” This enigmatic reference may refer to Ar or, more likely, to Aroer itself. Epexegetically the text might read, “From Aroer…, that is, the city in the wadi.” See D. L. Christensen, Deuteronomy 1-11 (WBC), 49.

37.text: However, you did not approach the land of the Ammonites, the Wadi Jabbok, the cities of the hill country, or any place else forbidden by the Lord our God.

notes.text: Wadi Jabbok. Now known as the Zerqa River, this is a major tributary of the Jordan that normally served as a boundary between Ammon and Gad (Deut 3:16).

1.text: Next we set out on the route to Bashan, but King Og of Bashan and his whole army came out to meet us in battle at Edrei.

notes.text: Heb “turned and went up.”
Bashan. This plateau country, famous for its oaks (Isa 2:13) and cattle (Deut 32:14; Amos 4:1), was north of Gilead along the Yarmuk River.
Heb “people.”
Edrei is probably modern Derʿa, 60 mi (95 km) south of Damascus (see Num 21:33; Josh 12:4; 13:12, 31; also mentioned in Deut 1:4).

2.text: The Lord, however, said to me, “Don’t be afraid of him because I have already given him, his whole army, and his land to you. You will do to him exactly what you did to King Sihon of the Amorites who lived in Heshbon.”

notes.text: Heb “people.”

3.text: So the Lord our God did indeed give over to us King Og of Bashan and his whole army, and we struck them down until not a single survivor was left.
