Heb “do not approach it.”
Heb “know.”

5.text: Joshua told the people, “Ritually consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the Lord will perform miraculous deeds among you.”

6.text: Joshua told the priests, “Pick up the ark of the covenant and pass on ahead of the people.” So they picked up the ark of the covenant and went ahead of the people.

7.text: The Lord told Joshua, “This very day I will begin to honor you before all Israel, so they will know that I am with you just as I was with Moses.

notes.text: Or more literally, “to exalt you in the eyes of all Israel.”

8.text: Instruct the priests carrying the ark of the covenant, ‘When you reach the bank of the Jordan River, wade into the water.’”

notes.text: Heb “the edge of the waters of the Jordan.” The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied for clarity.
Heb “stand in the Jordan.” Here the repetition of the word “Jordan” would be redundant according to contemporary English style, so it was not included in the translation.

9.text: Joshua told the Israelites, “Come here and listen to the words of the Lord your God!”

10.text: Joshua continued, “This is how you will know the living God is among you and that he will truly drive out before you the Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Amorites, and Jebusites.

notes.text: Heb “said.”

11.text: Look! The ark of the covenant of the Lord of the whole earth is ready to enter the Jordan ahead of you.

notes.text: Or “Ruler”; or “Master.”

12.text: Now select for yourselves twelve men from the tribes of Israel, one per tribe.

13.text: When the feet of the priests carrying the ark of the Lord, the Lord of the whole earth, touch the water of the Jordan, the water coming downstream toward you will stop flowing and pile up.”

notes.text: Heb “the soles of the feet.”
Or “Ruler”; or “Master.”
Or “rest in.”
Heb “the waters of the Jordan, the waters descending from above, will be cut off so that they will stand in one pile.”

14.text: So when the people left their tents to cross the Jordan, the priests carrying the ark of the covenant went ahead of them.

notes.text: The verb, though not in the Hebrew, is added for clarification.

15.text: When the ones carrying the ark reached the Jordan, and the feet of the priests carrying the ark touched the surface of the water—(the Jordan is at flood stage all during harvest time) —

notes.text: Heb “dipped into the edge.”
Heb “and the Jordan overflows all its banks all the days of harvest.”
The lengthy description of the priests’ arrival at the Jordan and the parenthetical reminder that the Jordan was at flood stage delay the climax of the story and add to its dramatic buildup.

16.text: the water coming downstream toward them stopped flowing. It piled up far upstream at Adam (the city near Zarethan); there was no water at all flowing to the sea of the rift valley (the Salt Sea). The people crossed the river opposite Jericho.

notes.text: Heb “the waters descending from above stood still.”
Heb “they stood in one pile very far away.”
Heb “the [waters] descending… were completely cut off.”
The Salt Sea is an ancient name for the Dead Sea.

17.text: The priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the Lord stood firmly on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan. All Israel crossed over on dry ground until the entire nation was on the other side.

notes.text: Heb “and all Israel was crossing over on dry ground until all the nation had finished crossing the Jordan.”

1.text: When the entire nation was on the other side, the Lord told Joshua,

notes.text: Heb “And when all the nation had finished crossing the Jordan.”

2.text: “Select for yourselves twelve men from the people, one per tribe.

3.text: Instruct them, ‘Pick up twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, from the very place where the priests stand firmly, and carry them over with you and put them in the place where you camp tonight.’”

notes.text: Heb “the feet of the priests.”

4.text: Joshua summoned the twelve men he had appointed from the Israelites, one per tribe.

5.text: Joshua told them, “Go in front of the ark of the Lord your God to the middle of the Jordan. Each of you is to put a stone on his shoulder, according to the number of the Israelite tribes.

6.text: The stones will be a reminder to you. When your children ask someday, ‘Why are these stones important to you?’

notes.text: Heb “that this may be”; the referent of “this” (the twelve stones) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “in order that this might be a sign among you.”

7.text: tell them how the water of the Jordan stopped flowing before the ark of the covenant of the Lord. When it crossed the Jordan, the water of the Jordan stopped flowing. These stones will be a lasting memorial for the Israelites.”

notes.text: Heb “were cut off from before.”
Heb “how the waters descending from above stood still.”

8.text: The Israelites did just as Joshua commanded. They picked up twelve stones, according to the number of the Israelite tribes, from the middle of the Jordan as the Lord had instructed Joshua. They carried them over with them to the camp and put them there.

9.text: Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan in the very place where the priests carrying the ark of the covenant stood. They remain there to this very day.

notes.text: Here “also” has been supplied in the translation to make it clear (as indicated by v. 20) that these are not the same stones the men took from the river bed.

10.text: Now the priests carrying the ark of the covenant were standing in the middle of the Jordan until everything the Lord had commanded Joshua to tell the people was accomplished, in accordance with all that Moses had commanded Joshua. The people went across quickly,

11.text: and when all the people had finished crossing, the ark of the Lord and the priests crossed as the people looked on.

notes.text: Heb “in the presence of the people.”

12.text: The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh crossed over armed for battle ahead of the Israelites, just as Moses had instructed them.

13.text: About 40,000 battle-ready troops marched past the Lord to fight on the rift valley plains of Jericho.

notes.text: Heb “men equipped for battle.”
Heb “for war.”

The ‏עֲרָבָה‎ (ʿaravah, “rift valley”) extends from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba. The ‏עַרְבוֹת‎ (ʿarevot) of Jericho” refer to the parts of the Jordan Valley in the vicinity of Jericho (see HALOT 880 s.v. ‏עֲרָבָה‎). The region is characterized by gently sloping plains which descend about 450 feet over the five miles from Jericho to the Jordan. Many translation say simply the “plains of Jericho” for the portion west of the Jordan and “plains of Moab” for the eastern portion. The translation here clarifies that the plains are part of the rift valley basin.

14.text: That day the Lord brought honor to Joshua before all Israel. They respected him all his life, just as they had respected Moses.

notes.text: Heb “feared.”
Heb “all the days of his life.”
Heb “had feared.”

15.text: The Lord told Joshua,

16.text: “Instruct the priests carrying the ark of the covenantal laws to come up from the Jordan.”

notes.text: Traditionally, “the ark of the testimony,” another name for the ark of the covenant. The Hebrew term ‏עֵדוּת‎ (ʿedut, “testimony” or “witness”) here refers to the Mosaic covenant and the body of stipulations contained within it (see HALOT 791 s.v. 2).

17.text: So Joshua instructed the priests, “Come up from the Jordan!”

18.text: The priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the Lord came up from the middle of the Jordan, and as soon as they set foot on dry land, the water of the Jordan flowed again and returned to flood stage.

notes.text: Heb “and the soles of the feet of the priests were brought up to the dry land.”
Heb “and the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and went as formerly over their banks.”
Verses 15-18 give a more detailed account of the priests’ crossing that had been briefly described in v. 11.

19.text: The people went up from the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and camped in Gilgal on the eastern border of Jericho.

notes.text: The first month was the month Abib (= late March-early April in the modern calendar). The preparations for Passover also began on the tenth day of the first month (Exod 12:2-3).

20.text: Now Joshua set up in Gilgal the twelve stones they had taken from the Jordan.

notes.text: Heb “these,” referring specifically to the twelve stones mentioned in vv. 3-7.

21.text: He told the Israelites, “When your children someday ask their fathers, ‘What do these stones represent?’

notes.text: Heb “What are these stones?”

22.text: explain to your children, ‘Israel crossed the Jordan River on dry ground.’

notes.text: Heb “make known to.”
Heb “crossed this Jordan”; the word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied to clarify the meaning.

23.text: For the Lord your God dried up the water of the Jordan before you while you crossed over. It was just like when the Lord your God dried up the Red Sea before us while we crossed it.

notes.text: Heb “just as the Lord your God did to the Red Sea when he dried [it] up before us while we crossed over.”

24.text: He has done this so all the nations of the earth might recognize the Lord’s power and so you might always obey the Lord your God.”

notes.text: Heb “in order that.”
Or “peoples.”
Heb “know the hand of the Lord that it is strong.”
Heb “fear.”

1.text: When all the Amorite kings on the west side of the Jordan and all the Canaanite kings along the seacoast heard how the Lord had dried up the water of the Jordan before the Israelites while they crossed, they lost their courage and could not even breathe for fear of the Israelites.

notes.text: Another textual tradition has, “while we crossed.”
Heb “their heart[s] melted and there was no longer in them breath (or perhaps “spirit”) because of the sons of Israel.”

2.text: At that time the Lord told Joshua, “Make flint knives and circumcise the Israelites once again.”

notes.text: Heb “return, circumcise the sons of Israel a second time.” The Hebrew term ‏שׁוּב‎ (shuv, “return”) is used here in an adverbial sense to indicate the repetition of an action.

3.text: So Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the Israelites at the Hill of the Foreskins.

notes.text: Or “Gibeath Haaraloth.” This name means “Hill of the Foreskins.” Many modern translations simply give the Hebrew name, although an explanatory note giving the meaning of the name is often included.
The name given to the place, Hill of the Foreskins was an obvious reminder of this important event.

4.text: This is why Joshua had to circumcise them: All the men old enough to fight when they left Egypt died on the journey through the wilderness after they left Egypt.

notes.text: Heb “All the people who went out from Egypt, the males, all the men of war, died in the wilderness in the way when they went out from Egypt.”

5.text: Now all the men who left were circumcised, but all the sons born on the journey through the wilderness after they left Egypt were uncircumcised.

notes.text: Or “indeed.”
Heb “people.”
Heb “all the people.”

6.text: Indeed, for forty years the Israelites traveled through the wilderness until all the men old enough to fight when they left Egypt, the ones who had disobeyed the Lord, died off. For the Lord had sworn a solemn oath to them that he would not let them see the land he had sworn by oath to their ancestors to give them, a land rich in milk and honey.

notes.text: Heb “all the nation, the men of war who went out from Egypt, who did not listen to the voice of the Lord, came to an end.”
Some Hebrew mss, as well as the Syriac version, support this reading. Most ancient witnesses read “us.”
Heb “flowing with.”
The word picture a land rich in milk and honey depicts the land as containing many grazing areas (which would produce milk) and flowering plants (which would support the bees that produced honey).

7.text: He replaced them with their sons, whom Joshua circumcised. They were uncircumcised; their fathers had not circumcised them along the way.

notes.text: Heb “their sons he raised up in their place.”

8.text: When all the men had been circumcised, they stayed there in the camp until they had healed.

notes.text: Heb “nation.”

9.text: The Lord said to Joshua, “Today I have taken away the disgrace of Egypt from you.” So that place is called Gilgal even to this day.

notes.text: Heb “rolled away.”

One might take the disgrace of Egypt as a reference to their uncircumcised condition (see Gen 34:14), but the generation that left Egypt was circumcised (see v. 5). It more likely refers to the disgrace they experienced in Egyptian slavery. When this new generation reached the promised land and renewed their covenantal commitment to the Lord by submitting to the rite of circumcision, the Lord’s deliverance of his people from slavery, which had begun with the plagues and the crossing of the Red Sea, reached its climax. See T. C. Butler, Joshua (WBC), 59.
The name Gilgal sounds like the Hebrew verb “roll away” (‏גַּלַל‎, galal).

10.text: So the Israelites camped in Gilgal and celebrated the Passover in the evening of the fourteenth day of the month in the rift valley plains of Jericho.

notes.text: This is the area of the rift valley basin in the vicinity of Jericho (see the note at Josh 4:13).

11.text: They ate some of the produce of the land the day after the Passover, including unleavened bread and roasted grain.

notes.text: The Hebrew text adds, “on this same day.” This is somewhat redundant in English and has not been translated.

12.text: The manna stopped appearing the day they ate some of the produce of the land; the Israelites never ate manna again. They ate from the produce of the land of Canaan that year.

notes.text: Heb “the day after, when they ate.” The present translation assumes this means the day after the Passover, though it is possible it refers to the day after they began eating the land’s produce.
Heb “and the sons of Israel had no more manna.”

13.text: When Joshua was near Jericho, he looked up and saw a man standing in front of him holding a drawn sword. Joshua approached him and asked him, “Are you on our side or allied with our enemies?”

notes.text: Heb “in.”

Heb “he lifted up his eyes and looked. And look, a man was standing in front of him, and his sword was drawn in his hand.” The verb ‏הִנֵּה‎ (hinneh, “look”) invites the reader to view the scene through Joshua’s eyes. By calling the stranger “a man,” the author reflects Joshua’s perspective. The text shortly reveals his true identity (vv. 14-15).
Heb “Are you for us or for our enemies?”

14.text: He answered, “Truly I am the commander of the Lord’s army. Now I have arrived!” Joshua bowed down with his face to the ground and asked, “What does my master want to say to his servant?”

notes.text: Heb “He said, “Neither.” An alternative reading is ‏לוֹ‎ (lo, “[He said] to him”; cf. NEB). This reading is supported by many Hebrew mss, as well as the LXX and Syriac versions. The traditional reading of the MT (‏לֹא‎, loʾ, “no, neither”) is probably the product of aural confusion (the two variant readings sound the same in Hebrew). Although followed by a number of modern translations (cf. NIV, NRSV), this reading is problematic, for the commander of the Lord’s army would hardly have declared himself neutral.

The Lord’s heavenly army, like an earthly army, has a commander who leads the troops. For the phrase ‏שַׂר־צְבָא‎ (sar tsevaʾ, “army commander”) in the human sphere, see among many other references Gen 21:22, 32; 26:26; Judg 4:2, 7; 1 Sam 12:9.
The commander’s appearance seems to be for Joshua’s encouragement. Joshua could now lead Israel into battle knowing that the Lord’s invisible army would ensure victory.
Heb “Joshua fell on his face to the ground and bowed down.”

15.text: The commander of the Lord’s army answered Joshua, “Remove your sandals from your feet, because the place where you stand is holy.” Joshua did so.

1.text: Now Jericho was shut tightly because of the Israelites. No one was allowed to leave or enter.

notes.text: Heb “was shutting and shut up.” HALOT 743 s.v. I ‏סגר‎ paraphrases, “blocking [any way of access] and blocked [against any who would leave].”
Heb “there was no one going out and there was no one coming in.”

2.text: The Lord told Joshua, “See, I am about to defeat Jericho for you, along with its king and its warriors.

notes.text: Heb “I have given into your hand Jericho.” The Hebrew verb ‏נָתַתִּי‎ (natatti, “I have given”) is probably best understood as a perfect of certitude, indicating the certainty of the action. The Hebrew pronominal suffix “your” is singular, being addressed to Joshua as the leader and representative of the nation. To convey to the modern reader what is about to happen and who is doing it, the translation “I am about to defeat Jericho for you” has been used.

3.text: Have all the warriors march around the city one time; do this for six days.

notes.text: Heb “and go around the city, all [you] men of war, encircling the city one time.” The Hebrew verb ‏וְסַבֹּתֶם‎ (vesabbotem, “and go around”) is plural, being addressed to the whole army.

4.text: Have seven priests carry seven rams’ horns in front of the ark. On the seventh day march around the city seven times, while the priests blow the horns.

notes.text: Heb “rams’ horns, trumpets.”

5.text: When you hear the signal from the ram’s horn, have the whole army give a loud battle cry. Then the city wall will collapse, and the warriors should charge straight ahead.”

notes.text: Heb “and it will be at the sounding of the horn, the ram’s horn, when you hear the sound of the ram’s horn.” The text of Josh 6:5 seems to be unduly repetitive, so for the sake of English style and readability, it is best to streamline the text here. The reading in the Hebrew looks like a conflation of variant readings, with the second (“when you hear the sound of the ram’s horn”) being an interpolation that assimilates the text to verse 20 (“when the army heard the sound of the horn”). Note that the words “when you hear the sound of the ram’s horn” do not appear in the LXX of verse 5.
Heb “all the people will shout with a loud shout.”
Heb “fall in its place.”
Heb “and the people will go up, each man straight ahead.”

6.text: So Joshua son of Nun summoned the priests and instructed them, “Pick up the ark of the covenant, and seven priests must carry seven rams’ horns in front of the ark of the Lord.”

7.text: And he told the army, “Move ahead and march around the city, with armed troops going ahead of the ark of the Lord.”

notes.text: An alternative reading is “and they said.” In this case the subject is indefinite and the verb should be translated as passive, “[the army] was told.”
Heb “the people.”
Heb “pass by.”

8.text: When Joshua gave the army its orders, the seven priests carrying the seven rams’ horns before the Lord moved ahead and blew the horns as the ark of the covenant of the Lord followed behind.

notes.text: Heb “when Joshua spoke to the people.”

9.text: Armed troops marched ahead of the priests blowing the horns, while the rear guard followed along behind the ark blowing rams’ horns.

10.text: Now Joshua had instructed the army, “Do not give a battle cry or raise your voices; say nothing until the day I tell you, ‘Give the battle cry.’ Then give the battle cry!”

notes.text: Heb “the people.”
Or “the shout.”
Heb “do not let a word come out of your mouths.”
Or “the shout.”
Or “the shout.”

11.text: So Joshua made sure they marched the ark of the Lord around the city one time. Then they went back to the camp and spent the night there.

notes.text: Heb “and he made the ark of the Lord go around the city, encircling one time.”
Heb “and they entered the camp and spent the night in the camp.”

12.text: Bright and early the next morning Joshua had the priests pick up the ark of the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “Joshua rose early in the morning and the priests picked up the ark of the Lord.”

13.text: The seven priests carrying the seven rams’ horns before the ark of the Lord marched along blowing their horns. Armed troops marched ahead of them, while the rear guard followed along behind the ark of the Lord blowing rams’ horns.

14.text: They marched around the city one time on the second day, then returned to the camp. They did this six days in all.

15.text: On the seventh day they were up at the crack of dawn and marched around the city as before—only this time they marched around it seven times.

notes.text: Heb “On the seventh day they rose early, when the dawn ascended.”
Heb “and they went around the city according to this manner seven times, only on that day they went around the city seven times.”

16.text: The seventh time around, the priests blew the rams’ horns, and Joshua told the army, “Give the battle cry, for the Lord is handing the city over to you!

notes.text: Heb “the people.”
Or “the shout.”
Heb “for the Lord has given to you the city.” The verbal form is a perfect, probably indicating certitude here.

17.text: The city and all that is in it must be set apart for the Lord; only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house will live, because she hid the spies we sent.

notes.text: Or “dedicated to the Lord.”
To make the city set apart for the Lord would involve annihilating all the people and animals and placing its riches in the Lord’s treasury (vv. 19, 21, 24).
Heb “messengers.”

18.text: But be careful when you are setting apart the riches for God. If you take any of it, then you will make the Israelite camp subject to annihilation and cause a disaster.

notes.text: Heb “Only you keep [away] from what is set apart [to God] so that you might not, as you are setting [it] apart, take some of what is set apart [to God] and turn the camp of Israel into what is set apart [to destruction by God] and bring trouble on it.”

19.text: All the silver and gold, as well as bronze and iron items, belong to the Lord. They must go into the Lord’s treasury.”

notes.text: Heb “it is holy to the Lord.”

20.text: The rams’ horns sounded, and when the army heard the signal, they gave a loud battle cry. The wall collapsed, and the warriors charged straight ahead into the city and captured it.

notes.text: Heb “and the people shouted and they blew the rams’ horns.” The initial statement (“and the people shouted”) seems premature, since the verse goes on to explain that the battle cry followed the blowing of the horns. The statement has probably been accidentally duplicated from what follows. It is omitted in the LXX.
Heb “the people.”
Heb “the sound of the horn.”
Heb “they shouted with a loud shout.”
Heb “fell in its place.”
Heb “and the people went up into the city, each one straight ahead, and they captured the city.”

21.text: They annihilated with the sword everything that breathed in the city, including men and women, young and old, as well as cattle, sheep, and donkeys.

notes.text: Heb “all which was in the city.”

22.text: Joshua told the two men who had spied on the land, “Enter the prostitute’s house and bring out the woman and all who belong to her as you promised her.”

notes.text: Heb “the house of the woman, the prostitute.”
Heb “and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her as you swore on oath to her.”

23.text: So the young spies went and brought out Rahab, her father, mother, brothers, and all who belonged to her. They brought out her whole family and took them to a place outside the Israelite camp.

notes.text: Or “placed them outside.”

24.text: But they burned the city and all that was in it, except for the silver, gold, and bronze and iron items they put in the treasury of the Lord’s house.

notes.text: The Hebrew text adds “with fire.”
Heb “the treasury of the house of the Lord.” Technically the Lord did not have a “house” yet, so perhaps this refers to the tabernacle using later terminology.

25.text: Yet Joshua spared Rahab the prostitute, her father’s family, and all who belonged to her. She lives in Israel to this very day because she hid the messengers Joshua sent to spy on Jericho.

notes.text: Heb “kept alive.”
Heb the house of her father.”
Or “among the Israelites”; Heb “in the midst of Israel.”

26.text: At that time Joshua made this solemn declaration: “The man who attempts to rebuild this city of Jericho will stand condemned before the Lord. He will lose his firstborn son when he lays its foundations and his youngest son when he erects its gates!”

notes.text: Normally the Hiphil of ‏שָׁבַע‎ (shavaʿ) has a causative sense (“make [someone] take an oath”; see Josh 2:17, 20), but here (see also Josh 23:7) no object is stated or implied. If Joshua is calling divine judgment down upon the one who attempts to rebuild Jericho, then “make a solemn appeal [to God as judge]” or “pronounce a curse” would be an appropriate translation. However, the tone seems stronger. Joshua appears to be announcing the certain punishment of the violator. 1 Kgs 16:34, which records the fulfillment of Joshua’s prediction, supports this. Casting Joshua in a prophetic role, it refers to Joshua’s statement as the “word of the Lord” spoken through Joshua.
Heb “rises up and builds.”
The LXX omits “Jericho.” It is probably a scribal addition.
The Hebrew phrase ‏אָרוּר לִפְנֵי יְהוָה‎ (ʾarur lifne yehvah, “cursed [i.e., condemned] before the Lord”) also occurs in 1 Sam 26:19.

Heb “With his firstborn he will lay its foundations and with his youngest he will erect its gates.” The Hebrew verb ‏יַצִּיב‎ (yatsiv, “he will erect”) is imperfect, not jussive, suggesting Joshua’s statement is a prediction, not an imprecation.

27.text: The Lord was with Joshua and he became famous throughout the land.

notes.text: Heb “and the report about him was in all the land.” The Hebrew term ‏אֶרֶץ‎ (ʾerets, “land”) may also be translated “earth.”

1.text: But the Israelites disobeyed the command about the city’s riches. Achan son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, from the tribe of Judah, stole some of the riches. The Lord was furious with the Israelites.

notes.text: Heb “But the sons of Israel were unfaithful with unfaithfulness concerning what was set apart [to the Lord].”
1 Chr 2:6 lists a “Zimri” (but no Zabdi) as one of the five sons of Zerah (cf. also Josh 7:17, 18).
Heb “took from what was set apart [to the Lord].”
Heb “the anger of the Lord burned against the sons of Israel.”
This incident illustrates well the principle of corporate solidarity and corporate guilt. The sin of one man brought the Lord’s anger down upon the entire nation.

2.text: Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai (which is located near Beth Aven, east of Bethel) and instructed them, “Go up and spy on the land.” So the men went up and spied on Ai.

3.text: They returned and reported to Joshua, “Don’t send the whole army. About two or three thousand men are adequate to defeat Ai. Don’t tire out the whole army, for Ai is small.”

notes.text: Heb “and they returned to Joshua and said to him.”
Heb “Don’t let all the people go up.”
Heb “Let about two thousand men or about three thousand men go up to defeat Ai.”
Heb “all the people for they are small.”

4.text: So about 3,000 men went up, but they fled from the men of Ai.

5.text: The men of Ai killed about thirty-six of them and chased them from in front of the city gate all the way to the fissures and defeated them on the steep slope. The people’s courage melted away like water.

notes.text: The meaning and correct translation of the Hebrew word ‏שְׁבָרִים‎ (shevarim) is uncertain. The translation “fissures” is based on usage of the plural form of the noun in Ps 60:4 HT (60:2 ET), where it appears to refer to cracks in the earth caused by an earthquake. Perhaps deep ravines or gorges are in view, or the word is a proper noun (“all the way to Shebarim”).
The precise geographical location of the Israelite defeat at this “steep slope” is uncertain.
Or “army’s.”
Heb “and the heart of the people melted and became water.”

6.text: Joshua tore his clothes; he and the leaders of Israel lay face down on the ground before the ark of the Lord until evening and threw dirt on their heads.

notes.text: Tearing one’s clothes was an outward expression of extreme sorrow (see Gen 37:34; 44:13).
Or “elders.”
Heb “and fell on his face to the ground before the ark of the Lord until evening, he and the elders of Israel.”
Throwing dirt on one’s head was an outward expression of extreme sorrow (see Lam 2:10; Ezek 27:30).

7.text: Joshua prayed, “O, Sovereign Lord! Why did you bring these people across the Jordan to hand us over to the Amorites so they could destroy us? If only we had been satisfied to live on the other side of the Jordan!

notes.text: Heb “said.”

8.text: O Lord, what can I say now that Israel has retreated before its enemies?

notes.text: Heb “turned [the] back.”

9.text: When the Canaanites and all who live in the land hear about this, they will turn against us and destroy the very memory of us from the earth. What will you do to protect your great reputation?”

notes.text: Heb “and cut off our name.”
Heb “What will you do for your great name?”

10.text: The Lord responded to Joshua, “Get up! Why are you lying there face down?

notes.text: Heb “said.”
Heb “Why are you falling on your face?”

11.text: Israel has sinned; they have violated my covenantal commandment! They have taken some of the riches; they have stolen them and deceitfully put them among their own possessions.

notes.text: Heb “They have violated my covenant which I commanded them.”
Heb “what was set apart [to the Lord].”
Heb “and also they have stolen, and also they have lied, and also they have placed [them] among their items.”

12.text: The Israelites are unable to stand before their enemies; they retreat because they have become subject to annihilation. I will no longer be with you, unless you destroy what has contaminated you.

notes.text: Heb “they turn [the] back before their enemies because they are set apart [to destruction by the Lord].”
The second person pronoun is plural in Hebrew, indicating these words are addressed to the entire nation.
Heb “what is set apart [to destruction by the Lord] from your midst.”

13.text: Get up! Ritually consecrate the people and tell them this: ‘Ritually consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, because this is what the Lord God of Israel has said, “You are contaminated, O Israel! You will not be able to stand before your enemies until you remove what is contaminating you.”

notes.text: Heb “what is set apart [to destruction by the Lord] [is] in your midst.”
Heb “remove what is set apart [i.e., to destruction by the Lord] from your midst.”

14.text: In the morning you must approach in tribal order. The tribe the Lord selects must approach by clans. The clan the Lord selects must approach by families. The family the Lord selects must approach man by man.

notes.text: Heb “by your tribes.”
Heb “takes forcefully, seizes.”
Heb “houses.”
Heb “by men.”

15.text: The one caught with the riches must be burned up along with all who belong to him, because he violated the Lord’s covenant and did such a disgraceful thing in Israel.’”

notes.text: Heb “with what was set apart [to the Lord].”
Heb “burned with fire.”

16.text: Bright and early the next morning Joshua made Israel approach in tribal order, and the tribe of Judah was selected.

notes.text: Heb “by tribes.”

17.text: He then made the clans of Judah approach, and the clan of the Zerahites was selected. He made the clan of the Zerahites approach, and Zabdi was selected.

notes.text: See the note on “Zabdi” in Jos 7:1.
Heb “and he selected Zabdi.” The Lord is the apparent subject. The LXX supports reading a passive (Niphal) form here, as does the immediate context.

18.text: He then made Zabdi’s family approach man by man and Achan son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, from the tribe of Judah, was selected.

notes.text: Heb “his”; the referent (Zabdi) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “by men.”

19.text: So Joshua said to Achan, “My son, honor the Lord God of Israel and give him praise! Tell me what you did; don’t hide anything from me.”

notes.text: Heb “give glory to.”

20.text: Achan told Joshua, “It is true. I have sinned against the Lord God of Israel in this way:

notes.text: Heb “like this and like this I did.”

21.text: I saw among the goods we seized a nice robe from Babylon, 200 silver pieces, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels. I wanted them, so I took them. They are hidden in the ground right in the middle of my tent, with the silver underneath.”

notes.text: Heb “Shinar,” a reference to Babylon (cf. Gen 10:10; 11:2; 14:1). Many modern translations retain the Hebrew name “Shinar” (cf. NEB, NRSV) but some use the more familiar “Babylon” (cf. NIV, NLT).
Heb “shekels.”

22.text: Joshua sent messengers who ran to the tent. The things were hidden right in his tent, with the silver underneath.

notes.text: Heb “Look, [it was] hidden in his tent, and the silver was beneath it.”

23.text: They took it all from the middle of the tent, brought it to Joshua and all the Israelites, and placed it before the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “poured out,” probably referring to the way the silver pieces poured out of their container.

24.text: Then Joshua and all Israel took Achan, son of Zerah, along with the silver, the robe, the bar of gold, his sons, daughters, oxen, donkeys, sheep, tent, and all that belonged to him and brought them up to the Valley of Disaster.

notes.text: Or “Trouble” The name is “Achor” in Hebrew, which means “disaster” or “trouble” (also in v. 26).

25.text: Joshua said, “Why have you brought disaster on us? The Lord will bring disaster on you today!” All Israel stoned him to death. (They also stoned and burned the others.)

notes.text: Or “trouble on.” The word is “achor” in Hebrew (also in the following clause).
Heb “and they burned them with fire and they stoned them with stones.” These words are somewhat parenthetical in nature and are omitted in the LXX; they may represent a later scribal addition.

26.text: Then they erected over him a large pile of stones (it remains to this very day) and the Lord’s anger subsided. So that place is called the Valley of Disaster to this very day.

notes.text: Heb “to this day.” The phrase “to this day” is omitted in the LXX and may represent a later scribal addition.

1.text: The Lord told Joshua, “Don’t be afraid and don’t panic! Take the whole army with you and march against Ai! See, I am handing over to you the king of Ai, along with his people, city, and land.

notes.text: Or perhaps “and don’t get discouraged!”
Heb “Take with you all the people of war and arise, go up against Ai!”
Heb “I have given into our hand.” The verbal form, a perfect, is probably best understood as a perfect of certitude, indicating the certainty of the action.

2.text: Do to Ai and its king what you did to Jericho and its king, except you may plunder its goods and cattle. Set an ambush behind the city.”

3.text: Joshua and the whole army marched against Ai. Joshua selected 30,000 brave warriors and sent them out at night.

notes.text: “And Joshua and all the people of war arose to go up [against] Ai.”

4.text: He ordered them, “Look, set an ambush behind the city. Don’t go very far from the city; all of you be ready!

5.text: I and all the troops who are with me will approach the city. When they come out to fight us like before, we will retreat from them.

notes.text: Heb “the people.”

6.text: They will attack us until we have lured them from the city, for they will say, ‘They are retreating from us like before.’ We will retreat from them.

notes.text: Heb “come out after.”

7.text: Then you rise up from your hiding place and seize the city. The Lord your God will hand it over to you.

notes.text: Heb “from the ambush.”
Heb “take possession of.”

8.text: When you capture the city, set it on fire in keeping with the Lord’s message. See, I have given you orders.”

notes.text: Heb “the city.”
Heb “I have commanded you.”

9.text: Joshua sent them away and they went to their hiding place west of Ai, between Bethel and Ai. Joshua spent that night with the army.

notes.text: Or “the place of ambush.”
Heb “and they stayed between Bethel and Ai, west of Ai.”
Heb “in the midst of the people.”

10.text: Bright and early the next morning Joshua gathered the army, and he and the leaders of Israel marched at the head of it to Ai.

notes.text: Or “summoned, mustered.”
Heb “the people.”
Or “elders.”
Heb “went up.”

Heb “them” (referring to “the people” in the previous clause, which requires a plural pronoun). Since the translation used “army” in the previous clause, a singular pronoun (“it”) is required in English.

11.text: All the troops that were with him marched up and drew near the city. They camped north of Ai on the other side of the valley.

notes.text: Heb “All the people of war who were with him went up and approached and came opposite the city.”
Heb “and the valley [was] between them and Ai.”

12.text: He took 5,000 men and set an ambush west of the city between Bethel and Ai.

13.text: The army was in position—the main army north of the city and the rear guard west of the city. That night Joshua went into the middle of the valley.

notes.text: Some Hebrew mss read, “spent the night in.”

14.text: When the king of Ai and all his people saw Israel, they rushed to get up early. Then the king and the men of the city went out to meet Israel in battle, at the meeting place near the rift valley. But he did not realize an ambush was waiting for him behind the city.

notes.text: This probably refers to the hill country at the edge of the rift valley between Ai and Jericho. This part of the battle was probably engaged where Israel would have come up to the hill country out of the rift valley from Jericho, an ascent of about 4000 feet (with ups and downs) over ten miles.
Heb “did not know that an ambush for him was behind the city.”

15.text: Joshua and all Israel pretended to be defeated by them, and they retreated along the way to the wilderness.

16.text: All the reinforcements in Ai were ordered to chase them; they chased Joshua and were lured away from the city.

notes.text: Heb “All the people.”
Some textual witnesses read “the city.”
Or “were summoned”; or “were mustered.”

17.text: No men were left in Ai or Bethel; they all went out after Israel. They left the city wide open and chased Israel.

notes.text: The LXX omits the words “or Bethel.”
Heb “who did not go out after Israel.”

18.text: The Lord told Joshua, “Hold out toward Ai the curved sword in your hand, for I am handing the city over to you.” So Joshua held out toward Ai the curved sword in his hand.

notes.text: Traditionally “spear,” but see HALOT 472 s.v. ‏כִּידוֹן‎, which argues based upon evidence from the Dead Sea Scrolls that this term refers to a curved sword of some type; note the definition “scimitar” given there.
Heb “it”; the referent (the city of Ai) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

19.text: When he held out his hand, the men waiting in ambush rose up quickly from their place and attacked. They entered the city, captured it, and immediately set it on fire.

notes.text: Heb “and ran.”

20.text: When the men of Ai turned around, they saw the smoke from the city ascending into the sky and were so shocked they were unable to flee in any direction. In the meantime the men who were retreating to the wilderness turned against their pursuers.

notes.text: Heb “and they saw, and look.” The Hebrew term ‏הִנֵּה‎ (hinneh, “look”) draws attention to the scene and invites the audience to view the events from the perspective of the men of Ai.
Heb “and there was not in them hands to flee here or there.” The Hebrew term ‏יָדַיִם‎ (yadayim, “hands”) is idiomatic for “strength.”

21.text: When Joshua and all Israel saw that the men in ambush had captured the city and that the city was going up in smoke, they turned around and struck down the men of Ai.

notes.text: Heb “and that the smoke of the city ascended.”

22.text: At the same time the men who had taken the city came out to fight, and the men of Ai were trapped in the middle. The Israelites struck them down, leaving no survivors or refugees.

notes.text: Heb “and these went out from the city to meet them and they were for Israel in the middle, some on this side, and others on the other side.”

23.text: But they captured the king of Ai alive and brought him to Joshua.

24.text: When Israel had finished killing all the men of Ai who had chased them toward the wilderness (they all fell by the sword), all Israel returned to Ai and put the sword to it.

notes.text: Heb “residents.”
Heb “in the field, in the wilderness in which they chased them.”
Heb “and all of them fell by the edge of the sword until they were destroyed.” The LXX omits the words, “and all of them fell by the edge of the sword.” They may represent a later scribal addition.

25.text: So 12,000 men and women died that day, including all the men of Ai.

notes.text: Heb “fell.”

26.text: Joshua kept holding out his curved sword until Israel had annihilated all who lived in Ai.

notes.text: Heb “Joshua did not draw back his hand which held out the curved sword until he had annihilated all the residents of Ai.”

27.text: But Israel did plunder the cattle and the goods of the city, in keeping with the Lord’s orders to Joshua.

notes.text: Heb “message, word.”

28.text: Joshua burned Ai and made it a permanently uninhabited mound (it remains that way to this very day).

notes.text: Heb “and made it a permanent mound, a desolation, to this day.”

29.text: He hung the king of Ai on a tree, leaving him exposed until evening. At sunset Joshua ordered that his corpse be taken down from the tree. They threw it down at the entrance of the city gate and erected over it a large pile of stones (it remains to this very day).

notes.text: Heb “on a tree until evening.” The words “leaving him exposed” are supplied in the translation for clarity.
For the legal background of this action, see Deut 21:22-23.
Heb “to this day.”

30.text: Then Joshua built an altar for the Lord God of Israel on Mount Ebal,

31.text: just as Moses the Lord’s servant had commanded the Israelites. As described in the law scroll of Moses, it was made with uncut stones untouched by an iron tool. On it they offered burnt sacrifices to the Lord and sacrificed tokens of peace.

notes.text: Heb “as it is written in the scroll of the law of Moses, an altar of whole stones on which no one had wielded iron.” The expression “whole stones” refers to stones in their natural condition, i.e., not carved or shaped artificially with tools (“wielded iron”).
Or “peace offerings.”

32.text: There, in the presence of the Israelites, Joshua inscribed on the stones a duplicate of the law written by Moses.

notes.text: Heb “and he wrote there on the stones a duplicate of the law of Moses which he wrote before the sons of Israel.”

33.text: All the people, rulers, leaders, and judges were standing on either side of the ark, in front of the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord. Both resident foreigners and native Israelites were there. Half the people stood in front of Mount Gerizim and the other half in front of Mount Ebal, as Moses the Lord’s servant had previously instructed them to do for the formal blessing ceremony.

notes.text: Heb “All Israel.”
Or “elders.”
Heb “like the resident foreigner, like the citizen.” The language is idiomatic, meaning that both groups were treated the same, at least in this instance.
Heb “as Moses, the Lord’s servant, commanded to bless the people, Israel, formerly.”
Moses’ earlier instructions are found in Deut 11:29.

34.text: Then Joshua read aloud all the words of the law, including the blessings and the curses, just as they are written in the law scroll.

notes.text: Or “afterward.”

35.text: Joshua read aloud every commandment Moses had given before the whole assembly of Israel, including the women, children, and resident foreigners who lived among them.

notes.text: Heb “There was not a word from all which Moses commanded that Joshua did not read aloud.”
Heb “walked in their midst.”

1.text: When the news reached all the kings on the west side of the Jordan —in the hill country, the foothills, and all along the Mediterranean coast as far as Lebanon (including the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites)—

notes.text: Heb “When all the kings who were beyond the Jordan heard.”
The foothills (‏שְׁפֵלָה‎, shephelah) are the transition region between the hill country and the coastal plains.
Heb “all the coast of the Great Sea.” The “Great Sea” was the typical designation for the Mediterranean Sea.
Heb “in front of.”

2.text: they formed an alliance to fight against Joshua and Israel.

notes.text: Heb “they gathered together to fight against Joshua and Israel [with] one mouth.”

3.text: When the residents of Gibeon heard what Joshua did to Jericho and Ai,

4.text: they did something clever. They collected some provisions and put worn-out sacks on their donkeys, along with worn-out wineskins that were ripped and patched.

notes.text: Heb “and they went and [?].” The root and meaning of the verb form ‏יִצְטַיָּרוּ‎ (yitstayyaru) are uncertain. The Hebrew text form most likely should be ‏יִצְטַיָּדוּ‎ (yitstayyadu), read by some Hebrew mss and ancient versions, from the root ‏צוּד‎ (tsud, “take provisions,” BDB 845 s.v. II ‏צוד‎) which also occurs in v. 11. Note NRSV “they went and prepared provisions”; cf. NEB “They went and disguised themselves”; NIV “they went as a delegation.”

5.text: They had worn-out, patched sandals on their feet and dressed in worn-out clothes. All their bread was dry and hard.

notes.text: Heb “all the bread of their provisions.”
Or “moldy.”

6.text: They came to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal and said to him and the men of Israel, “We have come from a distant land. Make a treaty with us.”

7.text: The men of Israel said to the Hivites, “Perhaps you live near us. So how can we make a treaty with you?”

notes.text: Heb “in our midst.”

8.text: But they said to Joshua, “We are willing to be your subjects.” So Joshua said to them, “Who are you and where do you come from?”

notes.text: Heb “we are your servants.”

9.text: They told him, “Your subjects have come from a very distant land because of the reputation of the Lord your God, for we have heard the news about all he did in Egypt

notes.text: Or “servants.”
Heb “name.”
Heb “the report about him, all that he did in Egypt.”

10.text: and all he did to the two Amorite kings on the other side of the Jordan—King Sihon of Heshbon and King Og of Bashan in Ashtaroth.

11.text: Our leaders and all who live in our land told us, ‘Take provisions for your journey and go meet them. Tell them, “We are willing to be your subjects. Make a treaty with us.”’

notes.text: Heb “your servants.”

12.text: This bread of ours was warm when we packed it in our homes the day we started out to meet you, but now it is dry and hard.

notes.text: Heb “in the day we went out to come to you.”
Or “moldy.”

13.text: These wineskins we filled were brand new, but look how they have ripped. Our clothes and sandals have worn out because it has been a very long journey.”

14.text: The men examined some of their provisions, but they failed to ask the Lord’s advice.

notes.text: Heb “took.” This probably means they tasted some of the food to make sure it was stale.
Heb “but they did not ask the mouth of the Lord.” This refers to seeking the Lord’s will and guidance through an oracle.

15.text: Joshua made a peace treaty with them and agreed to let them live. The leaders of the community sealed it with an oath.

notes.text: Or “assembly.”
Heb “Joshua made peace with them and made a treaty with them to let them live, and the leaders of the community swore an oath to them.”

16.text: Three days after they made the treaty with them, the Israelites found out they were from the local area and lived nearby.

notes.text: Heb “At the end of three days, after they made the treaty with them, they heard that they were neighbors to them and in their midst they were living.”

17.text: So the Israelites set out and on the third day arrived at their cities—Gibeon, Kephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath Jearim.

18.text: The Israelites did not attack them because the leaders of the community had sworn an oath to them in the name of the Lord God of Israel. The whole community criticized the leaders,

notes.text: Heb “by the Lord God of Israel.”
Or “grumbled against.”

19.text: but all the leaders told the whole community, “We swore an oath to them in the name of the Lord God of Israel! So now we can’t hurt them.

notes.text: Heb “to them by….”
Or “touch.”

20.text: We must let them live so we can escape the curse attached to the oath we swore to them.”

notes.text: Heb “This is what we will do to them, keeping them alive so there will not be upon us anger concerning the oath which we swore to them.”

21.text: The leaders then added, “Let them live.” So they became woodcutters and water carriers for the whole community, as the leaders had decided.

notes.text: Heb “and the leaders said to them.” The LXX omits the words “and the leaders said to them.”

The vav (‏ו‎) consecutive construction in the Hebrew text suggests that the narrative resumes at this point. The LXX reads here, “and they will be,” understanding what follows to be a continuation of the leaders’ words rather than a comment by the narrator.
Heb “as the leaders said to them.”

22.text: Joshua summoned the Gibeonites and said to them, “Why did you trick us by saying, ‘We live far away from you,’ when you really live nearby?

notes.text: Verses 22-27 appear to elaborate on v. 21b.
Heb “them.”
Or “deceive.”
Heb “live in our midst?”

23.text: Now you are condemned to perpetual servitude as woodcutters and water carriers for the house of my God.”

notes.text: Heb “Now you are cursed and a servant will not be cut off from you, woodcutters and water carriers for the house of my God.”

24.text: They said to Joshua, “It was carefully reported to your subjects how the Lord your God commanded Moses his servant to assign you the whole land and to destroy all who live in the land from before you. Because of you we were terrified we would lose our lives, so we did this thing.

notes.text: Heb “your servants.”
Or “we were very afraid.”

25.text: So now we are in your power. Do to us what you think is good and appropriate.”

notes.text: Heb “so now, look, we are in your hand.”
Heb “according to what is good and according to what is upright in your eyes to do us, do.”

26.text: Joshua did as they said; he kept the Israelites from killing them

notes.text: Heb “And he did to them so and he rescued them from the hand of the sons of Israel and they did not kill them.”

27.text: and that day made them woodcutters and water carriers for the community and for the altar of the Lord at the divinely chosen site. (They continue in that capacity to this very day.)

notes.text: Heb “and Joshua made them in that day woodcutters and water carriers for the community, and for the altar of the Lord to this day at the place which he chooses.”

1.text: Adoni-Zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard how Joshua captured Ai and annihilated it and its king as he did Jericho and its king. He also heard how the people of Gibeon made peace with Israel and lived among them.

notes.text: Heb “as he had done to Jericho and to its king, so he did to Ai and to its king.”
Heb “and how.”

2.text: All Jerusalem was terrified because Gibeon was a large city, like one of the royal cities. It was larger than Ai and all its men were warriors.

notes.text: This statement is subordinated to v. 1 in the Hebrew text, which reads literally, “When Adoni-Zedek…they feared greatly.” The subject of the plural verb at the beginning of v. 2 is probably the residents of Jerusalem.

3.text: So King Adoni-Zedek of Jerusalem sent this message to King Hoham of Hebron, King Piram of Jarmuth, King Japhia of Lachish, and King Debir of Eglon:

4.text: “Come to my aid so we can attack Gibeon, for it has made peace with Joshua and the Israelites.”

notes.text: Heb “Come up to me and help me.”

5.text: So the five Amorite kings (the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon) and all their troops gathered together and advanced. They deployed their troops and fought against Gibeon.

notes.text: Heb “and they camped against Gibeon and fought against it.”

6.text: The men of Gibeon sent this message to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal, “Do not abandon your subjects! Come up here quickly and rescue us! Help us! For all the Amorite kings living in the hill country are attacking us.”

notes.text: Heb “do not let your hand drop from us.”
Heb “your servants!”
Heb “have gathered against us.”

7.text: So Joshua and his whole army, including the bravest warriors, marched up from Gilgal.

notes.text: Heb “And Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of war with him, and all the brave warriors.”

8.text: The Lord told Joshua, “Don’t be afraid of them, for I am handing them over to you. Not one of them can resist you.”

notes.text: Heb “I have given them into your hand.” The verbal form is a perfect of certitude, emphasizing the certainty of the action.
Heb “and not a man [or “one”] of them will stand before you.”

9.text: Joshua attacked them by surprise after marching all night from Gilgal.

notes.text: Heb “Joshua came upon them suddenly, all the night he went up from Gilgal.”

10.text: The Lord routed them before Israel. Israel thoroughly defeated them at Gibeon. They chased them up the road to the pass of Beth Horon and struck them down all the way to Azekah and Makkedah.

notes.text: Or “caused to panic.”

Heb “he.” The referent is probably Israel (mentioned at the end of the previous sentence in the verse; cf. NIV, NRSV), but it is also possible that the Lord should be understood as the referent (cf. NASB “and He slew them with a great slaughter at Gibeon”), or even Joshua (cf. NEB “and Joshua defeated them utterly in Gibeon”).
Heb “struck them down with a great striking down.”
Or “ascent.”

11.text: As they fled from Israel on the slope leading down from Beth Horon, the Lord threw down on them large hailstones from the sky, all the way to Azekah. They died—in fact, more died from the hailstones than the Israelites killed with the sword.

notes.text: Heb “on the descent of.”
Or “heaven” (also in v. 13). The Hebrew term ‏שָׁמַיִם‎ (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.

12.text: The day the Lord delivered the Amorites over to the Israelites, Joshua prayed to the Lord before Israel: “O sun, stand still over Gibeon; O moon, over the Valley of Aijalon!”

notes.text: Heb “Then Joshua spoke to the Lord in the day the Lord placed the Amorites before the sons of Israel and he said in the eyes of Israel.” It is uncertain whether the phrase “before the sons of Israel” modifies the verb “placed” (as in the present translation, “delivered the Amorites over to the Israelites”) or the verb “spoke” (“Joshua spoke to the Lord before the sons of Israel in the day the Lord delivered over the Amorites”).

13.text: The sun stood still and the moon stood motionless while the nation took vengeance on its enemies. The event is recorded in the Scroll of the Upright One. The sun stood motionless in the middle of the sky and did not set for about a full day.

notes.text: Heb “Is it not written down in the Scroll of the Upright One?” Many modern translations render this as “the Book of Jashar.” Yashar (‏יָשָׁר‎) means “Upright One.”
The Scroll of the Upright One was apparently an ancient Israelite collection of songs and prayers (see also 2 Sam 1:18), but it has not been preserved.
Heb “and did not hurry to set [for] about a full day.”

The nature of the event described here is debated. Various options have been suggested, including (1) the earth stopped rotating, (2) the light of the sun somehow shone longer than normal, (3) the light of the sun was blocked by an eclipse, (4) the position of the sun and moon in the sky was interpreted as an omen, or (5) the language is figurative and metaphorical, describing the battle in poetic terms. For a good discussion of these options, see D. M. Howard, Jr., Joshua (NAC), 241-49.

14.text: There has not been a day like it before or since. The Lord listened to a human being, for the Lord fought for Israel!

15.text: Then Joshua and all Israel returned to the camp at Gilgal.

16.text: The five Amorite kings ran away and hid in the cave at Makkedah.

notes.text: Heb “these five kings.”

17.text: Joshua was told, “The five kings have been found hiding in the cave at Makkedah.”

18.text: Joshua said, “Roll large stones over the mouth of the cave and post guards in front of it.

notes.text: Heb “and appoint by it men to guard them.”

19.text: But don’t you delay! Chase your enemies and catch them. Don’t allow them to retreat to their cities, for the Lord your God is handing them over to you.”

notes.text: Heb “But [as for] you, don’t stand still, chase after your enemies and attack them from the rear.”
Or “enter into.”
Heb “has given them into your hand.” The verbal form is a perfect of certitude, emphasizing the certainty of the action.

20.text: Joshua and the Israelites almost totally wiped them out, but some survivors did escape to the fortified cities.

notes.text: Heb “When Joshua and the sons of Israel finished defeating them with a very great defeat until they were destroyed (now the survivors escaped to the fortified cities).” In the Hebrew text the initial temporal clause (“when Joshua…finished”) is subordinated to v. 21 (“the whole army returned”).

21.text: Then the whole army safely returned to Joshua at the camp in Makkedah. No one dared threaten the Israelites.

notes.text: Heb “all the people returned to the camp, to Joshua [at] Makkedah [in] peace.”
Heb “No man.” The lamed (‏ל‎) prefixed to ‏אִישׁ‎ (ʾish, “man”) is probably dittographic (note the immediately preceding ‏יִשְׂרָאֵל‎ [yisraʾel] which ends in lamed, ‏ל‎); cf. the LXX.

Heb “no man sharpened [or perhaps, “pointed”] his tongue against the sons of Israel.” Cf. NEB “not a man of the Israelites suffered so much as a scratch on his tongue,” which understands “sharpened” as “scratched” (referring to a minor wound). Most modern translations understand the Hebrew expression “sharpened his tongue” figuratively for opposition or threats against the Israelites.

22.text: Joshua said, “Open the cave’s mouth and bring the five kings out of the cave to me.”

notes.text: Heb “these five kings.”

23.text: They did as ordered; they brought the five kings out of the cave to him—the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon.

notes.text: Heb “they did so.”
Heb “these five kings.”

24.text: When they brought the kings out to Joshua, he summoned all the men of Israel and said to the commanders of the troops who accompanied him, “Come here and put your feet on the necks of these kings.” So they came up and put their feet on their necks.

notes.text: Heb “Joshua.” The translation has replaced the proper name with the pronoun (“he”) because a repetition of the proper name here would be redundant according to English style.
Or “Draw near.”
Or “drew near.”

25.text: Then Joshua said to them, “Don’t be afraid and don’t panic! Be strong and brave, for the Lord will do the same thing to all your enemies you fight.”

notes.text: Or perhaps “and don’t get discouraged!”

26.text: Then Joshua executed them and hung them on five trees. They were left hanging on the trees until evening.

notes.text: Heb “struck them down and killed them.”

27.text: At sunset Joshua ordered his men to take them down from the trees. They threw them into the cave where they had hidden and piled large stones over the mouth of the cave. (They remain to this very day.)

notes.text: For the legal background of the removal of the corpses before sundown, see Deut 21:22-23.
Heb “to this very day.” The words “They remain” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

28.text: That day Joshua captured Makkedah and put the sword to it and its king. He annihilated everyone who lived in it; he left no survivors. He did to its king what he had done to the king of Jericho.

29.text: Joshua and all Israel marched from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against it.

notes.text: Heb “Libnah.” Repetition of the proper name here would be redundant according to English style, so the pronoun (“it”) has been employed in the translation.

30.text: The Lord handed it and its king over to Israel, and Israel put the sword to all who lived there; they left no survivors. They did to its king what they had done to the king of Jericho.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the implied subject may be Israel, or Joshua (as the commanding general of the army).
Heb “he”; the implied subject may be Israel, or Joshua (as the commanding general of the army). So also for “They did to its king” and “they had done.”

31.text: Joshua and all Israel marched from Libnah to Lachish. He deployed his troops and fought against it.

notes.text: Heb “encamped against it.”

32.text: The Lord handed Lachish over to Israel, and they captured it on the second day. They put the sword to all who lived there, just as they had done to Libnah.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the implied subject may be Israel, or Joshua (as the commanding general of the army).

33.text: Then King Horam of Gezer came up to help Lachish, but Joshua struck him down, as well as his army, until no survivors remained.

notes.text: Heb “people.”

34.text: Joshua and all Israel marched from Lachish to Eglon. They deployed troops and fought against it.

notes.text: Heb “they encamped against it.”

35.text: That day they captured it and put the sword to all who lived there. That day they annihilated it just as they had done to Lachish.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the implied subject may be Israel, or Joshua (as the commanding general of the army). So also for “they had done to Lachish.”

36.text: Joshua and all Israel marched up from Eglon to Hebron and fought against it.

37.text: They captured it and put the sword to its king, all its surrounding cities, and all who lived in it; they left no survivors. As they had done at Eglon, they annihilated it and all who lived there.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the implied subject may be Israel, or Joshua (as the commanding general of the army). So also for “they had done” and “they annihilated.”

38.text: Joshua and all Israel turned to Debir and fought against it.

39.text: They captured it, its king, and all its surrounding cities and put the sword to them. They annihilated everyone who lived there; they left no survivors. They did to Debir and its king what they had done to Libnah and its king and to Hebron.

notes.text: Heb “He”; the implied subject may be Israel, or Joshua (as the commanding general of the army).
Heb “he”; the implied subject may be Israel, or Joshua (as the commanding general of the army). So also for “They did to Debir” and “they had done to Libnah.”
Heb “as he did to Hebron, so he did to Debir and its king, and as he did to Libnah and its king.” The clauses have been rearranged in the translation for stylistic reasons.

40.text: Joshua defeated the whole land, including the hill country, the Negev, the foothills, the slopes, and all their kings. He left no survivors. He annihilated everything that breathed, just as the Lord God of Israel had commanded.

notes.text: The Negev is an area of central southern Judah, south of the hill country and west of the rift valley. As a geographic feature it is a depression extending south to the Gulf of Aqabah, but the biblical reference is probably to the northern portion of the region.
The foothills (‏שְׁפֵלָה‎, shephelah) are the transition region from the hill country to the Mediterranean coastal plains.
In contrast to the foothills on the western side of the hill country, the slopes are on the eastern side leading down to the rift valley of the Dead Sea and Jordan river.

41.text: Joshua conquered the area between Kadesh Barnea and Gaza and the whole region of Goshen, all the way to Gibeon.

notes.text: Heb “and Joshua struck them down, from Kadesh Barnea even to Gaza, and all the land of Goshen, even to Gibeon.”

42.text: Joshua captured in one campaign all these kings and their lands, for the Lord God of Israel fought for Israel.

notes.text: Heb “at one time.”

43.text: Then Joshua and all Israel returned to the camp at Gilgal.

1.text: When King Jabin of Hazor heard the news about Israel’s victories, he organized a coalition, including King Jobab of Madon, the king of Shimron, the king of Acshaph,

notes.text: The words “about Israel’s victories” are not in the Hebrew text but have been supplied for clarity.
Heb “he sent to.”

2.text: and the northern kings who ruled in the hill country, in the rift valley south of Kinnereth, in the foothills, and on the heights of Dor to the west.

notes.text: Heb “and to the kings who [are] from the north in.”
Heb “Chinneroth,” a city and plain located in the territory of Naphtali in Galilee (BDB 490 s.v. ‏כִּנֶּרֶת‎, ‏כִּנֲרוֹת‎).

Kinnereth was a city in Galilee located near the Sea of Galilee (Deut 3:17). The surrounding region also became known by this name (1 Kgs 15:20; cf. Matt 14:34), and eventually even the lake itself (Josh 12:3; cf. Luke 5:1). The “rift valley south of” Galilee probably refers to the northern part of the Jordan Valley from the lake to where the Jezreel Valley joins the rift valley. Dor is nearly due west from that point.

3.text: Canaanites came from the east and west; Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, and Jebusites from the hill country; and Hivites from below Hermon in the area of Mizpah.

notes.text: The verb “came” is supplied in the translation (see v. 4).
Or “land.”

4.text: These kings came out with their armies; they were as numerous as the sand on the seashore and had a large number of horses and chariots.

notes.text: Heb “They and all their camps with them came out, a people as numerous as the sand which is on the edge of the sea in multitude, and [with] horses and chariots very numerous.”

5.text: All these kings gathered and joined forces at the Waters of Merom to fight Israel.

notes.text: Heb “and came and camped together.”

6.text: The Lord told Joshua, “Don’t be afraid of them, for about this time tomorrow I will cause all of them to lie dead before Israel. You must hamstring their horses and burn their chariots.”

notes.text: Heb “burn with fire”; the words “with fire” are redundant in English and have not been included in the translation.

7.text: Joshua and his whole army caught them by surprise at the Waters of Merom and attacked them.

notes.text: Heb “Joshua and all the people of war with him came upon them at the Waters of Merom suddenly and fell upon them.”

8.text: The Lord handed them over to Israel, and they struck them down and chased them all the way to Greater Sidon, Misrephoth Maim, and the Mizpah Valley to the east. They struck them down until no survivors remained.

notes.text: The meaning of the Hebrew name “Misrephoth Maim” is perhaps “lime-kilns by the water” (see HALOT 641 s.v. ‏מִשְׂרָפוֹת‎).

9.text: Joshua did to them as the Lord had commanded him; he hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots.

notes.text: Heb “burned with fire”; the words “with fire” are redundant in English and have not been included in the translation.

10.text: At that time Joshua turned, captured Hazor, and struck down its king with the sword, for Hazor was at that time the leader of all these kingdoms.

notes.text: Or “formerly.”

11.text: They annihilated everyone who lived there with the sword —no one who breathed remained—and burned Hazor.

notes.text: Heb “and they struck down all life which was in it with the edge of the sword, annihilating.”
Heb “burned with fire”; the words “with fire” are redundant in English and have not been included in the translation.

12.text: Joshua captured all these royal cities and all their kings and annihilated them with the sword, as Moses the Lord’s servant had commanded.

notes.text: Heb “and he struck them down with the edge of the sword, he annihilated them.”

13.text: But Israel did not burn any of the cities located on mounds except for Hazor; it was the only one Joshua burned.

notes.text: Heb “standing on their mounds.”

14.text: The Israelites plundered all the goods of these cities and the cattle, but they totally destroyed all the people and allowed no one who breathed to live.

notes.text: Heb “but all the people they struck down with the edge of the sword until they destroyed them.”

15.text: Moses the Lord’s servant passed on the Lord’s commands to Joshua, and Joshua did as he was told. He did not ignore any of the commands the Lord had given Moses.

notes.text: Heb “As the Lord commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and Joshua acted accordingly; he did not turn aside a thing from all which the Lord commanded Moses.”

16.text: Joshua conquered the whole land, including the hill country, all the Negev, all the land of Goshen, the foothills, the rift valley, the hill country of Israel and its foothills,

notes.text: Heb “Joshua took all this land.”

The Negev is an area south of the Judean hill country and west of the rift valley. As a geographic feature it is an arid depression extending south to the Gulf of Aqabah, but the biblical reference is probably to the northern part of this region.
The foothills (‏שְׁפֵלָה‎, “shephelah”) refer to the transition region between the Judean hill country and the Mediterranean coastal plain.

As a geographic feature, the rift valley (‏עֲרָבָה‎, ʿaravah) extends from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba. The reference here is probably to the Jordan Valley and the wider part of the rift valley below the Dead Sea.

17.text: from Mount Halak up to Seir, as far as Baal Gad in the Lebanon Valley below Mount Hermon. He captured all their kings and executed them.

notes.text: Heb “and struck them down and killed them.”

18.text: Joshua campaigned against these kings for quite some time.

notes.text: Heb “made war with.”
Heb “for many days.”

19.text: No city made peace with the Israelites (except the Hivites living in Gibeon); they had to conquer all of them,

notes.text: The LXX omits this parenthetical note, which may represent a later scribal addition.
Heb “the whole they took in battle.”

20.text: for the Lord determined to make them obstinate so they would attack Israel. He wanted Israel to annihilate them without mercy, as he had instructed Moses.

notes.text: Heb “for from the Lord it was to harden their heart[s] to meet for the battle with Israel, in order to annihilate them, so that they would receive no mercy, in order annihilate them, as the Lord commanded Moses.”

21.text: At that time Joshua attacked and eliminated the Anakites from the hill country —from Hebron, Debir, Anab, and all the hill country of Judah and Israel. Joshua annihilated them and their cities.

notes.text: Heb “went and cut off the Anakites from the hill country.”
Heb “and from all the hill country of Israel.”

22.text: No Anakites were left in Israelite territory, though some remained in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod.

23.text: Joshua conquered the whole land, just as the Lord had promised Moses, and he assigned Israel their tribal portions. Then the land was free of war.

notes.text: Heb “took.”

Heb “according to all which the Lord said to Moses.” The translation assumes this refers to the promise of the land (see 1:3). Another possibility is that it refers to the Lord’s instructions, in which case the phrase could be translated, “just as the Lord had instructed Moses” (so NLT; cf. also NIV “had directed Moses”).
Heb “and Joshua gave it for an inheritance to Israel according to their allotted portions by their tribes.”

1.text: Now these are the kings of the land whom the Israelites defeated and drove from their land on the east side of the Jordan, from the Arnon Valley to Mount Hermon, including all the eastern rift valley:

notes.text: Heb “and took possession of their land.”
Heb “beyond the Jordan, toward the rising of the sun.”

The rift valley is a geographic feature that extends from Mt. Hermon to the Gulf of Aqaba and includes the Sea of Galilee, the Jordan River, and the Dead Sea. The section described here extends from the border of Moab, the Arnon which runs into the middle of the Dead Sea, northward up the entire Jordan valley and beyond Galilee to Mt. Hermon at the border of Lebanon.

2.text: King Sihon of the Amorites who lived in Heshbon and ruled from Aroer (on the edge of the Arnon Valley)—including the city in the middle of the valley and half of Gilead—all the way to the Jabbok Valley bordering Ammonite territory.

notes.text: Or perhaps, “reigned.”
The MT reads here “and the middle of the valley,” but the reading “the city in the middle of valley” can be reconstructed on the basis of Josh 13:9, 16.

3.text: His kingdom included the eastern rift valley from the Sea of Kinnereth to the sea of the rift valley (the Salt Sea), including the route to Beth Jeshimoth and the area southward below the slopes of Pisgah.

notes.text: The words “his kingdom included” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
The Sea of Kinnereth is another name for the Sea of Galilee. See the note on the word “Kinnereth” in 11:2.
The Salt Sea is another name for the Dead Sea.
The slopes of Pisgah lie east of the northern tip of the Dead Sea.

4.text: The territory of King Og of Bashan, one of the few remaining Rephaites, who lived in Ashtaroth and Edrei

notes.text: Heb “from the remnant of the Rephaites.”
The Rephaites were apparently an extremely tall ethnic group. See Deut 2:10-11, 20; 3:11.
Or perhaps “who reigned.”

5.text: and ruled over Mount Hermon, Salecah, all Bashan to the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and half of Gilead as far as the border of King Sihon of Heshbon.

6.text: Moses the Lord’s servant and the Israelites defeated them and Moses the Lord’s servant assigned their land to Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.

notes.text: Heb “gave it for a possession.”

7.text: These are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the Israelites defeated on the west side of the Jordan, from Baal Gad in the Lebanon Valley to Mount Halak up to Seir. Joshua assigned this territory to the Israelite tribes,

notes.text: Heb “Joshua gave it to the tribes of Israel as a possession according to their allotted portions.”

8.text: including the hill country, the foothills, the rift valley, the slopes, the wilderness, and the Negev —the land of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites:

notes.text: The foothills (‏שְׁפֵלָה‎, shephelah) are the transition region between the Judean hill country and the Mediterranean coastal plain. These are areas of eocene limestone with a distinct pattern of erosion, soil, and vegetation cover.

The rift valley (‏עֲרָבָה‎, ʿaravah) is a geographic feature extending from Galilee to the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba. Here it probably refers to the Jordan valley and an area extending south of the Dead Sea by the Negev.
The slopes (‏אֲשֵׁדוֹת‎, ʾashedot) refer to the ascent from the rift valley up to the hill country and to the flatlands (or wilderness) south of the hill country.

The Negev is the area of central southern Judah, south of the hill country and west of the rift valley. As a geographic feature it is a depression extending south to the Gulf of Aqaba, but the biblical reference is probably to the northern portion of the region.
The words “the land of” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

9.text: the king of Jericho (one), the king of Ai—located near Bethel—(one),

10.text: the king of Jerusalem (one), the king of Hebron (one),

11.text: the king of Jarmuth (one), the king of Lachish (one),

12.text: the king of Eglon (one), the king of Gezer (one),

13.text: the king of Debir (one), the king of Geder (one),

14.text: the king of Hormah (one), the king of Arad (one),

15.text: the king of Libnah (one), the king of Adullam (one),

16.text: the king of Makkedah (one), the king of Bethel (one),

17.text: the king of Tappuah (one), the king of Hepher (one),

18.text: the king of Aphek (one), the king of Lasharon (one),

19.text: the king of Madon (one), the king of Hazor (one),

20.text: the king of Shimron Meron (one), the king of Acshaph (one),

21.text: the king of Taanach (one), the king of Megiddo (one),

22.text: the king of Kedesh (one), the king of Jokneam near Carmel (one),

23.text: the king of Dor—near Naphath Dor—(one), the king of Goyim—near Gilgal—(one),

24.text: the king of Tirzah (one), a total of thirty-one kings.

1.text: When Joshua was very old, the Lord told him, “You are very old, and a great deal of land remains to be conquered.

notes.text: Heb “was old, coming into the days.” This expression, referring to advancing in years, also occurs in the following clause.

2.text: This is the land that remains: all the territory of the Philistines and all the Geshurites,

3.text: from the Shihor River east of Egypt northward to the territory of Ekron (it is regarded as Canaanite territory), including the area belonging to the five Philistine lords who ruled in Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron, as well as Avvite land

notes.text: Heb “the Shihor”; the word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied to clarify the meaning.
Heb “in front of.”
Heb “it is reckoned to the Canaanites.”
Heb “the five lords of the Philistines, the Gazaite, the Ashdodite, the Ashkelonite, the Gathite, and the Ekronite, and the Avvites.”

4.text: to the south; all the Canaanite territory, from Arah in the region of Sidon to Aphek, as far as Amorite territory;

notes.text: Or “from Teman.” The phrase is especially problematic if taken with what follows, as the traditional verse division suggests. For further discussion see T. C. Butler, Joshua (WBC), 146.
Heb “all the land of the Canaanites.”
The reading “Arah” assumes a slight emendation of the Hebrew vowel pointing. The MT reads, “and a cave,” or “and Mearah” (if one understands the word as a proper noun).
Heb “which belongs to the Sidonians.”

5.text: the territory of Byblos and all Lebanon to the east, from Baal Gad below Mount Hermon to Lebo Hamath.

notes.text: Heb “and the land of the Gebalites.”

Or “the entrance to Hamath.” Most modern translations take the phrase “Lebo Hamath” to be a proper name, but often provide a note with the alternative, where “Hamath” is the proper name and ‏לְבוֹא‎ (levoʾ) is taken to mean “entrance to.”

6.text: I will drive out before the Israelites all who live in the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth Maim, all the Sidonians; you be sure to parcel it out to Israel as I instructed you.

notes.text: The meaning of the Hebrew name “Misrephoth Maim” is perhaps “lime-kilns by the water” (see HALOT 641 s.v. ‏מִשְׂרָפוֹת‎).
Heb “only you, assign it by lots to Israel as an inheritance as I commanded you.”

7.text: Now, divide up this land among the nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh.”

notes.text: Heb “now apportion this land as an inheritance.”

8.text: The other half of Manasseh, Reuben, and Gad received their allotted tribal lands on east side of the Jordan, just as Moses, the Lord’s servant, had assigned them.

notes.text: The MT reads “with him,” which is problematic, since the reference would be to the other half of the tribe of Manasseh (not the half mentioned in v. 7).
