Heb “received their inheritance, which Moses had assigned to them beyond the Jordan to the east.”

9.text: Their territory started from Aroer (on the edge of the Arnon Valley), included the city in the middle of the valley, the whole plain of Medeba as far as Dibon,

notes.text: The words “their territory started” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

10.text: and all the cities of King Sihon of the Amorites who ruled in Heshbon, and ended at the Ammonite border.

11.text: Their territory also included Gilead, Geshurite and Maacathite territory, all Mount Hermon, and all Bashan to Salecah—

notes.text: The words “their territory also included” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

12.text: the whole kingdom of Og in Bashan, who ruled in Ashtaroth and Edrei. (He was one of the few remaining Rephaites.) Moses defeated them and took their lands.

notes.text: Heb “from the remnant of the Rephaites.”
The Rephaites were apparently an extremely tall ethnic group. See Deut 2:10-11, 20; 3:11.
Or “dispossessed them.”

13.text: But the Israelites did not conquer the Geshurites and Maacathites; Geshur and Maacah live among Israel to this very day.

notes.text: Or “dispossess.”

14.text: However, Moses did not assign land as an inheritance to the Levites; their inheritance is the sacrificial offerings made to the Lord God of Israel, as he instructed them.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Moses) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “did not assign an inheritance.”
That is, “their source of food and life.”
Or “offerings made by fire.”
Or “promised” (Heb “spoke”).
For the background of this observation, see Deut 18:1-2.

15.text: Moses assigned land to the tribe of Reuben by its clans.

notes.text: Heb “assigned to the sons of Reuben.”

16.text: Their territory started at Aroer (on the edge of the Arnon Valley) and included the city in the middle of the valley, the whole plain of Medeba,

notes.text: Heb “their territory was from.”

17.text: Heshbon and all its surrounding cities on the plain, including Dibon, Bamoth Baal, Beth Baal Meon,

18.text: Jahaz, Kedemoth, Mephaath,

19.text: Kiriathaim, Sibmah, Zereth Shahar on the hill in the valley,

20.text: Beth Peor, the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth Jeshimoth.

21.text: It encompassed all the cities of the plain and the whole realm of King Sihon of the Amorites who ruled in Heshbon. Moses defeated him and the Midianite leaders Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba (they were subjects of Sihon and lived in his territory).

notes.text: The words “it encompassed” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “princes of Sihon, inhabitants of the land.”

22.text: The Israelites killed Balaam son of Beor, the omen reader, along with the others.

notes.text: Or “diviner.”
Heb “Balaam son of Beor, the omen-reader, the Israelites killed with the sword, along with their slain ones.”

23.text: The border of the tribe of Reuben was the Jordan. The land allotted to the tribe of Reuben by its clans included these cities and their towns.

notes.text: Heb “This is the inheritance of the sons of Reuben by their clans, the cities and their towns.”

24.text: Moses assigned land to the tribe of Gad by its clans.

notes.text: Heb “assigned to the tribe of Gad, to the sons of Gad.”

25.text: Their territory included Jazer, all the cities of Gilead, and half the Ammonite territory as far as Aroer near Rabbah.

notes.text: Heb “and half of the land of the sons of Ammon.”
Heb “which [is] in front of.”

26.text: Their territory ran from Heshbon to Ramath Mizpah and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the territory of Debir.

notes.text: The words “Their territory ran” are not in the Hebrew text, but have been supplied for clarification.

27.text: It included the valley of Beth Haram, Beth Nimrah, Sukkoth, and Zaphon, and the rest of the realm of King Sihon of Heshbon, the area east of the Jordan to the end of the Sea of Kinnereth.

notes.text: Or “it included in the valley, Beth Haram.”
The Sea of Kinnereth is another name for the Sea of Galilee. See the note on the word “Kinnereth” in 11:2.

28.text: The land allotted to the tribe of Gad by its clans included these cities and their towns.

notes.text: Heb “This is the inheritance of the sons of Gad by their clans, the cities and their towns.”

29.text: Moses assigned land to the half-tribe of Manasseh by its clans.

notes.text: Heb “assigned to the half-tribe of Manasseh, and it belonged to the half-tribe of Manasseh.”

30.text: Their territory started at Mahanaim and encompassed all Bashan, the whole realm of King Og of Bashan, including all sixty cities in Havvoth Jair in Bashan.

notes.text: The words “their territory started at” are not in the Hebrew text, but have been supplied for clarification.
The Hebrew name Havvoth Jair means “the tent villages of Jair.”

31.text: Half of Gilead, Ashtaroth, and Edrei, cities in the kingdom of Og in Bashan, were assigned to the descendants of Makir son of Manasseh, to half the descendants of Makir by their clans.

32.text: These are the land assignments made by Moses in the rift valley plains of Moab east of the Jordan River opposite Jericho.

notes.text: Heb “These are [the lands] which Moses gave as an inheritance.”

This is the area of rift valley basin to the north of the Dead Sea and east of the Jordan. Some translate as the “plains of Moab” (NASB, NIV, ESV) but this can give the wrong impression of the larger part of Moab above the rift valley. See the note at Num 22:1.
Heb “beyond the Jordan, east of Jericho.” The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied to clarify the meaning.

33.text: However, Moses did not assign land as an inheritance to the Levites; their inheritance is the Lord God of Israel, as he instructed them.

notes.text: Heb “Moses did not assign an inheritance.” The word “land” has been supplied in the translation to clarify what the inheritance consisted of.
That is, “their source of food and life.”
Or “as he promised”; Heb “as he spoke to.”
For the background of this observation, see Deut 18:1-2.

1.text: The following is a record of the territory assigned to the Israelites in the land of Canaan by Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the Israelite tribal leaders.

notes.text: Heb “These are [the lands] which the sons of Israel received as an inheritance in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the fathers of the tribes assigned as an inheritance to the sons of Israel.”

2.text: The land assignments to the nine-and-a-half tribes were made by drawing lots, as the Lord had instructed Moses.

notes.text: Heb “By lot was their inheritance, as the Lord had commanded by Moses, to the nine tribes and the half-tribe.”

3.text: Now Moses had assigned land to the two-and-a-half tribes east of the Jordan, but he assigned no land to the Levites.

notes.text: Or “assigned an inheritance.”
Or “no inheritance.”
The Hebrew text adds, “in their midst.”

4.text: The descendants of Joseph were considered as two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. The Levites were allotted no territory, though they were assigned cities in which to live, along with the grazing areas for their cattle and possessions.

notes.text: Heb “and they did not assign a portion to the Levites in the land, except cities [in which] to live and their pastures for their cattle and property.”

5.text: The Israelites followed the Lord’s instructions to Moses and divided up the land.

notes.text: Heb “Just as the Lord had commanded Moses, so the sons of Israel did, and they divided up the land.”

6.text: The men of Judah approached Joshua in Gilgal, and Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said to him, “You know what the Lord said about you and me to Moses, the man of God, at Kadesh Barnea.

notes.text: Heb “You know the word which the Lord spoke to Moses, the man of God, because of me and because of you in Kadesh Barnea.”
On this incident at Kadesh Barnea see Num 14:30.

7.text: I was forty years old when Moses, the Lord’s servant, sent me from Kadesh Barnea to spy on the land and I brought back to him an honest report.

notes.text: Heb “and I brought back to him a word just as [was] in my heart.”

8.text: My countrymen who accompanied me frightened the people, but I remained loyal to the Lord my God.

notes.text: Heb “brothers.”
Heb “went up with.”
Heb “made the heart[s] of the people melt.”
Heb “I filled up after the Lord my God,” an idiomatic statement meaning that Caleb remained loyal to the Lord.

9.text: That day Moses made this solemn promise: ‘Surely the land on which you walked will belong to you and your descendants permanently, for you remained loyal to the Lord your God.’

notes.text: Heb “swore an oath.”
Heb “on which your foot has walked.”
Heb “will belong to you for an inheritance, and to your sons forever.”

10.text: So now, look, the Lord has preserved my life, just as he promised, these past forty-five years since the Lord spoke these words to Moses, while Israel traveled through the wilderness. See here, I am today eighty-five years old!

11.text: Today I am still as strong as when Moses sent me out. I can fight and go about my daily activities with the same energy I had then.

notes.text: Heb “like my strength then, like my strength now, for battle and for going out and coming in.”

12.text: Now, assign me this hill country that the Lord promised me at that time! No doubt you heard then that the Anakites live there in large, fortified cities. But assuming the Lord is with me, I will conquer them, as the Lord promised.”

notes.text: Heb “are there and large, fortified cities.”
Or “will dispossess.”

13.text: Joshua asked God to empower Caleb son of Jephunneh and assigned him Hebron.

notes.text: Heb “Joshua blessed him and gave Hebron to Caleb son of Jephunneh as an inheritance.”

14.text: So Hebron remains the assigned land of Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite to this very day because he remained loyal to the Lord God of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “Therefore Hebron belongs to Caleb son of Jephunneh for an inheritance to this day.”

15.text: (Hebron used to be called Kiriath Arba. Arba was a famous Anakite.) Then the land was free of war.

notes.text: Heb “And he was the great man among the Anakites.”

1.text: The land allotted to the tribe of Judah by its clans reached to the border of Edom, to the wilderness of Zin in the Negev far to the south.

notes.text: Heb “The lot was to the tribe of the sons of Judah by their clans to the border of Edom, the wilderness of Zin toward the south, southward.”

2.text: Their southern border started at the southern tip of the Salt Sea,

notes.text: Heb “Their southern border was from the end of the Salt Sea, from the tongue that faces to the south.”
The Salt Sea is another name for the Dead Sea (also in v. 5).

3.text: extended south of the Scorpion Ascent, crossed to Zin, went up from the south to Kadesh Barnea, crossed to Hezron, went up to Addar, and turned toward Karka.

notes.text: Heb “went out.”
Or “the Ascent of Akrabbim” (‏עַקְרַבִּים‎ [ʿaqrabbim] means “scorpions” in Hebrew).

4.text: It then crossed to Azmon, extended to the Stream of Egypt, and ended at the Mediterranean Sea. This was their southern border.

notes.text: Traditionally “the Brook of Egypt,” although a number of recent translations have “the Wadi of Egypt” (cf. NAB, NIV, NRSV).
The translation follows the LXX at this point. The MT reads, “This will be your southern border.”

5.text: The eastern border was the Salt Sea to the mouth of the Jordan River. The northern border started north of the Salt Sea at the mouth of the Jordan,

notes.text: Heb “end.”
The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied for clarity.
Heb “the border on the northern side was from the tongue of the sea, from the end of the Jordan.”

6.text: went up to Beth Hoglah, crossed north of Beth Arabah, and went up to the Stone of Bohan son of Reuben.

7.text: It then went up to Debir from the Valley of Achor, turning northward to Gilgal (which is opposite the Pass of Adummim south of the valley), crossed to the waters of En Shemesh and extended to En Rogel.

notes.text: Or “ascent.”

8.text: It then went up the Valley of Ben Hinnom to the slope of the Jebusites on the south (that is, Jerusalem), going up to the top of the hill opposite the Valley of Ben Hinnom to the west, which is at the end of the Valley of the Rephaites to the north.

9.text: It then went from the top of the hill to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah, extended to the cities of Mount Ephron, and went to Baalah (that is, Kiriath Jearim).

10.text: It then turned from Baalah westward to Mount Seir, crossed to the slope of Mount Jearim on the north (that is Kesalon), descended to Beth Shemesh, and crossed to Timnah.

11.text: It then extended to the slope of Ekron to the north, went toward Shikkeron, crossed to Mount Baalah, extended to Jabneel, and ended at the sea.

12.text: The western border was the Mediterranean Sea. These were the borders of the tribe of Judah and its clans.

notes.text: Heb “the Great Sea,” the typical designation for the Mediterranean Sea.
Heb “this was the border of the sons of Judah round about, by their clans.”

13.text: Caleb son of Jephunneh was assigned Kiriath Arba (that is Hebron) within the tribe of Judah, according to the Lord’s instructions to Joshua. (Arba was the father of Anak.)

notes.text: Heb “To Caleb son of Jephunneh he gave a portion in the midst of the sons of Judah according to the mouth [i.e., command] of the Lord to Joshua, Kiriath Arba (the father of Anak), it is Hebron.”

14.text: Caleb drove out from there three Anakites—Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, descendants of Anak.

notes.text: Or “dispossessed.”

15.text: From there he attacked the people of Debir. (Debir used to be called Kiriath Sepher.)

notes.text: Heb “he went up against the inhabitants of Debir.”

16.text: Caleb said, “To the man who attacks and captures Kiriath Sepher I will give my daughter Achsah as a wife.”

17.text: When Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s brother, captured it, Caleb gave Achsah his daughter to him as a wife.

notes.text: “Caleb’s brother” may refer either to Othniel or to Kenaz. If Kenaz was the brother of Caleb, Othniel is Caleb’s nephew.
Heb “he”; the referent (Caleb) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

18.text: One time Achsah came and charmed her father so that she could ask him for some land. When she got down from her donkey, Caleb said to her, “What would you like?”

notes.text: Heb “she”; the referent (Achsah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Heb “him.” The referent of the pronoun could be Othniel, in which case the translation would be “she incited him [Othniel] to ask her father for a field.” This is problematic, however, for Achsah, not Othniel, makes the request in v. 19. The LXX has “he [Othniel] urged her to ask her father for a field.” This appears to be an attempt to reconcile the apparent inconsistency and probably does not reflect the original text. If Caleb is understood as the referent of the pronoun, the problem disappears. For a fuller discussion of the issue, see P. G. Mosca, “Who Seduced Whom? A Note on Joshua 15:18//Judges 1:14, ” CBQ 46 (1984): 18-22. This incident is also recorded in Judg 1:14.

19.text: She answered, “Please give me a special present. Since you have given me land in the Negev, now give me springs of water.” So he gave her both the upper and lower springs.

notes.text: Elsewhere this Hebrew word (‏בְּרָכָה‎, berakhah) is often translated “blessing,” but here it refers to a gift (as in Gen 33:11; 1 Sam 25:27; 30:26; 2 Kgs 5:15).

20.text: This is the land assigned to the tribe of Judah by its clans:

notes.text: Heb “This is the inheritance of the tribe of the sons of Judah by their clans.”

21.text: These cities were located at the southern extremity of Judah’s tribal land near the border of Edom: Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur,

notes.text: Heb “and the cities were at the end of the tribe of the sons of Judah, at the border of Edom, to the south.”

22.text: Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah,

23.text: Kedesh, Hazor, Ithnan,

24.text: Ziph, Telem, Bealoth,

25.text: Hazor Hadattah, Kerioth Hezron (that is, Hazor),

26.text: Amam, Shema, Moladah,

27.text: Hazar Gaddah, Heshbon, Beth Pelet,

28.text: Hazar Shual, Beer Sheba, Biziothiah,

29.text: Baalah, Iim, Ezem,

30.text: Eltolad, Kesil, Hormah,

31.text: Ziklag, Madmannah, Sansannah,

32.text: Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon—a total of twenty-nine cities and their towns.

notes.text: The total number of names in the list is thirty-six, not twenty-nine. Perhaps (1) some of the names are alternatives (though the text appears to delineate clearly such alternative names here and elsewhere, see vv. 8, 9, 10, 13, 25b) or (2), more likely, later scribes added to a list originally numbering twenty-nine and failed to harmonize the concluding summary statement with the expanded list.

33.text: These cities were in the foothills: Eshtaol, Zorah, Ashnah,

notes.text: The words “these cities were” have been supplied for English stylistic reasons.
The foothills (‏שְׁפֵלָה‎, shephelah) are the region between the Judean hill country and the Mediterranean coastal plain.

34.text: Zanoah, En Gannim, Tappuah, Enam,

35.text: Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, Azekah,

36.text: Shaaraim, Adithaim, and Gederah (or Gederothaim)—a total of fourteen cities and their towns.

37.text: Zenan, Hadashah, Migdal Gad,

38.text: Dilean, Mizpah, Joktheel,

39.text: Lachish, Bozkath, Eglon,

40.text: Cabbon, Lahmas, Kitlish,

41.text: Gederoth, Beth Dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah—a total of sixteen cities and their towns.

42.text: Libnah, Ether, Ashan,

43.text: Iphtah, Ashnah, Nezib,

44.text: Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah—a total of nine cities and their towns.

45.text: Ekron and its surrounding towns and settlements;

notes.text: Heb “daughters.”

46.text: from Ekron westward, all those in the vicinity of Ashdod and their towns;

47.text: Ashdod with its surrounding towns and settlements, and Gaza with its surrounding towns and settlements, as far as the Stream of Egypt and the border at the Mediterranean Sea.

notes.text: See the note on this place name in 15:4.
Heb “the Great Sea,” the typical designation for the Mediterranean Sea.

48.text: These cities were in the hill country: Shamir, Jattir, Socoh,

notes.text: The words “These cities were” have been supplied in the translation for English stylistic reasons.

49.text: Dannah, Kiriath Sannah (that is, Debir),

50.text: Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim,

51.text: Goshen, Holon, and Giloh—a total of eleven cities and their towns.

52.text: Arab, Dumah, Eshan,

notes.text: Some Hebrew mss and some mss of the LXX read “Rumah” in place of “Dumah.”

53.text: Janim, Beth Tappuah, Aphekah,

54.text: Humtah, Kiriath Arba (that is, Hebron), and Zior—a total of nine cities and their towns.

55.text: Maon, Carmel, Ziph, Juttah,

56.text: Jezreel, Jokdeam, Zanoah,

57.text: Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah—a total of ten cities and their towns.

58.text: Halhul, Beth Zur, Gedor,

59.text: Maarath, Beth Anoth, and Eltekon—a total of six cities and their towns.

60.text: Kiriath Baal (that is, Kiriath Jearim) and Rabbah—a total of two cities and their towns.

61.text: These cities were in the wilderness: Beth Arabah, Middin, Secacah,

notes.text: The words “These cities were” have been supplied for English stylistic reasons.

62.text: Nibshan, the City of Salt, and En Gedi—a total of six cities and their towns.

63.text: The men of Judah were unable to conquer the Jebusites living in Jerusalem. The Jebusites live with the people of Judah in Jerusalem to this very day.

notes.text: The statement to this very day reflects the perspective of the author, who must have written prior to David’s conquest of the Jebusites (see 2 Sam 5:6-7).

1.text: The land allotted to Joseph’s descendants extended from the Jordan at Jericho to the waters of Jericho to the east, through the desert and on up from Jericho into the hill country of Bethel.

notes.text: Heb “The lot went out to the sons of Joseph from the Jordan [at] Jericho to the waters of Jericho to the east, the desert going up from Jericho into the hill country of Bethel.”

2.text: The southern border extended from Bethel to Luz, and crossed to Arkite territory at Ataroth.

notes.text: Heb “it”; the referent (the southern border) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

In the Hebrew text the place name “Luz” has the directive ending, indicating that the border went from Bethel to Luz. Elsewhere Luz and Bethel appear to be names for the same site (cf. Judg 1:23), but here they appear to be distinct. Note that the NIV translates “from Bethel (that is, Luz)” here, following the reading of the LXX, εἰς Βαιθηλ Λουζα (eis Baithēl Louza, “from Bethel [Luz]”).

3.text: It then descended westward to Japhletite territory, as far as the territory of lower Beth Horon and Gezer, and ended at the sea.

4.text: Joseph’s descendants, Manasseh and Ephraim, were assigned their land.

notes.text: Or “received their inheritance.”

5.text: The territory of the tribe of Ephraim by its clans included the following: The border of their assigned land to the east was Ataroth Addar as far as upper Beth Horon.

notes.text: Heb “The territory of the sons of Ephraim was for their clans.”

6.text: It then extended on to the sea, with Micmethath on the north. It turned eastward to Taanath Shiloh and crossed it on the east to Janoah.

7.text: It then descended from Janoah to Ataroth and Naarah, touched Jericho, and extended to the Jordan River.

notes.text: The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

8.text: From Tappuah it went westward to the Valley of Kanah and ended at the sea. This is the land assigned to the tribe of Ephraim by its clans.

notes.text: Heb “This is the inheritance of the tribe of the sons of Ephraim.”

9.text: Also included were the cities set apart for the tribe of Ephraim within Manasseh’s territory, along with their towns.

notes.text: Heb “and the cities set apart for the sons of Ephraim in the midst of the inheritance of the sons of Manasseh, all the cities and their towns.”

10.text: The Ephraimites did not conquer the Canaanites living in Gezer. The Canaanites live among the Ephraimites to this very day and do hard labor as their servants.

notes.text: Heb “they”; the referent (the Ephraimites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

1.text: The tribe of Manasseh, Joseph’s firstborn son, was also allotted land. The descendants of Makir, Manasseh’s firstborn and the father of Gilead, received land, for they were warriors. They were assigned Gilead and Bashan.

notes.text: Heb “and the lot belonged to the tribe of Manasseh, for he was the firstborn of Joseph.”
Heb “to Makir, the firstborn of Manasseh, the father of Gilead, for he was a man of war.”
Heb “Gilead and Bashan belonged to him.”
On the assignment of Manasseh’s territory in Gilead and Bashan, see Josh 13:31.

2.text: The rest of Manasseh’s descendants were also assigned land by their clans, including the descendants of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida. These are the male descendants of Manasseh son of Joseph by their clans.

notes.text: Heb “and it belonged to the sons of Manasseh who remained.”

3.text: Now Zelophehad son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Makir, son of Manasseh, had no sons, only daughters. These are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.

4.text: They went before Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the leaders and said, “The Lord told Moses to assign us land among our relatives.” So Joshua assigned them land among their uncles, as the Lord had commanded.

notes.text: Heb “The Lord commanded Moses to assign to us an inheritance in the midst of our brothers.” Since Zelophehad had no sons, “brothers” must refer to their uncles, as the next sentence makes clear.
Heb “he.” The referent is probably Joshua, although Eleazar is mentioned first in the preceding list.
Heb “and he assigned to them in accordance with the mouth [i.e., command] of the Lord an inheritance in the midst of the brothers of their father.”

5.text: Manasseh was allotted ten shares of land, in addition to the land of Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan,

notes.text: Heb “and the allotted portions of Manasseh fell out ten.”

6.text: for the daughters of Manasseh were assigned land among his sons. The land of Gilead belonged to the rest of the descendants of Manasseh.

7.text: The border of Manasseh went from Asher to Micmethath, which is near Shechem. It then went south toward those who live by En Tappuah.

notes.text: Heb “was.”
Heb “in front of”; perhaps “east of.”
Or “the spring of Tappuah.”

8.text: (The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but Tappuah, located on the border of Manasseh, belonged to the tribe of Ephraim.)

9.text: The border then descended southward to the Valley of Kanah. Ephraim was assigned cities there among the cities of Manasseh, but the border of Manasseh was north of the valley and ended at the sea.

notes.text: Heb “these cities belonged to Ephraim in the midst of the cities of Manasseh.”

10.text: Ephraim’s territory was to the south, and Manasseh’s to the north. The sea was Manasseh’s western border and their territory touched Asher on the north and Issachar on the east.

notes.text: Heb “his”; the referent (Manasseh) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “they”; the referent (their territory) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

11.text: Within Issachar’s and Asher’s territories Manasseh was assigned Beth Shean, Ibleam, the residents of Dor, the residents of Endor, the residents of Taanach, the residents of Megiddo, the three of Napheth, and the towns surrounding all these cities.

notes.text: Or “the third [is] Napheth”; or “Napheth-dor.” The meaning of the Hebrew phrase is uncertain.

Heb “Beth Shean and its surrounding towns, Ibleam and its surrounding towns, the residents of Dor and its surrounding towns, the residents of Endor and its surrounding towns, the residents of Taanach and its surrounding towns, the residents of Megiddo and its surrounding towns, three of Nepheth.”

12.text: But the men of Manasseh were unable to conquer these cities; the Canaanites managed to remain in those areas.

notes.text: Heb “sons”; “men” has been used in the translation because the context involves the conquest of cities; therefore, warriors (hence males) would be in view here.
Or “were determined.”

13.text: Whenever the Israelites were strong militarily, they forced the Canaanites to do hard labor, but they never totally conquered them.

notes.text: On the Israelites’ failure to conquer the Canaanites completely, see Judg 1:27-28.

14.text: The descendants of Joseph said to Joshua, “Why have you assigned us only one tribal allotment? After all, we have many people, for until now the Lord has enabled us to increase in number.”

notes.text: Heb “Why have you given me as an inheritance one lot and one portion, though I am a great people until [the time] which, until now the Lord has blessed me?” The construction ‏עַד אֲשֶׁר־עַד־כֹּה‎ (ʿad ʾasher ʿad koh, “until [the time] which, until now”) is extremely awkward. An emendation of the first ‏עַד‎ (ʿad) to ‏עַל‎ (ʿal) yields a more likely reading: “for until now” (see HALOT 787 s.v. III ‏עַד‎).

15.text: Joshua replied to them, “Since you have so many people, go up into the forest and clear out a place to live in the land of the Perizzites and Rephaites, if the hill country of Ephraim is too small for you.”

notes.text: Heb “If you are a great people.”

16.text: The descendants of Joseph said, “The whole hill country is inadequate for us, and the Canaanites living down in the valley in Beth Shean and its surrounding towns and in the Valley of Jezreel have chariots with iron-rimmed wheels.”

notes.text: The Hebrew text has simply “the hill country,” which must here include the hill country of Ephraim and the forest regions mentioned in v. 15.

Heb “and there are iron chariots among all the Canaanites who live in the land of the valley, to those who are in Beth Shean and its daughters and to those who are in the Valley of Jezreel.” Regarding the translation “chariots with iron-rimmed wheels” see Y. Yadin, The Art of Warfare in Biblical Lands, 255 and R. Drews, “The ‘Chariots of Iron’ of Joshua and Judges,” JSOT 45 (1989): 15-23.

17.text: Joshua said to the family of Joseph—to both Ephraim and Manasseh: “You have many people and great military strength. You will not have just one tribal allotment.

notes.text: Heb “house.”

18.text: The whole hill country will be yours; though it is a forest, you can clear it, and it will be entirely yours. You can conquer the Canaanites, though they have chariots with iron-rimmed wheels and are strong.”

notes.text: The Hebrew text has simply “the hill country,” which must here include the hill country of Ephraim and the forest regions mentioned in v. 15.
Heb “and its limits will be yours.”

1.text: The entire Israelite community assembled at Shiloh and there they set up the tent of meeting. Though they had subdued the land,

notes.text: Heb “the tent of assembly.”
On the tent of meeting see Exod 33:7-11.
Heb “and the land was subdued before them.”

2.text: seven Israelite tribes had not been assigned their allotted land.

notes.text: Heb “there were left among the sons of Israel who had not divided up their inheritance seven tribes.”

3.text: So Joshua said to the Israelites: “How long do you intend to put off occupying the land the Lord God of your ancestors has given you?

notes.text: Heb “How long are you putting off entering and possessing.”
Or “fathers.”

4.text: Pick three men from each tribe. I will send them out to walk through the land and make a map of it for me.

notes.text: Heb “I will send them so they may arise and walk about in the land and describe it in writing according to their inheritance and come to me.”

5.text: Divide it into seven regions. Judah will stay in its territory in the south, and the family of Joseph in its territory in the north.

notes.text: Heb “portions.”
Heb “stand.”
Heb “the house.”

6.text: But as for you, map out the land into seven regions and bring it to me. I will draw lots for you here before the Lord our God.

7.text: But the Levites will not have an allotted portion among you, for their inheritance is to serve the Lord. Gad, Reuben, and the half-tribe of Manasseh have already received their allotted land east of the Jordan, which Moses the Lord’s servant assigned them.”

notes.text: Or “the priesthood of the Lord.”
Or “inheritance.”

8.text: When the men started out, Joshua told those going to map out the land, “Go, walk through the land, map it out, and return to me. Then I will draw lots for you before the Lord here in Shiloh.”

9.text: The men journeyed through the land and mapped it and its cities out into seven regions on a scroll. Then they came to Joshua at the camp in Shiloh.

notes.text: Heb “went and passed through.”

10.text: Joshua drew lots for them in Shiloh before the Lord and divided the land among the Israelites according to their allotted portions.

11.text: The first lot belonged to the tribe of Benjamin by its clans. Their allotted territory was between Judah and Joseph.

notes.text: Heb “and the lot came up for the tribe of the sons of Benjamin.”
Heb “and the territory of their allotment went out between the sons of Judah and the sons of Joseph.”

12.text: Their northern border started at the Jordan, went up to the slope of Jericho on the north, ascended westward to the hill country, and extended to the wilderness of Beth Aven.

13.text: It then crossed from there to Luz, to the slope of Luz to the south (that is, Bethel), and descended to Ataroth Addar located on the hill that is south of lower Beth Horon.

14.text: It then turned on the west side southward from the hill near Beth Horon on the south and extended to Kiriath Baal (that is, Kiriath Jearim), a city belonging to the tribe of Judah. This is the western border.

notes.text: Heb “sons,” here referring to the tribe.
Or “side.”

15.text: The southern side started on the edge of Kiriath Jearim and extended westward to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah.

16.text: The border then descended to the edge of the hill country near the Valley of Ben Hinnom located in the Valley of the Rephaites to the north. It descended through the Valley of Hinnom to the slope of the Jebusites to the south and then down to En Rogel.

17.text: It went northward, extending to En Shemesh and Geliloth opposite the Pass of Adummim, and descended to the Stone of Bohan son of Reuben.

notes.text: Or “ascent.”

18.text: It crossed to the slope in front of the rift valley to the north and descended into the rift valley.

notes.text: This section of the rift valley is to the north and west of the Dead Sea.

19.text: It then crossed to the slope of Beth Hoglah to the north and ended at the northern tip of the Salt Sea at the mouth of the Jordan River. This was the southern border.

notes.text: The Salt Sea is another name for the Dead Sea.

Heb “to the tongue of the Salt Sea to the north, to the end of the Jordan to the south.” The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarity (also in the following verse).

20.text: The Jordan River bordered it on the east. These were the borders of the land assigned to the tribe of Benjamin by its clans.

notes.text: Heb “This was the inheritance of the sons of Benjamin by its borders round about, by their clans.”

21.text: These cities belonged to the tribe of Benjamin by its clans: Jericho, Beth Hoglah, Emek Keziz,

notes.text: Heb “the sons,” here referring to the tribe.

22.text: Beth Arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel,

23.text: Avvim, Parah, Ophrah,

24.text: Kephar Ammoni, Ophni, and Geba—a total of twelve cities and their towns.

25.text: Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth,

26.text: Mizpah, Kephirah, Mozah,

27.text: Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah,

28.text: Zelah, Haeleph, the Jebusite city (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeah, and Kiriath—a total of fourteen cities and their towns. This was the land assigned to the tribe of Benjamin by its clans.

notes.text: The word “city” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

The structure of this list presents problems. In v. 28 no conjunction appears before “Haeleph” or “Kiriath” in the Hebrew text. This suggests they should be compounded with the preceding names, yielding “Zelah Haeleph” and “Gibeah Kiriath” respectively. This results in a list of only twelve cities, however, while the summary statement (v. 28) gives the number fourteen. One should note, however, that the city lists in chap. 15 do not consistently use the conjunction before the name of each city. See also Josh 19:7, where no conjunction appears before “Rimmon,” but the summary assumes that Ain and Rimmon are distinct.
Heb “This is the inheritance of the sons of Benjamin.”

1.text: The second lot belonged to the tribe of Simeon by its clans. Their assigned land was in the middle of Judah’s assigned land.

notes.text: Heb “and the second lot came out for Simeon, for the tribe of the sons of Simeon by their clans.”
The LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate omit “for Simeon.”

2.text: Their assigned land included Beer Sheba, Moladah,

notes.text: Heb “and they had in their inheritance.”

The MT has “and Sheba” listed after “Beer Sheba.” The LXX suggests “Shema.” The Hebrew text may be defective here, since the form “Sheba” duplicates the latter part of the preceding name. If Sheba (or Shema) is retained as a separate city, the list numbers fourteen, one more than the number given in the concluding summary (v. 6). Some translations treat it as an alternate shorter name for “Beer Sheba” rendering it as “or Sheba;” cf. HCSB, TNIV, and JPS.

3.text: Hazar Shual, Balah, Ezem,

4.text: Eltolad, Bethul, Hormah,

5.text: Ziklag, Beth Marcaboth, Hazar Susah,

6.text: Beth Lebaoth, and Sharuhen—a total of thirteen cities and their towns,

7.text: Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan—a total of four cities and their towns,

8.text: as well as all the towns around these cities as far as Baalath Beer (Ramah of the Negev). This was the land assigned to the tribe of Simeon by its clans.

notes.text: Heb “this was the inheritance of the tribe of the sons of Simeon.”

9.text: Simeon’s assigned land was taken from Judah’s allotted portion, for Judah’s territory was too large for them; so Simeon was assigned land within Judah.

notes.text: Heb “from the portion of the sons of Judah was the inheritance of the sons of Simeon for the portion of the sons of Judah was too large for them, and the sons of Simeon received an inheritance in the midst of their inheritance.”

10.text: The third lot belonged to the tribe of Zebulun by its clans. The border of their territory extended to Sarid.

notes.text: Heb “and the third lot came up for the sons of Zebulun.”
Or “inheritance.”

11.text: Their border went up westward to Maralah and touched Dabbesheth and the valley near Jokneam.

notes.text: Heb “in front of”; perhaps “east of.”

12.text: From Sarid it turned eastward to the territory of Kisloth Tabor, extended to Daberath, and went up to Japhia.

notes.text: Heb “eastward toward the rising of the sun.”

13.text: From there it crossed eastward to Gath Hepher and Eth Kazin and extended to Rimmon, turning toward Neah.

14.text: It then turned on the north to Hannathon and ended at the Valley of Iphtah El.

15.text: Their territory included Kattah, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem; in all they had twelve cities and their towns.

notes.text: Heb “Kattah, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem, twelve cities and their towns.” The words “their territory included” and “in all they had” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

16.text: This was the land assigned to the tribe of Zebulun by its clans, including these cities and their towns.

notes.text: Heb “this is the inheritance of the sons of Zebulun.”

17.text: The fourth lot belonged to the tribe of Issachar by its clans.

notes.text: Heb “the fourth lot came out for the sons of Issachar.”

18.text: Their assigned land included Jezreel, Kesulloth, Shunem,

notes.text: Or “their inheritance.”

19.text: Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath,

20.text: Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez,

21.text: Remeth, En Gannim, En Haddah and Beth Pazzez.

22.text: Their border touched Tabor, Shahazumah, and Beth Shemesh, and ended at the Jordan. They had sixteen cities and their towns.

23.text: This was the land assigned to the tribe of Issachar by its clans, including these cities and their towns.

notes.text: Heb “this was the inheritance of the tribe of the sons of Issachar.”

24.text: The fifth lot belonged to the tribe of Asher by its clans.

notes.text: Heb “and the fifth lot came out for the tribe of the sons of Asher.”

19.text: But if your own land is impure, cross over to the Lord’s own land, where the Lord himself lives, and settle down among us. But don’t rebel against the Lord or us by building for yourselves an altar other than the altar of the Lord our God.

notes.text: Heb “the land of your possession.”

The western tribes here imagine a possible motive for the action of the eastern tribes. T. C. Butler explains the significance of the land’s “impurity”: “East Jordan is impure because it is not Yahweh’s possession. Rather it is simply ‘your possession.’ That means it is land where Yahweh does not live, land which his presence has not sanctified and purified” (Joshua [WBC], 247).
Heb “the land of the possession of the Lord.”
Heb “where the dwelling place of the Lord resides.”
The phrase where the Lord himself lives refers to the tabernacle.
Heb “and take for yourselves in our midst.”

Heb “and us to you rebel.” The reading of the MT, the accusative sign with suffix (‏וְאֹתָנוּ‎, veʾotanu), is problematic with the verb “rebel” (‏מָרַד‎, marad). Many Hebrew mss correctly read the negative particle ‏אַל‎ (ʾal) for the preposition ‏אֶל‎ (ʾel, “to”).

20.text: When Achan son of Zerah disobeyed the command about the city’s riches, the entire Israelite community was judged, though only one man had sinned. He most certainly died for his sin!’”

notes.text: Heb “Is it not [true that] Achan son of Zerah was unfaithful with unfaithfulness concerning what was set apart [to the Lord] and against all the assembly of Israel there was anger?”

The second half of the verse reads literally, “and he [was] one man, he did not die for his sin.” There are at least two possible ways to explain this statement: (1) One might interpret the statement to mean that Achan was not the only person who died for his sin. In this case it could be translated, “and he was not the only one to die because of his sin.” (2) Another option, the one reflected in the translation, is to take the words ‏וְהוּא אִישׁ אֶחָד‎ (vehuʾ ʾish ʾekhad, “and he [was] one man”) as a concessive clause and join it with what precedes. The remaining words (‏לֹא גָוַע בַּעֲוֹנוֹ‎, loʾ gavaʿ baʿavono) must then be taken as a rhetorical question (“Did he not die for his sin?”). Taking the last sentence as interrogative is consistent with the first part of the verse, a rhetorical question introduced with the interrogative particle. The present translation has converted these rhetorical questions into affirmative statements to bring out more clearly the points they are emphasizing. For further discussion, see T. C. Butler, Joshua (WBC), 240.

The Hiphil of ‏שָׁבַע‎ (shavaʿ) without an object occurs only here and in Josh 6:26.
Or “serve.”

8.text: But you must be loyal to the Lord your God, as you have been to this very day.

notes.text: Heb “hug.”
Heb “done.”

9.text: “The Lord drove out from before you great and mighty nations; no one has been able to resist you to this very day.

notes.text: Heb “not a man has stood before you.”

10.text: One of you makes a thousand run away, for the Lord your God fights for you, as he promised you he would.

notes.text: Or “chases a thousand.”
Heb “for the Lord your God, he [is] the one who fights for you.”
Heb “as he said to you.”

11.text: Watch yourselves carefully! Love the Lord your God!

notes.text: Heb “Watch carefully yourselves so as to love the Lord your God.”

12.text: But if you ever turn away and make alliances with these nations that remain near you, and intermarry with them and establish friendly relations with them,

notes.text: Heb “and hug.”
Heb “the remnant of the these nations, these nations that are with you.”
Heb “and go into them, and they into you.”

13.text: know for certain that the Lord your God will no longer drive out these nations from before you. They will trap and ensnare you; they will be a whip that tears your sides and thorns that blind your eyes until you disappear from this good land the Lord your God gave you.

notes.text: Heb “be a trap and a snare to you.”
Heb “in.”
Heb “thorns in your eyes.”
Or “perish.”

14.text: “Look, today I am about to die. You know with all your heart and being that not even one of all the faithful promises the Lord your God made to you is left unfulfilled; every one was realized—not one promise is unfulfilled!

notes.text: Heb “go the way of all the earth.”
Or “soul.”
Heb “one word from all these words which the Lord your God spoke to you has not fallen, the whole has come to pass for you, one word from it has not fallen.”

15.text: But in the same way every faithful promise the Lord your God made to you has been realized, it is just as certain that if you disobey, then the Lord will bring on you every judgment until he destroys you from this good land that the Lord your God gave you.

notes.text: Heb “and it will be as every good word which the Lord your God spoke to you has come to pass.”
Heb “so the Lord will bring every injurious [or “evil”] word [or “thing”] upon you.”

16.text: If you violate the covenantal laws of the Lord your God which he commanded you to keep, and follow, worship, and bow down to other gods, then the Lord will be very angry with you and you will disappear quickly from the good land that he gave to you.”

notes.text: Heb “when you violate the covenant of the Lord your God which he commanded you.”
Heb “and you walk and serve other gods and bow down to them.”
Or “perish.”

1.text: Joshua assembled all the Israelite tribes at Shechem. He summoned Israel’s elders, rulers, judges, and leaders, and they appeared before God.

2.text: Joshua told all the people, “This is what the Lord God of Israel has said: ‘In the distant past your ancestors lived beyond the Euphrates River, including Terah the father of Abraham and Nahor. They worshiped other gods,

notes.text: Heb “the river,” referring to the Euphrates. This has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “served.”

3.text: but I took your father Abraham from beyond the Euphrates and brought him into the entire land of Canaan. I made his descendants numerous; I gave him Isaac,

notes.text: Heb “the river,” referring to the Euphrates. This has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “through.”

4.text: and to Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau. To Esau I assigned Mount Seir, while Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt.

notes.text: Heb “I gave to Esau Mount Seir to possess it.”

5.text: I sent Moses and Aaron, and I struck Egypt down when I intervened in their land. Then I brought you out.

notes.text: Heb “by that which I did in its midst.”

6.text: When I brought your fathers out of Egypt, you arrived at the sea. The Egyptians chased your fathers with chariots and horsemen to the Red Sea.

7.text: Your fathers cried out for help to the Lord; he made the area between you and the Egyptians dark, and then he drowned them in the sea. You witnessed with your very own eyes what I did in Egypt. You lived in the wilderness for a long time.

notes.text: Heb “they”; the referent (the fathers) has been specified in the translation for clarity (see the previous verse).
Or “put darkness between you and the Egyptians.”
Heb “and he brought over them the sea and covered them.”
Heb “your eyes saw.”
Heb “many days.”

8.text: Then I brought you to the land of the Amorites who lived east of the Jordan. They fought with you, but I handed them over to you; you conquered their land, and I destroyed them from before you.

notes.text: Or “took possession of.”

9.text: Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, launched an attack against Israel. He summoned Balaam son of Beor to call down judgment on you.

notes.text: Heb “arose and fought.”
Heb “sent and called.”
Or “to curse.”

10.text: I refused to respond to Balaam; he kept prophesying good things about you, and I rescued you from his power.

notes.text: The infinitive absolute follows the finite verb in the Hebrew text and indicates continuation or repetition of the action. Balaam pronounced several oracles of blessing over Israel (see Num 23-24).
Heb “blessing.” Balaam’s “blessings” were actually prophecies of how God would prosper Israel.
Heb “hand.”

11.text: You crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho. The leaders of Jericho, as well as the Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hittites, Girgashites, Hivites, and Jebusites, fought with you, but I handed them over to you.

notes.text: Or perhaps, “citizens.”

12.text: I sent terror ahead of you to drive out before you the two Amorite kings. I gave you the victory; it was not by your swords or bows.

notes.text: Traditionally, “the hornet” (so KJV, NKJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV) but the precise meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain (cf. NEB “panic”).
The LXX has “twelve,” apparently understanding this as a reference to Amorite kings west of the Jordan (see Josh 5:1, rather than the trans-Jordanian Amorite kings Sihon and Og (see Josh 2:10; 9:10).
Heb “and it drove them out from before you, the two kings of the Amorites, not by your sword and not by your bow.” The words “I gave you the victory” are supplied for clarification.

13.text: I gave you a land in which you had not worked hard; you took up residence in cities you did not build, and you are eating the produce of vineyards and olive groves you did not plant.’

notes.text: Or perhaps, “for.”
The words “the produce of” are supplied for clarification.

14.text: “Now obey the Lord and worship him with integrity and loyalty. Put aside the gods your ancestors worshiped beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, and worship the Lord.

notes.text: Joshua quotes the Lord’s words in vv. 2b-13 (note that the Lord speaks in the first person in these verses); in vv. 14-15 Joshua himself exhorts the people (note the third person references to the Lord).
Heb “fear.”
Or “and serve.”
Heb “your fathers.”
Or “served.”
Heb “the river,” referring to the Euphrates. This has been specified in the translation for clarity; see v. 3.
Or “and serve.”

15.text: If you have no desire to worship the Lord, then choose today whom you will worship, whether it be the gods whom your ancestors worshiped beyond the Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living. But I and my family will worship the Lord.”

notes.text: Heb “if it is bad in your eyes.”
Or “to serve.”
Or “will serve.”
Heb “your fathers.”
Or “served.”
Heb “the river,” referring to the Euphrates. This has been specified in the translation for clarity; see v. 3.
Heb “house.”
Or “will serve.”

16.text: The people responded, “Far be it from us to abandon the Lord so we can worship other gods!

notes.text: Heb “to.”
Or “can serve.”

17.text: For the Lord our God took us and our fathers out of slavery in the land of Egypt and performed these awesome miracles before our very eyes. He continually protected us as we traveled and when we passed through nations.

notes.text: Heb “of the house of slavery.”
Heb “for the Lord our God, he is the one who brought up us and our fathers from the land of Egypt, from the house of slaves.”
Or “great signs.”
Heb “and he guarded us in all the way in which we walked and among all the peoples through whose midst we passed.”

18.text: The Lord drove out from before us all the nations, including the Amorites who lived in the land. So we too will worship the Lord, for he is our God!”

notes.text: Or “will serve.”

19.text: Joshua warned the people, “You will not keep worshiping the Lord, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God who will not forgive your rebellion or your sins.

notes.text: Heb “said to.”
Heb “you are not able to serve.”
For an excellent discussion of Joshua’s logical argument here, see T. C. Butler, Joshua (WBC), 274-75.

In the Hebrew text both the divine name (‏אֱלֹהִים‎, ʾelohim) and the adjective (‏קְדֹשִׁים‎, qedoshim, “holy”) are plural. Normally the divine name, when referring to the one true God, takes singular modifiers, but this is a rare exception where the adjective agrees grammatically with the honorific plural noun. See GKC §124.i and IBHS 122.
Heb “lift up” or “take away.”

This assertion obviously needs qualification, for the OT elsewhere affirms that God does forgive. Joshua is referring to the persistent national rebellion against the Mosaic covenant that eventually causes God to decree unconditionally the nation’s exile.

20.text: If you abandon the Lord and worship foreign gods, he will turn against you; he will bring disaster on you and destroy you, though he once treated you well.”

notes.text: Or “when.”
Or “and serve.”
The words “against you” are added for clarification.
Heb “bring you to an end.”
Heb “after he did good for you.”

21.text: The people said to Joshua, “No! We really will worship the Lord.”

notes.text: The translation assumes that ‏כִּי‎ (ki) is emphatic. Another option is to take it as explanatory, “No, for we will….”
Or “will serve.”

22.text: Joshua said to the people, “Do you agree to be witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to worship the Lord?” They replied, “We are witnesses!”

notes.text: Heb “You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen for yourselves the Lord to serve him.”
Like witnesses in a court of law, Israel’s solemn vow to worship the Lord will testify against them in the divine court if the nation ever violates its commitment.

23.text: Joshua said, “Now put aside the foreign gods that are among you and submit to the Lord God of Israel.”

notes.text: The words “Joshua said” are supplied for clarification.
Heb “bend your heart toward.” The term ‏לֵבָב‎ (levav, “heart”) probably here refers to the people’s volition or will.

24.text: The people said to Joshua, “We will worship the Lord our God and obey him.”

notes.text: Or “will serve.”
Heb “and listen to his voice.”

25.text: That day Joshua drew up an agreement for the people, and he established rules and regulations for them in Shechem.

notes.text: Heb “cut a covenant.”
Heb “a statute and a judgment.”

26.text: Joshua wrote these words in the Law Scroll of God. He then took a large stone and set it up there under the oak tree near the Lord’s sanctuary.

27.text: Joshua said to all the people, “Look, this stone will be a witness against us, for it has heard everything the Lord said to us. It will be a witness against you if you deny your God.”

notes.text: Heb “all the words of the Lord which he spoke with us.”
Or “lest,” “so that you might not.”

28.text: When Joshua dismissed the people, they went to their allotted portions of land.

notes.text: Heb “And Joshua sent the people away, each to his inheritance.”

29.text: After all this Joshua son of Nun, the Lord’s servant, died at the age of 110.

notes.text: Heb “after these things.”

30.text: They buried him in his allotted territory in Timnath Serah in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.

notes.text: Heb “in the territory of his inheritance.”

31.text: Israel worshiped the Lord throughout Joshua’s lifetime and as long as the elderly men who outlived him remained alive. These men had experienced firsthand everything the Lord had done for Israel.

notes.text: Or “served.”
Heb “all the days of Joshua and all the days of the elders who outlived him.”
Heb “who knew all the work of the Lord which he had done for Israel.”

32.text: The bones of Joseph, which the Israelites had brought up from Egypt, were buried at Shechem in the part of the field that Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for 100 pieces of money. So it became the inheritance of the tribe of Joseph.

notes.text: Heb “one hundred qesitahs.” The Hebrew word ‏קְשִׂיטָה‎ (qesitah) is generally understood to refer to a unit of money, but the value and/or weight is unknown. The word occurs only here and in Gen 33:19 and Job 42:11.

Heb “and they became for the sons of Joseph an inheritance.” One might think “bones” is the subject of the verb “they became,” but the verb is masculine, while “bones” is feminine. The translation follows the emendation suggested in the BHS note, which appeals to the Syriac and Vulgate for support. The emended reading understands “the part (of the field)” as the subject of the verb “became.” The emended verb is feminine singular; this agrees with “the part” (of the field), which is feminine in Hebrew.

33.text: Eleazar son of Aaron died, and they buried him in Gibeah in the hill country of Ephraim, where his son Phinehas had been assigned land.

notes.text: Heb “in Gibeah of Phinehas, his son, which had been given to him in the hill country of Ephraim.”

1.text: After Joshua died, the Israelites asked the Lord, “Who should lead the invasion against the Canaanites and launch the attack?”

notes.text: The Hebrew verb translated “asked” (‏שָׁאַל‎, shaʾal) refers here to consulting the Lord through a prophetic oracle; cf. NAB “consulted.”
Heb “Who should first go up for us against the Canaanites to attack them?”

2.text: The Lord said, “The men of Judah should take the lead. Be sure of this! I am handing the land over to them.”

notes.text: Heb “Judah should go up.”

The Hebrew exclamation ‏הִנֵּה‎ (hinneh, traditionally, “Behold”), translated “Be sure of this,” draws attention to the following statement. The verb form in the following statement (a Hebrew perfect, indicating completed action from the standpoint of the speaker) emphasizes the certainty of the event. Though it had not yet taken place, the Lord speaks of it as a “done deal.”

3.text: The men of Judah said to their relatives, the men of Simeon, “Invade our allotted land with us and help us attack the Canaanites. Then we will go with you into your allotted land.” So the men of Simeon went with them.

notes.text: Heb “Judah said to Simeon, his brother.”
Heb “Come up with me into our allotted land and let us attack the Canaanites.”
Heb “I.” The Hebrew pronoun is singular, agreeing with the collective singular “Judah” earlier in the verse. English style requires a plural pronoun here, however.

4.text: The men of Judah attacked, and the Lord handed the Canaanites and Perizzites over to them. They killed 10,000 men at Bezek.

notes.text: Heb “Judah went up.”

5.text: They met Adoni-Bezek at Bezek and fought him. They defeated the Canaanites and Perizzites.

notes.text: Or “found.”

6.text: When Adoni-Bezek ran away, they chased him and captured him. Then they cut off his thumbs and big toes.

7.text: Adoni-Bezek said, “Seventy kings, with thumbs and big toes cut off, used to lick up food scraps under my table. God has repaid me for what I did to them.” They brought him to Jerusalem, where he died.

notes.text: Elsewhere this verb usually carries the sense of “to gather; to pick up; to glean,” but “lick up” seems best here in light of the peculiar circumstances described by Adoni-Bezek.
The words “food scraps” are not in the Hebrew text, but are implied.
Heb “Just as I did, so God has repaid me.” Note that the phrase “to them” has been supplied in the translation to clarify what is meant.

8.text: The men of Judah attacked Jerusalem and captured it. They put the sword to it and set the city on fire.

9.text: Later the men of Judah went down to attack the Canaanites living in the hill country, the Negev, and the foothills.

notes.text: The Negev is the area of central, southern Judah, south of the hill country and Beer Sheba and west of the rift valley.
The foothills (‏שְׁפֵלָה‎, shephelah) are the region between the Judean hill country and the Mediterranean coastal plain.

10.text: The men of Judah attacked the Canaanites living in Hebron. (Hebron used to be called Kiriath Arba.) They killed Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai.

11.text: From there they attacked the people of Debir. (Debir used to be called Kiriath Sepher.)

notes.text: Heb “they went from there against the inhabitants of Debir.” The LXX reads the verb as “they went up,” which suggests that the Hebrew text translated by the LXX read ‏וַיַּעַל‎ (vayyaʿal) rather than the MT’s ‏וַיֵּלֶךְ‎ (vayyelekh). It is possible that this is the text to be preferred in v. 11. Cf. Josh 15:15.

12.text: Caleb said, “To the man who attacks and captures Kiriath Sepher I will give my daughter Achsah as a wife.”

13.text: When Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, captured it, Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah as a wife.

notes.text: “Caleb’s younger brother” may refer to Othniel or to Kenaz (in which case Othniel was Caleb’s nephew; so CEV).
Heb “he”; the referent (Caleb) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

14.text: One time Achsah came and charmed her father so she could ask him for some land. When she got down from her donkey, Caleb said to her, “What would you like?”

notes.text: Heb “she”; the referent (Achsah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Heb “him.” The pronoun could refer to Othniel, in which case one would translate, “she incited him [Othniel] to ask her father for a field.” This is problematic, however, for Achsah, not Othniel, makes the request in v. 15. The LXX has “he [Othniel] urged her to ask her father for a field.” This appears to be an attempt to reconcile the apparent inconsistency and probably does not reflect the original text. If Caleb is understood as the referent of the pronoun, the problem disappears. For a fuller discussion of the issue, see P. G. Mosca, “Who Seduced Whom? A Note on Joshua 15:18 // Judges 1:14, ” CBQ 46 (1984): 18-22. The translation takes Caleb to be the referent, specified as “her father.”

15.text: She answered, “Please give me a special present. Since you have given me land in the Negev, now give me springs of water.” So Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs.

notes.text: Elsewhere the Hebrew word ‏בְרָכָה‎ (verakhah) is often translated “blessing,” but here it refers to a gift (as in Gen 33:11; 1 Sam 25:27; 30:26; 2 Kgs 5:15).
Some translations regard the expressions “springs of water” (‏גֻּלֹּת מָיִם‎, gullot mayim) and “springs” (‏גֻּלֹּת‎) as place names here (cf. NRSV).

16.text: Now the descendants of the Kenite, Moses’ father-in-law, went up with the people of Judah from the city of date palm trees to Arad in the wilderness of Judah, located in the Negev. They went and lived with the people of Judah.

notes.text: The city of date palm trees refers to Jericho. See Deut 34:3.
Part of the Greek ms tradition lacks the words “of Judah.”
Heb “[to] the wilderness of Judah in the Negev, Arad.”

The phrase “of Judah” is supplied here in the translation. Some ancient textual witnesses read, “They went and lived with the Amalekites.” This reading, however, is probably influenced by 1 Sam 15:6 (see also Num 24:20-21).

17.text: The men of Judah went with their brothers the men of Simeon and defeated the Canaanites living in Zephath. They wiped out Zephath. So people now call the city Hormah.

notes.text: Heb “Judah went with Simeon, his brother.”
Heb “it”; the referent (the city of Zephath) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The name Hormah (‏חָרְמָה‎, khormah) sounds like the Hebrew verb translated “wipe out” (‏חָרַם‎, kharam).

18.text: The men of Judah captured Gaza, Ashkelon, Ekron, and the territory surrounding each of these cities.

notes.text: Heb “The men of Judah captured Gaza and its surrounding territory, Ashkelon and its surrounding territory, and Ekron and its surrounding territory.”

19.text: The Lord was with the men of Judah. They conquered the hill country, but they could not conquer the people living in the coastal plain, because they had chariots with iron-rimmed wheels.

notes.text: Or “seized possession of”; or “occupied.”
Several textual witnesses support the inclusion of this verb.

Regarding the translation “chariots with iron-rimmed wheels,” see Y. Yadin, The Art of Warfare in Biblical Lands, 255, and the article by R. Drews, “The ‘Chariots of Iron’ of Joshua and Judges,” JSOT 45 (1989): 15-23.

20.text: Caleb received Hebron, just as Moses had promised. He drove out the three Anakites.

notes.text: Heb “they gave to Caleb.”

21.text: The men of Benjamin, however, did not conquer the Jebusites living in Jerusalem. The Jebusites live with the people of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this very day.

notes.text: The statement to this very day reflects the perspective of the author, who must have written prior to David’s conquest of the Jebusites (see 2 Sam 5:6-7).

22.text: When the men of Joseph attacked Bethel, the Lord was with them.

notes.text: Heb “house.” This is a metonymy for the warriors from the tribe.
Heb “went up.”

23.text: When the men of Joseph spied out Bethel (it used to be called Luz),

24.text: the spies spotted a man leaving the city. They said to him, “If you show us a secret entrance into the city, we will reward you.”

notes.text: Heb “saw.”

25.text: He showed them a secret entrance into the city, and they put the city to the sword. But they let the man and his extended family leave safely.

26.text: He moved to Hittite country and built a city. He named it Luz, and it has kept that name to this very day.

notes.text: Heb “the man.”

27.text: The men of Manasseh did not conquer Beth Shean, Taanach, or their surrounding towns. Nor did they conquer the people living in Dor, Ibleam, Megiddo or their surrounding towns. The Canaanites managed to remain in those areas.

notes.text: Heb “The men of Manasseh did not conquer Beth Shean and its surrounding towns, Taanach and its surrounding towns, the people living in Dor and its surrounding towns, the people living in Ibleam and its surrounding towns, or the people living in Megiddo and its surrounding towns.”
Or “were determined.”
Heb “in this land.”

28.text: Whenever Israel was strong militarily, they forced the Canaanites to do hard labor, but they never totally conquered them.

29.text: The men of Ephraim did not conquer the Canaanites living in Gezer. The Canaanites lived among them in Gezer.

30.text: The men of Zebulun did not conquer the people living in Kitron and Nahalol. The Canaanites lived among them and were forced to do hard labor.

notes.text: Heb “the people living in Kitron and the people living in Nahalol.”

31.text: The men of Asher did not conquer the people living in Acco or Sidon, nor did they conquer Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphek, or Rehob.

notes.text: Heb “The men of Asher did not conquer the people living in Acco, the people living in Sidon, Ahlab, Acco, Helbah, Aphek, or Rehob.”

32.text: The people of Asher live among the Canaanites residing in the land because they did not conquer them.

33.text: The men of Naphtali did not conquer the people living in Beth Shemesh or Beth Anath. They live among the Canaanites residing in the land. The Canaanites living in Beth Shemesh and Beth Anath were forced to do hard labor for them.

notes.text: Heb “the people living in Beth Shemesh or the people living in Beth Anath.”
The term “Canaanites” is supplied here both for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

34.text: The Amorites forced the people of Dan to live in the hill country. They did not allow them to live in the coastal plain.

notes.text: Heb “come down into.”

35.text: The Amorites managed to remain in Har Heres, Aijalon, and Shaalbim. Whenever the tribe of Joseph was strong militarily, the Amorites were forced to do hard labor.

notes.text: Or “were determined.”
Or “Mount Heres”; the term ‏הַר‎ (har) means “mount” or “mountain” in Hebrew.
Heb “Whenever the hand of the tribe of Joseph was heavy.”

36.text: The border of Amorite territory ran from the Scorpion Ascent to Sela and on up.

notes.text: Or “the Ascent of Scorpions” (‏עַקְרַבִּים‎ [ʿaqrabbim] means “scorpions” in Hebrew).
Or “Amorite territory started at the Pass of the Scorpions at Sela and then went on up.”

1.text: The angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to Bokim. He said, “I brought you up from Egypt and led you into the land I had solemnly promised to give to your ancestors. I said, ‘I will never break my covenant with you,

notes.text: Heb “the land that I had sworn to your fathers.”

2.text: but you must not make an agreement with the people who live in this land. You should tear down the altars where they worship.’ But you have disobeyed me. Why would you do such a thing?

notes.text: Heb “their altars.”
Heb “you have not listened to my voice.”
Heb “What is this you have done?”

3.text: At that time I also warned you, ‘If you disobey, I will not drive out the Canaanites before you. They will ensnare you and their gods will lure you away.’”

notes.text: Heb “And I also said.” The use of the perfect tense here suggests that the messenger is recalling an earlier statement (see Josh 23:12-13). However, some translate, “And I also say,” understanding the following words as an announcement of judgment upon those gathered at Bokim.
The words “If you disobey” are supplied in the translation for clarity. See Josh 23:12-13.
Heb “them”; the referent (the Canaanites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The meaning of the Hebrew word ‏צִדִּים‎ (tsiddim) is uncertain in this context. It may be related to an Akkadian cognate meaning “snare.” If so, a more literal translation would be “they will become snares to you.” Normally the term in question means “sides,” but this makes no sense here. On the basis of Num 33:55 some suggest the word for “thorns” has been accidentally omitted. If this word is added, the text would read, “they will become [thorns] in your sides” (cf. NASB, NIV, NLT).
Heb “their gods will become a snare to you.”

4.text: When the angel of the Lord finished speaking these words to all the Israelites, the people wept loudly.

notes.text: Heb “lifted their voices and wept.”

5.text: They named that place Bokim and offered sacrifices to the Lord there.

notes.text: Bokim means “weeping ones” and is derived from the Hebrew verb ‏בָּכָא‎ (bakhaʾ, “to weep”).

6.text: When Joshua dismissed the people, the Israelites went to their allotted portions of territory, intending to take possession of the land.

notes.text: Or “sent away.”
Heb “the Israelites went each to his inheritance.”

7.text: The people worshiped the Lord throughout Joshua’s lifetime and as long as the elderly men who outlived him remained alive. These men had witnessed all the great things the Lord had done for Israel.

notes.text: Or “served”; or “followed.”
Or perhaps “elders,” which could be interpreted to mean “leaders.”
Heb “all the days of Joshua and all the days of the old men who outlived him, who had seen.”
Heb “the great work of the Lord which he had done for Israel.”

8.text: Joshua son of Nun, the Lord’s servant, died at the age of 110.

9.text: The people buried him in his allotted land in Timnath Heres in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.

notes.text: Heb “they”; the referent (the people) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “in the territory of his inheritance.”

10.text: That entire generation passed away; a new generation grew up that had not personally experienced the Lord’s presence or seen what he had done for Israel.

notes.text: Heb “All that generation were gathered to their fathers.”
Heb “arose after them.”
Heb “that did not know the Lord or the work which he had done for Israel.” The expressions “personally experienced” and “seen” are interpretive.

11.text: The Israelites did evil before the Lord by worshiping the Baals.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”
Or “serving”; or “following.”

12.text: They abandoned the Lord God of their ancestors who brought them out of the land of Egypt. They followed other gods—the gods of the nations who lived around them. They worshiped them and made the Lord angry.

notes.text: Or “fathers.”
Or “bowed before” (the same expression occurs in the following verse).

13.text: They abandoned the Lord and worshiped Baal and the Ashtoreths.

notes.text: The Ashtoreths were local manifestations of the goddess Astarte.

14.text: The Lord was furious with Israel and handed them over to robbers who plundered them. He turned them over to their enemies who lived around them. They could no longer withstand their enemies’ attacks.

notes.text: Or “The Lord’s anger burned [or “raged”] against Israel.”
Heb “robbers who robbed them.” (The verb ‏שָׁסָה‎ [shasah] appears twice in the verse.)
The expression robbers who plundered them is a derogatory reference to the enemy nations, as the next line indicates.
Heb “sold them into the hand of.”
The word “attacks” is supplied in the translation both for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

15.text: Whenever they went out to fight, the Lord did them harm, just as he had warned and solemnly vowed he would do. They suffered greatly.

notes.text: The expression “to fight” is interpretive.
Heb “the Lord’s hand was against them for harm.”
Heb “just as he had said and just as he had sworn to them.”
Or “they experienced great distress.”

16.text: The Lord raised up leaders who delivered them from these robbers.

notes.text: Or more traditionally, “judges” (also in vv. 17, 18 [3x], 19). Since these figures carried out more than a judicial function, also serving as rulers and (in several instances) as military commanders, the translation uses the term “leaders.”
Heb “and they delivered them from the hand of the ones robbing them.”

17.text: But they did not obey their leaders. Instead they prostituted themselves to other gods and worshiped them. They quickly turned aside from the path their ancestors had walked. Their ancestors had obeyed the Lord’s commands, but they did not.

notes.text: Or “did not listen to.”
Or “bowed before.”
Or “way [of life].”
Or “fathers.”
Heb “…walked, obeying the Lord’s commands. They did not do this.”

18.text: When the Lord raised up leaders for them, the Lord was with each leader and delivered the people from their enemies while the leader remained alive. The Lord felt sorry for them when they cried out in agony because of what their harsh oppressors did to them.

notes.text: Heb “them”; the referent (the people) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The phrase “for them” is supplied in the translation for clarity.

Heb “the ones oppressing them and afflicting them.” The synonyms “oppressing” and “afflicting” are joined together in the translation as “harsh oppressors” to emphasize the cruel character of their enemies.

19.text: When a leader died, the next generation would again act more wickedly than the previous one. They would follow after other gods, worshiping them and bowing down to them. They did not give up their practices or their stubborn ways.

notes.text: Heb “they”; the referent (the next generation) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The verb ‏שׁוּב‎ (shuv, “to return; to turn”) is sometimes translated “turn back” here, but it is probably used in an adverbial sense, indicating that the main action (“act wickedly”) is being repeated.
Heb “their fathers.”
The statement the next generation would again act more wickedly than the previous one must refer to the successive sinful generations after Joshua, not Joshua’s godly generation (cf. vv. 7, 17).
Or “serving [them]”; or “following [them].”
Or “drop.”

20.text: The Lord was furious with Israel. He said, “This nation has violated the terms of the covenant I made with their ancestors by disobeying me.

notes.text: Or “The Lord’s anger burned [or “raged”] against Israel.”
Heb “Because this nation.”
Heb “my covenant which I commanded their fathers.”
Heb “and has not listened to my voice.” The expression “to not listen to [God’s] voice” is idiomatic here for disobeying him.

21.text: So I will no longer remove before them any of the nations that Joshua left unconquered when he died,

22.text: in order to test Israel. I want to see whether or not the people will carefully walk in the path marked out by the Lord, as their ancestors were careful to do.”

notes.text: The Hebrew text of v. 22 simply begins with “to test.” Some subordinate this phrase to “I will no longer remove” (v. 21). In this case the Lord announces that he has now decided to leave these nations as a test for Israel. Another possibility is to subordinate “to test” to “He said” (v. 20; see B. Lindars, Judges 1-5, 111). In this case the statement recorded in vv. 20b-21 is the test in that it forces Israel to respond either positively (through repentance) or negatively to the Lord’s declaration. A third possibility is to subordinate “to test” to “left unconquered” (v. 21). In this case the Lord recalls that Joshua left these nations as a test. Israel has failed the test (v. 20), so the Lord announces that the punishment threatened earlier (Josh 23:12-13; see also Judg 2:3) will now be implemented. As B. G. Webb (Judges [JSOTSup], 115) observes, “The nations which were originally left as a test are now left as a punishment.” This view harmonizes v. 23, which explains that the Lord did not give all the nations to Joshua, with v. 22. (For a grammatical parallel, where the infinitive construct of ‏נָסָה‎ [nasah] is subordinated to the perfect of ‏עָזַב‎ [ʿazav], see 2 Chr 32:31.)
The Hebrew text includes the phrase “by them,” but this is somewhat redundant in English and has been omitted from the translation for stylistic reasons.
The words “I [i.e., the Lord] want to see” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “they”; the referent (the people) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “way [of life].”
“The words “marked out by” are interpretive.
Or “fathers.”

23.text: This is why the Lord permitted these nations to remain and did not conquer them immediately; he did not hand them over to Joshua.

notes.text: The words “this is why” are interpretive and not in the original text.
Or “quickly.”

1.text: These were the nations the Lord permitted to remain so he could use them to test Israel—he wanted to test all those who had not experienced battle against the Canaanites.

notes.text: Heb “did not know the wars of Canaan.”

2.text: He left those nations simply because he wanted to teach the subsequent generations of Israelites, who had not experienced the earlier battles, how to conduct holy war.

notes.text: The Hebrew syntax of v. 2 is difficult. The Hebrew text reads literally, “only in order that the generations of the Israelites might know, to teach them war—only those who formerly did not know them.”

The stated purpose for leaving the nations (to teach the subsequent generations…how to conduct holy war) seems to contradict 2:22 and 3:4, which indicate the nations were left to test Israel’s loyalty to the Lord. However, the two stated purposes can be harmonized. The willingness of later generations to learn and engage in holy war would measure their allegiance to the Lord (see B. G. Webb, Judges [JSOTSup], 114-15).

3.text: These were the nations: the five lords of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites living in Mount Lebanon, from Mount Baal Hermon to Lebo Hamath.

notes.text: The words “These were the nations,” though not present in the Hebrew text, are supplied in the translation for clarity.
Or “the entrance to Hamath.”

4.text: They were left to test Israel, so the Lord would know if his people would obey the commands he gave their ancestors through Moses.

notes.text: Heb “to know if they would hear the commands of the Lord which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses.”

5.text: The Israelites lived among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.

6.text: They took the Canaanites’ daughters as wives and gave their daughters to the Canaanites; they worshiped their gods as well.

notes.text: Heb “to their sons.”
Or “served”; or “followed” (this term occurs in the following verse as well).

7.text: The Israelites did evil in the Lord’s sight. They forgot the Lord their God and worshiped the Baals and the Asherahs.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of the Lord.”
The Asherahs were local manifestations of the Canaanite goddess Asherah.

8.text: The Lord was furious with Israel and turned them over to King Cushan Rishathaim of Armon Haraim. They were Cushan Rishathaim’s subjects for eight years.

notes.text: Or “The Lord’s anger burned (or raged) against Israel.”
Heb “sold them into the hands of.”
Or “Cushan the Doubly Wicked.”

Armon Haraim. Traditionally Aram-Naharaim, and sometimes understood as a place in Mesopotamia. This reading accepts the consonantal text but divides the words after the nun (‏נ‎) instead of before. The consonants ‏ארמן הרים‎ could be read with a dual ending as ʾArmon Haraim, meaning “Citadel of the Two Mountains,” or with a plural ending as ʾArmon Harim, meaning “Citadel of the Mountains.” In either case, Cushan Rishathaim is probably a remaining Canaanite king with a fortress in the hill country of Israel. See Beitzel, The Moody Atlas of Bible Lands, 106.
Or “they served Cushan Rishathaim.”

9.text: When the Israelites cried out for help to the Lord, he raised up a deliverer for the Israelites who rescued them. His name was Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother.
