notes.text: Heb “navel.” On the background of the Hebrew expression “the navel of the land,” see R. G. Boling, Judges (AB), 178-79.
Heb “head.”
Some English translations simply transliterated this as a place name (Heb “Elon-meonenim”); cf. NAB, NRSV.

38.text: Zebul said to him, “Where now are your bragging words, ‘Who is Abimelech that we should serve him?’ Are these not the men you insulted? Go out now and fight them!”

notes.text: Heb “is your mouth that says.”
Heb “the people.”
Or “despised.”

39.text: So Gaal led the leaders of Shechem out and fought Abimelech.

notes.text: Heb “So Gaal went out before the leaders of Shechem.”

40.text: Abimelech chased him, and Gaal ran from him. Many Shechemites fell wounded at the entrance of the gate.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Gaal) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The word “Shechemites” is not in the Hebrew text, but is supplied for clarification.

41.text: Abimelech went back to Arumah; Zebul drove Gaal and his brothers out of Shechem.

notes.text: Heb “stayed.” Some scholars revise the vowel pointing on this verb from that of the MT, resulting in the translation “and he returned to.” The Lucianic recension of the LXX understands the word in this way.
Heb “drove…out from dwelling in Shechem.”

42.text: The next day the Shechemites came out to the field. When Abimelech heard about it,

notes.text: Heb “the people”; the referent (the Shechemites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “And they told Abimelech.”

43.text: he took his men and divided them into three units and set an ambush in the field. When he saw the people coming out of the city, he attacked and struck them down.

notes.text: Heb “his people.”
Heb “And he saw and, look, the people were coming out of the city.”
Heb “he arose against them and struck them.”

44.text: Abimelech and his units attacked and blocked the entrance to the city’s gate. Two units then attacked all the people in the field and struck them down.

notes.text: Or possibly, “the unit that was with him.”
Heb “stood [at].”

45.text: Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed all the people in it. Then he leveled the city and spread salt over it.

notes.text: Or “destroyed.”
Heb “sowed it with salt.”

The spreading of salt over the city was probably a symbolic act designed to place the site under a curse, deprive it of fertility, and prevent any future habitation. The practice is referred to outside the Bible as well. For example, one of the curses in the Aramaic Sefire treaty states concerning Arpad: “May Hadad sow in them salt and weeds, and may it not be mentioned again!” See J. A. Fitzmyer, The Aramaic Inscriptions of Sefire (BibOr), 15, 53. Deut 29:23, Jer 17:6, and Zeph 2:9 associate salt flats or salty regions with infertility and divine judgment.

46.text: When all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem heard the news, they went to the stronghold of the temple of El Berith.

notes.text: Perhaps the Tower of Shechem was a nearby town, distinct from Shechem proper, or a tower within the city.

Apparently this rare word refers here to the most inaccessible area of the temple, perhaps the inner sanctuary or an underground chamber. It appears only here and in 1 Sam 13:6, where it is paired with “cisterns” and refers to subterranean or cave-like hiding places.
The name El-Berith means “God of the Covenant.” It is probably a reference to the Canaanite high god El.

47.text: Abimelech heard that all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem were in one place.

notes.text: Heb “and it was told to Abimelech.”
Heb “were assembled.”

48.text: He and all his men went up on Mount Zalmon. He took an ax in his hand and cut off a tree branch. He put it on his shoulder and said to his men, “Quickly, do what you have just seen me do!”

notes.text: Heb “his people.”
Heb “Abimelech.” The proper name has been replaced with the pronoun (“he”) due to considerations of English style.
The Hebrew text has the plural here.
Heb “he lifted it and put [it].”
Heb “What you have seen me do, quickly do like me.”

49.text: So each of his men also cut off a branch and followed Abimelech. They put the branches against the stronghold and set fire to it. All the people of the Tower of Shechem died—about 1,000 men and women.

notes.text: The words “the branches” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “they kindled over them the stronghold with fire.”
Or “men,” but the word seems to have a more general sense here, as the conclusion to the sentence suggests.

50.text: Abimelech moved on to Thebez; he besieged and captured it.

notes.text: Or “went.”
Heb “he camped near Thebez and captured it.”

51.text: There was a fortified tower in the center of the city, so all the men and women, as well as the city’s leaders, ran into it and locked the entrance. Then they went up to the roof of the tower.

notes.text: Or “strong.”
Or “fortress.” The same Hebrew term occurs once more in this verse and twice in v. 52.

52.text: Abimelech came and attacked the tower. When he approached the entrance of the tower to set it on fire,

53.text: a woman threw an upper millstone down on his head and shattered his skull.

notes.text: A hand mill consisted of an upper stone and larger lower stone. One would turn the upper stone with a handle to grind the grain, which was placed between the stones. An upper millstone, which was typically about two inches thick and a foot or so in diameter, probably weighed 25-30 pounds (11.4-13.6 kg). See G. F. Moore, Judges (ICC), 268; C. F. Burney, Judges, 288.
Heb “Abimelech’s.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun “his” in the translation in keeping with conventions of English narrative style.

54.text: He quickly called to the young man who carried his weapons, “Draw your sword and kill me, so they will not say, ‘A woman killed him.’” So the young man stabbed him and he died.

notes.text: The Hebrew text adds, “and said to him.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.
The Hebrew text adds, “concerning me.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

55.text: When the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, they went home.

notes.text: Heb “each to his own place.”

56.text: God repaid Abimelech for the evil he did to his father by murdering his seventy half brothers.

notes.text: Heb “seventy brothers.”

57.text: God also repaid the men of Shechem for their evil deeds. The curse spoken by Jotham son of Jerub Baal fell on them.

notes.text: Heb “came.”

1.text: After Abimelech’s death, Tola son of Puah, grandson of Dodo, from the tribe of Issachar, rose up to deliver Israel. He lived in Shamir in the Ephraimite hill country.

notes.text: The word “death” has been supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “son.”
Heb “a man of Issachar.”

2.text: He led Israel for twenty-three years, then died and was buried in Shamir.

notes.text: Traditionally, “judged.”

3.text: Jair the Gileadite rose up after him; he led Israel for twenty-two years.

4.text: He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys and possessed thirty cities. To this day these towns are called Havvoth Jair —they are in the land of Gilead.

notes.text: The name Habboth Jair means “tent villages of Jair” in Hebrew.
Heb “they call them Havvoth Jair to this day—which are in the land of Gilead.”

5.text: Jair died and was buried in Kamon.

6.text: The Israelites again did evil in the Lord’s sight. They worshiped the Baals and the Ashtoreths, as well as the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, the Ammonites, and the Philistines. They abandoned the Lord and did not worship him.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of the Lord.”
Or “served;” or “followed.”
The Ashtoreths were local manifestations of the goddess Astarte.
Heb “the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines.”
Or “serve”; or “follow.”

7.text: The Lord was furious with Israel and turned them over to the Philistines and Ammonites.

notes.text: Or “the Lord’s anger burned [or “raged”] against Israel.”
Heb “sold them into the hands of.”

8.text: They ruthlessly oppressed the Israelites that eighteenth year —that is, all the Israelites living east of the Jordan in Amorite country in Gilead.

notes.text: Heb “shattered and crushed.” The repetition of similar sounding synonyms (‏רָעַץ‎ [raʿats] and ‏רָצַץ‎ [ratsats]) is for emphasis; ‏רָצַץ‎ appears in the Polel, adding further emphasis to the affirmation.

The phrase ‏שְׁמֹנֶה עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה‎ (shemoneh ʿesreh shanah) could be translated “eighteen years,” but this would be difficult after the reference to “that year.” It is possible that v. 8b is parenthetical, referring to an eighteen year long period of oppression east of the Jordan which culminated in hostilities against all Israel (including Judah, see v. 9) in the eighteenth year. It is simpler to translate the phrase as an ordinal number, though the context does not provide the point of reference. (See Gen 14:4-5 and R. G. Boling, Judges [AB], 191-92.) In this case, the following statement specifies which “Israelites” are in view.

9.text: The Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight with Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim. Israel suffered greatly.

notes.text: Heb “the house of Ephraim.”
Or “Israel experienced great distress.” Perhaps here the verb has the nuance “hemmed in.”

10.text: The Israelites cried out for help to the Lord: “We have sinned against you. We abandoned our God and worshiped the Baals.”

notes.text: Or “served”; or “followed.”

11.text: The Lord said to the Israelites, “Did I not deliver you from Egypt, the Amorites, the Ammonites, the Philistines,

12.text: the Sidonians, Amalek, and Midian when they oppressed you? You cried out for help to me, and I delivered you from their power.

notes.text: The translation follows the LXX which reads “Midian”; the Hebrew text has “Maon.”
The words “Did I not deliver you” are interpretive. The Hebrew text simply reads, “Is it not from Egypt…when they oppressed you?” Perhaps the incomplete sentence reflects the Lord’s frustration.
Heb “hand.”

13.text: But since you abandoned me and worshiped other gods, I will not deliver you again.

notes.text: Or “served”; or “followed.”

14.text: Go and cry for help to the gods you have chosen! Let them deliver you from trouble!”

notes.text: Heb “in your time of trouble.”

15.text: But the Israelites said to the Lord, “We have sinned. You do to us as you see fit, but deliver us today!”

notes.text: Heb “according to all whatever is good in your eyes.”

You do to us as you see fit, but deliver us today. The request seems contradictory, but it can be explained in one of two ways. They may be asking for relief from their enemies and direct discipline from God’s hand. Or they may mean, “In the future you can do whatever you like to us, but give us relief from what we’re suffering right now.”

16.text: They threw away the foreign gods they owned and worshiped the Lord. Finally the Lord grew tired of seeing Israel suffer so much.

notes.text: Heb “from their midst.”
Or “served”; or “followed.”

Heb “And his spirit grew short [i.e., impatient] with the suffering of Israel.” The Hebrew noun ‏נֶפֶשׁ‎ (nefesh) also appears as the subject of the verb ‏קָצַר‎ (qatsar) in Num 21:4 (the Israelites grow impatient wandering in the wilderness), Judg 16:16 (Samson grows impatient with Delilah’s constant nagging), and Zech 11:8 (Zechariah grows impatient with the three negligent “shepherds”).

17.text: The Ammonites assembled and camped in Gilead; the Israelites gathered together and camped in Mizpah.

notes.text: Or “were summoned;” or “were mustered.”

18.text: The leaders of Gilead said to one another, “Who is willing to lead the charge against the Ammonites? He will become the leader of all who live in Gilead!”

notes.text: Heb “the people, the officers.”
Heb “Who is the man who will begin fighting.”

1.text: Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a brave warrior. His mother was a prostitute, but Gilead was his father.

notes.text: Heb “Now he was the son of a woman, a prostitute, and Gilead fathered Jephthah.”

2.text: Gilead’s wife also gave him sons. When his wife’s sons grew up, they made Jephthah leave and said to him, “You are not going to inherit any of our father’s wealth, because you are another woman’s son.”

notes.text: Heb “bore.”
Heb “in the house of our father.”

3.text: So Jephthah left his half brothers and lived in the land of Tob. Lawless men joined Jephthah’s gang and traveled with him.

notes.text: Or “fled from.”
Heb “brothers.”
Heb “Empty men joined themselves to Jephthah and went out with him.”

4.text: It was some time after this when the Ammonites fought with Israel.

5.text: When the Ammonites attacked, the leaders of Gilead asked Jephthah to come back from the land of Tob.

notes.text: Heb “When the Ammonites fought with Israel.”
Or “elders.”
Heb “went to take Jephthah.”

6.text: They said, “Come, be our commander, so we can fight with the Ammonites.”

notes.text: Heb “to Jephthah.”

7.text: Jephthah said to the leaders of Gilead, “But you hated me and made me leave my father’s house. Why do you come to me now, when you are in trouble?”

notes.text: Heb “Did you not hate me and make me leave?”

8.text: The leaders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “That may be true, but now we pledge to you our loyalty. Come with us and fight with the Ammonites. Then you will become the leader of all who live in Gilead.”

notes.text: Heb “therefore”; “even so.” For MT ‏לָכֵן‎ (lakhen, “therefore”) the LXX has an opposite reading, “not so,” which seems to be based on the Hebrew words ‏לֹא כֵן‎ (loʾ khen).
Heb “we have returned to you.” For another example of ‏שׁוּב אֶל‎ (shuv ʾel) in the sense of “give allegiance to,” see 1 Kgs 12:27b.

Then you will become the leader. The leaders of Gilead now use the word ‏רֹאשׁ‎ (roʾsh, “head, leader”), the same term that appeared in their original, general offer (see 10:18). In their initial offer to Jephthah they had simply invited him to be their ‏קָצִין‎ (qatsin, “commander”; v. 6). When he resists they must offer him a more attractive reward—rulership over the region. See R. G. Boling, Judges (AB), 198.
Heb “leader of us and all who live in Gilead.”

9.text: Jephthah said to the leaders of Gilead, “All right. If you take me back to fight with the Ammonites and the Lord gives them to me, I will be your leader.”

notes.text: “All right” is supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “places them before me.”

Some translate the final statement as a question, “will I really be your leader?” An affirmative sentence is preferable. Jephthah is repeating the terms of the agreement in an official manner. In v. 10 the leaders legally agree to these terms.

10.text: The leaders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “The Lord will judge any grievance you have against us, if we do not do as you say.”

notes.text: Heb “The Lord will be the one who hears between us.” For the idiom ‏שָׁמַע בַּיִן‎ (shamaʿ bayin, “to hear between”), see Deut 1:16.
The Lord will judge…if we do not do as you say. The statement by the leaders of Gilead takes the form of a legally binding oath, which obligates them to the terms of the agreement.

11.text: So Jephthah went with the leaders of Gilead. The people made him their leader and commander. Jephthah repeated the terms of the agreement before the Lord in Mizpah.

notes.text: Heb “spoke all his words.” This probably refers to the “words” recorded in v. 9. Jephthah repeats the terms of the agreement at the Lord’s sanctuary, perhaps to ratify the contract or to emphasize the Gileadites’ obligation to keep their part of the bargain. Another option is to translate, “Jephthah conducted business before the Lord in Mizpah.” In this case, the statement is a general reference to the way Jephthah ruled. He recognized the Lord’s authority and made his decisions before the Lord.

12.text: Jephthah sent messengers to the Ammonite king, saying, “Why have you come against me to attack my land?”

notes.text: Heb “What to me and to you that…?”

13.text: The Ammonite king said to Jephthah’s messengers, “Because Israel stole my land when they came up from Egypt—from the Arnon River in the south to the Jabbok River in the north, and as far west as the Jordan. Now return it peaceably!”

notes.text: Or “took”; or “seized.”
Heb “he” (a collective singular).

Heb “from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan.” The word “River” has been supplied in the translation with “Arnon” and “Jabbok,” because these are less familiar to modern readers than the Jordan.
The translation assumes a singular suffix (“[return] it”); the Hebrew text has a plural suffix (“[return] them”), which, if retained, might refer to the cities of the land.

14.text: Jephthah sent messengers back to the Ammonite king

15.text: and said to him, “This is what Jephthah says, ‘Israel did not steal the land of Moab and the land of the Ammonites.

notes.text: Or “take”; or “seize.”

16.text: When they left Egypt, Israel traveled through the desert as far as the Red Sea and then came to Kadesh.

notes.text: Heb “For when they went up from.”
Or “went.”

17.text: Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, “Please allow us to pass through your land.” But the king of Edom rejected the request. Israel sent the same request to the king of Moab, but he was unwilling to cooperate. So Israel stayed at Kadesh.

notes.text: Heb “me.” (Collective Israel is the speaker.)
Heb “did not listen.”
Heb “Also to the king of Moab he sent, but he was unwilling.”

18.text: Then Israel went through the wilderness and bypassed the land of Edom and the land of Moab. They traveled east of the land of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon River; they did not go through Moabite territory (the Arnon was Moab’s border).

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Israel; the pronoun in the Hebrew text represents a collective singular) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

19.text: Israel sent messengers to King Sihon, the Amorite king who ruled in Heshbon, and said to him, “Please allow us to pass through your land to our land.”

notes.text: Heb “to my place.”

20.text: But Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory. He assembled his whole army, camped in Jahaz, and fought with Israel.

notes.text: Heb “Sihon.” The proper name (“Sihon”) has been replaced in the translation by the pronoun (“he”) because of English style; a repetition of the proper name here would be redundant in English.
Heb “all his people” (also in the following verse).

21.text: The Lord God of Israel handed Sihon and his whole army over to Israel and they defeated them. Israel took all the land of the Amorites who lived in that land.

notes.text: That is, took as its own possession.

22.text: They took all the Amorite territory from the Arnon River on the south to the Jabbok River on the north, from the desert in the east to the Jordan in the west.

notes.text: Heb “from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and from the desert to the Jordan.” The word “River” has been supplied in the translation with “Arnon” and “Jabbok,” because these are less familiar to modern readers than the Jordan.

23.text: Since the Lord God of Israel has driven out the Amorites before his people Israel, do you think you can just take it from them?

notes.text: Heb “Now.”
Or “dispossessed.”
Heb “will you dispossess him [i.e., Israel; or possibly “it,” i.e., the territory]?” There is no interrogative marker in the Hebrew text.

24.text: You have the right to take what Chemosh your god gives you, but we will take the land of all whom the Lord our God has driven out before us.

notes.text: Heb “Is it not so that what Chemosh your god causes you to possess, you possess, and all whom the Lord our God dispossesses before us we will possess?” Jephthah speaks of Chemosh as if he is on a par with the Lord God of Israel. This does not necessarily mean that Jephthah is polytheistic or that he recognizes the Lord as only a local deity. He may simply be assuming the Ammonite king’s perspective for the sake of argument. Other texts, as well as the extrabiblical Mesha inscription, associate Chemosh with Moab, while Milcom is identified as the god of the Ammonites. Why then does Jephthah refer to Chemosh as the Ammonite god? Ammon had likely conquered Moab and the Ammonite king probably regarded himself as heir of all territory formerly held by Moab. Originally Moab had owned the disputed territory (cf. Num 21:26-29), meaning that Chemosh was regarded as the god of the region (see R. G. Boling, Judges [AB], 203-4). Jephthah argues that Chemosh had long ago relinquished claim to the area (by allowing Sihon to conquer it), while the Lord had long ago established jurisdiction over it (by taking it from Sihon and giving it to Israel). Both sides should abide by the decisions of the gods which had stood firm for 300 years.

25.text: Are you really better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he dare to quarrel with Israel? Did he dare to fight with them?

notes.text: The Hebrew grammatical constructions of all three rhetorical questions indicate emphasis, which “really” and “dare to” are intended to express in the translation.
Jephthah argues that the Ammonite king should follow the example of Balak, who, once thwarted in his attempt to bring a curse on Israel, refused to attack Israel and returned home (Num 22-24).

26.text: Israel has been living in Heshbon and its nearby towns, in Aroer and its nearby towns, and in all the cities along the Arnon for 300 years! Why did you not reclaim them during that time?

27.text: I have not done you wrong, but you are doing wrong by attacking me. May the Lord, the Judge, judge this day between the Israelites and the Ammonites!’”

notes.text: Or “sinned against you.”
Or “evil.”

28.text: But the Ammonite king disregarded the message sent by Jephthah.

notes.text: Heb “did not listen to.”
Heb “Jephthah’s words which he sent to him.”

29.text: The Lord’s Spirit empowered Jephthah. He passed through Gilead and Manasseh and went to Mizpah in Gilead. From there he approached the Ammonites.

notes.text: Heb “was on.”
Heb “passed through.”
Heb “From Mizpah in Gilead he passed through [to] the Ammonites.”

30.text: Jephthah made a vow to the Lord, saying, “If you really do hand the Ammonites over to me,

31.text: then whoever is the first to come through the doors of my house to meet me when I return safely from fighting the Ammonites—he will belong to the Lord and I will offer him up as a burnt sacrifice.”

notes.text: Heb “the one coming out, who comes out from.” The text uses a masculine singular participle with prefixed article, followed by a relative pronoun and third masculine singular verb. The substantival masculine singular participle ‏הַיּוֹצֵא‎ (hayyotseʾ, “the one coming out”) is used elsewhere of inanimate objects (such as a desert [Num 21:13] or a word [Num 32:24]) or persons (Jer 5:6; 21:9; 38:2). In each case context must determine the referent. Jephthah may have envisioned an animal meeting him, since the construction of Iron Age houses would allow for an animal coming through the doors of a house (see R. G. Boling, Judges [AB], 208). But the fact that he actually does offer up his daughter indicates the language of the vow is fluid enough to encompass human beings, including women. He probably intended such an offering from the very beginning, but he obviously did not expect his daughter to meet him first.
The language is fluid enough to include women and perhaps even animals, but the translation uses the masculine pronoun because the Hebrew form is grammatically masculine.

Some translate “or,” suggesting that Jephthah makes a distinction between humans and animals. According to this view, if a human comes through the door, then Jephthah will commit him/her to the Lord’s service, but if an animal comes through the doors, he will offer it up as a sacrifice. However, it is far more likely that the Hebrew construction (vav [‏ו‎] + perfect) specifies how the subject will become the Lord’s, that is, by being offered up as a sacrifice. For similar constructions, where the apodosis of a conditional sentence has at least two perfects (each with vav) in sequence, see Gen 34:15-16; Exod 18:16.

32.text: Jephthah approached the Ammonites to fight with them, and the Lord handed them over to him.

notes.text: Heb “passed over to.”

33.text: He defeated them from Aroer all the way to Minnith—twenty cities in all, even as far as Abel Keramim. He wiped them out! The Israelites humiliated the Ammonites.

notes.text: Heb “with a very great slaughter.”
Heb “The Ammonites were humbled before the Israelites.”

34.text: When Jephthah came home to Mizpah, there was his daughter hurrying out to meet him, dancing to the rhythm of tambourines. She was his only child; except for her he had no son or daughter.

notes.text: Heb “Look! His daughter was coming out.”
Heb “with tambourines and dancing.”

35.text: When he saw her, he ripped his clothes and said, “Oh no! My daughter! You have completely ruined me! You have brought me disaster! I made an oath to the Lord, and I cannot break it.”

notes.text: Heb “you have brought me very low,” or “you have knocked me to my knees.” The infinitive absolute precedes the verb for emphasis.
Heb “You are among [or “like”] those who trouble me.”
Heb “I opened my mouth to the Lord and I am not able to return.”

36.text: She said to him, “My father, since you made an oath to the Lord, do to me as you promised. After all, the Lord vindicated you before your enemies, the Ammonites.”

notes.text: The conjunction “since” is supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “you opened your mouth to the Lord, do to me according to [what] went out from your mouth.”
Or “has given you vengeance against.”

37.text: She then said to her father, “Please grant me this one wish. For two months allow me to walk through the hills with my friends and mourn my virginity.”

notes.text: Heb “Let this thing be done for me.”
Heb “Leave me alone for two months so I can go and go down on the hills and weep over my virginity—I and my friends.”

38.text: He said, “You may go.” He permitted her to leave for two months. She went with her friends and mourned her virginity as she walked through the hills.

notes.text: Heb “he sent her.”
Heb “on the hills.” The words “as she walked” are supplied.

39.text: After two months she returned to her father, and he did to her as he had vowed. She died a virgin. Her tragic death gave rise to a custom in Israel.

notes.text: Heb “She had never known a man.” Some understand this to mean that her father committed her to a life of celibacy, but the disjunctive clause (note the vav + subject + verb pattern) more likely describes her condition at the time the vow was fulfilled. (See G. F. Moore, Judges [ICC], 302-3; C. F. Burney, Judges, 324.) She died a virgin and never experienced the joys of marriage and motherhood.
Heb “There was a custom in Israel.”

40.text: Every year Israelite women commemorate the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite for four days.

notes.text: Heb “From days to days,” a Hebrew idiom for “annually.”
Heb “go to commemorate.” The rare Hebrew verb ‏תָּנָה‎ (tanah, “to tell; to repeat; to recount”) occurs only here and in 5:11.
The Hebrew text adds, “in the year.” This is redundant (note “every year” at the beginning of the verse) and has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

1.text: The Ephraimites assembled and crossed over to Zaphon. They said to Jephthah, “Why did you go and fight with the Ammonites without asking us to go with you? We will burn your house down right over you!”

notes.text: Heb “the men of Ephraim were summoned [or “were mustered”].”
Heb “cross over to fight.”
Or “calling”; or “summoning.”
Heb “Your house we will burn over you with fire.”

2.text: Jephthah said to them, “My people and I were in a struggle and the Ammonites were oppressing me greatly. I asked for your help, but you did not deliver me from their power.

notes.text: Heb “A fighting man was I was and my people, and the Ammonites greatly.” The LXX reads “I was man fighting, and my people [also]. And the sons of Ammon were humiliating me greatly.” The imperfect form of ταπεινόω (tapeinoō) in the LXX probably represents the Hebrew verb ‏עָנָה‎ (ʿanah) as it commonly does elsewhere. Two nearby words begin with ‏ע‎ (ʿayin): ‏עַמִּי‎ (ʿammi; “my people”) and ‏עַמּוֹן‎ (ʿammōn; “Ammon”). So a form of ‏עָנָה‎ (ʿanah) could easily have been omitted by haplography. A piel perfect would begin with ʿayin, (‏עִנּוּ‎; ʿinnu), while a piel participle (as might be suggested by the Greek imperfect) would begin with mem and ʿayin, ‏מְעַנֶּה‎ (meʿanneh).
The Hebrew verb ‏רִיב‎ (riv) often appears in a legal setting, to contend a legal case, but does not have to. In non-legal settings it can mean to strive against, quarrel, brawl (HALOT, 1224).
Heb “hand.”

3.text: When I saw that you were not going to help, I risked my life and advanced against the Ammonites, and the Lord handed them over to me. Why have you come up to fight with me today?”

notes.text: Heb “you were no deliverer.” Codex Alexandrinus (A) of the LXX has “no one was helping.”
Heb “I put my life in my hand.”
Heb “crossed over to.”
The Hebrew adds “against me” here. This is redundant in English and has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

4.text: Jephthah assembled all the men of Gilead and they fought with Ephraim. The men of Gilead defeated Ephraim, because the Ephraimites insulted them, saying, “You Gileadites are refugees in Ephraim, living within Ephraim’s and Manasseh’s territory.”

notes.text: Heb “because they said.”

Heb “Refugees of Ephraim are you, O Gilead, in the midst of Ephraim and in the midst of Manasseh.” The LXX omits the entire second half of the verse (beginning with “because”). The words ‏כִּי אָמְרוּ פְּלִיטֵי אֶפְרַיִם‎ (ki ʾameru pelite ʾefrayim, “because they said, ‘Refugees of Ephraim’”) may have been accidentally copied from the next verse (cf. ‏כִּי יֹאמְרוּ פְּלִיטֵי אֶפְרַיִם‎, ki yoʾmeru pelite ʾefrayim) and the following words (“you, O Gilead…Manasseh”) then added in an attempt to make sense of the verse. See G. F. Moore, Judges (ICC), 307-8, and C. F. Burney, Judges, 327. If the Hebrew text is retained, then the Ephraimites appear to be insulting the Gileadites by describing them as refugees who are squatting on Ephraim’s and Manasseh’s land. The present translation assumes that “Ephraim” is a genitive of location after “refugees.”

5.text: The Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan River opposite Ephraim. Whenever an Ephraimite fugitive said, “Let me cross over,” the men of Gilead asked him, “Are you an Ephraimite?” If he said, “No,”

notes.text: The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarification.
Or “against Ephraim,” that is, so as to prevent Ephraim from crossing.
The Hebrew text has a plural form here.
Heb “say to.”

6.text: then they said to him, “Say ‘Shibboleth!’” If he said, “Sibboleth” (and could not pronounce the word correctly), they grabbed him and executed him right there at the fords of the Jordan. On that day 42,000 Ephraimites fell dead.

notes.text: The inability of the Ephraimites to pronounce the word shibboleth the way the Gileadites did served as an identifying test. It illustrates that during this period there were differences in pronunciation between the tribes. The Hebrew word shibboleth itself means “stream” or “flood,” and was apparently chosen simply as a test case without regard to its meaning.

Heb “and could not prepare to speak.” The precise meaning of ‏יָכִין‎ (yakhin) is unclear. Some understand it to mean “was not careful [to say it correctly]”; others emend to ‏יָכֹל‎ (yakhol, “was not able [to say it correctly]”) or ‏יָבִין‎ (yavin, “did not understand [that he should say it correctly]”), which is read by a few Hebrew mss.

7.text: Jephthah led Israel for six years; then he died and was buried in his town in Gilead.

notes.text: Traditionally, “judged.”
Heb “Jephthah the Gileadite.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.
The Hebrew text has “in the cities of Gilead.” The present translation has support from some ancient Greek textual witnesses.

8.text: After him Ibzan of Bethlehem led Israel.

notes.text: Traditionally, “judged.”

9.text: He had thirty sons. He arranged for thirty of his daughters to be married outside his extended family, and he arranged for thirty young women to be brought from outside as wives for his sons. Ibzan led Israel for seven years;

notes.text: Heb “thirty daughters he sent off outside.” Another option is to translate, “He arranged for his thirty daughters….” It is not clear if he had more than the “thirty daughters” mentioned in the text.
Heb “and thirty daughters he brought for his sons from the outside.”
Heb “He”; the referent (Ibzan) has been specified in the translation for clarity and for English stylistic reasons.
Traditionally, “judged.”

10.text: then he died and was buried in Bethlehem.

notes.text: Heb “Ibzan.” The pronoun “he” is used in the translation in keeping with English style, which tends to use a proper name first in a sentence followed by a pronoun rather than vice versa.

11.text: After him Elon the Zebulunite led Israel for ten years.

notes.text: Traditionally, “judged.”
Heb “…led Israel. He led Israel for ten years.”

12.text: Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.

13.text: After him Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite led Israel.

notes.text: Traditionally, “judged.”

14.text: He had forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode on seventy donkeys. He led Israel for eight years.

15.text: Then Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.

1.text: The Israelites again did evil in the Lord’s sight, so the Lord handed them over to the Philistines for forty years.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”

2.text: There was a man named Manoah from Zorah, from the Danite tribe. His wife was infertile and childless.

notes.text: Heb “and had not given birth.”

3.text: The angel of the Lord appeared to the woman and said to her, “You are infertile and childless, but you will conceive and have a son.

notes.text: Heb “Look, you.”
Heb “and have not given birth.”

4.text: Now be careful! Do not drink wine or beer, and do not eat any food that will make you ritually unclean.

notes.text: Heb “eat anything unclean.” Certain foods were regarded as ritually “unclean” (see Lev 11). Eating such food made one ritually “contaminated.”

5.text: Look, you will conceive and have a son. You must never cut his hair, for the child will be dedicated to God from birth. He will begin to deliver Israel from the power of the Philistines.”

notes.text: Another option is to translate, “you are already pregnant and will have a son.” The earlier reference to her being infertile (v. 3) suggests that her conception is still future, but it is possible that the earlier statement only reflects her perspective (as far as she is concerned, she is infertile). According to this interpretation, in v. 5 the angel reveals the truth to her—actually she has recently conceived and is now pregnant (see the translation in R. G. Boling, Judges [AB], 217). Usage favors this interpretation. The predicate adjective ‏הָרָה‎ (harah, “[be/become] pregnant”) elsewhere has a past (1 Sam 4:19) or present (Gen 16:11; 38:25; 2 Sam 11:5) translation value. (The usage in Isa 7:14 is debated, but a present translation is definitely possible there.) A final, but less likely possibility, is that she miraculously conceived during the angel’s speech, sometime between his statements recorded in vv. 3 and 5.
Heb “a razor should not go up on his head.”
Or “set apart to God.” Traditionally the Hebrew term ‏נָזִיר‎ (nazir) has been translated “Nazirite.” The word is derived from the verb ‏נָזַר‎ (nazar, “to dedicate; to consecrate; to set apart”).
Heb “hand.”

6.text: The woman went and said to her husband, “A man sent from God came to me! He looked like God’s angel—he was very awesome. I did not ask him where he came from, and he did not tell me his name.

notes.text: Heb “The man of God.”
Heb “His appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, very awesome.”

7.text: He said to me, ‘Look, you will conceive and have a son. So now, do not drink wine or beer and do not eat any food that will make you ritually unclean. For the child will be dedicated to God from birth till the day he dies.’”

notes.text: See the note on the word “son” in 13:5, where this same statement occurs.
Heb “eat anything unclean.” Certain foods were regarded as ritually “unclean” (see Lev 11). Eating such food made one ritually “contaminated.”
Traditionally “a Nazirite.”

8.text: Manoah prayed to the Lord, “Please, Lord, allow the man sent from God to visit us again, so he can teach us how we should raise the child who will be born.”

notes.text: The Hebrew text adds “and said.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “the man of God.”
Heb “come to.”
The LXX has “enlighten,” understanding the Hebrew to read ‏וִיאִירֵנוּ‎ (viʾirenu, “to give light”) rather than the reading of the MT, ‏וְיוֹרֵנוּ‎ (veyorenu, “to teach”).
Heb “what we should do for.”

9.text: God answered Manoah’s prayer. God’s angel visited the woman again while she was sitting in the field. But her husband Manoah was not with her.

notes.text: Heb “God listened to the voice of Manoah.”
Heb “came to.”

10.text: The woman ran at once and told her husband, “Come quickly, the man who visited me the other day has appeared to me!”

notes.text: Heb “and said to him.” This phrase has not been translated for stylistic reasons.
Heb “Look.”
Heb “came to.”

11.text: So Manoah got up and followed his wife. When he met the man, he said to him, “Are you the man who spoke to my wife?” He said, “Yes.”

notes.text: Heb “came to.”
Heb “the woman.”
Heb “I [am].”

12.text: Manoah said, “Now, when your announcement comes true, how should the child be raised and what should he do?”

notes.text: Heb “Now, [when] your word comes [to pass].”
Heb “what will be the child’s rule [i.e., way of life] and his work?”

13.text: The angel of the Lord told Manoah, “Your wife should pay attention to everything I told her.

notes.text: Or “said to.”

Heb “To everything I said to the woman she should pay attention.” The Hebrew word order emphasizes “to everything,” probably because Manoah’s wife did not tell her husband everything the angel had said to her (cf. vv. 3-5 with v. 7). If she had, Manoah probably would not have been so confused about the child’s mission.

14.text: She should not drink anything that the grapevine produces. She must not drink wine or beer, and she must not eat any food that will make her ritually unclean. She should obey everything I commanded her to do.”

notes.text: Heb “eat.”
Heb “eat anything unclean.” Certain foods were regarded as ritually “unclean” (see Lev 11). Eating such food made one ritually “contaminated.”

15.text: Manoah said to the angel of the Lord, “Please stay here awhile, so we can prepare a young goat for you to eat.”

notes.text: Heb “Please allow us to detain you.”
Heb “so we can prepare before you a young goat of the goats.”

16.text: The angel of the Lord said to Manoah, “If I stay, I will not eat your food. But if you want to make a burnt sacrifice to the Lord, you should offer it.” (He said this because Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the Lord.)

notes.text: Heb “If you detain me.”

The words “he said this” are supplied in the translation for clarification. Manoah should have known from these words that the angel represented the Lord. In the preceding narrative the narrator has informed the reader that the visitor is the angel of the Lord, but Manoah and his wife did not perceive this. In vv. 5 and 7 the angel refers to “God” (‏אֱלֹהִים‎, ʾelohim), not the Lord (‏יְהוַה‎, yehvah). Manoah’s wife calls the visitor “a man sent from God” and “God’s angel” (v. 6), while Manoah prays to the “Lord” (‏אֲדוֹנָי‎, ʾadonay) and calls the visitor “a man sent from God” (v. 8).

17.text: Manoah said to the angel of the Lord, “Tell us your name, so we can honor you when your announcement comes true.”

notes.text: Heb “Who your name? For [when] your word comes [to pass], we will honor you.” Manoah apparently gets tongue-tied and uses the wrong pronoun (“who” instead of “what”). He starts to say, “Who are you?” But then he switches to “your name” as if he began the sentence with “what.” See R. G. Boling, Judges (AB), 222.

18.text: The angel of the Lord said to him, “You should not ask me my name, because you cannot comprehend it.”

notes.text: Heb “Why do you ask for my name, for it is incomprehensible?” The Hebrew adjective e ‏פִּלְאִי‎ (pilʾi, “wonderful, incomprehensible”) refers to what is in a category of its own and is beyond full human understanding. Note the use of this word in Ps 139:6, where God’s knowledge is described as incomprehensible and unattainable.

19.text: Manoah took a young goat and a grain offering and offered them on a rock to the Lord. The Lord’s messenger did an amazing thing as Manoah and his wife watched.

notes.text: Heb “Doing an extraordinary deed while Manoah and his wife were watching.” The subject of the participle is missing. The translation assumes that the phrase “the Lord’s messenger” was lost by homoioteleuton. If the text originally read ‏לַיהוָה מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה‎ (layhvah malʾakh yehvah), the scribe’s eye could have jumped from the first ‏יְהוָה‎ to the second, accidentally omitting two of the three words. Later the conjunction ‏וּ‎ (shureq) would have been added to the following ‏מַפְלִא‎ (mafliʾ) for syntactical reasons. Another possibility is that a pronominal subject (‏הוּא‎, huʾ) has been lost in the MT due to haplography.

20.text: As the flame went up from the altar toward the sky, the angel of the Lord went up in it while Manoah and his wife watched. They fell facedown to the ground.

notes.text: Heb “in the flame from the altar.”
Heb “on their faces.”

21.text: The angel of the Lord did not appear again to Manoah and his wife. After all this happened Manoah realized that the visitor had been the angel of the Lord.

22.text: Manoah said to his wife, “We will certainly die, because we have seen a supernatural being!”

notes.text: Or “seen God.” Some take the Hebrew term ‏אֱלֹהִים‎ (ʾelohim) as the divine name (“God”) here, but this seems unlikely since v. 21 informs us that Manoah realized this was the Lord’s messenger, not God himself. Of course, he may be exaggerating for the sake of emphasis. Another option, the one followed in the translation, understands Manoah to be referring to a lesser deity. The term ‏אֱלֹהִים‎ (ʾelohim) is sometimes used of an individual deity other than the Lord (see BDB 43 s.v. 2.a). One cannot assume that Manoah was a theologically sophisticated monotheist.

23.text: But his wife said to him, “If the Lord wanted to kill us, he would not have accepted the burnt offering and the grain offering from us. He would not have shown us all these things, or have spoken to us like this just now.”

notes.text: Heb “our hand.”

24.text: Manoah’s wife gave birth to a son and named him Samson. The child grew and the Lord empowered him.

notes.text: Heb “the woman.” For clarity this has been specified in the translation as “Manoah’s wife.”
The name appears to mean “sun-like” or “solar.”
Traditionally, “blessed.”

25.text: The Lord’s Spirit began to control him in Mahaneh Dan between Zorah and Eshtaol.

notes.text: Or “move him to action”; or “stir him.”

1.text: Samson went down to Timnah, where a Philistine girl caught his eye.

notes.text: Heb “and he saw a woman in Timnah, one of the daughters of the Philistines.”

2.text: When he got home, he told his father and mother, “A Philistine girl in Timnah has caught my eye. Now get her for my wife.”

notes.text: Heb “and he went up.”
Heb “I have seen a woman in Timnah, one of the daughters of the Philistines.”

3.text: But his father and mother said to him, “Certainly you can find a wife among your relatives or among all our people! You should not have to go and get a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines.” But Samson said to his father, “Get her for me, because she is the right one for me.”

notes.text: Heb “my.” The singular may seem strange, since the introduction to the quotation attributes the words to his father and mother. But Samson’s father apparently speaks for both himself and his wife. However, the Lucianic recension of the LXX and the Syriac Peshitta have a second person pronoun here (“you”), and this may represent the original reading.
Heb “Is there not among the daughters of your brothers or among all my people a woman that you have to go to get a wife among the uncircumcised Philistines?”
“Her” is first in the Hebrew word order for emphasis. Samson wanted this Philistine girl, no one else. See C. F. Burney, Judges, 357.
Heb “because she is right in my eyes.”

4.text: Now his father and mother did not realize this was the Lord’s doing, because he was looking for an opportunity to stir up trouble with the Philistines (for at that time the Philistines were ruling Israel).

notes.text: Heb “this was from the LORD.”
Heb “for an opportunity he was seeking from the Philistines.”

5.text: Samson went down to Timnah. When he approached the vineyards of Timnah, he saw a roaring young lion attacking him.

notes.text: The Hebrew includes “and his father and his mother.” See the next note.

The MT reads “they approached,” while the LXX reads “he approached.” The previous sentence suggests that his parents were there, reading literally, “he went down, Samson and his father and his mother, to Timnah.” But the story line suggests that his parents were not there, as v. 6b reports that Samson did not tell them about the incident. The following sentence begins with ‏וְהִנֵּה‎ (vehinneh, “and behold”). This particle is used to focus or shift attention, typically pointing something out or introducing it into the scene (here the lion). But the scene that ‏וְהִנֵּה‎ comments on is set by the previous verb. If the verb “approached” were plural, then Samson’s parents should be with him when the lion attacks, something that contradicts the story as a whole. This indicates the verb should be singular. Since the previous verb, “went down,” is also singular (so also v. 7a), the phrase “and his father and his mother” may have been accidentally copied into the text under the influence of v. 4a. Later the verb was changed to “they approached” to account for the addition, but not until after the LXX was translated. Or one might suppose that his parents had gone on this trip down to Timnah (retaining “and his father and his mother”), but he had separated from them before approaching to the vineyards.
Heb “and look, a young lion of the lions was roaring to meet him.”

6.text: The Lord’s Spirit empowered him, and he tore the lion in two with his bare hands as easily as one would tear a young goat. But he did not tell his father or mother what he had done.

notes.text: Heb “rushed on.”
Heb “him” or “it”; the referent (the lion) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “and there was nothing in his hand.”

7.text: Samson continued on down to Timnah and spoke to the girl. In his opinion, she was just the right one.

notes.text: Heb “He went down.”
Heb “She was the right one in the eyes of Samson.”

8.text: Some time later, when he went back to marry her, he turned aside to see the lion’s remains. He saw a swarm of bees in the lion’s carcass, as well as some honey.

notes.text: Heb “get.”
Heb “and look, a swarm of bees….”

9.text: He scooped it up with his hands and ate it as he walked along. When he returned to his father and mother, he offered them some and they ate it. But he did not tell them he had scooped the honey out of the lion’s carcass.

notes.text: Heb “went.” Samson apparently went home to his parents before going to Timnah for the marriage. Seeing and tasting the honey appears to encourage Manoah to go with his son to Timnah. Perhaps both Samson and his father viewed the honey as a good omen of future blessing. Possibly Samson considered it a symbol of sexual pleasure or an aphrodisiac. Note the use of honey imagery in Song 4:11 and 5:1.
Touching the carcass of a dead animal undoubtedly violated Samson’s Nazirite status. See Num 6:6.

10.text: Then Samson’s father accompanied him to Timnah for the marriage. Samson hosted a party there, for this was customary for bridegrooms to do.

notes.text: Heb “And his father went down to the woman.”
Or “[wedding] feast.”
Heb “the young men.”

11.text: When the Philistines saw he had no attendants, they gave him thirty groomsmen who kept him company.

notes.text: Heb “When they saw him, they gave him thirty companions and they were with him.” Instead of ‏כִּרְאוֹתָם‎ (kirʾotam, “when they saw”) some ancient witnesses (e.g., some mss of the LXX) assume the reading ‏בְּיִרְאָתָם‎ (beyirʾatam, “because they feared”).

12.text: Samson said to them, “I will give you a riddle. If you really can solve it during the seven days the party lasts, I will give you thirty linen robes and thirty sets of clothes.

notes.text: Heb “If you really can tell it to me [during] the seven days of the feast and you find [its answer].”
Heb “changes.”

13.text: But if you cannot solve it, you will give me thirty linen robes and thirty sets of clothes.” They said to him, “Let us hear your riddle.”

notes.text: Heb “you are unable to tell me.”
Heb “Give your riddle so we can hear it.”

14.text: He said to them, “Out of the one who eats came something to eat; out of the strong one came something sweet.” They could not solve the riddle for three days.

15.text: On the fourth day they said to Samson’s bride, “Trick your husband into giving the solution to the riddle. If you refuse, we will burn up you and your father’s family. Did you invite us here to make us poor?”

notes.text: The MT reads “seventh.” In Hebrew there is a difference of only one letter between the words ‏רְבִיעִי‎ (reviʿi, “fourth”) and ‏שְׁבִיעִי‎ (sheviʿi, “seventh”). Some ancient textual witnesses (e.g., LXX and the Syriac Peshitta) read “fourth,” here, which certainly harmonizes better with the preceding verse (cf. “for three days”) and with v. 17. Another option is to change ‏שְׁלֹשֶׁת‎ (sheloshet, “three”) at the end of v. 14 to ‏שֵׁשֶׁת‎ (sheshet, “six”), but the resulting scenario does not account as well for v. 17, which implies the bride had been hounding Samson for more than one day.
Heb “Entice your husband so that he might tell us the riddle.”
Heb “lest.”
The Hebrew text expands the statement: “burn up with fire.” The words “with fire” are redundant in English and have been omitted from the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “house.”

The translation assumes the Hebrew form ‏הֲלֹם‎ (halom, “here,” attested in five Hebrew mss and supported by the Targum), instead of the inexplicable ‏הֲלֹא‎ (haloʾ), a negative particle with interrogative particle prefixed to it.
For discussion of this difficult form, see C. F. Burney, Judges, 364.

16.text: So Samson’s bride cried on his shoulder and said, “You must hate me; you do not love me! You told the young men a riddle, but you have not told me the solution.” He said to her, “Look, I have not even told my father or mother. Do you really expect me to tell you?”

notes.text: Heb “on him.”
Heb “only”; or “simply.”
Heb “the sons of my people.”
Heb “Should I tell you?”

17.text: She cried on his shoulder until the party was almost over. Finally, on the seventh day, he told her because she had nagged him so much. Then she told the young men the solution to the riddle.

notes.text: Heb “on him.”

Heb “the seven days [during] which they held the party.” This does not mean she cried for the entire seven days; v. 15 indicates otherwise. She cried for the remainder of the seven day period, beginning on the fourth day.
Heb “because she forced him.”
Heb “she told the riddle to the sons of her people.”

18.text: On the seventh day, before the sun set, the men of the city said to him, “What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?” He said to them, “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have solved my riddle!”

notes.text: Plowed with my heifer. This statement emphasizes that the Philistines had utilized a source of information which should have been off-limits to them. Heifers were used in plowing (Hos 10:11), but one typically used one’s own farm animals, not another man’s.

19.text: The Lord’s Spirit empowered him. He went down to Ashkelon and killed thirty men. He took their clothes and gave them to the men who had solved the riddle. He was furious as he went back home.

notes.text: Heb “equipment”; or “gear.”
Heb “changes [of clothes].”
Heb “he went up to his father’s house.”

20.text: Samson’s bride was then given to his best man.

notes.text: Heb “to his companion who had been his attendant.”

1.text: Sometime later, during the wheat harvest, Samson took a young goat as a gift and went to visit his bride. He said to her father, “I want to sleep with my bride in her bedroom!” But her father would not let him enter.

notes.text: The wheat harvest took place during the month of May. See O. Borowski, Agriculture in Iron Age Israel, 37, 88.
Heb “Samson visited his wife with a young goat.”
The words “to her father” are supplied in the translation (see the end of the verse).
Heb “I want to approach.” The verb ‏בּוֹא‎ (boʾ) with the preposition ‏אֶל‎ (ʾel) means “come to” or “approach,” but is also used as a euphemism for sexual relations.

Heb “I will go to my wife in the bedroom.” The Hebrew idiom ‏בּוֹא אֶל‎ (boʾ ʾel, “to go to”) often has sexual connotations. The cohortative form used by Samson can be translated as indicating resolve (“I want to go”) or request (“let me go”).

2.text: Her father said, “I really thought you absolutely despised her, so I gave her to your best man. Her younger sister is more attractive than she is. Take her instead!”

notes.text: Heb “saying, I said.” The first person form of ‏אָמַר‎ (ʾamar, “to say”) sometimes indicates self-reflection. The girl’s father uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis.
Heb “hating, you hated.” Once again the girl’s father uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis.
Heb “Is her younger sister not better than her? Let her [i.e., the younger sister] be yours instead of her [i.e., Samson’s ‘bride’]).”

3.text: Samson said to them, “This time I am justified in doing the Philistines harm!”

notes.text: Codex Alexandrinus (A) of the (original) LXX has the singular “to him.”
Heb “I am innocent this time from the Philistines when I do with them harm.”

4.text: Samson went and captured 300 jackals and got some torches. He tied the jackals in pairs by their tails and then tied a torch to each pair.

notes.text: Traditionally, “foxes.”
Heb “He turned tail to tail and placed one torch between the two tails in the middle.”

5.text: He lit the torches and set the jackals loose in the Philistines’ standing grain. He burned up the grain heaps and the standing grain, as well as the vineyards and olive groves.

notes.text: Heb “He set fire to the torches.”

6.text: The Philistines asked, “Who did this?” They were told, “Samson, the Timnite’s son-in-law, because the Timnite took Samson’s bride and gave her to his best man.” So the Philistines went up and burned her and her father.

notes.text: Or “said.”
Heb “and they said.” The subject of the plural verb is indefinite.
Heb “he”; the referent (the Timnite) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “his”; the referent (Samson) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The Hebrew text expands the statement with the additional phrase “burned with fire.” The words “with fire” are redundant in English and have been omitted from the translation for stylistic reasons. Some textual witnesses read “burned…her father’s house,” perhaps under the influence of 14:15. On the other hand, the shorter text may have lost this phrase due to haplography.

7.text: Samson said to them, “Because you did this, I will get revenge against you before I quit fighting.”

notes.text: The Niphal of ‏נָקָם‎ (naqam, “to avenge, to take vengeance”) followed by the preposition ‏ב‎ (bet) has the force “to get revenge against.” See 1 Sam 18:25; Jer 50:15; Ezek 25:12.
Heb “and afterward I will stop.”

8.text: He struck them down and defeated them. Then he went down and lived for a time in the cave in the cliff of Etam.

notes.text: Heb “He struck them, calf on thigh, [with] a great slaughter.” The precise meaning of the phrase “calf on thigh” is uncertain.

9.text: The Philistines went up and invaded Judah. They arrayed themselves for battle in Lehi.

notes.text: Or “camped in.”
Or “spread out.” The Niphal of ‏נָטָשׁ‎ (natash) has this same sense in 2 Sam 5:18, 22.

10.text: The men of Judah said, “Why are you attacking us?” The Philistines said, “We have come up to take Samson prisoner so we can do to him what he has done to us.”

notes.text: Or “come up against.”
Heb “they”; the referent (the Philistines) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

11.text: So 3,000 men of Judah went down to the cave in the cliff of Etam and said to Samson, “Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? Why have you done this to us?” He said to them, “I have only done to them what they have done to me.”

12.text: They said to him, “We have come down to take you prisoner so we can hand you over to the Philistines.” Samson said to them, “Promise me you will not kill me.”

notes.text: Or “swear to me.”
Heb “meet [with hostility]”; “harm.” In light of v. 13, “kill” is an appropriate translation.

13.text: They said to him, “We promise! We will only take you prisoner and hand you over to them. We promise not to kill you.” They tied him up with two brand new ropes and led him up from the cliff.

notes.text: Heb “No,” meaning that they will not harm him.

14.text: When he arrived in Lehi, the Philistines shouted as they approached him. But the Lord’s Spirit empowered him. The ropes around his arms were like flax dissolving in fire, and they melted away from his hands.

notes.text: Heb “rushed on.”
Heb “burned with.”
Heb “his bonds.”

15.text: He happened to see a solid jawbone of a donkey. He grabbed it and struck down 1,000 men.

notes.text: Heb “he found.”
Heb “fresh,” i.e., not decayed and brittle.
Heb “he reached out his hand and took it.”
The Hebrew text adds “with it.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

16.text: Samson then said, “With the jawbone of a donkey I have left them in heaps; with the jawbone of a donkey I have struck down a thousand men!”

notes.text: The precise meaning of the second half of the line (‏חֲמוֹר חֲמֹרָתָיִם‎, khamor khamoratayim) is uncertain. The present translation assumes that the phrase means, “a heap, two heaps” and refers to the heaps of corpses littering the battlefield. Other options include: (a) “I have made donkeys of them” (cf. NIV; see C. F. Burney, Judges, 373, for a discussion of this view, which understands a denominative verb from the noun “donkey”); (b) “I have thoroughly skinned them” (see HALOT 330 s.v. IV cj. ‏חמר‎, which appeals to an Arabic cognate for support); (c) “I have stormed mightily against them,” which assumes the verb ‏חָמַר‎ (khamar, “to ferment; to foam; to boil up”).

17.text: When he finished speaking, he threw the jawbone down and named that place Ramath Lehi.

notes.text: Heb “from his hand.”
The name Ramath Lehi means “Height of the Jawbone.”

18.text: He was very thirsty, so he cried out to the Lord and said, “You have given your servant this great victory. But now must I die of thirst and fall into the hands of these uncircumcised Philistines?”

notes.text: Heb “you have placed into the hand of your servant.”
Heb “the hand of uncircumcised.” “Hand” often represents power or control. “The uncircumcised [ones]” is used as a pejorative and in the context refers to the Philistines.

19.text: So God split open the basin at Lehi and water flowed out from it. When he took a drink, his strength was restored and he revived. For this reason he named the spring En Hakkore. It remains in Lehi to this very day.

notes.text: The word translated “basin” refers to a circular-shaped depression in the land’s surface.
Heb “spirit.”
Heb “named it”; the referent (the spring) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The name En Hakkore means “Spring of the one who cries out.”

20.text: Samson led Israel for twenty years during the days of Philistine prominence.

notes.text: Traditionally, “judged.”
Heb “in the days of the Philistines.”

1.text: Samson went to Gaza. There he saw a prostitute and slept with her.

notes.text: Heb “approached her.” The idiom ‏בּוֹא אֶל‎ (boʾ ʾel, “to go to”) is a euphemism for sexual relations.

2.text: The Gazites were told, “Samson has come here!” So they surrounded the town and hid all night at the city gate, waiting for him to leave. They relaxed all night, thinking, “He will not leave until morning comes; then we will kill him!”

notes.text: Heb “To the Gazites, saying.” A verb is missing from the MT; some ancient Greek witnesses add “it was reported.”

Heb “And they surrounded.” The rest of the verse suggests that “the town” is the object, not “the house.” Though the Gazites knew Samson was in the town, apparently they did not know exactly where he had gone. Otherwise, they could have just gone into or surrounded the house and would not have needed to post guards at the city gate.
Heb “and they lay in wait for him all night in the city gate.”
Heb “were silent.”
Heb “saying.”
The words “He will not leave” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “until the light of the morning.”

3.text: Samson spent half the night with the prostitute; then he got up in the middle of the night and left. He grabbed the doors of the city gate, as well as the two posts, and pulled them right off, bar and all. He put them on his shoulders and carried them up to the top of a hill east of Hebron.

notes.text: Heb “And Samson lay until the middle of the night and arose in the middle of the night.”
Heb “with the bar.”
Heb “which is upon the face of Hebron.”

4.text: After this Samson fell in love with a woman named Delilah, who lived in the Sorek Valley.

5.text: The rulers of the Philistines went up to visit her and said to her, “Trick him! Find out what makes him so strong and how we can subdue him and humiliate him. Each one of us will give you 1,100 silver pieces.”

notes.text: Heb “subdue him in order to humiliate him.”

6.text: So Delilah said to Samson, “Tell me what makes you so strong and how you can be subdued and humiliated.”

notes.text: Heb “how you can be subdued in order to be humiliated.”

7.text: Samson said to her, “If they tie me up with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, I will become weak and be just like any other man.”

notes.text: Or “moist.”
The word refers to a bowstring, probably made from animal tendons. See Ps 11:2; Job 30:11.

8.text: So the rulers of the Philistines brought her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she tied him up with them.

9.text: They hid in the bedroom and then she said to him, “The Philistines are here, Samson!” He snapped the bowstrings as easily as a thread of yarn snaps when it is put close to fire. The secret of his strength was not discovered.

notes.text: Heb “And the ones lying in wait were sitting for her.” The grammatically singular form ‏וְהָאֹרֵב‎ (vehaʾorev) is collective here, referring to the rulers as a group (so also in v. 16).
Heb “are upon you.”
Heb “when it smells fire.”
Heb “His strength was not known.”

10.text: Delilah said to Samson, “Look, you deceived me and told me lies! Now tell me how you can be subdued.”

notes.text: See Gen 31:7; Exod 8:29 [8:25 HT]; Job 13:9; Isa 44:20; Jer 9:4 for other uses of this Hebrew word (II ‏תָּלַל‎, talal), which also occurs in v. 13.

11.text: He said to her, “If they tie me tightly with brand new ropes that have never been used, I will become weak and be just like any other man.”

notes.text: Heb “with which no work has been done.”

12.text: So Delilah took new ropes and tied him with them and said to him, “The Philistines are here, Samson!” (The Philistines were hiding in the bedroom.) But he tore the ropes from his arms as if they were a piece of thread.

notes.text: Heb “are upon you.”
Heb “And the ones lying in wait were sitting in the bedroom.”
Heb “them”; the referent (the ropes) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

13.text: Delilah said to Samson, “Up to now you have deceived me and told me lies. Tell me how you can be subdued.” He said to her, “If you weave the seven braids of my hair into the fabric on the loom and secure it with the pin, I will become weak and be like any other man.”

notes.text: Heb “head” (also in the following verse). By metonymy the head is mentioned in the Hebrew text in place of the hair on it.
Heb “with the web.” For a discussion of how Delilah did this, see C. F. Burney, Judges, 381, and G. F. Moore, Judges (ICC), 353-54.

14.text: So she made him go to sleep, wove the seven braids of his hair into the fabric on the loom, fastened it with the pin, and said to him, “The Philistines are here, Samson!” He woke up and tore away the pin of the loom and the fabric.

notes.text: Heb “are upon you.”

The MT of vv. 13b-14a reads simply, “He said to her, ‘If you weave the seven braids of my head with the web.’ And she fastened with the pin and said to him.” The additional words in the translation, “and secure it with the pin, I will become weak and be like any other man.’ 16:14 So she made him go to sleep, wove the seven braids of his hair into the fabric on the loom,” which without doubt represent the original text, are supplied from the ancient Greek version. (In both vv. 13b and 14a the Greek version has “to the wall” after “with the pin,” but this is an interpretive addition that reflects a misunderstanding of ancient weaving equipment. See G. F. Moore, Judges [ICC], 353-54.) The Hebrew textual tradition was accidentally shortened during the copying process. A scribe’s eye jumped from the first instance of “with the web” to the second, causing him to leave out inadvertently the intervening words.
The Hebrew adds, “from his sleep.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

15.text: She said to him, “How can you say, ‘I love you,’ when you will not share your secret with me? Three times you have deceived me and have not told me what makes you so strong.”

notes.text: Heb “when your heart is not with me.”

16.text: She nagged him every day and pressured him until he was sick to death of it.

notes.text: Heb “forced him with her words.”
Heb “and his spirit was short [i.e., impatient] to the point of death.”

17.text: Finally he told her his secret. He said to her, “My hair has never been cut, for I have been dedicated to God from the time I was conceived. If my head were shaved, my strength would leave me; I would become weak and be just like all other men.”

notes.text: Heb “all his heart.”
Heb “a razor has not come upon my head.”
Or “set apart to God.” Traditionally the Hebrew term ‏נָזִיר‎ (nazir) has been translated “Nazirite.” The word is derived from the verb ‏נָזַר‎ (nazar, “to dedicate; to consecrate; to set apart”).
Heb “from the womb of my mother.”
Heb “I.” The referent has been made more specific in the translation (“my head”).

18.text: When Delilah saw that he had told her his secret, she sent for the rulers of the Philistines, saying, “Come up here again, for he has told me his secret.” So the rulers of the Philistines went up to visit her, bringing the silver in their hands.

notes.text: Heb “all his heart.”
Heb “she sent and summoned.”
The translation follows the Qere, ‏לִי‎ (li, “to me”) rather than the Kethib, ‏לָהּ‎ (lah, “to her”).
Heb “all his heart.”

19.text: She made him go to sleep on her lap and then called a man in to shave off the seven braids of his hair. She made him vulnerable and his strength left him.

notes.text: Heb “on her knees.” The expression is probably euphemistic for sexual intercourse. See HALOT 160-61 s.v. ‏בֶּרֶךְ‎.
Heb “she called for a man and she shaved off.” The point seems to be that Delilah acted through the instrumentality of the man. See J. A. Soggin, Judges (OTL), 254.
Heb “head.” By metonymy the hair of his head is meant.

Heb “She began to humiliate him.” Rather than referring to some specific insulting action on Delilah’s part after Samson’s hair was shaved off, this statement probably means that she, through the devious actions just described, began the process of Samson’s humiliation which culminates in the following verses.

20.text: She said, “The Philistines are here, Samson!” He woke up and thought, “I will do as I did before and shake myself free.” But he did not realize that the Lord had left him.

notes.text: Heb “are upon you.”
The Hebrew adds, “from his sleep.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “and said.”
Heb “I will go out as before.”

21.text: The Philistines captured him and gouged out his eyes. They brought him down to Gaza and bound him in bronze chains. He became a grinder in the prison.

22.text: His hair began to grow back after it had been shaved off.

notes.text: Heb “the hair of his head.”

23.text: The rulers of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to celebrate. They said, “Our god has handed Samson, our enemy, over to us.”

24.text: When the people saw him, they praised their god, saying, “Our god has handed our enemy over to us, the one who ruined our land and killed so many of us!”

notes.text: Most interpret this as a reference to Samson, but this seems premature, since v. 25 suggests he was not yet standing before them. Consequently some prefer to see this statement as displaced and move it to v. 25 (see C. F. Burney, Judges, 387). It seems more likely that the pronoun refers to an image of Dagon.
Heb “multiplied our dead.”

25.text: When they really started celebrating, they said, “Call for Samson so he can entertain us!” So they summoned Samson from the prison and he entertained them. They made him stand between two pillars.

notes.text: Heb “When their heart was good.”
Heb “before them.”

26.text: Samson said to the young man who held his hand, “Position me so I can touch the pillars that support the temple. Then I can lean on them.”

notes.text: Heb “the pillars upon which the house is founded.”

27.text: Now the temple was filled with men and women, and all the rulers of the Philistines were there. There were 3,000 men and women on the roof watching Samson entertain.

notes.text: Heb “house.”

28.text: Samson called to the Lord, “O Sovereign Lord, remember me! Strengthen me just one more time, O God, so I can get swift revenge against the Philistines for my two eyes!”

notes.text: The Hebrew has ‏אֲדֹנָי יֱהֹוִה‎ (ʾadonay yehovih, “Lord Yahweh”).
Heb “so I can get revenge with one act of vengeance.”

29.text: Samson took hold of the two middle pillars that supported the temple and he leaned against them, with his right hand on one and his left hand on the other.

notes.text: Heb “the pillars upon which the house was founded.”

30.text: Samson said, “Let me die with the Philistines!” He pushed hard, and the temple collapsed on the rulers and all the people in it. He killed many more people in his death than he had killed during his life.

notes.text: Heb “he stretched out with strength.”
Heb “And the ones whom he killed in his death were many more than he killed in his life.”

31.text: His brothers and all his family went down and brought him back. They buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father. He had led Israel for twenty years.

notes.text: Heb “and all the house of his father.”
Heb “and lifted him up and brought up.”
Traditionally, “judged.”

1.text: There was a man named Micah from the Ephraimite hill country.

2.text: He said to his mother, “You know the 1,100 pieces of silver which were stolen from you, about which I heard you pronounce a curse? Look here, I have the silver. I stole it, but now I am giving it back to you.” His mother said, “May the Lord reward you, my son!”

notes.text: The words “You know” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “taken.”
Heb “took.”

In the Hebrew text the statement, “but now I am giving it back to you,” appears at the end of v. 3 and is spoken by the mother. But v. 4 indicates that she did not give the money back to her son. Unless the statement is spoken by the woman to the Lord, it appears to be misplaced and fits much better in v. 2. It may have been accidentally omitted from a manuscript, written in the margin, and then later inserted in the wrong place in another manuscript.
Traditionally, “bless.”

3.text: When he gave back to his mother the 1,100 pieces of silver, his mother said, “I solemnly dedicate this silver to the Lord. It will be for my son’s benefit. We will use it to make a carved image and a metal image.”

notes.text: Heb “dedicating, I dedicate.” In this case the emphatic infinitive absolute lends a mood of solemnity to the statement.

Heb “to the Lord from my hand for my son to make a carved image and cast metal image.” She cannot mean that she is now taking the money from her hand and giving it back to her son so he can make an image. Verses 4-6 indicate she took back the money and used a portion of it to hire a silversmith to make an idol for her son to use. The phrase “a carved image and cast metal image” is best taken as referring to two idols (see 18:17-18), even though the verb at the end of v. 4, ‏וַיְהִי‎ (vayehi, “and it was [in the house of Micah]”), is singular.

4.text: When he gave the silver back to his mother, she took 200 pieces of silver to a silversmith, who made them into a carved image and a metal image. She then put them in Micah’s house.

notes.text: Heb “his mother.” The pronoun (“she”) has been substituted for the noun (“mother”) in the translation because of English style.
The Hebrew text has “and gave it.” The referent (the pieces of silver) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “and it was in Micah’s house.”

5.text: Now this man Micah owned a shrine. He made an ephod and some personal idols and hired one of his sons to serve as a priest.

notes.text: Heb “house of God.”
Here an ephod probably refers to a priestly garment (cf. Exod 28:4-6).
Heb “and he filled the hand of one of his sons and he became his priest.”

6.text: In those days Israel had no king. Each man did what he considered to be right.

notes.text: Heb “Each was doing what was right in his [own] eyes.”

7.text: There was a young man from Bethlehem in Judah. He was a Levite who had been temporarily residing among the tribe of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “There was a young man from Bethlehem of Judah, from the tribe of Judah, and he was a Levite, and he was temporarily residing there.”

8.text: This man left the town of Bethlehem in Judah to find another place to live. He came to the Ephraimite hill country and made his way to Micah’s house.

notes.text: Heb “He came to the Ephraimite hill country, to Micah’s house, making his way.”

9.text: Micah said to him, “Where do you come from?” He replied, “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah. I am looking for a new place to live.”

notes.text: Heb “father.” “Father” is here a title of honor that suggests the priest will give advice and protect the interests of the family, primarily by divining God’s will in matters, perhaps through the use of the ephod. Several ancient textual witnesses, including some LXX mss and the Vulgate, support the reading “Moses” (‏מֹשֶׁה‎, mosheh) here. notes.text: Heb “they were making their heart good.”
Heb “and look.”

Heb “the men of the city, men, the sons of wickedness.” The phrases are in apposition; the last phrase specifies what type of men they were. It is not certain if all the men of the city are in view, or just a group of troublemakers. In 20:5 the town leaders are implicated in the crime, suggesting that all the men of the city were involved. If so, the implication is that the entire male population of the town were good-for-nothings.
The Hitpael verb form appears to have an iterative force here, indicating repeated action.

Heb “know.” The expression ‏יָדַע‎ (yadaʿ) “to know” is a euphemism for sexual relations. Elsewhere NET employs the English euphemism “be intimate with” for this use of ‏יָדַע‎ (yadaʿ), but uses a different euphemism here because of the perverse overtones of force in this context. Their intent is to molest him, but their rhetoric tries to minimize their wickedness.

notes.text: The translation assumes the reading ‏מִנּוֹחָה‎ (minnokhah, “from Nohah”; cf. 1 Chr 8:2) rather than the MT’s ‏מְנוּחָה‎ (menukhah, “resting place”).
