According to DNWSI 2:915-16, the noun consistently refers to a spindle in Phoenician, as it does in Ugaritic (see UT 468).

33.text: The king chanted the following lament for Abner: “Should Abner have died like a fool?

34.text: Your hands were not bound, and your feet were not put into irons. You fell the way one falls before criminals.” All the people wept over him again.

notes.text: The translation follows many medieval Hebrew manuscripts and several ancient versions in reading “your hands,” rather than “your hand.”
4QSama lacks the words “all the people.”

35.text: Then all the people came and encouraged David to eat food while it was still day. But David took an oath saying, “God will punish me severely if I taste bread or anything whatsoever before the sun sets!”

notes.text: Heb “Thus God will do to me and thus he will add.”

36.text: All the people noticed this and it pleased them. In fact, everything the king did pleased all the people.

notes.text: Heb “it was good in their eyes.”

37.text: All the people and all Israel realized on that day that the killing of Abner son of Ner was not done at the king’s instigation.

notes.text: Heb “from the king.”

38.text: Then the king said to his servants, “Do you not realize that a great leader has fallen this day in Israel?

notes.text: Heb “a leader and a great one.” The expression is a hendiadys.

39.text: Today I am weak, even though I am anointed as king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too much for me to bear! May the Lord punish appropriately the one who has done this evil thing!”

notes.text: Heb “are hard from me.”
Heb “May the Lord repay the doer of the evil according to his evil” (NASB similar).

1.text: When Ish Bosheth the son of Saul heard that Abner had died in Hebron, he was very disheartened, and all Israel was afraid.

notes.text: The MT does not specify the subject of the verb here, but the reference is to Ish Bosheth, so the name has been supplied in the translation for clarity. 4QSama and the LXX mistakenly read “Mephibosheth.”
Heb “his hands went slack.”

2.text: Now Saul’s son had two men who were in charge of raiding units; one was named Baanah and the other Recab. They were sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, who was a Benjaminite. (Beeroth is regarded as belonging to Benjamin,

notes.text: The present translation, “Saul’s son had two men,” is based on the reading “to the son of Saul,” rather than the MT’s “the son of Saul.” The context requires the preposition to indicate the family relationship.

3.text: for the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have remained there as resident foreigners until the present time.)

notes.text: Heb “until this day.”

4.text: Now Saul’s son Jonathan had a son who was crippled in both feet. He was five years old when the news about Saul and Jonathan arrived from Jezreel. His nurse picked him up and fled, but in her haste to get away, he fell and was injured. Mephibosheth was his name.

notes.text: Heb “and was lame.”

5.text: Now the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite—Recab and Baanah—went at the hottest part of the day to the home of Ish Bosheth, as he was enjoying his midday rest.

6.text: They entered the house under the pretense of getting wheat and mortally wounded him in the stomach. Then Recab and his brother Baanah escaped.

notes.text: For the MT’s ‏וְהֵנָּה‎ (vehennah, “and they,” feminine) read ‏וְהִנֵּה‎ (vehinneh, “and behold”). See the LXX, Syriac Peshitta, and Targum.

The LXX (followed by NLT) reads, “behold the house doorkeeper was cleaning wheat and became drowsy and fell asleep and the brothers Rekcha and Baana avoided notice.” Josephus refers to the LXX with a slight expansion on the tradition in Ant. 7:48. The last sentence appears to follow the Hebrew MT, although understanding the final verb ‏נִמְלָטוּ‎ (nimlatu; Niphal of ‏מָלַט‎, malat) “to escape” as “escaping notice” is without parallel. The beginning of the verse in the LXX shares at least the words “midst of house” and “wheat” with the Hebrew MT. What sort of textual corruption through common scribal copying errors could lead to the different texts is unclear.

Heb “taking wheat.” The reference to getting wheat is obscure and traditionally inferred to mean that they came under the pretense of obtaining wheat (KJV, ESV, NASB, NIV, Holman). However the plausibility of this scenario is not culturally certain.
Heb “and they struck him down.”

7.text: They had entered the house while Ish Bosheth was resting on his bed in his bedroom. They mortally wounded him and then cut off his head. Taking his head, they traveled on the way of the rift valley all that night.

notes.text: After the concluding disjunctive clause at the end of v. 6, the author now begins a more detailed account of the murder and its aftermath.
Heb “he”; the referent (Ish Bosheth) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “they struck him down and killed him.” The expression is a verbal hendiadys.
Heb “and they removed his head.” The Syriac Peshitta and Vulgate lack these words.
The Lucianic Greek recension lacks the words “his head.”
The rift valley is a large geographic feature extending form Galilee to the gulf of Aqaba. The portion in view here runs along the west of the Dead Sea.

8.text: They brought the head of Ish Bosheth to David in Hebron, saying to the king, “Look! The head of Ish Bosheth son of Saul, your enemy who sought your life! The Lord has granted vengeance to my lord the king this day against Saul and his descendants!”

notes.text: Heb “from.”

9.text: David replied to Recab and his brother Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, “As surely as the Lord lives, who has delivered my life from all adversity,

10.text: when someone told me that Saul was dead—even though he thought he was bringing good news —I seized him and killed him in Ziklag. That was the good news I gave to him!

notes.text: Heb “and he was like a bearer of good news in his eyes.”

11.text: Surely when wicked men have killed an innocent man as he slept in his own house, should I not now require his blood from your hands and remove you from the earth?”

notes.text: Heb “on his bed.”
See HALOT 146 s.v. II ‏בער‎. Some derive the verb from a homonym meaning “to burn; to consume.”

12.text: So David issued orders to the soldiers and they put them to death. Then they cut off their hands and feet and hung them near the pool in Hebron. But they took the head of Ish Bosheth and buried it in the tomb of Abner in Hebron.

notes.text: The antecedent of the pronoun “them” (which is not present in the Hebrew text, but implied) is not entirely clear. Presumably it is the corpses that were hung and not merely the detached hands and feet; cf. NIV “hung the (their NRSV, NLT) bodies”; the alternative is represented by TEV “cut off their hands and feet, which they hung up.”
4QSama mistakenly reads “Mephibosheth” here.
The LXX adds “the son of Ner” by conformity with common phraseology elsewhere.
Some mss of the LXX lack the phrase “in Hebron.”

1.text: All the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron saying, “Look, we are your very flesh and blood!

notes.text: Heb “look we are your bone and your flesh.”

2.text: In the past, when Saul was our king, you were the real leader in Israel. The Lord said to you, ‘You will shepherd my people Israel; you will rule over Israel.’”

notes.text: Heb “you were the one leading out and the one leading in Israel.”

3.text: When all the leaders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, King David made an agreement with them in Hebron before the Lord. They designated David as king over Israel.

notes.text: Heb “elders.”
Heb “and the king, David, cut for them a covenant.”
Heb “anointed.”

4.text: David was thirty years old when he began to reign and he reigned for forty years.

5.text: In Hebron he reigned over Judah for seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned for thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.

6.text: Then the king and his men advanced to Jerusalem against the Jebusites who lived in the land. The Jebusites said to David, “You cannot invade this place! Even the blind and the lame will turn you back, saying, ‘David cannot invade this place!’”

notes.text: The Hebrew text has “he” rather than “the Jebusites.” The referent has been specified in the translation for clarity. In the Syriac Peshitta and some mss of the Targum the verb is plural rather than singular.

7.text: But David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David).

8.text: David said on that day, “Whoever attacks the Jebusites must approach the ‘lame’ and the ‘blind’ who are David’s enemies by going through the water tunnel.” For this reason it is said, “The blind and the lame cannot enter the palace.”

notes.text: There is some confusion among the witnesses concerning this word. The Kethib is the Qal perfect third common plural ‏שָׂנְאוּ‎ (saneʾu, “they hated”), referring to the Jebusites’ attitude toward David. The Qere is the Qal passive participle construct plural ‏שְׂנֻאֵי‎ (senuʾe, “hated”), referring to David’s attitude toward the Jebusites. 4QSama has the Qal perfect third person feminine singular ‏שָׂנְאָה‎ (saneʾah, “hated”), the subject of which would be “the soul of David.” The difference is minor and the translation adopted above works for either the Kethib or the Qere.
The meaning of the Hebrew term has been debated. For a survey of various views, see P. K. McCarter, II Samuel (AB), 139-40.

If a water tunnel is in view here, it is probably the so-called Warren’s Shaft that extends up from Hezekiah’s tunnel. It would have provided a means for surprise attack against the occupants of the City of David. The LXX seems not to understand the reference here, translating “by the water shaft” as “with a small knife.”
Heb “the house.” TEV takes this as a reference to the temple (“the Lord’s house”).

9.text: So David lived in the fortress and called it the City of David. David built all around it, from the terrace inwards.

10.text: David’s power grew steadily, for the Lord God of Heaven’s Armies was with him.

notes.text: 4QSama and the LXX lack the word “God,” probably due to harmonization with the more common biblical phrase “the Lord of hosts.”
Traditionally, “the Lord God of hosts” (KJV, NASB); NIV, NLT “the Lord God Almighty”; CEV “the Lord (+ God NCV) All-Powerful.”
The translation assumes that the disjunctive clause is circumstantial-causal, giving the reason for David’s success.

notes.text: Heb “a house.”

notes.text: Heb “anointed.”

notes.text: The infinitive absolute lends emphasis to the following verb.

notes.text: Heb “they”; the referent (the Philistines) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

notes.text: The words “what to do” are not in the Hebrew text.
The words “this time” are not in the Hebrew text.
Heb “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Some translate as “balsam trees” (cf. NASB, NIV, NRSV, NJB, NLT); cf. KJV, NKJV, ASV “mulberry trees”; NAB “mastic trees”; NEB, REB “aspens.” The exact identification of the type of tree or plant is uncertain.

notes.text: Heb “from Gibeon until you enter Gezer.”

notes.text: The translation understands the verb to be a defective spelling of ‏וַיֶּאֱסֹף‎ (vayyeʾesof) due to quiescence of the letter ‏א‎ (alef). The root therefore is ‏אָסַף‎ (ʾasaf, “to gather”). The Masoretes, however, pointed the verb as ‏וַיֹּסֶף‎ (vayyosef), understanding it to be a form of ‏יָסַף‎ (yasaf, “to add”). This does not fit the context, which calls for a verb of gathering.
Or “chosen.”

2.text: David and all the men who were with him traveled to Baalah in Judah to bring up from there the ark of God which is called by the name of the Lord of Heaven’s Armies, who sits enthroned between the cherubim that are on it.

notes.text: Heb “arose and went.”
Heb “from,” but the following context indicates they traveled to this location.
This is another name for Kiriath Jearim (see 1 Chr 13:6).

The MT has here a double reference to the name (‏שֵׁם שֵׁם‎, shem shem). Many medieval Hebrew mss in the first occurrence point the word differently and read the adverb ‏שָׁם‎ (sham, “there”). This is also the understanding of the Syriac Peshitta (Syr., taman). While this yields an acceptable understanding to the text, it is more likely that the MT reading results from dittography. If the word did occur twice, one might have expected the first occurrence to have the article. The present translation therefore reads ‏שֵׁם‎ only once.

Heb “God.”

notes.text: Heb “and David was dancing with all his strength before the Lord, and David was girded with a linen ephod.”

16.text: As the ark of the Lord entered the City of David, Saul’s daughter Michal looked out the window. When she saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, she despised him.

notes.text: The Hebrew text adds “in her heart.” Cf. CEV “she was disgusted (+ with him TEV)”; NLT “was filled with contempt for him”; NCV “she hated him.”

17.text: They brought the ark of the Lord and put it in its place in the middle of the tent that David had pitched for it. Then David offered burnt sacrifices and peace offerings before the Lord.

notes.text: The Syriac Peshitta lacks “in its place.”

18.text: When David finished offering the burnt sacrifices and peace offerings, he pronounced a blessing over the people in the name of the Lord of Heaven’s Armies.

19.text: He then handed out to each member of the entire assembly of Israel, both men and women, a portion of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake. Then all the people went home.

notes.text: Heb “to all the people, to all the throng of Israel.”

The Hebrew word used here ‏אֶשְׁפָּר‎ (ʾespar) is found in the OT only here and in the parallel passage found in 1 Chr 16:3. Its exact meaning is uncertain, although the context indicates that it was a food of some sort (cf. KJV “a good piece of flesh”; NRSV “a portion of meat”). The translation adopted here (“date cake”) follows the lead of the Greek translations of the LXX, Aquila, and Symmachus (cf. NASB, NIV, NLT).
Heb “and all the people went, each to his house.”

20.text: When David went home to pronounce a blessing on his own house, Michal, Saul’s daughter, came out to meet him. She said, “How the king of Israel has distinguished himself this day! He has exposed himself today before his servants’ slave girls the way a vulgar fool might do!”

notes.text: Heb “and David returned to bless his house.”
Heb “David.” The name has been replaced by the pronoun (“him”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “honored.”
Heb “one of the foolish ones.”

21.text: David replied to Michal, “It was before the Lord! I was celebrating before the Lord, who chose me over your father and his entire family and appointed me as leader over the Lord’s people Israel.

notes.text: Heb “all his house”; CEV “anyone else in your family.”

22.text: I am willing to shame and humiliate myself even more than this. But with the slave girls whom you mentioned, let me be distinguished.”

notes.text: Heb “and I will shame myself still more than this and I will be lowly in my eyes.”

23.text: Now Michal, Saul’s daughter, had no children to the day of her death.

1.text: The king settled into his palace, for the Lord gave him relief from all his enemies on all sides.

notes.text: Heb “house” (also in the following verse).
Or “rest.”
The translation understands the disjunctive clause in v. 1b as circumstantial-causal.

2.text: The king said to Nathan the prophet, “Look! I am living in a palace made from cedar, while the ark of God sits in the middle of a tent.”

3.text: Nathan replied to the king, “You should go and do whatever you have in mind, for the Lord is with you.”

notes.text: Several medieval Hebrew mss and the Syriac Peshitta lack this word.
Heb “all that is in your heart.”

4.text: That night the Lord’s message came to Nathan,

5.text: “Go, tell my servant David, ‘This is what the Lord has said: Do you really intend to build a house for me to live in?

6.text: I have not lived in a house from the time I brought the Israelites up from Egypt to the present day. Instead, I was traveling with them and living in a tent.

notes.text: Heb “in a tent and in a dwelling.” The expression is a hendiadys, using two terms to express one idea.

7.text: Wherever I moved among all the Israelites, I did not say to any of their leaders whom I appointed to care for my people Israel, “Why have you not built me a house made from cedar?”’

notes.text: Heb “Did I speak a word?” In the Hebrew text the statement is phrased as a rhetorical question.
Heb “tribes of Israel” (so KJV, NASB, NCV), but the parallel passage in 1 Chr 17:6 has “judges of Israel.”
Heb “whom I commanded to shepherd” (so NIV, NRSV).

8.text: “So now, say this to my servant David, ‘This is what the Lord of Heaven’s Armies has said: I took you from the pasture and from your work as a shepherd to make you leader of my people Israel.

notes.text: Heb “and from after the sheep.”

9.text: I was with you wherever you went, and I defeated all your enemies before you. Now I will make you as famous as the great men of the earth.

notes.text: Heb “cut off.”
Heb “and I will make for you a great name like the name of the great ones who are in the earth.”

10.text: I will establish a place for my people Israel and settle them there; they will live there and not be disturbed anymore. Violent men will not oppress them again, as they did in the beginning

notes.text: Heb “plant.”
Heb “shaken.”
Heb “the sons of violence.”

11.text: and during the time when I appointed judges to lead my people Israel. Instead, I will give you relief from all your enemies. The Lord declares to you that he himself will build a dynastic house for you.

notes.text: Or “rest.”

In the Hebrew text the verb is apparently perfect with vav consecutive, which would normally suggest a future sense (“he will declare”; so the LXX, ἀπαγγελεῖ [apangelei]). But the context seems instead to call for a present or past nuance (“he declares” or “he has declared”). The synoptic passage in 1 Chr 17:10 has ‏וָאַגִּד‎ (vaʾaggid, “and I declared”). The construction used in 2 Sam 7:11 highlights this important statement.
Heb “the Lord.”

Heb “house,” but used here in a metaphorical sense, referring to a royal dynasty. Here the Lord’s use of the word plays off the literal sense that David had in mind as he contemplated building a temple for the Lord. To reflect this in the English translation the adjective “dynastic” has been supplied.

12.text: When the time comes for you to die, I will raise up your descendant, one of your own sons, to succeed you, and I will establish his kingdom.

notes.text: Heb, “when your days are full and you lie down with your ancestors.”
Heb “your seed after you who comes out from your insides.”

13.text: He will build a house for my name, and I will make his dynasty permanent.

notes.text: Heb “and I will establish the throne of his kingdom permanently.”

14.text: I will become his father and he will become my son. When he sins, I will correct him with the rod of men and with wounds inflicted by human beings.

15.text: But my loyal love will not be removed from him as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before you.

16.text: Your house and your kingdom will stand before me permanently; your dynasty will be permanent.’”

notes.text: Heb “before you.” A few medieval Hebrew mss read instead “before me,” which makes better sense contextually. (See also the LXX and the Syriac Peshitta.) The MT reading is probably the result of dittography (note the ‏כ‎ [kaf] at the beginning of the next form), with the extra ‏כ‎ then being interpreted as a pronominal suffix.
Heb “throne.”

17.text: Nathan told David all these words that were revealed to him.

notes.text: Heb “according to all these words and according to all this revelation, so Nathan said to David.”

18.text: King David went in, sat before the Lord, and said, “Who am I, O Sovereign Lord, and what is my family, that you should have brought me to this point?

notes.text: Heb “house.”

19.text: And you didn’t stop there, O Lord God! You have also spoken about the future of your servant’s family. Is this your usual way of dealing with men, O Sovereign Lord?

notes.text: Heb “and this was small in your eyes, O Lord God, so you spoke concerning the house of your servant for a distance.”

Heb “and this [is] the law of man”; KJV “is this the manner of man, O Lord God?”; NAB “this too you have shown to man”; NRSV “May this be instruction for the people, O Lord God!” This part of the verse is very enigmatic; no completely satisfying solution has yet been suggested. The present translation tries to make sense of the MT by understanding the phrase as a question that underscores the uniqueness of God’s dealings with David as described here. The parallel passage in 1 Chr 17:17 reads differently (see the note there).

20.text: What more can David say to you? You have given your servant special recognition, O Sovereign Lord!

notes.text: Heb “and you know your servant.” The verb here refers to recognizing another in a special way and giving them special treatment (see 1 Chr 17:18). Some English versions take this to refer to the Lord’s knowledge of David himself: CEV “you know my thoughts”; NLT “know what I am really like.”

21.text: For the sake of your promise and according to your purpose you have done this great thing in order to reveal it to your servant.

notes.text: Heb “for the sake of your word and according to your heart.”
Heb “to make known, your servant.”

22.text: Therefore you are great, O Sovereign Lord, for there is none like you. There is no God besides you! What we have heard is true.

notes.text: Heb “in all which we heard with our ears.” The phrase translated “in all” ‏בְּכֹל‎ (bekhol) should probably be emended to “according to all” ‏כְּכֹל‎ (kekhol).

23.text: Who is like your people, Israel, a unique nation on the earth? Their God went to claim a nation for himself and to make a name for himself! You did great and awesome acts for your land, before your people whom you delivered for yourself from the Egyptian empire and its gods.

notes.text: Heb “a nation, one.”
Heb “whose God” or “because God.” In the Hebrew text this clause is subordinated to what precedes. The clauses are separated in the translation for stylistic reasons.
The verb is plural in Hebrew, agreeing grammatically with the divine name, which is a plural of degree.
Heb “redeem.”
Heb “and to do for you [plural form] the great [thing] and awesome [things] for your land.”
Heb “from Egypt, nations and their gods.” The LXX has “nations and tents,” which reflects a mistaken metathesis of letters in ‏אֶלֹהָיו‎ (ʾelohayv, “its gods”) and ‏אֹהָלָיו‎ (ʾohalayv, “its tents”).

24.text: You made Israel your very own people for all time. You, O Lord, became their God.

notes.text: Heb “and you established for yourself your people Israel for yourself for a people permanently.”

25.text: So now, O Lord God, make this promise you have made about your servant and his family a permanent reality. Do as you promised,

notes.text: Heb “and now, O Lord God, the word which you spoke concerning your servant and concerning his house, establish permanently.”
Heb “as you have spoken.”

26.text: so you may gain lasting fame, as people say, ‘The Lord of Heaven’s Armies is God over Israel!’ The dynasty of your servant David will be established before you,

notes.text: Heb “and your name might be great permanently.” Following the imperative in v. 23b, the prefixed verbal form with vav conjunctive indicates purpose/result.
Heb “saying.” The words “as people” are supplied in the translation for clarification and stylistic reasons.
Heb “the house.” See the note on “dynastic house” in the following verse.

27.text: for you, O Lord of Heaven’s Armies, the God of Israel, have told your servant, ‘I will build you a dynastic house.’ That is why your servant has had the courage to pray this prayer to you.

notes.text: Heb “have uncovered the ear of.”
Heb “a house.” This maintains the wordplay from v. 11 (see the note on the word “house” there) and is continued in v. 29.
Heb “has found his heart.”

28.text: Now, O Sovereign Lord, you are the true God. May your words prove to be true! You have made this good promise to your servant.

notes.text: Heb “the God.” The article indicates uniqueness here.
The translation understands the prefixed verb form as a jussive, indicating David’s wish/prayer. Another option is to take the form as an imperfect and translate “your words are true.”
Heb “and you have spoken to your servant this good thing.”

29.text: Now be willing to bless your servant’s dynasty so that it may stand permanently before you, for you, O Sovereign Lord, have spoken. By your blessing may your servant’s dynasty be blessed from now on into the future!”

notes.text: Heb “house” (again later in this verse). See the note on “dynastic house” in v. 27.
Or “permanently”; cf. NLT “it is an eternal blessing.”

1.text: Later David defeated the Philistines and subdued them. David took Metheg Ammah from the Philistines.

notes.text: Heb “the bridle of one cubit.” Many English versions treat this as a place name because the parallel text in 1 Chr 18:1 reads “Gath” (which is used by NLT here). It is possible that “the bridle of one cubit” is to be understood as “the token of surrender,” referring to the Philistine’s defeat rather than a specific place (cf. TEV, CEV).
Heb “from the hand [i.e., control] of the Philistines.”

2.text: He defeated the Moabites. He made them lie on the ground and then used a rope to measure them off. He put two-thirds of them to death and spared the other third. The Moabites became David’s subjects and brought tribute.

notes.text: Heb “and he measured [with] two [lengths] of rope to put to death and [with] the fullness of the rope to keep alive.”
Heb “and the Moabites were servants of David, carriers of tribute.”

3.text: David defeated King Hadadezer son of Rehob of Zobah when he came to reestablish his authority over the Euphrates River.

notes.text: The LXX has ἐπιστῆσαι (epistēsai, “cause to stand”). See the parallel text in 1 Chr 18:3.
Heb “hand.”

The MT does not have the name “Euphrates” in the text. It is supplied in the margin (Qere) as one of ten places where the Masoretes believed that something was “to be read although it was not written” in the text as they had received it. The ancient versions (LXX, Syriac Peshitta, Vulgate) include the word. See also the parallel text in 1 Chr 18:3.

4.text: David seized from him 1,700 charioteers and 20,000 infantrymen. David cut the hamstrings of all but 100 of the chariot horses.

notes.text: The LXX has “1,000 chariots and 7,000 charioteers,” a reading adopted in the text of the NIV. See the parallel text in 1 Chr 18:4.
Heb “and David cut the hamstrings of all the chariot horses, and he left from them 100 chariot horses.”

5.text: The Arameans of Damascus came to help King Hadadezer of Zobah, but David killed 22,000 of the Arameans.

6.text: David placed garrisons in the territory of the Arameans of Damascus; the Arameans became David’s subjects and brought tribute. The Lord protected David wherever he campaigned.

notes.text: Or “delivered.”
Or “wherever he went.”

7.text: David took the golden shields that belonged to Hadadezer’s servants and brought them to Jerusalem.

notes.text: The LXX includes seventeen words (in Greek) at the end of v. 7 that are not found in the MT. The LXX addition is as follows: “And Sousakim king of Egypt took them when he came up to Jerusalem in the days of Rehoboam the son of Solomon.” This Greek reading now finds Hebrew support in 4QSama. For a reconstruction of this poorly preserved Qumran text see E. C. Ulrich, Jr., The Qumran Text of Samuel and Josephus (HSM), 45-48.

8.text: From Tebah and Berothai, Hadadezer’s cities, King David took a great deal of bronze.

notes.text: Heb “Betah” (so KJV, NASB, NRSV), but the name should probably be corrected to “Tebah.” See the parallel text in 1 Chr 18:8.

9.text: When King Toi of Hamath heard that David had defeated the entire army of Hadadezer,

notes.text: The name is spelled “Tou” in the parallel text in 1 Chr 18:9. NIV adopts the spelling “Tou” here.

10.text: he sent his son Joram to King David to extend his best wishes and to pronounce a blessing on him for his victory over Hadadezer, for Toi had been at war with Hadadezer. He brought with him various items made of silver, gold, and bronze.

notes.text: Heb “Toi.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun in the translation for stylistic reasons.
The name appears as “Hadoram” in the parallel text in 1 Chr 18:10.
Heb “to ask concerning him for peace.”
Heb “and to bless him because he fought with Hadadezer and defeated him, for Hadadezer was a man of battles with Toi.”
Heb “and in his hand were items of silver and items of gold and items of bronze.”

11.text: King David dedicated these things to the Lord, along with the dedicated silver and gold that he had taken from all the nations that he had subdued,

notes.text: Heb “also them King David made holy to the Lord.”
Heb “with the silver and the gold that he had dedicated from.”

12.text: including Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and Amalek. This also included some of the plunder taken from King Hadadezer son of Rehob of Zobah.

notes.text: Heb “from.”

Heb “Aram.” A few Hebrew mss along with the LXX and Syriac read “Edom” (cf. 2 Sam 8:14 and 1 Chr 18:11). Aram and Edom are spelled similarly, the difference being a ‏ד‎ (dalet) vs. a ‏ר‎ (resh). Besides the textual witnesses, the geography in v. 13, the Valley of Salt, fits Edom and not Aram.
Heb “and from the plunder of.”

13.text: David became famous when he returned from defeating the Edomites in the Valley of Salt; he defeated 18,000 in all.

notes.text: Heb “made a name.”
See the note on “Aram” in v. 12.
The words “he defeated” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

14.text: He placed garrisons throughout Edom, and all the Edomites became David’s subjects. The Lord protected David wherever he campaigned.

notes.text: The MT is repetitious here: “He placed in Edom garrisons; in all Edom he placed garrisons.” The Vulgate lacks “in all Edom”; most of the Greek tradition (with the exception of the Lucianic recension and the recension of Origen) and the Syriac Peshitta lack “he placed garrisons.” The MT reading appears here to be the result of a conflation of variant readings.

15.text: David reigned over all Israel; he guaranteed justice for all his people.

notes.text: Heb “and David was doing what is just and fair for all his people.”

16.text: Joab son of Zeruiah was general in command of the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was secretary;

notes.text: Heb “was over.”

17.text: Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests; Seraiah was scribe;

notes.text: Here Ahimelech is called “the son of Abiathar,” but NCV, CEV, and REB reverse this to conform with 1 Sam 22:20. Most recent English versions (e.g., NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT) retain the order found in the MT.

18.text: Benaiah son of Jehoiada supervised the Kerethites and Pelethites; and David’s sons were priests.

notes.text: The translation follows the Syriac Peshitta, Targum, and Vulgate in reading “over,” rather than the simple conjunction that appears in MT. See also the parallel passage in 1 Chr 18:17.

That David’s sons could have been priests, in light of the fact that they were not of the priestly lineage, is strange. One must assume either (1) that the word “priest” (‏כֹּהֵן‎, kohen) during this period of time could be used in a broader sense of “chief ruler” (KJV); “chief minister” (ASV, NASB), or “royal adviser” (NIV), perhaps based on the parallel passage in 1 Chr 18:17 which has “the king’s leading officials”, or (2) that in David’s day members of the king’s family could function as a special category of “priests” (cf. NLT “priestly leaders”). The latter option seems to be the more straightforward way of understanding the word in 2 Sam 8:18.

1.text: Then David asked, “Is anyone still left from the family of Saul, so that I may extend kindness to him for the sake of Jonathan?”

notes.text: 2 Samuel 9-20 is known as the Succession Narrative. It is a literary unit that describes David’s efforts at consolidating his own kingdom following the demise of King Saul; it also provides the transition to subsequent leadership on the part of David’s successor Solomon.
Heb “house.”

2.text: Now there was a servant from Saul’s house named Ziba, so he was summoned to David. The king asked him, “Are you Ziba?” He replied, “At your service.”

notes.text: Heb “your servant.”

3.text: The king asked, “Is there not someone left from Saul’s family that I may extend God’s kindness to him?” Ziba said to the king, “One of Jonathan’s sons is left; both of his feet are crippled.”

notes.text: Heb “house.”

4.text: The king asked him, “Where is he?” Ziba told the king, “He is at the house of Makir son of Ammiel in Lo Debar.”

5.text: So King David had him brought from the house of Makir son of Ammiel in Lo Debar.

notes.text: Heb “sent and took him.”
Heb “from.”

6.text: When Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, he bowed low with his face toward the ground. David said, “Mephibosheth?” He replied, “Yes, at your service.”

notes.text: Heb “he fell on his face and bowed down.”
Heb “Look, your servant.”

7.text: David said to him, “Don’t be afraid, because I will certainly extend kindness to you for the sake of Jonathan your father. I will give back to you all the land that belonged to your grandfather Saul, and you will be a regular guest at my table.”

notes.text: Heb “and you will eat food at my table continually.”

8.text: Then Mephibosheth bowed and said, “Of what importance am I, your servant, that you show regard for a dead dog like me?”

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Mephibosheth) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “What is your servant, that you turn to a dead dog which is like me?”

9.text: Then the king summoned Ziba, Saul’s attendant, and said to him, “Everything that belonged to Saul and to his entire house I hereby give to your master’s grandson.

10.text: You will cultivate the land for him—you and your sons and your servants. You will bring its produce and it will be food for your master’s grandson to eat. But Mephibosheth, your master’s grandson, will be a regular guest at my table.” (Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.)

notes.text: Heb “work.”
The Hebrew text implies, but does not actually contain, the words “its produce” here.
The words “it will be,” though present in the MT, are absent from the LXX, the Syriac Peshitta, and Vulgate.
Heb “and he will eat it.”

11.text: Ziba said to the king, “Your servant will do everything that my lord the king has instructed his servant to do.” So Mephibosheth was a regular guest at David’s table, just as though he were one of the king’s sons.

notes.text: Heb “eating.”

Heb “my table.” But the first person reference to David is awkward here since the quotation of David’s words has already been concluded in v. 10; nor does the “my” refer to Ziba, since the latter part of v. 11 does not seem to be part of Ziba’s response to the king. The ancient versions are not unanimous in the way that they render the phrase. The LXX has “the table of David” (τῆς τραπέζης Δαυιδ, tēs trapezēs Dauid); the Syriac Peshitta has “the table of the king” (patureh demalkaʾ); the Vulgate has “your table” (mensam tuam). The present translation follows the LXX.

12.text: Now Mephibosheth had a young son whose name was Mica. All the members of Ziba’s household were Mephibosheth’s servants.

13.text: Mephibosheth was living in Jerusalem, for he was a regular guest at the king’s table. But both his feet were crippled.

1.text: Later the king of the Ammonites died and his son Hanun succeeded him.

notes.text: Heb “reigned in his place.”

2.text: David said, “I will express my loyalty to Hanun son of Nahash just as his father was loyal to me.” So David sent his servants with a message expressing sympathy over his father’s death. When David’s servants entered the land of the Ammonites,

notes.text: Heb “do loyalty.”
Heb “did loyalty.”
Heb “and David sent to console him by the hand of his servants concerning his father.”

3.text: the Ammonite officials said to their lord Hanun, “Do you really think David is trying to honor your father by sending these messengers to express his sympathy? No, David has sent his servants to you to get information about the city and spy on it so they can overthrow it!”

notes.text: Heb “Is David honoring your father in your eyes when he sends to you ones consoling?”
Heb “Is it not to explore the city and to spy on it and to overthrow it [that] David has sent his servants to you?”

4.text: So Hanun seized David’s servants and shaved off half of each one’s beard. He cut the lower part of their robes off so that their buttocks were exposed, and then sent them away.

notes.text: Heb “and he cut their robes in the middle unto their buttocks.”

5.text: Messengers told David what had happened, so he sent them to the men who were thoroughly humiliated. The king said, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown again; then you may come back.”

notes.text: Heb “they”; the referent (the messengers) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The words “what had happened” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

6.text: When the Ammonites realized that David was disgusted with them, they sent and hired 20,000 foot soldiers from Aram Beth Rehob and Aram Zobah, in addition to 1,000 men from the king of Maacah and 12,000 men from Ish Tob.

notes.text: Heb “that they were a stench [i.e., disgusting] with David.”
Heb “the Ammonites.”
Or “Arameans of Beth Rehob and Arameans of Zobah.”

Or perhaps “the men of Tob.” The ancient versions (the LXX, the Syriac Peshitta, and Vulgate) understand the name to be “Ish Tob.” It is possible that “Ish” is dittographic and that we should read simply “Tob,” a reading adopted by a number of recent English versions.

7.text: When David heard the news, he sent Joab and the entire army to meet them.

notes.text: The words “the news” and “to meet them” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons and for clarification.

8.text: The Ammonites marched out and were deployed for battle at the entrance of the city gate, while the men from Aram Zobah, Rehob, Ish Tob, and Maacah were by themselves in the field.

9.text: When Joab saw that the battle would be fought on two fronts, he chose some of Israel’s best men and deployed them against the Arameans.

notes.text: Heb “and Joab saw that the face of the battle was to him before and behind and he chose from all the best in Israel and arranged to meet Aram.”

10.text: He put his brother Abishai in charge of the rest of the army and they were deployed against the Ammonites.

notes.text: Heb “people.”
Heb “he arranged.”

11.text: Joab said, “If the Arameans start to overpower me, you come to my rescue. If the Ammonites start to overpower you, I will come to your rescue.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Joab) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “if Aram is stronger than me.”
Heb “if the sons of Ammon are stronger than you.”

12.text: Be strong! Let’s fight bravely for the sake of our people and the cities of our God! The Lord will do what he decides is best!”

notes.text: Heb “and the Lord will do what is good in his eyes.”

13.text: So Joab and his men marched out to do battle with the Arameans, and they fled before him.

notes.text: Heb “and the army which was with him.”

14.text: When the Ammonites saw the Arameans flee, they fled before his brother Abishai and went into the city. Joab withdrew from fighting the Ammonites and returned to Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “and Joab returned from against the sons of Ammon and entered.”

15.text: When the Arameans realized that they had been defeated by Israel, they consolidated their forces.

notes.text: Heb “were gathered together.”

16.text: Then Hadadezer sent for Arameans from beyond the Euphrates River, and they came to Helam. Shobach, the general in command of Hadadezer’s army, led them.

notes.text: Heb “and Hadadezer sent and brought out Aram which is.”
Heb “from beyond the River.” The name “Euphrates” has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
Heb “was before them.”

17.text: When David was informed, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan River, and came to Helam. The Arameans deployed their forces against David and fought with him.

notes.text: The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

18.text: The Arameans fled before Israel. David killed 700 Aramean charioteers and 40,000 foot soldiers. He also struck down Shobach, the general in command of the army, who died there.

notes.text: Heb “horsemen” (so KJV, NASB, NCV, NRSV, NLT) but the Lucianic recension of the LXX reads “foot soldiers,” as does the parallel text in 1 Chr 19:18. Cf. NAB, NIV.

19.text: When all the kings who were subject to Hadadezer saw they were defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and became subjects of Israel. The Arameans were no longer willing to help the Ammonites.

notes.text: Heb “the servants of Hadadezer.”
Heb “and they served them.”

1.text: In the spring of the year, at the time when kings normally conduct wars, David sent out Joab with his officers and the entire Israelite army. They defeated the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah. But David stayed behind in Jerusalem.

notes.text: Codex Leningrad (B19A), on which BHS is based, has here “messengers” (‏הַמַּלְאָכִים‎, hammalʾakhim), probably as the result of contamination from the occurrence of that word in v. 4. The present translation follows most Hebrew mss and the ancient versions, which read “kings” (‏הַמֶּלָאכִים‎, hammelakhim).
Heb “go out.”
Heb “and his servants with him.”
Heb “all Israel.”
The disjunctive clause contrasts David’s inactivity with the army’s activity.

2.text: One evening David got up from his bed and walked around on the roof of his palace. From the roof he saw a woman bathing. Now this woman was very attractive.

notes.text: Heb “on the roof of the house of the king.” So also in vv. 8, 9.
The disjunctive clause highlights this observation and builds the tension of the story.

3.text: So David sent someone to inquire about the woman. The messenger said, “Isn’t this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?”

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (the messenger) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

4.text: David sent some messengers to get her. She came to him and he went to bed with her. (Now at that time she was in the process of purifying herself from her menstrual uncleanness.) Then she returned to her home.

notes.text: Heb “and David sent messengers and he took her.”

The expression ‏בּוֹא אֶל‎ (boʾ ʾel) means “come to” or “approach,” but is also used as a euphemism for sexual relations, the implied purpose for approaching someone. Here it refers only to the stage of approaching while the next verb describes the result. That she is the subject of this verb (while David is the subject of the next verb) probably indicates that the act was consensual.
Heb “he lay down with her.” The verb ‏שָׁכַב‎ (shakav) “to lie down” can be a euphemism for going to bed for sexual relations.

The parenthetical disjunctive clause further heightens the tension by letting the reader know that Bathsheba, having just completed her menstrual cycle, is ripe for conception. See P. K. McCarter, II Samuel (AB), 286. Since she just had her period, it will also be obvious to those close to the scene that Uriah, who has been away fighting, cannot be the father of the child.

5.text: The woman conceived and then sent word to David saying, “I’m pregnant.”

6.text: So David sent a message to Joab that said, “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” So Joab sent Uriah to David.

7.text: When Uriah came to him, David asked about how Joab and the army were doing and how the campaign was going.

notes.text: Heb “concerning the peace of Joab and concerning the peace of the people and concerning the peace of the battle.”

8.text: Then David said to Uriah, “Go down to your home and relax.” When Uriah left the palace, the king sent a gift to him.

notes.text: Heb “and wash your feet.”
Heb “and there went out after him the gift of the king.”

9.text: But Uriah stayed at the door of the palace with all the servants of his lord. He did not go down to his house.

notes.text: The Lucianic recension of the Old Greek translation lacks the word “all.”

10.text: So they informed David, “Uriah has not gone down to his house.” So David said to Uriah, “Haven’t you just arrived from a journey? Why haven’t you gone down to your house?”

11.text: Uriah replied to David, “The ark and Israel and Judah reside in temporary shelters, and my lord Joab and my lord’s soldiers are camping in the open field. Should I go to my house to eat and drink and go to bed with my wife? As surely as you are alive, I will not do this thing!”

notes.text: Heb “lie with.” The verb ‏שָׁכַב‎ (shakav) “to lie down” can be a euphemism for going to bed for sexual relations.
Heb “as you live and as your soul lives.”

12.text: So David said to Uriah, “Stay here another day. Tomorrow I will send you back.” So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem both that day and the following one.

notes.text: On the chronology involved here see P. K. McCarter, II Samuel (AB), 287.

13.text: Then David summoned him. He ate and drank with him, and got him drunk. But in the evening he went out to sleep on his bed with the servants of his lord; he did not go down to his own house.

14.text: In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it with Uriah.

15.text: In the letter he wrote: “Station Uriah at the front in the thick of the battle and then withdraw from him so he will be cut down and killed.”

16.text: So as Joab kept watch on the city, he stationed Uriah at the place where he knew the best enemy soldiers were.

notes.text: Heb “the valiant men.” This refers in context to the strongest or most valiant defenders of the city Joab and the Israelite army were besieging, so the present translation uses “the best enemy soldiers” for clarity.

17.text: When the men of the city came out and fought with Joab, some of David’s soldiers fell in battle. Uriah the Hittite also died.

notes.text: Heb “some of the people from the servants of David.”

18.text: Then Joab sent a full battle report to David.

notes.text: Heb “Joab sent and related to David all the matters of the battle.”

19.text: He instructed the messenger as follows: “When you finish giving the battle report to the king,

20.text: if the king becomes angry and asks you, ‘Why did you go so close to the city to fight? Didn’t you realize they would shoot from the wall?

21.text: Who struck down Abimelech the son of Jerub-Besheth? Didn’t a woman throw an upper millstone down on him from the wall so that he died in Thebez? Why did you go so close to the wall?’ just say to him, ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead.’”

notes.text: The upper millstone (Heb “millstone of riding”) refers to the heavy circular stone that was commonly rolled over a circular base in order to crush and grind such things as olives.

22.text: So the messenger departed. When he arrived, he informed David of all the news that Joab had sent with him.

23.text: The messenger said to David, “The men overpowered us and attacked us in the field. But we forced them to retreat all the way to the door of the city gate.

notes.text: Heb “and came out to us.”
Heb “but we were on them.”

24.text: Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall and some of the king’s soldiers died. Your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead.”

notes.text: The translation follows the Qere (“your servants”) rather than the Kethib (“your servant”).

25.text: David said to the messenger, “Tell Joab, ‘Don’t let this thing upset you. There is no way to anticipate whom the sword will cut down. Press the battle against the city and conquer it.’ Encourage him with these words.”

notes.text: Heb “let not this matter be evil in your eyes.”
Heb “according to this and according to this the sword devours.”
Heb “overthrow.”
The Hebrew text does not have “with these words.” They are supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

26.text: When Uriah’s wife heard that her husband Uriah was dead, she mourned for him.

notes.text: Heb “for her lord.”

27.text: When the time of mourning passed, David had her brought to his palace. She became his wife and she bore him a son. But what David had done upset the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “David sent and gathered her to his house.”
Heb “and the thing which David had done was evil in the eyes of the Lord.” Note the verbal connection with v. 25. Though David did not regard the matter as evil, the Lord certainly did.

1.text: So the Lord sent Nathan to David. When he came to David, Nathan said, “There were two men in a certain city, one rich and the other poor.

notes.text: A few medieval Hebrew mss, the LXX, and the Syriac Peshitta add “the prophet.” The words are included in a few modern English version (e.g., TEV, CEV, NLT).
Heb “him”; the referent (David) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “he”; the referent (Nathan) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The Hebrew text repeats “to him.”

2.text: The rich man had a great many flocks and herds.

3.text: But the poor man had nothing except for a little lamb he had acquired. He raised it, and it grew up alongside him and his children. It used to eat his food, drink from his cup, and sleep in his arms. It was just like a daughter to him.

notes.text: Heb “his sons.”
The three Hebrew imperfect verbal forms in this sentence have a customary nuance; they describe past actions that were repeated or typical.
Heb “from his morsel.”
Heb “and on his chest [or perhaps, “lap”] it would lie.”

4.text: “When a traveler arrived at the rich man’s home, he did not want to use one of his own sheep or cattle to feed the traveler who had come to visit him. Instead, he took the poor man’s lamb and cooked it for the man who had come to visit him.”

notes.text: Heb “came to the rich man.” In the translation “arrived at the rich man’s home” has been used for stylistic reasons.
Heb “and he refused to take from his flock and from his herd to prepare [a meal] for.”
Heb “who had come to him” (also a second time later in this verse). The word “visit” has been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons and for clarity.
Heb “and prepared.”

5.text: Then David became very angry at this man. He said to Nathan, “As surely as the Lord lives, the man who did this deserves to die!

notes.text: Heb “the man doing this [is] a son of death.” See 1 Sam 20:31 for another use of this expression, which must mean “he is as good as dead” or “he deserves to die,” as 1 Sam 20:32 makes clear.

6.text: Because he committed this cold-hearted crime, he must pay for the lamb four times over!”

notes.text: With the exception of the Lucianic recension, the Old Greek translation has here “sevenfold” rather than “fourfold,” a reading that S. R. Driver thought probably to be the original reading (S. R. Driver, Notes on the Hebrew Text and the Topography of the Books of Samuel, 291). However, Exod 22:1 [21:37 HT] specifies fourfold repayment for a stolen sheep, which is consistent with 2 Sam 12:6. Some mss of the Targum and the Syriac Peshitta exaggerate the idea to “fortyfold.”
Heb “the lamb he must repay fourfold because he did this thing and because he did not have compassion.”

7.text: Nathan said to David, “You are that man! This is what the Lord God of Israel has said: ‘I chose you to be king over Israel and I rescued you from the hand of Saul.

notes.text: Heb “anointed.”

8.text: I gave you your master’s house, and put your master’s wives into your arms. I also gave you the house of Israel and Judah. And if all that somehow seems insignificant, I would have given you so much more as well!

notes.text: Heb “and the wives of your lord into your chest [or “lap”].” The words “I put” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons and for clarification.

9.text: Why have you shown contempt for the Lord’s decrees by doing evil in my sight? You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and you have taken his wife to be your own wife! You have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.

notes.text: Or “word, message.” The “word of the Lord” sometimes refers to a prophetic message from God and sometimes to his past revelation. Here it refers to the Lord’s laws which David has violated.
So the Qere; the Kethib has “his.”

10.text: So now the sword will never depart from your house. For you have despised me by taking the wife of Uriah the Hittite as your own!’

11.text: This is what the Lord has said: ‘I am about to bring disaster on you from inside your own household! Right before your eyes I will take your wives and hand them over to your companion. He will go to bed with your wives in broad daylight!

notes.text: Heb “raise up against you disaster.”
Heb “house” (so NAB, NRSV); NCV, TEV, CEV “family.”
Or “friend.”
Heb “will lie down with.” The verb ‏שָׁכַב‎ (shakhav) “to lie down” can be a euphemism for going to bed for sexual relations.
Heb “in the eyes of this sun.”

12.text: Although you have acted in secret, I will do this thing before all Israel, and in broad daylight.’”

notes.text: Heb “and before the sun.”

13.text: Then David exclaimed to Nathan, “I have sinned against the Lord!” Nathan replied to David, “Yes, and the Lord has forgiven your sin. You are not going to die.

notes.text: Heb “removed.”

14.text: Nonetheless, because you have treated the Lord with such contempt in this matter, the son who has been born to you will certainly die.”

notes.text: The MT has here “because you have caused the enemies of the Lord to treat the Lord with such contempt.” This is one of the so-called tiqqune sopherim, or “emendations of the scribes.” According to this ancient tradition, the scribes changed the text in order to soften somewhat the negative light in which David was presented. If that is the case, the MT reflects the altered text. The present translation departs from the MT here. Elsewhere the Piel stem of this verb means “treat with contempt,” but never “cause someone to treat with contempt.”

15.text: Then Nathan went to his home. The Lord struck the child that Uriah’s wife had borne to David, and the child became very ill.

notes.text: Heb “and the Lord struck the child…and he was ill.” It is necessary to repeat “the child” in the translation to make clear who became ill, since “the Lord struck the child that Uriah’s wife had borne to David, and he became very ill” could be understood to mean that David himself became ill.

16.text: Then David prayed to God for the child and fasted. He would even go and spend the night lying on the ground.

notes.text: Heb “sought” or “searched for.”
Heb “and David fasted.”
The three Hebrew verbs that follow in this verse are perfects with prefixed vav. They may describe repeated past actions or actions which accompanied David’s praying and fasting.

17.text: The elders of his house stood over him and tried to lift him from the ground, but he was unwilling, and refused to eat food with them.

18.text: On the seventh day the child died. But the servants of David were afraid to inform him that the child had died, for they said, “While the child was still alive he would not listen to us when we spoke to him. How can we tell him that the child is dead? He will do himself harm!”

notes.text: Heb “to our voice.”
Heb “he will do harm.” The object is not stated in the Hebrew text. The statement may be intentionally vague, meaning that he might harm himself or them!

19.text: When David saw that his servants were whispering to one another, he realized that the child was dead. So David asked his servants, “Is the child dead?” They replied, “Yes, he’s dead.”

notes.text: Heb “David.” The name has been replaced in the translation by the pronoun (“he”) for stylistic reasons.

20.text: So David got up from the ground, bathed, put on oil, and changed his clothes. He went to the house of the Lord and worshiped. Then, when he entered his palace, he requested that food be brought to him, and he ate.

21.text: His servants said to him, “What is this that you have done? While the child was still alive, you fasted and wept. Once the child was dead you got up and ate food!”

notes.text: For the MT ‏בַּעֲבוּר‎ (baʿavur, “for the sake of”) we should probably read ‏בְּעוֹד‎ (beʿod, “while”). See the Lucianic Greek recension, the Syriac Peshitta, and the Targum.

22.text: He replied, “While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept because I thought, ‘Perhaps the Lord will show pity and the child will live.’

notes.text: Heb “said.”
Heb “Who knows?”

23.text: But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Am I able to bring him back at this point? I will go to him, but he cannot return to me!”

24.text: So David comforted his wife Bathsheba. He came to her and went to bed with her. Later she gave birth to a son, and David named him Solomon. Now the Lord loved the child

notes.text: The combination of the verb ‏בּוֹא‎ (boʾ; “to come, enter”) and the preposition ‏אֶל‎ (ʾel; “to”) means “to approach, to come to” (HALOT 1:113). This common expression is also used as a euphemism for coming together for sexual relations. Although some take the phrase to be a graphic depiction of a man actions in sexual relations with a woman, certain factors clarify that it is a euphemism. First, the phrase also describes a woman approaching a man for sexual relations (2 Sam 11:4), a situation where this phrase cannot be explicitly descriptive. Second, the phrase is paired here with ‏שָׁכַב‎ (shakhav), “to lie down,” which only makes sense if the two are complementary (compare also Gen 19:33-34 which uses both verbs of Lot’s daughters, but without the preposition). The verb ‏שָׁכַב‎ can imply lying down for sleep or for sexual relations. When ‏בּוֹא אֶל‎ (boʾ ʾel) is used with ‏שָׁכַב‎ (shakhav), they state the natural progression of approaching and then lying with. Hebrew can use the two together, or either separately, as a euphemism for sexual relations. But if the phrase ‏בּוֹא אֶל‎ were already an explicit depiction of sex, then the latter phrase with ‏שָׁכַב‎, “to lie with,” would be pointless. So 2 Sam 11:4 and 2 Sam 12:24 are important evidence for how this phrase really works, and it is appropriate to also use euphemisms in translation.
Heb “and he lay with her.” The phrase is a euphemism for sexual relations.
The Kethiv reads “he named” while the Qere reads “she named.”

Heb “he”; the referent (David) has been specified in the translation for clarity. While some translations render the pronoun as third person plural (“they”), implying that both David and Bathsheba together named the child, it is likely that the name “Solomon,” which is related to the Hebrew word for “peace” (and may be derived from it) had special significance for David, who would have regarded the birth of a second child to Bathsheba as a confirming sign that God had forgiven his sin and was at peace with him.
Heb “him,” referring to the child.

25.text: and sent word through Nathan the prophet that he should be named Jedidiah for the Lord’s sake.

notes.text: The name Jedidiah means “loved by the Lord.”

26.text: So Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the royal city.

notes.text: Here the narrative resumes the battle story that began in 11:1 (see 11:25). The author has interrupted that story to give the related account of David’s sin with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah. He now returns to the earlier story and brings it to a conclusion.

27.text: Joab then sent messengers to David, saying, “I have fought against Rabbah and have captured the water supply of the city.

notes.text: The expression translated the water supply of the city (Heb “the city of the waters”) apparently refers to that part of the fortified city that guarded the water supply of the entire city. Joab had already captured this part of the city, but he now defers to King David for the capture of the rest of the city. In this way the king will receive the credit for this achievement.

28.text: So now assemble the rest of the army and besiege the city and capture it. Otherwise I will capture the city and it will be named for me.”

notes.text: Heb “people.” So also in vv. 29, 31.

29.text: So David assembled all the army and went to Rabbah and fought against it and captured it.

30.text: He took the crown of their king from his head—it was gold, weighed about seventy-five pounds, and held a precious stone—and it was placed on David’s head. He also took from the city a great deal of plunder.

notes.text: Part of the Greek tradition wrongly understands Hebrew ‏מַלְכָּם‎ (malkam, “their king”) as a proper name (“Milcom”). Some English versions follow the Greek here, rendering the phrase “the crown of Milcom” (so NRSV; cf. also NAB, CEV). TEV takes this as a reference not to the Ammonite king but to “the idol of the Ammonite god Molech.”
Heb “and its weight [was] a talent of gold.” The weight of this ornamental crown was approximately 75 lbs (34 kg). See P. K. McCarter, II Samuel (AB), 313.

31.text: He removed the people who were in it and made them labor with saws, iron picks, and iron axes, putting them to work at the brick kiln. This was his policy with all the Ammonite cities. Then David and all the army returned to Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “brought out.”
tnHeb “to pass through.”
Heb “and so he would do.”

1.text: Now David’s son Absalom had a beautiful sister named Tamar. In the course of time David’s son Amnon fell madly in love with her.

notes.text: Heb “Amnon the son of David loved her.” The following verse indicates the extreme nature of his infatuation, so the translation uses “madly in love” here.
Amnon was the half-brother of Tamar; Absalom was her full blood-brother.

2.text: But Amnon became frustrated because he was so lovesick over his sister Tamar. For she was a virgin, and to Amnon it seemed out of the question to do anything to her.

notes.text: Heb “and there was distress to Amnon so that he made himself sick.”

3.text: Now Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, the son of David’s brother Shimeah. Jonadab was a very crafty man.

4.text: He asked Amnon, “Why are you, the king’s son, so depressed every morning? Can’t you tell me?” So Amnon said to him, “I’m in love with Tamar the sister of my brother Absalom.”

notes.text: Heb “and he said to him.”
A more idiomatic translation might be “Why are you of all people…?”

5.text: Jonadab replied to him, “Lie down on your bed and pretend to be sick. When your father comes in to see you, say to him, ‘Please let my sister Tamar come in so she can fix some food for me. Let her prepare the food in my sight so I can watch. Then I will eat from her hand.’”

notes.text: This verb is used in the Hitpael stem only in this chapter of the Hebrew Bible. With the exception of v. 2 it describes not a real sickness but one pretended in order to entrap Tamar. The Hitpael sometimes, as here, describes the subject making oneself appear to be of a certain character. On this use of the stem, see GKC 149-50 §54.e.

6.text: So Amnon lay down and pretended to be sick. When the king came in to see him, Amnon said to the king, “Please let my sister Tamar come in so she can make a couple of cakes in my sight. Then I will eat from her hand.”

7.text: So David sent Tamar to the house saying, “Please go to the house of Amnon your brother and prepare some food for him.”

8.text: So Tamar went to the house of Amnon her brother, who was lying down. She took the dough, kneaded it, made some cakes while he watched, and baked them.

notes.text: Heb “in his sight.”
Heb “the cakes.”

9.text: But when she took the pan and set it before him, he refused to eat. Instead Amnon said, “Get everyone out of here!” So everyone left.

notes.text: Heb “from upon me.”

A few medieval Hebrew mss supported by the LXX and Vulgate read the Hiphil ‏וַיּוֹצִיאוּ‎ (vayyotsiʾu) “and they removed everyone,” rather than the MT’s Qal ‏וַיֵּצְאוּ‎ (vayyetseʾu, “they left”). This verb would then match the instructions more closely.

10.text: Then Amnon said to Tamar, “Bring the cakes into the bedroom; then I will eat from your hand.” So Tamar took the cakes that she had prepared and brought them to her brother Amnon in the bedroom.

11.text: As she brought them to him to eat, he grabbed her and said to her, “Come on! Get in bed with me, my sister!”

notes.text: Heb “lie with me” (so NAB, NASB, NRSV); NCV “come and have sexual relations with me.”

12.text: But she said to him, “No, my brother! Don’t humiliate me! This just isn’t done in Israel! Don’t do this foolish thing!

13.text: How could I ever be rid of my humiliation? And you would be considered one of the fools in Israel! Just speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you.”

notes.text: Heb “and you will be like one of the fools.”
Heb “Now.”

14.text: But he refused to listen to her. He overpowered her and humiliated her by raping her.

notes.text: Heb “to her voice.”
Heb “and he humiliated her and lay with her.”

15.text: Then Amnon greatly despised her. His disdain toward her surpassed the love he had previously felt toward her. Amnon said to her, “Get up and leave!”

notes.text: Heb “and Amnon hated her with very great hatred.”
Heb “for greater was the hatred with which he hated her than the love with which he loved her.”

16.text: But she said to him, “No I won’t, for sending me away now would be worse than what you did to me earlier!” But he refused to listen to her.

notes.text: Heb “No, because this great evil is [worse] than the other which you did with me, by sending me away.” Perhaps the broken syntax reflects her hysteria and outrage.

17.text: He called his personal attendant and said to him, “Take this woman out of my sight and lock the door behind her!”

notes.text: Heb “send this [one] from upon me to the outside.”

18.text: (Now she was wearing a long robe, for this is what the king’s virgin daughters used to wear.) So Amnon’s attendant removed her and bolted the door behind her.

notes.text: The Hebrew expression used here (‏כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּים‎, ketonet passim) is found only here and in Gen 37:3, 23, 32. Hebrew ‏פַּס‎ (pas) can refer to the palm of the hand or the sole of the foot; here the idea is probably that of a long robe reaching to the feet and having sleeves reaching to the wrists. The notion of a “coat of many colors” (KJV, ASV “garment of divers colors”), a familiar translation for the phrase in Genesis, is based primarily on the translation adopted in the LXX χιτῶνα ποικίλον (chitōna poikilon) and does not have a great deal of support.
Heb “his”; the referent (Amnon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The Hebrew verb is a perfect with nonconsecutive vav, probably indicating an action (locking the door) that complements the preceding one (pushing her out the door).

19.text: Then Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long robe she was wearing. She put her hands on her head and went on her way, wailing as she went.

20.text: Her brother Absalom said to her, “Was Amnon your brother with you? Now be quiet, my sister. He is your brother. Don’t take it so seriously!” Tamar, devastated, lived in the house of her brother Absalom.

notes.text: Heb “Don’t set your heart to this thing!” Elsewhere this phrase means to disregard or not pay attention to something (e.g. Exod 7:23). It is a callous thing to say to Tamar, but to the degree that what he said becomes known, it misleads people from understanding that he is personally plotting revenge (13:22, 28).

21.text: Now King David heard about all these things and was very angry.

notes.text: The LXX and part of the Old Latin tradition include the following addition to v. 21, also included in some English versions (e.g., NAB, NRSV, CEV): “But he did not grieve the spirit of Amnon his son, because he loved him, since he was his firstborn.” Note David’s attitude toward his son Adonijah in 1 Kgs 1:6.

22.text: But Absalom said nothing to Amnon, either bad or good, yet Absalom hated Amnon because he had humiliated his sister Tamar.

23.text: Two years later Absalom’s sheepshearers were in Baal Hazor, near Ephraim. Absalom invited all the king’s sons.

24.text: Then Absalom went to the king and said, “My shearers have begun their work. Let the king and his servants go with me.”

notes.text: Heb “your servant has sheepshearers.” The phrase “your servant” also occurs at the end of the verse and is translated as "me".

25.text: But the king said to Absalom, “No, my son. We shouldn’t all go. We shouldn’t burden you in that way.” Though Absalom pressed him, the king was not willing to go. Instead, David blessed him.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Absalom) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Here and in v. 27 the translation follows 4QSama ‏ויפצר‎ (vayyiftsar, “and he pressed”) rather than the MT ‏וַיִּפְרָץ‎ (vayyifrats, “and he broke through”). This emended reading seems also to underlie the translations of the LXX (καὶ ἐβιάσατο, kai ebiasato), the Syriac Peshitta (weʾalseh), and Vulgate (cogeret eum).
Heb “he”; the referent (the king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “he”; the referent (David) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

26.text: Then Absalom said, “If you will not go, then let my brother Amnon go with us.” The king replied to him, “Why should he go with you?”

notes.text: Heb “and not.”

27.text: But when Absalom pressed him, he sent Amnon and all the king’s sons along with him.

28.text: Absalom instructed his servants, “Look! When Amnon is drunk and I say to you, ‘Strike Amnon down,’ kill him then and there. Don’t fear! Is it not I who have given you these instructions? Be strong and courageous!”

notes.text: Heb “when good is the heart of Amnon with wine.”
Heb “and become sons of valor.”

29.text: So Absalom’s servants did to Amnon exactly what Absalom had instructed. Then all the king’s sons got up; each one rode away on his mule and fled.

30.text: While they were still on their way, the following report reached David: “Absalom has killed all the king’s sons; not one of them is left!”

31.text: Then the king stood up and tore his garments and lay down on the ground. All his servants were standing there with torn garments as well.

32.text: Jonadab, the son of David’s brother Shimeah, said, “My lord should not say, ‘They have killed all the young men who are the king’s sons.’ For only Amnon is dead. This is what Absalom has talked about from the day that Amnon humiliated his sister Tamar.

notes.text: Heb “it was placed on the mouth of Absalom.”
Heb “he”; the referent (Amnon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

33.text: Now don’t let my lord the king be concerned about the report that has come saying, ‘All the king’s sons are dead.’ It is only Amnon who is dead.”

34.text: In the meantime Absalom fled. When the servant who was the watchman looked up, he saw many people coming from the west on a road beside the hill.

notes.text: Heb “behind him.”

35.text: Jonadab said to the king, “Look! The king’s sons have come! It’s just as I said.”

36.text: Just as he finished speaking, the king’s sons arrived, wailing and weeping. The king and all his servants wept loudly as well.

notes.text: Heb “and they lifted their voice and wept.”
Heb “with a great weeping.”

37.text: But Absalom fled and went to King Talmai son of Ammihud of Geshur. And David grieved over his son every day.

notes.text: The Hebrew text leaves the word “David” to be inferred. The Syriac Peshitta and Vulgate add the word “David.” Most of the Greek tradition includes the words “King David” here.

38.text: After Absalom fled and went to Geshur, he remained there for three years.

39.text: The king longed to go to Absalom, for he had since been consoled over the death of Amnon.

notes.text: The translation follows 4QSama in reading ‏רוּחַ הַמֶּלֶךְ‎ (ruakh hammelekh, “the spirit of the king”) rather than the MT ‏דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ‎ (david hammelekh, “David the king”). The understanding reflected in the translation above is that David, though alienated during this time from his son Absalom, still had an abiding love and concern for him. He longed for reconciliation with him. A rather different interpretation of the verse supposes that David’s interest in taking military action against Absalom grew slack with the passing of time, and this in turn enabled David’s advisers to encourage him toward reconciliation with Absalom. For the latter view, see P. K. McCarter, II Samuel (AB), 344, and cf. CEV.
Heb “was consoled over Amnon, because he was dead.”

1.text: Now Joab son of Zeruiah realized that the king longed to see Absalom.

notes.text: Heb “the heart of the king was upon.” The Syriac Peshitta adds the verb ʾethreʿi (“was reconciled”).

2.text: So Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman. He told her, “Pretend to be in mourning and put on garments for mourning. Don’t anoint yourself with oil. Instead, act like a woman who has been mourning for the dead for some time.

notes.text: The Hebrew Hitpael verbal form here indicates pretended rather than genuine action.
Heb “these many days.”

3.text: Go to the king and speak to him in the following fashion.” Then Joab told her what to say.

notes.text: Heb “put the words in her mouth” (so NASB, NIV).

4.text: So the Tekoan woman went to the king. She bowed down with her face to the ground in deference to him and said, “Please help me, O king!”

notes.text: The translation follows many medieval Hebrew mss in reading ‏וַתַּבֹא‎ (vattavoʾ, “and she went”) rather than the MT ‏וַתֹּאמֶר‎ (vattoʾmer, “and she said”). The MT reading shows confusion with ‏וַתֹּאמֶר‎ later in the verse. The emendation suggested here is supported by the LXX, the Syriac Peshitta, some mss of the Targum, and Vulgate.
The word “me” is left to be inferred in the Hebrew text; it is present in the Syriac Peshitta and Vulgate.

5.text: The king replied to her, “What do you want?” She answered, “I am a widow; my husband is dead.

notes.text: Heb “What to you?”

6.text: Your servant has two sons. When the two of them got into a fight in the field, there was no one present who could intervene. One of them struck the other and killed him.

notes.text: Here and elsewhere (vv. 7, 12, 15a, 17, 19) the woman uses a term which suggests a lower level female servant. She uses the term to express her humility before the king. However, she uses a different term in vv. 15b-16. See the note at v. 15 for a discussion of the rhetorical purpose of this switch in terminology.

7.text: Now the entire family has risen up against your servant, saying, ‘Turn over the one who struck down his brother, so that we can execute him and avenge the death of his brother whom he killed. In so doing we will also destroy the heir.’ They want to extinguish my remaining coal, leaving no one on the face of the earth to carry on the name of my husband.”

notes.text: Heb “in exchange for the life.” The Hebrew preposition ‏ב‎ (bet, “in”) here is the so-called bet pretii, or bet (‏ב‎) of price, defining the value attached to someone or something.
My remaining coal is here metaphorical language, describing the one remaining son as her only source of lingering hope for continuing the family line.

8.text: Then the king told the woman, “Go to your home. I will give instructions concerning your situation.”

notes.text: Heb “concerning you.”

9.text: The Tekoan woman said to the king, “My lord the king, let any blame fall on me and on the house of my father. But let the king and his throne be innocent!”

10.text: The king said, “Bring to me whoever speaks to you, and he won’t bother you again!”

11.text: She replied, “In that case, let the king invoke the name of the Lord your God so that the avenger of blood may not add to the killing! Then they will not destroy my son!” He replied, “As surely as the Lord lives, not a single hair of your son’s head will fall to the ground.”

notes.text: The words “in that case” are not in the Hebrew text, but may be inferred from the context. They are supplied in the translation for the sake of clarification.
Heb “let the king remember.”
Heb “of your son.”

12.text: Then the woman said, “Please permit your servant to speak to my lord the king about another matter.” He replied, “Tell me.”

13.text: The woman said, “Why have you devised something like this against God’s people? When the king speaks in this fashion, he makes himself guilty, for the king has not brought back the one he has banished.

14.text: Certainly we must die, and are like water spilled on the ground that cannot be gathered up again. But God does not take away life; instead he devises ways for the banished to be restored.

notes.text: Heb “he devises plans for the one banished from him not to be banished.”

15.text: I have now come to speak with my lord the king about this matter, because the people have made me fearful. But your servant said, ‘I will speak to the king! Perhaps the king will do what his female servant asks.

notes.text: The LXX (ὄψεταί με, opsetai me) has misunderstood the Hebrew ‏יֵרְאֻנִי‎ (yereʾuni, Piel perfect, “they have made me fearful”), taking the verb to be a form of the verb ‏רָאָה‎ (raʾah, “to see”) rather than the verb ‏יָרֵא‎ (yareʾ, “to fear”). The fact that the Greek translators were working with an unvocalized Hebrew text (i.e., consonants only) made them very susceptible to this type of error.

Here and in v. 16 the woman refers to herself as the king’s ‏אָמָה‎ (ʾamah), a term that refers to a higher level female servant toward whom the master might have some obligation. Like the other term, this word expresses her humility, but it also suggests that the king might have some obligation to treat her in accordance with the principles of justice.

16.text: Yes! The king may listen and deliver his female servant from the hand of the man who seeks to remove both me and my son from the inheritance God has given us!’

notes.text: Or “for.”
Or “will.” The imperfect verbal form can have either an indicative or modal nuance. The use of “perhaps” in v. 15b suggests the latter here.
Heb “in order to deliver his maid.”
Heb “destroy.”
Heb “from the inheritance of God.” The expression refers to the property that was granted to her family line in the division of the land authorized by God.

17.text: So your servant said, ‘May the word of my lord the king be my security, for my lord the king is like the angel of God when it comes to deciding between right and wrong! May the Lord your God be with you!’”

18.text: Then the king replied to the woman, “Don’t hide any information from me when I question you.” The woman said, “Let my lord the king speak.”

19.text: The king said, “Did Joab put you up to all of this?” The woman answered, “As surely as you live, my lord the king, there is no deviation to the right or to the left from all that my lord the king has said. For your servant Joab gave me instructions. He has put all these words in your servant’s mouth.

notes.text: Heb “Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?”

20.text: Your servant Joab did this so as to change this situation. But my lord has wisdom like that of the angel of God, and knows everything that is happening in the land.”

notes.text: Heb “to know all that is in the land.”
