They are pictured as winged creatures (Exod 25:20; 37:9; 1 Kgs 6:24-27; Ezek 10:8, 19) and serve as the very throne of God when the ark of the covenant is in view (Pss 80:1; 99:1; see Num 7:89; 1 Sam 4:4; 2 Sam 6:2; 2 Kgs 19:15). The picture of the Lord seated on the cherubim suggests they might be used by him as a vehicle, a function they carry out in Ezek 1:22-28 (the “living creatures” mentioned here are identified as cherubim in Ezek 10:20). In Ps 18:10 the image of a cherub serves to personify the wind (see the next line).

The translation follows very many medieval Hebrew mss in reading ‏וַיֵּדֶא‎ (vayyedeʾ, “and he glided”; cf. NIV “soared”; NCV “raced”) rather than MT ‏וַיֵּרָא‎ (vayyeraʾ, “and he appeared,” so NASB, CEV). See as well the Syriac Peshitta, Targum, Vulgate, and the parallel version in Ps 18:10, which preserves the original reading (see the note there).

The wings of the wind. Verse 10 may depict the Lord mounting a cherub, which is in turn propelled by the wind current. Another option is that two different vehicles (a cherub and the wind) are envisioned. A third option is that the wind is personified as a cherub. For a discussion of ancient Near Eastern parallels to the imagery in v. 10, see M. Weinfeld, “‘Rider of the Clouds’ and ‘Gatherer of the Clouds’,” JANESCU 5 (1973): 422-24.

12.text: He shrouded himself in darkness, in thick rain clouds.

notes.text: Heb “he made darkness around him coverings.” The parallel text in Ps 18:11 reads “he made darkness his hiding place around him, his covering.” 2 Sam 22:12 omits “his hiding place” and pluralizes “covering.” Psalm 18:11 may include a conflation of synonyms (“his hiding place” and “his covering”) or 2 Sam 22:12 may be the result of haplography/homoioarcton. Note that three successive words in Ps 18:11 begin with the letter ‏ס‎ (samek): ‏ סִתְרוֹ סְבִיבוֹתָיו סֻכָּתוֹ‎ (sitro sevivotayv sukkato).

Heb “a sieve of water, clouds of clouds.” The form ‏חַשְׁרַת‎ (khashrat) is a construct of ‏חַשְׁרָה‎ (khashrah, “sieve”), which occurs only here in the OT. A cognate Ugaritic noun means “sieve,” and a related verb ‏חשׁר‎ (“to sift”) is attested in post-biblical Hebrew and Aramaic (see HALOT 363 s.v. *‏חשׁר‎). The phrase ‏חַשְׁרַת־מַיִם‎ (khashrat mayim) means literally “a sieve of water.” It pictures the rain clouds as a sieve through which the rain falls to the ground. (See F. M. Cross and D. N. Freedman, Studies in Ancient Yahwistic Poetry, 146, note 33.)

13.text: From the brightness in front of him came coals of fire.

notes.text: The parallel text in Ps 18:12 reads “from the brightness in front of him his clouds came, hail and coals of fire.” The Lucianic family of texts within the Greek tradition of 2 Sam 22:13 seems to assume the underlying Hebrew text: ‏מִנֹּגַהּ נֶגְדּוֹ עָבְרוּ בָּרָד וְגַחֲלֵי אֵשׁ‎ (minnogah negdo ʿaveru barad vegakhale ʾesh, “from the brightness in front of him came hail and coals of fire”) which is the basis for the present translation. The textual situation is perplexing and the identity of the original text uncertain. The verbs ‏עָבְרוּ‎ (ʿaveru; Ps 18:12) and ‏בָּעֲרוּ‎ (baʿaru, 2 Sam 22:13) appear to be variants involving a transposition of the first two letters. The noun ‏עָבָיו‎ (ʿavayv, “his clouds”; Ps 18:12) may be virtually dittographic (note the following ‏עָבְרוּ‎), or it could have accidentally dropped from the text of 2 Sam 22:13 by virtual haplography (note the preceding ‏בָּעֲרוּ‎ [baʿaru], which might have originally read ‏עָבְרוּ‎). The term ‏בָּרָד‎ (barad, “hail”; Ps 18:12) may be virtually dittographic (note the preceding ‏עָבְרוּ‎), or it could have dropped from 2 Sam 22:13 by virtual haplography (note the preceding ‏בָּעֲרוּ‎, which might have originally read ‏עָבְרוּ‎). For a fuller discussion of the text, see R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of Psalm 18/2 Samuel 22” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 74-76.

14.text: The Lord thundered from the sky; the Most High shouted loudly.

notes.text: The shortened theme vowel indicates that the prefixed verbal form is a preterite.
This divine title (‏עֶלְיוֹן‎, ʿelyon) pictures God as the exalted ruler of the universe who vindicates the innocent and judges the wicked. See especially Ps 47:2.

Heb “offered his voice.” In this poetic narrative context the prefixed verbal form is best understood as a preterite indicating past tense, not an imperfect. Note the preterite form in the preceding line. The text of Ps 18:13 adds at this point, “hail and coals of fire.” These words are probably accidentally added from v. 12b; they do not appear in 2 Sam 22:14.

Thunder is a common motif in Old Testament theophanies and in ancient Near Eastern portrayals of the storm god and warring kings. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of Psalm 18/2 Samuel 22” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 179-83.

15.text: He shot arrows and scattered them, lightning and routed them.

notes.text: Heb “sent.”

The pronominal suffixes on the verbs “scattered” and “routed” (see the next line) refer to David’s enemies. Some argue that the suffixes refer to the arrows, in which case one might translate “shot them far and wide” and “made them move noisily,” respectively. They argue that the enemies have not been mentioned since v. 4 and are not again mentioned until v. 17. However, usage of the verbs ‏פוּץ‎ (puts, “scatter”) and ‏הָמַם‎ (hamam, “rout”) elsewhere in Holy War accounts suggests the suffixes refer to enemies. Enemies are frequently pictured in such texts as scattered and/or routed (see Exod 14:24; 23:27; Num 10:35; Josh 10:10; Judg 4:15; 1 Sam 7:10; 11:11; Ps 68:1).

Lightning is a common motif in OT theophanies and in ancient Near Eastern portrayals of the storm god and warring kings. Arrows and lightning bolts are associated in other texts (see Pss 77:17-18; 144:6; Zech 9:14), as well as in ancient Near Eastern art. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of Psalm 18/2 Samuel 22” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 187, 190-92.

16.text: The depths of the sea were exposed; the inner regions of the world were uncovered by the Lord’s battle cry, by the powerful breath from his nose.

notes.text: Or “channels.”
Or “foundations.”

The noun is derived from the verb ‏גָעַר‎ (gaʿar) which is often understood to mean “rebuke.” In some cases it is apparent that scolding or threatening is in view (see Gen 37:10; Ruth 2:16; Zech 3:2). However, in militaristic contexts this translation is inadequate, for the verb refers in this setting to the warrior’s battle cry, which terrifies and paralyzes the enemy. See A. Caquot, TDOT 3:53, and note the use of the verb in Pss 68:30; 106:9; and Nah 1:4, as well as the related noun in Job 26:11; Pss 9:5; 76:6; 104:7; Isa 50:2; 51:20; 66:15.

Heb “blast of the breath” (literally, “breath of breath”) employs an appositional genitive. Synonyms are joined in a construct relationship to emphasize the single idea. For a detailed discussion of the grammatical point with numerous examples, see Y. Avishur, “Pairs of Synonymous Words in the Construct State (and in Appositional Hendiadys) in Biblical Hebrew,” Semitics 2 (1971): 17-81.

17.text: He reached down from above and grabbed me; he pulled me from the surging water.

notes.text: Heb “stretched.” Perhaps “his hand” should be supplied by ellipsis (see Ps 144:7). In this poetic narrative context the three prefixed verbal forms in this verse are best understood as preterites indicating past tense, not imperfects.
Heb “mighty waters.” The waters of the sea symbolize the psalmist’s powerful enemies, as well as the realm of death they represent (see v. 5 and Ps 144:7).

18.text: He rescued me from my strong enemy, from those who hate me, for they were too strong for me.

notes.text: The singular refers either to personified death or collectively to the psalmist’s enemies. The following line, which refers to “those [plural] who hate me,” favors the latter.

19.text: They confronted me in my day of calamity, but the Lord helped me.

notes.text: The same verb is translated “trapped” in v. 6. In this poetic narrative context the prefixed verbal form is best understood as a preterite indicating past tense, not imperfect. Cf. NAB, NCV, TEV, NLT “attacked.”
Heb “became my support.”

20.text: He brought me out into a wide open place; he delivered me because he was pleased with me.

notes.text: Or “delighted in me” (so KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV).

21.text: The Lord repaid me for my godly deeds; he rewarded my blameless behavior.

notes.text: In this poetic narrative context the prefixed verbal form is best understood as a preterite indicating past tense, not imperfect.

Heb “according to my righteousness.” As vv. 22-25 make clear, David refers here to his unwavering obedience to God’s commands. He explains that the Lord was pleased with him and willing to deliver him because he had been loyal to God and obedient to his commandments. Ancient Near Eastern literature contains numerous parallels. A superior (a god or king) would typically reward a subject (a king or the servant of a king, respectively) for loyalty and obedience. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of Psalm 18/2 Samuel 22” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 211-13.

The unreduced Hiphil prefixed verbal form appears to be an imperfect, in which case the psalmist would be generalizing. However, both the preceding and following contexts (see especially v. 25) suggest he is narrating his experience. Despite its unreduced form, the verb is better taken as a preterite. For other examples of unreduced Hiphil preterites, see Pss 55:14a; 68:9a, 10b; 80:8a; 89:43a; 107:38b; 116:6b.
Heb “according to the purity of my hands he repaid to me.” Hands suggest activity and behavior.

22.text: For I have obeyed the Lord’s commands; I have not rebelled against my God.

notes.text: Heb “for I have kept the ways of the Lord.” The phrase “ways of the Lord” refers here to the “conduct required” by the Lord (see HALOT 232 s.v. ‏דֶרֶךְ‎). In Ps 25 the Lord’s “ways” are associated with his covenantal demands (see vv. 4, 9-10). See also Ps 119:3 (cf. vv. 1, 4), as well as Deut 8:6; 10:12; 11:22; 19:9; 26:17; 28:9; 30:16.
Heb “I have not acted wickedly from my God.” The statement is elliptical, the idea being, “I have not acted wickedly and, in so doing, departed from my God.”

23.text: For I am aware of all his regulations, and I do not reject his rules.

notes.text: Heb “for all his regulations are before me.” The term ‏מִשְׁפָּטָו‎ (mishpatav, “his regulations”) refers to God’s covenantal requirements, especially those which the king is responsible to follow (cf Deut 17:18-20). See also Pss 19:9 (cf vv. 7-8); 89:30; 147:20 (cf v. 19), as well as the numerous uses of the term in Ps 119.

Heb “and his rules, I do not turn aside from it.” Ps 18:22 reads, “and his rules I do not turn aside from me.” The prefixed verbal form is probably an imperfect; David here generalizes about his loyalty to God’s commands. The Lord’s “rules” are the stipulations of the covenant which the king was responsible to obey (see Ps 89:31; cf v. 30 and Deut 17:18-20).

24.text: I was blameless before him; I kept myself from sinning.

notes.text: Heb “from my sin,” that is, from making it my own in any way. Leading a “blameless” life meant that the king would be loyal to God’s covenant, purge the government and society of evil and unjust officials, and reward loyalty to the Lord (see Ps 101).

25.text: The Lord rewarded me for my godly deeds; he took notice of my blameless behavior.

notes.text: Heb “according to my righteousness.” See v. 21.
Heb “according to my purity before his eyes.”

26.text: You prove to be loyal to one who is faithful; you prove to be trustworthy to one who is innocent.

notes.text: The imperfect verbal forms in vv. 26-30 draw attention to God’s characteristic actions. Based on his experience, the psalmist generalizes about God’s just dealings with people (vv. 26-28) and about the way in which God typically empowers him on the battlefield (vv. 29-30). The Hitpael stem is used in vv. 26-27 in a reflexive resultative (or causative) sense. God makes himself loyal, etc. in the sense that he conducts or reveals himself as such. On this use of the Hitpael stem, see GKC 149-50 §54.e.
Or “to a faithful follower.” A ‏חָסִיד‎ (khasid, “faithful follower”) is one who does what is right in God’s eyes and remains faithful to God (see Pss 4:3; 12:1; 16:10; 31:23; 37:28; 86:2; 97:10).
Or “innocent.”
Heb “a warrior of innocence.” The parallel text in Ps 18:25 reads, probably correctly, ‏גֶּבֶר‎ (gever, “man”) instead of ‏גִּבּוֹר‎ (gibbor, “warrior”).

27.text: You prove to be reliable to one who is blameless, but you prove to be deceptive to one who is perverse.

notes.text: Or “blameless.”

The translation follows two medieval Hebrew mss in reading ‏תִּתְפַּתָּל‎ (titpattal) from the root ‏פָּתַל‎ (patal, “to twist”), rather than the MT ‏תִּתַּפָּל‎ (tittappal, from the root ‏תָּפַל‎ (tafal, “to be tasteless,” “behave silly”; cf. KJV “unsavoury”). See as well the parallel passage in Ps 18:26. The verb ‏פָּתַל‎ (patal) is used in only three other texts. In Gen 30:8 it means literally “to wrestle,” or “to twist.” In Job 5:13 it refers to devious individuals, and in Prov 8:8 to deceptive words. Cf. NAB, NASB “astute”; NIV “shrewd”; NRSV “perverse”; TEV, NLT “hostile.”

The adjective ‏עִקֵּשׁ‎ (ʿiqqesh) has the basic nuance “twisted; crooked,” and by extension refers to someone or something that is morally perverse. It appears frequently in Proverbs, where it is used of evil people (22:5), speech (8:8; 19:1), thoughts (11:20; 17:20) and life styles (2:15; 28:6). A righteous king opposes such people (Ps 101:4). Verses 26-27 affirm God’s justice. He responds to people in accordance with their moral character. His response mirrors their actions. The faithful and blameless find God to be loyal and reliable in his dealings with them. But deceivers discover he is able and willing to use deceit to destroy them. For a more extensive discussion of the theme of divine deception in the OT, see R. B. Chisholm, “Does God Deceive?” BSac 155 (1998): 11-28.

28.text: You deliver oppressed people, but you watch the proud and bring them down.

notes.text: Or perhaps “humble” (so NIV, NRSV, NLT; note the contrast with those who are proud).
Heb “but your eyes are upon the proud, you bring low.” Psalm 18:27 reads “but proud eyes you bring low.”

29.text: Indeed, you are my lamp, Lord. The Lord illumines the darkness around me.

notes.text: Or “for.” The translation assumes that ‏כִּי‎ (ki) is asseverative here.

Many medieval Hebrew mss, some LXX mss, and the Syriac Peshitta support reading ‏תָּאִיר‎ (taʾir, “you cause to shine”) before the words “my lamp.” See Ps 18:28. The metaphor, which likens the Lord to a lamp or light, pictures him as the psalmist’s source of life. For other examples of “lamp” used in this way, see Job 18:6; 21:17; Prov 13:9; 20:20; 24:20. For other examples of “light” as a symbol for life, see Job 3:20; 33:30; Ps 56:13.

The Lucianic Greek recension and Vulgate understand this verb to be second person rather than third person as in the MT. But this is probably the result of reading the preceding word “Lord” as a vocative under the influence of the vocative in the first part of the verse.
Heb “my darkness.”

30.text: Indeed, with your help I can charge against an army; by my God’s power I can jump over a wall.

notes.text: Or “for.” The translation assumes that ‏כִּי‎ (ki) is asseverative here.
Heb “by you.”

Heb “I will run.” The imperfect verbal forms in v. 30 indicate the subject’s potential or capacity to perform an action. Though one might expect a preposition to follow the verb here, this need not be the case with the verb ‏רוּץ‎ (ruts; see 1 Sam 17:22). Some emend the Qal to a Hiphil form of the verb and translate, “I put to flight [literally, “cause to run”] an army.”

More specifically, the noun refers to a raiding party or to a contingent of troops (see HALOT 177 s.v. II ‏גְדוּד‎). The picture of a divinely empowered warrior charging against an army in almost superhuman fashion appears elsewhere in ancient Near Eastern literature. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of Psalm 18/2 Samuel 22” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 228.
Heb “by my God.”
David uses hyperbole to emphasize his God-given military superiority.

31.text: The one true God acts in a faithful manner; the Lord’s promise is reliable; he is a shield to all who take shelter in him.

notes.text: Heb “[As for] the God, his way is blameless.” The term ‏הָאֵל‎ (haʾel, “the God”) stands as a nominative (or genitive) absolute in apposition to the resumptive pronominal suffix on “way.” The prefixed article emphasizes his distinctiveness as the one true God (see BDB 42 s.v. II ‏אֵל‎ 6; Deut 33:26). God’s “way” in this context refers to his protective and salvific acts in fulfillment of his promise (see also Deut 32:4; Pss 67:2; 77:13 [note vv. 11-12, 14]; 103:7; 138:5; 145:17).

Heb “the word of the Lord is purified.” The Lord’s “word” probably refers here to his oracle(s) of victory delivered to the psalmist before the battle(s) described in the following context. See also Pss 12:5-7 and 138:2-3. David frequently received such oracles before going into battle (see 1 Sam 23:2, 4-5, 10-12; 30:8; 2 Sam 5:19). The Lord’s word of promise is absolutely reliable; it is compared to metal that has been refined in fire and cleansed of impurities. See Ps 12:6. In the ancient Near East kings would typically seek and receive oracles from their god(s) prior to battle. For examples, see R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of Psalm 18/2 Samuel 22” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 241-42.

32.text: Indeed, who is God besides the Lord? Who is a protector besides our God?

notes.text: Or “for.” The translation assumes that ‏כִּי‎ (ki) is asseverative here.
Heb “rocky cliff,” which is a metaphor of protection.

The rhetorical questions anticipate the answer, “No one.” In this way the psalmist indicates that the Lord is the only true God and reliable source of protection. See also Deut 32:39, where the Lord affirms that he is the only true God. Note as well the emphasis on his role as protector (‏צוּר‎, tsur, “rocky cliff”) in Deut 32:4, 15, 17-18, 30.

33.text: The one true God is my mighty refuge; he removes the obstacles in my way.

notes.text: Heb “the God.” See the note at v. 31.
4QSama has ‏מְאַזְּרֵנִי‎ (meʾazzereni, “the one girding me with strength”) rather than the MT ‏מָעוּזִּי‎ (maʿuzzi, “my refuge”). See as well Ps 18:32.
The prefixed verbal form with vav consecutive here carries along the generalizing tone of the preceding line.

Heb “and he sets free (from the verb ‏נָתַר‎, natar) [the] blameless, his [Kethib; “my” (Qere)] way.” The translation follows Ps 18:32 in reading “he made my path smooth.” The term ‏תָּמִים‎ (tamim, “smooth”) usually carries a moral or ethical connotation, “blameless, innocent.” However, in Ps 18:33 it refers to a pathway free of obstacles. The reality underlying the metaphor is the psalmist’s ability to charge into battle without tripping (see vv. 33, 36).

34.text: He gives me the agility of a deer; he enables me to negotiate the rugged terrain.

notes.text: Heb “[the one who] makes his feet like [those of] a deer.” The translation follows the Qere and many medieval Hebrew mss in reading ‏רַגְלַי‎ (raglay, “my feet”) rather than the MT ‏רַגְלָיו‎ (raglayv, “his feet”). See as well Ps 18:33.

Heb “and on my high places he makes me walk.” The imperfect verbal form emphasizes God’s characteristic provision. The psalmist compares his agility in battle to the ability of a deer to negotiate rugged, high terrain without falling or being injured. Habakkuk uses similar language to describe his faith during difficult times. See Hab 3:19.

35.text: He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend even the strongest bow.

notes.text: Heb “teaches.”
The psalmist attributes his skill with weapons to divine enabling. Egyptian reliefs picture gods teaching the king how to shoot a bow. See O. Keel, Symbolism of the Biblical World, 265.

Heb “and a bow of bronze is bent by my arms.” The verb ‏נָחֵת‎ (nakhet) apparently means “to pull back; to bend” here (see HALOT 692 s.v. ‏נחת‎). The bronze bow referred to here was probably laminated with bronze strips, or a purely ceremonial or decorative bow made entirely from bronze. In the latter case the language is hyperbolic, for such a weapon would not be functional in battle.

36.text: You give me your protective shield; your willingness to help enables me to prevail.

notes.text: Another option is to translate the prefixed verb with vav consecutive with a past tense, “you gave me.” Several prefixed verbal forms with vav consecutive also appear in vv. 38-44. The present translation understands this section as a description of what generally happened when the author charged into battle, but another option is to understand the section as narrative and translate accordingly.
Psalm 18:35 contains an additional line following this one, which reads “your right hand supports me.” It may be omitted here due to homoioarcton. See the note at Ps 18:35.

Heb “and you give me the shield of your deliverance”; KJV, ASV “the shield of thy (your NRSV, NLT) salvation”; NIV “your shield of victory.” Ancient Near Eastern literature often refers to a god giving a king special weapons. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of Psalm 18/2 Samuel 22” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 260-61.
Heb “your answer makes me great.” David refers to God’s willingness to answer his prayer.

37.text: You widen my path; my feet do not slip.

notes.text: Heb “step.” “Step” probably refers metonymically to the path upon which the psalmist walks. Another option is to translate, “you widen my stride.” This would suggest that God gives him the capacity to run quickly.
Heb “lower legs.” On the meaning of the Hebrew noun, which occurs only here, see H. R. Cohen, Biblical Hapax Legomena (SBLDS), 112. A cognate Akkadian noun means “lower leg.”

38.text: I chase my enemies and destroy them; I do not turn back until I wipe them out.

39.text: I wipe them out and beat them to death; they cannot get up; they fall at my feet.

40.text: You give me strength for battle; you make my foes kneel before me.

notes.text: Heb “you clothed me with strength for battle.”
Heb “you make those who rise against me kneel beneath me.”

41.text: You make my enemies retreat; I destroy those who hate me.

notes.text: Heb “and [as for] my enemies, you give to me [the] back [or “neck” ].” The idiom “give [the] back” means “to cause [one] to turn the back and run away.” See Exod 23:27 and HALOT 888 s.v. II ‏ערף‎.

42.text: They cry out, but there is no one to help them; they cry out to the Lord, but he does not answer them.

notes.text: The translation follows one medieval Hebrew ms and the ancient versions in reading the Piel ‏יְשַׁוְּעוּ‎ (yeshavveʿu, “they cry for help”) rather than the Qal of the MT ‏יִשְׁעוּ‎ (yishʿu, “they look about for help”). See Ps 18:41 as well.
Heb “but there is no deliverer.”

The words “they cry out” are not in the Hebrew text. This reference to the psalmists’ enemies crying out for help to the Lord suggests that the psalmist refers here to enemies within the covenant community, rather than foreigners. However, the militaristic context suggests foreign enemies are in view. Ancient Near Eastern literature indicates that defeated enemies would sometimes cry out for mercy to the god(s) of their conqueror. See R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of Psalm 18/2 Samuel 22” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 271.

43.text: I grind them as fine as the dust of the ground; I crush them and stomp them like clay in the streets.

notes.text: Or “mud” (so NAB, NIV, CEV). See HALOT 374 s.v. ‏טִיט‎.

44.text: You rescue me from a hostile army; you preserve me as a leader of nations; people over whom I had no authority are now my subjects.

notes.text: Heb “from the strivings of my people.” In this context ‏רִיב‎ (riv, “striving”) probably has a militaristic sense (as in Judg 12:2; Isa 41:11), and ‏עַם‎ (ʿam, “people”) probably refers more specifically to an army (for other examples, see the verses listed in BDB 766 s.v. ‏עַם‎ 2.d). The suffix “my” suggests David is referring to attacks by his own countrymen, the “people” being Israel. However, the parallel text in Ps 18:43 omits the suffix.

Heb “a people whom I did not know serve me.” In this context the verb “know” (‏יָדַע‎, yadaʿ) probably refers to formal recognition by treaty. People who were once not under the psalmist’s authority now willingly submit to his rulership to avoid being conquered militarily (see vv. 45-46). The language may recall the events recorded in 2 Sam 8:9-10 and 10:19.

45.text: Foreigners are powerless before me; when they hear of my exploits, they submit to me.

notes.text: For the meaning “to be weak; to be powerless” for the verb ‏כָּחַשׁ‎ (kakhash), see Ps 109:24. Verse 46, which also mentions foreigners, favors this interpretation. Another option is to translate “cower in fear” (see Deut 33:29; Pss 66:3; 81:15).
Heb “at a report of an ear they submit to me.” The report of David’s exploits is so impressive that those who hear it submit to his rulership without putting up a fight.

46.text: Foreigners lose their courage; they shake with fear as they leave their strongholds.

notes.text: Heb “wither, wear out.”
The translation assumes a reading ‏וְיַחְרְגוּ‎ (veyakhregu, “and they quaked”) rather than the MT ‏וְיַחְגְּרוּ‎ (veyakhgeru, “and they girded themselves”). See the note at Ps 18:45.
Heb “from.”
Heb “prisons.” Their besieged cities are compared to prisons.

47.text: The Lord is alive! My Protector is praiseworthy! The God who delivers me is exalted as king!

notes.text: Elsewhere the construction ‏חַי־יְהוָה‎ (khay yehvah) is used exclusively as an oath formula, but this is not the case here, for no oath follows. Here the statement is an affirmation of the Lord’s active presence and intervention. In contrast to pagan deities, he demonstrates that he is the living God by rescuing and empowering the psalmist.
Heb “my rocky cliff,” which is a metaphor for protection.
Or “blessed [i.e., praised] be.”

Heb “the God of the rock of my deliverance.” The term ‏צוּר‎ (tsur, “rock”) is probably accidentally repeated from the previous line. The parallel version in Ps 18:46 has simply “the God of my deliverance.”

The words “as king” are supplied in the translation for clarification. In the Psalms the verb ‏רוּם‎ (rum, “be exalted”) when used of God, refers to his exalted position as king (Pss 99:2; 113:4; 138:6) and/or his self-revelation as king through his mighty deeds of deliverance (Pss 21:13; 46:10; 57:5, 11).

48.text: The one true God completely vindicates me; he makes nations submit to me.

notes.text: Heb “The God is the one who grants vengeance to me.” The plural form of the noun “vengeance” indicates degree here, suggesting complete vengeance or vindication. In the ancient Near East military victory was sometimes viewed as a sign that one’s God had judged in favor of the victor, avenging and/or vindicating him. See, for example, Judg 11:27, 32-33, 36.
Heb “and [is the one who] brings down nations beneath me.”

49.text: He delivers me from my enemies; you snatch me away from those who attack me; you rescue me from violent men.

notes.text: Heb “and [the one who] brings me out from my enemies.”

Heb “you lift me up.” In light of the preceding and following references to deliverance, the verb ‏רוּם‎ (rum) probably here refers to being rescued from danger (see Ps 9:13). However, it could mean “exalt; elevate” here, indicating that the Lord has given him victory over his enemies and forced them to acknowledge the psalmist’s superiority.
Heb “from those who rise against me.”

50.text: So I will give you thanks, O Lord, before the nations! I will sing praises to you.

notes.text: This probably alludes to the fact that David will praise the Lord in the presence of the defeated nations when they, as his subjects, bring their tribute payments. Ideally God’s chosen king was to testify to the nations of God’s greatness. See J. Eaton, Kingship and the Psalms (SBT), 182-85.

Heb “to your name.” God’s “name” refers metonymically to his divine characteristics as suggested by his name, in this case “Lord,” the primary name of Israel’s covenant God which suggests his active presence with his people (see Exod 3:12-15).

51.text: He gives his king magnificent victories; he is faithful to his chosen ruler, to David and to his descendants forever!”

notes.text: The translation follows the Kethib and the ancient versions in reading ‏מַגְדִּיל‎ (magdil, “he magnifies”) rather than the Qere and many medieval Hebrew mss of the MT which read ‏מִגְדּוֹל‎ (migdol, “tower”). See Ps 18:50.
Heb “[the one who] does loyalty to his anointed one.”

1.text: These are the final words of David: “The oracle of David son of Jesse, the oracle of the man raised up as the ruler chosen by the God of Jacob, Israel’s beloved singer of songs:

notes.text: Heb “the anointed one of the God of Jacob.”
Or “pleasant.”

2.text: The Lord’s Spirit spoke through me; his word was on my tongue.

3.text: The God of Israel spoke, the Protector of Israel spoke to me. The one who rules fairly among men, the one who rules in the fear of God,

notes.text: Heb “rock,” used as a metaphor of divine protection.

4.text: is like the light of morning when the sun comes up, a morning in which there are no clouds. He is like the brightness after rain that produces grass from the earth.

5.text: My dynasty is approved by God, for he has made a perpetual covenant with me, arranged in all its particulars and secured. He always delivers me, and brings all I desire to fruition.

notes.text: Heb “For not thus [is] my house with God?”
Heb “for all my deliverance and every desire, surely does he not make [it] grow?”

6.text: But evil people are like thorns— all of them are tossed away, for they cannot be held in the hand.

7.text: The one who touches them must use an iron instrument or the wooden shaft of a spear. They are completely burned up right where they lie!”

notes.text: Heb “and with fire they are completely burned up in [the place where they] remain.” The infinitive absolute is used before the finite verb to emphasize that they are completely consumed by the fire.

8.text: These are the names of David’s warriors: Josheb Basshebeth, a Tahkemonite, was head of the officers. He killed 800 men with his spear in one battle.

notes.text: The Hebrew word is sometimes rendered as “the three,” but BDB is probably correct in taking it to refer to military officers (BDB 1026 s.v. ‏שְׁלִישִׁי‎). In that case the etymological connection of this word to the Hebrew numerical adjective for “three” can be explained as originating with a designation for the third warrior in a chariot.

The translation follows some LXX mss (see 1 Chr 11:11 as well) in reading ‏הוּא עוֹרֵר אֶת־חֲנִיתוֹ‎ (huʾ ʿorer ʾet khanito, “he raised up his spear”) rather than the MT’s ‏הוּא עֲדִינוֹ הָעֶצְנִי‎ (huʾ ʿadino haʿetsni [Kethib = ‏הָעֶצְנוֹ‎, haʿetsno]; “Adino the Ezenite”). The emended text reads literally “he was wielding his spear against eight hundred, [who were] slain at one time.”

9.text: Next in command was Eleazar son of Dodo, the son of Ahohi. He was one of the three warriors who were with David when they defied the Philistines who were assembled there for battle. When the men of Israel retreated,

notes.text: Heb “after him.”
This follows the Qere and many medieval Hebrew mss in reading ‏דֹּדוֹ‎ (dodo) rather than the Kethib of the MT ‏דֹּדַי‎ (doday; cf. ASV, NIV, NLT). But see 1 Chr 27:4.
Heb “went up.”

10.text: he stood his ground and fought the Philistines until his hand grew so tired that it seemed stuck to his sword. The Lord gave a great victory on that day. When the army returned to him, the only thing left to do was to plunder the corpses.

notes.text: Heb “arose.”
Heb “his hand.”

11.text: Next in command was Shammah son of Agee the Hararite. When the Philistines assembled at Lehi, where there happened to be an area of a field that was full of lentils, the army retreated before the Philistines.

notes.text: Heb “after him.”

The Hebrew text is difficult here. The MT reads ‏לַחַיָּה‎ (lachayyah), which implies a rare use of the word ‏חַיָּה‎ (chayyah). The word normally refers to an animal, but if the MT is accepted it would here have the sense of a troop or community of people. BDB 312 s.v. II. ‏חַיָּה‎, for example, understands the similar reference in v. 13 to be to “a group of allied families, making a raid together.” But this works better in v. 13 than it does in v. 11, where the context seems to suggest a particular staging location for a military operation. (See 1 Chr 11:15.) It therefore seems best to understand the word in v. 11 as a place name with ‏ה‎ (he) directive. In that case the Masoretes mistook the word for the common term for an animal and then tried to make sense of it in this context.

12.text: But he made a stand in the middle of that area. He defended it and defeated the Philistines; the Lord gave them a great victory.

notes.text: Heb “delivered.”

13.text: At the time of the harvest three of the thirty leaders went down to David at the cave of Adullam. A band of Philistines was camped in the valley of Rephaim.

notes.text: The meaning of Hebrew ‏אֶל־קָצִיר‎ (ʾel qatsir) seems here to be “at the time of harvest,” although this is an unusual use of the phrase. As S. R. Driver points out, this preposition does not normally have the temporal sense of “in” or “during” (S. R. Driver, Notes on the Hebrew Text and the Topography of the Books of Samuel, 366).

The translation follows the Qere and many medieval Hebrew mss in reading ‏שְׁלֹשָׁה‎ (sheloshah, “three”) rather than the Kethib of the MT ‏שְׁלֹשִׁים‎ (sheloshim, “thirty”). “Thirty” is due to dittography of the following word and makes no sense in the context.
Heb “went down…and approached.”

14.text: David was in the stronghold at the time, while a Philistine garrison was in Bethlehem.

15.text: David was thirsty and said, “How I wish someone would give me some water to drink from the cistern in Bethlehem near the gate!”

16.text: So the three elite warriors broke through the Philistine forces and drew some water from the cistern in Bethlehem near the gate. They carried it back to David, but he refused to drink it. He poured it out as a drink offering to the Lord

17.text: and said, “O Lord, I will not do this! It is equivalent to the blood of the men who risked their lives by going.” So he refused to drink it. Such were the exploits of the three elite warriors.

notes.text: Heb “Far be it to me, O Lord, from doing this.”
Heb “[Is it not] the blood of the men who were going with their lives?”
Heb “These things the three warriors did.”

18.text: Abishai son of Zeruiah, the brother of Joab, was head of the three. He killed 300 men with his spear and gained fame among the three.

notes.text: The translation follows the Qere, many medieval Hebrew mss, the LXX, and Vulgate in reading ‏הַשְּׁלֹשָׁה‎ (hashelosha, “the three”) rather than the Kethib of the MT ‏הַשָּׁלִשִׁי‎ (hashalishi, “the third,” or “adjutant”). Two medieval Hebrew mss and the Syriac Peshitta have “thirty.”
Heb “and he was wielding his spear against three hundred, [who were] slain, and to him there was a name among the three.”

19.text: From the three he was given honor and he became their officer, even though he was not one of the three.

notes.text: Or “more than.”

20.text: Benaiah son of Jehoiada was a brave warrior from Kabzeel who performed great exploits. He struck down the two sons of Ariel of Moab. He also went down and killed a lion in a cistern on a snowy day.

notes.text: The translation follows the Qere and many medieval Hebrew mss in reading ‏חַיִל‎ (khayil, “valor”) rather than the Kethib of the MT, ‏חַי‎ (khay, “life”).

Heb “the two of Ariel, Moab.” The precise meaning of ‏אריאל‎ is uncertain; some read “warrior.” The present translation assumes that the word is a proper name and that ‏בני‎, “sons of,” has accidentally dropped from the text by homoioarcton (note the preceding ‏שׁני‎), so originally: ‏שְׁנֵי בְנֵי אֲרִיאֵל‎ (shene vene ʾariʾel).

21.text: He also killed an impressive-looking Egyptian. The Egyptian wielded a spear, while Benaiah attacked him with a club. He grabbed the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand and killed him with his own spear.

notes.text: The translation follows the Qere and many medieval Hebrew mss in reading ‏אִישׁ‎ (ʾish, “man”) rather than the Kethib of the MT, ‏אֲשֶׁר‎ (ʾasher, “who”).
Heb “and he went down to.”

22.text: Such were the exploits of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who gained fame among the three elite warriors.

23.text: He received honor from the thirty warriors, though he was not one of the three elite warriors. David put him in charge of his bodyguard.

notes.text: Or “more than.”

24.text: Included with the thirty were the following: Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan son of Dodo from Bethlehem,

25.text: Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite,

26.text: Helez the Paltite, Ira son of Ikkesh from Tekoa,

27.text: Abiezer the Anathothite, Mebunnai the Hushathite,

28.text: Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite,

29.text: Heled son of Baanah the Netophathite, Ittai son of Ribai from Gibeah in Benjamin,

notes.text: The translation follows many medieval Hebrew mss in reading ‏חֵלֶד‎ (kheled; cf. NAB, NIV, NLT) rather than the MT ‏חֵלֶב‎ (khelev).

30.text: Benaiah the Pirathonite, Hiddai from the wadis of Gaash,

31.text: Abi-Albon the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Barhumite,

32.text: Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan

33.text: son of Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam son of Sharar the Hararite,

notes.text: The Hebrew text does not have “the son of.”

34.text: Eliphelet son of Ahasbai the Maacathite, Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite,

notes.text: Heb “the son of.”

35.text: Hezrai the Carmelite, Paarai the Arbite,

notes.text: The translation follows the Qere and many medieval Hebrew mss in reading ‏חֶצְרַי‎ (khetsray; cf. KJV, NAB) rather than the Kethib of the MT, ‏חֶצְרוֹ‎ (khetsro).

36.text: Igal son of Nathan from Zobah, Bani the Gadite,

37.text: Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite (the armor-bearer of Joab son of Zeruiah),

notes.text: The translation follows the Qere and many medieval Hebrew mss in reading the singular rather than the plural of the Kethib of the MT.

38.text: Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,

39.text: and Uriah the Hittite. Altogether there were thirty-seven.

1.text: The Lord’s anger again raged against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, “Go count Israel and Judah.”

notes.text: The parallel text in 1 Chr 21:1 says, “An adversary opposed Israel, inciting David to count how many warriors Israel had.” The Samuel version gives an underlying theological perspective, while the Chronicler simply describes what happened from a human perspective. The adversary in 1 Chr 21:1 is likely a human enemy, probably a nearby nation whose hostility against Israel pressured David into numbering the people so he could assess his military strength. See the note at 1 Chr 21:1.

2.text: The king told Joab, the general in command of his army, “Go through all the tribes of Israel from Dan to Beer Sheba and muster the army, so I may know the size of the army.”

3.text: Joab replied to the king, “May the Lord your God make the army a hundred times larger right before the eyes of my lord the king! But why does my master the king want to do this?”

4.text: But the king’s edict stood, despite the objections of Joab and the leaders of the army. So Joab and the leaders of the army left the king’s presence in order to muster the Israelite army.

notes.text: Heb “and the word of the king was stronger than.”

5.text: They crossed the Jordan and camped at Aroer, on the south side of the city, at the wadi of Gad, near Jazer.

notes.text: Heb “in the middle of.”

6.text: Then they went on to Gilead and to the region of Tahtim Hodshi, coming to Dan Jaan and on around to Sidon.

7.text: Then they went to the fortress of Tyre and all the cities of the Hivites and the Canaanites. Then they went on to the Negev of Judah, to Beer Sheba.

8.text: They went through all the land and after nine months and twenty days came back to Jerusalem.

9.text: Joab reported the number of warriors to the king. In Israel there were 800,000 sword-wielding warriors, and in Judah there were 500,000 soldiers.

notes.text: Heb “and Joab gave the number of the numbering of the people.”

10.text: David felt guilty after he had numbered the army. David said to the Lord, “I have sinned greatly by doing this! Now, O Lord, please remove the guilt of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.”

notes.text: Heb “and the heart of David struck him.”

11.text: When David got up the next morning, the Lord’s message had already come to the prophet Gad, David’s seer:

12.text: “Go, tell David, ‘This is what the Lord has said: I am offering you three forms of judgment. Pick one of them and I will carry it out against you.’”

13.text: Gad went to David and told him, “Shall seven years of famine come upon your land? Or shall you flee for three months from your enemies with them in hot pursuit? Or shall there be three days of plague in your land? Now decide what I should tell the one who sent me.”

notes.text: The LXX has here “three” rather than “seven,” and is followed by NAB, NIV, NCV, NRSV, TEV, NLT. See 1 Chr 21:12.
Heb “now know and see.”

14.text: David said to Gad, “I am very upset! I prefer that we be attacked by the Lord, for his mercy is great; I do not want to be attacked by human hands!”

notes.text: Heb “There is great distress to me. Let us fall into the hand of the Lord, for great is his mercy, but into the hand of man let me not fall.”

15.text: So the Lord sent a plague through Israel from the morning until the completion of the appointed time, and 70,000 people died from Dan to Beer Sheba.

16.text: When the angel extended his hand to destroy Jerusalem, the Lord relented from his judgment. He told the angel who was killing the people, “That’s enough! Stop now!” (Now the angel of the Lord was near the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.)

notes.text: Heb “messenger.”
Heb “concerning the calamity.”
Heb “Now, drop your hand.”

17.text: When he saw the angel who was destroying the people, David said to the Lord, “Look, it is I who have sinned and done this evil thing! As for these sheep—what have they done? Attack me and my family.”

notes.text: Heb “let your hand be against me and against the house of my father.”

18.text: So Gad went to David that day and told him, “Go up and build an altar for the Lord on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.”

19.text: So David went up as Gad instructed him to do, according to the Lord’s instructions.

20.text: When Araunah looked out and saw the king and his servants approaching him, he went out and bowed to the king with his face to the ground.

notes.text: Heb “Araunah.” The name has been replaced in the translation by the pronoun (“he”) for stylistic reasons.
Heb “nostrils.”

21.text: Araunah said, “Why has my lord the king come to his servant?” David replied, “To buy from you the threshing floor so I can build an altar for the Lord, so that the plague may be removed from the people.”

22.text: Araunah told David, “My lord the king may take whatever he wishes and offer it. Look! Here are oxen for burnt offerings, and threshing sledges and harnesses for wood.

notes.text: Heb “what is good in his eyes.”

Threshing sledges were heavy boards used in ancient times for loosening grain from husks. On the bottom sides of these boards sharp stones were embedded, and the boards were then dragged across the grain on a threshing floor by an ox or donkey.
Heb “the equipment of the oxen.”

23.text: I, the servant of my lord the king, give it all to the king!” Araunah also told the king, “May the Lord your God show you favor!”

notes.text: The Hebrew text is difficult here. The translation reads ‏עֶבֶד אֲדֹנִי‎ (ʿeved ʾadoni, “the servant of my lord”) rather than the MT’s ‏אֲרַוְנָה‎ (ʾAravnah). In normal court etiquette a subject would not use his own name in this way, but would more likely refer to himself in the third person. The MT probably first sustained loss of ‏עֶבֶד‎ (ʿeved, “servant”), leading to confusion of the word for “my lord” with the name of the Jebusite referred to here.

24.text: But the king said to Araunah, “No, I insist on buying it from you! I will not offer to the Lord my God burnt sacrifices that cost me nothing.” So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty pieces of silver.

notes.text: Heb “fifty shekels of silver.” This would have been about 20 ounces (568 grams) of silver by weight.

25.text: Then David built an altar for the Lord there and offered burnt sacrifices and peace offerings. And the Lord accepted prayers for the land, and the plague was removed from Israel.

1.text: King David was very old; even when they covered him with blankets, he could not get warm.

notes.text: Heb “was old, coming into the days” (i.e., advancing in years).
Or “garments.”

2.text: His servants advised him, “A young virgin must be found for our master, the king, to take care of the king’s needs and serve as his nurse. She can also sleep with you and keep our master, the king, warm.”

notes.text: Heb “said to.”

Heb “let them seek for my master, the king, a young girl, a virgin.” The third person plural subject of the verb is indefinite (see GKC 460 §144.f). The appositional expression, “a young girl, a virgin,” is idiomatic; the second term specifically defines the more general first term (see IBHS 230 §12.3b).
Heb “and she will stand before the king.” The Hebrew phrase “stand before” can mean “to attend; to serve” (BDB 764 s.v. ‏עָמַד‎).

Heb “and she will lie down in your bosom.” The expression might imply sexual intimacy (see 2 Sam 12:3 [where the lamb symbolizes Bathsheba] and Mic 7:5), though v. 4b indicates that David did not actually have sex with the young woman.
Heb “and my master, the king, will be warm.”

3.text: So they looked through all Israel for a beautiful young woman and found Abishag, a Shunammite, and brought her to the king.

notes.text: Heb “through all the territory of Israel.”

4.text: The young woman was very beautiful; she became the king’s nurse and served him, but the king was not intimate with her.

notes.text: Heb “did not know her.” The verb ‏יָדַע‎ (yadaʿ, “to know”) is a euphemism for sexual relations.

5.text: Now Adonijah, son of David and Haggith, was promoting himself, boasting, “I will be king!” He managed to acquire chariots and horsemen, as well as fifty men to serve as his royal guard.

notes.text: Heb “son of Haggith,” but since this formula usually designates the father (who in this case was David), the translation specifies that David was Adonijah’s father.
Haggith was one of David’s wives (2 Sam 3:4; 2 Chr 3:2).
Heb “lifting himself up.”
Heb “saying.”
Or “he acquired for himself.”
Heb “to run ahead of him.”

6.text: (Now his father had never corrected him by saying, “Why do you do such things?” He was also very handsome and had been born right after Absalom.)

notes.text: Or “disciplined.”
Heb “did not correct him from his days.” The phrase “from his days” means “from his earliest days,” or “ever in his life.” See GKC 382 §119.w, n. 2.
Heb “and she gave birth to him after Absalom.” This does not imply they had the same mother; Absalom’s mother was Maacah, not Haggith (2 Sam 3:4).

7.text: He collaborated with Joab son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest, and they supported him.

notes.text: Heb “his words were.”
Heb “helped after” (i.e., stood by).
Heb “Adonijah.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“him”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.

8.text: But Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and David’s elite warriors did not ally themselves with Adonijah.

notes.text: Or “bodyguard” (Heb “mighty men”).
Heb “were not.”

9.text: Adonijah sacrificed sheep, cattle, and fattened steers at the Stone of Zoheleth near En Rogel. He invited all his brothers, the king’s sons, as well as all the men of Judah, the king’s servants.

notes.text: The ancient Greek version omits this appositional phrase.

10.text: But he did not invite Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the elite warriors, or his brother Solomon.

notes.text: Or “bodyguard” (Heb “mighty men”).

11.text: Nathan said to Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother, “Has it been reported to you that Haggith’s son Adonijah has become king behind our master David’s back?

notes.text: Heb “Have you not heard?”
Heb “and our master David does not know.”

12.text: Now let me give you some advice as to how you can save your life and your son Solomon’s life.

notes.text: Heb “now, come.” The imperative of ‏הָלַךְ‎ (halakh) is here used as an introductory interjection. See BDB 234 s.v. ‏חָלַךְ‎.
Or “so that.”

13.text: Visit King David and say to him, ‘My master, O king, did you not solemnly promise your servant, “Surely your son Solomon will be king after me; he will sit on my throne”? So why has Adonijah become king?’

notes.text: Heb “come, go to.” The imperative of ‏הָלַךְ‎ (halakh) is here used as an introductory interjection. See BDB 234 s.v. ‏חָלַךְ‎.
Or “swear an oath to.”

14.text: While you are still there speaking to the king, I will arrive and verify your report.”

notes.text: In the Hebrew text the sentence is introduced by the particle ‏הִנֵּה‎ (hinneh, “look”), which here draws attention to Nathan’s concluding word of assurance and support. For this use of the word, see HALOT 252 s.v. ‏הִנֵּה‎.
The Hebrew text reads, “I will come after you.”
Heb “fill up [i.e., confirm] your words.”

15.text: So Bathsheba visited the king in his private quarters. (The king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was serving the king.)

notes.text: Or “bedroom.”

16.text: Bathsheba bowed down on the floor before the king. The king said, “What do you want?”

notes.text: Heb “bowed low and bowed down to.”

17.text: She replied to him, “My master, you swore an oath to your servant by the Lord your God, ‘Solomon your son will be king after me and he will sit on my throne.’

18.text: But now, look, Adonijah has become king! But you, my master the king, are not even aware of it!

notes.text: Instead of ‏עַתָּה‎ (ʿattah, “now”) many Hebrew mss, along with the Old Greek, Syriac Peshitta, and Latin Vulgate, have the similar sounding independent pronoun ‏אַתָּה‎ (ʾattah, “you”). This reading is followed in the present translation.
Heb “you do not know [about it].”

19.text: He has sacrificed many cattle, steers, and sheep and has invited all the king’s sons, Abiathar the priest, and Joab, the commander of the army, but he has not invited your servant Solomon.

20.text: Now, my master, O king, all Israel is watching anxiously to see who is named to succeed my master the king on the throne.

notes.text: Many Hebrew mss have ‏עַתָּה‎ (ʿattah, “now”) rather than the similar sounding independent pronoun ‏אַתָּה‎ (ʾattah, “you”).
Heb “the eyes of all Israel are upon you to declare to them who will sit on the throne of my master the king after him.”

21.text: If a decision is not made, when my master the king is buried with his ancestors, my son Solomon and I will be considered state criminals.”

notes.text: The words “if a decision is not made” are added for clarification.
Heb “lies down with his fathers.”
Heb “I and my son Solomon.” The order has been reversed in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “will be guilty”; NASB “considered offenders”; TEV “treated as traitors.”

22.text: Just then, while she was still speaking to the king, Nathan the prophet arrived.

notes.text: Heb “look.” The particle ‏הִנֵּה‎ (hinneh) here draws attention to Nathan’s arrival and invites the audience to view the scene through the eyes of the participants.

23.text: The king was told, “Nathan the prophet is here.” Nathan entered and bowed before the king with his face to the floor.

notes.text: Heb “ground.” Since this was indoors, “floor” is more appropriate than “ground.”

24.text: Nathan said, “My master, O king, did you announce, ‘Adonijah will be king after me; he will sit on my throne’?

25.text: For today he has gone down and sacrificed many cattle, steers, and sheep and has invited all the king’s sons, the army commanders, and Abiathar the priest. At this moment they are having a feast in his presence, and they have declared, ‘Long live King Adonijah!’

notes.text: Heb “look.”
Heb “eating and drinking.”
Heb “let the king, Adonijah, live!”

26.text: But he did not invite me—your servant—or Zadok the priest, or Benaiah son of Jehoiada, or your servant Solomon.

27.text: Has my master the king authorized this without informing your servants who should succeed my master the king on his throne?”

notes.text: Many Hebrew mss and ancient textual witnesses agree with the Qere in reading this as singular, “your servant.”
Heb “From my master the king is this thing done, and you did not make known to your servants who will sit on the throne of my master the king after him?”

28.text: King David responded, “Summon Bathsheba!” She came and stood before the king.

notes.text: Heb “answered and said.”
Summon Bathsheba. Bathsheba must have left the room when Nathan arrived (see 1:22).
Heb “she came before the king and stood before the king.”

29.text: The king swore an oath: “As certainly as the Lord lives (he who has rescued me from every danger),

notes.text: Or “ransomed my life.”

30.text: I will keep today the oath I swore to you by the Lord God of Israel: ‘Surely Solomon your son will be king after me; he will sit in my place on my throne.’”

notes.text: Or “carry out, perform.”

31.text: Bathsheba bowed down to the king with her face to the floor and said, “May my master, King David, live forever!”

notes.text: Heb “bowed low, face [to] the ground, and bowed down to the king.”

32.text: King David said, “Summon Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada.” They came before the king,

notes.text: Summon…Nathan. Nathan must have left the room when Bathsheba reentered.

33.text: and he told them, “Take your master’s servants with you, put my son Solomon on my mule, and lead him down to Gihon.

notes.text: Heb “the king.”
The plural form is used in the Hebrew text to indicate honor and authority.
Heb “mount Solomon my son on the mule that belongs to me and take him down to Gihon.”

34.text: There Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet will anoint him king over Israel; then blow the trumpet and declare, ‘Long live King Solomon!’

notes.text: Or “designate” (i.e., by anointing with oil).

35.text: Then follow him up as he comes and sits on my throne. He will be king in my place; I have decreed that he will be ruler over Israel and Judah.”

notes.text: Or “commanded.”

36.text: Benaiah son of Jehoiada responded to the king: “So be it! May the Lord God of my master the king confirm it!

notes.text: Heb “answered and said.”
Or “Amen.”
Heb “So may the Lord God of my master the king say.”

37.text: As the Lord is with my master the king, so may he be with Solomon, and may he make him an even greater king than my master King David!”

notes.text: Heb “and may he make his throne greater than the throne of my master King David.”

38.text: So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the Kerethites, and the Pelethites went down, put Solomon on King David’s mule, and led him to Gihon.

notes.text: The Kerethites and Pelethites were members of David’s royal guard (see 2 Sam 8:18). The Kerethites may have been descendants of an ethnic group originating in Crete.

39.text: Zadok the priest took a horn filled with olive oil from the tent and poured it on Solomon; the trumpet was blown and all the people declared, “Long live King Solomon!”

notes.text: Heb “the horn of oil.” This has been specified as olive oil in the translation for clarity.
A horn filled with oil. An animal’s horn was used as an oil flask in the anointing ceremony.
Or “anointed.”

40.text: All the people followed him up, playing flutes and celebrating so loudly they made the ground shake.

notes.text: Heb “and all the people went up after him, and the people were playing flutes and rejoicing with great joy and the ground split open at the sound of them.” The verb ‏בָּקַע‎ (baqaʿ, “to split open”), which elsewhere describes the effects of an earthquake, is obviously here an exaggeration for the sake of emphasis.

41.text: Now Adonijah and all his guests heard the commotion just as they had finished eating. When Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he asked, “Why is there such a noisy commotion in the city?”

notes.text: Heb “And Adonijah and all the guests who were with him heard, now they had finished eating.”
Heb “Why is the city’s sound noisy?”

42.text: As he was still speaking, Jonathan son of Abiathar the priest arrived. Adonijah said, “Come in, for an important man like you must be bringing good news.”

notes.text: The Hebrew text has “look” at this point. The particle ‏הִנֵּה‎ (hinneh), “look” draws attention to Jonathan’s arrival and invites the audience to view the scene through the eyes of the participants.
Or “surely.”

Heb “you are a man of strength [or “ability”] and you bring a message [that is] good.” Another option is to understand the phrase ‏אִישׁ חַיִל‎ (ʾish khayil) in the sense of “a worthy man,” that is “loyal.” See also 1 Kgs 1:52 and HALOT 311 s.v. ‏חַיִל‎.

43.text: Jonathan replied to Adonijah: “No! Our master King David has made Solomon king.

notes.text: Heb “answered and said.”
For a similar use of ‏אֲבָל‎ (ʾaval), see Gen 17:19, where God rejects Abraham’s proposal and offers an alternative.
The plural form is used in the Hebrew text to indicate honor and authority.

44.text: The king sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the Kerethites, and the Pelethites and they put him on the king’s mule.

45.text: Then Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anointed him king in Gihon. They went up from there rejoicing, and the city is in an uproar. That is the sound you hear.

notes.text: I.e., designated by anointing with oil.

46.text: Furthermore, Solomon has assumed the royal throne.

notes.text: Heb “And also Solomon sits on the throne of the kingdom.”

47.text: The king’s servants have even come to congratulate our master King David, saying, ‘May your God make Solomon more famous than you and make him an even greater king than you!’ Then the king leaned on the bed

notes.text: Heb “to bless.”
The plural form is used in the Hebrew text to indicate honor and authority.
Many Hebrew mss agree with the Qere in reading simply “God.”
Heb “make the name of Solomon better than your name, and make his throne greater than your throne.” The term ‏שֵׁם‎ (shem, “name”) is used here of one’s fame and reputation.
Or “bowed down; worshiped.”

48.text: and said this: ‘The Lord God of Israel is worthy of praise because today he has placed a successor on my throne and allowed me to see it.’”

notes.text: The Hebrew text reads, “and the king said.”
Or “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who….” In this blessing formula ‏אֲשֶׁר‎ (ʾasher, “who; because”) introduces the reason why the one being blessed deserves the honor.
Heb “and my eyes are seeing.”

49.text: All of Adonijah’s guests panicked; they jumped up and rushed off their separate ways.

notes.text: Or “were afraid, trembled.”

50.text: Adonijah feared Solomon, so he got up and went and grabbed hold of the horns of the altar.

notes.text: Grabbed hold of the horns of the altar. The “horns” of the altar were the horn-shaped projections on the four corners of the altar (see Exod 27:2). By going to the holy place and grabbing hold of the horns of the altar, Adonijah was seeking asylum from Solomon.

51.text: Solomon was told, “Look, Adonijah fears you; see, he has taken hold of the horns of the altar, saying, ‘May King Solomon solemnly promise me today that he will not kill his servant with the sword.’”

notes.text: Heb “King Solomon.” The name and title have been replaced by the pronoun (“you”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Or “swear an oath to.”

52.text: Solomon said, “If he is a loyal subject, not a hair of his head will be harmed, but if he is found to be a traitor, he will die.”

notes.text: Heb “if he is a man of strength [or ability].” In this context, where Adonijah calls himself a “servant,” implying allegiance to the new king, the phrase ‏אִישׁ חַיִל‎ (ʾish khayil) probably carries the sense of “a worthy man,” that is, “loyal” (see HALOT 311 s.v. ‏חַיִל‎).
Heb “but if evil is found in him.”

53.text: King Solomon sent men to bring him down from the altar. He came and bowed down to King Solomon, and Solomon told him, “Go home.”

notes.text: Heb “sent and they brought him down.”
Heb “Go to your house.”

1.text: When David was close to death, he told Solomon his son:

notes.text: Heb “and the days of David approached to die.”
Or “commanded.”

2.text: “I am about to die. Be strong and become a man!

notes.text: Heb “going the way of all the earth.”

3.text: Do the job the Lord your God has assigned you by following his instructions and obeying his rules, commandments, regulations, and laws as written in the law of Moses. Then you will succeed in all you do and seek to accomplish,

notes.text: Heb “keep the charge of the Lord your God.”
Heb “by walking in his ways.”
Or “keeping.”
Heb “then you will cause to succeed all which you do and all which you turn there.”

4.text: and the Lord will fulfill his promise to me, ‘If your descendants watch their step and live faithfully in my presence with all their heart and being, then,’ he promised, ‘you will not fail to have a successor on the throne of Israel.’

notes.text: Heb “then the Lord will establish his word which he spoke to me, saying.”
Heb “guard their way.”
Heb “by walking before me in faithfulness.”
Or “soul.”
Heb “saying.”
Heb “there will not be cut off from you a man from upon the throne of Israel.”

5.text: “You know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me—how he murdered two commanders of the Israelite armies, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether. During peacetime he struck them down as if in battle; when he shed their blood, he stained the belt on his waist and the sandals on his feet.

notes.text: Heb “what he did to the two commanders…and he killed them.”
Heb “he shed the blood of battle in peace.”

Heb “and he shed the blood of battle on his belt which is on his waist and on his sandal[s] which are on his feet.” That is, he covered himself with guilt and his guilt was obvious to all who saw him.

6.text: Do to him what you think is appropriate, but don’t let him live long and die a peaceful death.

notes.text: Heb “according to your wisdom.”
Heb “and do not bring down his grey hair in peace [to] Sheol.”

7.text: “Treat fairly the sons of Barzillai of Gilead and provide for their needs, because they helped me when I had to flee from your brother Absalom.

notes.text: Heb “do loyalty with”; or “act faithfully toward.”
Heb “and let them be among the ones who eat [at] your table.”
Heb “thus drew near to.”

8.text: “Note well, you still have to contend with Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, who tried to call down upon me a horrible judgment when I went to Mahanaim. He came down and met me at the Jordan, and I solemnly promised him by the Lord, ‘I will not strike you down with the sword.’

notes.text: Heb “Look, with you is Shimei….”
Heb “and he cursed me with a horrible curse on the day I went to Mahanaim.”
Or “swore an oath to.”
Heb “kill you.”

9.text: But now don’t treat him as if he were innocent. You are a wise man and you know how to handle him; make sure he has a bloody death.”

notes.text: The Lucianic recension of the Old Greek and the Vulgate have here “you” rather than “now.” The two words are homonyms in Hebrew.
Heb “what you should do to him.”
Heb “bring his grey hair down in blood [to] Sheol.”

10.text: Then David passed away and was buried in the City of David.

notes.text: Heb “and David lay down with his fathers.”
The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

11.text: David reigned over Israel forty years; he reigned in Hebron seven years, and in Jerusalem thirty-three years.

12.text: Solomon sat on his father David’s throne, and his royal authority was firmly solidified.

notes.text: Or “kingship.”

13.text: Haggith’s son Adonijah visited Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother. She asked, “Do you come in peace?” He answered, “Yes.”

notes.text: Heb “[in] peace.”

14.text: He added, “I have something to say to you.” She replied, “Speak.”

notes.text: Heb “and he said.”

15.text: He said, “You know that the kingdom was mine and all Israel considered me king. But then the kingdom was given to my brother, for the Lord decided it should be his.

notes.text: Or “kingship.”
Heb “set their face to me to be king.”
Heb “and the kingdom turned about and became my brother’s, for from the Lord it became his.”

16.text: Now I’d like to ask you for just one thing. Please don’t refuse me.” She said, “Go ahead and ask.”

notes.text: Heb “Do not turn back my face.”
Heb “She said, ‘Speak!’”

17.text: He said, “Please ask King Solomon if he would give me Abishag the Shunammite as a wife, for he won’t refuse you.”

notes.text: Heb “Say to Solomon the king, for he will not turn back your face, that he might give to me Abishag the Shunammite for a wife.”

18.text: Bathsheba replied, “That’s fine; I’ll speak to the king on your behalf.”

notes.text: Heb “[It is] good!”

19.text: So Bathsheba visited King Solomon to speak to him on Adonijah’s behalf. The king got up to greet her, bowed to her, and then sat on his throne. He ordered a throne to be brought for the king’s mother, and she sat at his right hand.

notes.text: Or “meet.”
Heb “he set up a throne for the mother of the king.”

20.text: She said, “I would like to ask you for just one small favor. Please don’t refuse me.” He said, “Go ahead and ask, my mother, for I would not refuse you.”

notes.text: Or “I’d like to make just one request of you.”
Heb “Do not turn back my face.”
Heb “and the king said to her.”

21.text: She said, “Allow Abishag the Shunammite to be given to your brother Adonijah as a wife.”

22.text: King Solomon answered his mother, “Why just request Abishag the Shunammite for him? Since he is my older brother, you should also request the kingdom for him, for Abiathar the priest, and for Joab son of Zeruiah!”

notes.text: Heb “for Adonijah.”

23.text: King Solomon then swore an oath by the Lord, “May God judge me severely, if Adonijah does not pay for this request with his life!

notes.text: Heb “So may God do to me, and so may he add.”
Heb “if with his life Adonijah has not spoken this word.”

24.text: Now, as certainly as the Lord lives (he who made me secure, allowed me to sit on my father David’s throne, and established a dynasty for me as he promised), Adonijah will be executed today!”

notes.text: Heb “house.”

25.text: King Solomon then sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he killed Adonijah.

notes.text: The Hebrew text adds, “by the hand of.”
Heb “and he struck him and he died.”

26.text: The king then told Abiathar the priest, “Go back to your property in Anathoth. You deserve to die, but today I will not kill you because you did carry the ark of the Sovereign Lord before my father David and you suffered with my father through all his difficult times.”

notes.text: Or “field.”
Heb “you are a man of death,” an idiom.
Heb “and because you suffered through all which my father suffered.”

27.text: Solomon removed Abiathar from being a priest for the Lord, fulfilling the Lord’s message that he had pronounced against the family of Eli in Shiloh.

28.text: When the news reached Joab (for Joab had supported Adonijah, although he had not supported Absalom), he ran to the tent of the Lord and grabbed hold of the horns of the altar.

notes.text: Heb “turned after” (also later in this verse).
Heb “Joab.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.

Grabbed hold of the horns of the altar. The “horns” of the altar were the horn-shaped projections on the four corners of the altar (see Exod 27:2). By going to the holy place and grabbing hold of the horns of the altar, Joab was seeking asylum from Solomon.

29.text: When King Solomon heard that Joab had run to the tent of the Lord and was right there beside the altar, he ordered Benaiah son of Jehoiada, “Go, strike him down.”

notes.text: Heb “and it was related to King Solomon.”
Heb “so Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, saying.”

30.text: When Benaiah arrived at the tent of the Lord, he said to him, “The king says, ‘Come out!’” But he replied, “No, I will die here!” So Benaiah sent word to the king and reported Joab’s reply.

notes.text: Heb “saying, “In this way Joab spoke and in this way he answered me.”

31.text: The king told him, “Do as he said! Strike him down and bury him. Take away from me and from my father’s family the guilt of Joab’s murderous, bloody deeds.

notes.text: Heb “house.”
Heb “take away the undeserved bloodshed which Joab spilled from upon me and from upon the house of my father.”

32.text: May the Lord punish him for the blood he shed; behind my father David’s back he struck down and murdered with the sword two men who were more innocent and morally upright than he —Abner son of Ner, commander of Israel’s army, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of Judah’s army.

notes.text: Heb “The Lord will cause his blood to return upon his head.”
Heb “because he struck down two men more innocent and better than he and he killed them with the sword, and my father David did not know.”

33.text: May Joab and his descendants be perpetually guilty of their shed blood, but may the Lord give perpetual peace to David, his descendants, his family, and his dynasty.”

notes.text: Heb “house.”
Heb “his throne.”

34.text: So Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up and executed Joab; he was buried at his home in the wilderness.

notes.text: Heb “struck him and killed him.” The referent (Joab) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

35.text: The king appointed Benaiah son of Jehoiada to take his place at the head of the army, and the king appointed Zadok the priest to take Abiathar’s place.

notes.text: Heb “over.”
The Old Greek translation includes after v. 35 some fourteen verses that are absent from the MT.

36.text: Next the king summoned Shimei and told him, “Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and live there, but you may not leave there to go anywhere.

notes.text: Heb “sent and summoned.”
Heb “and you may not go out from there here or there.”

37.text: If you ever do leave and cross the Kidron Valley, know for sure that you will certainly die. You will be responsible for your own death.”

notes.text: Heb “your blood will be upon your head.”

38.text: Shimei said to the king, “My master the king’s proposal is acceptable. Your servant will do as you say.” So Shimei lived in Jerusalem for a long time.

notes.text: Heb “Good is the word, as my master the king has spoken.”
Heb “so your servant will do.”
Heb “many days.”

39.text: Three years later two of Shimei’s servants ran away to King Achish son of Maacah of Gath. Shimei was told, “Look, your servants are in Gath.”

40.text: So Shimei got up, saddled his donkey, and went to Achish at Gath to find his servants; Shimei went and brought back his servants from Gath.

41.text: When Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and had then returned,

42.text: the king summoned Shimei and said to him, “You will recall that I made you take an oath by the Lord, and I solemnly warned you, ‘If you ever leave and go anywhere, know for sure that you will certainly die.’ You said to me, ‘The proposal is acceptable; I agree to it.’

notes.text: Heb “sent and summoned.”
Heb “Is it not [true]…?” In the Hebrew text the statement is interrogative; the rhetorical question expects the answer, “Of course it is.”
Heb “here or there.”
Heb “good is the word; I have heard.”

43.text: Why then have you broken the oath you made before the Lord and disobeyed the order I gave you?”

notes.text: Heb “Why have you not kept the oath [to] the Lord and the commandment I commanded you?”

44.text: Then the king said to Shimei, “You are well aware of the way you mistreated my father David. The Lord will punish you for what you did.

notes.text: Heb “You know all the evil, for your heart knows, which you did to David my father.”
Heb “The Lord will cause your evil to return upon your head.”

45.text: But King Solomon will be empowered, and David’s dynasty will endure permanently before the Lord.”

notes.text: Or “blessed.”
Heb “throne.”

46.text: The king then gave the order to Benaiah son of Jehoiada who went and executed Shimei. So Solomon took firm control of the kingdom.

notes.text: “The king commanded Benaiah son of Jehoiada and he went out and struck him down and he died.”
“And the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.”

1.text: Solomon made an alliance by marriage with Pharaoh, king of Egypt; he married Pharaoh’s daughter. He brought her to the City of David until he could finish building his residence and the temple of the Lord and the wall around Jerusalem.

notes.text: The phrase City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

2.text: Now the people were offering sacrifices at the high places, because in those days a temple had not yet been built to honor the Lord.

notes.text: Offering sacrifices at the high places. The “high places” were places of worship that were naturally or artificially elevated.

Heb “for the name of the Lord.” The word “name” sometimes refers to one’s reputation or honor (thus the translation here, “to honor the Lord”). The “name” of the Lord sometimes designates the Lord himself, being indistinguishable from the proper name.

3.text: Solomon demonstrated his loyalty to the Lord by following the practices of his father David, except that he offered sacrifices and burned incense on the high places.

notes.text: Heb “by walking in.”
Or “policies, rules.”

4.text: The king went to Gibeon to offer sacrifices, for it had the most prominent of the high places. Solomon would offer up 1,000 burnt sacrifices on the altar there.

notes.text: Heb “for it was the great high place.”
Or, “customarily offered up.” The verb form is an imperfect, which is probably used here in a customary sense to indicate continued or repeated action in past time. See GKC 314 §107.b.

5.text: One night in Gibeon the Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream. God said, “Tell me what I should give you.”

notes.text: Or “revealed himself.”
Heb “ask.”

6.text: Solomon replied, “You demonstrated great loyalty to your servant, my father David, as he served you faithfully, properly, and sincerely. You have maintained this great loyalty to this day by allowing his son to sit on his throne.

notes.text: Heb “did.”
Heb “walked before.”
Heb “in faithfulness and in innocence and in uprightness of heart with you.”
Heb “and you have kept to him this great loyalty and you gave to him a son [who] sits on his throne as this day.”

7.text: Now, O Lord my God, you have made your servant king in my father David’s place, even though I am only a young man and am inexperienced.

notes.text: Heb “and I do not know going out or coming in.”

8.text: Your servant stands among your chosen people; they are a great nation that is too numerous to count or number.

notes.text: There is no verb expressed in the Hebrew text; “stands” is supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “your people whom you have chosen.”

9.text: So give your servant a discerning mind so he can make judicial decisions for your people and distinguish right from wrong. Otherwise no one is able to make judicial decisions for this great nation of yours.”

notes.text: Heb “a hearing heart.” (The Hebrew term translated “heart” often refers to the mental faculties.)
Heb “to judge.”
Heb “to understand between good and evil.”
Heb “for”; the word “otherwise” is used to reflect the logical sense of the statement.
Heb “who is able?” The rhetorical question anticipates the answer, “no one.”
Heb “to judge.”
Heb “your numerous people.”

10.text: The Lord was pleased that Solomon made this request.

notes.text: The Hebrew term translated “Lord” here and in v.15 is ‏אֲדֹנָי‎ (ʾadonay).
Heb “And the thing was good in the eyes of the Lord, for Solomon asked for this thing.”

11.text: God said to him, “Because you asked for the ability to make wise judicial decisions, and not for long life, or riches, or vengeance on your enemies,

notes.text: Heb “because you asked for this thing, and did not ask for yourself many days and did not ask for yourself riches and did not ask for the life of your enemies, but you asked for yourself understanding to hear judgment.”

12.text: I grant your request and give you a wise and discerning mind superior to that of anyone who has preceded or will succeed you.

notes.text: This statement is introduced in the Hebrew text by the particle ‏הִנֵּה‎ (hinneh, “look”) which draws attention to and emphasizes what follows.
Heb “I am doing according to your words.” The perfect tense is sometimes used of actions occurring at the same time a statement is made.

This statement is introduced by the particle ‏הִנֵּה‎ (hinneh, “look”) which draws attention to and emphasizes what follows. The translation assumes that the perfect tense here indicates that the action occurs as the statement is made (i.e., “right now I give you”).
Heb “heart.” (The Hebrew term translated “heart” often refers to the mental faculties.)
Heb “so that there has not been one like you prior to you, and after you one will not arise like you.”

13.text: Furthermore, I am giving you what you did not request—riches and honor so that you will be the greatest king of your generation.

notes.text: The translation assumes that the perfect tense here indicates that the action occurs as the statement is made.
Heb “so that there is not one among the kings like you all your days.” The LXX lacks the words “all your days.”

14.text: If you follow my instructions by obeying my rules and regulations, just as your father David did, then I will grant you long life.”

notes.text: Heb “walk in my ways.”
Or “keeping.”
Heb “walked.”
Heb “I will lengthen your days.”

15.text: Solomon then woke up and realized it was a dream. He went to Jerusalem, stood before the ark of the Lord’s covenant, offered up burnt sacrifices, presented peace offerings, and held a feast for all his servants.

notes.text: Heb “and look, a dream.”
Or “tokens of peace”; NIV, TEV “fellowship offerings.”

16.text: Then two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him.

17.text: One of the women said, “My master, this woman and I live in the same house. I had a baby while she was with me in the house.

18.text: Then three days after I had my baby, this woman also had a baby. We were alone; there was no one else in the house except the two of us.
