notes.text: There was no one else in the house except the two of us. In other words, there were no other witnesses to the births who could identify which child belonged to which mother.

19.text: This woman’s child suffocated during the night when she rolled on top of him.

notes.text: Heb “died.”
Heb “lay, slept.”

20.text: She got up in the middle of the night and took my son from my side, while your servant was sleeping. She put him in her arms, and put her dead son in my arms.

21.text: I got up in the morning to nurse my son, and there he was, dead! But when I examined him carefully in the morning, I realized it was not my baby.”

notes.text: Heb “look.”
Heb “look, it was not my son to whom I had given birth.”

22.text: The other woman said, “No! My son is alive; your son is dead!” But the first woman replied, “No, your son is dead; my son is alive.” Each presented her case before the king.

notes.text: Heb “they spoke before the king.” Another option is to translate, “they argued before the king.”

23.text: The king said, “One says, ‘My son is alive; your son is dead,’ while the other says, ‘No, your son is dead; my son is alive.’”

24.text: The king ordered, “Get me a sword.” So they placed a sword before the king.

25.text: The king then said, “Cut the living child in two, and give half to one and half to the other!”

26.text: The real mother spoke up to the king, for her motherly instincts were awakened. She said, “My master, give her the living child! Whatever you do, don’t kill him!” But the other woman said, “Neither one of us will have him. Let them cut him in two!”

notes.text: Heb “the woman whose son was alive.”
Heb “for her compassions grew warm for her son.”
The infinitive absolute before the negated jussive emphasizes the main verb.

27.text: The king responded, “Give the first woman the living child; don’t kill him. She is the mother.”

28.text: When all Israel heard about the judicial decision which the king had rendered, they respected the king, for they realized that he possessed divine wisdom to make judicial decisions.

notes.text: Heb “feared,” perhaps in the sense, “stood in awe of.”
Heb “saw.”

Heb “the wisdom of God was in his midst for performing justice.” The phrase “wisdom of God” may be taken as an attributive genitive, “divine wisdom,” or as a genitive of source, “wisdom from God.” Even in English they are basically the same, since wisdom from God is divine in character.

1.text: King Solomon ruled over all Israel.

2.text: These were his officials: Azariah son of Zadok was the priest.

3.text: Elihoreph and Ahijah, the sons of Shisha, wrote down what happened. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was in charge of the records.

notes.text: Heb “were scribes”; NASB, NIV, NRSV “secretaries”; TEV, NLT “court secretaries.”

4.text: Benaiah son of Jehoiada was commander of the army. Zadok and Abiathar were priests.

notes.text: Heb “was over.”

5.text: Azariah son of Nathan was supervisor of the district governors. Zabud son of Nathan was a priest and adviser to the king.

notes.text: Heb “was over.”
Heb “close associate of”; KJV, ASV, NASB “the king’s friend” (a title for an adviser, not just an acquaintance).

6.text: Ahishar was supervisor of the palace. Adoniram son of Abda was supervisor of the work crews.

notes.text: Heb “over the house.”
Heb “was over.”
The work crews. This Hebrew word (‏מַס‎, mas) refers to a group of laborers conscripted for royal or public service.

7.text: Solomon had twelve district governors appointed throughout Israel who acquired supplies for the king and his palace. Each was responsible for one month in the year.

8.text: These were their names: Ben Hur was in charge of the hill country of Ephraim.

9.text: Ben Deker was in charge of Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth Shemesh, and Elon Beth Hanan.

10.text: Ben Hesed was in charge of Arubboth; he controlled Socoh and all the territory of Hepher.

11.text: Ben Abinadab was in charge of Naphath Dor. (He was married to Solomon’s daughter Taphath.)

12.text: Baana son of Ahilud was in charge of Taanach and Megiddo, as well as all of Beth Shean next to Zarethan below Jezreel, from Beth Shean to Abel Meholah and on past Jokmeam.

13.text: Ben Geber was in charge of Ramoth Gilead; he controlled the villages of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead, as well as the region of Argob in Bashan, including sixty large walled cities with bronze bars locking their gates.

14.text: Ahinadab son of Iddo was in charge of Mahanaim.

15.text: Ahimaaz was in charge of Naphtali. (He married Solomon’s daughter Basemath.)

16.text: Baana son of Hushai was in charge of Asher and Aloth.

17.text: Jehoshaphat son of Paruah was in charge of Issachar.

18.text: Shimei son of Ela was in charge of Benjamin.

19.text: Geber son of Uri was in charge of the land of Gilead (the territory which had once belonged to King Sihon of the Amorites and to King Og of Bashan). He was sole governor of the area.

20.text: The people of Judah and Israel were as innumerable as the sand on the seashore; they had plenty to eat and drink and were happy.

21.text: (5:1) Solomon ruled all the kingdoms from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines, as far as the border of Egypt. These kingdoms paid tribute as Solomon’s subjects throughout his lifetime.

notes.text: Beginning with 4:21, the verse numbers through 5:18 in the English Bible differ from the verse numbers in the Hebrew text (BHS), with 4:21 ET = 5:1 HT, 4:22 ET = 5:2 HT, etc., through 5:18 ET = 5:32 HT. Beginning with 6:1 the numbering of verses in the English Bible and the Hebrew text is again the same.
Heb “the River” (also in v. 24). This is the standard designation for the Euphrates River in biblical Hebrew.
Heb “[They] were bringing tribute and were serving Solomon all the days of his life.”

22.text: Each day Solomon’s royal court consumed thirty cors of finely milled flour, sixty cors of cereal,

notes.text: Heb “the food of Solomon for each day was.”
As a unit of dry measure a cor was roughly equivalent to six bushels.

23.text: ten calves fattened in the stall, 20 calves from the pasture, and 100 sheep, not to mention rams, gazelles, deer, and well-fed birds.

notes.text: The words “in the stall” are added for clarification; note the immediately following reference to cattle from the pasture.

24.text: His royal court was so large because he ruled over all the kingdoms west of the Euphrates River from Tiphsah to Gaza; he was at peace with all his neighbors.

notes.text: Heb “because.” The words “his royal court was so large” are added to facilitate the logical connection with the preceding verse.
Tiphsah. This was located on the Euphrates River.
Heb “for he was ruling over all [the region] beyond the River, from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kingdoms beyond the River, and he had peace on every side all around.”

25.text: All the people of Judah and Israel had security; everyone from Dan to Beer Sheba enjoyed the produce of their vines and fig trees throughout Solomon’s lifetime.

notes.text: Heb “Judah and Israel lived securely, each one under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan to Beer Sheba, all the days of Solomon.”

26.text: Solomon had 4,000 stalls for his chariot horses and 12,000 horses.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has “40,000,” but this is probably an inflated number (nevertheless it is followed by KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV, TEV, CEV). Some Greek mss of the OT and the parallel in 2 Chr 9:25 read “4,000” (cf. NAB, NIV, NCV, NLT).

27.text: The district governors acquired supplies for King Solomon and all who ate in his royal palace. Each was responsible for one month in the year; they made sure nothing was lacking.

notes.text: Heb “everyone who drew near to the table of King Solomon.”

28.text: Each one also brought to the assigned location his quota of barley and straw for the various horses.

notes.text: Heb “barley and straw for the horses and the steeds they brought to the place which was there, each according to his measure.”

29.text: God gave Solomon wisdom and very great discernment; the breadth of his understanding was as infinite as the sand on the seashore.

notes.text: Heb “heart,” i.e., mind. (The Hebrew term translated “heart” often refers to the mental faculties.)

30.text: Solomon was wiser than all the men of the east and all the sages of Egypt.

notes.text: Heb “the wisdom of Solomon was greater than the wisdom of all the sons of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt.”

31.text: He was wiser than any man, including Ethan the Ezrahite or Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol. He was famous in all the neighboring nations.

notes.text: Heb “his name was in all the surrounding nations.”

32.text: He composed 3,000 proverbs and 1,005 songs.

notes.text: Heb “spoke.”

33.text: He produced manuals on botany, describing every kind of plant, from the cedars of Lebanon to the hyssop that grows on walls. He also produced manuals on biology, describing animals, birds, insects, and fish.

notes.text: Heb “he spoke about plants.”
Heb “he spoke about.”

34.text: People from all nations came to hear Solomon’s display of wisdom; they came from all the kings of the earth who heard about his wisdom.

notes.text: Heb “the wisdom of Solomon.”

1.text: (5:15) King Hiram of Tyre sent messengers to Solomon when he heard that he had been anointed king in his father’s place. (Hiram had always been an ally of David.)

notes.text: The verse numbers in the English Bible differ from those in the Hebrew text (BHS) here; 5:1-18 in the English Bible corresponds to 5:15-32 in the Hebrew text. See the note at 4:21.
Heb “his servants.”

2.text: Solomon then sent this message to Hiram:

3.text: “You know that my father David was unable to build a temple to honor the Lord his God, for he was busy fighting battles on all fronts while the Lord subdued his enemies.

notes.text: Heb “a house for the name of the Lord.” The word “name” sometimes refers to one’s reputation or honor. The “name” of the Lord sometimes designates the Lord himself, being indistinguishable from the proper name.
Heb “because of the battles which surrounded him until the Lord placed them under the soles of his feet.”

4.text: But now the Lord my God has made me secure on all fronts; there is no adversary or dangerous threat.

5.text: So I have decided to build a temple to honor the Lord my God, as the Lord instructed my father David, ‘Your son, whom I will put on your throne in your place, is the one who will build a temple to honor me.’

notes.text: Heb “Look, I am saying.”

Heb “a house for the name of the Lord.” The word “name” sometimes refers to one’s reputation or honor. The “name” of the Lord sometimes designates the Lord himself, being indistinguishable from the proper name.
Heb “a house for my name.”

6.text: So now order some cedars of Lebanon to be cut for me. My servants will work with your servants. I will pay your servants whatever you say is appropriate, for you know that we have no one among us who knows how to cut down trees like the Sidonians.”

7.text: When Hiram heard Solomon’s message, he was very happy. He said, “The Lord is worthy of praise today because he has given David a wise son to rule over this great nation.”

notes.text: Or “Blessed be the Lord today, who….”

8.text: Hiram then sent this message to Solomon: “I received the message you sent to me. I will give you all the cedars and evergreens you need.

notes.text: Heb “heard.”
Heb “I will satisfy all your desire with respect to cedar wood and with respect to the wood of evergreens.”

9.text: My servants will bring the timber down from Lebanon to the sea. I will send it by sea in raft-like bundles to the place you designate. There I will separate the logs and you can carry them away. In exchange you will supply the food I need for my royal court.”

notes.text: Heb “I will place them [on? as?] rafts in the sea to the place where you designate to me.” This may mean he would send them by raft, or that he would tie them in raft-like bundles, and have ships tow them down to an Israelite port.
Heb “smash them,” i.e., untie the bundles.
Heb “as for you, you will satisfy my desire by giving food for my house.”

10.text: So Hiram supplied the cedars and evergreens Solomon needed,

notes.text: Heb “and Hiram gave to Solomon cedar wood and the wood of evergreens, all his desire.”

11.text: and Solomon supplied Hiram annually with 20,000 cors of wheat as provision for his royal court, as well as 120,000 gallons of pure olive oil.

notes.text: As a unit of dry measure a cor was roughly equivalent to six bushels.
Heb “his house.”
The Hebrew text has “twenty cors,” but the ancient Greek version and the parallel text in 2 Chr 2:10 read “20,000 baths.”
A bath was a liquid measure roughly equivalent to six gallons (about 22 liters), so this was a quantity of about 120,000 gallons (440,000 liters).
Or “pressed.”
Heb “and Solomon supplied Hiram with 20,000 cors of wheat…pure olive oil. So Solomon would give to Hiram year by year.”

12.text: So the Lord gave Solomon wisdom, as he had promised him. And Hiram and Solomon were at peace and made a treaty.

notes.text: Heb “a covenant,” referring to a formal peace treaty or alliance.

13.text: King Solomon conscripted work crews from throughout Israel, 30,000 men in all.

notes.text: Heb “raised up.”
Work crews. This Hebrew word (‏מַס‎, mas) refers to a group of laborers conscripted for royal or public service.

14.text: He sent them to Lebanon in shifts of 10,000 men per month. They worked in Lebanon for one month, and then spent two months at home. Adoniram was supervisor of the work crews.

notes.text: Heb “was over.”

15.text: Solomon also had 70,000 common laborers and 80,000 stonecutters in the hills,

notes.text: Heb “carriers of loads.”
Heb “cutters” (probably of stones).

16.text: besides 3,300 officials who supervised the workers.

notes.text: Some Greek mss of the OT read “3,600”; cf. 2 Chr 2:2, 18 and NLT.
Heb “besides thirty-three hundred from the officials of Solomon’s governors who were over the work, the ones ruling over the people, the ones doing the work.”

17.text: By royal order they supplied large valuable stones in order to build the temple’s foundation with chiseled stone.

notes.text: Heb “and the king commanded.”

18.text: Solomon’s and Hiram’s construction workers, along with men from Byblos, did the chiseling and prepared the wood and stones for the building of the temple.

notes.text: Heb “builders.”
Heb “the Gebalites.” The reading is problematic and some emend to a verb form meaning, “set the borders.”
The LXX includes the words “for three years.”

1.text: In the four hundred and eightieth year after the Israelites left Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, during the month Ziv (the second month), he began building the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: During the month Ziv. This would be April-May, 966 b.c. by modern reckoning.

2.text: The temple King Solomon built for the Lord was 90 feet long, 30 feet wide, and 45 feet high.

notes.text: Heb “60 cubits.” A cubit was a unit of measure roughly equivalent to 18 inches or 45 cm. Measurements in vv. 2-10 have been converted to feet in the translation for clarity.
Heb “20 [cubits].”
Heb “30 cubits.”

3.text: The porch in front of the main hall of the temple was 30 feet long, corresponding to the width of the temple. It was 15 feet wide, extending out from the front of the temple.

notes.text: Heb “20 cubits.”
Heb “10 cubits.”

4.text: He made framed windows for the temple.

5.text: He built an extension all around the walls of the temple’s main hall and Holy Place and constructed side rooms in it.

notes.text: Heb “and he built on the wall of the temple an extension all around, the walls of the temple all around, for the main hall and for the holy place, and he made side rooms all around.”

6.text: The bottom floor of the extension was 7½ feet wide, the middle floor 9 feet wide, and the third floor 10½ feet wide. He made ledges on the temple’s outer walls so the beams would not have to be inserted into the walls.

notes.text: Heb “five cubits.”
Heb “six cubits.”
Heb “7 cubits.”
Or “offsets” (ASV, NAB, NASB, NRSV); NIV “offset ledges.”
Heb “so that [the beams] would not have a hold in the walls of the temple.”

7.text: As the temple was being built, only stones shaped at the quarry were used; the sound of hammers, pickaxes, or any other iron tool was not heard at the temple while it was being built.

notes.text: Heb “finished stone of the quarry,” i.e., stones chiseled and shaped at the time they were taken out of the quarry.

8.text: The entrance to the bottom level of side rooms was on the south side of the temple; stairs went up to the middle floor and then on up to the third floor.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has “middle,” but the remainder of the verse suggests this is an error.
Heb “by stairs they went up.” The word translated “stairs” occurs only here. Other options are “trapdoors” or “ladders.”
The translation reads with a few medieval Hebrew mss, the Syriac Peshitta, and Vulgate ‏הַשְּׁלִשִׁית‎ (hashelishit, “the third”) rather than MT ‏הַשְּׁלִשִׁים‎ (hashelishim, “the thirty”).

9.text: He finished building the temple and covered it with rafters and boards made of cedar.

notes.text: Heb “ built the house and completed it.”
Heb “the house.”
The word occurs only here; the precise meaning is uncertain.
Heb “and rows with cedar wood.”

10.text: He built an extension all around the temple; it was 7½ feet high and it was attached to the temple by cedar beams.

notes.text: Heb “5 cubits.” This must refer to the height of each floor or room.

11.text: The Lord’s message came to Solomon:

notes.text: The LXX lacks vv. 11-14.

12.text: “As for this temple you are building, if you follow my rules, observe my regulations, and obey all my commandments, I will fulfill through you the promise I made to your father David.

notes.text: Heb “walk in.”
Heb “do.”
Heb “and keep all my commandments by walking in them.”
Heb “I will establish my word with you which I spoke to David your father.”

13.text: I will live among the Israelites and will not abandon my people Israel.”

14.text: So Solomon finished building the temple.

notes.text: Heb “ built the house and completed it.”

15.text: He constructed the walls inside the temple with cedar planks; he paneled the inside with wood from the floor of the temple to the rafters of the ceiling. He covered the temple floor with boards made from the wood of evergreens.

notes.text: The MT reads ‏קִירוֹת‎ (qirot, “walls”), but this should be emended to ‏קוֹרוֹת‎ (qorot, “rafters”). See BDB 900 s.v. ‏קוֹרָה‎.

16.text: He built a wall 30 feet in from the rear of the temple as a partition for an inner sanctuary that would be the Most Holy Place. He paneled the wall with cedar planks from the floor to the rafters.

notes.text: Heb “He built 20 cubits from the rear areas of the temple with cedar planks from the floor to the walls, and he built it on the inside for an inner sanctuary, for a holy place of holy places.”
The MT reads ‏קִירוֹת‎ (qirot, “walls”), but this should be emended to ‏קוֹרוֹת‎ (qorot, “rafters”). See BDB 900 s.v. ‏קוֹרָה‎.

17.text: The main hall in front of the inner sanctuary was 60 feet long.

notes.text: Heb “and the house was 40 cubits, that is, the main hall before it.”

18.text: The inside of the temple was all cedar and was adorned with carvings of round ornaments and of flowers in bloom. Everything was cedar; no stones were visible.

notes.text: Heb “Cedar was inside the temple, carvings of gourds (i.e., gourd-shaped ornaments) and opened flowers; the whole was cedar, no stone was seen.”

19.text: He prepared the inner sanctuary inside the temple so that the ark of the covenant of the Lord could be placed there.

20.text: The inner sanctuary was 30 feet long, 30 feet wide, and 30 feet high. He plated it with gold, as well as the cedar altar.

notes.text: Heb “20 cubits” (this measurement occurs three times in this verse).
Heb “with plated gold” (or perhaps, “with pure gold”).
Heb “he plated [the] altar of cedar.”

21.text: Solomon plated the inside of the temple with gold. He hung golden chains in front of the inner sanctuary and plated the inner sanctuary with gold.

notes.text: Heb “with plated gold” (or perhaps, “with pure gold”).
Heb “it.”

22.text: He plated the entire inside of the temple with gold, as well as the altar inside the inner sanctuary.

notes.text: Heb “all the temple he plated with gold until all the temple was finished; and the whole altar which was in the inner sanctuary he plated with gold.”

23.text: In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olive wood; each stood 15 feet high.

notes.text: Heb “10 cubits” (a cubit was a unit of measure roughly equivalent to 18 inches or 45 cm).

24.text: Each of the first cherub’s wings was 7½ feet long; its entire wingspan was 15 feet.

notes.text: Heb “The first wing of the [one] cherub was 5 cubits, and the second wing of the cherub was 5 cubits, 10 cubits from the tips of his wings to the tips of his wings.”

25.text: The second cherub also had a wingspan of 15 feet; it was identical to the first in measurements and shape.

notes.text: Heb “and the second cherub was 10 cubits, the two cherubim had one measurement and one shape.”

26.text: Each cherub stood 15 feet high.

notes.text: Heb “the height of the first cherub was 10 cubits; and so was the second cherub.”

27.text: He put the cherubim in the inner sanctuary of the temple. Their wings were spread out. One of the first cherub’s wings touched one wall and one of the other cherub’s wings touched the opposite wall. The first cherub’s other wing touched the second cherub’s other wing in the middle of the room.

notes.text: Heb “in the midst of the inner house,” i.e., in the inner sanctuary.
Heb “and their wings were in the middle of the room, touching wing to wing.”

28.text: He plated the cherubim with gold.

29.text: On all the walls around the temple, inside and out, he carved cherubim, palm trees, and flowers in bloom.

notes.text: Inside and out probably refers to the inner and outer rooms within the building.
Heb “carved engravings of carvings.”

30.text: He plated the floor of the temple with gold, inside and out.

notes.text: Inside and out probably refers to the inner and outer rooms within the building.

31.text: He made doors of olive wood at the entrance to the inner sanctuary; the pillar on each doorpost was five-sided.

notes.text: Heb “the pillar, doorposts, a fifth part” (the precise meaning of this description is uncertain).

32.text: On the two doors made of olive wood he carved cherubim, palm trees, and flowers in bloom, and he plated them with gold. He plated the cherubim and the palm trees with hammered gold.

notes.text: Heb “carved carvings of.”
Heb “he plated [with] gold” (the precise object is not stated).
Heb “and he hammered out the gold on the cherubim and the palm trees.”

33.text: In the same way he made doorposts of olive wood for the entrance to the main hall, only with four-sided pillars.

notes.text: Heb “and so he did at the entrance of the main hall, doorposts of olive wood, from a fourth.”

34.text: He also made two doors out of wood from evergreens; each door had two folding leaves.

notes.text: The words “he also made” are added for stylistic reasons.

Heb “two of the leaves of the first door were folding, and two of the leaves of the second door were folding.” In the second half of the description, the MT has ‏קְלָעִים‎ (qelaʿim, “curtains”), but this probably should be emended to ‏צְלָעִים‎ (tselaʿim, “leaves”), which appears in the first half of the statement. One Hebrew ms, the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate support ‏צְלָעִים‎ (tselaʿim, “leaves”).

35.text: He carved cherubim, palm trees, and flowers in bloom and plated them with gold, leveled out over the carvings.

36.text: He built the inner courtyard with three rows of chiseled stones and a row of cedar beams.

37.text: In the month of Ziv in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign the foundation was laid for the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: In the month of Ziv. This would be April-May, 966 b.c. by modern reckoning.
The words “of Solomon’s reign” are added for clarification. See v. 1.

38.text: In the eleventh year, in the month of Bul (the eighth month) the temple was completed in accordance with all its specifications and blueprints. It took seven years to build.

notes.text: In the month Bul. This would be October-November 959 b.c. in modern reckoning.
Heb “he built it in seven years.”

1.text: Solomon took thirteen years to build his palace.

notes.text: Heb “His house Solomon built in thirteen years and he completed all his house.”

2.text: He named it “The Palace of the Lebanon Forest”; it was 150 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 45 feet high. It had four rows of cedar pillars and cedar beams above the pillars.

notes.text: Heb “he built.”

The Palace of the Lebanon Forest. This name was appropriate because of the large amount of cedar, undoubtedly brought from Lebanon, used in its construction. The cedar pillars in the palace must have given it the appearance of a forest.
Heb “100 cubits.”
Heb “50 cubits.”
Heb “30 cubits.”

3.text: The roof above the beams supported by the pillars was also made of cedar; there were forty-five beams, fifteen per row.

4.text: There were three rows of windows arranged in sets of three.

notes.text: Heb “and framed [windows in] three rows, and opening to opening three times.” The precise meaning of this description is uncertain. Another option might be, “overhung [in] three rows.” This might mean they were positioned high on the walls.

5.text: All the entrances were rectangular in shape and they were arranged in sets of three.

notes.text: Heb “all of the doors and doorposts.”
Rectangular in shape. That is, rather than arched.
Heb “and all the entrances and the doorposts [had] four frames, and in front of opening to opening three times” (the precise meaning of the description is uncertain).

6.text: He made a colonnade 75 feet long and 45 feet wide. There was a porch in front of this and pillars and a roof in front of the porch.

notes.text: Heb “a porch of pillars.”
Heb “50 cubits.”
Heb “30 cubits.”

Heb “and a porch was in front of them (i.e., the aforementioned pillars) and pillars and a roof in front of them (i.e., the aforementioned pillars and porch).” The precise meaning of the term translated “roof” is uncertain; it occurs only here and in Ezek 41:25-26.

7.text: He also made a throne room, called “The Hall of Judgment,” where he made judicial decisions. It was paneled with cedar from the floor to the rafters.

notes.text: Heb “and a porch for the throne, where he was making judicial decisions, the Porch of Judgment, he made.”

The Hebrew text reads, “from the floor to the floor.” The second occurrence of the term ‏הַקַּרְקָע‎ (haqqarqaʿ, “the floor”) is probably an error; one should emend to ‏הַקּוֹרוֹת‎ (haqqorot, “the rafters”). See 6:16.

8.text: The palace where he lived was constructed in a similar way. He also constructed a palace like this hall for Pharaoh’s daughter, whom he had married.

notes.text: Heb “and his house where he lived, the other court [i.e., as opposed to the great court], separated from the house belonging to the hall, was like this work [i.e., this style of architecture].”
Heb “and a house he was making for the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Solomon had taken, like this porch.”

9.text: All these were built with the best stones, chiseled to the right size and cut with a saw on all sides, from the foundation to the edge of the roof and from the outside to the great courtyard.

notes.text: Or “valuable” (see 5:17).
Heb “according to the measurement of chiseled [stone].”
Heb “inside and out.”
The precise meaning of the Hebrew word ‏טְפָחוֹת‎ (tefakhot) is uncertain, but it is clear that the referent stands in opposition to the foundation.

10.text: The foundation was made of large valuable stones, measuring either 15 feet or 12 feet.

notes.text: Heb “stones of 10 cubits and stones of 8 cubits” (it is unclear exactly what dimension is being measured). If both numbers refer to the length of the stones (cf. NCV, CEV, NLT), then perhaps stones of two different sizes were used in some alternating pattern.

11.text: Above the foundation the best stones, chiseled to the right size, were used along with cedar.

notes.text: Heb “on top,” or “above.”
Or “valuable” (see 5:17).
Heb “according to the measurement of chiseled [stone].”

12.text: Around the great courtyard were three rows of chiseled stones and one row of cedar beams, like the inner courtyard of the Lord’s temple and the hall of the palace.

notes.text: Or “the porch of the temple.”

13.text: King Solomon sent for Hiram of Tyre.

notes.text: Heb “King Solomon sent and took Hiram from Tyre.” In 2 Chr 2:13 (MT v. 12) and 4:11, 16 his name is spelled “Huram.”

14.text: He was the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a craftsman in bronze from Tyre. He had the skill and knowledge to make all kinds of works of bronze. He reported to King Solomon and did all the work he was assigned.

notes.text: 2 Chr 2:14 (13 HT) says “from the daughters of Dan.”
Heb “he was filled with the skill, understanding, and knowledge.”

15.text: He fashioned two bronze pillars; each pillar was 27 feet high and 18 feet in circumference.

notes.text: Heb “18 cubits.”
Heb “12 cubits.”

16.text: He made two bronze tops for the pillars; each was 7½ feet high.

notes.text: Heb “two capitals he made to place on the tops of the pillars, cast in bronze; 5 cubits was the height of the first capital, and 5 cubits was the height of the second capital.”

17.text: The latticework on the tops of the pillars was adorned with ornamental wreaths and chains; the top of each pillar had seven groupings of ornaments.

notes.text: Heb “there were seven for the first capital, and seven for the second capital.”

18.text: When he made the pillars, there were two rows of pomegranate-shaped ornaments around the latticework covering the top of each pillar.

notes.text: Heb “he made the pillars, and two rows surrounding one latticework to cover the capitals which were on top of the pomegranates, and so he did for the second latticework.” The translation supplies “pomegranates” after “two rows,” and understands “pillars,” rather than “pomegranates,” to be the correct reading after “on top of.” The latter change finds support from many Hebrew mss and the ancient Greek version.

19.text: The tops of the two pillars in the porch were shaped like lilies and were six feet high.

notes.text: Heb “the capitals which were on the top of the pillars were the work of lilies, in the porch, 4 cubits.” It is unclear exactly what dimension is being measured.

20.text: On the top of each pillar, right above the bulge beside the latticework, there were 200 pomegranate-shaped ornaments arranged in rows all the way around.

notes.text: Heb “and the capitals on the two pillars, also above, close beside the bulge which was beside the latticework, two hundred pomegranates in rows around, on the second capital.” The precise meaning of the word translated “bulge” is uncertain.

21.text: He set up the pillars on the porch in front of the main hall. He erected one pillar on the right side and called it Yakin; he erected the other pillar on the left side and called it Boaz.

notes.text: Or “south.”
The name “Yakin” appears to be a verbal form and probably means, “he establishes.”
Or “north.”

The meaning of the name Boaz is uncertain. For various proposals, see BDB 126-27 s.v. ‏בעז‎. One attractive option is to revocalize the name as ‏בְּעֹז‎ (beʿoz, “in strength”) and to understand it as completing the verbal form on the first pillar. Taking the words together and reading from right to left, one can translate the sentence, “he establishes [it] in strength.”

22.text: The tops of the pillars were shaped like lilies. So the construction of the pillars was completed.

23.text: He also made the large bronze basin called “The Sea.” It measured 15 feet from rim to rim, was circular in shape, and stood 7½ feet high. Its circumference was 45 feet.

notes.text: Heb “He made the sea, cast.”
This large basin was mounted on twelve bronze bulls and contained water for the priests to bathe themselves (2 Chr 4:6; cf. Exod 30:17-21).
Heb “10 cubits.”
Heb “5 cubits.”

Heb “and a measuring line went around it 30 cubits all around.” The measurements are an approximation. The LXX has the number 33. Neither fit a strict calculation of the diameter time pi, but the precise details of measuring (e.g. the width of the lip or other factors) are not known and numbers may be rounded.

24.text: Under the rim all the way around it were round ornaments arranged in settings 15 feet long. The ornaments were in two rows and had been cast with “The Sea.”

notes.text: Or “gourd-shaped ornaments.”
Heb “10 cubits surrounding the sea all around.” The precise meaning of this description is uncertain.
Heb “the gourd-shaped ornaments were in two rows, cast in its casting.”

25.text: “The Sea” stood on top of twelve bulls. Three faced northward, three westward, three southward, and three eastward. “The Sea” was placed on top of them, and they all faced outward.

notes.text: Heb “It.” The proper noun “The Sea” has been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “all their hindquarters were toward the inside.”

26.text: It was four fingers thick and its rim was like that of a cup shaped like a lily blossom. It could hold about 12,000 gallons.

notes.text: Heb “2,000 baths” (a bath was a liquid measure roughly equivalent to six gallons).

27.text: He also made ten bronze movable stands. Each stand was 6 feet long, 6 feet wide, and 4½ feet high.

notes.text: Heb “4 cubits.”
Heb “4 cubits.”
Heb “3 cubits.”

28.text: The stands were constructed with frames between the joints.

29.text: On these frames and joints were ornamental lions, bulls, and cherubim. Under the lions and bulls were decorative wreaths.

notes.text: The precise meaning of these final words is uncertain. A possible literal translation would be, “wreaths, the work of descent.”

30.text: Each stand had four bronze wheels with bronze axles and four supports. Under the basin the supports were fashioned on each side with wreaths.

notes.text: Heb “and four its feet, supports to them.”
The precise meaning of this last word, translated “wreaths,” is uncertain.

31.text: Inside the stand was a round opening that was 18 inches deep; it had a support that was 27 inches long. On the edge of the opening were carvings in square frames.

notes.text: Heb “And its opening from the inside to the top and upwards [was] a cubit, and its opening was round, the work of a stand, a cubit-and-a-half.” The precise meaning of this description is uncertain.
Heb “also over its opening were carvings and their frames [were] squared, not round.”

32.text: The four wheels were under the frames, and the crossbars of the axles were connected to the stand. Each wheel was 27 inches high.

notes.text: Heb “a cubit-and-a-half” (a cubit was a unit of measure roughly equivalent to 18 inches or 45 cm).

33.text: The wheels were constructed like chariot wheels; their crossbars, rims, spokes, and hubs were made of cast metal.

34.text: Each stand had four supports, one per side projecting out from the stand.

notes.text: Heb “four shoulders to the four sides of each stand, from the stand its shoulders.” The precise meaning of the description is uncertain.

35.text: On top of each stand was a round opening three-quarters of a foot deep; there were also supports and frames on top of the stands.

notes.text: Heb “and on top of the stand, a half cubit [in] height, round all around” (the meaning of this description is uncertain).

36.text: He engraved ornamental cherubim, lions, and palm trees on the plates of the supports and frames wherever there was room, with wreaths all around.

notes.text: Heb “according to the space of each.”
The precise meaning of this last word, translated “wreaths,” is uncertain.

37.text: He made the ten stands in this way. All of them were cast in one mold and were identical in measurements and shape.

38.text: He also made ten bronze basins, each of which could hold about 240 gallons. Each basin was 6 feet in diameter; there was one basin for each stand.

notes.text: Heb “forty baths” (a bath was a liquid measure roughly equivalent to six gallons).
Heb “4 cubits, each basin.” It is unclear which dimension is being measured.

39.text: He put five basins on the south side of the temple and five on the north side. He put “The Sea” on the south side, in the southeast corner.

40.text: Hiram also made basins, shovels, and bowls. He finished all the work on the Lord’s temple he had been assigned by King Solomon.

notes.text: Heb “Hiram.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “Hiram finished doing all the work which he did for King Solomon [on] the house of the Lord.”

41.text: He made the two pillars, the two bowl-shaped tops of the pillars, the latticework for the bowl-shaped tops of the two pillars,

notes.text: The words “he made” are added for stylistic reasons.

42.text: the 400 pomegranate-shaped ornaments for the latticework of the two pillars (each latticework had two rows of these ornaments at the bowl-shaped top of the pillar),

43.text: the ten movable stands with their ten basins,

44.text: the big bronze basin called “The Sea” with its twelve bulls underneath,

notes.text: Heb “underneath ‘The Sea.’”

45.text: and the pots, shovels, and bowls. All these items King Solomon assigned Hiram to make for the Lord’s temple were made from polished bronze.

notes.text: Heb “which Hiram made for King Solomon [for] the house of the Lord.”

46.text: The king had them cast in earth foundries in the region of the Jordan between Sukkoth and Zarethan.

notes.text: Or perhaps, “molds.”

47.text: Solomon left all these items unweighed; there were so many of them they did not weigh the bronze.

notes.text: Heb “Solomon left all the items, due to their very great abundance; the weight of the bronze was not sought.”

48.text: Solomon also made all these items for the Lord’s temple: the gold altar, the gold table on which was kept the Bread of the Presence,

notes.text: Heb “the bread of the face [or presence].” Many recent English versions employ “the bread of the Presence,” although this does not convey much to the modern reader.
This bread was viewed as a perpetual offering to God and was regarded as holy. See Lev 24:5-9.

49.text: the pure gold lampstands at the entrance to the inner sanctuary (five on the right and five on the left), the gold flower-shaped ornaments, lamps, and tongs,

50.text: the pure gold bowls, trimming shears, basins, pans, and censers, and the gold door sockets for the inner sanctuary (the Most Holy Place) and for the doors of the main hall of the temple.

51.text: When King Solomon finished constructing the Lord’s temple, he put the holy items that belonged to his father David (the silver, gold, and other articles) in the treasuries of the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: Heb “Solomon.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.

1.text: Then Solomon convened in Jerusalem Israel’s elders, all the leaders of the Israelite tribes and families, so they could witness the transferal of the ark of the Lord’s covenant from the City of David (that is, Zion).

notes.text: The Old Greek translation includes the following words at the beginning of ch. 8: “It so happened that when Solomon finished building the Lord’s temple and his own house, after twenty years.”

Heb “Then Solomon convened the elders of Israel, the heads of the tribes, the chiefs of the fathers belonging to the sons of Israel to King Solomon [in] Jerusalem to bring up the ark of the covenant of the Lord from the City of David (it is Zion).”

2.text: All the men of Israel assembled before King Solomon during the festival in the month of Ethanim (the seventh month).

notes.text: The festival. This was the Feast of Tabernacles, see Lev 23:34.
The month Ethanim. This would be September-October in modern reckoning.

3.text: When all Israel’s elders had arrived, the priests lifted the ark.

4.text: The priests and Levites carried the ark of the Lord, the tent of meeting, and all the holy items in the tent.

notes.text: Heb “the tent of assembly.”
The tent of meeting. See Exod 33:7-11.
Heb “and they carried the ark of the Lord…. The priests and the Levites carried them.”

5.text: Now King Solomon and all the Israelites who had assembled with him went on ahead of the ark and sacrificed more sheep and cattle than could be counted or numbered.

notes.text: Heb “And King Solomon and all the assembly of Israel, those who had been gathered to him, [were] before the ark, sacrificing sheep and cattle which could not be counted or numbered because of the abundance.”

6.text: The priests brought the ark of the Lord’s covenant to its assigned place in the inner sanctuary of the temple, in the Most Holy Place, under the wings of the cherubim.

notes.text: The word “assigned” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

7.text: The cherubim’s wings extended over the place where the ark sat; the cherubim overshadowed the ark and its poles.

notes.text: And its poles. These poles were used to carry the ark. See Exod 25:13-15.

8.text: The poles were so long their ends were visible from the Holy Place in front of the inner sanctuary, but they could not be seen from beyond that point. They have remained there to this very day.

notes.text: Heb “they could not be seen outside.”

9.text: There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets Moses had placed there in Horeb. It was there that the Lord made a covenant with the Israelites after he brought them out of the land of Egypt.

notes.text: Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai.
Heb “in Horeb where.”

10.text: Once the priests left the Holy Place, a cloud filled the Lord’s temple.

11.text: The priests could not carry out their duties because of the cloud; the Lord’s glory filled his temple.

notes.text: Heb “were not able to stand to serve.”
Heb “the house of the Lord.”

12.text: Then Solomon said, “The Lord has said that he lives in thick darkness.

13.text: O Lord, truly I have built a lofty temple for you, a place where you can live permanently.”

notes.text: The words “O Lord” do not appear in the original text, but they are supplied for clarification; Solomon addresses the Lord in prayer at this point.

14.text: Then the king turned around and pronounced a blessing over the whole Israelite assembly as they stood there.

notes.text: Heb “turned his face.”
Heb “and he blessed all the assembly of Israel, and all the assembly of Israel was standing.”

15.text: He said, “The Lord God of Israel is worthy of praise because he has fulfilled what he promised my father David.

notes.text: The Hebrew text reads, “by his hand he has fulfilled.”
The Hebrew text reads, “he promised by his mouth.”

16.text: He told David, ‘Since the day I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I have not chosen a city from all the tribes of Israel to build a temple in which to live. But I have chosen David to lead my people Israel.’

notes.text: Heb “saying.” The word is carried over from the end of verse 15.
Heb “to build a house for my name to be there.”

To build a temple in which to live (Heb “to build a house for my name to be there”). In the OT, the word “name” sometimes refers to one’s reputation or honor. The “name” of the Lord sometimes designates the Lord himself, being indistinguishable from the proper name.

17.text: Now my father David had a strong desire to build a temple to honor the Lord God of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “and it was with the heart of David my father.”

Heb “to build a house for the name of the Lord God of Israel.” The word “name” in the OT sometimes refers to one’s reputation or honor. The “name” of the Lord sometimes designates the Lord himself, being indistinguishable from the proper name.

18.text: The Lord told my father David, ‘It is right for you to have a strong desire to build a temple to honor me.

notes.text: Heb “Because it was with your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was with your heart.”

19.text: But you will not build the temple; your very own son will build the temple for my honor.’

notes.text: Heb “your son, the one who came out of your body, he will build the temple for my name.”

20.text: The Lord has kept the promise he made. I have taken my father David’s place and have occupied the throne of Israel, as the Lord promised. I have built this temple for the honor of the Lord God of Israel

notes.text: Heb “his word that he spoke.”
Heb “name.”

21.text: and set up in it a place for the ark containing the covenant the Lord made with our ancestors when he brought them out of the land of Egypt.”

notes.text: Heb “fathers” (also in vv. 34, 40, 48, 53, 57, 58).

22.text: Solomon stood before the altar of the Lord in front of the entire assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward the sky.

notes.text: Or “heaven.”

23.text: He prayed: “O Lord, God of Israel, there is no god like you in heaven above or on earth below! You maintain covenantal loyalty to your servants who obey you with sincerity.

notes.text: Heb “said.”
Heb “one who keeps the covenant and the loyal love.” The expression is a hendiadys.
Heb “who walk before you with all their heart.”

24.text: You have kept your word to your servant, my father David; this very day you have fulfilled what you promised.

notes.text: Heb “[you] who kept to your servant David my father that which you spoke to him.”
Heb “you spoke by your mouth and by your hand you fulfilled, as this day.”

25.text: Now, O Lord, God of Israel, keep the promise you made to your servant, my father David, when you said, ‘You will never fail to have a successor ruling before me on the throne of Israel, provided that your descendants watch their step and serve me as you have done.’

notes.text: Heb “there will not be cut off from you a man from before me sitting on the throne of Israel.”
Heb “watch their way.” The Hebrew and English colloquialisms are similar. The related ideas “way” and “steps” represent behavior in a broad sense in each language.
Heb “guard their way by walking before me as you have walked before me.”

26.text: Now, O God of Israel, may the promise you made to your servant, my father David, be realized.

notes.text: Heb “the words that you spoke.”
Or “prove to be reliable.”

27.text: “God does not really live on the earth! Look, if the sky and the highest heaven cannot contain you, how much less this temple I have built!

notes.text: Heb “Indeed, can God really live on the earth?” The rhetorical question expects the answer, “Of course not,” the force of which the translation above seeks to reflect.

28.text: But respond favorably to your servant’s prayer and his request for help, O Lord my God. Answer the desperate prayer your servant is presenting to you today.

notes.text: Heb “turn to.”
Heb “by listening to.”
Heb “the loud cry and the prayer.”
Heb “praying before you.”

29.text: Night and day may you watch over this temple, the place where you promised you would live. May you answer your servant’s prayer for this place.

notes.text: Heb “so your eyes might be open toward this house night and day, toward the place about which you said, ‘My name will be there.’”
Heb “by listening to the prayer which your servant is praying concerning this place.”

30.text: Respond to the request of your servant and your people Israel for this place. Hear from inside your heavenly dwelling place and respond favorably.

notes.text: Heb “listen to the request of your servant and your people Israel which they are praying concerning this place.”

Heb “and you, hear inside your dwelling place, inside heaven.” The precise nuance of the preposition ‏אֶל‎ (ʾel), used here with the verb “hear,” is unclear. One expects the preposition “from,” which appears in the parallel text in 2 Chr 6:21. The nuance “inside; among” is attested for ‏אֶל‎ (see Gen 23:19; 1 Sam 10:22; Jer 4:3), but in each case a verb of motion is employed with the preposition, unlike 1 Kgs 8:30. The translation above (“from inside”) is based on the demands of the immediate context rather than attested usage elsewhere.
Heb “hear and forgive.”

31.text: “When someone is accused of sinning against his neighbor and the latter pronounces a curse on the alleged offender before your altar in this temple, be willing to forgive the accused if the accusation is false.

notes.text: Heb “and forgive the man who sins against his neighbor when one takes up against him a curse to curse him and the curse comes before your altar in this house.” In the Hebrew text the words “and forgive” conclude v. 30, but the accusative sign at the beginning of v. 31 suggests the verb actually goes with what follows in v. 31. The parallel text in 2 Chr 6:22 begins with “and if,” rather than the accusative sign. In this case “forgive” must be taken with what precedes, and v. 31 must be taken as the protasis (“if” clause) of a conditional sentence, with v. 32 being the apodosis (“then” clause) that completes the sentence.

Be willing to forgive the accused if the accusation is false. At first it appears that Solomon is asking God to forgive the guilty party. But in v. 32 Solomon asks the Lord to discern who is guilty and innocent, so v. 31 must refer to a situation where an accusation has been made, but not yet proven. The very periphrastic translation reflects this interpretation.

32.text: Listen from heaven and make a just decision about your servants’ claims. Condemn the guilty party, declare the other innocent, and give both of them what they deserve.

notes.text: Heb “and you, hear [from] heaven and act and judge your servants by declaring the guilty to be guilty, to give his way on his head, and to declare the innocent to be innocent, to give to him according to his innocence.”

33.text: “The time will come when your people Israel are defeated by an enemy because they sinned against you. If they come back to you, renew their allegiance to you, and pray for your help in this temple,

notes.text: Heb “when.” In the Hebrew text vv. 33-34 actually contain one lengthy conditional sentence, which the translation has divided into two sentences for stylistic reasons.
Or “are struck down before an enemy.”
Heb “confess [or perhaps, “praise”] your name.”
Heb “and they pray and ask for help.”

34.text: then listen from heaven, forgive the sin of your people Israel, and bring them back to the land you gave to their ancestors.

35.text: “The time will come when the skies are shut up tightly and no rain falls because your people sinned against you. When they direct their prayers toward this place, renew their allegiance to you, and turn away from their sin because you punish them,

notes.text: Heb “when.” In the Hebrew text vv. 35-36a actually contain one lengthy conditional sentence, which the translation has divided into two sentences for stylistic reasons.
Heb “they”; the referent (your people) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “confess [or perhaps, “praise”] your name.”

The Hebrew text has “because you answer them,” as if the verb is from ‏עָנָה‎ (ʿanah, “to answer”). However, this reference to a divine answer is premature, since the next verse asks for God to intervene in mercy. It is better to revocalize the consonantal text as ‏תְעַנֵּם‎ (teʿannem, “you afflict them”), a Piel verb form from the homonym ‏עָנָה‎ (ʿanah, “to afflict”).

36.text: then listen from heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel. Certainly you will then teach them the right way to live and send rain on your land that you have given your people to possess.

notes.text: The translation understands ‏כִּי‎ (ki) in an emphatic or asseverative sense.
Heb “the good way in which they should walk.”
Or “for an inheritance.”

37.text: “The time will come when the land suffers from a famine, a plague, blight and disease, or a locust invasion, or when their enemy lays siege to the cities of the land, or when some other type of plague or epidemic occurs.

notes.text: Actually two Hebrew terms appear here, both of which are usually taken as referring to locusts. Perhaps different stages of growth or different varieties are in view.
Heb “in the land, his gates.”

38.text: When all your people Israel pray and ask for help, as they acknowledge their pain and spread out their hands toward this temple,

notes.text: Heb “every prayer, every request for help which will be to all the people, to all your people Israel.”
Heb “which they know, each the pain of his heart.”

39.text: then listen from your heavenly dwelling place, forgive their sin, and act favorably toward each one based on your evaluation of his motives. (Indeed you are the only one who can correctly evaluate the motives of all people.)

notes.text: The words “their sin” are added for clarification.

Heb “and act and give to each one according to all his ways because you know his heart.” In the Hebrew text vv. 37-39a actually contain one lengthy conditional sentence, which the translation has divided up for stylistic reasons.
Heb “Indeed you know, you alone, the heart of all the sons of mankind.”

40.text: Then they will obey you throughout their lifetimes as they live on the land you gave to our ancestors.

notes.text: Heb “fear.”
Heb “all the days [in] which.”

51.text: After all, they are your people and your special possession whom you brought out of Egypt, from the middle of the iron-smelting furnace.

notes.text: Or “for.”
Heb “inheritance.”

The Hebrew term ‏כּוּר‎ (kur, “furnace,” cf. Akkadian kūru) is a metaphor for the intense heat of purification. A ‏כּוּר‎ was not a source of heat but a crucible (“iron-smelting furnace”) in which precious metals were melted down and their impurities burned away (see I. Cornelius, NIDOTTE 2:618-19). Thus Egypt served not as a place of punishment for the Israelites, but as a place of refinement to bring Israel to a place of submission to divine sovereignty.
From the middle of the iron-smelting furnace. The metaphor of a furnace suggests fire and heat and is an apt image to remind the people of the suffering they endured while slaves in Egypt.

1.text: When the queen of Sheba heard about Solomon, she came to challenge him with difficult questions.

The Hebrew text also has, “to the name of the Lord,” which is very awkward due to its unusual syntax. The phrase is omitted in the parallel passage in 2 Chr 9:1. 1.text: King Solomon fell in love with many foreign women (besides Pharaoh’s daughter), including Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Sidonians, and Hittites.

2.text: They came from nations about which the Lord had warned the Israelites, “You must not establish friendly relations with them! If you do, they will surely shift your allegiance to their gods.” But Solomon was irresistibly attracted to them.

notes.text: Heb “you must not go into them, and they must not go into you.”
Heb “Surely they will bend your heart after their gods.” The words “if you do” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

Heb “Solomon clung to them for love.” The pronominal suffix, translated “them,” is masculine here, even though it appears the foreign women are in view. Perhaps this is due to attraction to the masculine forms used of the nations earlier in the verse.

3.text: He had 700 royal wives and 300 concubines; his wives had a powerful influence over him.

notes.text: Heb “wives, princesses.”

Concubines were slave women in ancient Near Eastern societies who were the legal property of their master, but who could have legitimate sexual relations with their master. A concubine’s status was more elevated than a mere servant, but she was not free and did not have the legal rights of a free wife. The children of a concubine could, in some instances, become equal heirs with the children of the free wife. The usage in the present passage suggests that after the period of the Judges concubines may have become more of a royal prerogative (cf. also 2 Sam 21:10-14).
Heb “his wives bent his heart.”

4.text: When Solomon became old, his wives shifted his allegiance to other gods; he was not wholeheartedly devoted to the Lord his God, as his father David had been.

notes.text: Heb “bent his heart after.”

7.text: Furthermore, on the hill east of Jerusalem Solomon built a high place for the detestable Moabite god Chemosh and for the detestable Ammonite god Milcom.

notes.text: Heb “then.”
The hill east of Jerusalem refers to the Mount of Olives.
A high place. The “high places” were places of worship that were naturally or artificially elevated (see 1 Kgs 3:2).
Heb “Chemosh, the detestable thing of Moab.”
The MT reads “Molech,” but Milcom must be intended (see vv. 5, 33).

8.text: He built high places for all his foreign wives so they could burn incense and make sacrifices to their gods.

notes.text: Heb “and the same thing he did for all his foreign wives, [who] were burning incense and sacrificing to their gods.”

9.text: The Lord was angry with Solomon because he had shifted his allegiance away from the Lord, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him on two occasions

notes.text: Heb “bent his heart.”
These two occasions are mentioned in 1 Kgs 3:5 and 9:2.

10.text: and had warned him about this very thing, so that he would not follow other gods. But he did not obey the Lord’s command.

notes.text: Heb “and had commanded him concerning this thing not to walk after other gods.”
Or “keep.”

11.text: So the Lord said to Solomon, “Because you insist on doing these things and have not kept the covenantal rules I gave you, I will surely tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant.

notes.text: Heb “Because this is with you, and you have not kept my covenant and my rules which I commanded you.”

12.text: However, for your father David’s sake I will not do this while you are alive. I will tear it away from your son’s hand instead.

13.text: But I will not tear away the entire kingdom; I will leave your son one tribe for my servant David’s sake and for the sake of my chosen city Jerusalem.”

notes.text: Heb “give.”

14.text: The Lord brought against Solomon an enemy, Hadad the Edomite, a descendant of the Edomite king.

notes.text: Or “raised up.”

15.text: During David’s campaign against Edom, Joab, the commander of the army, while on a mission to bury the dead, killed every male in Edom.

notes.text: Heb “when David was [fighting (?)] with Edom.”

16.text: For Joab and the entire Israelite army stayed there six months until they had exterminated every male in Edom.

notes.text: Heb “and all Israel.”
Heb “until he had cut off every male in Edom.”

17.text: Hadad, who was only a small boy at the time, escaped with some of his father’s Edomite servants and headed for Egypt.

notes.text: The MT reads “Adad,” an alternate form of the name Hadad.
Heb “and Adad fled, he and Edomite men from the servants of his father, to go to Egypt, and Hadad was a small boy.”

18.text: They went from Midian to Paran; they took some men from Paran and went to Egypt. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, gave him a house and some land and supplied him with food.

notes.text: Heb “and they arose from Midian and went to Paran and they took men with them from Paran and went to Egypt to Pharaoh king of Egypt and he gave to him a house and food he said to him, and a land he gave to him.”

19.text: Pharaoh liked Hadad so well he gave him his sister-in-law (Queen Tahpenes’ sister) as a wife.

notes.text: Heb “and Hadad found great favor in the eyes of Pharaoh.”
Heb “and he gave to him a wife, the sister of his wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen.”

20.text: Tahpenes’ sister gave birth to his son, named Genubath. Tahpenes raised him in Pharaoh’s palace; Genubath grew up in Pharaoh’s palace among Pharaoh’s sons.

notes.text: Heb “bore him Genubath his son.”

The Hebrew text reads ‏וַתִּגְמְלֵהוּ‎ (vattigmelehu, “weaned him”) but a slight alteration of the consonantal text yields ‏וַתִּגְדְלֵהוּ‎ (vattigdelehu, “raised him”), which seems to make better sense.

21.text: While in Egypt Hadad heard that David had passed away and that Joab, the commander of the army, was dead. So Hadad asked Pharaoh, “Give me permission to leave so I can return to my homeland.”

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”
Heb “send me away.”

22.text: Pharaoh said to him, “What do you lack here that makes you want to go to your homeland?” Hadad replied, “Nothing, but please give me permission to leave.”

notes.text: Heb “Indeed what do you lack with me, that now you are seeking to go to your land?”
Heb “and he said.”

So Hadad asked Pharaoh…. This lengthy description of Hadad’s exile in Egypt explains why Hadad wanted to oppose Solomon and supports the author’s thesis that his hostility to Solomon found its ultimate source in divine providence. Though Hadad enjoyed a comfortable life in Egypt, when the Lord raised him up (apparently stirring up his desire for vengeance) he decided to leave the comforts of Egypt and return to Edom.

23.text: God also brought against Solomon another enemy, Rezon son of Eliada who had run away from his master, King Hadadezer of Zobah.

notes.text: Heb “him”; the referent (Solomon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

24.text: He gathered some men and organized a raiding band. When David tried to kill them, they went to Damascus, where they settled down and gained control of the city.

notes.text: Heb “and he was the officer of a raiding band.”

The Hebrew text reads “when David killed them.” This phrase is traditionally joined with what precedes. The ancient Greek version does not reflect the phrase and some suggest that it has been misplaced from the end of v. 23.

25.text: He was Israel’s enemy throughout Solomon’s reign and, like Hadad, caused trouble. He loathed Israel and ruled over Syria.

notes.text: The construction (Qal of ‏קוּץ‎ + ‏בְּ‎ [quts + bet] preposition) is rare, but not without parallel (see Lev 20:23).

26.text: Jeroboam son of Nebat, one of Solomon’s servants, rebelled against the king. He was an Ephraimite from Zeredah whose mother was a widow named Zeruah.

notes.text: Heb “raised a hand against.”
Heb “Ephrathite,” which here refers to an Ephraimite (see HALOT 81 s.v. ‏אֶפְרַיִם‎).

27.text: This is what prompted him to rebel against the king: Solomon built a terrace, and he closed up a gap in the wall of the city of his father David.

notes.text: Heb “this is the matter concerning which he raised a hand against the king.”
The city of his father David. The phrase refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

28.text: Jeroboam was a talented man; when Solomon saw that the young man was an accomplished worker, he made him the leader of the work crew from the tribe of Joseph.

notes.text: Heb “man of strength.”
Heb “house.”

29.text: At that time, when Jeroboam had left Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite met him on the road; the two of them were alone in the open country. Ahijah was wearing a brand new robe,

notes.text: The Hebrew text has simply “he,” making it a bit unclear whether Jeroboam or Ahijah is the subject, but in the Hebrew word order Ahijah is the nearer antecedent, and this is followed by the present translation.

30.text: and he grabbed the robe and tore it into twelve pieces.

notes.text: Heb “and Ahijah grabbed the new robe that was on him.”

31.text: Then he told Jeroboam, “Take ten pieces, for this is what the Lord God of Israel has said: ‘Look, I am about to tear the kingdom from Solomon’s hand and I will give ten tribes to you.

32.text: He will retain one tribe, for my servant David’s sake and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel.

33.text: I am taking the kingdom from him because they have abandoned me and worshiped the Sidonian goddess Astarte, the Moabite god Chemosh, and the Ammonite god Milcom. They have not followed my instructions by doing what I approve and obeying my rules and regulations, as Solomon’s father David did.

notes.text: The words “I am taking the kingdom from him” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
This is the reading of the MT; the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate read “he has.”
Heb “walked in my ways.”
Heb “by doing what is right in my eyes, my rules and my regulations, like David his father.”

34.text: I will not take the whole kingdom from his hand. I will allow him to be ruler for the rest of his life for the sake of my chosen servant David who kept my commandments and rules.

35.text: I will take the kingdom from the hand of his son and give ten tribes to you.

notes.text: Heb “and I will give it to you, ten tribes.”

36.text: I will leave his son one tribe so my servant David’s dynasty may continue to serve me in Jerusalem, the city I have chosen as my home.

notes.text: Heb “give.”

Heb “so there might be a lamp for David my servant all the days before me in Jerusalem.” The metaphorical “lamp” symbolizes the Davidic dynasty. Because this imagery is unfamiliar to the modern reader, the translation “so my servant David’s dynasty may continue to serve me” has been used.
Heb “so there might be a lamp for David my servant all the days before me in Jerusalem, the city which I have chosen for myself to put my name there.”

37.text: I will select you; you will rule over all you desire to have and you will be king over Israel.

notes.text: Heb “take.”

38.text: You must obey all I command you to do, follow my instructions, do what I approve, and keep my rules and commandments, as my servant David did. Then I will be with you and establish for you a lasting dynasty, as I did for David; I will give you Israel.

notes.text: Heb “If you obey.” In the Hebrew text v. 38 is actually one long conditional sentence, which has been broken into two parts in the translation for stylistic purposes.
Heb “walk in my ways.”
Heb “do what is right in my eyes.”
Heb “I will build for you a permanent house, like I built for David.”

39.text: I will humiliate David’s descendants because of this, but not forever.’”

notes.text: Because of this. Reference is made to the idolatry mentioned earlier.
Heb “but not all the days.”

40.text: Solomon tried to kill Jeroboam, but Jeroboam escaped to Egypt and found refuge with King Shishak of Egypt. He stayed in Egypt until Solomon died.

notes.text: Heb “but Jeroboam arose and ran away to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt.”

41.text: The rest of the events of Solomon’s reign, including all his accomplishments and his wise decisions, are recorded in the scroll called the Annals of Solomon.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Solomon, and all which he did, and his wisdom, are they not written on the scroll of the events of Solomon?”

42.text: Solomon ruled over all Israel from Jerusalem for forty years.

43.text: Then Solomon passed away and was buried in the city of his father David. His son Rehoboam replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”
The city of his father David. The phrase refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

Before this sentence the Old Greek translation includes the following words: “And it so happened that when Jeroboam son of Nebat heard—now he was in Egypt where he had fled from before Solomon and was residing in Egypt—he came straight to his city in the land of Sarira which is on mount Ephraim. And king Solomon slept with his fathers.”

1.text: Rehoboam traveled to Shechem, for all Israel had gathered in Shechem to make Rehoboam king.

notes.text: Heb “come [to].”
Heb “him”; the referent (Rehoboam) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

2.text: When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard the news, he was still in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon and had been living ever since.

notes.text: Verse 2 is not included in the Old Greek translation. See the note on 11:43.

Heb “and Jeroboam lived in Egypt.” The parallel text in 2 Chr 10:2 reads, “and Jeroboam returned from Egypt.” In a purely consonantal text the forms “and he lived” and “and he returned” are identical (‏וישׁב‎).

3.text: They sent for him, and Jeroboam and the whole Israelite assembly came and spoke to Rehoboam, saying,

notes.text: Heb “They sent and called for him.”

4.text: “Your father made us work too hard. Now if you lighten the demands he made and don’t make us work as hard, we will serve you.”

notes.text: Heb “made our yoke burdensome.”

Heb “but you, now, lighten the burdensome work of your father and the heavy yoke which he placed on us, and we will serve you.” In the Hebrew text the prefixed verbal form with vav (‏וְנַעַבְדֶךָ‎, [venaʿavdekha] “and we will serve you”) following the imperative (‏הָקֵל‎ [haqel], “lighten”) indicates purpose (or result). The conditional sentence used in the translation above is an attempt to bring out the logical relationship between these forms.

5.text: He said to them, “Go away for three days, then return to me.” So the people went away.

6.text: King Rehoboam consulted with the older advisers who had served his father Solomon when he had been alive. He asked them, “How do you advise me to answer these people?”

notes.text: Heb “stood before.”
Heb “saying.”

7.text: They said to him, “Today if you will be a servant to these people and grant their request, speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants from this time forward.”

notes.text: Heb “and serve them and answer them,” understood as “serve them in how you answer them,” hence “grant their request.”
Heb “and speak to them good words.”
Heb “all the days.” The Hebrew phrase contrasts what he is asked to do “today” (literally “the day”) with the benefit for “all the days.”

8.text: But Rehoboam rejected their advice and consulted the young advisers who served him, with whom he had grown up.

notes.text: Heb “He rejected the advice of the elders which they advised and he consulted the young men with whom he had grown up, who stood before him.” The referent (Rehoboam) of the initial pronoun (“he”) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

9.text: He asked them, “How do you advise me to respond to these people who said to me, ‘Lessen the demands your father placed on us’?”

notes.text: In the Hebrew text the verb “we will respond” is plural, although it can be understood as an editorial “we.” The ancient versions have the singular here.
Heb “Lighten the yoke which your father placed on us.”

10.text: The young advisers with whom Rehoboam had grown up said to him, “Say this to these people who have said to you, ‘Your father made us work hard, but now lighten our burden.’ Say this to them: ‘I am a lot harsher than my father!

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Rehoboam) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “Your father made our yoke heavy, but make it lighter upon us.”

Heb “My little one is thicker than my father’s hips.” The referent of “my little one” is not clear. The traditional view is that it refers to the little finger. As the following statement makes clear, Rehoboam’s point is that he is more harsh and demanding than his father.

11.text: My father imposed heavy demands on you; I will make them even heavier. My father punished you with ordinary whips; I will punish you with whips that really sting your flesh.’”

notes.text: Heb “and now my father placed upon you a heavy yoke, but I will add to your yoke.”

Heb “My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions.” “Scorpions” might allude to some type of torture using poisonous insects, but more likely it refers to a type of whip that inflicts an especially biting, painful wound. Cf. CEV “whips with pieces of sharp metal.”

12.text: Jeroboam and all the people reported to Rehoboam on the third day, just as the king had ordered when he said, “Return to me on the third day.”

notes.text: Heb “came.”

13.text: The king responded to the people harshly. He rejected the advice of the older men

14.text: and followed the advice of the younger ones. He said, “My father imposed heavy demands on you; I will make them even heavier. My father punished you with ordinary whips; I will punish you with whips that really sting your flesh.”

notes.text: Heb “and spoke to them according to.”
Heb “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke.”
Heb “My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions.” See the note on the same phrase in v. 11.

15.text: The king refused to listen to the people, because the Lord was instigating this turn of events so that he might bring to pass the prophetic announcement he had made through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.

notes.text: Heb “because this turn of events was from the Lord.”
Heb “so that he might bring to pass his word which the Lord spoke.”

16.text: When all Israel saw that the king refused to listen to them, the people answered the king, “We have no portion in David, no share in the son of Jesse! Return to your homes, O Israel! Now, look after your own dynasty, O David!” So Israel returned to their homes.

notes.text: We have no portion in David; no share in the son of Jesse. Their point seems to be that they have no familial relationship with David that brings them any benefits or places upon them any obligations. They are being treated like outsiders.
Heb “to your tents, Israel.” The word “return” is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “Now see your house, David.”
Heb “went to their tents.”

17.text: (Rehoboam continued to rule over the Israelites who lived in the cities of Judah.)

18.text: King Rehoboam sent Adoniram, the supervisor of the work crews, out after them, but all Israel stoned him to death. King Rehoboam managed to jump into his chariot and escape to Jerusalem.

notes.text: The MT has “Adoram” here, but the Old Greek translation and Syriac Peshitta have “Adoniram.” Cf. 1 Kgs 4:6.
The work crews. See the note on this expression in 4:6.

19.text: So Israel has been in rebellion against the Davidic dynasty to this very day.

20.text: When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they summoned him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel. No one except the tribe of Judah remained loyal to the Davidic dynasty.

notes.text: Heb “there was no one [following] after the house of David except the tribe of Judah, it alone.”

21.text: When Rehoboam arrived in Jerusalem, he summoned 180,000 skilled warriors from all Judah and the tribe of Benjamin to attack Israel and restore the kingdom to Rehoboam son of Solomon.

notes.text: Heb “he summoned all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, 180,000 chosen men, accomplished in war.”

22.text: But God told Shemaiah the prophet,

notes.text: Heb “and the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God, saying.”

23.text: “Say this to King Rehoboam son of Solomon of Judah, and to all Judah and Benjamin, as well as the rest of the people,

24.text: ‘This is what the Lord has said: “Do not attack and make war with your brothers, the Israelites. Each of you go home. Indeed this thing has happened because of me.”’” So they obeyed the Lord’s message. They went home in keeping with the Lord’s message.

25.text: Jeroboam built up Shechem in the Ephraimite hill country and lived there. From there he went out and built up Penuel.

notes.text: The Old Greek translation has here a lengthy section consisting of twenty-three verses that are not found in the MT.

26.text: Jeroboam then thought to himself: “Now the Davidic dynasty could regain the kingdom.

notes.text: Heb “said in his heart.”

Heb “Now the kingdom could return to the house of David.” The imperfect verbal form translated “could return” is understood as having a potential force here. Perhaps this is not strong enough; another option is “will return.”

27.text: If these people go up to offer sacrifices in the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem, their loyalty could shift to their former master, King Rehoboam of Judah. They might kill me and return to King Rehoboam of Judah.”

notes.text: Heb “the heart of these people could return to their master.”

28.text: After the king had consulted with his advisers, he made two golden calves. Then he said to the people, “It is too much trouble for you to go up to Jerusalem. Look, Israel, here are your gods who brought you up from the land of Egypt.”

notes.text: The words “with his advisers” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “to them.”

29.text: He put one in Bethel and the other in Dan.

30.text: This caused Israel to sin; the people went to Bethel and Dan to worship the calves.

notes.text: Heb “and this thing became a sin.”

The MT reads “and the people went before the one to Dan.” It is likely that some words have been accidentally omitted and that the text originally said, “and the people went before the one at Bethel and before the one at Dan.”

31.text: He built temples on the high places and appointed as priests common people who were not Levites.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has the singular, but the plural is preferable here (see 1 Kgs 13:32). The Old Greek translation and the Vulgate have the plural.

32.text: Jeroboam inaugurated a festival on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, like the festival celebrated in Judah. On the altar in Bethel he offered sacrifices to the calves he had made. In Bethel he also appointed priests for the high places he had made.

notes.text: The eighth month would correspond to October-November in modern reckoning.
The festival celebrated in Judah probably refers to the Feast of Tabernacles (i.e., Booths or Temporary Shelters), held in the seventh month (September-October). See also 1 Kgs 8:2.
Heb “and he offered up [sacrifices] on the altar; he did this in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves which he had made.”

33.text: After this happened, Jeroboam still did not change his evil ways; he continued to appoint common people as priests at the high places. Anyone who wanted the job he consecrated as a priest.

notes.text: Heb “did not turn from his evil way.”
The expression common people refers to people who were not Levites. See 1 Kgs 12:31.
Heb “and one who had the desire he was filling his hand so that he became [one of] the priests of the high places.”

1.text: Just then a prophet arrived from Judah with the Lord’s message for Bethel, as Jeroboam was standing near the altar ready to offer a sacrifice.

notes.text: Heb The Hebrew particle ‏הִנֵּה‎ (hinneh) is a rhetorical device by which the author invites the reader to visualize the scene for dramatic effect.
Heb “the man of God.” Also in vv. 4-8.
Or “in keeping with” (also at vv. 2, 5, 9, 17, 18, 32).

2.text: He cried out against the altar with the Lord’s message, “O altar, altar! This is what the Lord has said, ‘Look, a son named Josiah will be born to the Davidic dynasty. He will sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who offer sacrifices on you. Human bones will be burned on you.’”

notes.text: “Look…you.” For the fulfillment of this prophecy see 2 Kgs 23:15-20.

3.text: That day he had also given a sign, saying, “This is the sign that the Lord has declared: The altar will split open and the ashes on it will pour out.”

notes.text: Heb “the fat,” i.e., fat mixed with ashes from the altar (HALOT 234 s.v. ‏דשׁן‎).
