4.text: When the king heard the prophet’s message that he had cried out against the altar in Bethel, Jeroboam took his hand from the altar and pointed it saying, “Seize him!” Then the hand that he had pointed at him stiffened up, and he could not pull it back.

notes.text: Heb “extended his hand from the altar.”

Heb The verb ‏יָבֵשׁ‎ (yavesh) usually describes water sources as dry or plants as dry and withered. Applied to a hand or an arm (Zech 11:17), it probably means to be(come) stiff, feeble, or both. TEV and NLT interpret this as “became paralyzed.”

5.text: Meanwhile the altar split open, and the ashes poured from the altar in fulfillment of the sign the prophet had given with the Lord’s message.

notes.text: The fat mixed with ashes. See note v. 3.

6.text: The king responded to the prophet, “Seek the favor of the Lord your God and pray for me, so that my hand may be restored.” So the prophet sought the Lord’s favor and the king’s hand was restored as it was at first.

notes.text: Heb “answered and said to.”
Heb “appease” or “soften the face of,” twice in this verse.

7.text: The king then said to the prophet, “Come home with me and have something to eat, so that I may give you a gift.”

notes.text: Or “reward.”

8.text: But the prophet said to the king, “Even if you were to give me half your possessions, I would not go with you. I am not allowed to eat food or drink water in this place.

notes.text: Heb “house,” representing one’s estate or possessions.

9.text: For this is how I was commanded in the Lord’s message, ‘Eat no food. Drink no water. And do not return by the way you came.’”

10.text: So he started back on another road; he did not travel back on the same road he had taken to Bethel.

11.text: Now there was an old prophet living in Bethel. When his sons came home, they told him everything the prophet had done in Bethel that day. And they told their father all the words that he had spoken to the king.

notes.text: The MT has the singular but the LXX, Syriac, some Latin manuscripts and two medieval Hebrew manuscripts have the plural, which consistent with the end of the verse and vv. 12-13.
Heb “the man of God.” Also in vv. 12, 14.
Heb “the words which he had spoken to the king, and they told them to their father.”

12.text: Their father asked them, “Which road did he take?” His sons showed him the road the prophet from Judah had taken.

notes.text: The MT reads ‏וַיִּרְאוּ‎ (vayyirʾu, “they saw”) the Qal preterite of ‏רָאָה‎ (raʾah, “to see”). Some translations render this as pluperfect “they had seen” (KJV, NASB), but then the verb should have been preceded by a different construction. Other translations (NIV, ESV, NRSV) follow some ancient versions and emend the verbal form to a Hiphil with pronominal suffix ‏וַיַּרְאֻהוּ‎ (vayyarʾuhu, “and they showed him”).

13.text: He then told his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me.” When they had saddled the donkey for him, he mounted it

14.text: and took off after the prophet, whom he found sitting under an oak tree. He asked him, “Are you the prophet from Judah?” He answered, “Yes, I am.”

15.text: He then said to him, “Come home with me and eat something.”

16.text: But he replied, “I can’t go back with you. I am not allowed to eat food or to drink water with you in this place.

notes.text: Heb “I am unable to return with you or to go with you.”

17.text: For an order came to me in the Lord’s message, ‘Eat no food. Drink no water there. And do not return by the way you came.’”

18.text: Then the old prophet said, “I too am a prophet like you. And an angel has told me in a message from the Lord, ‘Bring him back with you to your house so he can eat food and drink water.’” But he had lied to him.

notes.text: Heb “he.”

He had lied to him. The motives and actions of the old prophet are difficult to understand. The old man’s response to the prophet’s death (see vv. 26-32) suggests he did not trick him with malicious intent. Perhaps the old prophet wanted the honor of entertaining such a celebrity, or perhaps simply desired some social interaction with a fellow prophet.

19.text: So the prophet went back with him. He ate food in his house and he drank water.

notes.text: Heb “he.”

20.text: While they were sitting at the table, the Lord’s message came to the old prophet who had brought him back.

21.text: So he cried out to the prophet who had come from Judah, “This is what the Lord has said, ‘You have rebelled against the Lord’s instruction and have not obeyed the command the Lord your God gave you.

notes.text: Heb “man of God.”

The Hebrew text has “because” at the beginning of the sentence. In the Hebrew text vv. 21-22 are one long sentence comprised of a causal clause giving the reason for divine punishment (vv. 21-22a) and the main clause announcing the punishment (v. 22b). The translation divides this lengthy sentence for stylistic reasons.
Heb “mouth.”

22.text: You went back. You ate food. And you drank water in the place of which he had said to you, “Eat no food. Drink no water.” Therefore your corpse will not be buried in your ancestral tomb.’”

notes.text: “Therefore” is added for stylistic reasons. See the note at 1 Kgs 13:21 pertaining to the grammatical structure of vv. 21-22.
Heb “will not come to the tomb of your fathers.”

23.text: So this is what happened after he had eaten food and drunk water. The old prophet saddled the donkey for the prophet whom he had brought back.

notes.text: The MT does not include “water” though it is implied and included in the LXX and Syriac versions.
Heb “he.”

24.text: So the prophet from Judah travelled on. Then a lion attacked him on the road and killed him. There was his body lying on the road, with the donkey standing next to it, and the lion just standing there by the body.

25.text: Then some men came passing by and saw the body lying in the road with the lion standing next to the body. They went and reported what they had seen in the city where the old prophet lived.

notes.text: The words “what they had seen” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

26.text: When the old prophet who had invited him to his house heard the news, he said, “It is the prophet who rebelled against the Lord. The Lord delivered him over to the lion and it tore him up and killed him, in keeping with the Lord’s message that he had spoken to him.”

notes.text: Heb “and the prophet who had brought him back from the road heard.”
Heb “the man of God.”
Heb “the mouth of the Lord.”
Heb “destroyed him,” or “maimed him.”

27.text: He told his sons, “Saddle my donkey.” So they saddled it.

28.text: He went and found the body lying in the road with the donkey and the lion standing beside it; the lion had neither eaten the body nor attacked the donkey.

notes.text: Heb “the body.”

29.text: The old prophet picked up the prophet’s body, put it on the donkey, and brought it back. The old prophet then entered the city to mourn him and to bury him.

notes.text: Heb “the prophet.” The word “old” has been supplied in the translation to distinguish this individual from the other prophet.
Heb “the man of God.”

30.text: He put the body into his own tomb, and they mourned over him, saying, “Ah, my brother!”

notes.text: “They” is the reading of the Hebrew text here; perhaps this is meant to include not only the old prophet but his sons (cf. v. 31).

31.text: After he buried him, he said to his sons, “When I die, bury me in the tomb where the prophet is buried; put my bones right beside his bones,

notes.text: Heb “the man of God.”

32.text: because the message that he announced as the Lord’s message against the altar in Bethel and against all the temples on the high places in the cities of the north will certainly be fulfilled.”

notes.text: Heb “Samaria.” The name of Israel’s capital city here stands for the northern kingdom as a whole. Actually Samaria was not built and named until several years after this (see 1 Kgs 16:24), so it is likely that the author of Kings, writing at a later time, is here adapting the old prophet’s original statement.

34.text: This sin caused Jeroboam’s dynasty to come to an end and to be destroyed from the face of the earth.

notes.text: Heb “house.”

1.text: At that time Jeroboam’s son Abijah became sick.

notes.text: Some mss of the Old Greek lack vv. 1-20.

2.text: Jeroboam told his wife, “Disguise yourself so that people cannot recognize you are Jeroboam’s wife. Then go to Shiloh; Ahijah the prophet, who told me I would rule over this nation, lives there.

notes.text: Heb “Get up, change yourself.”
Heb “look, Ahijah the prophet is there; he spoke about me as king over this nation.”

3.text: Take ten loaves of bread, some small cakes, and a container of honey and visit him. He will tell you what will happen to the boy.”

notes.text: Heb “take in your hand.”

4.text: Jeroboam’s wife did as she was told. She went to Shiloh and visited Ahijah. Now Ahijah could not see; he had lost his eyesight in his old age.

notes.text: Heb “and the wife of Jeroboam did so; she arose and went to Shiloh and entered the house of Ahijah.”
Heb “his eyes were set because of his old age.”

5.text: But the Lord had told Ahijah, “Look, Jeroboam’s wife is coming to find out from you what will happen to her son, for he is sick. Tell her such and such. When she comes, she will be in a disguise.”

notes.text: Heb “like this and like this.”

Tell her such and such. Certainly the Lord gave Ahijah a specific message to give to Jeroboam’s wife (see vv. 6-16), but the author of Kings here condenses the Lord’s message with the words “so-and-so.” For dramatic effect he prefers to have us hear the message from Ahijah’s lips as he speaks to the king’s wife.

6.text: When Ahijah heard the sound of her footsteps as she came through the door, he said, “Come on in, wife of Jeroboam! Why are you pretending to be someone else? I have been commissioned to give you bad news.

notes.text: Heb “I am sent to you [with] a hard [message].”

7.text: Go, tell Jeroboam, ‘This is what the Lord God of Israel has said: “I raised you up from among the people and made you ruler over my people Israel.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has “because” at the beginning of the sentence. In the Hebrew text vv. 7-11 are one long sentence comprised of a causal clause giving the reason for divine punishment (vv. 7-9) and the main clause announcing the punishment (vv. 10-11). The translation divides this lengthy sentence for stylistic reasons.

8.text: I tore the kingdom away from the Davidic dynasty and gave it to you. But you are not like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me wholeheartedly by doing only what I approve.

notes.text: Heb “what was right in my eyes.”

9.text: You have sinned more than all who came before you. You went and angered me by making other gods, formed out of metal; you have completely disregarded me.

notes.text: Heb “you went and you made for yourself other gods, and metal [ones], angering me, and you threw me behind your back.”

10.text: So I am ready to bring disaster on the dynasty of Jeroboam. I will cut off every last male belonging to Jeroboam in Israel, including even the weak and incapacitated. I will burn up the dynasty of Jeroboam, just as one burns manure until it is completely consumed.

notes.text: Disaster. There is a wordplay in the Hebrew text. The word translated “disaster” (‏רָעָה‎, raʿah) is from the same root as the expression “you have sinned” in v. 9 (‏וַתָּרַע‎ [vattaraʿ], from ‏רָעַע‎, [raʿaʿ]). Jeroboam’s sins would receive an appropriate punishment.
Heb “house.”

Heb “and I will cut off from Jeroboam those who urinate against a wall (including both those who are) restrained and let free (or “abandoned”) in Israel.” The precise meaning of the idiomatic phrase ‏עָצוּר וְעָזוּב‎ (ʿatsur veʿazuv) is uncertain. For various options see HALOT 871 s.v. ‏עצר‎ 6 and M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 107. The two terms are usually taken as polar opposites (“slaves and freemen” or “minors and adults”), but Cogan and Tadmor, on the basis of contextual considerations (note the usage with ‏אֶפֶס‎ [ʾefes], “nothing but”) in Deut 32:36 and 2 Kgs 14:26, argue convincingly that the terms are synonyms, meaning “restrained and abandoned,” and refer to incapable or incapacitated individuals.

The traditional view understands the verb ‏בָּעַר‎ (baʿar) to mean “burn.” Manure was sometimes used as fuel (see Ezek 4:12, 15). However, an alternate view takes ‏בָּעַר‎ as a homonym meaning “sweep away” (HALOT 146 s.v. II ‏בער‎). In this case one might translate, “I will sweep away the dynasty of Jeroboam, just as one sweeps away manure it is gone” (cf. ASV, NASB, TEV). Either metaphor emphasizes the thorough and destructive nature of the coming judgment.

11.text: Dogs will eat the members of your family who die in the city, and the birds of the sky will eat the ones who die in the country.”’ Indeed, the Lord has announced it!

notes.text: The Hebrew text has “belonging to Jeroboam” here.

12.text: “As for you, get up and go home. When you set foot in the city, the boy will die.

13.text: All Israel will mourn him and bury him. He is the only one in Jeroboam’s family who will receive a decent burial, for he is the only one in whom the Lord God of Israel found anything good.

notes.text: Heb “house.”

14.text: The Lord will raise up a king over Israel who will cut off Jeroboam’s dynasty. It is ready to happen!

notes.text: Heb “house.”
Heb “This is the day. What also now?” The precise meaning of the second half of the statement is uncertain.

15.text: The Lord will attack Israel, making it like a reed that sways in the water. He will remove Israel from this good land he gave to their ancestors and scatter them beyond the Euphrates River, because they angered the Lord by making Asherah poles.

notes.text: The elliptical Hebrew text reads literally “and the Lord will strike Israel as a reed sways in the water.”
Heb “fathers” (also in vv. 22, 31).
Heb “the River.” In biblical Hebrew this is a typical reference to the Euphrates River. The name “Euphrates” has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
Heb “because they made their Asherah poles that anger the Lord”; or “their images of Asherah”; ASV, NASB “their Asherim”; NCV “they set up idols to worship Asherah.”

Asherah was a leading deity of the Canaanite pantheon, wife/sister of El and goddess of fertility. She was commonly worshiped at shrines in or near groves of evergreen trees, or, failing that, at places marked by wooden poles. These were to be burned or cut down (Deut 12:3; 16:21; Judg 6:25, 28, 30; 2 Kgs 18:4).

16.text: He will hand Israel over to their enemies because of the sins which Jeroboam committed and which he made Israel commit.”

notes.text: Heb “and he will give [up] Israel.”

17.text: So Jeroboam’s wife got up and went back to Tirzah. As she crossed the threshold of the house, the boy died.

notes.text: Heb “went and entered.”

18.text: All Israel buried him and mourned for him, in keeping with the Lord’s message that he had spoken through his servant, the prophet Ahijah.

19.text: The rest of the events of Jeroboam’s reign, including the details of his battles and rule, are recorded in the scroll called the Annals of the Kings of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Jeroboam, how he fought and how he ruled, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Israel?”

20.text: Jeroboam ruled for twenty-two years; then he passed away. His son Nadab replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”

21.text: Now Rehoboam son of Solomon ruled in Judah. He was forty-one years old when he became king and he ruled for seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the Lord chose from all the tribes of Israel to be his home. His mother was an Ammonite woman named Naamah.

notes.text: Heb “Rehoboam.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “the city where the Lord chose to place his name from all the tribes of Israel.”
Heb “an Ammonite”; the word “woman” is implied by the gender of the word.

22.text: Judah did evil in the sight of the Lord. They made him more jealous by their sins than their ancestors had done.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”
Heb “and they made him jealous more than all which their fathers had done by their sins which they sinned.”

23.text: They even built for themselves high places, sacred pillars, and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree.

24.text: There were also male cultic prostitutes in the land. They committed the same horrible sins as the nations that the Lord had driven out from before the Israelites.

notes.text: The Old Greek translation has “a conspiracy” rather than “male cultic prostitutes.”
Heb “they did according to all the abominable acts of the nations.”

25.text: In King Rehoboam’s fifth year, King Shishak of Egypt attacked Jerusalem.

26.text: He took away the treasures of the Lord’s temple and of the royal palace; he took everything, including all the golden shields that Solomon had made.

27.text: King Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace them and assigned them to the officers of the royal guard who protected the entrance to the royal palace.

notes.text: Heb “runners.”

28.text: Whenever the king visited the Lord’s temple, the royal guard carried them and then brought them back to the guardroom.

29.text: The rest of the events of Rehoboam’s reign, including his accomplishments, are recorded in the scroll called the Annals of the Kings of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Rehoboam, and all which he did, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Judah?”

30.text: Rehoboam and Jeroboam were continually at war with each other.

31.text: Rehoboam passed away and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His mother was an Ammonite named Naamah. His son Abijah replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”
In the Hebrew text the name is spelled “Abijam” here and in 1 Kgs 15:1-8.

1.text: In the eighteenth year of the reign of Jeroboam son of Nebat, Abijah became king over Judah.

notes.text: The Old Greek also has the phrase “the son of Rehoboam.”

2.text: He ruled for three years in Jerusalem. His mother was Maacah, the daughter of Abishalom.

notes.text: Abishalom (also in v. 10) is a variant of the name Absalom (cf. 2 Chr 11:20). The more common form is used by TEV, NLT.

3.text: He followed all the sinful practices of his father before him. He was not wholeheartedly devoted to the Lord his God, as his ancestor David had been.

notes.text: Heb “his heart was not complete with the Lord his God, like the heart of David his father.”

4.text: Nevertheless for David’s sake the Lord his God maintained his dynasty in Jerusalem by giving him a son to succeed him and by protecting Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “gave him a lamp.”
The Old Greek has the plural “his sons.”
Heb “by raising up his son after him.”
Heb “and by causing Jerusalem to stand firm.”

5.text: He did this because David had done what he approved and had not disregarded any of his commandments his entire lifetime, except for the incident involving Uriah the Hittite.

notes.text: The words “he did this” are added for stylistic reasons.
Heb “what was right in the eyes of the Lord.”
Heb “and had not turned aside from all which he commanded him.”

6.text: Rehoboam and Jeroboam were continually at war with each other throughout Abijah’s lifetime.

notes.text: Most Hebrew mss read “Rehoboam”; a few Hebrew mss and the Syriac read “Abijam” (a variant of Abijah).
Heb “his”; the referent (Abijah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

7.text: The rest of the events of Abijah’s reign, including all his accomplishments, are recorded in the scroll called the Annals of the Kings of Judah. Abijah and Jeroboam had been at war with each other.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Abijah, and all which he did, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Judah?”

8.text: Abijah passed away and was buried in the City of David. His son Asa replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.” The Old Greek also has these words: “in the twenty-eighth year of Jeroboam.”
Heb “and they buried him.”

9.text: In the twentieth year of Jeroboam’s reign over Israel, Asa became the king of Judah.

10.text: He ruled for forty-one years in Jerusalem. His grandmother was Maacah daughter of Abishalom.

notes.text: Heb “mother,” but Hebrew often uses the terms “father” and “mother” for grandparents and more remote ancestors.

11.text: Asa did what the Lord approved as his ancestor David had done.

notes.text: Heb “what was right in the eyes of the Lord.”
Heb “father,” but Hebrew often uses the terms “father” and “mother” for grandparents and more remote ancestors.

12.text: He removed the male cultic prostitutes from the land and got rid of all the disgusting idols his ancestors had made.

notes.text: The word used here, ‏גִלּוּלִים‎ [gillulim], is always used as a disdainful reference to idols. It is generally thought to have originally referred to “dung pellets” (cf. KBL 183 s.v. ‏גִלּוּלִים‎). It is only one of several terms used in this way, such as “worthless things” (‏אֱלִילִים‎, ʾelilim), “vanities” or “empty winds” (‏הֲבָלִים‎, havalim).
Heb “fathers” (also in v. 24).

13.text: He also removed Maacah his grandmother from her position as queen mother because she had made a loathsome Asherah pole. Asa cut down her loathsome pole and burned it in the Kidron Valley.

notes.text: Heb “mother,” but Hebrew often uses the terms “father” and “mother” for grandparents and more remote ancestors.
The Hebrew term ‏גְּבִירָה‎ (gevirah) can denote “queen” or “queen mother” depending on the context. Here the latter is indicated, since Maacah was the wife of Rehoboam and mother of Abijah.

14.text: The high places were not eliminated, yet Asa was wholeheartedly devoted to the Lord throughout his lifetime.

notes.text: Heb “yet the heart of Asa was complete with the Lord all his days.”

15.text: He brought the holy items that he and his father had made into the Lord’s temple, including the silver, gold, and other articles.

notes.text: Heb “and he brought the holy things of his father and his holy things (into) the house of the Lord, silver, gold, and items.” Instead of “his holy things,” a marginal reading (Qere) in the Hebrew text has “the holy things of [the house of the Lord].”

16.text: Now Asa and King Baasha of Israel were continually at war with each other.

notes.text: Heb “There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.”

17.text: King Baasha of Israel attacked Judah and established Ramah as a military outpost to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the land of King Asa of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “and he built up Ramah so as to not permit going out or coming in to Asa king of Judah.”

18.text: Asa took all the silver and gold that was left in the treasuries of the Lord’s temple and of the royal palace and handed it to his servants. He then told them to deliver it to Ben Hadad son of Tabrimmon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, ruler in Damascus, along with this message:

notes.text: Heb “King Asa sent it.”

19.text: “I want to make a treaty with you, like the one our fathers made. See, I have sent you silver and gold as a present. Break your treaty with King Baasha of Israel, so he will retreat from my land.”

notes.text: Heb “[May there be] a covenant between me and you [as there was] between my father and your father.”
Heb “so he will go up from upon me.”

20.text: Ben Hadad accepted King Asa’s offer and ordered his army commanders to attack the cities of Israel. They conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel Beth Maacah, and all the territory of Naphtali, including the region of Kinnereth.

notes.text: Heb “and Ben Hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of the armies which belonged to him against the cities of Israel.”
Heb “he struck down.”
A city in Galilee (Deut 3:17) along with its surrounding region; Kinnereth was also another name for the Sea of Galilee.

21.text: When Baasha heard the news, he stopped fortifying Ramah and settled down in Tirzah.

notes.text: Heb “building.”

22.text: King Asa ordered all the men of Judah (no exemptions were granted) to carry away the stones and wood that Baasha had used to build Ramah. King Asa used the materials to build up Geba (in Benjamin) and Mizpah.

notes.text: Heb “and King Asa made a proclamation to all Judah, there was no one exempt, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and its wood which Baasha had built.”
Heb “and King Asa built with them.”

23.text: The rest of the events of Asa’s reign, including all his successes and accomplishments, as well as a record of the cities he built, are recorded in the scroll called the Annals of the Kings of Judah. Yet when he was very old he developed a foot disease.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of all the events of Asa, and all his strength and all which he did and the cities which he built, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Judah?”
Heb “Yet in the time of his old age he became sick in his feet.”

24.text: Asa passed away and was buried with his ancestors in the city of his ancestor David. His son Jehoshaphat replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”

25.text: In the second year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Jeroboam’s son Nadab became the king of Israel; he ruled Israel for two years.

26.text: He did evil in the sight of the Lord. He followed in his father’s footsteps and encouraged Israel to sin.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”
Heb “and he walked in the way of his father and in his sin which he made Israel sin.”

27.text: Baasha son of Ahijah, from the tribe of Issachar, conspired against Nadab and assassinated him in Gibbethon, which was in Philistine territory. This happened while Nadab and all the Israelite army were besieging Gibbethon.

notes.text: Heb “against him”; the referent (Nadab) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

28.text: Baasha killed him in the third year of Asa’s reign over Judah and replaced him as king.

29.text: When he became king, he executed Jeroboam’s entire family. He wiped out everyone who breathed, in keeping with the Lord’s message that he had spoken through his servant Ahijah the Shilonite.

notes.text: Heb “house,” meaning “family” by metonymy.
Heb “He did not allow to survive.”

30.text: This happened because of the sins which Jeroboam committed and which he made Israel commit. These sins angered the Lord God of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “because of Jeroboam which he committed and which he made Israel commit, by his provocation by which he made the Lord God of Israel angry.”

31.text: The rest of the events of Nadab’s reign, including all his accomplishments, are recorded in the scroll called the Annals of the Kings of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Nadab, and all which he did, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Israel?”

32.text: Asa and King Baasha of Israel were continually at war with each other.

33.text: In the third year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Baasha son of Ahijah became king over all Israel in Tirzah; he ruled for twenty-four years.

34.text: He did evil in the sight of the Lord; he followed in Jeroboam’s footsteps and encouraged Israel to sin.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”
Heb “and he walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he made Israel sin.”

1.text: The Lord’s message against Baasha came to Jehu son of Hanani:

notes.text: LXX “by the hand of,” meaning “through.”

2.text: “I raised you up from the dust and made you ruler over my people Israel. Yet you followed in Jeroboam’s footsteps and encouraged my people Israel to sin; their sins have made me angry.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has “because” at the beginning of the sentence. In the Hebrew text vv. 2-3 are one sentence comprised of a causal clause giving the reason for divine punishment (v. 2) and the main clause announcing the punishment (v. 3). The translation divides this sentence for stylistic reasons.
Heb “walked in the way of Jeroboam.”
Heb “angering me by their sins.”

3.text: So I am ready to burn up Baasha and his family, and make your family like the family of Jeroboam son of Nebat.

notes.text: The traditional view understands the verb ‏בָּעַר‎ (baʿar) to mean “burn.” However, an alternate view takes ‏בָּעַר‎ (baʿar) as a homonym meaning “sweep away” (HALOT 146 s.v. II ‏בער‎). In this case one might translate, “I am ready to sweep away Baasha and his family.” Either metaphor emphasizes the thorough and destructive nature of the coming judgment.
The Old Greek, Syriac Peshitta, and some mss of the Targum have here “his house.”

4.text: Dogs will eat the members of Baasha’s family who die in the city, and the birds of the sky will eat the ones who die in the country.”

notes.text: Heb “the ones belonging to Baasha.”

5.text: The rest of the events of Baasha’s reign, including his accomplishments and successes, are recorded in the scroll called the Annals of the Kings of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Baasha, and that which he did and his strength, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Israel?”

6.text: Baasha passed away and was buried in Tirzah. His son Elah replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”

7.text: And so it was the Lord’s message came through the prophet Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha and his family. This was because of all the evil he had done in the Lord’s view, by angering him with his deeds and becoming like Jeroboam’s dynasty, and because of how he had destroyed Jeroboam’s dynasty.

notes.text: Heb “house,” by extension meaning the members of one’s household or a dynasty.
Heb “house.”
Heb “he struck him down” or “…it down.”

8.text: In the twenty-sixth year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Baasha’s son Elah became king over Israel; he ruled in Tirzah for two years.

9.text: His servant Zimri, a commander of half of his chariot force, conspired against him. While Elah was in Tirzah drinking heavily at the house of Arza, who supervised the palace in Tirzah,

notes.text: Heb “while he was in Tirzah drinking and drunken.”

10.text: Zimri came in and struck him dead. (This happened in the twenty-seventh year of Asa’s reign over Judah.) Zimri replaced Elah as king.

notes.text: Heb “and he became king in his place.”

11.text: When he became king and occupied the throne, he killed Baasha’s entire family. He did not spare any male belonging to him; he killed his relatives and his friends.

notes.text: Heb “and he did not spare any belonging to him who urinate against a wall, [including] his kinsmen redeemers and his friends.”

12.text: Zimri destroyed Baasha’s entire family, in keeping with the Lord’s message which he had spoken against Baasha through Jehu the prophet.

13.text: This happened because of all the sins which Baasha and his son Elah committed and which they made Israel commit. They angered the Lord God of Israel with their worthless idols.

notes.text: Heb “angering the Lord God of Israel with their empty things.”

14.text: The rest of the events of Elah’s reign, including all his accomplishments, are recorded in the scroll called the Annals of the Kings of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Elah, and all which he did, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Israel?”

15.text: In the twenty-seventh year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Zimri became king over Israel; he ruled for seven days in Tirzah. Zimri’s revolt took place while the army was deployed in Gibbethon, which was in Philistine territory.

notes.text: Heb “Now the people were encamped.

16.text: While deployed there, the army received this report: “Zimri has conspired against the king and assassinated him.” So all Israel made Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel that very day in the camp.

notes.text: Heb “and the people who were encamped heard, saying.”
Heb “has conspired against and also has struck down the king.”

17.text: Omri and all Israel went up from Gibbethon and besieged Tirzah.

18.text: When Zimri saw that the city was captured, he went into the fortified area of the royal palace. He set the palace on fire and died in the flames.

notes.text: Heb “and he burned the house of the king over him with fire and he died.”

19.text: This happened because of the sins he committed. He did evil in the sight of the Lord and followed in Jeroboam’s footsteps and encouraged Israel to continue sinning.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”
Heb “walking in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he did to make Israel sin.”

20.text: The rest of the events of Zimri’s reign, including the details of his revolt, are recorded in the scroll called the Annals of the Kings of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Zimri, and his conspiracy which he conspired, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Israel?”

21.text: At that time the people of Israel were divided in their loyalties. Half the people supported Tibni son of Ginath and wanted to make him king; the other half supported Omri.

22.text: Omri’s supporters were stronger than those who supported Tibni son of Ginath. Tibni died; Omri became king.

23.text: In the thirty-first year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Omri became king over Israel. He ruled for twelve years, six of them in Tirzah.

24.text: He purchased the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver. He launched a construction project there and named the city he built after Shemer, the former owner of the hill of Samaria.

notes.text: The Hebrew term ‏כִּכָּר‎ (kikkar, “circle”) refers generally to something that is round. When used of metals it can refer to a disk-shaped weight made of the metal or to a standard unit of weight, generally regarded as a talent. Since the accepted weight for a talent of metal is about 75 pounds, this would have amounted to about 150 pounds of silver.
Heb “he built up the hill.”

25.text: Omri did more evil in the sight of the Lord than all who were before him.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”

26.text: He followed in the footsteps of Jeroboam son of Nebat and encouraged Israel to sin; they angered the Lord God of Israel with their worthless idols.

notes.text: Heb “walked in all the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat and in his sin which he made Israel sin.”
Heb “angering the Lord God of Israel with their empty things.”

27.text: The rest of the events of Omri’s reign, including his accomplishments and successes, are recorded in the scroll called the Annals of the Kings of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the acts of Omri which he did, and his strength which he demonstrated, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Israel?”

28.text: Omri passed away and was buried in Samaria. His son Ahab replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”
The Old Greek has eight additional verses here. Cf. 1 Kgs 22:41-44.

29.text: In the thirty-eighth year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Omri’s son Ahab became king over Israel. Ahab son of Omri ruled over Israel for twenty-two years in Samaria.

30.text: Ahab son of Omri did more evil in the sight of the Lord than all who were before him.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”

31.text: As if following in the sinful footsteps of Jeroboam son of Nebat were not bad enough, he married Jezebel the daughter of King Ethbaal of the Sidonians. Then he worshiped and bowed to Baal.

notes.text: Heb “and he went and served Baal and bowed down to him.”
The Canaanites worshiped Baal as a storm and fertility god.

32.text: He set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal he had built in Samaria.

33.text: Ahab also made an Asherah pole; he did more to anger the Lord God of Israel than all the kings of Israel who were before him.

notes.text: Heb “Ahab”; the proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.

34.text: During Ahab’s reign, Hiel the Bethelite rebuilt Jericho. Abiram, his firstborn son, died when he laid the foundation; Segub, his youngest son, died when he erected its gates, in keeping with the Lord’s message that he had spoken through Joshua son of Nun.

notes.text: Heb “in his days.”
Heb “with Abiram, his firstborn, he founded it.”
Heb “with Segub, his youngest, he set up its gates.”

Warned through Joshua son of Nun. For the background to this statement, see Josh 6:26, where Joshua pronounces a curse on the one who dares to rebuild Jericho. Here that curse is viewed as a prophecy spoken by God through Joshua.

1.text: Elijah the Tishbite, from Tishbe in Gilead, said to Ahab, “As certainly as the Lord God of Israel lives (whom I serve), there will be no dew or rain in the years ahead unless I give the command.”

notes.text: Heb “before whom I stand.”
Heb “except at the command of my word.”

2.text: The Lord’s message came to him:

3.text: “Leave here and travel eastward. Hide out in the Kerith Valley near the Jordan.

4.text: Drink from the stream; I have already told the ravens to bring you food there.”

notes.text: Heb “commanded.”
Heb “to provide for you.”

5.text: So he carried out the Lord’s message; he went and lived in the Kerith Valley near the Jordan.

notes.text: Heb “acted according to.”

6.text: The ravens would bring him bread and meat each morning and evening, and he would drink from the stream.

7.text: After a while, the stream dried up because there had been no rain in the land.

notes.text: Heb “And it came about at the end of days.”

8.text: The Lord’s message came to him,

9.text: “Get up, go to Zarephath in Sidonian territory, and live there. I have already told a widow who lives there to provide for you.”

notes.text: Heb “Look, I have commanded.”

10.text: So he got up and went to Zarephath. When he went through the city gate, there was a widow gathering wood. He called out to her, “Please give me a little water in a cup, so I can take a drink.”

11.text: As she went to get it, he called out to her, “Please bring me a piece of bread.”

notes.text: The Hebrew text also includes the phrase “in your hand.”

12.text: She said, “As certainly as the Lord your God lives, I have no food, except for a handful of flour in a jar and a little olive oil in a jug. Right now I am gathering a couple of sticks for a fire. Then I’m going home to make one final meal for my son and myself. After we have eaten that, we will die of starvation.”

notes.text: Heb “Look, I am gathering two sticks and then I will go and make it for me and my son and we will eat it and we will die.”

13.text: Elijah said to her, “Don’t be afraid. Go and do as you planned. But first make me a small cake and bring it to me; then make something for yourself and your son.

notes.text: Heb “according to your word.”
Heb “cake from there.”

14.text: For this is what the Lord God of Israel has said: ‘The jar of flour will not be empty and the jug of oil will not run out until the day the Lord makes it rain on the surface of the ground.’”

15.text: She went and did as Elijah told her; there was always enough food for Elijah and for her and her family.

notes.text: Heb “and she ate, she and he and her house [for] days.”

16.text: The jar of flour was never empty and the jug of oil never ran out, in keeping with the Lord’s message that he had spoken through Elijah.

17.text: After this the son of the woman who owned the house got sick. His illness was so severe he could no longer breathe.

notes.text: Heb “after these things.”

18.text: She asked Elijah, “Why, prophet, have you come to me to confront me with my sin and kill my son?”

notes.text: Heb “What to me and to you, man of God, that you have come.”
Heb “to make me remember.”

19.text: He said to her, “Hand me your son.” He took him from her arms, carried him to the upper room where he was staying, and laid him down on his bed.

20.text: Then he called out to the Lord, “O Lord, my God, are you also bringing disaster on this widow I am staying with by killing her son?”

21.text: He stretched out over the boy three times and called out to the Lord, “O Lord, my God, please let this boy’s breath return to him.”

22.text: The Lord answered Elijah’s prayer; the boy’s breath returned to him and he lived.

23.text: Elijah took the boy, brought him down from the upper room to the house, and handed him to his mother. Elijah then said, “See, your son is alive!”

24.text: The woman said to Elijah, “Now I know that you are a prophet and that the Lord’s message really does come through you.”

notes.text: Heb “man of God.”
Heb “is truly in your mouth.”

This episode is especially significant in light of Ahab’s decision to promote Baal worship in Israel. In Canaanite mythology the drought that swept over the region (v. 1) would signal that Baal, a fertility god responsible for providing food for his subjects, had been defeated by the god of death and was imprisoned in the underworld. While Baal was overcome by death and unable to function like a king, Israel’s God demonstrated his sovereignty and superiority to death by providing food for a widow and restoring life to her son. And he did it all in Sidonian territory, Baal’s back yard, as it were. The episode demonstrates that Israel’s God, not Baal, is the true king who provides food and controls life and death. This polemic against Baalism reaches its climax in the next chapter, when the Lord proves that he, not Baal, controls the elements of the storm and determines when the rains will fall.

1.text: Some time later, in the third year of the famine, the Lord’s message came to Elijah, “Go, make an appearance before Ahab, so I may send rain on the surface of the ground.”

notes.text: The words “of the famine” do not appear in the original text but are supplied for clarification.

2.text: So Elijah went to make an appearance before Ahab. Now the famine was severe in Samaria.

3.text: So Ahab summoned Obadiah, who supervised the palace. (Now Obadiah was a very loyal follower of the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “now Obadiah greatly feared the Lord.” “Fear” refers here to obedience and allegiance, the products of healthy respect for the Lord’s authority.

4.text: When Jezebel was killing the Lord’s prophets, Obadiah took 100 prophets and hid them in two caves in two groups of fifty. He also brought them food and water.)

notes.text: Heb “cutting off.”

5.text: Ahab told Obadiah, “Go through the land to all the springs and valleys. Maybe we can find some grazing areas so we can keep the horses and mules alive and not have to kill some of the animals.”

notes.text: Heb “grass.”
Heb “to cut off.”

6.text: They divided up the land between them to search it; Ahab went one way by himself and Obadiah went the other way by himself.

7.text: As Obadiah was traveling along, Elijah met him. When he recognized him, he fell facedown to the ground and said, “Is it really you, my master, Elijah?”

notes.text: Heb “look, Elijah [came] to meet him.”

8.text: He replied, “Yes, go and say to your master, ‘Elijah is back.’”

notes.text: Heb “[It is] I.”
Heb “Look, Elijah”; or “Elijah is here.”

9.text: Obadiah said, “What sin have I committed that you are ready to hand your servant over to Ahab for execution?

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Obadiah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “to kill me.”

10.text: As certainly as the Lord your God lives, my master has sent to every nation and kingdom in an effort to find you. When they say, ‘He’s not here,’ he makes them swear an oath that they could not find you.

notes.text: Heb “he makes the kingdom or the nation swear an oath.”

11.text: Now you say, ‘Go and say to your master, “Elijah is back.”’

notes.text: Heb “Look, Elijah”; or “Elijah is here.”

12.text: But when I leave you, the Lord’s Spirit will carry you away so I can’t find you. If I go tell Ahab I’ve seen you, he won’t be able to find you and he will kill me. That would not be fair, because your servant has been a loyal follower of the Lord from my youth.

notes.text: Heb “to [a place] which I do not know.”
Heb “and I will go to inform Ahab and he will not find you and he will kill me.”
The words “that would not be fair” are added to clarify the logic of Obadiah’s argument.
Heb “has feared the Lord” (also see the note at 1 Kgs 18:3).

13.text: Certainly my master is aware of what I did when Jezebel was killing the Lord’s prophets. I hid 100 of the Lord’s prophets in two caves in two groups of fifty and I brought them food and water.

notes.text: Heb “Has it not been told to my master what I did…?” The rhetorical question expects an answer, “Of course it has!”

14.text: Now you say, ‘Go and say to your master, “Elijah is back,”’ but he will kill me.”

notes.text: Heb “Look, Elijah”; or “Elijah is here.”

15.text: But Elijah said, “As certainly as the Lord of Heaven’s Armies lives (whom I serve), I will make an appearance before him today.”

notes.text: Traditionally, “the Lord of Hosts.”
Heb “(before whom I stand).”

16.text: When Obadiah went and informed Ahab, the king went to meet Elijah.

notes.text: Heb “Obadiah went to meet Ahab and told him, and Ahab went to meet Elijah.”

17.text: When Ahab saw Elijah, he said to him, “Is it really you, the one who brings disaster on Israel?”

notes.text: Heb “Ahab.”
Or “brings trouble on.”

18.text: Elijah replied, “I have not brought disaster on Israel. But you and your father’s dynasty have, by abandoning the Lord’s commandments and following the Baals.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Elijah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “brought trouble on.”

19.text: Now send out messengers and assemble all Israel before me at Mount Carmel, as well as the 450 prophets of Baal and 400 prophets of Asherah whom Jezebel supports.”

notes.text: The word “messengers” is supplied in the translation both here and in v. 20 for clarification.
Heb “who eat at the table of Jezebel.”

20.text: Ahab sent messengers to all the Israelites and had the prophets assemble at Mount Carmel.

21.text: Elijah approached all the people and said, “How long are you going to be paralyzed by indecision? If the Lord is the true God, then follow him, but if Baal is, follow him!” But the people did not say a word.

notes.text: Heb “How long are you going to limp around on two crutches?” (see HALOT 762 s.v. ‏סְעִפִּים‎). In context this idiomatic expression refers to indecision rather than physical disability.
Heb “the God.”

22.text: Elijah said to them: “I am the only prophet of the Lord who is left, but there are 450 prophets of Baal.

notes.text: Heb “to the people.”

23.text: Let them bring us two bulls. Let them choose one of the bulls for themselves, cut it up into pieces, and place it on the wood. But they must not set it on fire. I will do the same to the other bull and place it on the wood. But I will not set it on fire.

24.text: Then you will invoke the name of your god, and I will invoke the name of the Lord. The god who responds with fire will demonstrate that he is the true God.” All the people responded, “This will be a fair test.”

notes.text: Elijah now directly addresses the prophets.
Heb “the God.”
Heb “The matter [i.e., proposal] is good [i.e., acceptable].”

25.text: Elijah told the prophets of Baal, “Choose one of the bulls for yourselves and go first, for you are the majority. Invoke the name of your god, but do not light a fire.”

notes.text: The last sentence of v. 25 is absent in the Syriac Peshitta.

26.text: So they took a bull, as he had suggested, and prepared it. They invoked the name of Baal from morning until noon, saying, “Baal, answer us.” But there was no sound and no answer. They jumped around on the altar they had made.

notes.text: Heb “and they took the bull which he allowed them.”
Heb “limped” (the same verb is used in v. 21).
The MT has “which he made,” but some medieval Hebrew mss and the ancient versions have the plural form of the verb.

27.text: At noon Elijah mocked them, “Yell louder! After all, he is a god; he may be deep in thought, or perhaps he stepped out for a moment or has taken a trip. Perhaps he is sleeping and needs to be awakened.”

notes.text: Elijah’s sarcastic proposals would have been especially offensive and irritating to Baal’s prophets, for they believed Baal was imprisoned in the underworld as death’s captive during this time of drought. Elijah’s apparent ignorance of their theology is probably designed for dramatic effect; indeed the suggestion that Baal is away on a trip or deep in sleep comes precariously close to the truth as viewed by the prophets.

28.text: So they yelled louder and, in accordance with their prescribed ritual, mutilated themselves with swords and spears until their bodies were covered with blood.

notes.text: Or “as was their custom.”
Heb “until blood poured out on them.”
mutilated…covered with blood. This self-mutilation was a mourning rite designed to facilitate Baal’s return from the underworld.

29.text: Throughout the afternoon they were in an ecstatic frenzy, but there was no sound, no answer, and no response.

notes.text: Heb “when noon passed they prophesied until the offering up of the offering.”

The Old Greek translation and Syriac Peshitta include the following words here: “When it was time to offer the sacrifice, Elijah the Tishbite spoke to the prophets of the abominations: ‘Stand aside for the time being, and I will offer my burnt offering.’ So they stood aside and departed.”
In 2 Kgs 4:31 the words “there was no sound and there was no response” are used to describe a dead boy. Similar words are used here to describe the god Baal as dead and therefore unresponsive.

30.text: Elijah then told all the people, “Approach me.” So all the people approached him. He repaired the altar of the Lord that had been torn down.

notes.text: Torn down. The condition of the altar symbolizes the spiritual state of the people.

31.text: Then Elijah took twelve stones, corresponding to the number of tribes that descended from Jacob, to whom the Lord’s message had come, “Israel will be your name.”

notes.text: Israel will be your name. See Gen 32:28; 35:10.

32.text: With the stones he constructed an altar for the Lord. Around the altar he made a trench large enough to contain two seahs of seed.

notes.text: Heb “and he built the stones into an altar in the name of the Lord.”
A seah was a dry measure equivalent to about seven quarts.

33.text: He arranged the wood, cut up the bull, and placed it on the wood. Then he said, “Fill four water jars and pour the water on the offering and the wood.”

34.text: When they had done so, he said, “Do it again.” So they did it again. Then he said, “Do it a third time.” So they did it a third time.

notes.text: The words “when they had done so” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

35.text: The water flowed down all sides of the altar and filled the trench.

36.text: When it was time for the evening offering, Elijah the prophet approached the altar and prayed: “O Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, prove today that you are God in Israel and that I am your servant and have done all these things at your command.

notes.text: Heb “at the offering up of the offering.”
The words “the altar” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “let it be known.”

37.text: Answer me, O Lord, answer me, so these people will know that you, O Lord, are the true God and that you are winning back their allegiance.”

notes.text: Heb “the God.”
Heb “that you are turning their heart[s] back.”

38.text: Then fire from the Lord fell from the sky. It consumed the offering, the wood, the stones, and the dirt, and licked up the water in the trench.

notes.text: The words “from the sky” are added for stylistic reasons.

39.text: When all the people saw this, they threw themselves down with their faces to the ground and said, “The Lord is the true God! The Lord is the true God!”

notes.text: Heb “the God” (the phrase occurs twice in this verse).

40.text: Elijah told them, “Seize the prophets of Baal! Don’t let even one of them escape!” So they seized them, and Elijah led them down to the Kishon Valley and executed them there.

notes.text: Or “slaughtered.”

41.text: Then Elijah told Ahab, “Go on up and eat and drink, for the sound of a heavy rainstorm can be heard.”

notes.text: Heb “for [there is] the sound of the roar of the rain.”

42.text: So Ahab went on up to eat and drink, while Elijah climbed to the top of Carmel. He bent down toward the ground and put his face between his knees.

43.text: He told his servant, “Go on up and look in the direction of the sea.” So he went on up, looked, and reported, “There is nothing.” Seven times Elijah sent him to look.

notes.text: So he went on up, looked, and reported, “There is nothing.” Several times in this chapter those addressed by Elijah obey his orders. In vv. 20 and 42 Ahab does as instructed, in vv. 26 and 28 the prophets follow Elijah’s advice, and in vv. 30, 34, 40 and 43 the people and servants do as they are told. By juxtaposing Elijah’s commands with accounts of those commands being obeyed, the narrator emphasizes the authority of the Lord’s prophet.
Heb “He said, ‘Return,’ seven times.”

44.text: The seventh time the servant said, “Look, a small cloud, the size of the palm of a man’s hand, is rising up from the sea.” Elijah then said, “Go and tell Ahab, ‘Hitch up the chariots and go down, so that the rain won’t overtake you.’”

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (the servant) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “he”; the referent (Elijah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “so that the rain won’t restrain you.”

45.text: Meanwhile the sky was covered with dark clouds, the wind blew, and there was a heavy rainstorm. Ahab rode toward Jezreel.

notes.text: Heb “rode and went to.”

46.text: Now the Lord energized Elijah with power; he tucked his robe into his belt and ran ahead of Ahab all the way to Jezreel.

notes.text: Heb “and the hand of the Lord was on Elijah.”
Heb “and girded up his loins.” The idea is that of gathering up the robes and tucking them into the sash or belt so that they do not get in the way of the legs when running (or working or fighting).

1.text: Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, including a detailed account of how he killed all the prophets with the sword.

2.text: Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah with this warning, “May the gods judge me severely if by this time tomorrow I do not take your life as you did theirs!”

notes.text: Heb “saying.”
Heb “So may the gods do to me, and so may they add.”
Heb “I do not make your life like the life of one of them.”

3.text: Elijah was afraid, so he got up and fled for his life to Beer Sheba in Judah. He left his servant there,

notes.text: The MT has “and he saw,” but some medieval Hebrew mss as well as several ancient versions support the reading “he was afraid.” The consonantal text (‏וַיַּרְא‎, vayyarʾ) is ambiguous and can be vocalized ‏וַיַּרְא‎ (from ‏רָאָה‎, raʾah, “to see”) or ‏וַיִּרָא‎ (vayyiraʾ, from ‏יָרֵא‎, yareʾ, “to fear”).

4.text: while he went a day’s journey into the wilderness. He went and sat down under a shrub and asked the Lord to take his life: “I’ve had enough! Now, O Lord, take my life. After all, I’m no better than my ancestors.”

notes.text: Or “broom tree” (also in v. 5).
Heb “and asked with respect to his life to die.”
Heb “fathers.”

5.text: He stretched out and fell asleep under the shrub. Suddenly an angelic messenger touched him and said, “Get up and eat.”

notes.text: Or “lay down.”
Heb “Look, this messenger.”

6.text: He looked and right there by his head was a cake baking on hot coals and a jug of water. He ate and drank and then slept some more.

notes.text: Heb “and again lay down.”

7.text: The angel of the Lord came back again, touched him, and said, “Get up and eat, for otherwise you won’t be able to make the journey.”

notes.text: Heb “for the journey is too great for you.”

8.text: So he got up and ate and drank. That meal gave him the strength to travel forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God.

9.text: He went into a cave there and spent the night. Suddenly the Lord’s message came to him, “Why are you here, Elijah?”

10.text: He answered, “I have been absolutely loyal to the Lord God of Heaven’s Armies, even though the Israelites have abandoned the covenant they made with you, torn down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I alone am left and now they want to take my life.”

notes.text: Or “very zealous.” The infinitive absolute preceding the finite verb emphasizes the degree of his zeal and allegiance.
Traditionally, “the God of hosts.”
Heb “abandoned your covenant.”
Heb “and they are seeking my life to take it.”

11.text: The Lord said, “Go out and stand on the mountain before the Lord. Look, the Lord is ready to pass by.” A very powerful wind went before the Lord, digging into the mountain and causing landslides, but the Lord was not in the wind. After the windstorm there was an earthquake, but the Lord was not in the earthquake.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “tearing away the mountains and breaking the cliffs” (or perhaps, “breaking the stones”).

12.text: After the earthquake, there was a fire, but the Lord was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a soft whisper.

notes.text: Heb “a voice, calm, soft.”

13.text: When Elijah heard it, he covered his face with his robe and went out and stood at the entrance to the cave. Suddenly a voice asked him, “Why are you here, Elijah?”

notes.text: Heb “look.”

14.text: He answered, “I have been absolutely loyal to the Lord God of Heaven’s Armies, even though the Israelites have abandoned the covenant they made with you, torn down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I alone am left and now they want to take my life.”

notes.text: Or “very zealous.” The infinitive absolute preceding the finite verb emphasizes the degree of his zeal and allegiance.
Traditionally, “the God of hosts.”
Heb “and they are seeking my life to take it.”

15.text: The Lord said to him, “Go back the way you came and then head for the wilderness of Damascus. Go and anoint Hazael king over Syria.

16.text: You must anoint Jehu son of Nimshi king over Israel, and Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel Meholah to take your place as prophet.

17.text: Jehu will kill anyone who escapes Hazael’s sword, and Elisha will kill anyone who escapes Jehu’s sword.

18.text: I still have left in Israel 7,000 followers who have not bowed their knees to Baal or kissed the images of him.”

notes.text: Heb “I have kept in Israel 7,000, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal, and all the mouths that have not kissed him.”

19.text: Elijah went from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat. He was plowing with twelve pairs of oxen; he was near the twelfth pair. Elijah passed by him and threw his robe over him.

20.text: He left the oxen, ran after Elijah, and said, “Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye, then I will follow you.” Elijah said to him, “Go back! Indeed, what have I done to you?”

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Elijah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

21.text: Elisha went back and took his pair of oxen and slaughtered them. He cooked the meat over a fire that he made by burning the harness and yoke. He gave the people meat and they ate. Then he got up and followed Elijah and became his assistant.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Elisha) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “and with the equipment of the oxen he cooked them, the flesh.”

1.text: Now King Ben Hadad of Syria assembled all his army, along with thirty-two other kings with their horses and chariots. He marched against Samaria and besieged and attacked it.

notes.text: Heb “and he went up and besieged Samaria and fought against it.”

2.text: He sent messengers to King Ahab of Israel, who was in the city. He said to him, “This is what Ben Hadad says:

notes.text: Heb “to the city.”

3.text: ‘Your silver and your gold are mine, as well as the best of your wives and sons.’”

4.text: The king of Israel replied, “It is just as you say, my master, O king. I and all I own belong to you.”

5.text: The messengers came again and said, “This is what Ben Hadad says: ‘I sent this message to you, “You must give me your silver, gold, wives, and sons.”

6.text: But now at this time tomorrow I will send my servants to you and they will search through your palace and your servants’ houses. They will carry away all your valuables.’”

notes.text: Heb “all that is desirable to your eyes they will put in their hand and take.”

7.text: The king of Israel summoned all the leaders of the land and said, “Notice how this man is looking for trouble. Indeed, he demanded my wives, sons, silver, and gold, and I did not resist him.”

notes.text: Heb “elders.”
Heb “Know and see that this [man] is seeking trouble.”

8.text: All the leaders and people said to him, “Do not give in or agree to his demands.”

notes.text: Heb “Do not listen and do not be willing.”

9.text: So he said to the messengers of Ben Hadad, “Say this to my master, the king: ‘I will give you everything you demanded at first from your servant, but I am unable to agree to this latest demand.’” So the messengers went back and gave their report.

notes.text: Heb “all which you sent to your servant in the beginning I will do, but this thing I am unable to do.”

10.text: Ben Hadad sent another message to him, “May the gods judge me severely if there is enough dirt left in Samaria for all my soldiers to scoop up in their hands.”

notes.text: Heb “So may the gods do to me, and so may they add.”
Heb “if the dirt of Samaria suffices for the handfuls of all the people who are at my feet.”

11.text: The king of Israel replied, “Tell him the one who puts on his battle gear should not boast like one who is taking it off.”

notes.text: The point of the saying is that someone who is still preparing for a battle should not boast as if he has already won the battle. A modern parallel would be, “Don’t count your chickens before they’re hatched.”

12.text: When Ben Hadad received this reply, he and the other kings were drinking in their quarters. He ordered his servants, “Get ready to attack!” So they got ready to attack the city.

notes.text: Heb “When he heard this word.”
Heb “in the temporary shelters.” This is probably referring to tents.

13.text: Now a prophet visited King Ahab of Israel and said, “This is what the Lord has said: ‘Do you see this huge army? Look, I am going to hand it over to you this very day. Then you will know that I am the Lord.’”

notes.text: Heb “see all this great horde.”

14.text: Ahab asked, “By whom will this be accomplished?” He answered, “This is what the Lord has said, ‘By the servants of the district governors.’” Ahab asked, “Who will launch the attack?” He answered, “You will.”

notes.text: The words “will this be accomplished” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “he”; the referent (Ahab) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

15.text: So Ahab assembled the 232 servants of the district governors. After that he assembled all the Israelite army, numbering 7,000.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Ahab) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

16.text: They marched out at noon, while Ben Hadad and the 32 kings allied with him were drinking heavily in their quarters.

notes.text: Heb “drinking and drunken.”
Heb “in the temporary shelters.” This is probably referring to tents.

17.text: The servants of the district governors led the march. When Ben Hadad sent messengers, they reported back to him, “Men are marching out of Samaria.”

18.text: He ordered, “Whether they come in peace or to do battle, take them alive.”

notes.text: Heb “if they come in peace, take them alive; if they come for battle, take them alive.”

19.text: They marched out of the city with the servants of the district governors in the lead and the army behind them.

20.text: Each one struck down an enemy soldier; the Syrians fled and Israel chased them. King Ben Hadad of Syria escaped on horseback with some horsemen.

notes.text: Heb “each struck down his man.”

21.text: Then the king of Israel marched out and struck down the horses and chariots; he thoroughly defeated Syria.

notes.text: Heb “struck down Aram with a great striking down.”

22.text: The prophet visited the king of Israel and instructed him, “Go, fortify your defenses. Determine what you must do, for in the spring the king of Syria will attack you.”

notes.text: The definite article indicates previous reference, that is, “the prophet mentioned earlier” (see v. 13).
Heb “strengthen yourself.”
Heb “know and see.”
Heb “at the turning of the year.”
Heb “go up against.”

23.text: Now the advisers of the king of Syria said to him: “Their God is a god of the mountains. That’s why they overpowered us. But if we fight them in the plains, we will certainly overpower them.

notes.text: Or “servants.”

24.text: So do this: Dismiss the kings from their command, and replace them with military commanders.

25.text: Muster an army like the one you lost, with the same number of horses and chariots. Then we will fight them in the plains; we will certainly overpower them.” He approved their plan and did as they advised.

notes.text: Heb “And you, you muster an army like the one that fell from you, horse like horse and chariot like chariot.”
Heb “he listened to their voice and did so.”

26.text: In the spring Ben Hadad mustered the Syrian army and marched to Aphek to fight Israel.

notes.text: Heb “at the turning of the year.”
Heb “mustered Aram.”
Heb “and went up to Aphek for battle with Israel.”

27.text: When the Israelites had mustered and received their supplies, they marched out to face them in battle. When the Israelites deployed opposite them, they were like two small flocks of goats, but the Syrians filled the land.

notes.text: The noun translated “small flocks” occurs only here. The common interpretation derives the word from the verbal root ‏חשׂף‎, “to strip off; to make bare.” In this case the noun refers to something “stripped off” or “made bare.” HALOT 359 s.v. II ‏חשׂף‎ derives the noun from a proposed homonymic verbal root (which occurs only in Ps 29:9) meaning “cause a premature birth.” In this case the derived noun could refer to goats that are undersized because they are born prematurely.

28.text: The prophet visited the king of Israel and said, “This is what the Lord has said: ‘Because the Syrians said, “The Lord is a god of the mountains and not a god of the valleys,” I will deliver this entire huge army into to your control. Then you will know that I am the Lord.’

notes.text: Heb “the man of God.”

29.text: The armies were deployed opposite each other for seven days. On the seventh day the battle began, and the Israelites killed 100,000 Syrian foot soldiers in one day.

30.text: The remaining 27,000 ran to Aphek and went into the city, but the wall fell on them. Now Ben Hadad ran into the city and hid in an inner room.

notes.text: Heb “and the remaining ones fled to Aphek to the city and the wall fell on 27,000 men, the ones who remained.”
Heb “and Ben Hadad fled and went into the city, [into] an inner room in an inner room.”

31.text: His advisers said to him, “Look, we have heard that the kings of the Israelite dynasty are kind. Allow us to put sackcloth around our waists and ropes on our heads and surrender to the king of Israel. Maybe he will spare our lives.”

notes.text: Or “servants.”

Heb “that the kings of the house of Israel, that kings of kindness [are] they.” Or “merciful” rather than “kind.” The word used here often means “devoted” or “loyal.” Perhaps the idea is that the Israelite kings are willing to make treaties with other kings.

Sackcloth was worn as a sign of sorrow and repentance. The precise significance of the ropes on the head is uncertain, but it probably was a sign of submission. These actions were comparable to raising a white flag on the battlefield or throwing in the towel in a boxing match.
Heb “go out.”

32.text: So they put sackcloth around their waists and ropes on their heads and went to the king of Israel. They said, “Your servant Ben Hadad says, ‘Please let me live!’” Ahab replied, “Is he still alive? He is my brother.”

notes.text: Your servant. By referring to Ben Hadad as Ahab’s servant, they are suggesting that Ahab make him a subject in a vassal treaty arrangement.
Heb “he”; the referent (Ahab) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
He is my brother. Ahab’s response indicates that he wants to make a parity treaty and treat Ben Hadad as an equal partner.

33.text: The men took this as a good omen and quickly accepted his offer, saying, “Ben Hadad is your brother.” Ahab then said, “Go, get him.” So Ben Hadad came out to him, and Ahab pulled him up into his chariot.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Ahab) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

34.text: Ben Hadad said, “I will return the cities my father took from your father. You may set up markets in Damascus, just as my father did in Samaria.” Ahab then said, “I want to make a treaty with you before I dismiss you.” So he made a treaty with him and then dismissed him.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Ben Hadad) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “streets,” but this must refer to streets set up with stalls for merchants to sell their goods. See HALOT 299 s.v. ‏חוּץ‎.

Heb “I will send you away with a treaty.” The words “Ahab then said” are supplied in the translation. There is nothing in the Hebrew text to indicate that the speaker has changed from Ben Hadad to Ahab. Some suggest adding “and he said” before “I will send you away.” Others prefer to maintain Ben Hadad as the speaker and change the statement to, “Please send me away with a treaty.”

35.text: One of the members of the prophetic guild told his companion a message from the Lord, “Please wound me!” But the man refused to wound him.

notes.text: Heb “of the sons of the prophets.”

36.text: So the prophet said to him, “Because you have disobeyed the Lord, as soon as you leave me a lion will kill you.” When he left him, a lion attacked and killed him.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (the prophet) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

37.text: He found another man and said, “Wound me!” So the man wounded him severely.

notes.text: Heb “and the man wounded him, wounding and bruising.”

38.text: The prophet then went and stood by the road, waiting for the king. He also disguised himself by putting a bandage down over his eyes.

39.text: When the king passed by, he called out to the king, “Your servant went out into the heat of the battle, and then a man turned aside and brought me a prisoner. He told me, ‘Guard this prisoner. If he ends up missing for any reason, you will pay with your life or with a talent of silver.’

notes.text: Heb “middle.”
Heb “man” (also a second time later in this verse).
Heb “if being missed, he is missed.” The emphatic infinitive absolute before the finite verbal form lends solemnity to the warning.

The Hebrew term ‏כִּכָּר‎ (kikkar, “circle”) refers generally to something that is round. When used of metals it can refer to a disk-shaped weight made of the metal or to a standard unit of weight, generally regarded as a talent. Since the accepted weight for a talent of metal is about 75 pounds, this would have amounted to about 75 pounds of silver.
Heb “your life will be in place of his life, or a unit of silver you will pay.”

40.text: Well, it just so happened that while your servant was doing this and that, he disappeared.” The king of Israel said to him, “Your punishment is already determined by your own testimony.”

notes.text: Heb “so [i.e., in accordance with his testimony] is your judgment, you have determined [it].”

41.text: The prophet quickly removed the bandage from his eyes, and the king of Israel recognized he was one of the prophets.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (the prophet) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

42.text: The prophet then said to him, “This is what the Lord has said: ‘Because you released a man I had determined should die, you will pay with your life, and your people will suffer instead of his people.’”

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (the prophet) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Heb “Because you sent away the man of my destruction [i.e., that I determined should be destroyed] from [my/your?] hand, your life will be in place of his life, and your people in place of his people.”

43.text: The king of Israel went home to Samaria bitter and angry.

1.text: After this the following episode took place. Naboth the Jezreelite owned a vineyard in Jezreel adjacent to the palace of King Ahab of Samaria.

notes.text: Heb “after these things.” The words “the following episode took place” are added for stylistic reasons.
King Ahab of Samaria. Samaria, as the capital of the northern kingdom, here stands for the nation of Israel.

2.text: Ahab said to Naboth, “Give me your vineyard so I can make a vegetable garden out of it, for it is adjacent to my palace. I will give you an even better vineyard in its place, or if you prefer, I will pay you silver for it.”

notes.text: Heb “if it is good in your eyes.”
The Old Greek translation includes the following words: “And it will be mine as a garden of herbs.”

3.text: But Naboth replied to Ahab, “The Lord forbid that I should sell you my ancestral inheritance.”

notes.text: Heb “Far be it from me, by the Lord, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers to you.”

4.text: So Ahab went into his palace, bitter and angry that Naboth the Jezreelite had said, “I will not sell to you my ancestral inheritance.” He lay down on his bed, pouted, and would not eat.

notes.text: Heb “on account of the word that Naboth the Jezreelite spoke to him and he said.”
Heb “I will not give to you the inheritance of my fathers.”
Heb “turned away his face.”

5.text: Then his wife Jezebel came in and said to him, “Why do you have a bitter attitude and refuse to eat?”

6.text: He answered her, “While I was talking to Naboth the Jezreelite, I said to him, ‘Sell me your vineyard for silver, or if you prefer, I will give you another vineyard in its place.’ But he said, ‘I will not sell you my vineyard.’”

notes.text: Heb “While I was talking…, I said…, he said….” Ahab’s explanation is one lengthy sentence in the Hebrew text, which is divided in the English translation for stylistic reasons.

7.text: His wife Jezebel said to him, “You are the king of Israel! Get up, eat some food, and have a good time. I will get the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite for you.”

notes.text: Heb “You, now, you are exercising kingship over Israel.”
Heb “so your heart [i.e., disposition] might be well.”

8.text: She wrote out orders, signed Ahab’s name to them, and sealed them with his seal. She then sent the orders to the leaders and to the nobles who lived in Naboth’s city.

notes.text: Heb “scrolls.”
Heb “in the name of Ahab.”
Heb “scrolls.”
Heb “elders.”
Heb “to the nobles who were in his city, the ones who lived with Naboth.”

9.text: This is what she wrote: “Observe a time of fasting and seat Naboth in front of the people.

notes.text: Heb “she wrote on the scrolls, saying.”

10.text: Also seat two villains opposite him and have them testify, ‘You cursed God and the king.’ Then take him out and stone him to death.”

11.text: The men of the city, the leaders, and the nobles who lived there followed the written orders Jezebel had sent them.

notes.text: Heb “his.”
Heb “elders.”
Heb “and the nobles who were living in his city.”
Heb “did as Jezebel sent to them, just as was written in the scrolls which she sent to them.”

12.text: They observed a time of fasting and put Naboth in front of the people.

13.text: The two villains arrived and sat opposite him. Then the villains testified against Naboth right before the people, saying, “Naboth cursed God and the king.” So they dragged him outside the city and stoned him to death.

notes.text: Heb “led him.”
Heb “and they stoned him with stones and he died.”

14.text: Then they reported to Jezebel, “Naboth has been stoned to death.”

notes.text: Heb “Naboth was stoned and he died.” So also in v. 15.

15.text: When Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned to death, she said to Ahab, “Get up, take possession of the vineyard Naboth the Jezreelite refused to sell you for silver, for Naboth is no longer alive; he’s dead.”

notes.text: Heb “Jezebel”; the proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“she”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.

16.text: When Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, he got up and went down to take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.

notes.text: The Old Greek translation includes the following words here: “he tore his garments and put on sackcloth. After these things.”

17.text: The Lord’s message came to Elijah the Tishbite:

18.text: “Get up, go down and meet King Ahab of Israel who lives in Samaria. He is at the vineyard of Naboth; he has gone down there to take possession of it.

19.text: Say to him, ‘This is what the Lord has said: “Haven’t you committed murder and taken possession of the property of the deceased?”’ Then say to him, ‘This is what the Lord has said: “In the spot where dogs licked up Naboth’s blood they will also lick up your blood—yes, yours!”’”

notes.text: The words “of the property of the deceased” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

20.text: When Elijah arrived, Ahab said to him, “So, you have found me, my enemy!” Elijah replied, “I have found you, because you are committed to doing evil in the sight of the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “and Ahab said to Elijah.” The narrative is elliptical and streamlined. The words “when Elijah arrived” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “he”; the referent (Elijah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “you have sold yourself.”
Heb “in the eyes of.”

21.text: The Lord says, ‘Look, I am ready to bring disaster on you. I will destroy you and cut off every last male belonging to Ahab in Israel, including even the weak and incapacitated.

notes.text: The introductory formula “the Lord says” is omitted in the Hebrew text, but supplied in the translation for clarification.

Disaster. There is a wordplay in the Hebrew text. The word translated “disaster” (‏רָעָה‎, raʿah) is similar to the word translated “evil” (v. 20, ‏הָרַע‎, haraʿ). Ahab’s sins would receive an appropriate punishment.
Heb “I will burn after you.” Some take the verb ‏בָּעַר‎ (baʿar) to mean here “sweep away.” See the discussion of this verb in the notes at 14:10 and 16:3.

Heb “and I will cut off from Ahab those who urinate against a wall, [including both those who are] restrained and let free [or “abandoned”] in Israel.” The precise meaning of the idiomatic phrase ‏עָצוּר וְעָזוּב‎ (ʿatsur veʿazuv, translated here “weak and incapacitated”) is uncertain. For various options see HALOT 871 s.v. ‏עצר‎ and M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 107.
