So he ordered the bones from the tombs to be brought; he burned them on the altar and defiled it, just as in the Lord’s message that was announced by the prophet while Jeroboam stood by the altar during a festival. Then the king turned and saw the grave of the prophet who had foretold this.

notes.text: Heb “and he sent and took the bones from the tombs.”

The MT is much shorter than this. It reads, “according to the word of the Lord which the man of God proclaimed, who proclaimed these words.” The LXX has a much longer text at this point. It reads: “[which was proclaimed by the man of God] while Jeroboam stood by the altar at a celebration. Then he turned and saw the grave of the man of God [who proclaimed these words].” The extra material attested in the LXX was probably accidentally omitted in the Hebrew tradition when a scribe’s eye jumped from the first occurrence of the phrase “man of God” (which appears right before the extra material) and the second occurrence of the phrase (which appears at the end of the extra material).
This recalls the prophecy recorded in 1 Kgs 13:2.

17.text: He asked, “What is this grave marker I see?” The men from the city replied, “It’s the grave of the prophet who came from Judah and foretold these very things you have done to the altar of Bethel.”

notes.text: Heb “man of God.”

18.text: The king said, “Leave it alone! No one must touch his bones.” So they left his bones undisturbed, as well as the bones of the Israelite prophet buried beside him.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (the king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Heb “and they left undisturbed his bones, the bones of the prophet who came from Samaria.” If the phrase “the bones of the prophet” were appositional to “his bones,” one would expect the sentence to end “from Judah” (see v. 17). Apparently the “prophet” referred to in the second half of the verse is the old prophet from Bethel who buried the man of God from Judah in his own tomb and instructed his sons to bury his bones there as well (1 Kgs 13:30-31). One expects the text to read “from Bethel,” but “Samaria” (which was not even built at the time of the incident recorded in 1 Kgs 13) is probably an anachronistic reference to the northern kingdom in general. See the note at 1 Kgs 13:32 and the discussion in M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 290.

19.text: Josiah also removed all the shrines on the high places in the cities of Samaria. The kings of Israel had made them and angered the Lord. He did to them what he had done to the high place in Bethel.

notes.text: Heb “which the kings of Israel had made, angering.” The object has been accidentally omitted in the MT. It appears in the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate versions.
Heb “and he did to them according to all the deeds he had done in Bethel.”

20.text: He sacrificed all the priests of the high places on the altars located there, and burned human bones on them. Then he returned to Jerusalem.

21.text: The king ordered all the people, “Observe the Passover of the Lord your God, as prescribed in this scroll of the covenant.”

22.text: He issued this edict because a Passover like this had not been observed since the days of the judges who led Israel; it was neglected for the entire period of the kings of Israel and Judah.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has simply “because.” The translation attempts to reflect more clearly the logical connection between the king’s order and the narrator’s observation. Another option is to interpret ‏כִּי‎ (ki) as asseverative and translate, “indeed.”
Heb “because there had not been observed [one] like this Passover from the days of the judges who judged Israel and all the days of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah.”

23.text: But in the eighteenth year of King Josiah’s reign, such a Passover of the Lord was observed in Jerusalem.

24.text: Josiah also got rid of the ritual pits used to conjure up spirits, the magicians, personal idols, disgusting images, and all the detestable idols that had appeared in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem. In this way he carried out the terms of the law recorded on the scroll that Hilkiah the priest had discovered in the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: Here ‏בִּעֵר‎ (biʿer) is not the well attested verb “burn,” but the less common homonym meaning “devastate, sweep away, remove.” See HALOT 146 s.v. ‏בער‎.
See the note at 2 Kgs 21:6.
See the note at 1 Kgs 15:12.
Heb “carrying out the words of the law.”

25.text: No king before or after repented before the Lord as he did, with his whole heart, soul, and being in accordance with the whole law of Moses.

notes.text: Heb “and like him there was not a king before him who returned to the Lord with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his being according to all the law of Moses, and after him none arose like him.”
The description of Josiah’s devotion as involving his whole “heart, soul, and being” echoes the language of Deut 6:5.

26.text: Yet the Lord’s great anger against Judah did not subside; he was still infuriated by all the things Manasseh had done.

notes.text: Heb “Yet the Lord did not turn away from the fury of his great anger, because his anger raged against Judah on account of all the infuriating things by which Manasseh had made him angry.”

27.text: The Lord announced, “I will also spurn Judah, just as I spurned Israel. I will reject this city that I chose—both Jerusalem and the temple, about which I said, ‘I will live there.’

notes.text: Heb “Also Judah I will turn away from my face.”
Heb “My name will be there.”

28.text: The rest of the events of Josiah’s reign and all his accomplishments are recorded in the scroll called the Annals of the Kings of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Josiah, and all which he did, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Judah?”

29.text: During Josiah’s reign Pharaoh Necho king of Egypt marched toward the Euphrates River to help the king of Assyria. King Josiah marched out to fight him, but Necho killed him at Megiddo when he saw him.

notes.text: Heb “In his days.”
Heb “went up to.” The idiom ‏עַל‎…‏עָלָה‎ (ʿalah…ʿal) can sometimes mean “go up against,” but here it refers to Necho’s attempt to aid the Assyrians in their struggle with the Babylonians.
Heb “he”; the referent (Necho) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

30.text: His servants transported his dead body from Megiddo in a chariot and brought it to Jerusalem, where they buried him in his tomb. The people of the land took Josiah’s son Jehoahaz, poured olive oil on his head, and made him king in his father’s place.

notes.text: Heb “him, dead.”
Or “anointed him.”

31.text: Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. His mother was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah.

notes.text: Heb “the name of his mother.”

32.text: He did evil in the sight of the Lord as his ancestors had done.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”
Heb “according to all that his fathers had done.”

33.text: Pharaoh Necho imprisoned him in Riblah in the land of Hamath and prevented him from ruling in Jerusalem. He imposed on the land a special tax of 100 talents of silver and a talent of gold.

notes.text: The consonantal text (Kethib) has “when [he was] ruling in Jerusalem,” but the marginal reading (Qere), which has support from Hebrew, Greek, Aramaic, and Latin witnesses, has “[preventing him] from ruling in Jerusalem.”
Or “fine.”

The Hebrew term ‏כִּכָּר‎ (kikkar, “circle”) refers generally to something that is round. When used of metals it can refer to a disk-shaped weight made of the metal or to a standard unit of weight, generally regarded as a talent. Since the accepted weight for a talent of metal is about 75 pounds, this would have amounted to about 7,500 pounds of silver and 75 pounds of gold (cf. NCV, NLT); CEV “almost four tons of silver and about seventy-five pounds of gold.”

34.text: Pharaoh Necho made Josiah’s son Eliakim king in Josiah’s place, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. He took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died.

notes.text: Heb “and he took Jehoahaz, and he came to Egypt and he died there.”

35.text: Jehoiakim paid Pharaoh the required amount of silver and gold, but to meet Pharaoh’s demands Jehoiakim had to tax the land. He collected an assessed amount from each man among the people of the land in order to pay Pharaoh Necho.

notes.text: Heb “And the silver and the gold Jehoiakim gave to Pharaoh, but he taxed the land to give the silver at the command of Pharaoh, [from] each according to his tax he collected the silver and the gold, from the people of the land, to give to Pharaoh Necho.”

36.text: Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned for eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother was Zebidah the daughter of Pedaiah, from Rumah.

notes.text: Heb “the name of his mother.”

37.text: He did evil in the sight of the Lord as his ancestors had done.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”

1.text: During Jehoiakim’s reign, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon attacked. Jehoiakim was his subject for three years, but then he rebelled against him.

notes.text: Heb “In his days.”
Heb “came up.” Perhaps an object (“against him”) has been accidentally omitted from the text. See M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 306.
The Hebrew text has “and he turned and rebelled against him.”

2.text: The Lord sent against him Babylonian, Syrian, Moabite, and Ammonite raiding bands; he sent them to destroy Judah, just as in the Lord’s message that he had announced through his servants the prophets.

3.text: Just as the Lord had announced, he rejected Judah because of all the sins that Manasseh had committed.

notes.text: Heb “Certainly according to the word of the Lord this happened against Judah, to remove [them] from his face because of the sins of Manasseh according to all which he did.”

4.text: Because he killed innocent people and stained Jerusalem with their blood, the Lord was unwilling to forgive them.

notes.text: Heb “and also the blood of the innocent which he shed, and he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the Lord was not willing to forgive.”

5.text: The rest of the events of Jehoiakim’s reign and all his accomplishments, are recorded in the scroll called the Annals of the Kings of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Jehoiakim, and all which he did, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Judah?”

6.text: He passed away and his son Jehoiachin replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”

7.text: The king of Egypt did not march out from his land again, for the king of Babylon conquered all the territory that the king of Egypt had formerly controlled between the Stream of Egypt and the Euphrates River.

8.text: Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. His mother was Nehushta the daughter of Elnathan, from Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “the name of his mother.”

9.text: He did evil in the sight of the Lord as his ancestors had done.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”

10.text: At that time the generals of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon marched to Jerusalem and besieged the city.

notes.text: Heb “servants.”
Heb “went up [to] Jerusalem and the city entered into siege.”

11.text: King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon came to the city while his generals were besieging it.

12.text: King Jehoiachin of Judah, along with his mother, his servants, his officials, and his eunuchs surrendered to the king of Babylon. The king of Babylon, in the eighth year of his reign, took Jehoiachin prisoner.

notes.text: Heb “came out.”
That is, the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, 597 b.c.
Heb “him”; the referent (Jehoiachin) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

13.text: Nebuchadnezzar took from there all the riches in the treasuries of the Lord’s temple and of the royal palace. He removed all the gold items that King Solomon of Israel had made for the Lord’s temple, just as the Lord had warned.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Nebuchadnezzar) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

14.text: He deported all the residents of Jerusalem, including all the officials and all the soldiers (10,000 people in all). This included all the craftsmen and those who worked with metal. No one was left except for the poorest among the people of the land.

15.text: He deported Jehoiachin from Jerusalem to Babylon, along with the king’s mother and wives, his eunuchs, and the high-ranking officials of the land.

notes.text: Heb “and he deported Jehoiachin to Babylon; the mother of the king and the wives of the king and his eunuchs and the mighty of the land he led into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon.”

16.text: The king of Babylon deported to Babylon all the soldiers (there were 7,000), as well as 1,000 craftsmen and metal workers. This included all the best warriors.

notes.text: Heb “the entire [group], mighty men, doers of war.”

17.text: The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s uncle, king in Jehoiachin’s place. He renamed him Zedekiah.

notes.text: Heb “his.”

18.text: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he ruled for eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah.

notes.text: Heb “the name of his mother.”
Some textual witnesses support the consonantal text (Kethib) in reading “Hamital.”

19.text: He did evil in the sight of the Lord, as Jehoiakim had done.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”
Heb “according to all which Jehoiakim had done.”

20.text: Nebuzaradan, captain of the royal guard, took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.

1.text: So King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon came against Jerusalem with his whole army and set up camp outside it. They built siege ramps all around it. He arrived on the tenth day of the tenth month in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign.

notes.text: Or “against.”
This would have been Jan 15, 588 b.c. The reckoning is based on the calendar that begins the year in the spring (Nisan = March/April).

2.text: The city remained under siege until King Zedekiah’s eleventh year.

3.text: By the ninth day of the fourth month the famine in the city was so severe the residents had no food.

notes.text: The MT has simply “of the month,” but the parallel passage in Jer 52:6 has “fourth month,” and this is followed by almost all English translations. The word “fourth,” however, is not actually present in the MT of 2 Kgs 25:3.
According to modern reckoning that would have been July 18, 586 b.c. The siege thus lasted almost a full eighteen months.
Heb “the people of the land.”

4.text: The enemy broke through the city walls, and all the soldiers tried to escape. They left the city during the night. They went through the gate between the two walls, which is near the king’s garden. (The Babylonians were all around the city.) Then they headed for the rift valley.

notes.text: Heb “the city was breached.”
The Hebrew text is abrupt here: “And all the men of war by the night.” The translation attempts to capture the sense.

The king’s garden is mentioned again in Neh 3:15 in conjunction with the pool of Siloam and the stairs that go down from the City of David. This would have been in the southern part of the city near the Tyropean Valley which agrees with the reference to the “two walls” which were probably the walls on the eastern and western hills.

The rift valley (‏עֲרָבָה‎, ʿarabah) extends northward of the Dead Sea past Galilee and southward to the Gulf of Aqaba. Here the southern part of the Jordan Valley is in view with the intention to escape across the Jordan river to Moab or Ammon. It appears from Jer 40:14; 41:15 that the Ammonites were known to harbor fugitives from the Babylonians.

5.text: But the Babylonian army chased after the king. They caught up with him in the rift valley plains of Jericho, and his entire army deserted him.

notes.text: The rift valley plains of Jericho refer to the parts of the Jordan Valley in the vicinity of Jericho (see HALOT 880 s.v. ‏עֲרָבָה‎). There the terrain is fairly level and slopes gently down to the Jordan, a descent of about 450 feet over five miles. Many translations render this as “the plains of Jericho” (ESV, NASB, NIV, KJV). See the note at Num 22:1.

6.text: They captured the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where he passed sentence on him.

notes.text: Riblah was a strategic town on the Orontes River in Syria. It was at a crossing of the major roads between Egypt and Mesopotamia. Pharaoh Necho had earlier received Jehoahaz there and put him in chains (2 Kgs 23:33) prior to taking him captive to Egypt. Nebuchadnezzar had set up his base camp for conducting his campaigns against the Palestinian states there and was now sitting in judgment on prisoners brought to him.
The Hebrew text has the plural form of the verb, but the parallel passage in Jer 52:9 has the singular.

7.text: Zedekiah’s sons were executed while Zedekiah was forced to watch. The king of Babylon then had Zedekiah’s eyes put out, bound him in bronze chains, and carried him off to Babylon.

notes.text: Heb “were killed before his eyes.”
Heb “he”; the referent (the king of Babylon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

8.text: On the seventh day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, Nebuzaradan, the captain of the royal guard, who served the king of Babylon, arrived in Jerusalem.

notes.text: The parallel account in Jer 52:12 has “tenth.”
The seventh day of the month would have been August 14, 586 b.c. in modern reckoning.
For the meaning of this phrase see BDB 371 s.v. ‏טַבָּח‎ 2, and compare the usage in Gen 39:1.

9.text: He burned down the Lord’s temple, the royal palace, and all the houses in Jerusalem, including every large house.

notes.text: Heb “and every large house he burned down with fire.”

10.text: The whole Babylonian army that came with the captain of the royal guard tore down the walls that surrounded Jerusalem.

11.text: Nebuzaradan, the captain of the royal guard, deported the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the craftsmen.

notes.text: The MT has “the multitude.” But ‏הֶהָמוֹן‎ (hehamon) should probably be emended to ‏הֶאָמוֹן‎ (heʾamon). See Jeremiah 52:15.

12.text: But he left behind some of the poor of the land and gave them fields and vineyards.

notes.text: Heb “the captain of the royal guard.” However, the subject is clear from the preceding and contemporary English style would normally avoid repeating the proper name and title.

13.text: The Babylonians broke the two bronze pillars in the Lord’s temple, as well as the movable stands and the big bronze basin called “The Sea.” They took the bronze to Babylon.

notes.text: Heb “the bronze pillars that were in the Lord’s house and the stands and the bronze sea that were in the Lord’s house the Babylonians broke.”
See the note at 1 Kgs 7:23.

14.text: They also took the pots, shovels, trimming shears, pans, and all the bronze utensils used by the priests.

notes.text: These shovels were used to clean the altar.
These were used to trim the wicks.
Heb “with which they served [or, ‘fulfilled their duty’].”

15.text: The captain of the royal guard took the golden and silver censers and basins.

notes.text: These held the embers used for the incense offerings.

16.text: The bronze of the items that King Solomon made for the Lord’s temple—including the two pillars, the big bronze basin called “The Sea,” the twelve bronze bulls under “The Sea,” and the movable stands—was too heavy to be weighed.

notes.text: The MT lacks “the twelve bronze bulls under ‘the Sea,’” but these words have probably been accidentally omitted by homoioarcton. The scribe’s eye may have jumped from the ‏וְהָ‎ (veha) on ‏וְהַבָּקָר‎ (vehabbaqar), “and the bulls,” to the ‏וְהָ‎ on ‏וְהַמְּכֹנוֹת‎ (vehammekhonot), “and the movable stands,” causing him to leave out the intervening words. See the parallel passage in Jer 52:20.

17.text: Each of the pillars was about twenty-seven feet high. The bronze top of one pillar was about 4½ feet high and had bronze latticework and pomegranate-shaped ornaments all around it. The second pillar with its latticework was like it.

notes.text: Heb “18 cubits.” The standard cubit in the OT is assumed by most authorities to be about 18 inches (45 cm) long.
Heb “3 cubits.” The parallel passage in Jer 52:22 has “five.”

18.text: The captain of the royal guard took Seraiah, the chief priest, and Zephaniah, the priest who was second in rank, and the three doorkeepers.

19.text: From the city he took a eunuch who was in charge of the soldiers, five of the king’s advisers who were discovered in the city, an official army secretary who drafted citizens for military service, and sixty citizens from the people of the land who were discovered in the city.

notes.text: The parallel passage in Jer 52:25 has “seven.”
Heb “five men seeing the king’s face.”
Heb “the people of the land.”

21.text: The king of Babylon ordered them to be executed at Riblah in the territory of Hamath. So Judah was deported from its land.

notes.text: Heb “struck them down and killed them.”
Heb “land.”

22.text: Now King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as governor over the people whom he allowed to remain in the land of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “And the people who were left in the land of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon left, he appointed over them Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan.”

23.text: All the officers of the Judahite army and their troops heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah to govern. So they came to Gedaliah at Mizpah. The officers who came were Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah son of the Maacathite.

notes.text: Heb “of the army.” The word “Judahite” has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

24.text: Gedaliah took an oath so as to give them and their troops some assurance of safety. He said, “You don’t need to be afraid to submit to the Babylonian officials. Settle down in the land and submit to the king of Babylon. Then things will go well for you.”

notes.text: The words “so as to give them…some assurance of safety” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

25.text: But in the seventh month Ishmael son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, who was a member of the royal family, came with ten of his men and murdered Gedaliah, as well as the Judeans and Babylonians who were with him at Mizpah.

notes.text: It is not altogether clear whether this is in the same year that Jerusalem fell or not. The wall was breached in the fourth month (= early July; Jer 39:2) and Nebuzaradan came and burned the palace, the temple, and many of the houses and tore down the wall in the fifth month (= early August; Jer 52:12). That would have left time between the fifth month and the seventh month (October) to gather in the harvest of grapes, dates and figs, and olives (Jer 40:12). However, many commentators feel that too much activity takes place in too short a time for this to have been in the same year and posit that it happened the following year or even five years later when a further deportation took place, possibly in retaliation for the murder of Gedaliah and the Babylonian garrison at Mizpah (Jer 52:30). The assassination of Gedaliah had momentous consequences and was commemorated in one of the post exilic fast days lamenting the fall of Jerusalem (Zech 8:19).
Heb “[was] from the seed of the kingdom.”
Heb “and they struck down Gedaliah and he died.”

26.text: Then all the people, from the youngest to the oldest, as well as the army officers, left for Egypt, because they were afraid of what the Babylonians might do.

notes.text: Heb “arose and went to.”

27.text: In the thirty-seventh year of the exile of King Jehoiachin of Judah, on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month, King Evil Merodach of Babylon, in the first year of his reign, pardoned King Jehoiachin of Judah and released him from prison.

notes.text: The parallel account in Jer 52:31 has “twenty-fifth.”
The twenty-seventh day would be March 22, 561 b.c. in modern reckoning.
Heb “lifted up the head of.”
The words “released him” are supplied in the translation on the basis of Jer 52:31.

28.text: He spoke kindly to him and gave him a more prestigious position than the other kings who were with him in Babylon.

notes.text: Heb “made his throne above the throne of.”

29.text: Jehoiachin took off his prison clothes and ate daily in the king’s presence for the rest of his life.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Jehoiachin) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

30.text: He was given daily provisions by the king for the rest of his life until the day he died.

notes.text: The words “until the day he died” do not appear in the MT, but they are included in the parallel passage in Jer 52:34. Probably they have been accidentally omitted by homoioteleuton. A scribe’s eye jumped from the final vav (‏ו‎) on ‏בְּיוֹמוֹ‎ (beyomo), “in his day,” to the final vav (‏ו‎) on ‏מוֹתוֹ‎ (moto), “his death,” leaving out the intervening words.

1.text: Adam, Seth, Enosh,

2.text: Kenan, Mahalalel, Jered,

3.text: Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech,

4.text: Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

notes.text: The LXX reads “Noah; the sons of Noah [were] Shem, Ham, and Japheth.” Several English translations (e.g., NIV, NLT) follow the LXX.
Shem, Ham, and Japheth were Noah’s three sons (Gen 6:10).

5.text: The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.

6.text: The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah.

notes.text: Many medieval Hebrew mss, along with the LXX and Vulgate, read “Riphath” (see Gen 10:3). This is followed by several English translations (e.g., NAB, NIV, NLT), while others (e.g., ASV, NASB, NRSV) follow the MT reading (“Diphath”).

7.text: The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, the Kittites, and the Rodanites.

notes.text: Or in this case, “descendants.”

The Kethib has ‏רוֹדָנִים‎ (Rodanim), which probably refers to the island of Rhodes. The Qere has ‏דּוֹדָנִים‎ (Dodanim), which refers to one of the most ancient and revered locations in ancient Greece. The MT and most medieval Hebrew mss of the parallel list in Gen 10:4 read “Dodanim,” but a few have “Rodanim.”
Heb “Kittim and Rodanim.”

8.text: The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.

notes.text: That is, “Egypt.”

9.text: The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabta, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.

10.text: Cush was the father of Nimrod, who established himself as a mighty warrior on earth.

notes.text: Heb “he began to be a mighty warrior in the earth.”

11.text: Mizraim was the father of the Ludites, Anamites, Lehabites, Naphtuhites,

12.text: Pathrusites, Casluhites (from whom the Philistines descended) , and the Caphtorites.

notes.text: Heb “came forth.”

13.text: Canaan was the father of Sidon—his firstborn—and Heth,

14.text: as well as the Jebusites, Amorites, Girgashites,

15.text: Hivites, Arkites, Sinites,

16.text: Arvadites, Zemarites, and Hamathites.

17.text: The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram. The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech.

notes.text: The words “the sons of Aram” do not appear in the Hebrew text. Apparently the phrase ‏וּבְנֵי אֲרָם‎ (uvene ʾaram) has accidentally dropped out of the text by homoioteleuton (note the presence of ‏אֲרָם‎ just before this). The phrase is included in Gen 10:23.
The MT of the parallel geneaology in Gen 10:23 reads “Mash,” but the LXX there reads “Meshech” in agreement with 1 Chr 1:17.

18.text: Arphaxad was the father of Shelah, and Shelah was the father of Eber.

19.text: Two sons were born to Eber: the first was named Peleg, for during his lifetime the earth was divided; his brother’s name was Joktan.

notes.text: Perhaps this refers to the scattering of the people at Babel (Gen 11:1-9).

20.text: Joktan was the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,

21.text: Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah,

22.text: Ebal, Abimael, Sheba,

notes.text: Some medieval Hebrew mss and the Syriac read “Obal” (see Gen 10:28).

23.text: Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were the sons of Joktan.

24.text: Shem, Arphaxad, Shelah,

notes.text: Some LXX mss read “Arphaxad, Cainan, Shelah” (see also the notes on Gen 10:24; 11:12-13).

25.text: Eber, Peleg, Reu,

26.text: Serug, Nahor, Terah,

27.text: Abram (that is, Abraham).

28.text: The sons of Abraham: Isaac and Ishmael.

29.text: These were their descendants: Ishmael’s firstborn son was Nebaioth; the others were Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,

notes.text: The words “the others were” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

30.text: Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema,

31.text: Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These were the sons of Ishmael.

32.text: The sons to whom Keturah, Abraham’s concubine, gave birth: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, Shuah. The sons of Jokshan: Sheba and Dedan.

notes.text: A concubine was a slave woman in ancient Near Eastern societies who was the legal property of her master, but who could have legitimate sexual relations with her master. A concubine’s status was more elevated than a mere servant, but she was not free and did not have the legal rights of a free wife. The children of a concubine could, in some instances, become equal heirs with the children of the free wife. After the period of the Judges concubines may have become more of a royal prerogative (2 Sam 21:10-14; 1 Kgs 11:3).

33.text: The sons of Midian: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the sons of Keturah.

34.text: Abraham was the father of Isaac. The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel.

35.text: The sons of Esau: Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.

36.text: The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, Omar, Zephi, Gatam, Kenaz, and (by Timna) Amalek.

notes.text: Many medieval Hebrew mss, along with some LXX mss and the Syriac, read “Zepho” (see Gen 36:11).

The Hebrew text has simply, “and Timna and Amalek,” but Gen 36:12 indicates that Timna, a concubine of Eliphaz, was the mother of Amalek. See also v. 39 below, which states that Timna was the sister of Lotan.

37.text: The sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah.

38.text: The sons of Seir: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan.

39.text: The sons of Lotan: Hori and Homam. (Timna was Lotan’s sister.)

notes.text: Perhaps this is the Timna mentioned in v. 36.

40.text: The sons of Shobal: Alyan, Manahath, Ebal, Shephi, and Onam. The sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah.

notes.text: Some medieval Hebrew mss and a few LXX mss read “Alvan” (see Gen 36:23).
A few medieval Hebrew mss read “Shepho” (see Gen 36:23).

41.text: The son of Anah: Dishon. The sons of Dishon: Hamran, Eshban, Ithran, and Keran.

notes.text: Heb “sons.” The Hebrew text has the plural, but only one son is listed. For stylistic reasons the singular “son” was used in the translation.
The parallel geneaology in Gen 36:26 has the variant spelling “Hemdan.” Some English versions follow the variant spelling here (e.g., NAB, NIV, NCV, CEV, NLT).

42.text: The sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, Jaakan. The sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.

notes.text: The parallel geneaology in Gen 36:27 has the variant spelling “Akan.” Among English versions that use the variant spelling here are NIV, NCV, NLT.
The MT reads “Dishon” here, but this should be emended to “Dishan.” See the list in v. 38 and Gen 36:28.

43.text: These were the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king ruled over the Israelites: Bela son of Beor; the name of his city was Dinhabah.

44.text: When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah, succeeded him.

notes.text: Heb “ruled in his place,” here and in vv. 45-50.

45.text: When Jobab died, Husham from the land of the Temanites succeeded him.

46.text: When Husham died, Hadad son of Bedad succeeded him. He struck down the Midianites in the plains of Moab; the name of his city was Avith.

47.text: When Hadad died, Samlah from Masrekah succeeded him.

48.text: When Samlah died, Shaul from Rehoboth on the River succeeded him.

notes.text: Or “near the river.”
The river may refer to the Euphrates River (cf. NRSV, CEV, NLT).

49.text: When Shaul died, Baal Hanan son of Achbor succeeded him.

50.text: When Baal Hanan died, Hadad succeeded him; the name of his city was Pai. His wife was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred, daughter of Me-Zahab.

notes.text: Many medieval Hebrew mss, along with some LXX mss, the Syriac, and Vulgate, read “Pau.” See also Gen 36:39.
Heb “The name of his wife.”

51.text: Hadad died. The tribal chiefs of Edom were: Timna, Alvah, Jetheth,

52.text: Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon,

53.text: Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar,

notes.text: The parallel genealogy in Gen 36:42 has the variant spelling “Temam.”

54.text: Magdiel, and Iram. These were the tribal chiefs of Edom.

notes.text: Each of the names in this list is preceded by the word “chief” in the Hebrew text. This has not been included in the translation because it would appear very redundant to the modern reader.

1.text: These were the sons of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah; Issachar and Zebulun;

notes.text: The groupings in the list that follows, as well as the conjunctions (vav-consecutives in Hebrew), reflect those of the Hebrew text.

2.text: Dan, Joseph, and Benjamin; Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.

3.text: The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, and Shelah. These three were born to him by Bathshua, a Canaanite woman. Er, Judah’s firstborn, displeased the Lord, so the Lord killed him.

notes.text: The name means “daughter of Shua.” Shua is identified in Gen 38:2 as a “Canaanite man.”
Heb “was evil in the eyes of the Lord, so he [i.e., the Lord] killed him [i.e., Er].”

4.text: Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, bore to him Perez and Zerah. Judah had five sons in all.

notes.text: Heb “his”; the referent (Judah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

5.text: The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul.

6.text: The sons of Zerah: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Kalkol, Dara —five in all.

notes.text: Many medieval Hebrew mss, some LXX mss, and Syriac read “Darda” (see 1 Kgs 4:31 ET = 1 Kgs 5:11 HT).

7.text: The son of Carmi: Achan, who brought the disaster on Israel when he stole what was devoted to God.

notes.text: Heb “sons.” The Hebrew text has the plural, but only one son is listed.
The Hebrew text has “Achar,” which means “disaster,” but a few medieval Hebrew mss read “Achan.” See Josh 7:1.
Heb “the troubler of Israel who was unfaithful with respect to the devoted [things].”

8.text: The son of Ethan: Azariah.

notes.text: Heb “sons.” The Hebrew text has the plural, but only one son is listed.

9.text: The sons born to Hezron: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Caleb.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has “Celubai,” but see v. 18, where Caleb is described as the son of Hezron.

10.text: Ram was the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab was the father of Nahshon, the tribal chief of Judah.

11.text: Nahshon was the father of Salma, and Salma was the father of Boaz.

notes.text: The LXX reads “Salmon” (cf. Ruth 4:21) and is followed by some English versions (e.g., NIV, NCV, TEV, NLT).

12.text: Boaz was the father of Obed, and Obed was the father of Jesse.

13.text: Jesse was the father of Eliab, his firstborn; Abinadab was born second, Shimea third,

14.text: Nethanel fourth, Raddai fifth,

15.text: Ozem sixth, and David seventh.

16.text: Their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail. Zeruiah’s three sons were Abshai, Joab, and Asahel.

notes.text: In 2 Sam 2:18 this name appears as “Abishai,” a spelling followed by many English versions here.

17.text: Abigail bore Amasa, whose father was Jether the Ishmaelite.

18.text: Caleb son of Hezron fathered sons by his wife Azubah (also known as Jerioth). Her sons were Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon.

notes.text: Heb “and Caleb son of Hezron fathered [children] with Azubah, a wife, and with Jerioth.” Jerioth could be viewed as a second wife (so NLT; cf. also NASB, NIV, NRSV), but the following context mentions only “her [presumably Azubah’s] sons.” Another option, the one chosen in the translation, is that Jerioth is another name for Azubah.

19.text: When Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, who bore him Hur.

notes.text: Heb “took for himself.”

20.text: Hur was the father of Uri, and Uri was the father of Bezalel.

21.text: Later Hezron slept with the daughter of Makir, the father of Gilead. (He had married her when he was sixty years old.) She bore him Segub.

notes.text: This means “later” in relation to the births of the three sons (Jerahmeel, Ram and Caleb) mentioned in v. 9.
The expression ‏בּוֹא אֶל‎ (boʾ ʾel) means “come to” or “approach,” but is also used as a euphemism for sexual relations.
Heb “he took,” referring to taking in marriage.

22.text: Segub was the father of Jair, who owned twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead.

23.text: (Geshur and Aram captured the towns of Jair, along with Kenath and its sixty surrounding towns.) All these were descendants of Makir, the father of Gilead.

notes.text: Or “Havvoth Jair” (NIV, NRSV). Some translations do not translate the phrase (“havvoth” = “the towns of”), but treat it as part of the place name.

24.text: After Hezron’s death, Caleb slept with Ephrath, his father Hezron’s widow, and she bore to him Ashhur the father of Tekoa.

notes.text: Heb “And after the death of Hezron in Caleb Ephrathah, and the wife of Hezron, Abijah, and she bore to him Ashhur the father of Tekoa.” The translations assumes three diferences from the MT. 1) Where the MT preserves only the preposition ‏ב‎ (bet, “in”), the NET agrees with the text behind the LXX and Vulgate in reading ‏בָּא ב‎ (baʾ b-, “went to”). Caleb is thus the subject of the verb rather than an otherwise unattested place name, and Ephrath(a) is a reference to his wife (see vv. 19 and 50). A directional he on the end of Ephratha would be unusual on a personal name but the he also appears in v. 50 where it cannot be a directional he. Also the phrase ‏בָּא ב‎ is viewed as a euphemism for sexual relations, rather than a description of entering the town of Ephrath (or Bethlehem). 2) The ‏ו‎ (vav, “and”) is not read before “wife of Hezron.” 3) A ‏ו‎ (vav) is restored after ‏אֲבִיָּה‎ (ʾaviyyah, “Abijah”) to make ‏אָבִיהוּ‎ (ʾavihu, “his father”). This less common form of the noun with the suffix also occurs in 1 Chron 26:10 and 2 Chron 3:1. Thus “the wife of Hezron his father” is a descriptor of Caleb’s second wife, Ephrath. Some translations follow the MT on the first point to make Abijah the subject of the following verb as in “after Hezron died in Caleb Ephrathah, Abijah, Hezron’s wife, bore to him Ashhur, the father of Tekoa” (cf. NASB, NIV, NRSV). However, the preterite verb form cannot properly be preceded by its subject in this fashion. One would need to suppose that the phrase “and the wife of Hezron, Abijah” is not appositional but rather a parenthetic clause “and the wife of Hezron was Abijah.” R. Braun (1 Samuel [WBC], 40) is favorable to the idea that “the name of Hezron’s wife represents a misplaced gloss on v 21” (citing Williamson, JBL 98, 355). In the reading adopted here, this would mean that Caleb’s second wife, Ephrath, had actually been his late father’s wife (probably Caleb’s stepmother). Perhaps the text was subsequently altered because Caleb’s actions appeared improper in light of the injunctions in Lev 18:8; 20:11; Deut 22:30; 27:20 (which probably refer, however, to a son having sexual relations with his stepmother while his father is still alive).

25.text: The sons of Jerahmeel, Hezron’s firstborn, were Ram, the firstborn, Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah.

26.text: Jerahmeel had another wife named Atarah; she was Onam’s mother.

27.text: The sons of Ram, Jerahmeel’s firstborn, were Maaz, Jamin, and Eker.

28.text: The sons of Onam were Shammai and Jada. The sons of Shammai: Nadab and Abishur.

29.text: Abishur’s wife was Abihail, who bore him Ahban and Molid.

30.text: The sons of Nadab: Seled and Appaim. (Seled died without having sons.)

31.text: The son of Appaim: Ishi. The son of Ishi: Sheshan. The son of Sheshan: Ahlai.

notes.text: Heb “sons.” The Hebrew text has the plural “sons” in all three instances in this verse, even though the following lists have only one name each.

32.text: The sons of Jada, Shammai’s brother: Jether and Jonathan. (Jether died without having sons.)

33.text: The sons of Jonathan: Peleth and Zaza. These were the descendants of Jerahmeel.

34.text: Sheshan had no sons, only daughters. Sheshan had an Egyptian servant named Jarha.

35.text: Sheshan gave his daughter to his servant Jarha as a wife; she bore him Attai.

36.text: Attai was the father of Nathan, and Nathan was the father of Zabad.

37.text: Zabad was the father of Ephlal, and Ephlal was the father of Obed.

38.text: Obed was the father of Jehu, and Jehu was the father of Azariah.

39.text: Azariah was the father of Helez, and Helez was the father of Eleasah.

40.text: Eleasah was the father of Sismai, and Sismai was the father of Shallum.

41.text: Shallum was the father of Jekamiah, and Jekamiah was the father of Elishama.

42.text: The sons of Caleb, Jerahmeel’s brother: His firstborn Mesha, the father of Ziph, and his second son Mareshah, the father of Hebron.

notes.text: Heb “and the sons of Mareshah,” but this does not fit contextually. Perhaps the text originally had ‏וּבְנוֹ מִשְׁנֶה מָרֵשָׁה‎ (uveno mishneh mareshah, “and his second son, Mareshah”), with ‏מִשְׁנֶה‎ (“second”) later accidentally falling out by homoioteleuton (cf. the note in BHS here).

43.text: The sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem, and Shema.

44.text: Shema was the father of Raham, the father of Jorkeam. Rekem was the father of Shammai.

45.text: Shammai’s son was Maon, who was the father of Beth Zur.

46.text: Caleb’s concubine Ephah bore Haran, Moza, and Gazez. Haran was the father of Gazez.

notes.text: See the note on the word “concubine” in 1:32.

47.text: The sons of Jahdai: Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph.

48.text: Caleb’s concubine Maacah bore Sheber and Tirhanah.

49.text: She also bore Shaaph the father of Madmannah and Sheva the father of Machbenah and Gibea. Caleb’s daughter was Achsah.

50.text: These were the descendants of Caleb. The sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrath: Shobal, the father of Kiriath Jearim,

notes.text: Heb “son.” The Hebrew text has the singular, but the following list contains more than one name.
The Hebrew text reads “Ephrathah” here, but see v. 19, which mentions “Ephrath” as the wife of Caleb and mother of Hur.

51.text: Salma, the father of Bethlehem, and Hareph, the father of Beth Gader.

52.text: The sons of Shobal, the father of Kiriath Jearim, were Haroeh, half the Manahathites,

notes.text: The Hebrew text has “Menuchites” here, but v. 54 has “Manachathites.”

53.text: the clans of Kiriath Jearim—the Ithrites, Puthites, Shumathites, and Mishraites. (The Zorathites and Eshtaolites descended from these groups.)

notes.text: Heb “from these went forth the Zorathites and Eshtaolites.”

54.text: The sons of Salma: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth Beth Joab, half the Manahathites, the Zorites,

55.text: and the clans of the scribes who lived in Jabez: the Tirathites, Shimeathites, and Sucathites. These are the Kenites who descended from Hammath, the father of Beth Rechab.

notes.text: Or perhaps “the Sopherim.” The NAB transliterates this term and treats it as a proper name.
Heb “came.”
Or (if ‏בֵּית‎ [beth] is translated as “house” rather than considered to be part of the name) “the father of the house [i.e., family] of Rechab.”

1.text: These were the sons of David who were born to him in Hebron: The firstborn was Amnon, whose mother was Ahinoam from Jezreel; the second was Daniel, whose mother was Abigail from Carmel;

2.text: the third was Absalom whose mother was Maacah, daughter of King Talmai of Geshur; the fourth was Adonijah, whose mother was Haggith;

3.text: the fifth was Shephatiah, whose mother was Abital; the sixth was Ithream, whose mother was Eglah, David’s wife.

notes.text: Heb “his wife.”

4.text: These six were born to David in Hebron, where he ruled for seven years and six months. He ruled thirty-three years in Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “him”; the referent (David) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

5.text: These were the sons born to him in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon—the mother of these four was Bathsheba the daughter of Ammiel.

notes.text: “Shimea” (‏שִׁמְעָא‎, shimʿaʾ) is a variant spelling of “Shammua” (‏שַׁמּוּעַ‎, shammuaʿ; see 2 Sam 5:14). Some English versions use the spelling “Shammua” here (e.g., NIV, NCV).

Most Hebrew mss read “Bathshua” here, but 2 Sam 12:24 makes it clear Bathsheba was Solomon’s mother. “Bathsheba” is read by one Hebrew ms and the Vulgate. Many English translations (e.g., NAB, NIV, NLT) render the name “Bathsheba” to avoid confusion.
In 2 Sam 11:3 Bathsheba is called “the daughter of Eliam,” while here her father’s name is given as “Ammiel.”

6.text: The other nine were Ibhar, Elishua, Elpelet,

notes.text: All but two Hebrew mss read “Elishama” here, but 1 Chr 14:5 lists the name as “Elishua,” and is followed by a number of English versions here (e.g., NAB, NIV, NCV, TEV, CEV, NLT). Another son named “Elishama” is listed in 3:8.
The MT reads “Eliphelet” here, but 1 Chr 14:5 lists the name as “Elpelet” and is followed by some English versions here (e.g., TEV, NLT). Another son named “Eliphelet” is listed in 3:8.

7.text: Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia,

8.text: Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.

9.text: These were all the sons of David, not counting the sons of his concubines. Tamar was their sister.

notes.text: See the note on the word “concubine” in 1:32.

10.text: Solomon’s son was Rehoboam, followed by Abijah his son, Asa his son, Jehoshaphat his son,

11.text: Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son,

notes.text: Joram is a variant spelling of the name “Jehoram.”

12.text: Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son,

13.text: Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son,

14.text: Amon his son, Josiah his son.

15.text: The sons of Josiah: Johanan was the firstborn; Jehoiakim was born second; Zedekiah third; and Shallum fourth.

16.text: The sons of Jehoiakim: his son Jehoiachin and his son Zedekiah.

notes.text: Heb “Jeconiah,” a variation of the name “Jehoiachin” (also in v. 17).

17.text: The sons of Jehoiachin the exile: Shealtiel his son,

notes.text: Heb “prisoner.” Jehoiachin was carried off to Babylon as a prisoner. See 2 Chr 36:10.

18.text: Malkiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah.

19.text: The sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei. The sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah. Shelomith was their sister.

20.text: The five others were Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab Hesed.

21.text: The descendants of Hananiah: Pelatiah, Jeshaiah, the sons of Rephaiah, of Arnan, of Obadiah, and of Shecaniah.

22.text: The descendants of Shecaniah: Shemaiah and his sons: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat—six in all.

23.text: The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam—three in all.

24.text: The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani—seven in all.

1.text: The descendants of Judah: Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal.

2.text: Reaiah the son of Shobal was the father of Jahath, and Jahath was the father of Ahumai and Lahad. These were the clans of the Zorathites.

3.text: These were the sons of Etam: Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash. Their sister was Hazzelelponi.

4.text: Penuel was the father of Gedor, and Ezer was the father of Hushah. These were the descendants of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah and the father of Bethlehem.

5.text: Ashhur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah.

6.text: Naarah bore him Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah.

7.text: The sons of Helah: Zereth, Zohar, Ethnan,

8.text: and Koz, who was the father of Anub, Hazzobebah, and the clans of Aharhel the son of Harum.

9.text: Jabez was more respected than his brothers. His mother had named him Jabez, for she said, “I experienced pain when I gave birth to him.”

notes.text: In Hebrew the name ‏יַעְבֵּץ‎ (yaʿbets, “Jabez”) sounds like the noun ‏עֹצֶב‎ (ʿotsev) which means “pain.”

10.text: Jabez called out to the God of Israel, “If only you would greatly bless me and expand my territory. May your hand be with me! Keep me from harm so I might not endure pain.” God answered his prayer.

notes.text: Here the word ‏אִם‎ (ʾim, “if only”) begins an oath formula (see HALOT 60 s.v. and GKC 151e, 159dd, 167a). A full reporting of the oath would include both the request made of God and the promise made to God (cf. Gen 28:20; Num 21:2; Judg 11:30; 1 Sam 1:11; 2 Sam 15:8; Ps 81:9-14). Jabez’ promise is not recorded here, only that God granted his request. Perhaps Jabez’ vow in return had not been preserved by tradition and so the author could not include it, or perhaps those details were simply less important to the purpose of the book. Likely the author wants to emphasize to the post-exilic community (the original audience of the book) that God answers prayer, including concerns for their borders. That God granted his request implies that Jabez was faithful to his vow, so that his destiny was different than the expectation arising from his namesake. This should challenge the audience to consider their own faithfulness to God.

It is not certain whether the person Jabez should be connected with the town Jabez mentioned in 1 Chr 2:55. If Jabez were the head of the town (“more respected than his brothers” v. 9), then the request for an enlarged territory would not be a simple request for his own benefit, but an example of a leader of character whose faithfulness to God benefits those under his leadership.

The Hebrew text is difficult. As it stands in the MT, it says “and do some harm so that I might not be hurt.” When directly modifying ‏עָשָׂה‎ (ʿasah; “to do”), the preposition ‏מִן‎ (min; “from,”) can indicate the source or type of action, hence “do some harm” (cf. Lev 4:22; 18:30). But this makes little sense in context unless we suppose with no other basis that it refers to harming enemies. There is no other example of the privative use of ‏מִן‎ (min) with the verb ‏עָשָׂה‎ (ʿasah), which would have meant “act so as to prevent” harm. And one expects it would be confusing to use ‏מִן‎ (min) for both the type of action done and the type of action excluded or prevented. On the basis of a parallel to Isa 26:18, BHS suggests inserting ‏יְשׁוּעָתִי‎ (yeshuati; “my salvation”) on the possibility that it was omitted by haplography (as “do” and “my salvation,” ‏עָשִׂיתָ‎ and ‏יְשׁוּעָתִי‎, share similar consonants). This would mean “perform my salvation from harm.” Instead of ‏מֵרָעָה‎ (meraʿah; “from harm”), the LXX has γνῶσιν (gnosin; “knowledge”) which normally stands for Hebrew ‏דַעַת‎ (daʿat) or ‏דֵעָה‎ (deʿah) “knowledge; wisdom,” implying a simple confusion of dalet (‏ד‎) and resh (‏ר‎). The Greek text says “do/produce wisdom so that I will not be humiliated,” though the Hebrew behind this would be “act wisely so that I will not be grieved.” Rather than ask God to act wisely, we might suppose that the verb was first singular “may your hand be with me so that I may act wisely in order to not be grieved.” This would involve the loss of a yod at the end of the verb, which matches the verbal forms preceding it. Finally one might suppose that instead of ‏רָעָה‎ (raʿah; “harm”), some form of the root of ‏רֵעָה‎ (reʿah; “friend”) was original, meaning something like, “act from friendship…” but there is no direct parallel for this.
Heb “and God brought about what he had asked.”

11.text: Kelub, the brother of Shuhah, was the father of Mehir, who was the father of Eshton.

12.text: Eshton was the father of Beth Rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah, the father of Ir Nahash. These were the men of Recah.

notes.text: Or “of the city of Nahash.”

13.text: The sons of Kenaz: Othniel and Seraiah. The sons of Othniel: Hathath and Meonothai.

notes.text: “Meonothai” is read here by some mss of the LXX, along with the Vulgate. The name apparently was dropped from the Hebrew text by haplography. Note that the name appears at the beginning of the next verse as well.

14.text: Meonothai was the father of Ophrah. Seraiah was the father of Joab, the father of those who live in the Valley of the Craftsmen, for they were craftsmen.

notes.text: Heb “Ge-harashim,” which could be left untranslated as a place name.

15.text: The sons of Caleb son of Jephunneh: Iru, Elah, and Naam. The son of Elah: Kenaz.

notes.text: Heb “and the sons of Elah and Kenaz.” Kenaz was actually the son of Elah.

16.text: The sons of Jehallelel: Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asarel.

17.text: The sons of Ezrah: Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon. Mered’s wife Bithiah gave birth to Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has simply, “and she gave birth to,” without identifying the subject. The words “Mered’s wife Bithiah” are added in the translation for clarification. See v. 18b, which mentions “Bethiah, whom Mered married.”

18.text: (His Judahite wife gave birth to Jered the father of Gedor, Heber the father of Soco, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah.) These were the sons of Pharaoh’s daughter Bithiah, whom Mered married.

notes.text: Heb “took,” referring to taking in marriage.

19.text: The sons of Hodiah’s wife, the sister of Naham: the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maacathite.

20.text: The sons of Shimon: Amnon, Rinnah, Ben Hanan, and Tilon. The descendants of Ishi: Zoheth and Ben Zoheth.

notes.text: Or “and the son of Zoheth” (NAB). The word ‏בֶּן‎ (ben) in Hebrew means “son [of].”

21.text: The sons of Shelah son of Judah: Er the father of Lecah, Laadah the father of Mareshah, the clans of the linen workers at Beth Ashbea,

22.text: Jokim, the men of Cozeba, and Joash and Saraph, both of whom ruled in Moab and Jashubi Lehem. (This information is from ancient records.)

notes.text: Heb “and the words are old.”

23.text: They were the potters who lived in Netaim and Gederah; they lived there and worked for the king.

notes.text: Heb “and those who lived in Netaim and Gederah; with the king in his work they lived there.”

24.text: The descendants of Simeon: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, Shaul,

25.text: his son Shallum, his son Mibsam, and his son Mishma.

26.text: The descendants of Mishma: his son Hammuel, his son Zaccur, and his son Shimei.

27.text: Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters. But his brothers did not have many sons, so their whole clan was not as numerous as the sons of Judah.

28.text: They lived in Beer Sheba, Moladah, Hazar Shual,

29.text: Bilhah, Ezem, Tolad,

30.text: Bethuel, Hormah, Ziklag,

31.text: Beth Marcaboth, Hazar Susim, Beth Biri, and Shaaraim. These were their towns until the reign of David.

32.text: Their settlements also included Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan—five towns,

33.text: along with all their settlements that surrounded these towns as far as Baal. These were the places where they lived; they kept genealogical records.

notes.text: Some LXX mss read “Baalath” (cf. Josh 19:8). This is followed by some English versions (e.g., NIV, NCV, TEV, NLT).

34.text: Their clan leaders were: Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah son of Amaziah,

notes.text: The words “their clan leaders were” are added in the translation for clarification. See v. 38a, which makes this clear.

35.text: Joel, Jehu son of Joshibiah (son of Seraiah, son of Asiel),

36.text: Eleoenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, Benaiah,

37.text: Ziza son of Shipi (son of Allon, son of Jedaiah, son of Shimri, son of Shemaiah).

38.text: These who are named above were the leaders of their clans. Their extended families increased greatly in numbers.

39.text: They went to the entrance of Gedor, to the east of the valley, looking for pasture for their sheep.

40.text: They found fertile and rich pasture; the land was very broad, undisturbed and peaceful. Indeed some Hamites had been living there before that.

41.text: The men whose names are listed came during the time of King Hezekiah of Judah and attacked the Hamites’ settlements, as well as the Meunites they discovered there, and they wiped them out, as can be seen to this very day. They dispossessed them, for they found pasture for their sheep there.

notes.text: The Hebrew text reads “their tents,” apparently referring to those of the Hamites mentioned at the end of v. 40. Some prefer to emend the text to read, “the tents of Ham.”
Heb “and they lived in place of them.”

42.text: Five hundred men of Simeon, led by Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi, went to the hill country of Seir

43.text: and defeated the rest of the Amalekite refugees; they live there to this very day.

notes.text: Heb “and struck down the remnant that had escaped belonging to Amalek.”

1.text: The sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn— (Now he was the firstborn, but when he defiled his father’s bed, his rights as firstborn were given to the sons of Joseph, Israel’s son. So Reuben is not listed as firstborn in the genealogical records.

notes.text: The phrase when he defiled his father’s bed refers to Reuben having sexual relations with his father Jacob’s concubine Bilhah. This incident is recorded in Gen 35:22.
Heb “and not to be listed in the genealogical records as (having) the right of the firstborn.”

2.text: Though Judah was the strongest among his brothers and a leader descended from him, the right of the firstborn belonged to Joseph.)

notes.text: Heb “and [one] for a leader [was] from him.” This probably refers to the Davidic king.

3.text: The sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.

4.text: The descendants of Joel: his son Shemaiah, his son Gog, his son Shimei,

5.text: his son Micah, his son Reaiah, his son Baal,

6.text: and his son Beerah, whom King Tiglath-Pileser of Assyria carried into exile. Beerah was the tribal leader of Reuben.

notes.text: Heb “Tilgath-Pilneser,” a variant spelling of Tiglath-Pileser (also in v. 26).
Heb “he”; the referent (Beerah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

7.text: His brothers by their clans, as listed in their genealogical records: The leader Jeiel, Zechariah,

8.text: and Bela son of Azaz, son of Shema, son of Joel. They lived in Aroer as far as Nebo and Baal Meon.

9.text: In the east they settled as far as the entrance to the wilderness that stretches to the Euphrates River, for their cattle had increased in numbers in the land of Gilead.

10.text: During the time of Saul they attacked the Hagrites and defeated them. They took over their territory in the entire eastern region of Gilead.

notes.text: Heb “and in the days of Saul they made war with the Hagrites and they fell by their hand and they lived in their tents unto all the face of the east of Gilead.”

11.text: The descendants of Gad lived near them in the land of Bashan, as far as Salecah.

12.text: They included Joel the leader, Shapham the second in command, Janai, and Shaphat in Bashan.

13.text: Their relatives, listed according to their families, included Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia, and Eber—seven in all.

notes.text: Heb “and their brothers by the house of their fathers.”

14.text: These were the sons of Abihail son of Huri, son of Jaroah, son of Gilead, son of Michael, son of Jeshishai, son of Jahdo, son of Buz.

15.text: Ahi son of Abdiel, son of Guni, was the leader of the family.

notes.text: Heb “was the head of the house of their fathers.”

16.text: They lived in Gilead, in Bashan and its surrounding settlements, and in the pasturelands of Sharon to their very borders.

notes.text: Heb “unto their extremities.”

17.text: All of them were listed in the genealogical records in the time of King Jotham of Judah and in the time of King Jeroboam of Israel.

18.text: The Reubenites, Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had 44,760 men in their combined armies, warriors who carried shields and swords, were equipped with bows, and were trained for war.

notes.text: Heb “the sons of Reuben and the Gadites and half of the tribe of Manasseh, from the sons of bravery, men carrying a shield and sword and treading a bow and trained for war, 44,760 going out for warfare.”

19.text: They attacked the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab.

notes.text: Heb “made war with.”

20.text: They received divine help in fighting them, and the Hagrites and all their allies were handed over to them. They cried out to God during the battle; he responded to their prayers because they trusted in him.

notes.text: Heb “and they were helped against them and they were given over into their hand, the Hagrites and all who were with them, for to God they cried out in the battle and he was entreated [or “allowed himself to be entreated”] by them for they trusted in him.”

21.text: They seized the Hagrites’ animals, including 50,000 camels, 250,000 sheep, and 2,000 donkeys. They also took captive 100,000 people.

notes.text: Heb “their”; the referent (the Hagrites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

22.text: Because God fought for them, they killed many of the enemy. They dispossessed the Hagrites and lived in their land until the exile.

notes.text: Heb “from God [was] the battle.”
Heb “many slain fell.”
Heb “and they lived in place of them until the exile.” The referent of “them” (the Hagrites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

23.text: The half-tribe of Manasseh settled in the land from Bashan as far as Baal Hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon. They grew in number.

24.text: These were the leaders of their families: Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, and Jahdiel. They were skilled warriors, men of reputation, and leaders of their families.

notes.text: Heb “and these [were] the heads of the house of their fathers.”
Heb “men of names.”

25.text: But they were unfaithful to the God of their ancestors and worshiped instead the gods of the native peoples whom God had destroyed before them.

notes.text: Heb “fathers.”
Heb “prostituted themselves after.”
Heb “the peoples of the land.”

26.text: So the God of Israel stirred up King Pul of Assyria (that is, King Tiglath-Pileser of Assyria), and he carried away the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh and took them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan, where they remain to this very day.

notes.text: Heb “stirred up the spirit of.”
Heb “and the spirit of Tilgath-Pilneser king of Assyria.” “Pul” and “Tilgath-Pilneser” were names of the same Assyrian ruler, more commonly known as Tiglath-Pileser (cf. 2 Kgs 15:29).

1.text: (5:27) The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.

notes.text: Beginning with 6:1, the verse numbers through 6:81 in the English Bible differ from the verse numbers in the Hebrew text (BHS), with 6:1 ET = 5:27 HT, 6:2 ET = 5:28 HT, 6:16 ET = 6:1 HT, etc., through 6:81 ET = 6:66 HT. Beginning with 7:1 the verse numbers in the ET and HT are again the same.

2.text: The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel.

3.text: The children of Amram: Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.

4.text: Eleazar was the father of Phinehas, and Phinehas was the father of Abishua.

5.text: Abishua was the father of Bukki, and Bukki was the father of Uzzi.

6.text: Uzzi was the father of Zerahiah, and Zerahiah was the father of Meraioth.

7.text: Meraioth was the father of Amariah, and Amariah was the father of Ahitub.

8.text: Ahitub was the father of Zadok, and Zadok was the father of Ahimaaz.

9.text: Ahimaaz was the father of Azariah, and Azariah was the father of Johanan.

10.text: Johanan was the father of Azariah, who served as a priest in the temple Solomon built in Jerusalem.

11.text: Azariah was the father of Amariah, and Amariah was the father of Ahitub.

12.text: Ahitub was the father of Zadok, and Zadok was the father of Shallum.

13.text: Shallum was the father of Hilkiah, and Hilkiah was the father of Azariah.

14.text: Azariah was the father of Seraiah, and Seraiah was the father of Jehozadak.

15.text: Jehozadak went into exile when the Lord sent the people of Judah and Jerusalem into exile by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.

notes.text: The words “the people of” are added in the translation for clarification.

16.text: (6:1) The sons of Levi: Gershom, Kohath, and Merari.

notes.text: Chapter 6 of 1 Chr begins here in the Hebrew text; 6:16-81 ET = 6:1-66 HT. See the note at 6:1.
The name “Gershom” (also in vv. 17, 20, 43, 62, 71) appears as “Gershon” in 1 Chr 6:1.

17.text: These are the names of the sons Gershom: Libni and Shimei.

18.text: The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel.

19.text: The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites by their families.

notes.text: Heb “by their fathers.”

20.text: To Gershom: his son Libni, his son Jahath, his son Zimmah,

21.text: his son Joah, his son Iddo, his son Zerah, and his son Jeatherai.

22.text: The sons of Kohath: his son Amminadab, his son Korah, his son Assir,

notes.text: Or perhaps, “descendants,” since the list differs from the one in v. 18.

23.text: his son Elkanah, his son Ebiasaph, his son Assir,

24.text: his son Tahath, his son Uriel, his son Uzziah, and his son Shaul.

25.text: The sons of Elkanah: Amasai, Ahimoth,

notes.text: Heb “and Achimoth.”

26.text: his son Elkanah, his son Zophai, his son Nahath,

notes.text: The consonantal Hebrew text (Kethib) has, “Elkanah, his son, Elkanah.” The marginal reading (Qere) is “Elkanah, the sons of Elkanah.” The text probably originally read simply, “Elkanah his son.”

27.text: his son Eliab, his son Jeroham, and his son Elkanah.

notes.text: After the last named individual (“Elkanah” in v. 27) some LXX mss insert the words “Samuel his son” to facilitate a transition to the following verse, which begins “and the sons of Samuel.” Among the English versions that include this added phrase are NAB, NIV, and NLT.

28.text: The sons of Samuel: Joel the firstborn and Abijah the second oldest.

notes.text: The Hebrew text lacks the name ‏יוֹאֵל‎ (yoʾel, “Joel”), which has probably dropped out due to homoioteleuton (note the last three letters of the preceding name ‏שְׁמוּאֵל‎ (shemuel, “Samuel”).

29.text: The descendants of Merari: Mahli, his son Libni, his son Shimei, his son Uzzah,

30.text: his son Shimea, his son Haggiah, and his son Asaiah.

31.text: These are the men David put in charge of music in the Lord’s sanctuary, after the ark was placed there.

notes.text: Heb “house.”

32.text: They performed music before the sanctuary of the meeting tent until Solomon built the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem. They carried out their tasks according to regulations.

notes.text: Heb “they were serving…with music.”
Or traditionally “tabernacle.”

33.text: These are the ones who served along with their sons: From the Kohathites: Heman the musician, son of Joel, son of Samuel,

34.text: son of Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Eliel, son of Toah,

35.text: son of Zuph, son of Elkanah, son of Mahath, son of Amasai,

36.text: son of Elkanah, son of Joel, son of Azariah, son of Zephaniah,

37.text: son of Tahath, son of Assir, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah,

38.text: son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Israel.

39.text: Serving beside him was his fellow Levite Asaph, son of Berechiah, son of Shimea,

notes.text: Heb “and his brother Asaph, the one who stood at his right hand.”

40.text: son of Michael, son of Baaseiah, son of Malkijah,

notes.text: A few Hebrew mss, one LXX ms, and the Syriac read “Maaseiah.”

41.text: son of Ethni, son of Zerah, son of Adaiah,

42.text: son of Ethan, son of Zimmah, son of Shimei,

43.text: son of Jahath, son of Gershom, son of Levi.

44.text: Serving beside them were their fellow Levites, the descendants of Merari, led by Ethan, son of Kishi, son of Abdi, son of Malluch,

notes.text: Heb “and the sons of Merari, their brothers, on the left.”

45.text: son of Hashabiah, son of Amaziah, son of Hilkiah,

46.text: son of Amzi, son of Bani, son of Shemer,

47.text: son of Mahli, son of Mushi, son of Merari, son of Levi.

48.text: The rest of their fellow Levites were assigned to perform the remaining tasks at God’s sanctuary.

notes.text: Heb “their brothers, the Levites.”
Heb “were assigned to all the work of the tabernacle of the house of God.”

49.text: But Aaron and his descendants offered sacrifices on the altar for burnt offerings and on the altar for incense as they had been assigned to do in the Most Holy Sanctuary. They made atonement for Israel, just as God’s servant Moses had ordered.

notes.text: Heb “for all the work of the holy of holies.”
Heb “making atonement for Israel according to all which Moses the servant of God commanded.”

50.text: These were the descendants of Aaron: His son Eleazar, his son Phinehas, his son Abishua,

51.text: his son Bukki, his son Uzzi, his son Zerahiah,

52.text: his son Meraioth, his son Amariah, his son Ahitub,

53.text: his son Zadok, and his son Ahimaaz.

54.text: These were the areas where Aaron’s descendants lived: The following belonged to the Kohathite clan, for they received the first allotment:

notes.text: Heb “and these were their dwelling places according to their encampments in their territory to the sons of Aaron.”
Heb “to the clan of the Kohathites for to them was the lot.”

55.text: They were allotted Hebron in the territory of Judah, as well as its surrounding pasturelands.

56.text: (But the city’s land and nearby towns were allotted to Caleb son of Jephunneh.)

57.text: The descendants of Aaron were also allotted as cities of refuge Hebron, Libnah and its pasturelands, Jattir, Eshtemoa and its pasturelands,

notes.text: The parallel account in Josh 21:13 has the singular “city,” which apparently refers only to Hebron.

58.text: Hilez and its pasturelands, Debir and its pasturelands,

notes.text: The MT reads “Hilez” here; the place name appears as “Holon” in Josh 21:15.

59.text: Ashan and its pasturelands, and Beth Shemesh and its pasturelands.

notes.text: The MT reads “Ashan” here; the place name appears as “Ain” in Josh 21:16.
The LXX and Syriac (following the parallel list in Josh 21:16) add “Juttah and its pasturelands” here. Cf. NAB “Jetta”; also NIV, NCV, NLT “Juttah.”

60.text: Within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin they were allotted Geba and its pasturelands, Alemeth and its pasturelands, and Anathoth and its pasturelands. Their clans were allotted thirteen cities in all.

notes.text: The parallel passage in Josh 21:17 adds “Gibeon and its pasturelands” (cf. NAB, NIV, NCV, NLT). The words “they were allotted” are supplied in the translation for both clarity and stylistic reasons.

61.text: The rest of Kohath’s descendants were allotted ten cities in the territory of the half-tribe of Manasseh.

notes.text: Heb “to the sons of Kohath who were left from the clan of the tribe, from the half of the tribe of the half of Manasseh by lot ten cities.”

62.text: The clans of Gershom’s descendants received thirteen cities within the territory of the tribes of Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Manasseh (in Bashan).

notes.text: Heb “and to the sons of Gershom by their clans from the tribe of Issachar, and from the tribe of Asher, and from the tribe of Naphtali, and from the tribe of Manasseh in Bashan, thirteen cities.”

63.text: The clans of Merari’s descendants were allotted twelve cities within the territory of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun.

notes.text: Heb “and to the sons of Merari by their clans from the tribe of Reuben, and from the tribe of Gad, and from the tribe of Zebulun by lot, twelve cities.”

64.text: So the Israelites gave to the Levites these cities and their pasturelands.

65.text: They allotted these previously named cities from the territory of the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin.

notes.text: Heb “and they gave by lot from the tribe of the sons of Judah, and from the tribe of the sons of Simeon, and from the tribe of the sons of Benjamin these cities, which they called them by names.”

66.text: The clans of Kohath’s descendants also received cities as their territory within the tribe of Ephraim.

notes.text: Heb “and from [it is probably preferable to read “to” here] the clans of the sons of Kohath and there were the cities of their territory from the tribe of Ephraim.”

67.text: They were allotted as cities of refuge Shechem and its pasturelands (in the hill country of Ephraim), Gezer and its pasturelands,

notes.text: The parallel account in Josh 21:21 has the singular “city,” referring only to Shechem.

68.text: Jokmeam and its pasturelands, Beth Horon and its pasturelands,

69.text: Aijalon and its pasturelands, and Gath Rimmon and its pasturelands.

70.text: Within the territory of the half-tribe of Manasseh, the rest of Kohath’s descendants received Aner and its pasturelands and Bileam and its pasturelands.

notes.text: Heb “and from the half of the tribe of Manasseh, Aner and its pasturelands and Bileam and its pasturelands to the clan, to the sons of Kohath who were left.”

71.text: The following belonged to Gershom’s descendants: Within the territory of the half-tribe of Manasseh: Golan in Bashan and its pasturelands and Ashtaroth and its pasturelands.

notes.text: Heb “to the sons of Gershom.”

72.text: Within the territory of the tribe of Issachar: Kedesh and its pasturelands, Daberath and its pasturelands,

73.text: Ramoth and its pasturelands, and Anem and its pasturelands.

74.text: Within the territory of the tribe of Asher: Mashal and its pasturelands, Abdon and its pasturelands,

75.text: Hukok and its pasturelands, and Rehob and its pasturelands.

76.text: Within the territory of the tribe of Naphtali: Kedesh in Galilee and its pasturelands, Hammon and its pasturelands, and Kiriathaim and its pasturelands.

77.text: The following belonged to the rest of Merari’s descendants: Within the territory of the tribe of Zebulun: Rimmono and its pasturelands, and Tabor and its pasturelands.

notes.text: Heb “to the sons of Merari, who were left.”

Before “Rimmono” the LXX (following the parallel passage in Josh 21:34) adds “Jokneam and its pasturelands, Kartah and its pasturelands.” This addition is included in some English versions (e.g., NAB, NIV, NCV, NLT).

78.text: Within the territory of the tribe of Reuben across the Jordan River east of Jericho: Bezer in the wilderness and its pasturelands, Jahzah and its pasturelands,

notes.text: Heb “and from across the Jordan at Jericho, on the east of the Jordan, from the tribe of Reuben.” The word “River” is supplied in the translation for clarity.

79.text: Kedemoth and its pasturelands, and Mephaath and its pasturelands.

80.text: Within the territory of the tribe of Gad: Ramoth in Gilead and its pasturelands, Mahanaim and its pasturelands,

81.text: Heshbon and its pasturelands, and Jazer and its pasturelands.

1.text: The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron—four in all.

2.text: The sons of Tola: Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Jibsam, and Samuel. They were leaders of their families. In the time of David there were 22,600 warriors listed in Tola’s genealogical records.

notes.text: Many English versions spell this name “Ibsam.”
Many English versions retain a form of this name closer to the Hebrew, i.e., “Shemuel.”
Heb “heads of the house of their fathers.”
Heb “to Tola [there were] warriors by their generations, their number in the days of David [was] 22,600.”

3.text: The son of Uzzi: Izrahiah. The sons of Izrahiah: Michael, Obadiah, Joel, and Isshiah. All five were leaders.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has the plural “sons,” but only one son is listed.

4.text: According to the genealogical records of their families, they had 36,000 warriors available for battle, for they had numerous wives and sons.

notes.text: Heb “and unto them by their generations to the house of their fathers [were] troops of war of battle, 36,000, for they had many wives and sons.”

5.text: Altogether the genealogical records of the clans of Issachar listed 87,000 warriors.

notes.text: Heb “and their brothers, according to all the clans of Issachar, the warriors [were] 87,000 listed in the genealogical records for all.”

6.text: The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Beker, and Jediael—three in all.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has simply “Benjamin,” but ‏בְּנֵי‎ (bene, “sons of”) has dropped out by haplography (‏בְּנֵי בִּנְיָמִן‎, bene binyamin).

7.text: The sons of Bela: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, and Iri. The five of them were leaders of their families. There were 22,034 warriors listed in their genealogical records.

8.text: The sons of Beker: Zemirah, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alemeth. All these were the sons of Beker.

9.text: There were 20,200 family leaders and warriors listed in their genealogical records.

10.text: The son of Jediael: Bilhan. The sons of Bilhan: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Kenaanah, Zethan, Tarshish, and Ahishahar.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has the plural “sons,” but only one son is listed.

11.text: All these were the sons of Jediael. There were 17,200 family leaders and warriors who were capable of marching out to battle.

12.text: The Shuppites and Huppites were descendants of Ir; the Hushites were descendants of Aher.

notes.text: The name “Aher” appears as “Ahiram” in Num 26:38.

13.text: The sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer, and Shallum —sons of Bilhah.

notes.text: The name “Jahziel” appears as “Jahzeel” in Gen 46:24.
Most Hebrew mss read “Shallum”; some Hebrew mss and some LXX mss read “Shillem,” the form of the name that appears in Gen 46:24 and Num 26:49.

14.text: The sons of Manasseh: Asriel, who was born to Manasseh’s Aramean concubine. She also gave birth to Makir the father of Gilead.

notes.text: See the note on the word “concubine” in 1:32.

15.text: Now Makir married a wife from the Huppites and Shuppites. (His sister’s name was Maacah.) Zelophehad was Manasseh’s second son; he had only daughters.

notes.text: Some translations treat the terms ‏שֻׁפִּים‎ (shuppim) and ‏חֻפִּים‎ (khuppim) as proper names of individuals (“Huppim” and “Shuppim”), but others consider these forms to be plurals and refer to tribal or clan names.
Heb “and the name of the second was Zelophehad.”

16.text: Maacah, Makir’s wife, gave birth to a son, whom she named Peresh. His brother was Sheresh, and his sons were Ulam and Rekem.

17.text: The son of Ulam: Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead, son of Makir, son of Manasseh.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has the plural “sons,” but only one son is listed.

18.text: His sister Hammoleketh gave birth to Ishhod, Abiezer, and Mahlah.

19.text: The sons of Shemida were Ahian, Shechem, Likhi, and Aniam.

20.text: The descendants of Ephraim: Shuthelah, his son Bered, his son Tahath, his son Eleadah, his son Tahath,

21.text: his son Zabad, his son Shuthelah (Ezer and Elead were killed by the men of Gath, who were natives of the land, when they went down to steal their cattle.

22.text: Their father Ephraim mourned for them many days and his brothers came to console him.

23.text: He slept with his wife; she became pregnant and gave birth to a son. Ephraim named him Beriah because tragedy had come to his family.
