notes.text: The expression ‏בּוֹא אֶל‎ (boʾ ʾel) means “come to” or “approach,” but is also used as a euphemism for sexual relations.
Heb “he”; the referent (Ephraim) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Heb “because in tragedy there had come to his house.” The preposition prefixed to ‏רָעָה‎ (raʿah) should probably be omitted. The Hebrew noun ‏רָעָה‎ (“tragedy”) should be understood as the subject of the feminine verb form that follows.

24.text: His daughter was Sheerah, who built Lower and Upper Beth Horon, as well as Uzzen Sheerah),

25.text: his son Rephah, his son Resheph, his son Telah, his son Tahan,

notes.text: The antecedent of the pronoun “his” is not clear. The translation assumes that v. 25 resumes the list of Ephraim’s descendants (see vv. 20-21a) after a lengthy parenthesis (vv. 21b-24).
The Hebrew text has simply “Resheph,” but the phrase “his son” has probably been accidentally omitted, since the names before and after this one include the phrase.

26.text: his son Ladan, his son Ammihud, his son Elishama,

27.text: his son Nun, and his son Joshua.

notes.text: Heb “Non” (so KJV, NASB; cf. Exod 33:11, where the more familiar spelling “Nun” occurs).

28.text: Their property and settlements included Bethel and its surrounding towns, Naaran to the east, Gezer and its surrounding towns to the west, and Shechem and its surrounding towns as far as Ayyah and its surrounding towns.

29.text: On the border of Manasseh’s territory were Beth Shean and its surrounding towns, Taanach and its surrounding towns, Megiddo and its surrounding towns, and Dor and its surrounding towns. The descendants of Joseph, Israel’s son, lived here.

notes.text: “Beth Shean” is a variant spelling of “Beth Shan.”

30.text: The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, and Beriah. Serah was their sister.

31.text: The sons of Beriah: Heber and Malkiel, who was the father of Birzaith.

32.text: Heber was the father of Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham, and Shua their sister.

33.text: The sons of Japhlet: Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath. These were Japhlet’s sons.

34.text: The sons of his brother Shemer: Rohgah, Hubbah, and Aram.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has ‏אֲחִי‎ (ʾakhi, “the brother of”), but this should probably be emended to ‏אֲחִיו‎ (ʾakhiv, “his brother”). Cf. v. 35. Most English versions treat this Hebrew word as a proper name (“Ahi”) and list it before “Rohgah.”
Or “Shomer,” cf. v. 32.
“Hubbah” is the marginal reading (Qere); the consonantal text (Kethib) has “Jachbah.”

35.text: The sons of his brother Helem: Zophah, Imna, Shelesh, and Amal.

notes.text: Or “Hotham,” cf. v. 32.

36.text: The sons of Zophah: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah,

37.text: Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran, and Beera.

notes.text: The name “Ithran” is sometimes understood to be another name for “Jether” (v. 38).

38.text: The sons of Jether: Jephunneh, Pispah, and Ara.

39.text: The sons of Ulla: Arah, Hanniel, and Rizia.

40.text: All these were the descendants of Asher. They were the leaders of their families, the most capable men, who were warriors and served as head chiefs. There were 26,000 warriors listed in their genealogical records as capable of doing battle.

notes.text: Heb “all these were the sons of Asher, heads of the house of the fathers, selected, warriors, heads of the leaders, and there was listed in the genealogical records in war, in battle, their number, men, 26,000.”

1.text: Benjamin was the father of Bela, his firstborn; Ashbel was born second, Aharah third,

notes.text: Aharah is called “Ahiram” in Num 26:38.

2.text: Nohah fourth, and Rapha fifth.

3.text: Bela’s sons were Addar, Gera, Abihud,

4.text: Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah,

5.text: Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram.

6.text: These were the descendants of Ehud who were leaders of the families living in Geba who were forced to move to Manahath:

7.text: Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera, who moved them. Gera was the father of Uzzah and Ahihud.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Gera) has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

8.text: Shaharaim fathered sons in Moab after he divorced his wives Hushim and Baara.

9.text: By his wife Hodesh he fathered Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malkam,

10.text: Jeuz, Sakia, and Mirmah. These were his sons; they were family leaders.

11.text: By Hushim he fathered Abitub and Elpaal.

12.text: The sons of Elpaal: Eber, Misham, Shemed (who built Ono and Lod, as well as its surrounding towns),

13.text: Beriah, and Shema. They were leaders of the families living in Aijalon and chased out the inhabitants of Gath.

14.text: Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth,

15.text: Zebadiah, Arad, Eder,

16.text: Michael, Ishpah, and Joha were the sons of Beriah.

17.text: Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber,

18.text: Ishmerai, Izliah, and Jobab were the sons of Elpaal.

19.text: Jakim, Zikri, Zabdi,

20.text: Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel,

21.text: Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath were the sons of Shimei.

22.text: Ishpan, Eber, Eliel,

23.text: Abdon, Zikri, Hanan,

24.text: Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah,

25.text: Iphdeiah, and Penuel were the sons of Shashak.

26.text: Shamsherai, Shechariah, Athaliah,

27.text: Jaareshiah, Elijah, and Zikri were the sons of Jeroham.

28.text: These were the family leaders listed in the genealogical records; they lived in Jerusalem.

29.text: The father of Gibeon lived in Gibeon; his wife’s name was Maacah.

notes.text: Some LXX mss supply the name “Jeiel,” which is not in the MT (cf. 1 Chr 9:35). The addition of the name here is followed by many English versions (e.g., ASV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).

30.text: His firstborn son was Abdon, followed by Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab,

notes.text: Some LXX mss add “Ner” here (cf. 1 Chr 9:36 and v. 33 below, where Ner is mentioned as the father of Kish). The form ‏וְנֵר‎ (vener) could have been accidentally omitted by homoioarcton since each name in the list has the conjunction prefixed to it. Some English versions follow the LXX here and add “Ner” (e.g., NAB, NIV, NLT).

31.text: Gedor, Ahio, Zeker, and Mikloth.

notes.text: The Hebrew text omits the name “Mikloth,” but it may have fallen out accidentally by haplography. Note that the name immediately follows at the beginning of v. 32; cf. NAB.

32.text: Mikloth was the father of Shimeah. They also lived near their relatives in Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “and also they, opposite their brothers, lived in Jerusalem with their brothers.” This redundancy has been removed in the translation.

33.text: Ner was the father of Kish, and Kish was the father of Saul. Saul was the father of Jonathan, Malki-Shua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal.

notes.text: Eshbaal is called “Ishbosheth” in 2 Sam 2:8.

34.text: The son of Jonathan: Meribbaal. Meribbaal was the father of Micah.

notes.text: Meribbaal is called “Mephibosheth” in 2 Sam 4:4.

35.text: The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz.

36.text: Ahaz was the father of Jehoaddah, and Jehoaddah was the father of Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. Zimri was the father of Moza,

37.text: and Moza was the father of Binea. His son was Raphah, whose son was Eleasah, whose son was Azel.

38.text: Azel had six sons: Azrikam his firstborn, followed by Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel.

notes.text: Heb “sons and these were their names.”

The Hebrew text has ‏בֹּכְרוּ‎ (bokheru), which some understand as a name: “Bocheru” (so, e.g., NEB, NASB, NIV, NRSV). But the form should probably be revocalized ‏בְּכֹרוֹ‎ (bekhoro, “his firstborn”). A name has accidentally dropped from the list, and a scribe apparently read ‏בֹּכְרוּ‎ as one of the names.

The Lucianic recension of the LXX inserts another name here, καὶ Ἀζαριας (kai Azarias, “and Azariah”), presumably to make up the six sons mentioned at the beginning of the verse (see the previous tc note on “firstborn”). Cf. NAB.

39.text: The sons of his brother Eshek: Ulam was his firstborn, Jeush second, and Eliphelet third.

40.text: The sons of Ulam were warriors who were adept archers. They had many sons and grandsons, a total of 150. All these were the descendants of Benjamin.

notes.text: Heb “and the sons of Ulam were men, warriors and treaders of a bow.”

1.text: Genealogical records were kept for all Israel; they are recorded in the Scroll of the Kings of Israel. The people of Judah were carried away to Babylon because of their unfaithfulness.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has simply “Judah,” though the verb ‏הָגְלוּ‎ (hoglu, “carried away”) is plural.

2.text: The first to resettle on their property and in their cities were some Israelites, priests, Levites, and temple servants.

notes.text: Heb “and the inhabitants, the first who [were] in their property in their cities, Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants.”

3.text: Some from the tribes of Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim and Manasseh settled in Jerusalem.

4.text: The settlers included: Uthai son of Ammihud, son of Omri, son of Imri, son of Bani, who was a descendant of Perez son of Judah.

notes.text: The words “the settlers included” are supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

5.text: From the Shilonites: Asaiah the firstborn and his sons.

6.text: From the descendants of Zerah: Jeuel. Their relatives numbered 690.

7.text: From the descendants of Benjamin: Sallu son of Meshullam, son of Hodaviah, son of Hassenuah;

8.text: Ibneiah son of Jeroham; Elah son of Uzzi, son of Mikri; and Meshullam son of Shephatiah, son of Reuel, son of Ibnijah.

9.text: Their relatives, listed in their genealogical records, numbered 956. All these men were leaders of their families.

notes.text: Heb “and all these men were heads of fathers for the house of their fathers.”

10.text: From the priests: Jedaiah; Jehoiarib; Jakin;

11.text: Azariah son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub the leader in God’s temple;

12.text: Adaiah son of Jeroham, son of Pashhur, son of Malkijah; and Maasai son of Adiel, son of Jahzerah, son of Meshullam, son of Meshillemith, son of Immer.

13.text: Their relatives, who were leaders of their families, numbered 1,760. They were capable men who were assigned to carry out the various tasks of service in God’s temple.

notes.text: Heb “capable [for] the work of the task of the house of God.”

14.text: From the Levites: Shemaiah son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah a descendant of Merari;

15.text: Bakbakkar; Heresh; Galal; Mattaniah son of Mika, son of Zikri, son of Asaph;

16.text: Obadiah son of Shemaiah, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun; and Berechiah son of Asa, son of Elkanah, who lived among the settlements of the Netophathites.

17.text: The gatekeepers were: Shallum, Akkub, Talmon, Ahiman, and their brothers. Shallum was the leader;

18.text: he serves to this day at the King’s Gate on the east. These were the gatekeepers from the camp of the descendants of Levi.

19.text: Shallum son of Kore, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, and his relatives from his family (the Korahites) were assigned to guard the entrance to the sanctuary. Their ancestors had guarded the entrance to the Lord’s dwelling place.

notes.text: Heb “and his brothers belonging to the house of his father, the Korachites, to the work of the task, guardians of the threshold of the tent.”

Heb “and their fathers to the camp of the Lord, guardians of the entrance.” Here “fathers” is used in a more general sense of “forefathers” or “ancestors” and is not limited specifically to their fathers only.

20.text: Phinehas son of Eleazar had been their leader in earlier times, and the Lord was with him.

21.text: Zechariah son of Meshelemiah was the guard at the entrance to the meeting tent.

22.text: All those selected to be gatekeepers at the entrances numbered 212. Their names were recorded in the genealogical records of their settlements. David and Samuel the prophet had appointed them to their positions.

notes.text: The Hebrew term is ‏רֹאֶה‎ (roʾeh, “seer”), an older word for ‏נָבִיא‎ (naviʾ, “prophet”).
Heb “they—David appointed, and Samuel the seer, in their position.”

23.text: They and their descendants were assigned to guard the gates of the Lord’s sanctuary (that is, the tabernacle).

notes.text: Heb “and they and their sons to the gates of the house of the Lord, of the house of the tent, [were assigned] as guards.”

24.text: The gatekeepers were posted on all four sides—east, west, north, and south.

25.text: Their relatives, who lived in their settlements, came from time to time and served with them for seven-day periods.

26.text: The four head gatekeepers, who were Levites, were assigned to guard the storerooms and treasuries in God’s sanctuary.

notes.text: Heb “in the house of God.”

27.text: They would spend the night in their posts all around God’s sanctuary, for they were assigned to guard it and would open it with the key every morning.

notes.text: Heb “in the house of God.”

28.text: Some of them were in charge of the articles used by those who served; they counted them when they brought them in and when they brought them out.

notes.text: Heb “and from them over the articles of the task, for by number they would bring them in, and by number they would bring them out.”

29.text: Some of them were in charge of the equipment and articles of the sanctuary, as well as the flour, wine, olive oil, incense, and spices.

notes.text: Heb “holy place.”

30.text: (But some of the priests mixed the spices.)

31.text: Mattithiah, a Levite, the firstborn son of Shallum the Korahite, was in charge of baking the bread for offerings.

notes.text: The word “son” is not in the Hebrew text, but is implied.

32.text: Some of the Kohathites, their relatives, were in charge of preparing the bread that is displayed each Sabbath.

33.text: The musicians and Levite family leaders stayed in rooms at the sanctuary and were exempt from other duties, for day and night they had to carry out their assigned tasks.

notes.text: Heb “were in rooms.” The words “at the sanctuary” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

34.text: These were the family leaders of the Levites, as listed in their genealogical records. They lived in Jerusalem.

35.text: Jeiel (the father of Gibeon) lived in Gibeon. His wife was Maacah.

notes.text: Heb “The name of his wife.”

36.text: His firstborn son was Abdon, followed by Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab,

37.text: Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth.

38.text: Mikloth was the father of Shimeam. They also lived near their relatives in Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “and also they, opposite their brothers, lived in Jerusalem with their brothers.” This redundancy has been removed in the translation.

39.text: Ner was the father of Kish, and Kish was the father of Saul. Saul was the father of Jonathan, Malki-Shua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal.

notes.text: Eshbaal is called “Ishbosheth” in 2 Sam 2:8.

40.text: The son of Jonathan: Meribbaal, who was the father of Micah.

notes.text: Meribbaal is called “Mephibosheth” in 2 Sam 4:4.

41.text: The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, and Ahaz.

notes.text: The name “Ahaz” is included in the Vulgate and Syriac, but omitted in the MT. It probably was accidentally omitted by haplography. Note that the name appears at the beginning of the next verse. Cf. also 8:35.

42.text: Ahaz was the father of Jarah, and Jarah was the father of Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. Zimri was the father of Moza,

notes.text: So MT; some Hebrew mss and the LXX read “Jadah” (cf. NIV, NCV, NLT) while in 8:36 the name “Jehoaddah’ appears (cf. NAB).

43.text: and Moza was the father of Binea. His son was Rephaiah, whose son was Eleasah, whose son was Azel.

44.text: Azel had six sons: Azrikam his firstborn, followed by Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. These were the sons of Azel.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has ‏בֹּכְרוּ‎ (bokheru), which some understand as a name: “Bocheru” (so, e.g., NEB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT). But the form should probably be revocalized ‏בְֹּכרוֹ‎ (bekhoro, “his firstborn”). A name has accidentally dropped from the list, and a scribe apparently read ‏בֹּכְרוּ‎ as one of the names. Cf. also 1 Chr 8:38.

1.text: Now the Philistines fought against Israel. The Israelites fled before the Philistines and many of them fell dead on Mount Gilboa.

2.text: The Philistines stayed right on the heels of Saul and his sons. They struck down Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malki-Shua.

notes.text: Heb “stuck close after.”
Heb “the Philistines.” The translation has substituted the pronoun “they” to avoid redundancy.

3.text: The battle was thick around Saul; the archers spotted him and wounded him.

notes.text: Heb “heavy.”
Heb “and they found him, the ones who shoot with the bow, and he was in pain from the ones shooting.”

4.text: Saul told his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and stab me with it. Otherwise these uncircumcised people will come and torture me.” But his armor-bearer refused to do it, because he was very afraid. So Saul took the sword and fell on it.

notes.text: Heb “so these uncircumcised ones might not come and abuse me.”

5.text: When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell on his sword and died.

6.text: So Saul and his three sons died; his whole household died together.

notes.text: Heb “all his house.” This is probably to be understood as a general summary statement. It could include other males in Saul’s household besides his three sons, cf. 1 Sam 31:6. If it refers only to the male members of his household who would have stood in succession to the throne (cf. NLT, “bringing his dynasty to an end,”) even here there is an exception, since one of Saul’s sons, Eshbaal (or “Ishbosheth” in 2 Sam 2:8) was not killed in the battle and became king over Israel, which he ruled for two years (2 Sam 2:10) until he was assassinated by Rechab and Baanah (2 Sam 4:5-6). The tribe of Judah never acknowledged Ishbosheth as king; instead they followed David (2 Sam 2:10).

7.text: When all the Israelites who were in the valley saw that the army had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled. The Philistines came and occupied them.

notes.text: Heb “they”; the referent (the army) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

8.text: The next day, when the Philistines came to strip loot from the corpses, they discovered Saul and his sons lying dead on Mount Gilboa.

9.text: They stripped his corpse, and then carried off his head and his armor. They sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines proclaiming the news to their idols and their people.

10.text: They placed his armor in the temple of their gods and hung his head in the temple of Dagon.

notes.text: Or “god.” The Hebrew term may be translated as singular or plural depending on the context.

11.text: When all the residents of Jabesh Gilead heard about everything the Philistines had done to Saul,

12.text: all the warriors went and recovered the bodies of Saul and his sons and brought them to Jabesh. They buried their remains under the oak tree in Jabesh and fasted for seven days.

notes.text: Heb “arose and carried away the corpse of Saul and the corpses of his sons.”
Heb “their bones.”

13.text: So Saul died because he was unfaithful to the Lord and did not obey the Lord’s instructions; he even tried to conjure up underworld spirits.

notes.text: Heb “and Saul died in his unfaithfulness by which he acted unfaithfully against the Lord, concerning the Lord’s message which he did not keep, also to inquire of a medium to seek [an oracle].” The LXX adds “and the prophet Samuel answered him.” The text alludes to the incident recorded in 1 Sam 28.

14.text: He did not seek the Lord’s guidance, so the Lord killed him and transferred the kingdom to David son of Jesse.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

1.text: All Israel joined David at Hebron and said, “Look, we are your very flesh and blood!

notes.text: Heb “look, your bone and your flesh [are] we.”

2.text: In the past, even when Saul was king, you were Israel’s commanding general. The Lord your God said to you, ‘You will shepherd my people Israel; you will rule over my people Israel.’”

notes.text: Heb “you were the one who led out and the one who brought in Israel.”

3.text: When all the leaders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the Lord. They anointed David king over Israel, in keeping with the Lord’s message that came through Samuel.

notes.text: Heb “elders.”
Heb “by the hand of Samuel.”

4.text: David and the whole Israelite army advanced to Jerusalem (that is, Jebus). (The Jebusites, the land’s original inhabitants, lived there.)

notes.text: Heb “all Israel.”
Jebus was an older name for the city of Jerusalem (cf. Josh 15:8; Judg 1:21).
Heb “and there [were] the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land.”

5.text: The residents of Jebus said to David, “You cannot invade this place!” But David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David).

6.text: David said, “Whoever attacks the Jebusites first will become commanding general!” So Joab son of Zeruiah attacked first and became commander.

notes.text: Verse 6 inserts into the narrative parenthetical information about Joab’s role in the conquest of the city. Verse 7 then picks up where v. 5 left off.
Or perhaps “strikes down.”
Heb “head and officer.”
Heb “went up.”
Heb “head.”

7.text: David lived in the fortress; for this reason it is called the City of David.

8.text: He built up the city around it, from the terrace to the surrounding walls; Joab restored the rest of the city.

notes.text: Heb “to that which surrounds.” On the referent here as “the surrounding walls,” see HALOT 740 s.v. ‏סָבִיב‎.

9.text: David’s power steadily grew, for the Lord of Heaven’s Armies was with him.

notes.text: Heb “and David went, going and becoming great, and the Lord of Heaven’s Armies [traditionally, Lord of hosts] was with him.”

10.text: These were the leaders of David’s warriors who, together with all Israel, stood courageously with him in his kingdom by installing him as king, in keeping with the Lord’s message concerning Israel.

11.text: This is the list of David’s warriors: Jashobeam, a Hacmonite, was head of the officers. He killed 300 men with his spear in a single battle.

notes.text: Heb “and these are the number of the warriors who were David’s.”
The marginal reading (Qere) has “officers;” the consonantal text (Kethib) has “the Thirty” (see v. 15).
Heb “he was wielding his spear against 300, [who were] slain at one time.”

12.text: Next in command was Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite. He was one of the three elite warriors.

notes.text: Heb “after him.”

13.text: He was with David in Pas Dammim when the Philistines assembled there for battle. In an area of the field that was full of barley, the army retreated before the Philistines,

notes.text: Some read here “Ephes Dammim.” See 1 Sam 17:1.

14.text: but then they made a stand in the middle of that area. They defended it and defeated the Philistines; the Lord gave them a great victory.

notes.text: Heb “delivered it.”
Heb “and the Lord delivered [with] a great deliverance.”

15.text: Three of the thirty leaders went down to David at the rocky cliff at the cave of Adullam, while a Philistine force was camped in the Valley of Rephaim.

16.text: David was in the stronghold at the time, while a Philistine garrison was in Bethlehem.

17.text: David was thirsty and said, “How I wish someone would give me some water to drink from the cistern in Bethlehem near the city gate!”

notes.text: Heb “Who will give me water to drink?” On the rhetorical use of ‏מִי‎ (mi) here, see BDB 566 s.v. f.

18.text: So the three elite warriors broke through the Philistine forces and drew some water from the cistern in Bethlehem near the city gate. They carried it back to David, but David refused to drink it. He poured it out as a drink offering to the Lord

notes.text: Heb “the three,” referring to the three elite warriors mentioned in v. 12.

19.text: and said, “God forbid that I should do this! Should I drink the blood of these men who risked their lives?” Because they risked their lives to bring it to him, he refused to drink it. Such were the exploits of the three elite warriors.

notes.text: Heb “Far be it to me from my God from doing this.”
Heb “with their lives.” The same expression occurs later in this verse.
Heb “These things the three warriors did.”

20.text: Abishai the brother of Joab was head of the three elite warriors. He killed 300 men with his spear and gained fame along with the three elite warriors.

notes.text: The Syriac reads “thirty” here and at the beginning of v. 21; this reading is followed by some English translations (cf. NAB, NASB, NRSV, NLT).
Heb “he was wielding his spear against three hundred, [who were] slain.”
Heb “and to him [reading with the Qere] there was a name among the three.”

21.text: From the three he was given double honor and he became their officer, even though he was not one of them.

notes.text: Or “more than.”
Heb “of the three.”

22.text: Benaiah son of Jehoiada was a brave warrior from Kabzeel who performed great exploits. He struck down the two sons of Ariel of Moab; he also went down and killed a lion inside a cistern on a snowy day.

notes.text: Heb “the two of Ariel, Moab.” The precise meaning of ‏אֲרִיאֵל‎ (ʾariʾel) is uncertain; some read “warrior.” The present translation assumes that the word is a proper name and that ‏בְּנֵי‎ (bene, “sons of”) has accidentally dropped from the text by homoioarcton (note the preceding ‏שְׁנֵי‎, shene).

23.text: He even killed an Egyptian who was 7½ feet tall. The Egyptian had a spear in his hand as big as the crossbeam of a weaver’s loom; Benaiah attacked him with a club. He grabbed the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand and killed him with his own spear.

notes.text: Heb “5 cubits.” Assuming a length of 18 inches for the standard cubit, this individual would be 7.5 feet (2.3 m) tall.
Heb “went down to.”

24.text: Such were the exploits of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who gained fame along with the three elite warriors.

25.text: He received honor from the thirty warriors, though he was not one of the three elite warriors. David put him in charge of his bodyguard.

notes.text: Or “more than.”

26.text: The mighty warriors were: Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan son of Dodo, from Bethlehem,

27.text: Shammoth the Harorite, Helez the Pelonite,

notes.text: The parallel text of 2 Sam 23:25 has the variant spelling of “Shammah.”
The parallel text of 2 Sam 23:26 has the variant spelling of “Paltite.”

28.text: Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Abiezer the Anathothite,

29.text: Sibbekai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite,

notes.text: In 2 Sam 23:27 this individual’s name is given as “Mebunnai.”
The parallel text of 2 Sam 23:28 has the variant “Zalmon.”

30.text: Maharai the Netophathite, Heled son of Baanah the Netophathite,

31.text: Ithai son of Ribai from Gibeah in Benjaminite territory, Benaiah the Pirathonite,

notes.text: The parallel text of 2 Sam 23:29 has the variant spelling “Ittai.”

32.text: Hurai from the valleys of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite,

notes.text: The parallel text of 2 Sam 23:28 has the variant spelling “Hiddai.”
The parallel text of 2 Sam 23:31 has the variant spelling “Abi-Albon.”

33.text: Azmaveth the Baharumite, Eliahba the Shaalbonite,

notes.text: The parallel text of 2 Sam 23:31 has the variant spelling “Barhumite.”

34.text: the sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan son of Shageh the Hararite,

notes.text: In 2 Sam 23:32 this individual’s name is given as “Jashen.”
The parallel text of 2 Sam 23:33 has the variant spelling “Shammah.”

35.text: Ahiam son of Sakar the Hararite, Eliphal son of Ur,

notes.text: In 2 Sam 23:33 this individual’s name is given as “Sharar.”
The parallel text of 2 Sam 23:34 has the variant “Eliphelet son of Ahasbai the Maacathite.”

36.text: Hepher the Mekerathite, Ahijah the Pelonite,

37.text: Hezro the Carmelite, Naarai son of Ezbai,

notes.text: The parallel text of 2 Sam 23:35 has the variant spelling “Hezrai.”

38.text: Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar son of Hagri,

notes.text: The parallel text of 2 Sam 23:36 has the variant “Igal son of Nathan from Zobah.”

39.text: Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite, the armor-bearer of Joab son of Zeruiah,

40.text: Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,

41.text: Uriah the Hittite, Zabad son of Achli,

42.text: Adina son of Shiza the Reubenite, leader of the Reubenites and the thirty warriors with him,

43.text: Hanan son of Maacah, Joshaphat the Mithnite,

44.text: Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jeiel, the sons of Hotham the Aroerite,

45.text: Jediael son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite,

46.text: Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite,

47.text: Eliel, and Obed, and Jaasiel the Mezobaite.

1.text: These were the men who joined David in Ziklag, when he was banished from the presence of Saul son of Kish. (They were among the warriors who assisted him in battle.

notes.text: Heb “kept from.”

2.text: They were armed with bows and could shoot arrows or sling stones right or left-handed. They were fellow tribesmen of Saul from Benjamin.) These were:

notes.text: Heb “ones armed with bow[s], using the right hand and the left hand with stones and with arrows with the bow, from the brothers of Saul from Benjamin.”
The words “These were” have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons, because of the length of the intervening material since the beginning of the verse.

3.text: Ahiezer, the leader, and Joash, the sons of Shemaah the Gibeathite; Jeziel and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; Berachah, Jehu the Anathothite,

4.text: Ishmaiah the Gibeonite, one of the thirty warriors and their leader, (12:5) Jeremiah, Jahaziel, Johanan, Jozabad the Gederathite,

notes.text: In the Hebrew text (BHS) a verse division occurs at this point, and for the remainder of the chapter the verse numbers of the Hebrew Bible differ by one from the English Bible. Thus 1 Chr 12:4b ET = 12:5 HT, and 12:5-40 ET = 12:6-41 HT. Beginning with 13:1 the verse numbers in the ET and HT are again the same.

5.text: (12:6) Eluzai, Jerimoth, Bealiah, Shemariah, Shephatiah the Haruphite,

6.text: Elkanah, Isshiah, Azarel, Joezer, and Jashobeam, who were Korahites,

7.text: and Joelah and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham from Gedor.

8.text: Some of the Gadites joined David at the stronghold in the wilderness. They were warriors who were trained for battle; they carried shields and spears. They were as fierce as lions and could run as quickly as gazelles across the hills.

notes.text: Heb “warriors, men of battle for war, prepared with shield and spear, and [like] the face of a lion were their faces, and like gazelles on the hills to hurry.”

9.text: Ezer was the leader, Obadiah the second in command, Eliab the third,

10.text: Mishmannah the fourth, Jeremiah the fifth,

11.text: Attai the sixth, Eliel the seventh,

12.text: Johanan the eighth, Elzabad the ninth,

13.text: Jeremiah the tenth, and Machbannai the eleventh.

14.text: These Gadites were military leaders; the least led a hundred men, the greatest a thousand.

notes.text: Heb “one for a hundred the small, and the great for a thousand.” Another option is to translate the preposition ‏ל‎ (lamed) as “against” and to understand this as a hyperbolic reference to their prowess: “the least could stand against a hundred, the greatest against a thousand.”

15.text: They crossed the Jordan River in the first month, when it was overflowing its banks, and routed those living in all the valleys to the east and west.

notes.text: The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied for clarity.
That is, March-April.
Heb “and they chased all the valleys to the east and to the west.”

16.text: Some from Benjamin and Judah also came to David’s stronghold.

17.text: David went out to meet them and said, “If you come to me in peace and want to help me, then I will make an alliance with you. But if you come to betray me to my enemies when I have not harmed you, may the God of our ancestors take notice and judge!”

notes.text: Heb “and David went out before them and answered and said to them.”
Heb “there will be to me concerning you a heart for unity.”
Heb “with no violence in my hands.”
Heb “fathers.”

18.text: But a spirit empowered Amasai, the leader of the group of warriors known as the Thirty, and he said: “We are yours, O David! We support you, O son of Jesse! May you greatly prosper. May those who help you prosper. Indeed your God helps you!” So David accepted them and made them leaders of raiding bands.

notes.text: Perhaps “the Spirit,” but the text has simply ‏רוּחַ‎ (ruakh) with no article (suggesting an indefinite reference).
Heb “clothed.”
The words “and he said” are supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.
Heb “are with.”
Heb “Peace, peace to you.” The Hebrew term ‏שָׁלוֹם‎ (shalom, “peace”) is repeated to emphasize degree.
Heb “and peace to the one who helps you.”
Or “for.”

19.text: Some men from Manasseh joined David when he went with the Philistines to fight against Saul. (But in the end they did not help the Philistines because, after taking counsel, the Philistine lords sent David away, saying, “It would be disastrous for us if he deserts to his master Saul.”)

notes.text: Heb “fell upon,” here in a good sense.
Heb “and they did not help them for by counsel they sent him away, the lords of the Philistines, saying, ‘With our heads he will fall to his master Saul.’”

20.text: When David went to Ziklag, the men of Manasseh who joined him were Adnach, Jozabad, Jediael, Michael, Jozabad, Elihu, and Zillethai, leaders of 1,000 soldiers each in the tribe of Manasseh.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (David) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

21.text: They helped David fight against raiding bands, for all of them were warriors and leaders in the army.

22.text: Each day men came to help David until his army became very large.

notes.text: Heb “for at the time of day in a day they were coming to David to help him until [there was] a great camp like the camp of God.” The term ‏אֱלֹהִים‎ (ʾelohim, “God”) is probably used idiomatically here to indicate the superlative.

23.text: The following is a record of the armed warriors who came with their leaders and joined David in Hebron in order to make David king in Saul’s place, in accordance with the Lord’s decree:

notes.text: Heb “these are the numbers of the heads of the forces armed for battle [who] came to David in Hebron to turn over the kingdom of Saul to him according to the mouth of the Lord.”

24.text: From Judah came 6,800 trained warriors carrying shields and spears.

notes.text: Heb “the sons of Judah, carrying shield and spear, [were] 6,800 armed for battle.”

25.text: From Simeon there were 7,100 warriors.

26.text: From Levi there were 4,600.

27.text: Jehoiada, the leader of Aaron’s descendants, brought 3,700 men with him,

28.text: along with Zadok, a young warrior, and 22 leaders from his family.

29.text: From Benjamin, Saul’s tribe, there were 3,000, most of whom, up to that time, had been loyal to Saul.

notes.text: Heb “from the sons of Benjamin, the brothers of Saul.”
Heb “and until then, the majority of them were keeping the charge of the house of Saul.”

30.text: From Ephraim there were 20,800 warriors, who had brought fame to their families.

notes.text: Heb “men of names for the house of their fathers.”

31.text: From the half-tribe of Manasseh there were 18,000 who had been designated by name to come and make David king.

32.text: From Issachar there were 200 leaders and all their relatives at their command—they understood the times and knew what Israel should do.

notes.text: Heb “from the sons of Issachar, knowers of understanding for times to know what Israel should do, their heads [were] 200, and all their brothers according to their mouth.”

33.text: From Zebulun there were 50,000 warriors who were prepared for battle, equipped with all kinds of weapons, and ready to give their undivided loyalty.

notes.text: Heb “from Zebulun, those going out for battle, prepared for war with all weapons of war, 50,000, and to help without a heart and a heart.”

34.text: From Naphtali there were 1,000 officers, along with 37,000 men carrying shields and spears.

35.text: From Dan there were 28,600 men prepared for battle.

36.text: From Asher there were 40,000 warriors prepared for battle.

37.text: From the other side of the Jordan, from Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, there were 120,000 men armed with all kinds of weapons.

38.text: All these men were warriors who were ready to march. They came to Hebron to make David king over all Israel by acclamation; all the rest of the Israelites also were in agreement that David should become king.

notes.text: Heb “all these [were] men of war, helpers of the battle line.” The present translation assumes an emendation of ‏עֹדְרֵי‎ (ʿodere, “helpers of”) to ‏עֹרְכֵי‎, (ʿorekhe, “prepared for”).
Heb “with a complete heart they came to Hebron to make David king over all Israel.”
Heb “and also all the rest of Israel [was of] one mind to make David king.”

39.text: They spent three days feasting there with David, for their relatives had given them provisions.

notes.text: Heb “eating and drinking.”

40.text: Also their neighbors, from as far away as Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali, were bringing food on donkeys, camels, mules, and oxen. There were large supplies of flour, fig cakes, raisins, wine, olive oil, beef, and lamb, for Israel was celebrating.

notes.text: Heb “cattle and sheep.”
Heb “for there was joy in Israel.”

1.text: David consulted with his military officers, including those who led groups of a thousand and those who led groups of a hundred.

notes.text: Heb “and David consulted with the officers of thousands and hundreds, to every ruler.”

2.text: David said to the whole Israelite assembly, “If you so desire and the Lord our God approves, let’s spread the word to our brothers who remain in all the regions of Israel, and to the priests and Levites in their cities, so they may join us.

notes.text: Heb “If to you [it is] good and from the Lord our God.”
Heb “let us spread and let us send.” The words “the word” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “in the cities of their pasturelands.”

3.text: Let’s move the ark of our God back here, for we did not seek his will throughout Saul’s reign.”

notes.text: Heb “to us.”
Heb “him.” In this case, seeking God’s will is what is implied.
Heb “in the days of Saul.”

4.text: The whole assembly agreed to do this, for the proposal seemed right to all the people.

notes.text: Heb “all the assembly said to do so.”
Heb “for right was the word in the eyes of all the people.”

5.text: So David assembled all Israel from the Shihor River in Egypt to Lebo Hamath, to bring the ark of God from Kiriath Jearim.

notes.text: The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied for clarity.
The Shihor River was a river on the border of Egypt, probably the eastern branch of the Nile.
Or “the entrance to Hamath.”

6.text: David and all Israel went up to Baalah (that is, Kiriath Jearim) in Judah to bring up from there the ark of God the Lord, who sits enthroned between the cherubim—the ark that is called by his Name.

notes.text: Heb “the ark of God the Lord who sits [between] the cherubim which is called [by his] name.”

7.text: They transported the ark of God on a new cart from the house of Abinadab; Uzzah and Ahio were guiding the cart,

8.text: while David and all Israel were energetically celebrating before God, singing and playing various stringed instruments, tambourines, cymbals, and trumpets.

notes.text: Heb “with all strength.”
Heb “with songs and with zithers [meaning uncertain] and with harps.” Due to the collocation with “harps,” some type of stringed instrument is probably in view.

9.text: When they arrived at the threshing floor of Kidon, Uzzah reached out his hand to take hold of the ark, because the oxen stumbled.

notes.text: Or “to steady.”

10.text: The Lord was so furious with Uzzah, he killed him, because he reached out his hand and touched the ark. He died right there before God.

notes.text: Heb “and the anger of the Lord burned against Uzzah.”
Heb “because he stretched out his hand over the ark.”

The modern reader might think God seemed to overreact here, but Israel needed a vivid object lesson of God’s holiness. By loading the ark on a cart, David had violated the instructions in God’s law (Exod 25:12-14; Num 4:5-6, 15). Uzzah’s action, however innocent it may seem, betrayed a certain lack of reverence for God’s presence. God had to remind his people that his holiness could not under any circumstances be violated.

11.text: David was angry because the Lord attacked Uzzah; so he called that place Perez Uzzah, which remains its name to this very day.

notes.text: Heb “because the Lord broke out [with] breaking out [i.e., an outburst] against Uzzah.”
The name Perez Uzzah means in Hebrew “the outburst [against] Uzzah.”

12.text: David was afraid of God that day and said, “How will I ever be able to bring the ark of God up here?”

13.text: So David did not move the ark to the City of David; he left it in the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite.

notes.text: The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

14.text: The ark of God remained in Obed-Edom’s house for three months; the Lord blessed Obed-Edom’s family and everything that belonged to him.

1.text: King Hiram of Tyre sent messengers to David, along with cedar logs, stonemasons, and carpenters to build a palace for him.

notes.text: Heb “craftsman of a wall,” that is, masons skilled at building stone walls.

2.text: David realized that the Lord had established him as king over Israel and that he had elevated his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.

notes.text: Heb “was lifted upwards.”

3.text: In Jerusalem David married more wives and fathered more sons and daughters.

notes.text: Heb “took.”

4.text: These are the names of children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,

5.text: Ibhar, Elishua, Elpelet,

6.text: Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia,

7.text: Elishama, Beeliada, and Eliphelet.

notes.text: In 1 Chr 3:8 and 2 Sam 5:16 this name appears as “Eliada.” The form here represents a variant spelling of the name.

8.text: When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king of all Israel, all the Philistines marched up to confront him. When David heard about it, he marched out against them.

notes.text: Or “designated”; NCV “had been made king”; CEV “had become king.”
Heb “to seek David.”
Heb “went out before.”

9.text: Now the Philistines had come and raided the Valley of Rephaim.

notes.text: Heb “stripped.”

10.text: David asked God, “Should I march up against the Philistines? Will you hand them over to me?” The Lord said to him, “March up! I will hand them over to you!”

11.text: So they marched against Baal Perazim and David defeated them there. David said, “Using me as his instrument, God has burst out against my enemies like water bursts out.” So that place is called Baal Perazim.

notes.text: Heb “by my hand.”
The name Baal Perazim means “Lord of outbursts” in Hebrew.

12.text: The Philistines left their idols there, so David ordered that they be burned.

notes.text: Heb “they abandoned.”
Heb “gods.”

13.text: The Philistines again raided the valley.

14.text: So David again asked God what he should do. This time God told him, “Don’t march up after them; circle around them and come against them in front of the trees.

notes.text: Heb “and David again consulted with God.”
The words “this time” are not in the Hebrew text.
The Hebrew word translated “trees” is defined by HALOT 129 s.v. ‏בָּכָא‎ as “shrubs.” Some translate “balsam trees” (see BDB 113 s.v. ‏בָּכָא‎), cf. NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT.

15.text: When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the trees, then attack. For at that moment God is going before you to strike down the army of the Philistines.”

notes.text: Heb “go out in battle.”
Heb “camp.”

16.text: David did just as God commanded him, and they struck down the Philistine army from Gibeon to Gezer.

17.text: So David became famous in all the lands; the Lord caused all the nations to fear him.

notes.text: Heb “the name of David went out.”
Heb “and the Lord placed fear of him upon all the nations.”

1.text: David constructed buildings in the City of David; he then prepared a place for the ark of God and pitched a tent for it.

2.text: Then David said, “Only the Levites may carry the ark of God, for the Lord chose them to carry the ark of the Lord and to serve before him perpetually.”

3.text: David assembled all Israel at Jerusalem to bring the ark of the Lord up to the place he had prepared for it.

4.text: David gathered together the descendants of Aaron and the Levites:

5.text: From the descendants of Kohath: Uriel the leader and 120 of his relatives.

6.text: From the descendants of Merari: Asaiah the leader and 220 of his relatives.

7.text: From the descendants of Gershom: Joel the leader and 130 of his relatives.

notes.text: Gershom is a variant spelling of the name Gershon.

8.text: From the descendants of Elizaphan: Shemaiah the leader and 200 of his relatives.

9.text: From the descendants of Hebron: Eliel the leader and 80 of his relatives.

10.text: From the descendants of Uzziel: Amminadab the leader and 112 of his relatives.

11.text: David summoned the priests Zadok and Abiathar, along with the Levites Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel, and Amminadab.

12.text: He told them: “You are the leaders of the Levites’ families. You and your relatives must consecrate yourselves and bring the ark of the Lord God of Israel up to the place I have prepared for it.

13.text: The first time you did not carry it; that is why the Lord God attacked us, because we did not ask him about the proper way to carry it.”

notes.text: Heb “because for what was at first [i.e., formerly] you [were] not, the Lord our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him concerning the procedure.”

14.text: The priests and Levites consecrated themselves so they could bring up the ark of the Lord God of Israel.

15.text: The descendants of Levi carried the ark of God on their shoulders with poles, just as Moses had commanded in keeping with the Lord’s instruction.

notes.text: Heb “word, message.”

16.text: David told the leaders of the Levites to appoint some of their relatives as musicians; they were to play various instruments, including stringed instruments and cymbals, and to sing loudly and joyfully.

notes.text: Heb “causing to be heard to lift up with a voice of joy.”

17.text: So the Levites appointed Heman son of Joel; one of his relatives, Asaph son of Berechiah; one of the descendants of Merari, Ethan son of Kushaiah;

notes.text: The Hebrew text adds, “their brothers.”

18.text: along with some of their relatives who were second in rank, including Zechariah, Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-Edom, and Jeiel, the gatekeepers.

notes.text: The Hebrew text adds ‏בֶּן‎ (ben, “son”) here; the word is omitted in three Hebrew mss and most LXX mss. If the word is original, perhaps the name of Zechariah’s father was accidentally omitted. Some English versions treat the word as an additional name in the list (“Ben”; e.g., KJV, ASV, NASB).

19.text: The musicians Heman, Asaph, and Ethan were to sound the bronze cymbals;

20.text: Zechariah, Aziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Maaseiah, and Benaiah were to play the harps according to the alamoth style;

notes.text: The meaning of the Hebrew word ‏עֲלָמוֹת‎ (ʿalamot) is uncertain; perhaps it refers to a particular style of music. See HALOT 835-36 s.v. ‏עַלְמָה‎.

21.text: Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-Edom, Jeiel, and Azaziah were to play the lyres according to the sheminith style, as led by the director;

notes.text: The meaning of the Hebrew word ‏שְׁמִינִית‎ (sheminit) is uncertain; perhaps it refers to a particular style of music. See HALOT 1562 s.v. ‏שְׁמִינֹי‎.
Heb “for” or “according to.”

22.text: Kenaniah, the leader of the Levites, was in charge of transport, for he was well-informed on this matter;

notes.text: The MT reads ‏בְּמַשָּׂא יָסֹר בַּמַּשָּׂא‎ (bemassa’ yasor bammassa’), leader of the Levites “in [the] lifting up, an instructor in lifting up.” The LXX reads ἄρχων τῶν ᾠδῶν (archōn tōn ōdōn) “ruler/leader of the songs,” apparently omitting the first Hebrew ‏בְּמַשָּׂא‎ (bemassa’) and then reading the similar sounding ‏יָשֹׂר‎ (yasor) “one who rules” for ‏יָסֹר‎ (yasor) “instructor.” The Vulgate associates the first Hebrew ‏בְּמַשָּׂא‎ (bemassa’) with prophesy (see note below) and the second with song. Luther renders “the master in song to teach them to sing” (see Keil and Delitzsch, The First Book of Chronicles, 204).

Or “in charge of the singing,” i.e., was the director or conductor of music. The difficulties are: 1) the meaning of “lifting up,” 2) where to supply the verb “to be,” 3) choosing which elements of context to rely on. 1) The verb ‏נָשָׂא‎ (nasaʾ; “to lift, carry”) can mean to carry a load, but is also used in many idiomatic expressions, including to “raise” the voice. The noun ‏מַשָּׂא‎ (massaʾ) most often means a load or a prophetic announcement. DCH, a recent major dictionary, includes “perhaps music” under ‏מַשָּׂא‎ I, while noting that ‏מַשָּׂא‎ II is used at Qumran specifically as an “utterance or praise.” So ‏מַשָּׂא‎ likely refers either to carrying [the ark of the covenant] or to raising the voice/sound (‏קוֹל‎; qol) [of music]. A third possibility is that the expression is a technical term, a shorthand for the raising of hands in the conducting of music. 2) As a noun clause, the verb “to be” must be understood at some point, either “Kenaniah was leader of the Levites in [the] lifting up, an instructor in lifting up” or “Kenaniah, leader of the Levites in [the] lifting up, was an instructor in lifting up. 3) There are a four primary contextual considerations. A) Chapter 15 is about transporting the ark; verse 2 (but not 12-13) uses the root ‏נָשָׂא‎ (nasaʾ). B) Identifying what transporting activity Kenaniah would be trained/wise in and instructor of. They were no longer moving the tabernacle from place to place. C) Verse 16 appears to set the agenda for vss 19-22; it identifies musical instruments that Levites are appointed to in 19-21. Verse 16 last lists “causing the voice/sound (‏קוֹל‎; qol) to rise with joy.” The Hebrew root is ‏רוּם‎ (rum; “to be/make high”) not ‏נָשָׂא‎, but this may only be due to the Hiphil stem. ‏נָשָׂא‎ is a very common verb but only occurs twice in the Hiphil, possibly due to a preference to switch verbs for the causative concept. D) A Kenaniah mentioned in 1 Chr 26:29 is in charge of external responsibilities, officers and judges. If this is the same Kenaniah, that would represent a significant change in responsibilities for an instructor of musical conducting, but may embrace oversight of transportation.
This is a Hiphil participle of ‏בִּין‎ (bin; “to understand”). In the Hiphil it means to act with skill or understanding, or to give understanding, i.e., to explain or teach.

23.text: Berechiah and Elkanah were guardians of the ark;

notes.text: Heb “gatekeepers.”

24.text: Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer the priests were to blow the trumpets before the ark of God; Obed-Edom and Jehiel were also guardians of the ark.

notes.text: Heb “gatekeepers.”

25.text: So David, the leaders of Israel, and the commanders of units of a thousand went to bring up the ark of the Lord’s covenant from the house of Obed-Edom with celebration.

26.text: When God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the Lord’s covenant, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.

27.text: David was wrapped in a linen robe, as were all the Levites carrying the ark, the musicians, and Kenaniah the supervisor of transport and the musicians; David also wore a linen ephod.

notes.text: Heb “the leader, the lifting up, the musicians.” See also the note on the word “matter” in v. 22.
An ephod was a priestly garment worn over the robe.

28.text: All Israel brought up the ark of the Lord’s covenant; they were shouting, blowing trumpets, sounding cymbals, and playing stringed instruments.

29.text: As the ark of the Lord’s covenant entered the City of David, Michal, Saul’s daughter, looked out the window. When she saw King David jumping and celebrating, she despised him.

notes.text: The Hebrew text adds “in her heart.”

1.text: They brought the ark of God and put it in the middle of the tent David had pitched for it. Then they offered burnt sacrifices and peace offerings before God.

notes.text: Or “tokens of peace”; NIV “fellowship offerings.”

2.text: When David finished offering burnt sacrifices and peace offerings, he pronounced a blessing over the people in the Lord’s name.

3.text: He then handed out to each Israelite man and woman a loaf of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake.

4.text: He appointed some of the Levites to serve before the ark of the Lord, to offer prayers, songs of thanks, and hymns to the Lord God of Israel.

5.text: Asaph was the leader and Zechariah second-in-command, followed by Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-Edom, and Jeiel. They were to play stringed instruments, Asaph was to sound the cymbals,

6.text: and the priests Benaiah and Jahaziel were to blow trumpets regularly before the ark of God’s covenant.

7.text: That day David first gave to Asaph and his colleagues this song of thanks to the Lord.

8.text: Give thanks to the Lord! Call on his name! Make known his accomplishments among the nations.

9.text: Sing to him! Make music to him! Tell about all his miraculous deeds.

10.text: Boast about his holy name. Let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice.

11.text: Seek the Lord and the strength he gives. Seek his presence continually!

notes.text: Heb “face.”

12.text: Recall the miraculous deeds he performed, his mighty acts and the judgments he decreed,

notes.text: Heb “and the judgments of his mouth.”

13.text: O children of Israel, God’s servant, you descendants of Jacob, God’s chosen ones!

notes.text: Heb “seed.”
Heb “his”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “his”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

14.text: He is the Lord our God; he carries out judgment throughout the earth.

notes.text: Heb “in all the earth [are] his judgments.”

15.text: Remember continually his covenantal decree, the promise he made to a thousand generations—

notes.text: The Hebrew text has a masculine plural imperative, addressed to the people. Some LXX mss harmonize the wording here to Ps 105:8, which has ‏זָכַר‎ (zakhar), the perfect third masculine singular form of the verb, “He (the Lord) remembers” (so NIV; NEB reads “He called to mind his covenant”).
Heb “[the] word he commanded.” The text refers here to God’s unconditional covenantal promise to Abraham and the patriarchs, as vv. 16-18 make clear.

16.text: the promise he made to Abraham, the promise he made by oath to Isaac!

notes.text: Heb “which.”
Heb “his oath to Isaac.”

17.text: He gave it to Jacob as a decree, to Israel as a lasting promise,

notes.text: Or “eternal covenant.”

18.text: saying, “To you I will give the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance.”

19.text: When they were few in number, just a very few, and foreign residents within it,

20.text: they wandered from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another.

notes.text: Heb “and from a kingdom to another people.”

21.text: He let no one oppress them; he disciplined kings for their sake,

22.text: saying, “Don’t touch my anointed ones! Don’t harm my prophets!”

notes.text: The word “saying” is supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.

23.text: Sing to the Lord, all the earth! Announce every day how he delivers.

notes.text: Heb “from day to day.”

24.text: Tell the nations about his splendor, tell all the nations about his miraculous deeds.

notes.text: The verb “tell” is understood by ellipsis (note the preceding line).

25.text: For the Lord is great and certainly worthy of praise, he is more awesome than all gods.

notes.text: Or “feared above.”

26.text: For all the gods of the nations are worthless, but the Lord made the heavens.

notes.text: The Hebrew word ‏אֱלִילִים‎ (ʾelilim, “worthless”) sounds like ‏אֱלֹהִים‎ (ʾelohim, “gods”). The sound play draws attention to the statement. Many modern English translations render this term as “idols” here.
Or “the sky” (also in v. 31). The Hebrew term ‏שָׁמַיִם‎ (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.

27.text: Majestic splendor emanates from him, he is the source of strength and joy.

notes.text: Heb “majesty and splendor [are] before him.”
Heb “strength and joy [are] in his place.”

28.text: Ascribe to the Lord, O families of the nations, ascribe to the Lord splendor and strength!

29.text: Ascribe to the Lord the splendor he deserves! Bring an offering and enter his presence! Worship the Lord in holy attire!

notes.text: Heb “the splendor of [i.e., due] his name.”
Or “in holy splendor.”

30.text: Tremble before him, all the earth! The world is established, it cannot be moved.

31.text: Let the heavens rejoice, and the earth be happy! Let the nations say, “The Lord reigns!”

notes.text: Heb “let them say among the nations.”

32.text: Let the sea and everything in it shout! Let the fields and everything in them celebrate!

33.text: Then let the trees of the forest shout with joy before the Lord, for he comes to judge the earth!

34.text: Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good and his loyal love endures.

notes.text: Or “is eternal.”

35.text: Say this prayer: “Deliver us, O God who delivers us! Gather us! Rescue us from the nations! Then we will give thanks to your holy name, and boast about your praiseworthy deeds.”

notes.text: The words “this prayer” are supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.
Heb “to give thanks.” The infinitive construct indicates result after the imperative.
Heb “to boast in your praise.”

36.text: May the Lord God of Israel be praised, in the future and forevermore. Then all the people said, “We agree! Praise the Lord.”

notes.text: Heb “from everlasting to everlasting.”
This is the Hebrew term ‏אָמֵן‎ (ʾamen, “surely”), traditionally transliterated “amen.”

37.text: David left Asaph and his colleagues there before the ark of the Lord’s covenant to serve before the ark regularly and fulfill each day’s requirements,

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (David) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “according to the matter of the day in its day.”

38.text: including Obed-Edom and sixty-eight colleagues. Obed-Edom son of Jeduthun and Hosah were gatekeepers.

39.text: Zadok the priest and his fellow priests served before the Lord’s tabernacle at the worship center in Gibeon,

notes.text: The word “served” is supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.
Or “high place.”

40.text: regularly offering burnt sacrifices to the Lord on the altar for burnt sacrifice, morning and evening, according to what is prescribed in the law of the Lord which he charged Israel to observe.

notes.text: Heb “which he laid as a charge upon Israel.”

41.text: Joining them were Heman, Jeduthun, and the rest of those chosen and designated by name to give thanks to the Lord. (For his loyal love endures!)

notes.text: Perhaps this refers to the refrain of their songs of praise (see Ps 136). In this case one could translate, “to give thanks to the Lord with songs using the refrain, ‘For his loyal love endures.’”

42.text: Heman and Jeduthun were in charge of the music, including the trumpets, cymbals, and the other musical instruments used in praising God. The sons of Jeduthun guarded the entrance.

notes.text: Heb “and with them, Heman and Jeduthun, trumpets and cymbals for sounding, and the instrument of song of God, and the sons of Jeduthun [were] at the gate.”

43.text: Then all the people returned to their homes, and David went to pronounce a blessing on his family.

notes.text: Heb “to bless his house.” Elsewhere when “house” is the object of “bless,” it refers to a household or family. See, for example, 1 Chr 13:14; 17:27. However, since ‏בֵּית‎ (bet, “house”) refers to a literal house or home earlier in the verse and to David’s palace in 17:1, one might translate here, “David went to pronounce a blessing on [i.e., dedicate] his house [i.e., palace].”

1.text: When David had settled into his palace, he said to Nathan the prophet, “Look, I am living in a palace made from cedar, while the ark of the Lord’s covenant is under a tent.”

notes.text: Heb “house.”
Heb “David.” The pronoun “he” has been used in the translation here to avoid redundancy in keeping with contemporary English style.
Heb “house.”
Heb “tent curtains.”

2.text: Nathan said to David, “You should do whatever you have in mind, for God is with you.”

notes.text: Heb “all that is in your heart.”

3.text: That night God told Nathan,

notes.text: Heb “the word of God was [i.e., came] to Nathan.”

4.text: “Go, tell my servant David: ‘This is what the Lord says: “You must not build me a house in which to live.

5.text: For I have not lived in a house from the time I brought Israel up from Egypt to the present day. I have lived in a tent that has been in various places.

notes.text: The words “from Egypt” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

Heb “and I was from tent to tent and from tabernacle.” The words ‏אֶל־מִשְׁכָּן‎ (ʾel mishkan, “to tabernacle”) should probably be added at the end of the sentence to complete this prepositional phrase and produce symmetry with the preceding prepositional phrase. The words probably fell from the text by homoioteleuton.
I have lived in a tent that has been in various places. The point here is that the Lord moved with the tabernacle as it moved from place to place; he did not confine himself to a particular location.

6.text: Wherever I moved throughout Israel, I did not say to any of the leaders whom I appointed to care for my people Israel, ‘Why have you not built me a house made from cedar?’”’

notes.text: In the Hebrew text the statement is phrased as a rhetorical question (“Did I say a word?”) meaning “I did not say a word.”
Heb “to one of the judges of Israel whom I commanded to shepherd my people.”

7.text: “So now, say this to my servant David: ‘This is what the Lord of Heaven’s Armies says: “I took you from the pasture and from your work as a shepherd to make you a leader of my people Israel.

notes.text: Traditionally, “Lord of hosts.”
Heb “and from after sheep.”

8.text: I was with you wherever you went and I defeated all your enemies before you. Now I will make you as famous as the great men of the earth.

notes.text: Heb “cut off.”
Heb “and I will make for you a name like the name of the great men who are in the earth.”

9.text: I will establish a place for my people Israel and settle them there; they will live there and not be disturbed anymore. Violent men will not oppress them again, as they did in the beginning

notes.text: Heb “plant.”
Heb “shaken.”
Heb “and sons of violence will no longer consume them as in the beginning.”

10.text: and during the time when I appointed judges to lead my people Israel. I will subdue all your enemies. “‘“I declare to you that the Lord will build a dynastic house for you!

notes.text: Here the word “house” is used in a metaphorical sense, referring to a royal dynasty. The Lord’s use of the word here plays off the literal sense that David had in mind as he contemplated building a temple (“house”) for the Lord. In the translation the adjective “dynastic” is supplied to indicate that the term is used metaphorically.

11.text: When the time comes for you to die, I will raise up your descendant, one of your own sons, to succeed you, and I will establish his kingdom.

notes.text: Heb “and it will be when your days are full to go with your ancestors.”
Heb “your seed.”

12.text: He will build me a house, and I will make his dynasty permanent.

notes.text: Heb “and I will establish his throne permanently.”

13.text: I will become his father and he will become my son. I will never withhold my loyal love from him, as I withheld it from the one who ruled before you.

notes.text: The one who ruled before you is a reference to Saul, from whom the kingdom was taken and given to David.

14.text: I will put him in permanent charge of my house and my kingdom; his dynasty will be permanent.”’”

notes.text: Heb “and his throne will be established permanently.”

15.text: Nathan told David all these words that were revealed to him.

notes.text: Heb “according to all these words and according to all this revelation, so Nathan said to David.”

16.text: King David went in, sat before the Lord, and said: “Who am I, O Lord God, and what is my family, that you should have brought me to this point?

notes.text: Heb “house.”

17.text: And you did not stop there, O God! You have also spoken about the future of your servant’s family. You have revealed to me what men long to know, O Lord God.

notes.text: Heb “and this was small in your eyes, O God, so you spoke concerning the house of your servant for a distance.”

The translation “You have revealed to me what men long to know” is very tentative; the meaning of the Hebrew text is unclear. The text appears to read literally, “and you see me like the searching of man, that which is upward,” which is nonsensical. The translation above assumes the following: (1) The Qal verb translated “you see me” is repointed as a Hiphil, “you showed me,” (2) ‏תּוֹר‎ (tor) is understood in the sense of “searching, exploring,” and (3) ‏הַמַּעֲלָה‎ (hammaʿalah) is taken in a temporal sense of “that which lies beyond.” Thus one could translate, “you have shown me what men search for, what lies beyond.”

18.text: What more can David say to you? You have honored your servant; you have given your servant special recognition.

notes.text: The word “say” is supplied in the translation for clarification. The Hebrew verb means “add.”
Heb “for honoring your servant, and you, your servant, know.”

19.text: O Lord, for the sake of your servant and according to your will, you have done this great thing in order to reveal your greatness.

notes.text: Heb “heart.”
Heb “to make known all the great deeds.”

20.text: O Lord, there is none like you; there is no God besides you! What we heard is true!

notes.text: The Hebrew text reads literally, “in all which we heard with our ears,” but ‏בְּכֹל‎ (bekhol, “in all”) should probably be emended to ‏כְּכֹל‎ (kekhol, “according to all”).

21.text: And who is like your people, Israel, a unique nation in the earth? Their God went to claim a nation for himself! You made a name for yourself by doing great and awesome deeds when you drove out nations before your people whom you had delivered from the Egyptian empire and its gods.

notes.text: Heb “a nation, one.”
Heb “whose God,” or “because God.” In the Hebrew text this clause is subordinated to what precedes. The clauses are separated in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “redeem” or “deliver.”
Heb “to make for yourself a name [with] great and awesome [deeds].”
Heb “to drive out.”
Heb “from Egypt, nations.” The parallel text in 2 Sam 7:23 reads “from Egypt, nations and its gods.”

22.text: You made Israel your very own nation for all time. You, O Lord, became their God.

notes.text: Heb “and you made your people Israel your own for a people permanently.”

23.text: So now, O Lord, may the promise you made about your servant and his family become a permanent reality! Do as you promised,

notes.text: Heb “and now, O Lord, the word which you spoke concerning your servant and concerning his house, may it be established permanently.”
Heb “as you have spoken.”

24.text: so it may become a reality and you may gain lasting fame, as people say, ‘The Lord of Heaven’s Armies is the God of Israel.’ The dynasty of your servant David will be established before you,

notes.text: Following the imperative in v. 23b, the prefixed verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result: “so it might become a reality.”
Heb “so it might be established.”

Heb “and your name might be great permanently.” Following the imperative in v. 23b, the prefixed verbal form with vav conjunctive indicates purpose/result (parallel to the previous purpose/result clause): “[so]…you might gain lasting fame.”
Heb “saying.” The words “as people” are supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.

Heb “the Lord of Heaven’s Armies [traditionally, the Lord of hosts], the God of Israel, Israel’s God.” The phrases ‏אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל‎ (ʾelohey yisraʾel, “God of Israel”) and ‏אֱלֹהִים לְיִשְׂרָאֵל‎ (ʾelohim leyisraʾel, “Israel’s God”) are probably alternative readings that have been conflated in the text.
Heb “house.”

25.text: for you, my God, have revealed to your servant that you will build a dynasty for him. That is why your servant has had the courage to pray to you.

notes.text: Heb “house.”
Heb “That is why your servant found to pray before you.” Perhaps the phrase ‏אֶת לִבּוֹ‎ (ʾet libbo, “his heart”) should be supplied as the object of the verb “found.”

26.text: Now, O Lord, you are the true God; you have made this good promise to your servant.

notes.text: Heb “the God.” The article indicates uniqueness here.
Heb “and you have spoken to your servant this good thing.”

27.text: Now you are willing to bless your servant’s dynasty so that it may stand permanently before you, for you, O Lord, have blessed it and it will be blessed from now on into the future.”

notes.text: Heb “house.”
Heb “for you, O Lord, have blessed and [it is] blessed permanently.”

1.text: Later David defeated the Philistines and subdued them. He took Gath and its surrounding towns away from the Philistines.

notes.text: 2 Sam 8:1 identifies this region as “Metheg Ammah.”
Heb “from the hand of the Philistines.” Here “hand” is figurative language for “control.”

2.text: He defeated the Moabites; the Moabites became David’s subjects and brought tribute.

notes.text: Heb “carriers of tribute,” i.e., tribute payers.

3.text: David defeated King Hadadezer of Zobah as far as Hamath, when he went to extend his authority to the Euphrates River.

notes.text: Heb “hand.”

Heb “when he went to set up his hand at the Euphrates River.” The Hebrew word ‏יָד‎ (yad, “hand”) is usually understood to mean “control” or “dominion” here. However, since ‏יָד‎ does occasionally refer to a monument, perhaps one could translate, “to set up his monument at the Euphrates River” (i.e., as a visible marker of the limits of his dominion). For another example of the Hiphil of ‏נָצַב‎ (natsav) used with ‏יָד‎ (“monument”), see 1 Sam 15:12.

4.text: David seized from him 1,000 chariots, 7,000 charioteers, and 20,000 infantrymen . David cut the hamstrings of all but 100 of Hadadezer’s chariot horses.

notes.text: Or “horsemen.”
Heb “his”; the referent (Hadadezer) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “and David cut the hamstrings of all the chariot horses, and he left from them one hundred chariot horses.”

5.text: The Arameans of Damascus came to help King Hadadezer of Zobah, but David killed 22,000 of the Arameans.

6.text: David placed garrisons in the territory of the Arameans of Damascus; the Arameans became David’s subjects and brought tribute. The Lord protected David wherever he campaigned.

notes.text: Heb “and David placed in Aram of Damascus.” The object ‏נְצִיבִים‎ (netsivim, “garrisons”) appears to have been accidentally omitted from the text. See v. 13, as well as the parallel passage in 2 Sam 8:6, which includes it.
Or “delivered.”
Or “wherever he went.”

7.text: David took the golden shields which Hadadezer’s servants had carried and brought them to Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “which were upon the servants of Hadadezer.”

8.text: From Tibhath and Kun, Hadadezer’s cities, David took a great deal of bronze. (Solomon used it to make the big bronze basin called “The Sea,” the pillars, and other bronze items.)

notes.text: The MT reads “Tibhath” here, a variant name for Tebah (cf. 2 Sam 8:8). Some English translations substitute the other version of the name here (e.g., NIV, NLT), while others follow the reading of the Hebrew text at this point (e.g., NAB, NASB, NRSV).
The parallel text of 2 Sam 8:8 has the variant name “Berothai.”
Heb “the sea of bronze,” or “[the] sea, the bronze one.” See the note at 1 Kgs 7:23.

9.text: When King Tou of Hamath heard that David had defeated the entire army of King Hadadezer of Zobah,

notes.text: The name is spelled “Toi” in the parallel text in 2 Sam 8:9.

10.text: he sent his son Hadoram to King David to extend his best wishes and to pronounce a blessing on him for his victory over Hadadezer, for Tou had been at war with Hadadezer. He also sent various items made of gold, silver, and bronze.

notes.text: The name is spelled “Joram” in the parallel text in 2 Sam 8:10.
Heb “to ask concerning him for peace.”
Heb “and to bless him because he fought with Hadadezer and defeated him, for Hadadezer was a man of battles with Tou.”
Heb “[along with] all items of gold and silver and bronze.”

11.text: King David dedicated these things to the Lord, along with the silver and gold which he had carried off from all the nations, including Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and Amalek.

notes.text: Heb “also them King David made holy to the Lord.”
Heb “from.”
The parallel text of 2 Sam 8:12 of the MT reads “Aram.” However, a few Hebrew mss along with the LXX and Syriac of 2 Sam 8:12 read “Edom” in agreement with 1 Chr 18:11 (cf. 2 Sam 8:14).

12.text: Abishai son of Zeruiah killed 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt.

notes.text: The parallel text of 2 Sam 8:13 attributes this victory to David.

13.text: He placed garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites became David’s subjects. The Lord protected David wherever he campaigned.

notes.text: Or “delivered.”
Or “wherever he went.”

14.text: David reigned over all Israel; he guaranteed justice for all his people.

notes.text: Heb “and he was doing what is just and fair for all his people.”

15.text: Joab son of Zeruiah was commanding general of the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was secretary;

notes.text: Heb “over.”

16.text: Zadok son of Ahitub and Abimelech son of Abiathar were priests; Shavsha was scribe;

notes.text: The parallel text of 2 Sam 8:17 has the variant spelling “Seraiah.”

17.text: Benaiah son of Jehoiada supervised the Kerethites and Pelethites; and David’s sons were the king’s leading officials.

notes.text: Heb “[was] over.”
Heb “and the sons of David [were] the first ones at the hand of David.” The parallel text of 2 Sam 8:18 identifies them as “priests” (see sn there on the word “priests”).

1.text: Later King Nahash of the Ammonites died and his son succeeded him.

2.text: David said, “I will express my loyalty to Hanun son of Nahash, for his father was loyal to me.” So David sent messengers to express his sympathy over his father’s death. When David’s servants entered Ammonite territory to visit Hanun and express the king’s sympathy,

notes.text: Heb “do loyalty.”
Heb “did loyalty.”
Heb “to console him concerning his father.”
Heb “and the servants of David came to the land of the sons of Ammon to Hanun to console him.”

3.text: the Ammonite officials said to Hanun, “Do you really think David is trying to honor your father by sending these messengers to express his sympathy? No, his servants have come to you so they can get information and spy out the land!”

notes.text: Heb “Is David honoring your father in your eyes when he sends to you ones consoling?”

Heb “Is it not to explore and to overturn and to spy out the land (that) his servants have come to you?” The Hebrew term ‏לַהֲפֹךְ‎ (lahafokh, “to overturn”) seems misplaced in the sequence. Some emend the form to ‏לַחְפֹּר‎ (lakhpor, “to spy out”). The sequence of three infinitives may be a conflation of alternative readings.

4.text: So Hanun seized David’s servants and shaved their beards off. He cut off the lower part of their robes so that their buttocks were exposed and then sent them away.

notes.text: Heb “shaved them.” See v. 5.
Heb “and he cut their robes in the middle unto the buttocks.”

5.text: People came and told David what had happened to the men, so he sent messengers to meet them, for the men were thoroughly humiliated. The king said, “Stay in Jericho until your beards grow again; then you may come back.”

notes.text: Heb “they.” The logical referent, though not specified in the Hebrew text, has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

6.text: When the Ammonites realized that David was disgusted with them, Hanun and the Ammonites sent 1,000 talents of silver to hire chariots and charioteers from Aram Naharaim, Aram Maacah, and Zobah.

notes.text: Heb “that they were a stench [i.e., disgusting] with David.”

The Hebrew word ‏כִּכַּר‎ (kikkar, “circle”) refers generally to something that is round. When used of metals it can refer to a disk-shaped weight made of the metal or, by extension, to a standard unit of weight. According to the older (Babylonian) standard the “talent” weighed 130 lbs. (58.9 kg), but later this was lowered to 108.3 lbs. (49.1 kg). More recent research suggests the “light” standard talent was 67.3 lbs. (30.6 kg). Using this as the standard for calculation, the Ammonites hired chariots and charioteers for about 33.7 tons (30,600 kg) of silver.
The parallel text of 2 Sam 10:6 has “Aram Beth Rehob and Aram Zobah.”

7.text: They hired 32,000 chariots, along with the king of Maacah and his army, who came and camped in front of Medeba. The Ammonites also assembled from their cities and marched out to do battle.

8.text: When David heard the news, he sent Joab and the entire army to meet them.

notes.text: The words “the news” and “to meet them” are added in the translation for stylistic reasons and for clarification.

9.text: The Ammonites marched out and were deployed for battle at the entrance to the city, while the kings who had come were by themselves in the field.

10.text: When Joab saw that the battle would be fought on two fronts, he chose some of Israel’s best men and deployed them against the Arameans.

notes.text: The parallel text of 2 Sam 10:10 has “the Ammonites” in place of “the Arameans” here.
Heb “and Joab saw that the face of the battle was to him before and behind and he chose from all the best in Israel and arranged to meet Aram.”

11.text: He put his brother Abishai in charge of the rest of the army and they were deployed against the Ammonites.

12.text: Joab said, “If the Arameans start to overpower me, you come to my rescue. If the Ammonites start to overpower you, I will come to your rescue.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Joab) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “if Aram is stronger than me.”
Heb “if the sons of Ammon are stronger than you.”

13.text: Be strong! Let’s fight bravely for the sake of our people and the cities of our God! The Lord will do what he decides is best!”

notes.text: Heb “and the Lord, what is good in his eyes, he will do.”
