14.text: So Joab and his men marched toward the Arameans to do battle, and they fled before him.

notes.text: Heb “and the army which was with him.”

15.text: When the Ammonites saw the Arameans flee, they fled before Joab’s brother Abishai and withdrew into the city. Joab went back to Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “his”; the referent (Joab) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

16.text: When the Arameans realized they had been defeated by Israel, they sent for reinforcements from beyond the Euphrates River, led by Shophach the commanding general of Hadadezer’s army.

notes.text: Heb “the River,” referring to the Euphrates. This has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Heb “and Aram saw that they were struck down before Israel and they sent messengers and brought out Aram which is beyond the River, and Shophach the commander of the army of Hadadezer [was] before them.”

17.text: When David was informed, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan River, and marched against them. David deployed his army against the Arameans for battle and they fought against him.

notes.text: The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
The parallel text of 2 Sam 10:17 “he came to Helam.”
Heb “and he came to them and was deployed against them.”
Heb “and David was deployed to meet Aram [for] battle and they fought with him.”

18.text: The Arameans fled before Israel. David killed 7,000 Aramean charioteers and 40,000 infantrymen; he also killed Shophach the commanding general.

notes.text: The parallel text of 2 Sam 10:18 has “seven hundred.”
The parallel text of 2 Sam 10:18 has the variant spelling “Shobach.”

19.text: When Hadadezer’s subjects saw they were defeated by Israel, they made peace with David and became his subjects. The Arameans were no longer willing to help the Ammonites.

1.text: In the spring, at the time when kings normally conduct wars, Joab led the army into battle and devastated the land of the Ammonites. He went and besieged Rabbah, while David stayed in Jerusalem. Joab defeated Rabbah and tore it down.

notes.text: Heb “and it was at the time of the turning of the year, at the time of the going out of kings.”

2.text: David took the crown from the head of their king and wore it (its weight was a talent of gold and it was set with precious stones). He took a large amount of plunder from the city.

notes.text: The translation follows the MT, which reads “of their king”; the LXX and Vulgate read “of Milcom” (cf. 1 Kgs 11:5). Milcom, also known as Molech, was the god of the Ammonites.
Heb “and it was on the head of David.”
See the note on the word “talents” in 19:6.

3.text: He removed the city’s residents and made them labor with saws, iron picks, and axes. This was his policy with all the Ammonite cities. Then David and all the army returned to Jerusalem.

notes.text: The Hebrew text reads “saws,” but since saws were just mentioned, it is preferable to emend ‏מְגֵרוֹת‎ (megerot, “saws”) to ‏מַגְזְרוֹת‎ (magzerot, “axes”).
Heb “and so he would do.”

4.text: Later there was a battle with the Philistines in Gezer. At that time Sibbekai the Hushathite killed Sippai, one of the descendants of the Rephaim, and the Philistines were subdued.

notes.text: Heb “battle stood.”
The parallel text in 2 Sam 21:18 identifies this site as “Gob.”
The parallel text in 2 Sam 21:18 has the variant spelling “Saph.”
Heb “they”; the referent (the Philistines) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

5.text: There was another battle with the Philistines in which Elhanan son of Jair the Bethlehemite killed the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear had a shaft as big as the crossbeam of a weaver’s loom.

notes.text: The Hebrew text reads, “Elchanan son of Jair killed Lachmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite.” But it is likely that the accusative marker in front of ‏לַחְמִי‎ (lakhmi, “Lachmi”) was originally ‏בֵּית‎ (bet), and that ‏אֶת־לַחְמִי‎ (ʾet lakhmi) should be emended to ‏בֵּית הַלַּחְמִי‎ (bet hallakhmi, “the Bethlehemite”). See 2 Sam 21:19.
See tc note on the parallel passage in 2 Sam 21:19.

6.text: In a battle in Gath there was a large man who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot—twenty-four in all! He too was a descendant of Rapha.

notes.text: Heb “and there was another battle, in Gath.”

7.text: When he taunted Israel, Jonathan son of Shimea, David’s brother, killed him.

notes.text: The parallel text in 2 Sam 21:21 has the variant spelling “Shimeah.”

8.text: These were the descendants of Rapha who lived in Gath; they were killed by the hand of David and his soldiers.

notes.text: Heb “they fell.”
Heb “his servants.”

1.text: An adversary opposed Israel, inciting David to count how many warriors Israel had.

notes.text: Or “Satan.” The Hebrew word ‏שָׂטָן‎ (satan) refers to an adversary, typically used without the article to refer to anyone in an adversarial role. Used with the article in Job 1-2 and Zech 3:1-2, it refers to “The Satan,” the demonic opponent. Of the heavenly accuser in those passages NIDOTTE (IV, 1231) says that “it is improbable that a specific demonic being is referred to (a possible exception may be 1 Chr 21:1).” TLOT (p. 1269) believes that 1 Chr 21:1 represents the first use of “satan” without the article as a personal name. But see the study note at the end of the verse.
Heb “stood against.”
Heb “and incited David to count Israel.” As v. 5 indicates, David was not interested in a general census, but in determining how much military strength he had.

The parallel text in 2 Sam 24:1 says, “The Lord’s anger again raged against Israel and he incited David against them, saying: ‘Go, count Israel and Judah!’” The version of the incident in the Book of 2 Samuel gives an underlying theological perspective, while the Chronicler simply describes what happened from a human perspective. Many interpreters and translations render the Hebrew ‏שָׂטָן‎ as a proper name here, “Satan” (NEB, NASB, NIV, NRSV). However, the Hebrew term ‏שָׂטָן‎, which means “adversary,” is used here without the article. Elsewhere when it appears without the article, it refers to a personal or national adversary in the human sphere, the lone exception being Num 22:22, 32, where the angel of the Lord assumes the role of an adversary to Balaam. When referring elsewhere to the spiritual entity known in the NT as Satan, the noun has the article and is used as a title, “the Adversary” (see Job 1:6-9, 12; 2:1-4, 6-7; Zech 3:1-2). In light of usage elsewhere the adversary in 1 Chr 21:1 is likely a human enemy, probably a nearby nation whose hostility against Israel pressured David into numbering the people so he could assess his military strength. For compelling linguistic and literary arguments against taking the noun as a proper name here, see S. Japhet, I & II Chronicles (OTL), 374-75.

2.text: David told Joab and the leaders of the army, “Go, count the number of warriors from Beer Sheba to Dan. Then bring back a report to me so I may know how many we have.”

notes.text: Or “people.”
Heb “Go, count Israel.” See the note on “had” in v. 1.
Heb “their number.”

3.text: Joab replied, “May the Lord make his army a hundred times larger! My master, O king, do not all of them serve my master? Why does my master want to do this? Why bring judgment on Israel?”

notes.text: Or “people.”
Heb “Why should it become guilt for Israel?” David’s decision betrays an underlying trust in his own strength rather than in divine provision. See also 1 Chr 27:23-24.

4.text: But the king’s edict stood, despite Joab’s objections. So Joab left and traveled throughout Israel before returning to Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “and the word of the king was stronger than Joab.”

5.text: Joab reported to David the number of warriors. In all Israel there were 1,100,000 sword-wielding soldiers; Judah alone had 470,000 sword-wielding soldiers.

notes.text: Heb “and Joab gave to David the number of the numbering of the army [or “people”].”
Heb “a thousand thousands and 100,000.”
The parallel text in 2 Sam 24:9 has variant figures: “In Israel there were 800,000 sword-wielding warriors, and in Judah there were 500,000 soldiers.”

6.text: Now Joab did not number Levi and Benjamin, for the king’s edict disgusted him.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the proper name (“Joab”) has been substituted for the pronoun here for stylistic reasons; the proper name occurs at the end of the verse in the Hebrew text, where it has been replaced by the pronoun (“him”) in the translation.

7.text: God was also offended by it, so he attacked Israel.

notes.text: Heb “There was displeasure in the eyes of God concerning this thing.”

8.text: David said to God, “I have sinned greatly by doing this! Now, please remove the guilt of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.”

9.text: The Lord told Gad, David’s prophet,

notes.text: Heb “seer.”

10.text: “Go, tell David, ‘This is what the Lord says: “I am offering you three forms of judgment from which to choose. Pick one of them.”’”

notes.text: Heb “Three I am extending to you; choose for yourself one of them and I will do it to you.”

11.text: Gad went to David and told him, “This is what the Lord says: ‘Pick one of these:

12.text: three years of famine, or three months being chased by your enemies and struck down by their swords, or three days being struck down by the Lord, during which a plague will invade the land and the angel of the Lord will destroy throughout Israel’s territory.’ Now, decide what I should tell the one who sent me.”

notes.text: The parallel text in the MT of 2 Sam 24:13 has “seven,” but LXX has “three” there.

Heb “or three months being swept away from before your enemies and the sword of your enemies overtaking.” The Hebrew term ‏נִסְפֶּה‎ (nispeh, Niphal participle from ‏סָפָה‎, safah) should probably be emended to ‏נֻסְכָה‎ (nusekhah, Qal infinitive from ‏נוּס‎ [nus] with second masculine singular suffix). See 2 Sam 24:13.
Heb “or three days of the sword of the Lord and plague in the land, and the angel of the Lord destroying in all the territory of Israel.”

13.text: David said to Gad, “I am very upset! I prefer to be attacked by the Lord, for his mercy is very great; I do not want to be attacked by men!”

notes.text: Heb “There is great distress to me; let me fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercy is very great, but into the hand of men let me not fall.”

14.text: So the Lord sent a plague through Israel, and 70,000 Israelite men died.

15.text: God sent an angel to ravage Jerusalem. As he was doing so, the Lord watched and relented from his judgment. He told the angel who was destroying, “That’s enough! Stop now!” Now the angel of the Lord was standing near the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

notes.text: The parallel text of 2 Sam 24:15 reports that God sent a plague, while 24:16-17 attributes this to the instrumentality of an angel.
Or “destroy.”
Heb “while he was destroying.”
Or “saw.”
Or “was grieved because of.”
Heb “concerning the calamity.”
For this nuance of the Hebrew word ‏רַב‎ (rav), see BDB 913 s.v. 1.f.
Heb “Now, drop your hand.”
In the parallel text in 2 Sam 24:16 this individual is called ‏אֲרַוְנָא‎ (ʾaravnaʾ, “Aravna”), traditionally “Araunah.” The form of the name found here also occurs in vv. 18-28.

16.text: David looked up and saw the angel of the Lord standing between the earth and sky with his sword drawn and in his hand, stretched out over Jerusalem. David and the leaders, covered with sackcloth, threw themselves down with their faces to the ground.

notes.text: Heb “and David and the elders, covered with sackcloth, fell on their faces.”

17.text: David said to God, “Was I not the one who decided to number the army? I am the one who sinned and committed this awful deed! As for these sheep—what have they done? O Lord my God, attack me and my family, but remove the plague from your people!”

notes.text: “and doing evil I did evil.” The infinitive absolute precedes the finite form of the verb for emphasis.
Heb “let your hand be on me and on the house of my father.”
Heb “but on your people not for a plague.”

18.text: So the angel of the Lord told Gad to instruct David to go up and build an altar for the Lord on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

notes.text: Heb “that he should go up to raise up.”

19.text: So David went up as Gad instructed him to do in the name of the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “and David went up by the word of Gad which he spoke in the name of the Lord.”

20.text: While Ornan was threshing wheat, he turned and saw the messenger, and he and his four sons hid themselves.

21.text: When David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David; he came out from the threshing floor and bowed to David with his face to the ground.

notes.text: Heb “nostrils.”

22.text: David said to Ornan, “Sell me the threshing floor so I can build on it an altar for the Lord—I’ll pay top price —so that the plague may be removed from the people.”

notes.text: Heb “the place of the threshing floor.”
Following the imperative, the prefixed verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive here indicates the immediate purpose: “so I can build.”
Heb “For full silver sell to me.”

Following the imperative and first person prefixed verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive, this third person prefixed verbal form with vav conjunctive introduces the ultimate purpose: “so the plague may be removed.”

23.text: Ornan told David, “You can have it! My master, the king, may do what he wants. Look, I am giving you the oxen for burnt sacrifices, the threshing sledges for wood, and the wheat for an offering. I give it all to you.”

notes.text: Heb “take for yourself.”
Heb “what is good in his eyes.”

24.text: King David replied to Ornan, “No, I insist on buying it for top price. I will not offer to the Lord what belongs to you or offer a burnt sacrifice that cost me nothing.

notes.text: Heb “No, for buying I will buy for full silver.” The infinitive absolute precedes the finite verb for emphasis.
The parallel text in 2 Sam 24:24 has the plural “burnt sacrifices.”
Or “without [paying] compensation.”

25.text: So David bought the place from Ornan for 600 pieces of gold.

notes.text: The parallel text of 2 Sam 24:24 says David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for “fifty pieces of silver.” This would have been about 20 ounces (568 grams) of silver by weight.
Heb “six hundred shekels of gold.” This would have been about 15 lbs. (6.8 kg) of gold by weight.

26.text: David built there an altar to the Lord and offered burnt sacrifices and peace offerings. He called out to the Lord, and the Lord responded by sending fire from the sky and consuming the burnt sacrifice on the altar.

notes.text: Or “tokens of peace.”
Heb “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

27.text: The Lord ordered the messenger to put his sword back into its sheath.

notes.text: Heb “spoke to the messenger.”

28.text: At that time, when David saw that the Lord responded to him at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, he sacrificed there.

29.text: Now the Lord’s tabernacle (which Moses had made in the wilderness) and the altar for burnt sacrifices were at that time at the worship center in Gibeon.

notes.text: Or “high place.”

30.text: But David could not go before it to seek God’s will, for he was afraid of the sword of the angel of the Lord.

1.text: David then said, “This is the place where the temple of the Lord God will be, along with the altar for burnt sacrifices for Israel.”

2.text: David ordered the resident foreigners in the land of Israel to be called together. He appointed some of them to be stonecutters to chisel stones for the building of God’s temple.

notes.text: The term ‏גֵּר‎ (ger) refers to a foreign resident, but with different social implications in different settings. In Mosaic Law the resident foreigner was essentially a naturalized citizen and convert to worshiping the God of Israel (see Exod 12:19, 48; Deut 29:10-13).

3.text: David supplied a large amount of iron for the nails of the doors of the gates and for braces, more bronze than could be weighed,

4.text: and more cedar logs than could be counted. (The Sidonians and Tyrians had brought a large amount of cedar logs to David.)

5.text: David said, “My son Solomon is just an inexperienced young man, and the temple to be built for the Lord must be especially magnificent so it will become famous and be considered splendid by all the nations. Therefore I will make preparations for its construction.” So David made extensive preparations before he died.

notes.text: Heb “a young man and tender.”
Heb “and the house to build to make exceedingly great for a name and for splendor for all the lands.”

6.text: He summoned his son Solomon and charged him to build a temple for the Lord God of Israel.

7.text: David said to Solomon: “My son, I really wanted to build a temple to honor the Lord my God.

notes.text: Heb “I was with my heart.”
Heb “for the name of.”

8.text: But this was the Lord’s message to me: ‘You have spilled a great deal of blood and fought many battles. You must not build a temple to honor me, for you have spilled a great deal of blood on the ground before me.

notes.text: Heb “for my name.”

9.text: Look, you will have a son, who will be a peaceful man. I will give him rest from all his enemies on every side. Indeed, Solomon will be his name; I will give Israel peace and quiet during his reign.

notes.text: Heb “man of rest.”
Heb “his enemies all around.”
The name Solomon (‏שְׁלֹמֹה‎, shelomoh) sounds like (and may be derived from) the Hebrew word for “peace” (‏שָׁלוֹם‎, shalom).
Heb “in his days.”

10.text: He will build a temple to honor me; he will become my son, and I will become his father. I will grant to his dynasty permanent rule over Israel.’

notes.text: Heb “for my name.”
Heb “and I will establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel permanently.”

11.text: “Now, my son, may the Lord be with you! May you succeed and build a temple for the Lord your God, just as he announced you would.

notes.text: Heb “as he spoke concerning you.”

12.text: Only may the Lord give you insight and understanding when he places you in charge of Israel, so you may obey the law of the Lord your God.

notes.text: Or “keep.”

13.text: Then you will succeed, if you carefully obey the rules and regulations which the Lord ordered Moses to give to Israel. Be strong and brave! Don’t be afraid and don’t panic!

notes.text: Heb “which the Lord commanded Moses concerning Israel.”
Or perhaps, “and don’t get discouraged.”

14.text: Now, look, I have made every effort to supply what is needed to build the Lord’s temple. I have stored up 100,000 talents of gold, 1,000,000 talents of silver, and so much bronze and iron it cannot be weighed, as well as wood and stones. Feel free to add more!

notes.text: Heb “and look, in my affliction [or perhaps, “poverty”] I have supplied for the house of the Lord.”
See the note on the word “talents” in 19:6.
Heb “a thousand thousands.”

15.text: You also have available many workers, including stonecutters, masons, carpenters, and an innumerable array of workers who are skilled

notes.text: Heb “craftsmen of stone and wood.”

16.text: in using gold, silver, bronze, and iron. Get up and begin the work! May the Lord be with you!”

notes.text: Heb “and every kind of skilled one in all work, concerning gold, concerning silver, and concerning bronze, and concerning iron, there is no numbering.”

17.text: David ordered all the officials of Israel to support his son Solomon.

notes.text: Or “help.”

18.text: He told them, “The Lord your God is with you! He has made you secure on every side, for he handed over to me the inhabitants of the region and the region is subdued before the Lord and his people.

notes.text: The words “he told them” are added in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

In the Hebrew text the statement is phrased as a rhetorical question, “Is not the Lord your God with you?” The question anticipates the response, “Of course he is!” Thus in the translation the positive statement “The Lord your God is with you!” has been used.
Heb “and he gives rest to you all around.”
Or “earth.”
Or “earth.”

19.text: Now seek the Lord your God wholeheartedly and with your entire being! Get up and build the sanctuary of the Lord God! Then you can bring the ark of the Lord’s covenant and the holy items dedicated to God’s service into the temple that is built to honor the Lord.”

notes.text: Heb “now give your heart and your being to seek the Lord your God.”
Heb “to bring.”
Heb “items of holiness of God.”
Heb “for the name of the Lord.”

1.text: When David was old and approaching the end of his life, he made his son Solomon king over Israel.

notes.text: Heb “and full of years.”

2.text: David assembled all the leaders of Israel, along with the priests and the Levites.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (David) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

3.text: The Levites who were thirty years old and up were counted; there were 38,000 men.

notes.text: Heb “and their number by their heads, by men, was 38,000.”

4.text: David said, “Of these, 24,000 are to direct the work of the Lord’s temple; 6,000 are to be officials and judges;

notes.text: The words “David said” are supplied here in the translation for clarification. The appearance of the first person verb “I supplied” in v. 5 indicates that David is speaking here.

5.text: 4,000 are to be gatekeepers; and 4,000 are to praise the Lord with the instruments I supplied for worship.”

notes.text: Heb “made to [or “for”] praise.”

6.text: David divided them into groups corresponding to the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.

7.text: The Gershonites included Ladan and Shimei.

8.text: The sons of Ladan: Jehiel the oldest, Zetham, and Joel—three in all.

9.text: The sons of Shimei: Shelomoth, Haziel, and Haran—three in all. These were the leaders of the family of Ladan.

10.text: The sons of Shimei: Jahath, Zina, Jeush, and Beriah. These were Shimei’s sons—four in all.

notes.text: The MT reads “Zina” here and “Zizah” in v. 11. One Hebrew ms, the LXX, and the Vulgate, harmonizing the form of the name to that found in v. 11, read “Zizah” here.

Verses 8-10 are confusing. Two different lists of Shimei’s sons appear. In between these lists is the statement “these were the leaders of the family of Ladan,” suggesting that the list just before this includes the sons of Ladan, not Shimei. But verse 8 already lists Ladan’s sons. Apparently the text as it stands is a conflation of differing traditions.

11.text: Jahath was the oldest and Zizah the second oldest. Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, so they were considered one family with one responsibility.

12.text: The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel—four in all.

13.text: The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses. Aaron and his descendants were chosen on a permanent basis to consecrate the most holy items, to offer sacrifices before the Lord, to serve him, and to praise his name.

notes.text: Heb “and Aaron was set apart to consecrate it, the most holy things, he and his sons, permanently, to sacrifice before the Lord, to serve him, and to bless his name permanently.”

14.text: The descendants of Moses the man of God were considered Levites.

notes.text: Heb “and Moses the man of God, his sons were called to the tribe of Levi.”

15.text: The sons of Moses: Gershom and Eliezer.

16.text: The son of Gershom: Shebuel the oldest.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has the plural “sons,” but only one name appears after this. The attached phrase “the oldest” might indicate that Shebuel was not Gershom’s only son, but note v. 17.
The LXX reads Σουβαηλ (Soubaēl) here, a reading followed by NAB, NIV, NCV, CEV (“Shubael”); cf. 24:20.

17.text: The son of Eliezer was Rehabiah, the oldest. Eliezer had no other sons, but Rehabiah had many descendants.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has “the sons of Eliezer were,” but only one name appears after this in the verse, and we are specifically told that Eliezer had no other sons.

18.text: The son of Izhar: Shelomith the oldest.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has the plural “sons,” but only one name appears after this. The attached phrase “the oldest” might indicate that Shelomith was not Izhar’s only son, but note v. 17.

19.text: The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the oldest, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth.

20.text: The sons of Uzziel: Micah the oldest, and Isshiah the second.

21.text: The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The sons of Mahli: Eleazar and Kish.

22.text: Eleazar died without having sons; he had only daughters. The sons of Kish, their cousins, married them.

notes.text: Heb “the sons of Kish, their brothers [i.e., relatives/cousins] lifted them up.” For other uses of ‏נָאָשׂ‎ (naʾas, “lift up”) in the sense of “marry,” see BDB 671 s.v. Qal.3.d.

23.text: The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth—three in all.

24.text: These were the descendants of Levi according to their families, that is, the leaders of families as counted and individually listed who carried out assigned tasks in the Lord’s temple and were twenty years old and up.

notes.text: Heb “these were the sons of Levi according to the house of their fathers, heads of the fathers, according to their numberings, by number of names, according to their heads, doer[s] of the work for the service of the house of the Lord, from a son of twenty years and upwards.”

25.text: For David said, “The Lord God of Israel has given his people rest and has permanently settled in Jerusalem.

26.text: So the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle or any of the items used in its service.”

27.text: According to David’s final instructions, the Levites twenty years old or older were counted.

notes.text: Heb “for by the final words of David, they were the number of the sons of Levi, from a son of twenty years and upward.”

28.text: Their job was to help Aaron’s descendants in the service of the Lord’s temple. They were to take care of the courtyards, the rooms, ceremonial purification of all holy items, and other jobs related to the service of God’s temple.

notes.text: Heb “For their assignment was at the hand of the sons of Aaron for the work of the house of the Lord concerning the courtyards and concerning the rooms and concerning the purification of all holiness and the work of the service of the house of God.”

29.text: They also took care of the bread that is displayed, the flour for offerings, the unleavened wafers, the round cakes, the mixing, and all the measuring.

notes.text: Heb “with respect to.”
The Hebrew terms ‏מְשׂוּרָה‎ (mesurah) and ‏מִדָּה‎ (middah) refer to different types of measurements.

30.text: They also stood in a designated place every morning and offered thanks and praise to the Lord. They also did this in the evening

notes.text: Heb “and to stand.”

31.text: and whenever burnt sacrifices were offered to the Lord on the Sabbath and at new moon festivals and assemblies. A designated number were to serve before the Lord regularly in accordance with regulations.

notes.text: Heb “by number according to the manner upon them, regularly before the Lord.”

32.text: They were in charge of the meeting tent and the Holy Place, and helped their relatives, the descendants of Aaron, in the service of the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: Heb “and they kept the charge of the tent of meeting and the charge of the holy place and the charge of the sons of Aaron, their brothers, for the service of the house of the Lord.”

1.text: The divisions of Aaron’s descendants were as follows: The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.

2.text: Nadab and Abihu died before their father did; they had no sons. Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests.

3.text: David, Zadok (a descendant of Eleazar), and Ahimelech (a descendant of Ithamar) divided them into groups to carry out their assigned responsibilities.

notes.text: Heb “for their assignment in their service.”

4.text: The descendants of Eleazar had more leaders than the descendants of Ithamar, so they divided them up accordingly; the descendants of Eleazar had sixteen leaders, while the descendants of Ithamar had eight.

notes.text: Heb “And the sons of Eleazar were found to be more, with respect to the heads of men, than the sons of Ithamar, and they divided them. To the sons of Eleazar there were sixteen heads, according to the house of the fathers; and to the sons of Ithamar there were eight, according to the house of their fathers.”

5.text: They divided them by lots, for there were officials of the Holy Place and officials designated by God among the descendants of both Eleazar and Ithamar.

notes.text: Heb “and they divided them by lots, these with these, for the officials of the holy place and the officials of God were from the sons of Eleazar and among the sons of Ithamar.”

6.text: The scribe Shemaiah son of Nethanel, a Levite, wrote down their names before the king, the officials, Zadok the priest, Ahimelech son of Abiathar, and the leaders of the priestly and Levite families. One family was drawn by lot from Eleazar, and then the next from Ithamar.

notes.text: Heb “one house of a father was drawn by lot for Eleazar, and one [this assumes an emendation of ‏אָחֻז‎ (ʾakhuz) to ‏אֶחָד‎ (ʾekhad, “one”)] was drawn by lot for Ithamar.”

7.text: The first lot went to Jehoiarib, the second to Jedaiah,

8.text: the third to Harim, the fourth to Seorim,

9.text: the fifth to Malkijah, the sixth to Mijamin,

10.text: the seventh to Hakkoz, the eighth to Abijah,

11.text: the ninth to Jeshua, the tenth to Shecaniah,

12.text: the eleventh to Eliashib, the twelfth to Jakim,

13.text: the thirteenth to Huppah, the fourteenth to Jeshebeab,

14.text: the fifteenth to Bilgah, the sixteenth to Immer,

15.text: the seventeenth to Hezir, the eighteenth to Happizzez,

16.text: the nineteenth to Pethahiah, the twentieth to Jehezkel,

17.text: the twenty-first to Jakin, the twenty-second to Gamul,

18.text: the twenty-third to Delaiah, the twenty-fourth to Maaziah.

19.text: This was the order in which they carried out their assigned responsibilities when they entered the Lord’s temple, according to the regulations given them by their ancestor Aaron, just as the Lord God of Israel had instructed him.

notes.text: Heb “father.”
Heb “these were their responsibilities for their service to enter the house of the Lord according to their manner [given] by the hand of Aaron their father, as the Lord God of Israel commanded him.”

20.text: The rest of the Levites included: Shubael from the sons of Amram, Jehdeiah from the sons of Shubael,

notes.text: Heb “Belonging to the rest of the sons of Levi.”
This appears to be a variant of the name Shebuel (cf. 1 Chr 23:16 and 26:24).

21.text: the firstborn Isshiah from Rehabiah and the sons of Rehabiah,

22.text: Shelomoth from the Izharites, Jahath from the sons of Shelomoth.

23.text: The sons of Hebron: Jeriah, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth.

notes.text: Most Hebrew mss omit “Hebron” here, but see 1 Chr 23:19. The name is included in two Hebrew mss and some LXX mss.

24.text: The son of Uzziel: Micah; Shamir from the sons of Micah.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has the plural “sons,” but only one name appears after this.

25.text: The brother of Micah: Isshiah. Zechariah from the sons of Isshiah.

26.text: The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The son of Jaaziah: Beno.

notes.text: Heb “the sons of Jaaziah, Beno.” Apparently ‏בְנוֹ‎ (veno), which could be translated “his son,” is a proper name here. The text, however, may be defective at this point; a list of Jaaziah’s sons may have been accidentally omitted. See v. 27.

27.text: The sons of Merari, from Jaaziah: Beno, Shoham, Zaccur, and Ibri.

notes.text: Or “from Jaaziah his son.” See the note on “Beno” in v. 26.

28.text: From Mahli: Eleazar, who had no sons.

29.text: From Kish: Jerahmeel.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has, “Belonging to [i.e., from] Kish, the sons of Kish, Jerahmeel.” There appears to be a conflation of headings.

30.text: The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jerimoth. These were the Levites, listed by their families.

31.text: Like their relatives, the descendants of Aaron, they also cast lots before King David, Zadok, Ahimelech, the leaders of families, the priests, and the Levites. The families of the oldest son cast lots along with those of the youngest.

notes.text: Heb “the fathers [i.e., families] of the head [i.e., oldest] just like his youngest brother.”

1.text: David and the army officers selected some of the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun to prophesy as they played stringed instruments and cymbals. The following men were assigned this responsibility:

notes.text: Heb “David and the officers of the army set apart for service the sons of Asaph and Heman and Jeduthun, the ones prophesying by harps, by lyres, and by cymbals.”
Heb “and their number was, the men of work for their service.”

2.text: From the sons of Asaph: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asarelah. The sons of Asaph were supervised by Asaph, who prophesied under the king’s supervision.

notes.text: Heb “the sons of Asaph [were] upon the hand of Asaph, the one prophesying upon the hands of the king.”

3.text: From the sons of Jeduthun: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah—six in all, under supervision of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied as he played a harp, giving thanks and praise to the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “belonging to Jeduthun, the sons of Jeduthun.”
This name appears as “Izri” in v. 11.
One Hebrew ms and some LXX mss supply the name “Shimei” after “Jeshaiah.” Most Hebrew mss omit the name here (but cf. v. 17).
The list includes only five names. Apparently the name “Shimei” (see v. 17), which appears in one medieval Hebrew ms and in the LXX, has been accidentally omitted from the Hebrew text.

4.text: From the sons of Heman: Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel, Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, Romamti-Ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, and Mahazioth.

notes.text: Heb “belonging to Heman, the sons of Heman.”

5.text: All these were the sons of Heman, the king’s prophet. God had promised him these sons in order to make him prestigious. God gave Heman fourteen sons and three daughters.

notes.text: Heb “by the words of God to exalt a horn.” An animal’s horn is sometimes used metaphorically as a symbol of strength and honor. See BDB 901-2 s.v. ‏קֶרֶן‎.

6.text: All these were under the supervision of their fathers; they were musicians in the Lord’s temple, playing cymbals and stringed instruments as they served in God’s temple. Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman were under the supervision of the king.

7.text: They and their relatives, all of them skilled and trained to make music to the Lord, numbered 288.

notes.text: Heb “and their number with their brothers, trained in music to the Lord, all skilled, was 288.”

8.text: They cast lots to determine their responsibilities—oldest as well as youngest, teacher as well as student.

notes.text: Heb “and they cast lots [for] service, just as like small, like great, teacher with student.”

9.text: The first lot went to Asaph’s son Joseph and his relatives and sons—twelve in all, the second to Gedaliah and his relatives and sons—twelve in all,

notes.text: Heb “The first lot went to Asaph, to Joseph.” Apparently the recurring formula, “and his sons and his relatives, twelve” has been accidentally omitted from the Hebrew text at this point (see vv. 10-31; the formula is slightly different in v. 9b). If the number “twelve” is not supplied here, the total comes to only 276, not the 288 required by v. 7.

10.text: the third to Zaccur and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

11.text: the fourth to Izri and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

notes.text: “Izri” is a variant of the name “Zeri” (cf. 25:3).

12.text: the fifth to Nethaniah and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

13.text: the sixth to Bukkiah and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

14.text: the seventh to Jesharelah and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

notes.text: “Jesharelah” is a variant of the name “Asarelah” (cf. 25:2).

15.text: the eighth to Jeshaiah and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

16.text: the ninth to Mattaniah and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

17.text: the tenth to Shimei and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

18.text: the eleventh to Azarel and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

notes.text: “Azarel” is a variant of the name “Uzziel” (cf. 25:4).

19.text: the twelfth to Hashabiah and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

20.text: the thirteenth to Shubael and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

21.text: the fourteenth to Mattithiah and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

22.text: the fifteenth to Jerimoth and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

23.text: the sixteenth to Hananiah and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

24.text: the seventeenth to Joshbekashah and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

25.text: the eighteenth to Hanani and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

26.text: the nineteenth to Mallothi and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

27.text: the twentieth to Eliathah and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

28.text: the twenty-first to Hothir and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

29.text: the twenty-second to Giddalti and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

30.text: the twenty-third to Mahazioth and his sons and relatives—twelve in all,

31.text: the twenty-fourth to Romamti-Ezer and his sons and relatives—twelve in all.

1.text: The divisions of the gatekeepers: From the Korahites: Meshelemiah, son of Kore, one of the sons of Asaph.

2.text: Meshelemiah’s sons: The firstborn Zechariah, the second Jediael, the third Zebadiah, the fourth Jathniel,

3.text: the fifth Elam, the sixth Jehohanan, and the seventh Elihoenai.

4.text: Obed-Edom’s sons: The firstborn Shemaiah, the second Jehozabad, the third Joah, the fourth Sakar, the fifth Nethanel,

5.text: the sixth Ammiel, the seventh Issachar, and the eighth Peullethai. (Indeed, God blessed Obed-Edom.)

notes.text: Heb “blessed him.”

6.text: His son Shemaiah also had sons, who were leaders of their families, for they were highly respected.

7.text: The sons of Shemaiah: Othni, Rephael, Obed, and Elzabad. His relatives Elihu and Semakiah were also respected.

notes.text: Or “brothers.”

8.text: All these were the descendants of Obed-Edom. They and their sons and relatives were respected men, capable of doing their responsibilities. There were sixty-two of them related to Obed-Edom.

9.text: Meshelemiah had sons and relatives who were respected—eighteen in all.

10.text: Hosah, one of the descendants of Merari, had sons: The firstborn Shimri (he was not actually the firstborn, but his father gave him that status),

11.text: the second Hilkiah, the third Tebaliah, and the fourth Zechariah. All Hosah’s sons and relatives numbered thirteen.

12.text: These divisions of the gatekeepers, corresponding to their leaders, had assigned responsibilities, like their relatives, as they served in the Lord’s temple.

13.text: They cast lots, both young and old, according to their families, to determine which gate they would be responsible for.

notes.text: Heb “for a gate and a gate,” i.e., for each gate.

14.text: The lot for the east gate went to Shelemiah. They then cast lots for his son Zechariah, a wise adviser, and the lot for the north gate went to him.

notes.text: “Shelemiah” is a variant of the name “Meshelemiah” (cf. 26:2).

15.text: Obed-Edom was assigned the south gate, and his sons were assigned the storehouses.

16.text: Shuppim and Hosah were assigned the west gate, along with the Shalleketh gate on the upper road. One guard was adjacent to another.

notes.text: Heb “a guard alongside a guard.”

17.text: Each day there were six Levites posted on the east, four on the north, and four on the south. At the storehouses they were posted in pairs.

18.text: At the court on the west there were four posted on the road and two at the court.

19.text: These were the divisions of the gatekeepers who were descendants of Korah and Merari.

20.text: Their fellow Levites were in charge of the storehouses in God’s temple and the storehouses containing consecrated items.

notes.text: Following the LXX; the Hebrew reads, "And the Levites: Ahijah was"
Or “treasuries.”

21.text: The descendants of Ladan, who were descended from Gershon through Ladan and were leaders of the families of Ladan the Gershonite, included Jehieli

notes.text: “Ladan” is a variant of the name “Libni” (cf. 6:17).
“Jehieli” is a variant of the name “Jehiel” (cf. 23:8).

22.text: and the sons of Jehieli, Zetham and his brother Joel. They were in charge of the storehouses in the Lord’s temple.

23.text: As for the Amramites, Izharites, Hebronites, and Uzzielites:

24.text: Shebuel son of Gershom, the son of Moses, was the supervisor of the storehouses.

notes.text: A number of English versions follow the LXX and Vulgate and read “Shubael” here (e.g., NAB, NIV, NCV, CEV).

25.text: His relatives through Eliezer included: Rehabiah his son, Jeshaiah his son, Joram his son, Zikri his son, and Shelomith his son.

notes.text: The marginal reading (Qere) is “Shelomith,” while the consonantal text (Kethib) has “Shelomoth.”

26.text: Shelomith and his relatives were in charge of all the storehouses containing the consecrated items dedicated by King David, the family leaders who led units of a thousand and a hundred, and the army officers.

notes.text: The MT reads “Shelomoth”; the name is spelled “Shelomith” in the marginal reading (Qere) of v. 25.

27.text: They had dedicated some of the plunder taken in battles to be used for repairs on the Lord’s temple.

28.text: They were also in charge of everything dedicated by Samuel the prophet, Saul son of Kish, Abner son of Ner, and Joab son of Zeruiah; Shelomith and his relatives were in charge of everything that had been dedicated.

notes.text: Or “seer.”

29.text: As for the Izharites: Kenaniah and his sons were given responsibilities outside the temple as officers and judges over Israel.

notes.text: The words “the temple” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

30.text: As for the Hebronites: Hashabiah and his relatives, 1,700 respected men, were assigned responsibilities in Israel west of the Jordan; they did the Lord’s work and the king’s service.

31.text: As for the Hebronites: Jeriah was the leader of the Hebronites according to the genealogical records. In the fortieth year of David’s reign, they examined the records and discovered there were highly respected men in Jazer in Gilead.

notes.text: Heb “and they were searched and there were found in them.”

32.text: Jeriah had 2,700 relatives who were respected family leaders. King David placed them in charge of the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh; they took care of all matters pertaining to God and the king.

notes.text: Heb “and his brothers, sons of respect, [were] 2,700, heads of fathers.”
Heb “with respect to every matter of God and matter of the king.”

1.text: What follows is a list of Israelite family leaders and commanders of units of a thousand and a hundred, as well as their officers who served the king in various matters. Each division was assigned to serve for one month during the year; each consisted of 24,000 troops.

notes.text: Heb “and the sons of Israel according to their number, heads of the fathers and the commanders of the thousands and the hundreds and their officers who served the king with respect to every matter of the divisions, [that which] comes and goes out month by month according to all the months of the year, one division [was] twenty-four thousand.”

2.text: Jashobeam son of Zabdiel was in charge of the first division, which was assigned the first month. His division consisted of 24,000 troops.

3.text: He was a descendant of Perez; he was in charge of all the army officers for the first month.

4.text: Dodai the Ahohite was in charge of the division assigned the second month; Mikloth was the next in rank. His division consisted of 24,000 troops.

notes.text: Heb “and his division and Mikloth, the leader.”

5.text: The third army commander, assigned the third month, was Benaiah son of Jehoiada the priest. He was the leader of his division, which consisted of 24,000 troops.

6.text: Benaiah was the leader of the thirty warriors and his division; his son was Ammizabad.

notes.text: Heb “That [was the] Benaiah [who was] a warrior of the thirty and over the thirty, and his division, Ammizabad his son.”

7.text: The fourth, assigned the fourth month, was Asahel, brother of Joab; his son Zebadiah succeeded him. His division consisted of 24,000 troops.

notes.text: Heb “[was] after him.”

8.text: The fifth, assigned the fifth month, was the commander Shamhuth the Izrahite. His division consisted of 24,000 troops.

9.text: The sixth, assigned the sixth month, was Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite. His division consisted of 24,000 troops.

10.text: The seventh, assigned the seventh month, was Helez the Pelonite, an Ephraimite. His division consisted of 24,000 troops.

11.text: The eighth, assigned the eighth month, was Sibbekai the Hushathite, a Zerahite. His division consisted of 24,000 troops.

12.text: The ninth, assigned the ninth month, was Abiezer the Anathothite, a Benjaminite. His division consisted of 24,000 troops.

13.text: The tenth, assigned the tenth month, was Maharai the Netophathite, a Zerahite. His division consisted of 24,000 troops.

14.text: The eleventh, assigned the eleventh month, was Benaiah the Pirathonite, an Ephraimite. His division consisted of 24,000 troops.

15.text: The twelfth, assigned the twelfth month, was Heldai the Netophathite, a descendant of Othniel. His division consisted of 24,000 troops.

16.text: The officers of the Israelite tribes: Eliezer son of Zikri was the leader of the Reubenites, Shephatiah son of Maacah led the Simeonites,

17.text: Hashabiah son of Kemuel led the Levites, Zadok led the descendants of Aaron,

18.text: Elihu, a brother of David, led Judah, Omri son of Michael led Issachar,

19.text: Ishmaiah son of Obadiah led Zebulun, Jerimoth son of Azriel led Naphtali,

20.text: Hoshea son of Azaziah led the Ephraimites, Joel son of Pedaiah led the half-tribe of Manasseh,

21.text: Iddo son of Zechariah led the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Jaasiel son of Abner led Benjamin,

22.text: Azarel son of Jeroham led Dan. These were the commanders of the Israelite tribes.

23.text: David did not count the males twenty years old and under, for the Lord had promised to make Israel as numerous as the stars in the sky.

24.text: Joab son of Zeruiah started to count the men but did not finish. God was angry with Israel because of this, so the number was not recorded in the scroll called The Annals of King David.

notes.text: Heb “anger was on Israel.”

The Hebrew text has “in the number,” but ‏מִסְפַּר‎ (mispar) is probably dittographic—note that the same word appears immediately before this. The form should be emended to ‏בְּסֵפֶר‎ (besefer, “in the scroll”).

25.text: Azmaveth son of Adiel was in charge of the king’s storehouses; Jonathan son of Uzziah was in charge of the storehouses in the field, in the cities, in the towns, and in the towers.

26.text: Ezri son of Kelub was in charge of the field workers who farmed the land.

notes.text: Heb “with respect to the work of the land.” The phrase refers to agricultural labor; see HALOT 776-77 s.v. ‏עֲבֹדָה‎.

27.text: Shimei the Ramathite was in charge of the vineyards; Zabdi the Shiphmite was in charge of the wine stored in the vineyards.

notes.text: Heb “and over [that] which is in the vineyards, with respect to the storehouses of the wine, [was] Zabdi the Shiphmite.”

28.text: Baal Hanan the Gederite was in charge of the olive and sycamore trees in the foothills; Joash was in charge of the storehouses of olive oil.

notes.text: The foothills (‏שְׁפֵלָה‎, shephelah) are the region between the Judean hill country and the Mediterranean coastal plain.

29.text: Shitrai the Sharonite was in charge of the cattle grazing in Sharon; Shaphat son of Adlai was in charge of the cattle in the valleys.

30.text: Obil the Ishmaelite was in charge of the camels; Jehdeiah the Meronothite was in charge of the donkeys.

31.text: Jaziz the Hagrite was in charge of the sheep. All these were the officials in charge of King David’s property.

32.text: Jonathan, David’s uncle, was a wise adviser and scribe; Jehiel son of Hacmoni cared for the king’s sons.

notes.text: Heb “was an adviser, a man of insight, and he was a scribe.”
Heb “[was] with” (so KJV, ASV); NASB “tutored”; NRSV “attended”; NLT “was responsible to teach.’

33.text: Ahithophel was the king’s adviser; Hushai the Arkite was the king’s confidant.

notes.text: Heb “friend.”

34.text: Ahithophel was succeeded by Jehoiada son of Benaiah and by Abiathar. Joab was the commanding general of the king’s army.

1.text: David assembled in Jerusalem all the officials of Israel, including the commanders of the tribes, the commanders of the army divisions that served the king, the commanders of units of a thousand and a hundred, the officials who were in charge of all the property and livestock of the king and his sons, the eunuchs, and the warriors, including the most skilled of them.

2.text: King David rose to his feet and said: “Listen to me, my brothers and my people. I wanted to build a temple where the ark of the Lord’s covenant could be placed as a footstool for our God. I have made the preparations for building it.

notes.text: Heb “I, [it was] with my heart to build a house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the Lord and for a stool of the feet of our God.”

3.text: But God said to me, ‘You must not build a temple to honor me, for you are a warrior and have spilled blood.’

notes.text: Heb “for my name.”

4.text: The Lord God of Israel chose me out of my father’s entire family to become king over Israel and have a permanent dynasty. Indeed, he chose Judah as leader, and my father’s family within Judah, and then he picked me out from among my father’s sons and made me king over all Israel.

notes.text: Heb “out of all the house of my father to become king over all Israel permanently.”
Or “for.”
Heb “and among the sons of my father he desired to make me king over all Israel.”

5.text: From all the many sons the Lord has given me, he chose Solomon my son to rule on his behalf over Israel.

notes.text: Heb “from all my sons, for many sons the Lord has given to me, he chose Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the Lord over Israel.”

6.text: He said to me, ‘Solomon your son is the one who will build my temple and my courts, for I have chosen him to become my son and I will become his father.

7.text: I will establish his kingdom permanently, if he remains committed to obeying my commands and regulations, as you are doing this day.’

notes.text: Heb “if he is strong to do my commands and my regulations like this day.”

8.text: So now, in the sight of all Israel, the Lord’s assembly, and in the hearing of our God, I say this: Carefully observe all the commands of the Lord your God, so that you may possess this good land and may leave it as a permanent inheritance for your children after you.

notes.text: The words “I say this” are not in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.
Heb “Keep and seek”

9.text: “And you, Solomon my son, obey the God of your father and serve him with a submissive attitude and a willing spirit, for the Lord examines all minds and understands every motive of one’s thoughts. If you seek him, he will let you find him, but if you abandon him, he will reject you permanently.

notes.text: Heb “know.”
Heb “with a complete heart and a willing being.”
Heb “he will allow himself to be found by you.”

10.text: Realize now that the Lord has chosen you to build a temple as his sanctuary. Be strong and do it!”

notes.text: Heb “see.”

11.text: David gave to his son Solomon the blueprints for the temple porch, its buildings, its treasuries, its upper areas, its inner rooms, and the room for atonement.

notes.text: Heb “for the porch.” The word “temple” was supplied in the translation for clarity.
Or “storerooms.”
Heb “house.”

12.text: He gave him the blueprints of all he envisioned for the courts of the Lord’s temple, all the surrounding rooms, the storehouses of God’s temple, and the storehouses for the holy items.

notes.text: The words “he gave him” are supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.
Heb “the pattern of all which was in the spirit with him.”

13.text: He gave him the regulations for the divisions of priests and Levites, for all the assigned responsibilities within the Lord’s temple, and for all the items used in the service of the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: The words “he gave him the regulations” are supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

14.text: He gave him the prescribed weight for all the gold items to be used in various types of service in the Lord’s temple, for all the silver items to be used in various types of service,

notes.text: The words “he gave him” are supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.
Heb “for the gold, by the weight, for the gold, for all the items of service and service, for all the items of silver by weight for all the items of service and service.”

15.text: for the gold lampstands and their gold lamps, including the weight of each lampstand and its lamps, for the silver lampstands, including the weight of each lampstand and its lamps, according to the prescribed use of each lampstand,

16.text: for the gold used in the display tables, including the amount to be used in each table, for the silver to be used in the silver tables,

17.text: for the pure gold used for the meat forks, bowls, and jars, for the small gold bowls, including the weight for each bowl, for the small silver bowls, including the weight for each bowl,

18.text: and for the refined gold of the incense altar. He gave him the blueprint for the seat of the gold cherubim that spread their wings and provide shelter for the ark of the Lord’s covenant.

notes.text: The words “he gave him” are supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

The Hebrew text reads ‏מֶרְכָּבָה‎ (merkavah, “chariot”), but the final he (‏ה‎) is probably dittographic—note the prefixed he (‏ה‎) on the immediately following word. It is preferable to read ‏מֶרְכָּב‎ (merkav, “seat”).

The Hebrew text does not have “their wings,” but the word ‏כְּנָפַיִם‎ (kenafayim, “wings”) has probably been accidentally omitted by homoioteleuton. Note that the immediately preceding ‏לְפֹרְשִׂים‎ (leforsim) also ends in mem (‏ם‎).

19.text: David said, “All this I put in writing as the Lord directed me and gave me insight regarding the details of the blueprints.”

notes.text: The words “David said” are supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.
Heb “the whole in writing from the hand of the Lord upon me, he gave insight [for] all the workings of the plan.”

20.text: David said to his son Solomon: “Be strong and brave! Do it! Don’t be afraid and don’t panic! For the Lord God, my God, is with you. He will not leave you or abandon you before all the work for the service of the Lord’s temple is finished.

notes.text: Or perhaps, “don’t be discouraged.”

21.text: Here are the divisions of the priests and Levites who will perform all the service of God’s temple. All the willing and skilled men are ready to assist you in all the work and perform their service. The officials and all the people are ready to follow your instructions.”

notes.text: Heb “and with you in all work, for every willing [one] in skill for all service.”
Heb “and the officials and all the people to all your words.”

1.text: King David said to the entire assembly: “My son Solomon, the one whom God has chosen, is just an inexperienced young man, and the task is great, for this palace is not for man, but for the Lord God.

notes.text: Heb “a young man and tender.”

2.text: So I have made every effort to provide what is needed for the temple of my God, including the gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, as well as a large amount of onyx, settings of antimony and other stones, all kinds of precious stones, and alabaster.

notes.text: Heb “and according to all my strength.”
Heb “the gold for the gold, and the silver for the silver, and the bronze for the bronze, the iron for the iron, and the wood for the wood.”

3.text: Now, to show my commitment to the temple of my God, I donate my personal treasure of gold and silver to the temple of my God, in addition to all that I have already supplied for this holy temple.

4.text: This includes 3,000 talents of gold from Ophir and 7,000 talents of refined silver for overlaying the walls of the buildings,

notes.text: See the note on the word “talents” in 19:6. Using the “light” standard talent of 67.3 lbs. (30.6 kg) as the standard for calculation, David had supplied 101 tons (91,800 kg) of gold and 235.5 tons (214,200 kg) of silver.

5.text: for gold and silver items, and for all the work of the craftsmen. Who else wants to contribute to the Lord today?”

6.text: The leaders of the families, the leaders of the Israelite tribes, the commanders of units of a thousand and a hundred, and the supervisors of the king’s work contributed willingly.

7.text: They donated for the service of God’s temple 5,000 talents and 10,000 darics of gold, 10,000 talents of silver, 18,000 talents of bronze, and 100,000 talents of iron.

notes.text: See the note on the word “talents” in 19:6. Using the “light” standard talent of 67.3 lbs. (30.6 kg) as the standard for calculation, the people donated 168.3 tons (153,000 kg) of gold, 336.5 tons (306,000 kg) of silver, 605.7 tons (550,800 kg) of bronze, and 3,365 tons (3,060,000 kg) of iron.
On the “daric” as a unit of measure, see BDB 204 s.v. ‏דַּרְכְּמוֹן‎. Some have regarded the daric as a minted coin, perhaps even referring to the Greek drachma, but this is less likely.

The daric was a unit of weight perhaps equal to between 8 and 9 grams (just under one-third of an ounce), so 10,000 darics of gold would weigh between 80 and 90 kilograms (between 176 and 198 pounds).

8.text: All who possessed precious stones donated them to the treasury of the Lord’s temple, which was under the supervision of Jehiel the Gershonite.

notes.text: The word “precious” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

9.text: The people were delighted with their donations, for they contributed to the Lord with a willing attitude; King David was also very happy.

notes.text: Heb “with a complete heart.”
Heb “And also David the king rejoiced with great joy.”

10.text: David praised the Lord before the entire assembly: “O Lord God of our father Israel, you deserve praise forevermore!

notes.text: Heb “assembly, and David said.” The words “and David said” are redundant according to contemporary English style and have not been included in the translation.

11.text: O Lord, you are great, mighty, majestic, magnificent, glorious, and sovereign over all the sky and earth! You, Lord, have dominion and exalt yourself as the ruler of all.

notes.text: The words “and sovereign” are added in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.
Heb “head.”

12.text: You are the source of wealth and honor; you rule over all. You possess strength and might to magnify and give strength to all.

notes.text: Heb “wealth and honor [are] from before you.”
Heb “and in your hand [is] strength and might, and [it is] in your hand to magnify and to give strength to all.”

13.text: Now, our God, we give thanks to you and praise your majestic name!

14.text: “But who am I and who are my people, that we should be in a position to contribute this much? Indeed, everything comes from you, and we have simply given back to you what is yours.

notes.text: Heb “that we should retain strength to contribute like this.”
Heb “and from you we have given to you.”

15.text: For we are resident foreigners and temporary settlers in your presence, as all our ancestors were; our days are like a shadow on the earth, without security.

notes.text: The Hebrew terms ger (‏גֵּר‎; “resident foreigner”) and toshav (‏תּוֹשָׁב‎; “resident/dweller”) have similar meanings. They are not used here with the technical distinctions of most references in Mosaic Law. 1 Chron 29:15 takes up this language from Lev 25:23 where the terms emphasize that Israel would be a guest on God’s land. This is a privileged but dependent position; they did not own the land. Cf. also Ps 39:12 and Gen 23:4.
Heb “fathers” (also in vv. 18, 20).
Or perhaps “hope.”

16.text: O Lord our God, all this wealth, which we have collected to build a temple for you to honor your holy name, comes from you; it all belongs to you.

17.text: I know, my God, that you examine thoughts and are pleased with integrity. With pure motives I contribute all this; and now I look with joy as your people who have gathered here contribute to you.

notes.text: Heb “a heart.”
Heb “with integrity of heart.”

18.text: O Lord God of our ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, always maintain these motives of your people and keep them devoted to you.

notes.text: Heb “keep this permanently with respect to the motive of the thoughts of the heart of your people, and make firm their heart to you.”

19.text: Make my son Solomon willing to obey your commands, rules, and regulations, and to complete building the palace for which I have made preparations.”

notes.text: Heb “and to Solomon my son give a complete heart to keep your commands, your rules and your regulations, and to do everything, and to build the palace [for] which I have prepared.”

20.text: David told the entire assembly: “Praise the Lord your God!” So the entire assembly praised the Lord God of their ancestors; they bowed down and stretched out flat on the ground before the Lord and the king.

21.text: The next day they made sacrifices and offered burnt sacrifices to the Lord (1,000 bulls, 1,000 rams, 1,000 lambs), along with their accompanying drink offerings and many other sacrifices for all Israel.

22.text: They held a feast before the Lord that day and celebrated. Then they designated Solomon, David’s son, as king a second time; before the Lord they anointed him as ruler and Zadok as priest.

notes.text: Heb “they ate and drank.”
Heb “with great joy.”
See 1 Chr 23:1, where David had previously designated Solomon as king over Israel.

23.text: Solomon sat on the Lord’s throne as king in place of his father David; he was successful and all Israel was loyal to him.

notes.text: Heb “listened to him.”

24.text: All the officers and warriors, as well as all of King David’s sons, pledged their allegiance to King Solomon.

notes.text: Heb “placed a hand under Solomon the king.”

25.text: The Lord greatly magnified Solomon before all Israel and bestowed on him greater majesty than any king of Israel before him.

notes.text: Heb “and gave to him glory of kingship which there was not concerning every king before him over Israel.”

26.text: David son of Jesse reigned over all Israel.

27.text: He reigned over Israel forty years; he reigned in Hebron seven years and in Jerusalem thirty-three years.

28.text: He died at a good old age, having enjoyed long life, wealth, and honor. His son Solomon succeeded him.

notes.text: Heb “satisfied with days, wealth, and honor.”

29.text: King David’s accomplishments, from start to finish, are recorded in the Annals of Samuel the prophet, the Annals of Nathan the prophet, and the Annals of Gad the prophet.

notes.text: Heb “and the events of David the king, the former and the latter, look they are written in the annals of Samuel the seer, and in the annals of Nathan the prophet, and in the annals of Gad the seer.”

30.text: Recorded there are all the facts about his reign and accomplishments, and an account of the events that involved him, Israel, and all the neighboring kingdoms.

notes.text: Heb “with all his reign and his might, and the times which passed over him and over Israel and over all the kingdoms of the lands.”

1.text: Solomon son of David solidified his royal authority, for the Lord his God was with him and magnified him greatly.

notes.text: Heb “and Solomon son of David strengthened himself over his kingdom.”
The disjunctive clause (note the vav [‏ו‎] + subject pattern) probably has a causal nuance here.

2.text: Solomon addressed all Israel, including those who commanded units of a thousand and a hundred, the judges, and all the leaders of all Israel who were heads of families.

3.text: Solomon and the entire assembly went to the worship center in Gibeon, for the tent where they met God was located there, which Moses the Lord’s servant had made in the wilderness.

notes.text: Or “high place.”
Heb “the tent of meeting of God.”

4.text: (Now David had brought up the ark of God from Kiriath Jearim to the place he had prepared for it, for he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem.

5.text: But the bronze altar made by Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, was in front of the Lord’s tabernacle. Solomon and the entire assembly prayed to him there.)

notes.text: The tabernacle was located in Gibeon; see 1 Chr 21:29.
Heb “sought [or “inquired of”] him.”

6.text: Solomon went up to the bronze altar before the Lord which was at the meeting tent, and he offered up 1,000 burnt sacrifices.

7.text: That night God appeared to Solomon and said to him, “Tell me what I should give you.”

notes.text: Or “revealed himself.”
Heb “ask.”

8.text: Solomon replied to God, “You demonstrated great loyalty to my father David and have made me king in his place.

notes.text: Heb “did.”

9.text: Now, Lord God, may your promise to my father David be realized, for you have made me king over a great nation as numerous as the dust of the earth.

notes.text: Heb “your word.”
Or “be firm, established.”

10.text: Now give me wisdom and discernment so I can effectively lead this nation. Otherwise no one is able to make judicial decisions for this great nation of yours.”

notes.text: The cohortative with prefixed vav (‏ו‎) following the imperative here indicates purpose/result.
Heb “so I may go out before this nation and come in.” The expression “go out…and come in” here means “to lead” (see HALOT 425 s.v. ‏יצא‎ qal.4).
Heb “for.” The word “otherwise” is used to reflect the logical sense of the statement.
Heb “who is able?” The rhetorical question anticipates the answer, “no one.”
Heb “to judge.”
Heb “these numerous people of yours.”

11.text: God said to Solomon, “Because you desire this, and did not ask for riches, wealth, and honor, or for vengeance on your enemies, and because you did not ask for long life, but requested wisdom and discernment so you can make judicial decisions for my people over whom I have made you king,

notes.text: Heb “because this was in your heart.”
Heb “the life of those who hate you.”
Heb “many days.”

12.text: you are granted wisdom and discernment. Furthermore I am giving you riches, wealth, and honor surpassing that of any king before or after you.”

notes.text: Heb “wisdom and discernment are given to you.”
Heb “which was not so for the kings who were before you, and after you there will not be so.”

13.text: Solomon left the meeting tent at the worship center in Gibeon and went to Jerusalem, where he reigned over Israel.

notes.text: Heb “and Solomon came from the high place which was in Gibeon [to] Jerusalem, from before the tent of meeting, and he reigned over Israel.”

14.text: Solomon accumulated chariots and horses. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses . He kept them in assigned cities and in Jerusalem.

notes.text: Or “gathered.”
Heb “he placed them in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.”

15.text: The king made silver and gold as plentiful in Jerusalem as stones; cedar was as plentiful as sycamore fig trees are in the foothills.

notes.text: The words “as plentiful” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “he made.”
The foothills (‏שְׁפֵלָה‎, shephelah) are the region between the Judean hill country and the Mediterranean coastal plain.

16.text: Solomon acquired his horses from Egypt and from Que; the king’s traders purchased them from Que.

notes.text: Because Que is also mentioned, some prefer to see v. 16-17 as a reference to Mutsur. Que and Mutsur were located in Cilicia or Cappadocia (in modern southern Turkey). See HALOT 625 s.v. ‏מִצְרַיִם‎.

17.text: They paid 600 silver pieces for each chariot from Egypt, and 150 silver pieces for each horse. They also sold chariots and horses to all the kings of the Hittites and to the kings of Syria.

notes.text: Heb “and they brought up and brought out from Egypt a chariot for 600 silver (pieces), and a horse for 150, and in the same way to all the kings of the Hittites and to the kings of Aram by their hand they brought out.”

1.text: (1:18) Solomon ordered a temple to be built to honor the Lord, as well as a royal palace for himself.

notes.text: Beginning with 2:1, the verse numbers through 2:18 in the English Bible differ from the verse numbers in the Hebrew text (BHS), with 2:1 ET = 1:18 HT, 2:2 ET = 2:1 HT, 2:3 ET = 2:2 HT, etc., through 2:18 ET = 2:17 HT. Beginning with 3:1 the verse numbers in the ET and HT are again the same.
Heb “and Solomon said to build a house for the name of the Lord and house for his kingship.”

2.text: (2:1) Solomon had 70,000 common laborers and 80,000 stonecutters in the hills, in addition to 3,600 supervisors.

notes.text: Heb “counted,” perhaps “conscripted” (so NAB, NIV, NRSV).
Heb “men, carriers of loads.”
Or “quarry workers”; Heb “cutters” (probably referring to stonecutters).
The parallel text of MT in 1 Kgs 5:16 has “thirty-three hundred,” but some Greek mss there read “thirty-six hundred” in agreement with 2 Chr 2:2, 18.
Heb “and 3,600 supervisors over them.”

3.text: Solomon sent a message to King Huram of Tyre: “Help me as you did my father David, when you sent him cedar logs for the construction of his palace.

notes.text: Heb “Huram.” Some medieval Hebrew mss, along with the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate spell the name “Hiram,” agreeing with 1 Chr 14:1. “Huram” is a variant spelling referring to the same individual.
The words “help me” are supplied in the translation for clarification and stylistic reasons.
Heb “cedars.” The word “logs” has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
Heb “to build for him a house to live in it.”

4.text: Look, I am ready to build a temple to honor the Lord my God and to dedicate it to him in order to burn fragrant incense before him, to set out the bread that is regularly displayed, and to offer burnt sacrifices each morning and evening, and on Sabbaths, new moon festivals, and at other times appointed by the Lord our God. This is something Israel must do on a permanent basis.

notes.text: Heb “for the name of.”
Heb “and the regular display.”
Heb “permanently [is] this upon Israel.”

5.text: I will build a great temple, for our God is greater than all gods.

6.text: Of course, who can really build a temple for him, since the sky and the highest heavens cannot contain him? Who am I that I should build him a temple! It will really be only a place to offer sacrifices before him.

notes.text: Or “heavens” (also in v. 12). The Hebrew term ‏שָׁמַיִם‎ (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.
Heb “Who retains strength to build for him a house, for the heavens and the heavens of heavens do not contain him? And who am I that I should build for him a house, except to sacrifice before him?”

7.text: “Now send me a man who is skilled in working with gold, silver, bronze, and iron, as well as purple-, crimson-, and blue-colored fabrics, and who knows how to engrave. He will work with my skilled craftsmen here in Jerusalem and Judah, whom my father David provided.

8.text: Send me cedars, evergreens, and algum trees from Lebanon, for I know your servants are adept at cutting down trees in Lebanon. My servants will work with your servants

notes.text: This is probably a variant name for almug trees; see 9:10-11 and the parallel passage in 1 Kgs 10:11-12; cf. NLT. One or the other probably arose through metathesis of letters.
Heb “know.”

9.text: to supply me with large quantities of timber, for I am building a great, magnificent temple.

10.text: Look, I will pay your servants who cut the timber 20,000 cors of ground wheat, 20,000 cors of barley, 120,000 gallons of wine, and 120,000 gallons of olive oil.”

notes.text: As a unit of dry measure a cor was roughly equivalent to six bushels (about 220 liters).

Heb “20,000 baths” (also a second time later in this verse). A bath was a liquid measure roughly equivalent to six gallons (about 22 liters), so this was a quantity of about 120,000 gallons (440,000 liters).

11.text: King Huram of Tyre sent this letter to Solomon: “Because the Lord loves his people, he has made you their king.”

notes.text: Heb “Huram” (also in v. 12). Some medieval Hebrew mss, along with the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate spell the name “Hiram,” agreeing with 1 Chr 14:1. “Huram” is a variant spelling referring to the same individual.

12.text: Huram also said, “Worthy of praise is the Lord God of Israel, who made the sky and the earth! He has given King David a wise son who has discernment and insight and will build a temple for the Lord, as well as a royal palace for himself.

notes.text: Heb “who has given to King David a wise son knowing discernment and insight, who will build a house for the Lord and house for his kingship.”

13.text: Now I am sending you Huram Abi, a skilled and capable man,

notes.text: The name Huram Abi means “Huram [is] my father.”

14.text: whose mother is a Danite and whose father is a Tyrian. He knows how to work with gold, silver, bronze, iron, stones, and wood, as well as purple, blue, white, and crimson fabrics. He knows how to do all kinds of engraving and understands any design given to him. He will work with your skilled craftsmen and the skilled craftsmen of my lord David your father.

notes.text: Heb “a son of a woman from the daughters of Dan, and his father a man of Tyre.”

15.text: Now let my lord send to his servants the wheat, barley, olive oil, and wine he has promised;

16.text: we will get all the timber you need from Lebanon and bring it in raft-like bundles by sea to Joppa. You can then haul it on up to Jerusalem.”

notes.text: Heb “and we will cut down trees from Lebanon according to all your need.”
Heb “to you,” but this phrase has not been translated for stylistic reasons—it is somewhat redundant.
Or “on rafts.” See the note at 1 Kgs 5:9.

17.text: Solomon took a census of all the male resident foreigners in the land of Israel, after the census his father David had taken. There were 153,600 in all.

notes.text: Heb “Solomon counted.”

The term ‏גֵּר‎ (ger) refers to a foreign resident, but with different social implications in different settings. In Mosaic Law the resident foreigner was essentially a naturalized citizen and convert to worshiping the God of Israel (see Exod 12:19, 48; Deut 29:10-13).

18.text: He designated 70,000 as common laborers, 80,000 as stonecutters in the hills, and 3,600 as supervisors to make sure the people completed the work.

notes.text: Heb “appointed from them.”
Heb “carriers of loads.”
Or “quarry workers”; Heb “cutters” (probably referring to stonecutters).
Heb “and thirty-six hundred [as] supervisors to compel the people to work.”

1.text: Solomon began building the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the Lord had appeared to his father David. This was the place that David prepared at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

notes.text: Heb “where he.” “Lord” has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
In 2 Sam 24:16 this individual is called ‏אֲרַוְנָא‎ (ʾaravna; traditionally “Araunah”). The form of the name found here also occurs in 1 Chr 21:15; 18-28.

2.text: He began building on the second day of the second month of the fourth year of his reign.

notes.text: This would be April-May, 966 b.c. by modern reckoning.

3.text: Solomon laid the foundation for God’s temple; its length (determined according to the old standard of measure) was 90 feet, and its width 30 feet.

notes.text: Heb “and these are the founding of Solomon to build the house of God.”

Heb “the length [in] cubits by the former measure was 60 cubits, and a width of 20 cubits.” Assuming a length of 18 inches (45 cm) for the standard cubit, the length of the foundation would be 90 feet (27 m) and its width 30 feet (9 m).

4.text: The porch in front of the main hall was 30 feet long, corresponding to the width of the temple, and its height was 30 feet. He plated the inside with pure gold.

notes.text: Heb “and the porch which was in front of the length corresponding to the width of the house, 20 cubits.” The phrase ‏הֵיכַל הַבַּיִת‎ (hekhal habbayit, “the main hall of the temple,” which appears in the parallel account in 1 Kgs 6:3) has been accidentally omitted by homoioarcton after ‏עַל־פְּנֵי‎ (’al pene, “in front of”). Note that the following form, ‏הָאֹרֶךְ‎ (haʿorekh, “the length”), also begins with the Hebrew letter he (‏ה‎). A scribe’s eye probably jumped from the initial he on ‏הֵיכַל‎ to the initial he on ‏הָאֹרֶךְ‎, leaving out the intervening letters in the process.

The Hebrew text has “one hundred and 20 cubits,” i.e., (assuming a cubit of 18 inches) 180 feet (54 m). An ancient Greek witness and the Syriac version read “20 cubits,” i.e., 30 feet (9 m). It is likely that ‏מֵאָה‎ (meʾah, “a hundred”) should be emended to ‏אַמּוֹת‎ (ʾammot, “cubits”).

5.text: He paneled the main hall with boards made from evergreen trees and plated it with fine gold, decorated with palm trees and chains.

notes.text: Heb “covered.”
Heb “the large house.”
Heb “wood of evergreens.”
Heb “and he put up on it palm trees and chains.”

6.text: He decorated the temple with precious stones; the gold he used came from Parvaim.

notes.text: Heb “and he plated the house [with] precious stone for beauty, and the gold was the gold of Parvaim.”

The location of Parvaim, the source of the gold for Solomon’s temple, is uncertain. Some have identified it with modern Farwa in Yemen; others relate it to the Sanskrit parvam and understand it to be a general term for the regions east of Israel.

7.text: He overlaid the temple’s rafters, thresholds, walls and doors with gold; he carved decorative cherubim on the walls.

8.text: He made the Most Holy Place; its length was 30 feet, corresponding to the width of the temple, and its width 30 feet. He plated it with 600 talents of fine gold.

notes.text: Heb “the house of the holy place of holy places.”
Heb “20 cubits.” Assuming a cubit of 18 inches (45 cm), this would give a length of 30 feet (9 m).
Heb “20 cubits.” Some suggest adding, “and its height 20 cubits” (see 1 Kgs 6:20). The phrase could have been omitted by homoioteleuton.

The Hebrew word ‏כִּכַּר‎ (kikkar, “circle”) refers generally to something that is round. When used of metals it can refer to a disk-shaped weight made of the metal or, by extension, to a standard unit of weight. According to the older (Babylonian) standard the “talent” weighed 130 lbs. (58.9 kg), but later this was lowered to 108.3 lbs. (49.1 kg). More recent research suggests the “light” standard talent was 67.3 lbs. (30.6 kg).
