Using this as the standard for calculation, the weight of the gold plating was 40,380 lbs. (18,360 kg).

9.text: The gold nails weighed 50 shekels; he also plated the upper areas with gold.

10.text: In the Most Holy Place he made two images of cherubim and plated them with gold.

11.text: The combined wing span of the cherubim was 30 feet. One of the first cherub’s wings was 7½ long and touched one wall of the temple; its other wing was also 7½ long and touched one of the second cherub’s wings.

notes.text: Heb “and the wings of the cherubim, their length was 20 cubits.” Assuming a cubit of 18 inches (45 cm), the wingspan of the cherubim would have been 30 feet (9 m).

Heb “the wing of the one was 5 cubits from the touching of the wall of the house, and the other wing was 5 cubits from the touching of the wing of the other cherub.” Assuming a cubit of 18 inches (45 cm), each wing would have been 7.5 feet (2.25 m) long.

12.text: Likewise one of the second cherub’s wings was 7½ long and touched the other wall of the temple; its other wing was also 7½ long and touched one of the first cherub’s wings.

notes.text: Heb “and the wing of the one (‏הָאֶחָד‎, haʾekhad, “the one”; this should probably be emended to ‏הָאַחֵר‎, haʾakher, “the other”) cherub was 5 cubits, touching the wall of the house, and the other wing was 5 cubits, clinging to the wing of the other cherub.”

13.text: The combined wingspan of these cherubim was 30 feet. They stood upright, facing inward.

notes.text: Heb “the wings of these cherubim were spreading 20 cubits.”
Heb “and they were standing on their feet, with their faces to the house.” An alternative translation of the last clause would be, “with their faces to the main hall.”

14.text: He made the curtain out of blue, purple, crimson, and white fabrics, and embroidered on it decorative cherubim.

15.text: In front of the temple he made two pillars which had a combined length of 52½ feet, with each having a plated capital 7½ high.

notes.text: The figure given here appears to refer to the combined length of both pillars (perhaps when laid end-to-end on the ground prior to being set up; cf. v. 17); the figure given for the height of the pillars in 1 Kgs 7:15, 2 Kgs 25:17, and Jer 52:21 is half this (i.e., 18 cubits).
The Syriac reads “18 cubits” (27 feet). This apparently reflects an attempt at harmonization with 1 Kgs 7:15, 2 Kgs 25:17, and Jer 52:21.

Heb “and he made before the house two pillars, 35 cubits [in] length, and the plated capital which was on its top [was] 5 cubits.” The significance of the measure “35 cubits” (52.5 feet or 15.75 m, assuming a cubit of 18 inches) for the “length” of the pillars is uncertain. According to 1 Kgs 7:15, each pillar was 18 cubits (27 feet or 8.1 m) high. Perhaps the measurement given here was taken with the pillars lying end-to-end on the ground before they were set up.

16.text: He made ornamental chains and put them on top of the pillars. He also made 100 pomegranate-shaped ornaments and arranged them within the chains.

notes.text: The Hebrew text adds here, “in the inner sanctuary,” but the description at this point is of the pillars, not the inner sanctuary.

17.text: He set up the pillars in front of the temple, one on the right side and the other on the left. He named the one on the right Yakin, and the one on the left Boaz.

notes.text: Or “one on the south and the other on the north.”
The name “Yakin” appears to be a verbal form and probably means, “he establishes.”

The meaning of the name “Boaz” is uncertain. For various proposals, see BDB 126-27 s.v. ‏בֹּעַז‎. One attractive option is to revocalize the name as ‏בְּעֹז‎ (beʿoz, “in strength”) and to understand it as completing the verbal form on the first pillar. Taking the words together and reading from right to left, one can translate the sentence, “he establishes [it] in strength.”

1.text: He made a bronze altar, 30 feet long, 30 feet wide, and 15 feet high.

notes.text: Heb “20 cubits.” Assuming a cubit of 18 inches (45 cm), the length would have been 30 feet (9 m).
Heb “20 cubits.”
Heb “10 cubits.” Assuming a cubit of 18 inches (45 cm), the height would have been 15 feet (4.5 m).

2.text: He also made the big bronze basin called “The Sea.” It measured 15 feet from rim to rim, was circular in shape, and stood 7½ high. Its circumference was 45 feet.

notes.text: Heb “He made the sea, cast.”
The large bronze basin known as “The Sea” was mounted on twelve bronze bulls and contained water for the priests to bathe themselves (see v. 6; cf. Exod 30:17-21).
Heb “10 cubits.” Assuming a cubit of 18 inches (45 cm), the diameter would have been 15 feet (4.5 m).
Heb “5 cubits.” Assuming a cubit of 18 inches (45 cm), the height would have been 7.5 feet (2.25 m).
Heb “and a measuring line went around it 30 cubits all around.”

3.text: Images of bulls were under it all the way around, ten every 18 inches all the way around. The bulls were in two rows and had been cast with “The Sea.”

notes.text: Heb “ten every cubit.”
Heb “rows being cast with its casting.”

4.text: “The Sea” stood on top of twelve bulls. Three faced northward, three westward, three southward, and three eastward. “The Sea” was placed on top of them, and they all faced outward.

notes.text: Heb “all their hindquarters were toward the inside.”

5.text: It was four fingers thick, and its rim was like that of a cup shaped like a lily blossom. It could hold 18,000 gallons.

notes.text: Heb “3,000 baths” (note that the capacity is given in 1 Kings 7:26 as “2,000 baths”). A bath was a liquid measure roughly equivalent to six gallons (about 22 liters), so 3,000 baths was a quantity of about 18,000 gallons (66,000 liters).

6.text: He made ten washing basins; he put five on the south side and five on the north side. In them they rinsed the items used for burnt sacrifices; the priests washed in “The Sea.”

7.text: He made ten gold lampstands according to specifications and put them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left.

8.text: He made ten tables and set them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left. He also made 100 gold bowls.

9.text: He made the courtyard of the priests and the large enclosure and its doors; he plated their doors with bronze.

notes.text: Heb “and the doors for the enclosure.”

10.text: He put “The Sea” on the south side, in the southeast corner.

11.text: Huram Abi made the pots, shovels, and bowls. He finished all the work on God’s temple he had been assigned by King Solomon.

notes.text: Heb “Huram,” but here this refers to Huram Abi (2 Chr 2:13). The complete name has been used in the translation to avoid possible confusion with King Huram of Tyre.
Heb “Huram finished doing all the work which he did for King Solomon [on] the house of God.”

12.text: He made the two pillars, the two bowl-shaped tops of the pillars, the latticework for the bowl-shaped tops of the two pillars,

notes.text: The words “he made” are added for stylistic reasons.

13.text: the 400 pomegranate-shaped ornaments for the latticework of the two pillars (each latticework had two rows of these ornaments at the bowl-shaped top of the pillar),

14.text: the ten movable stands with their ten basins,

notes.text: The Hebrew text has ‏עָשָׂה‎ (ʿasah, “he made”), which probably should be emended to ‏עֶשֶׂר‎ (ʿeser, “ten”; see 1 Kgs 7:43).
The Hebrew text has ‏עָשָׂה‎ (ʿasah, “he made”), which probably should be emended to ‏עֲשָׂרָה‎ (ʿasarah, “ten”; see 1 Kgs 7:43).

15.text: the big bronze basin called “The Sea” with its twelve bulls underneath,

16.text: and the pots, shovels, and meat forks. All the items King Solomon assigned Huram Abi to make for the Lord’s temple were made from polished bronze.

notes.text: Some prefer to read here “bowls,” see v. 11 and 1 Kgs 7:45.
Heb “Huram Abi made for King Solomon [for] the house of the Lord.”

17.text: The king had them cast in earth foundries in the region of the Jordan between Sukkoth and Zarethan.

notes.text: Or perhaps, “molds.”

18.text: Solomon made so many of these items they did not weigh the bronze.

notes.text: Heb “Solomon made all these items in great abundance so that the weight of the bronze was not sought.”

19.text: Solomon also made these items for God’s temple: the gold altar, the tables on which the Bread of the Presence was kept,

notes.text: Heb “the bread of the face/presence.”
This bread offered to God was viewed as a perpetual offering to God. See Lev 24:5-9.

20.text: the pure gold lampstands and their lamps which burned as specified at the entrance to the inner sanctuary,

21.text: the pure gold flower-shaped ornaments, lamps, and tongs,

22.text: the pure gold trimming shears, basins, pans, and censers, and the gold door sockets for the inner sanctuary (the Most Holy Place) and for the doors of the main hall of the temple.

1.text: When Solomon had finished constructing the Lord’s temple, he put the holy items that belonged to his father David (the silver, gold, and all the other articles) in the treasuries of God’s temple.

2.text: Then Solomon convened Israel’s elders—all the leaders of the Israelite tribes and families—in Jerusalem, so they could witness the transferal of the ark of the covenant of the Lord from the City of David (that is, Zion).

notes.text: The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

Heb “Then Solomon convened the elders of Israel, the heads of the tribes, the chiefs of the fathers belonging to the sons of Israel to Jerusalem to bring up the ark of the covenant of the Lord from the City of David (it is Zion).”

3.text: All the men of Israel assembled before the king during the festival in the seventh month.

notes.text: This festival in the seventh month was the Feast of Tabernacles, see Lev 23:34.
The seventh month would be September-October in modern reckoning.

4.text: When all Israel’s elders had arrived, the Levites lifted the ark.

5.text: The priests and Levites carried the ark, the tent where God appeared to his people, and all the holy items in the tent.

notes.text: Heb “the tent of assembly.”
See Exod 33:7-11.
Heb “and they carried the ark of the Lord…. The priests and the Levites carried them.”

6.text: Now King Solomon and all the Israelites who had assembled with him went on ahead of the ark and sacrificed more sheep and cattle than could be counted or numbered.

notes.text: Heb “And King Solomon and all the assembly of Israel, those who had been gathered to him, [were] before the ark, sacrificing sheep and cattle which could not be counted or numbered because of the abundance.”

7.text: The priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord to its assigned place in the inner sanctuary of the temple, in the Most Holy Place under the wings of the cherubim.

notes.text: The word “assigned” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

8.text: The cherubim’s wings extended over the place where the ark sat; the cherubim overshadowed the ark and its poles.

notes.text: These poles were used to carry the ark. The Levites were to carry it with the poles on their shoulders. See Exod 25:13-15; 1 Chr 15:15.

9.text: The poles were so long their ends extending out from the ark were visible from in front of the inner sanctuary, but they could not be seen from beyond that point. They have remained there to this very day.

notes.text: Heb “they could not be seen outside.”

10.text: There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets Moses had placed there in Horeb. (It was there that the Lord made a covenant with the Israelites after he brought them out of the land of Egypt.)

notes.text: Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai (cf. Exod 3:1).
Heb “in Horeb where.”

11.text: The priests left the Holy Place. All the priests who participated had consecrated themselves, no matter which division they represented.

notes.text: Heb “and when the priests went from the holy place.” The syntactical relationship of this temporal clause to the following context is unclear. Perhaps the thought is completed in v. 14 after a lengthy digression.
Heb “Indeed [or “for”] all the priests who were found consecrated themselves without guarding divisions.”

12.text: All the Levites who were musicians, including Asaph, Heman, Jeduthun, and their sons and relatives, wore linen. They played cymbals and stringed instruments as they stood east of the altar. They were accompanied by 120 priests who blew trumpets.

13.text: The trumpeters and musicians played together, praising and giving thanks to the Lord. Accompanied by trumpets, cymbals, and other instruments, they loudly praised the Lord, singing: “Certainly he is good; certainly his loyal love endures!” Then a cloud filled the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: Heb “like one were the trumpeters and the musicians, causing one voice to be heard, praising and giving thanks to the Lord, and while raising a voice with trumpets and with cymbals and with instruments of music, and while praising the Lord.”
Heb “and the house was filled with a cloud, the house of the Lord.”

14.text: The priests could not carry out their duties because of the cloud; the Lord’s splendor filled God’s temple.

notes.text: Heb “were not able to stand to serve.”

1.text: Then Solomon said, “The Lord has said that he lives in thick darkness.

2.text: O Lord, I have built a lofty temple for you, a place where you can live permanently.”

notes.text: The words “O Lord” do not appear in the Hebrew text, but they are supplied in the translation for clarification; Solomon addresses the Lord in prayer at this point.

3.text: Then the king turned around and pronounced a blessing over the whole Israelite assembly as they stood there.

notes.text: Heb “turned his face.”
Heb “and he blessed all the assembly of Israel, and all the assembly of Israel was standing.”

4.text: He said, “The Lord God of Israel is worthy of praise because he has fulfilled what he promised my father David.

notes.text: The Hebrew text reads, “fulfilled by his hand,” but the phrase “by his hand” is somewhat redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
The Hebrew text reads, “promised by his mouth,” but the phrase “by his mouth” is somewhat redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.

5.text: He told David, ‘Since the day I brought my people out of the land of Egypt, I have not chosen a city from all the tribes of Israel to build a temple in which to live. Nor did I choose a man as leader of my people Israel.

notes.text: Heb “saying.”

Heb “to build a house for my name to be there.” Here “name” is used by metonymy for the Lord himself, and thus the expression “to be there” refers to his taking up residence there (hence the translation, “a temple in which to live”). In this case the temple is referred to as a “house” where the Lord himself can reside.

6.text: But now I have chosen Jerusalem as a place to live, and I have chosen David to lead my people Israel.’

notes.text: Heb “for my name to be there.” See also the note on the word “live” in v. 5.

7.text: Now my father David had a strong desire to build a temple to honor the Lord God of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “and it was with the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the Lord God of Israel.”
On the significance of the Lord’s “name,” see the note on the word “live” in v. 5.

8.text: The Lord told my father David, ‘It is right for you to have a strong desire to build a temple to honor me.

notes.text: Heb “Because it was with your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was with your heart.”

9.text: But you will not build the temple; your very own son will build the temple for my honor.’

notes.text: Heb “your son, the one who came out of your body, he will build the temple for my name.”

10.text: The Lord has kept the promise he made. I have taken my father David’s place and have occupied the throne of Israel, as the Lord promised. I have built this temple for the honor of the Lord God of Israel

11.text: and set up in it a place for the ark containing the covenant the Lord made with the Israelites.”

12.text: He stood before the altar of the Lord in front of the entire assembly of Israel and spread out his hands.

13.text: Solomon had made a bronze platform and had placed it in the middle of the enclosure. It was 7½ long, 7½ wide, and 4½ feet high. He stood on it and then got down on his knees in front of the entire assembly of Israel. He spread out his hands toward the sky,

notes.text: Heb “5 cubits.” Assuming a cubit of 18 inches (45 cm), the length would have been 7.5 feet (2.25 m).
Heb “5 cubits.”
Heb “3 cubits.” Assuming a cubit of 18 inches (45 cm), the height would have been 4.5 feet (1.35 m).

14.text: and prayed: “O Lord God of Israel, there is no god like you in heaven or on earth! You maintain covenantal loyalty to your servants who obey you with sincerity.

notes.text: Heb “said.”
Heb “one who keeps the covenant and the loyal love.”
Heb “who walk before you with all their heart.”

15.text: You have kept your word to your servant, my father David; this very day you have fulfilled what you promised.

notes.text: Heb “[you] who kept to your servant David my father that which you spoke to him.”
Heb “you spoke by your mouth and by your hand you fulfilled, as this day.”

16.text: Now, O Lord God of Israel, keep the promise you made to your servant, my father David, when you said, ‘You will never fail to have a successor ruling before me on the throne of Israel, provided that your descendants watch their step and obey my law as you have done.’

notes.text: Heb “there will not be cut off from you a man from before me sitting on the throne of Israel.”
Heb “guard their way by walking in my law as you have walked before me.”

17.text: Now, O Lord God of Israel, may the promise you made to your servant David be realized.

notes.text: Or “prove to be reliable.”

18.text: “God does not really live with humankind on the earth! Look, if the sky and the highest heaven cannot contain you, how much less this temple I have built!

notes.text: Heb “Indeed, can God really live with mankind on the earth?” The rhetorical question expects the answer, “Of course not,” the force of which is reflected in the translation “God does not really live with mankind on the earth.”

19.text: But respond favorably to your servant’s prayer and his request for help, O Lord my God. Answer the desperate prayer your servant is presenting to you.

notes.text: Heb “turn to.”
Heb “by listening to.”
Heb “the loud cry and the prayer.”
Heb “praying before you.”

20.text: Night and day may you watch over this temple, the place where you promised you would live. May you answer your servant’s prayer for this place.

notes.text: Heb “so your eyes might be open toward this house night and day, toward the place about which you promised to place your name there.”
Heb “by listening to the prayer which your servant is praying concerning this place.”

21.text: Respond to the requests of your servant and your people Israel for this place. Hear from your heavenly dwelling place and respond favorably and forgive.

notes.text: Heb “listen to the requests of your servant and your people Israel which they are praying concerning this place.”
Heb “hear and forgive.”

22.text: “When someone is accused of sinning against his neighbor and the latter pronounces a curse on the alleged offender before your altar in this temple,

notes.text: Heb “and if the man who sins against his neighbor when one takes up against him a curse to curse him and the curse comes before your altar in this house.”

23.text: listen from heaven and make a just decision about your servants’ claims. Condemn the guilty party, declare the other innocent, and give both of them what they deserve.

notes.text: Heb “and you, hear [from] heaven and act and judge your servants by repaying the guilty, to give his way on his head, and to declare the innocent to be innocent, to give to him according to his innocence.”

24.text: “If your people Israel are defeated by an enemy because they sinned against you, then if they come back to you, renew their allegiance to you, and pray for your help before you in this temple,

notes.text: Or “are struck down before an enemy.”
Heb “confess [or perhaps, “praise”] your name.”
Heb “and they pray and ask for help.”

25.text: then listen from heaven, forgive the sin of your people Israel, and bring them back to the land you gave to them and their ancestors.

notes.text: Heb “fathers” (also in vv. 31, 38).

26.text: “The time will come when the skies are shut up tightly and no rain falls because your people sinned against you. When they direct their prayers toward this place, renew their allegiance to you, and turn away from their sin because you punish them,

notes.text: Heb “when.” In the Hebrew text vv. 26-27a actually contain one lengthy conditional sentence, which the translation has divided into two sentences for stylistic reasons.
Or “heavens” (also in v. 12). The Hebrew term ‏שָׁמַיִם‎ (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.
Heb “they.”
Heb “confess [or perhaps, “praise”] your name.”

The Hebrew text reads “because you answer them,” as if the verb is from ‏עָנָה‎ (ʿanah, “answer”). However, this reference to a divine answer is premature, since the next verse asks for God to intervene in mercy. It is better to revocalize the consonantal text as ‏תְעַנֵּם‎ (teʿannem, “you afflict them”), a Piel verb form from the homonym ‏עָנָה‎ (“afflict”).

27.text: then listen from heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel. Certainly you will then teach them the right way to live and send rain on your land that you have given your people to possess.

notes.text: The present translation understands ‏כִּי‎ (ki) in an emphatic or asseverative sense (“Certainly”). Other translations have “indeed” (NASB), “when” (NRSV), “so” (NEB), or leave the word untranslated (NIV).
Heb “the good way in which they should walk.”
Or “for an inheritance.”

28.text: “The time will come when the land suffers from a famine, a plague, blight, and disease, or a locust invasion, or when their enemy lays siege to the cities of the land, or when some other type of plague or epidemic occurs.

notes.text: Actually two Hebrew words appear here, both of which are usually (but not always) taken as referring to locusts. Perhaps different stages of growth or different varieties are in view, but this is uncertain. NEB has “locusts new-sloughed or fully grown”; NASB has “locust or grasshopper”; NIV has “locusts or grasshoppers”; NRSV has “locust, or caterpillar.”
Heb “in the land, his gates.”

29.text: When all your people Israel pray and ask for help, as they acknowledge their intense pain and spread out their hands toward this temple,

notes.text: Heb “every prayer, every request for help which will be to all the people, to all your people Israel.”
Heb “which they know, each his pain and his affliction.”

30.text: then listen from your heavenly dwelling place, forgive their sin, and act favorably toward each one based on your evaluation of their motives. (Indeed you are the only one who can correctly evaluate the motives of all people.)

notes.text: The words “their sin” are not in the Hebrew text, but are supplied for clarification.

Heb “and give to each one according to all his ways because you know his heart.” In the Hebrew text vv. 28-30a actually contain one lengthy conditional sentence, which the translation has divided up for stylistic reasons.
Heb “Indeed you know, you alone, the heart of the sons of mankind.”

31.text: Then they will honor you by obeying you throughout their lifetimes as they live on the land you gave to our ancestors.

notes.text: Heb “fear.”
Heb “by walking in your ways.”
Heb “all the days [in] which.”

32.text: “Foreigners who do not belong to your people Israel will come from a distant land because of your great reputation and your ability to accomplish mighty deeds; they will come and direct their prayers toward this temple.

notes.text: Heb “your great name.” The word “name” sometimes refers to one’s reputation or honor (thus the translation here, “your great reputation”).
Heb “and your strong hand and your outstretched arm.”

33.text: Then listen from your heavenly dwelling place and answer all the prayers of the foreigners. Then all the nations of the earth will acknowledge your reputation, obey you as your people Israel do, and recognize that this temple I built belongs to you.

notes.text: Heb “and do all which the foreigner calls to [i.e., “requests of”] you.”
Heb “name.” See the note on “reputation” in v. 32.
Heb “fear.”
Heb “that your name is called over this house which I built.” The Hebrew idiom “call the name over” indicates ownership. See 2 Sam 12:28.

34.text: “When you direct your people to march out and fight their enemies, and they direct their prayers to you toward this chosen city and this temple I built for your honor,

notes.text: Heb “When your people go out for battle against their enemies in the way which you send them.”
Heb “toward this city which you have chosen and the house which I built for your name.”

35.text: then listen from heaven to their prayers for help and vindicate them.

notes.text: Heb “their prayer and their request for help.”
Heb “and accomplish their justice.”

36.text: “The time will come when your people will sin against you (for there is no one who is sinless!) and you will be angry at them and deliver them over to their enemies, who will take them as prisoners to their land, whether far away or close by.

notes.text: Heb “they”; the referent (God’s people) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

37.text: When your people come to their senses in the land where they are held prisoner, they will repent and beg for your mercy in the land of their imprisonment, admitting, ‘We have sinned and gone astray, we have done evil!’

notes.text: Heb “they”; the referent (God’s people) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “stop and reflect”; Heb “bring back to their heart.”
Or “done wrong.”

38.text: When they return to you with all their heart and being in the land where they are held prisoner and direct their prayers toward the land you gave to their ancestors, your chosen city, and the temple I built for your honor,

notes.text: Or “soul.”
Heb “your name.” The word “name” sometimes refers to one’s reputation or honor (thus the translation here, “your honor”).

39.text: then listen from your heavenly dwelling place to their prayers for help, vindicate them, and forgive your sinful people.

notes.text: Heb “their prayer and their requests for help.”
Heb “and accomplish their justice.”

40.text: “Now, my God, may you be attentive and responsive to the prayers offered in this place.

notes.text: Heb “May your eyes be open and your ears attentive to the prayer of this place.”

41.text: Now ascend, O Lord God, to your resting place, you and the ark of your strength! May your priests, O Lord God, experience your deliverance. May your loyal followers rejoice in the prosperity you give.

notes.text: Heb “be clothed with deliverance.”
Heb “and may your loyal ones rejoice in good.”

42.text: O Lord God, do not reject your chosen ones! Remember the faithful promises you made to your servant David!”

notes.text: Heb “do not turn away the face of your anointed ones.” Many medieval Hebrew mss, as well as the ancient versions, read the singular, “your anointed,” which would probably refer to Solomon specifically, rather than the people.

1.text: When Solomon finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the Lord’s splendor filled the temple.

notes.text: Or “the sky.” The Hebrew term ‏שָׁמַיִם‎ (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.

2.text: The priests were unable to enter the Lord’s temple because the Lord’s splendor filled the Lord’s temple.

3.text: When all the Israelites saw the fire come down and the Lord’s splendor over the temple, they got on their knees with their faces downward toward the pavement. They worshiped and gave thanks to the Lord, saying, “Certainly he is good; certainly his loyal love endures!”

notes.text: The word “saying” is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

4.text: The king and all the people were presenting sacrifices to the Lord.

5.text: King Solomon sacrificed 22,000 cattle and 120,000 sheep. Then the king and all the people dedicated God’s temple.

6.text: The priests stood in their assigned spots, along with the Levites who had the musical instruments used for praising the Lord. (These were the ones King David made for giving thanks to the Lord and which were used by David when he offered praise, saying, “Certainly his loyal love endures.”) Opposite the Levites, the priests were blowing the trumpets, while all Israel stood there.

notes.text: Heb “and the priests were standing at their posts, and the Levites with the instruments of music of the Lord.”
Heb “which David the king made to give thanks to the Lord, for lasting is his loyal love, when David praised by them.”
Heb “opposite them”; the referent (the Levites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

7.text: Solomon consecrated the middle of the courtyard that is in front of the Lord’s temple. He offered burnt sacrifices, grain offerings, and the fat from the peace offerings there, because the bronze altar that Solomon had made was too small to hold all these offerings.

notes.text: The Hebrew text omits reference to the grain offerings at this point, but note that they are included both in the list in the second half of the verse (see note on “offerings” at the end of this verse) and in the parallel account in 1 Kgs 8:64. The construction ‏וְאֶת־הַמִּנְחָה‎ (veʾet-hamminkhah; vav [‏ו‎] + accusative sign + noun with article; “grain offerings”) was probably omitted accidentally by homoioarcton. Note the ‏וְאֶת‎ (veʾet) that immediately follows.
Heb “to hold the burnt sacrifice, the grain offering, and the fat portions.” Because this is redundant, the translation employs a summary phrase: “all these offerings.”

8.text: At that time Solomon and all Israel with him celebrated a festival for seven days. This great assembly included people from Lebo Hamath in the north to the Stream of Egypt in the south.

notes.text: Heb “Solomon held the festival at that time for seven days, and all Israel was with him, a very great assembly from Lebo Hamath to the wadi of Egypt.”

9.text: On the eighth day they held an assembly, for they had dedicated the altar for seven days and celebrated the festival for seven more days.

10.text: On the twenty-third day of the seventh month, Solomon sent the people home. They left happy and contented because of the good the Lord had done for David, Solomon, and his people Israel.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Solomon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The words “they left” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “good of heart.”

11.text: After Solomon finished building the Lord’s temple and the royal palace and accomplished all his plans for the Lord’s temple and his royal palace,

notes.text: Heb “and all that entered the heart of Solomon to do in the house of the Lord and in his house he successfully accomplished.”

12.text: the Lord appeared to Solomon at night and said to him: “I have answered your prayer and chosen this place to be my temple where sacrifices are to be made.

notes.text: Heb “I have heard.”
Heb “temple of sacrifice.” This means the Lord designated the temple as the place for making sacrifices, and this has been clarified in the translation.

13.text: When I close up the sky so that it doesn’t rain, or command locusts to devour the land’s vegetation, or send a plague among my people,

notes.text: Or “if.”
Or “heavens.” The Hebrew term ‏שָׁמַיִם‎ (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.
Heb “the land,” which stands here by metonymy for the vegetation growing in it.

14.text: if my people, who belong to me, humble themselves, pray, seek to please me, and repudiate their sinful practices, then I will respond from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land.

notes.text: Heb “over whom my name is called.” The Hebrew idiom “call the name over” indicates ownership. See 2 Sam 12:28.
Heb “seek my face,” where “my face” is figurative for God’s presence and acceptance.
Heb “and turn from their sinful ways.”
Heb “hear.”
Here the phrase heal their land means restore the damage done by the drought, locusts and plague mentioned in v. 13.

15.text: Now I will be attentive and responsive to the prayers offered in this place.

notes.text: Heb “my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer of this place.” Note Solomon’s request in 6:40.

16.text: Now I have chosen and consecrated this temple by making it my permanent home; I will be constantly present there.

notes.text: Heb “for my name to be there perpetually [or perhaps, “forever”].”
Heb “and my eyes and my heart will be there all the days.”

17.text: You must serve me as your father David did. Do everything I commanded and obey my rules and regulations.

notes.text: Heb “As for you, if you walk before me, as David your father walked, by doing all which I commanded you, [and] you keep my rules and my regulations.”
Verse 17 is actually a lengthy protasis (“if” section) of a conditional sentence, the apodosis (“then” section) of which appears in v. 18.

18.text: Then I will establish your dynasty, just as I promised your father David, ‘You will not fail to have a successor ruling over Israel.’

notes.text: Heb “I will establish the throne of your kingdom.”
Heb “there will not be cut off from you a man ruling over Israel.”

19.text: “But if you people ever turn away from me, fail to obey the regulations and rules I instructed you to keep, and decide to serve and worship other gods,

notes.text: The Hebrew pronoun is plural, suggesting that Solomon and all Israel (or perhaps Solomon and his successors) are in view. To convey this to the English reader, the translation “you people” has been employed.
Heb “which I placed before you.”
Heb “and walk and serve other gods and bow down to them.”

20.text: then I will remove you from my land I have given you, I will abandon this temple I have consecrated with my presence, and I will make you an object of mockery and ridicule among all the nations.

notes.text: Heb “them.” The switch from the second to the third person pronoun is rhetorically effective, for it mirrors God’s rejection of his people—he has stopped addressing them as “you” and begun addressing them as “them.” However, the switch is awkward and confusing in English, so the translation maintains the direct address style.
Heb “them.” See the note on “you” earlier in this verse.
Instead of “I will throw away,” the parallel text in 1 Kgs 9:7 has “I will send away.” The two verbs sound very similar in Hebrew, so the discrepancy is likely due to an oral transmissional error.
Heb “and this temple which I consecrated for my name I will throw away from before my face.”
Heb “him,” which appears in context to refer to Israel (i.e., “you” in direct address). Many translations understand the direct object of the verb “make” to be the temple (NEB, NASB, NIV, NRSV “it”).
Heb “and I will make him [i.e., Israel] a proverb and a taunt,” that is, a proverbial example of destruction and an object of reproach.

21.text: As for this temple, which was once majestic, everyone who passes by it will be shocked and say, ‘Why did the Lord do this to this land and this temple?’

notes.text: Heb “and this house which was high/elevated.” The statement makes little sense in this context, which predicts the desolation that judgment will bring. Some treat the clause as concessive, “Even though this temple is lofty [now].” Others, following the lead of several ancient versions, emend the text to, “this temple will become a heap of ruins.”

22.text: Others will then answer, ‘Because they abandoned the Lord God of their ancestors, who led them out of Egypt. They embraced other gods whom they worshiped and served. That is why he brought all this disaster down on them.’”

notes.text: Heb “and they will say.”
Heb “fathers.”
Heb “and they took hold of other gods and bowed down to them and served them.”

1.text: After twenty years, during which Solomon built the Lord’s temple and his royal palace,

2.text: Solomon rebuilt the cities that Huram had given him and settled Israelites there.

notes.text: Heb “Huram” (also in v. 18). Some medieval Hebrew mss, along with the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate spell the name “Hiram,” agreeing with 1 Chr 14:1. “Huram” is a variant spelling referring to the same individual.

3.text: Solomon went to Hamath Zobah and seized it.

4.text: He built up Tadmor in the wilderness and all the storage cities he had built in Hamath.

5.text: He made upper Beth Horon and lower Beth Horon fortified cities with walls and barred gates,

notes.text: Heb “and he built…[as] cities of fortification, [with] walls, doors, and a bar.”

6.text: and built up Baalath, all the storage cities that belonged to him, and all the cities where chariots and horses were kept. He built whatever he wanted in Jerusalem, Lebanon, and throughout his entire kingdom.

notes.text: Heb “Solomon.” The recurrence of the proper name is unexpected in terms of contemporary English style, so the pronoun has been used in the translation instead.
Heb “the cities of the chariots and the cities of the horses.”
Heb “and all the desire of Solomon which he desired to build in Jerusalem and in Lebanon and in all the land of his kingdom.”

7.text: Now several non-Israelite peoples were left in the land after the conquest of Joshua, including the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.

notes.text: Heb “all the people who were left from the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not from Israel.”

8.text: Their descendants remained in the land (the Israelites were unable to wipe them out). Solomon conscripted them for his work crews, and they continue in that role to this very day.

notes.text: Heb “from their sons who were left after them in the land, whom the sons of Israel did not wipe out, and Solomon raised them up for a work crew to this day.”

9.text: Solomon did not assign Israelites to these work crews; the Israelites served as his soldiers, officers, charioteers, and commanders of his chariot forces.

notes.text: Heb “and from the sons of Israel whom Solomon did not assign to the laborers for his work.”
Heb “officers of his chariots and his horses.”

10.text: These men worked for King Solomon as supervisors; there were a total of 250 of them who were in charge of the people.

notes.text: Heb “these [were] the officials of the governors who belonged to the king, Solomon, 250, the ones ruling over the people.”

11.text: Solomon moved Pharaoh’s daughter up from the City of David to the palace he had built for her, for he said, “My wife must not live in the palace of King David of Israel, for the places where the ark of the Lord has entered are holy.”

notes.text: The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

12.text: Then Solomon offered burnt sacrifices to the Lord on the altar of the Lord which he had built in front of the temple’s porch.

notes.text: Heb “the porch.”

13.text: He observed the daily requirements for sacrifices that Moses had specified for Sabbaths, new moon festivals, and the three annual celebrations—the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Shelters.

notes.text: The Hebrew phrase ‏ הַסֻּכּוֹת‎[‏חַג‎] (khag hassukkot, “[Feast of] shelters” [or “huts”]) is traditionally known as the Feast of Tabernacles. The rendering “booths” (cf. NAB, NASB, NRSV) is probably better than the traditional “tabernacles” in light of the meaning of the term ‏סֻכָּה‎ (sukkah, “hut; booth”), but “booths” are frequently associated with trade shows and craft fairs in contemporary American English. The nature of the celebration during this feast as a commemoration of the wanderings of the Israelites after they left Egypt suggests that a translation like “shelters” is more appropriate.

14.text: As his father David had decreed, Solomon appointed the divisions of the priests to do their assigned tasks, the Levitical orders to lead worship and help the priests with their daily tasks, and the divisions of the gatekeepers to serve at their assigned gates. This was what David the man of God had ordered.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Solomon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “and the Levites, according to their posts, to praise and to serve opposite the priests according to the matter of a day in its day.”
Heb “and the gatekeepers by their divisions for a gate and a gate.”
Heb “for so [was] the command of David the man of God.”

15.text: They did not neglect any detail of the king’s orders pertaining to the priests, Levites, and treasuries.

notes.text: Heb “and they did not turn aside from the command of the king concerning the priests and the Levites with regard to any matter and with regard to the treasuries.”

16.text: All the work ordered by Solomon was completed, from the day the foundation of the Lord’s temple was laid until it was finished; the Lord’s temple was completed.

17.text: Then Solomon went to Ezion Geber and to Elat on the coast in the land of Edom.

18.text: Huram sent him ships and some of his sailors, men who were well acquainted with the sea. They sailed with Solomon’s men to Ophir and took from there 450 talents of gold, which they brought back to King Solomon.

notes.text: Heb “and Huram sent to him by the hand of his servants, ships, and servants [who] know the sea, and they came with the servants of Solomon to Ophir.”

The Hebrew word ‏כִּכַּר‎ (kikkar, “circle”) refers generally to something that is round. When used of metals it can refer to a disk-shaped weight made of the metal or, by extension, to a standard unit of weight. According to the older (Babylonian) standard the “talent” weighed 130 lbs. (58.9 kg), but later this was lowered to 108.3 lbs. (49.1 kg). More recent research suggests the “light” standard talent was 67.3 lbs. (30.6 kg). Using this as the standard for calculation, the weight of the gold was 30,285 lbs. (13,770 kg).

1.text: When the queen of Sheba heard about Solomon, she came to challenge him with difficult questions. She arrived in Jerusalem with a great display of pomp, bringing with her camels carrying spices, a very large quantity of gold, and precious gems. She visited Solomon and discussed with him everything that was on her mind.

notes.text: Heb “the report about Solomon.”
Or “test.”
Heb “Solomon.” The recurrence of the proper name here is redundant in terms of contemporary English style, so the pronoun has been used in the translation instead.
Or “riddles.”
Heb “with very great strength.” The Hebrew word ‏חַיִל‎ (khayil, “strength”) may refer here to the size of her retinue or to the great wealth she brought with her.
Or “balsam oil.”

2.text: Solomon answered all her questions; there was no question too complex for the king.

notes.text: Heb “Solomon declared to her all her words; there was not a word hidden from the king which he did not declare to her.” If riddles are specifically in view (see v. 1), then one might translate, “Solomon explained to her all her riddles; there was no riddle too complex for the king.”

3.text: When the queen of Sheba saw for herself Solomon’s wisdom, the palace he had built,

notes.text: Heb “house.”

4.text: the food in his banquet hall, his servants and attendants in their robes, his cupbearers in their robes, and his burnt sacrifices which he presented in the Lord’s temple, she was amazed.

notes.text: Heb “the food on his table.”
Heb “the seating of his servants and the standing of his attendants.”

The Hebrew text has here, “and his upper room [by] which he was going up to the house of the Lord.” But ‏עֲלִיָּתוֹ‎ (ʿaliyyato, “his upper room”) should be emended to ‏עֹלָתוֹ‎, (ʿolato, “his burnt sacrifice[s]”). See the parallel account in 1 Kgs 10:5.
Or “it took her breath away”; Heb “there was no breath still in her.”

5.text: She said to the king, “The report I heard in my own country about your wise sayings and insight was true!

notes.text: Heb “about your words [or perhaps, “deeds”] and your wisdom.”

6.text: I did not believe these things until I came and saw them with my own eyes. Indeed, I didn’t hear even half the story! Your wisdom surpasses what was reported to me.

notes.text: Heb “the half was not told to me.”

7.text: Your attendants, who stand before you at all times and hear your wise sayings, are truly happy!

notes.text: Heb “How happy are your men! How happy are these servants of yours, who stand before you continually, who hear your wisdom!”

8.text: May the Lord your God be praised because he favored you by placing you on his throne as the one ruling on his behalf. Because of your God’s love for Israel and his lasting commitment to them, he made you king over them so you could make just and right decisions.”

notes.text: Or “delighted in.”
Heb “as king for the Lord your God.”
Heb “to make him stand permanently.”
Heb “to do justice and righteousness.”

9.text: She gave the king 120 talents of gold and a very large quantity of spices and precious gems. The quantity of spices the queen of Sheba gave King Solomon has never been matched.

notes.text: The Hebrew word ‏כִּכַּר‎ (kikkar, “circle”) refers generally to something that is round. When used of metals it can refer to a disk-shaped weight made of the metal or, by extension, to a standard unit of weight. According to the older (Babylonian) standard the “talent” weighed 130 lbs. (58.9 kg), but later this was lowered to 108.3 lbs. (49.1 kg). More recent research suggests the “light” standard talent was 67.3 lbs. (30.6 kg). Using this as the standard for calculation, the weight of the gold was 8,076 lbs. (3,672 kg).
Heb “there has not been like those spices which the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.”

10.text: (Huram’s servants, aided by Solomon’s servants, brought gold from Ophir, as well as fine timber and precious gems.

notes.text: Heb “Huram’s” (also in v. 21). Some medieval Hebrew mss, along with the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate spell the name “Hiram,” agreeing with 1 Chr 14:1. “Huram” is a variant spelling referring to the same individual.
Heb “who brought gold from Ophir, brought.”
Heb “algum.”

11.text: With the timber the king made steps for the Lord’s temple and royal palace as well as stringed instruments for the musicians. No one had seen anything like them in the land of Judah before that.)

notes.text: Heb “tracks.” The parallel text in 1 Kgs 10:12 has a different term whose meaning is uncertain: “supports,” perhaps “banisters” or “parapets.”
Two types of stringed instruments are specifically mentioned in the Hebrew text, the ‏כִּנּוֹר‎ (kinnor, “zither”) and ‏נֶבֶל‎ (nevel, “harp”).
Heb “there was not seen like these formerly in the land of Judah.”

12.text: King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she requested, more than what she had brought him. Then she left and returned to her homeland with her attendants.

notes.text: Heb “besides what she brought to the king.”
Heb “turned and went.”

13.text: Solomon received 666 talents of gold per year,

notes.text: The Hebrew word ‏כִּכַּר‎ (kikkar, “circle”) refers generally to something that is round. When used of metals it can refer to a disk-shaped weight made of the metal or, by extension, to a standard unit of weight. According to the older (Babylonian) standard the “talent” weighed 130 lbs. (58.9 kg), but later this was lowered to 108.3 lbs. (49.1 kg). More recent research suggests the “light” standard talent was 67.3 lbs. (30.6 kg). Using this as the standard for calculation, the weight of the gold Solomon received annually was 44,822 lbs. (20,380 kg).
Heb “the weight of the gold which came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold.”

14.text: besides what he collected from the merchants and traders. All the Arabian kings and the governors of the land also brought gold and silver to Solomon.

notes.text: Heb “traveling men.”

15.text: King Solomon made 200 large shields of hammered gold; 600 measures of hammered gold were used for each shield.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has simply “600,” with no unit of measure given.

16.text: He also made 300 small shields of hammered gold; 300 measures of gold were used for each of those shields. The king placed them in the Palace of the Lebanon Forest.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has simply “300,” with no unit of measure given.

This name was appropriate because of the large amount of cedar, undoubtedly brought from Lebanon, used in its construction. The cedar pillars in the palace must have given it the appearance of a forest. See 1 Kgs 7:2.

17.text: The king made a large throne decorated with ivory and overlaid it with pure gold.

18.text: There were six steps leading up to the throne, and a gold footstool was attached to the throne. The throne had two armrests with a statue of a lion standing on each side.

notes.text: The parallel text of 1 Kgs 10:19 has instead “and the back of it was rounded on top.”
Heb “[There were] armrests on each side of the place of the seat, and two lions standing beside the armrests.”

19.text: There were twelve statues of lions on the six steps, one lion at each end of each step. There was nothing like it in any other kingdom.

notes.text: Heb “nothing like it had been made for any kingdom.”

20.text: All of King Solomon’s cups were made of gold, and all the household items in the Palace of the Lebanon Forest were made of pure gold. There were no silver items, for silver was not considered very valuable in Solomon’s time.

notes.text: Heb “there was no silver regarded as anything in the days of Solomon.”

21.text: The king had a fleet of large merchant ships manned by Huram’s men that sailed the sea. Once every three years the fleet came into port with cargoes of gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.

notes.text: Heb “for ships belonging to the king were going [to] Tarshish.” This probably refers to large ships either made in or capable of traveling to the distant western port of Tarshish.
Heb “servants.”
Heb “the fleet of Tarshish [ships].”
Heb “the ships of Tarshish came carrying.”
The meaning of this word is unclear; some suggest it refers to “baboons.” NEB has “monkeys,” NASB, NRSV “peacocks,” and NIV “baboons.”

22.text: King Solomon was wealthier and wiser than any of the kings of the earth.

notes.text: Heb “King Solomon was greater than all the kings of the earth with respect to wealth and wisdom.”

23.text: All the kings of the earth wanted to visit Solomon to see him display his God-given wisdom.

notes.text: Heb “and all the kings of the earth were seeking the face of Solomon to hear his wisdom which God had placed in his heart.”

24.text: Year after year visitors brought their gifts, which included items of silver, items of gold, clothes, perfume, spices, horses, and mules.

notes.text: Heb “and they were bringing each one his gift, items of silver…and mules, the matter of a year in a year.”

25.text: Solomon had 4,000 stalls for his chariot horses and 12,000 horses. He kept them in assigned cities and also with him in Jerusalem.

notes.text: The parallel text of 1 Kgs 10:26 reads “fourteen hundred chariots.”
Heb “he placed them in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.”

26.text: He ruled all the kingdoms from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines as far as the border of Egypt.

notes.text: Heb “the River.” In biblical Hebrew the Euphrates River was typically referred to simply as “the River.”

27.text: The king made silver as plentiful in Jerusalem as stones; cedar was as plentiful as sycamore fig trees are in the foothills.

notes.text: The words “as plentiful” are supplied for clarification.
Heb “he made cedar.”
The foothills (‏שְׁפֵלָה‎, shephelah) are the region between the Judean hill country and the Mediterranean coastal plain.

28.text: Solomon acquired horses from Egypt and from all the lands.

29.text: The rest of the events of Solomon’s reign, from start to finish, are recorded in the Annals of Nathan the Prophet, the Prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and the Vision of Iddo the Seer pertaining to Jeroboam son of Nebat.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Solomon, the former and the latter, are they not written?”

30.text: Solomon ruled over all Israel from Jerusalem for forty years.

31.text: Then Solomon passed away and was buried in the city of his father David. His son Rehoboam replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”

1.text: Rehoboam traveled to Shechem, for all Israel had gathered in Shechem to make Rehoboam king.

notes.text: Heb “come [to].”
Heb “him”; the referent (Rehoboam) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

2.text: When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard the news, he was still in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon. Jeroboam returned from Egypt.

3.text: They sent for him, and Jeroboam and all Israel came and spoke to Rehoboam, saying,

notes.text: Heb “They sent and called for him.”

4.text: “Your father made us work too hard! Now if you lighten the demands he made and don’t make us work as hard, we will serve you.”

notes.text: Heb “made our yoke burdensome.”

Heb “but you, now, lighten the burdensome work of your father and the heavy yoke which he placed on us, and we will serve you.” In the Hebrew text the prefixed verbal form with vav (‏וְנַעַבְדֶךָ‎, venaʿavedekha, “and we will serve you”) following the imperative (‏הָקֵל‎, haqel, “lighten”) indicates purpose/result. The conditional sentence used in the present translation is an attempt to bring out the logical relationship between these forms.

5.text: He said to them, “Go away for three days, then return to me.” So the people went away.

6.text: King Rehoboam consulted with the older advisers who had served his father Solomon when he had been alive. He asked them, “How do you advise me to answer these people?”

notes.text: Heb “stood before.”
Heb “saying.”

7.text: They said to him, “If you are fair to these people, grant their request, and are cordial to them, they will be your servants from this time forward.”

notes.text: Heb “If you are for good to these people and you are favorable to them and speak to them good words, they will be your servants all the days.”

8.text: But Rehoboam rejected their advice and consulted the young advisers who served him, with whom he had grown up.

notes.text: Heb “Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders which they advised and he consulted the young men with whom he had grown up, who stood before him.”

9.text: He asked them, “How do you advise me to respond to these people who said to me, ‘Lessen the demands your father placed on us’?”

notes.text: Heb “Lighten the yoke which your father placed on us.”

10.text: The young advisers with whom Rehoboam had grown up said to him, “Say this to these people who have said to you, ‘Your father made us work hard, but now lighten our burden’ —say this to them: ‘I am a lot harsher than my father!

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Rehoboam) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “Your father made our yoke heavy, but make it lighter upon us.”

Heb “My little one is thicker than my father’s hips.” The referent of “my little one” is not clear. The traditional view is that it refers to the little finger (so NEB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT). As the following statement makes clear, Rehoboam’s point is that he is more harsh and demanding than his father.

11.text: My father imposed heavy demands on you; I will make them even heavier. My father punished you with ordinary whips; I will punish you with whips that really sting your flesh.’”

notes.text: Heb “and now my father placed upon you a heavy yoke, but I will add to your yoke.”

Heb “My father punished you with whips, but I [will punish you] with scorpions.” “Scorpions” might allude to some type of torture, but more likely it refers to a type of whip that inflicts an especially biting, painful wound.

12.text: Jeroboam and all the people reported to Rehoboam on the third day, just as the king had ordered when he said, “Return to me on the third day.”

13.text: The king responded to the people harshly. He rejected the advice of the older men

notes.text: Heb “King Rehoboam.” The pronoun “he” has been used in the translation in place of the proper name in keeping with contemporary English style.

14.text: and followed the advice of the younger ones. He said, “My father imposed heavy demands on you; I will make them even heavier. My father punished you with ordinary whips; I will punish you with whips that really sting your flesh.”

notes.text: The Hebrew text reads, “I will make heavy your yoke,” but many medieval Hebrew mss and other ancient textual witnesses have, “my father made heavy your yoke.”
Heb “but I will add to your yoke.”

Heb “My father punished you with whips, but I [will punish you] with scorpions.” “Scorpions” might allude to some type of torture, but more likely it refers to a type of whip that inflicts an especially biting, painful wound.

15.text: The king refused to listen to the people, because God was instigating this turn of events so that he might bring to pass the prophetic announcement he had made through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.

notes.text: Heb “because this turn of events was from God.”
Heb “so that the Lord might bring to pass his word which he spoke.”

16.text: When all Israel saw that the king refused to listen to them, the people answered the king, “We have no portion in David—no share in the son of Jesse! Return to your homes, O Israel! Now, look after your own dynasty, O David!” So all Israel returned to their homes.

notes.text: The MT does not include the word “saw,” but many medieval Hebrew mss as well as several ancient versions have it. See the parallel text of 1 Kings 12:16, which has the verb ‏וַיַּרְא‎ (from ‏רָאָה‎, raʾah, “to see”).
The people’s point seems to be that they have no familial relationship with David that brings them any benefits or places upon them any obligations. They are being treated like outsiders.
Heb “each one to your tents, Israel.” The word “return” is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “Now see your house, David.”
Heb “went to their tents.”

17.text: (Rehoboam continued to rule over the Israelites who lived in the cities of Judah.)

18.text: King Rehoboam sent Hadoram, the supervisor of the work crews, out after them, but the Israelites stoned him to death. King Rehoboam managed to jump into his chariot and escape to Jerusalem.

notes.text: In the parallel account in 1 Kgs 12:18 this name appears as “Adoniram.”

19.text: So Israel has been in rebellion against the Davidic dynasty to this very day.

1.text: When Rehoboam arrived in Jerusalem, he summoned 180,000 skilled warriors from Judah and Benjamin to attack Israel and restore the kingdom to Rehoboam.

notes.text: Heb “he summoned the house of Judah and Benjamin, 180,000 chosen men, accomplished in war.”

2.text: But the Lord’s message came to the prophet Shemaiah,

notes.text: Heb “man of God.”

3.text: “Say this to King Rehoboam son of Solomon of Judah and to all the Israelites in Judah and Benjamin,

4.text: ‘The Lord says this: “Do not attack and make war with your brothers. Each of you go home, for I have caused this to happen.”’” They obeyed the Lord and called off the attack against Jeroboam.

notes.text: Heb “for this thing is from me.”
Heb “and they heard the words of the Lord and returned from going against Jeroboam.”

5.text: Rehoboam lived in Jerusalem; he built up these fortified cities throughout Judah:

6.text: Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa,

7.text: Beth Zur, Soco, Adullam,

8.text: Gath, Mareshah, Ziph,

9.text: Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah,

10.text: Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron. These were the fortified cities in Judah and Benjamin.

11.text: He fortified these cities and placed officers in them, as well as storehouses of food, olive oil, and wine.

12.text: In each city there were shields and spears; he strongly fortified them. Judah and Benjamin belonged to him.

notes.text: Heb “he strengthened them greatly, very much.”

13.text: The priests and Levites who lived throughout Israel supported him, no matter where they resided.

notes.text: Heb “and the priests and the Levites who were in all Israel supported him from all their territory.”

14.text: The Levites even left their pasturelands and their property behind and came to Judah and Jerusalem, for Jeroboam and his sons prohibited them from serving as the Lord’s priests.

15.text: Jeroboam appointed his own priests to serve at the worship centers and to lead in the worship of the goat idols and calf idols he had made.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Jeroboam) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “for the high places.”
Heb “and for the goats and for the calves that he had made.”

16.text: Those among all the Israelite tribes who were determined to worship the Lord God of Israel followed them to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the Lord God of their ancestors.

notes.text: Heb “and after them from all the tribes of Israel, the ones giving their heart[s] to seek the Lord God of Israel came [to] Jerusalem.”
Heb “fathers.”

17.text: They supported the kingdom of Judah and were loyal to Rehoboam son of Solomon for three years; they followed the edicts of David and Solomon for three years.

notes.text: Or “strengthened.”
Or “strengthened.”
Heb “they walked in the way of.”

18.text: Rehoboam married Mahalath the daughter of David’s son Jerimoth and of Abihail, the daughter of Jesse’s son Eliab.

notes.text: Heb “took for himself a wife.”
The words “and of” are supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.

19.text: She bore him sons named Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham.

20.text: He later married Maacah the daughter of Absalom. She bore to him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.

21.text: Rehoboam loved Maacah daughter of Absalom more than his other wives and concubines. He had eighteen wives and sixty concubines; he fathered twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters.

notes.text: Concubines were slave women in ancient Near Eastern societies who were the legal property of their master, but who could have legitimate sexual relations with their master. A concubine’s status was more elevated than a mere servant, but she was not free and did not have the legal rights of a free wife. The children of a concubine could, in some instances, become equal heirs with the children of the free wife. After the period of the Judges concubines may have become more of a royal prerogative (2 Sam 21:10-14; 1 Kgs 11:3).

22.text: Rehoboam appointed Abijah son of Maacah as the leader over his brothers, for he intended to name him his successor.

notes.text: Heb “and Rehoboam appointed for a head Abijah son of Maacah for ruler among his brothers, indeed to make him king.”

23.text: He wisely placed some of his many sons throughout the regions of Judah and Benjamin in the various fortified cities. He supplied them with abundant provisions and acquired many wives for them.

notes.text: Heb “and he was discerning and broke up from all his sons to all the lands of Judah and Benjamin, to all the fortified cities.”
“and he asked for a multitude of wives.”

1.text: After Rehoboam’s rule was established and solidified, he and all Israel rejected the law of the Lord.

2.text: Because they were unfaithful to the Lord, in King Rehoboam’s fifth year, King Shishak of Egypt attacked Jerusalem.

3.text: He had 1,200 chariots, 60,000 horsemen, and an innumerable number of soldiers who accompanied him from Egypt, including Libyans, Sukkites, and Cushites.

4.text: He captured the fortified cities of Judah and marched against Jerusalem.

5.text: Shemaiah the prophet visited Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah who were assembled in Jerusalem because of Shishak. He said to them, “This is what the Lord says: ‘You have rejected me, so I have rejected you and will hand you over to Shishak.’”

notes.text: Heb “also I have rejected you into the hand of Shishak.”

6.text: The leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, “The Lord is just.”

notes.text: Or “fair,” meaning the Lord’s punishment of them was just or fair.

7.text: When the Lord saw that they humbled themselves, the Lord’s message came to Shemaiah: “They have humbled themselves, so I will not destroy them. I will deliver them soon. My anger will not be unleashed against Jerusalem through Shishak.

notes.text: Heb “I will give them deliverance soon.”
Heb “pour out on.”

8.text: Yet they will become his subjects, so they can experience how serving me differs from serving the surrounding nations.”

notes.text: Heb “so they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms of the lands.”

9.text: King Shishak of Egypt attacked Jerusalem and took away the treasures of the Lord’s temple and of the royal palace; he took everything, including the gold shields that Solomon had made.

10.text: King Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace them and assigned them to the officers of the royal guard who protected the entrance to the royal palace.

notes.text: Heb “runners” (also in v. 11).

11.text: Whenever the king visited the Lord’s temple, the royal guards carried them and then brought them back to the guardroom.

notes.text: Heb “to the chamber of the runners.”

12.text: So when Rehoboam humbled himself, the Lord relented from his anger and did not annihilate him; Judah experienced some good things.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Rehoboam) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “the anger of the Lord turned from him and did not destroy completely.”
Heb “and also in Judah there were good things.”

13.text: King Rehoboam solidified his rule in Jerusalem; he was forty-one years old when he became king, and he ruled for seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the Lord chose from all the tribes of Israel to be his home. Rehoboam’s mother was an Ammonite named Naamah.

notes.text: Heb “and the king, Rehoboam, strengthened himself in Jerusalem and ruled.”
Heb “Rehoboam.” The recurrence of the proper name here is redundant in terms of contemporary English style, so the pronoun has been used in the translation instead.
Heb “the city where the Lord chose to place his name from all the tribes of Israel.”
Heb “his”; the referent has been specified in the translation for clarity.

14.text: He did evil because he was not determined to follow the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “because he did not set his heart to seek the Lord.”

15.text: The events of Rehoboam’s reign, from start to finish, are recorded in the Annals of Shemaiah the Prophet and of Iddo the Seer that include genealogical records. There were wars between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually.

notes.text: Heb “As for the events of Rehoboam, the former and the latter, are they not written?”

16.text: Then Rehoboam passed away and was buried in the City of David. His son Abijah replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”
The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

1.text: In the eighteenth year of the reign of King Jeroboam, Abijah became king over Judah.

2.text: He ruled for three years in Jerusalem. His mother was Michaiah, the daughter of Uriel from Gibeah. There was war between Abijah and Jeroboam.

notes.text: tnHeb “The name of his mother.”

The parallel text in 1 Kgs 15:2 identifies his mother as “Maacah, the daughter of Abishalom” (=Absalom, 2 Chr 11:20). Although most English versions identify the mother’s father as Uriel of Gibeah, a number of English versions substitute the name “Maacah” here for the mother (e.g., NIV, NCV, CEV, NLT).

3.text: Abijah launched the attack with 400,000 well-trained warriors, while Jeroboam deployed against him 800,000 well-trained warriors.

notes.text: Heb “and Abijah bound [i.e., began] the battle with a force of men of war, 400,000 chosen men.”
Heb “and Jeroboam arranged with him [for] battle with 800,000 chosen men, strong warrior[s].”

4.text: Abijah ascended Mount Zemaraim, in the Ephraimite hill country, and said: “Listen to me, Jeroboam and all Israel!

5.text: Don’t you realize that the Lord God of Israel has given David and his dynasty lasting dominion over Israel by a formal covenant?

notes.text: Heb “Do you not know that the Lord God of Israel has given kingship to David over Israel permanently, to him and to his sons [by] a covenant of salt?”
For other references to a “covenant of salt,” see Lev 2:13 and Num 18:19.

6.text: Jeroboam son of Nebat, a servant of Solomon son of David, rose up and rebelled against his master.

7.text: Lawless good-for-nothing men gathered around him and conspired against Rehoboam son of Solomon, when Rehoboam was an inexperienced young man and could not resist them.

notes.text: Heb “empty men, sons of wickedness.”
Heb “strengthened themselves.”
Heb “a young man and tender of heart.”

8.text: Now you are declaring that you will resist the Lord’s rule through the Davidic dynasty. You have a huge army, and bring with you the gold calves that Jeroboam made for you as gods.

notes.text: Heb “the kingdom of the Lord by the hand of the sons of David.”
Or “horde”; or “multitude.”

9.text: But you banished the Lord’s priests, Aaron’s descendants, and the Levites, and appointed your own priests just as the surrounding nations do! Anyone who comes to consecrate himself with a young bull or seven rams becomes a priest of these fake gods!

notes.text: In the Hebrew text this is phrased as a rhetorical question, “Did you not banish?” The rhetorical question expects the answer, “Of course you did,” the force of which is reflected in the translation “But you banished.”
Heb “whoever comes to fill his hand with a bull, a son of cattle, and seven rams, and he is a priest to no-gods.”

10.text: But as for us, the Lord is our God and we have not rejected him. Aaron’s descendants serve as the Lord’s priests, and the Levites assist them with the work.

notes.text: Heb “and priests serving the Lord [are] the sons of Aaron and the Levites in the work.”

11.text: They offer burnt sacrifices to the Lord every morning and every evening, along with fragrant incense. They arrange the Bread of the Presence on a ritually clean table and light the lamps on the gold lampstand every evening. Certainly we are observing the Lord our God’s regulations, but you have rejected him.

notes.text: Or “for.”

12.text: Now look, God is with us as our leader. His priests are ready to blow the trumpets to signal the attack against you. You Israelites, don’t fight against the Lord God of your ancestors, for you will not win!”

notes.text: Heb “and his priests and the trumpets of the war alarm [are ready] to sound out against you.”
Heb “fathers” (also in v. 18).

13.text: Now Jeroboam had sent some men to ambush the Judahite army from behind. The main army was in front of the Judahite army; the ambushers were behind it.

notes.text: Heb “and Jeroboam had caused to circle around an ambush to come from behind them.”
Heb “Judah.”

14.text: The men of Judah turned around and realized they were being attacked from the front and the rear. So they cried out to the Lord for help. The priests blew their trumpets,

notes.text: Heb “and Judah turned, and, look, to them [was] the battle in front and behind.”

15.text: and the men of Judah gave the battle cry. As the men of Judah gave the battle cry, God struck down Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah.

16.text: The Israelites fled from before the Judahite army, and God handed them over to the men of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “Judah.”
Heb “them”; the referent (the men of Judah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

17.text: Abijah and his army thoroughly defeated them; 500,000 well-trained Israelite men fell dead.

notes.text: Heb “struck them down with a great striking down.”
Heb “and [the] slain from Israel fell, 500,000 chosen men.”

18.text: That day the Israelites were defeated; the men of Judah prevailed because they relied on the Lord God of their ancestors.

notes.text: Heb “at that time.”

19.text: Abijah chased Jeroboam; he seized from him these cities: Bethel and its surrounding towns, Jeshanah and its surrounding towns, and Ephron and its surrounding towns.

20.text: Jeroboam did not regain power during the reign of Abijah. The Lord struck him down and he died.

notes.text: Heb “and the strength of Jeroboam was not retained again in the days of Abijah.”

21.text: Abijah’s power grew; he had fourteen wives and fathered twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.

notes.text: Heb “lifted up for himself.”

22.text: The rest of the events of Abijah’s reign, including his deeds and sayings, are recorded in the writings of the prophet Iddo.

notes.text: Heb “and his ways and his words.”

1.text: (13:23) Abijah passed away and was buried in the City of David. His son Asa replaced him as king. During his reign the land had rest for ten years.

notes.text: Beginning with 14:1, the verse numbers through 14:15 in the English Bible differ from the verse numbers in the Hebrew text (BHS), with 14:1 ET = 13:23 HT, 14:2 ET = 14:1 HT, 14:3 ET = 14:2 HT, etc., through 14:15 ET = 14:14 HT. Beginning with 15:1 the verse numbers in the ET and HT are again the same.
Heb “lay down with his fathers.”
The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.
Heb “in his days.”

2.text: (14:1) Asa did what the Lord his God desired and approved.

notes.text: Heb “and Asa did the good and the right in the eyes of the Lord his God.”

3.text: He removed the pagan altars and the high places, smashed the sacred pillars, and cut down the Asherah poles.

notes.text: Heb “the altars of the foreigner.”

Asherah poles. A leading deity of the Canaanite pantheon was Asherah, wife/sister of El and goddess of fertility. She was commonly worshiped at shrines in or near groves of evergreen trees, or, failing that, at places marked by wooden poles (Hebrew ‏אֲשֵׁרִים‎ [ʾasherim], as here). They were to be burned or cut down (Deut 7:5; 12:3; 16:21; Judg 6:25, 28, 30; 2 Kgs 18:4).

4.text: He ordered Judah to seek the Lord God of their ancestors and to observe his law and commands.

notes.text: Heb “fathers.”
Heb “the law and the command.”

5.text: He removed the high places and the incense altars from all the towns of Judah. The kingdom had rest under his rule.

notes.text: Heb “before him.”

6.text: He built fortified cities throughout Judah, for the land was at rest and there was no war during those years; the Lord gave him peace.

7.text: He said to the people of Judah: “Let’s build these cities and fortify them with walls, towers, and barred gates. The land remains ours because we have followed the Lord our God; we have followed him, and he has made us secure on all sides.” So they built the cities and prospered.

notes.text: The words “the people of” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The Hebrew text uses the name “Judah” by metonymy for the people of Judah.
Heb “and we will surround [them] with wall[s] and towers, doors, and bars.”
Heb “sought.”
Heb “we sought him, and he has given us rest all around.”
The words “the cities” are supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.

8.text: Asa had an army of 300,000 men from Judah, equipped with large shields and spears. He also had 280,000 men from Benjamin who carried small shields and were adept archers; they were all skilled warriors.

9.text: Zerah the Cushite marched against them with an army of 1,000,000 men and 300 chariots . He arrived at Mareshah,

notes.text: Heb “a thousand thousands.”

10.text: and Asa went out to oppose him. They deployed for battle in the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah.

11.text: Asa prayed to the Lord his God: “O Lord, there is no one but you who can help the weak when they are vastly outnumbered. Help us, O Lord our God, for we rely on you and have marched on your behalf against this huge army. O Lord, you are our God; don’t let men prevail against you!”

notes.text: Heb “called out.”
Heb “there is not except you to help between many with regard to [the one] without strength.”
Heb “and in your name we have come against this multitude.”
Heb “let not man retain [strength] with you.”

12.text: The Lord struck down the Cushites before Asa and Judah. The Cushites fled,

13.text: and Asa and his army chased them as far as Gerar. The Cushites were wiped out; they were shattered before the Lord and his army. The men of Judah carried off a huge amount of plunder.

notes.text: Heb “and there fell from the Cushites so that there was not to them preservation of life.”
Heb “they”; the referent (the men of Judah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

14.text: They defeated all the towns surrounding Gerar, for the Lord caused them to panic. The men of Judah looted all the towns, for they contained a huge amount of goods.

notes.text: Heb “for the terror of the Lord was upon them.”
Heb “they”; the referent (the men of Judah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “for great plunder was in them.”

15.text: They also attacked the tents of the herdsmen in charge of the livestock. They carried off many sheep and camels and then returned to Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “and also they struck down the tents of the livestock.”

1.text: God’s Spirit came upon Azariah son of Oded.

2.text: He met Asa and told him, “Listen to me, Asa and all Judah and Benjamin! The Lord is with you when you are loyal to him. If you seek him, he will respond to you, but if you reject him, he will reject you.

notes.text: Heb “went out before.”
Heb “when you are with him.”
Heb “he will allow himself to be found by you.”

3.text: For a long time Israel had not sought the one true God, or a priest to instruct them, or the law.

notes.text: Heb “Many days.”

4.text: Because of their distress, they turned back to the Lord God of Israel. They sought him and he responded to them.

notes.text: Heb “and he allowed himself to be found by them.”

5.text: In those days no one could travel safely, for total chaos had overtaken all the people of the surrounding lands.

notes.text: Heb “times.”
Heb “there was no peace for the one going out or the one coming in.”
Heb “for great confusion was upon all the inhabitants of the lands.”

6.text: One nation was crushed by another, and one city by another, for God caused them to be in great turmoil.

notes.text: Heb “threw them into confusion with all distress.”

7.text: But as for you, be strong and don’t get discouraged, for your work will be rewarded.”

notes.text: Heb “and let not your hands drop.”
Heb “for there is payment for your work.”

8.text: When Asa heard these words and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he was encouraged. He removed the detestable idols from the entire land of Judah and Benjamin and from the cities he had seized in the Ephraimite hill country. He repaired the altar of the Lord in front of the porch of the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: Heb “strengthened himself.”
Heb “the porch of the Lord.”
