9.text: He assembled all Judah and Benjamin, as well as the settlers from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who had come to live with them. Many people from Israel had come there to live when they saw that the Lord his God was with him.

notes.text: Or “foreign residents.”
Heb “had fallen upon him.”

10.text: They assembled in Jerusalem in the third month of the fifteenth year of Asa’s reign.

11.text: At that time they sacrificed to the Lord some of the plunder they had brought back, including 700 head of cattle and 7,000 sheep.

notes.text: Or “In that day.”

The Hebrew term ‏צֹאן‎ (tsoʾn) denotes smaller livestock in general; depending on context it can refer to sheep only or goats only, but their is nothing in the immediate context here to specify one or the other.

12.text: They solemnly agreed to seek the Lord God of their ancestors with their whole heart and being.

notes.text: Heb “entered into a covenant.”
Heb “fathers.”

13.text: Anyone who would not seek the Lord God of Israel would be executed, whether they were young or old, male or female.

notes.text: Heb “whether small or great.”

14.text: They swore their allegiance to the Lord, shouting their approval loudly and sounding trumpets and horns.

notes.text: Heb “with a loud voice and with a shout of joy and with trumpets and with horns.”

15.text: All Judah was happy about the oath, because they made the vow with their whole heart. They willingly sought the Lord and he responded to them. He made them secure on every side.

notes.text: Heb “and with all their desire they sought him and he allowed himself to be found by them.”
Heb “and the Lord gave them rest all around.”

16.text: King Asa also removed Maacah his grandmother from her position as queen mother because she had made a loathsome Asherah pole. Asa cut down her loathsome pole and crushed and burned it in the Kidron Valley.

notes.text: Heb “mother,” but Hebrew often uses “father” and “mother” for grandparents and even more remote ancestors.
The Hebrew term ‏גְּבִירָה‎ (gevirah) can denote “queen” or “queen mother” depending on the context. Here the latter is indicated, since Maacah was the wife of Rehoboam and mother of Abijah.

17.text: The high places were not eliminated from Israel, yet Asa was wholeheartedly devoted to the Lord throughout his lifetime.

notes.text: Heb “yet the heart of Asa was complete all his days.”

18.text: He brought the holy items that his father and he had made into God’s temple, including the silver, gold, and other articles.

notes.text: Heb “and he brought the holy things of his father and his holy things [into] the house of God, silver, gold, and items.”

19.text: There was no more war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa’s reign.

1.text: In the thirty-sixth year of Asa’s reign, King Baasha of Israel attacked Judah, and he established Ramah as a military outpost to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the land of King Asa of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “and he built up Ramah so as to not permit going out or coming in to Asa king of Judah.”

2.text: Asa took all the silver and gold that was left in the treasuries of the Lord’s temple and of the royal palace and sent it to King Ben Hadad of Syria, ruler in Damascus, along with this message:

3.text: “I want to make a treaty with you, like the one our fathers made. See, I have sent you silver and gold. Break your treaty with King Baasha of Israel, so he will retreat from my land.”

notes.text: Heb “[May there be] a covenant between me and you [as there was] between my father and your father.”
Heb “so he will go up from upon me.”

4.text: Ben Hadad accepted King Asa’s offer and ordered his army commanders to attack the cities of Israel. They conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel Maim, and all the storage cities of Naphtali.

notes.text: Heb “and Ben Hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of the armies which belonged to him against the cities of Israel.”
Heb “They struck down.”
In the parallel passage in 1 Kgs 15:20, this city’s name appears as Abel Beth Maacah. These appear to be variant names for the same place.

5.text: When Baasha heard the news, he stopped fortifying Ramah and abandoned the project.

notes.text: Heb “building.”
Heb “and he caused his work to cease.”

6.text: King Asa ordered all the men of Judah to carry away the stones and wood that Baasha had used to build Ramah. He used the materials to build up Geba and Mizpah.

notes.text: Heb “and King Asa took all Judah and they carried away the stones of Ramah and its wood which Baasha had built.”
Heb “and he built with them.”

7.text: At that time Hanani the prophet visited King Asa of Judah and said to him: “Because you relied on the king of Syria and did not rely on the Lord your God, the army of the king of Syria has escaped from your hand.

notes.text: Heb “the seer.”

8.text: Did not the Cushites and Libyans have a huge army with chariots and a very large number of horsemen? But when you relied on the Lord, he handed them over to you!

9.text: Certainly the Lord watches the whole earth carefully and is ready to strengthen those who are devoted to him. You have acted foolishly in this matter; from now on you will have war.”

notes.text: Or “for.”
Heb “the eyes of the Lord move quickly through all the earth.”
Heb “to strengthen himself with their heart, [the one] complete toward him.”

10.text: Asa was so angry at the prophet, he put him in jail. Asa also oppressed some of the people at that time.

notes.text: Heb “and Asa was angry at the seer, and he put him [in] the house of stocks, because of his rage with him over this.”

11.text: The events of Asa’s reign, from start to finish, are recorded in the Scroll of the Kings of Judah and Israel.

notes.text: Heb “Look, the events of Asa, the former and the latter, look, they are written on the scroll of the kings of Judah and Israel.”

12.text: In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa developed a foot disease and his disease became severe. Yet even in his disease, he did not seek the Lord, but only the doctors.

13.text: Asa passed away in the forty-first year of his reign.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers, and he died.”

14.text: He was buried in the tomb he had carved out in the City of David. They laid him to rest on a platform covered with spices and assorted mixtures of ointments. They made a huge bonfire to honor him.

notes.text: The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.
The Hebrew term ‏מִשְׁכָּב‎ (mishkav) most often refers to a bed. In this setting it was most likely a raised platform within the tomb where the body was laid to rest, technically similar to a bier.
Heb “and they burned for him a large fire, very great.”

1.text: His son Jehoshaphat replaced him as king and solidified his rule over Israel.

notes.text: Heb “and strengthened himself over Israel.”

2.text: He placed troops in all Judah’s fortified cities and posted garrisons throughout the land of Judah and in the cities of Ephraim that his father Asa had seized.

notes.text: Or perhaps, “governors.”

3.text: The Lord was with Jehoshaphat because he followed in his ancestor David’s footsteps at the beginning of his reign. He did not seek the Baals,

notes.text: Heb “father.”
Heb “for he walked in the ways of David his father [in] the beginning [times].”

4.text: but instead sought the God of his ancestors and obeyed his commands, unlike the Israelites.

notes.text: Heb “fathers.”
Heb “walked in.”
Heb “and not like the behavior of Israel.”

5.text: The Lord made his kingdom secure; all Judah brought tribute to Jehoshaphat, and he became very wealthy and greatly respected.

notes.text: Heb “established the kingdom in his hand.”
Heb “and he had wealth and honor in abundance.”

6.text: He was committed to following the Lord; he even removed the high places and Asherah poles from Judah.

notes.text: Heb “and his heart was high in the ways of the Lord.” Perhaps ‏גָּבַהּ‎ (gavah, “be high”) here means “be cheerful” (HALOT 171 s.v.) or “be encouraged” (BDB 147 s.v. 3.a).

7.text: In the third year of his reign he sent his officials Ben Hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah to teach in the cities of Judah.

8.text: They were accompanied by the Levites Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tob-Adonijah, and by the priests Elishama and Jehoram.

9.text: They taught throughout Judah, taking with them the scroll of the law of the Lord. They traveled to all the cities of Judah and taught the people.

10.text: The Lord put fear into all the kingdoms surrounding Judah; they did not make war with Jehoshaphat.

notes.text: Heb “and the terror of the Lord was upon all the kingdoms of the lands which were surrounding Judah.”

11.text: Some of the Philistines brought Jehoshaphat tribute, including a load of silver. The Arabs brought him 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats from their flocks.

12.text: Jehoshaphat’s power kept increasing. He built fortresses and storage cities throughout Judah.

13.text: He had many supplies stored in the cities of Judah and an army of skilled warriors stationed in Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “and many supplies were his in the cities of Judah, and men of war, warriors of skill in Jerusalem.”

14.text: These were their divisions by families: There were 1,000 officers from Judah. Adnah the commander led 300,000 skilled warriors,

notes.text: Or perhaps “from Judah, commanders of the thousands.”

15.text: Jehochanan the commander led 280,000,

16.text: and Amasiah son of Zikri, who volunteered to serve the Lord, led 200,000 skilled warriors.

17.text: From Benjamin, Eliada, a skilled warrior, led 200,000 men who were equipped with bows and shields,

18.text: and Jehozabad led 180,000 trained warriors.

19.text: These were the ones who served the king, besides those whom the king placed in the fortified cities throughout Judah.

1.text: Jehoshaphat was very wealthy and greatly respected. He made an alliance by marriage with Ahab,

2.text: and after several years went down to visit Ahab in Samaria. Ahab slaughtered many sheep and cattle to honor Jehoshaphat and those who came with him. He persuaded him to join in an attack against Ramoth Gilead.

notes.text: Heb “at the end of years.”
The word “visit” is supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.
Heb “and Ahab slaughtered for him sheep and cattle in abundance, and for the people who were with him.”
Heb “to go up.”

3.text: King Ahab of Israel said to King Jehoshaphat of Judah, “Will you go with me to attack Ramoth Gilead?” He replied, “I will support you; my army is at your disposal and will support you in battle.”

notes.text: Heb “Like me, like you; and like your people, my people; and with you in battle.”

4.text: Then Jehoshaphat said further to the king of Israel, “First, please seek an oracle from the Lord.”

notes.text: The word “further” has been added on the basis that this is a second speech act. The narrator uses the title “king of Israel” to convey a sense of formality.
Or “even today,” “right away.”

Heb “inquire for the Lord’s message.” Jehoshaphat is requesting a prophetic oracle revealing the Lord’s will in the matter and their prospects for success. For examples of such oracles, see 2 Sam 5:19, 23-24.

5.text: So the king of Israel assembled 400 prophets and asked them, “Should we attack Ramoth Gilead or not?” They said, “Attack! God will hand it over to the king.”

notes.text: Heb “Should we go against Ramoth Gilead for war or should I refrain?”

Though Jehoshaphat had requested an oracle from “the Lord” (‏יְהוָה‎, yehvah, “Yahweh”), the Israelite prophets stop short of actually using this name and substitute the title ‏הָאֱלֹהִים‎ (haʾelohim, “the God”). This ambiguity may explain in part Jehoshaphat’s hesitancy and caution (vv. 7-8). He seems to doubt that the 400 are genuine prophets of the Lord.

6.text: But Jehoshaphat asked, “Is there not a prophet of the Lord still here, that we may ask him?”

7.text: The king of Israel answered Jehoshaphat, “There is still one man through whom we can seek the Lord’s will, but I despise him because he does not prophesy prosperity for me, but always disaster—Micaiah son of Imlah.” Jehoshaphat said, “The king should not say such things!”

notes.text: Heb “to seek the Lord from him.”
Or “hate.”
Heb “all his days.”

8.text: The king of Israel summoned an officer and said, “Quickly bring Micaiah son of Imlah.”

9.text: Now the king of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah were sitting on their respective thrones, dressed in their royal robes, at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria. All the prophets were prophesying before them.

notes.text: Heb “at,” which in this case probably means “near.”

10.text: Zedekiah son of Kenaanah made iron horns and said, “This is what the Lord says, ‘With these you will gore Syria until they are destroyed.’”

11.text: All the prophets were prophesying the same, saying, “Attack Ramoth Gilead! You will succeed; the Lord will hand it over to the king.”

12.text: Now the messenger who went to summon Micaiah said to him, “Look, the prophets are in complete agreement that the king will succeed. Your words must agree with theirs; you must predict success!”

notes.text: Heb “the words of the prophets are [with] one mouth good for the king.”
Heb “let your words be like one of them and speak good.”

13.text: But Micaiah said, “As certainly as the Lord lives, I will say what my God tells me to say!”

14.text: Micaiah came before the king and the king asked him, “Micaiah, should we attack Ramoth Gilead or not?” He answered him, “Attack! You will succeed; they will be handed over to you.”

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Micaiah) has been specified in the translation both for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

One does not expect Micaiah, having just vowed to speak only what the Lord tells him, to agree with the other prophets and give the king an inaccurate prophecy. Micaiah’s actions became understandable later, when we discover that the Lord desires to deceive the king and lead him to his demise. The Lord even dispatches a lying spirit to deceive Ahab’s prophets. Micaiah can lie to the king because he realizes this lie is from the Lord. It is important to note that in v. 13 Micaiah only vows to speak the word of his God; he does not necessarily say he will tell the truth. In this case the Lord’s word is deliberately deceptive. Only when the king adjures him to tell the truth (v. 15), does Micaiah do so.

15.text: The king said to him, “How many times must I make you solemnly promise in the name of the Lord to tell me only the truth?”

notes.text: Or “swear an oath by.”

16.text: Micaiah replied, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep that have no shepherd. Then the Lord said, ‘They have no master. They should go home in peace.’”

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Micaiah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

17.text: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Didn’t I tell you he does not prophesy prosperity for me, but disaster?”

18.text: Micaiah said, “That being the case, listen to the Lord’s message. I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, with all the heavenly assembly standing on his right and on his left.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Micaiah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

19.text: The Lord said, ‘Who will deceive King Ahab of Israel, so he will attack Ramoth Gilead and die there?’ One said this and another that.

20.text: Then a spirit stepped forward and stood before the Lord. He said, ‘I will deceive him.’ The Lord asked him, ‘How?’

notes.text: Heb “the spirit.” The significance of the article prefixed to ‏רוּחַ‎ (ruakh) is uncertain, but it could contain a clue as to this spirit’s identity, especially when interpreted in light of verse 23. It is certainly possible, and probably even likely, that the article is used in a generic or dramatic sense and should be translated, “a spirit.” In the latter case it would show that this spirit was vivid and definite in the mind of Micaiah the storyteller. However, if one insists that the article indicates a well-known or universally known spirit, the following context provides a likely referent. Verse 23 tells how Zedekiah slapped Micaiah in the face and then asked sarcastically, “Which way did the spirit from the Lord (‏רוּחַ־יְהוָה‎, ruakh yehvah) go when he went from me to speak to you?” When the phrase “the spirit of the Lord” refers to the divine spirit (rather than the divine breath or mind, as in Isa 40:7, 13) elsewhere, the spirit energizes an individual or group for special tasks or moves one to prophesy. This raises the possibility that the deceiving spirit of vv. 20-22 is the same as the divine spirit mentioned by Zedekiah in v. 23. This would explain why the article is used on ‏רוּחַ‎ (ruakh); he can be called “the spirit” because he is the well-known spirit who energizes the prophets.

21.text: He replied, ‘I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.’ The Lord said, ‘Deceive and overpower him. Go out and do as you have proposed.’

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The Hebrew text has two imperfects connected by ‏וְגַם‎ (vegam). These verbs could be translated as specific futures, “you will deceive and also you will prevail,” in which case the Lord is assuring the spirit of success on his mission. However, in a commissioning context (note the following imperatives) such as this, it is more likely that the imperfects are injunctive, in which case one could translate, “Deceive, and also overpower.”

22.text: So now, look, the Lord has placed a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours, but the Lord has decreed disaster for you.”

23.text: Zedekiah son of Kenaanah approached, hit Micaiah on the jaw, and said, “Which way did the Lord’s Spirit go when he went from me to speak to you?”

24.text: Micaiah replied, “Look, you will see in the day when you go into an inner room to hide.”

25.text: Then the king of Israel said, “Take Micaiah and return him to Amon the city official and Joash the king’s son.

26.text: Say, ‘This is what the king says: “Put this man in prison. Give him only a little bread and water until I return safely.”’”

notes.text: Heb “the bread of affliction and the water of affliction.”

27.text: Micaiah said, “If you really do return safely, then the Lord has not spoken through me!” Then he added, “Take note, all you people.”

notes.text: Heb “Listen.”

28.text: The king of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah attacked Ramoth Gilead.

29.text: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “I will disguise myself and then enter the battle, but you wear your royal attire.” So the king of Israel disguised himself and they entered the battle.

notes.text: The Hebrew verbal forms could be imperatives (“Disguise yourself and enter”), but this would make no sense in light of the immediately following context. The forms are better interpreted as infinitives absolute functioning as cohortatives (see IBHS 594 §35.5.2a). Some prefer to emend the forms to imperfects.

30.text: Now the king of Syria had ordered his chariot commanders, “Do not fight common soldiers or high ranking officers; fight only the king of Israel!”

notes.text: Heb “small or great.”

31.text: When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they said, “He must be the king of Israel!” So they turned and attacked him, but Jehoshaphat cried out. The Lord helped him; God lured them away from him.

32.text: When the chariot commanders realized he was not the king of Israel, they turned away from him.

33.text: Now an archer shot an arrow at random, and it struck the king of Israel between the plates of his armor. The king ordered his charioteer, “Turn around and take me from the battle line, for I am wounded.”

notes.text: Heb “now a man drew a bow in his innocence” (i.e., with no specific target in mind, or at least without realizing his target was the king of Israel).
Heb “he”; the referent (the king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “camp.”

34.text: While the battle raged throughout the day, the king of Israel stood propped up in his chariot opposite the Syrians. He died in the evening as the sun was setting.

1.text: When King Jehoshaphat of Judah returned home safely to Jerusalem,

2.text: the prophet Jehu son of Hanani confronted him; he said to King Jehoshaphat, “Is it right to help the wicked and be an ally of those who oppose the Lord? Because you have done this, the Lord is angry with you!

notes.text: Or “seer.”
Heb “went out to his face.”
Heb “and love those who hate the Lord?”
Heb “and because of this upon you is anger from before the Lord.”

3.text: Nevertheless you have done some good things; you removed the Asherah poles from the land and you were determined to follow God.”

notes.text: Heb “nevertheless good things are found with you.”
Here ‏בָּעַר‎ (baʿar) is not the well attested verb “burn,” but the less common homonym meaning “devastate, sweep away, remove.” See HALOT 146 s.v. II ‏בער‎.
Heb “and you set your heart to seek God.”

4.text: Jehoshaphat lived in Jerusalem. He went out among the people from Beer Sheba to the hill country of Ephraim and encouraged them to follow the Lord God of their ancestors.

notes.text: Heb “and turned them back to.”
Heb “fathers.”

5.text: He appointed judges throughout the land and in each of the fortified cities of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “in the land in all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city.”

6.text: He told the judges, “Be careful what you do, for you are not judging for men, but for the Lord, who will be with you when you make judicial decisions.

notes.text: Heb “see what you are doing.”

7.text: Respect the Lord and make careful decisions, for the Lord our God disapproves of injustice, partiality, and bribery.”

notes.text: Heb “and now let the terror of the Lord be upon you, be careful and act for there is not with the Lord our God injustice, lifting up of a face, and taking a bribe.”

8.text: In Jerusalem Jehoshaphat appointed some Levites, priests, and Israelite family leaders to judge on behalf of the Lord and to settle disputes among the residents of Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “for the judgment of the Lord.”

Heb “and to conduct a case [or “for controversy”], and they returned [to] Jerusalem.” Some emend ‏וַיָּשֻׁבוּ‎ (vayyashuvu, “and they returned”) to ‏וַיֵּשְׁבוּ‎ (vayyeshevu, “and they lived [in]”). The present translation assumes an emendation to ‏יֹשְׁבֵי‎ (yoshevey, “residents of”).

9.text: He commanded them: “Carry out your duties with respect for the Lord, with honesty, and with pure motives.

notes.text: Heb “This you must do with the fear of the Lord, with honesty, and with a complete heart.”

10.text: Whenever your countrymen who live in the cities bring a case before you (whether it involves a violent crime or other matters related to the law, commandments, rules, and regulations), warn them that they must not sin against the Lord. If you fail to do so, God will be angry with you and your colleagues, but if you obey, you will be free of guilt.

notes.text: Heb “and every case which comes to you from your brothers who live in their cities.”
Heb “between blood pertaining to blood.”
Heb “and anger will be upon you and your brothers; do this and you will not be guilty.”

11.text: Take note, Amariah the chief priest will oversee you in every matter pertaining to the Lord and Zebadiah son of Ishmael, the leader of the family of Judah, in every matter pertaining to the king. The Levites will serve as officials before you. Act courageously, and may the Lord be with those who do well!”

notes.text: Heb “will be over you.”
Heb “Be strong and act!”

1.text: Later the Moabites and Ammonites, along with some of the Meunites, attacked Jehoshaphat.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has “Ammonites,” but they are mentioned just before this. Most translations, following some mss of the LXX, read “Meunites” (see 2 Chr 26:7; so NASB, NIV, NRSV).

2.text: Messengers arrived and reported to Jehoshaphat, “A huge army is attacking you from the other side of the Dead Sea, from the direction of Edom. Look, they are in Hazazon Tamar (that is, En Gedi).”

notes.text: Heb “they”; the implied referent (messengers) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “the Sea”; in context (“from the direction of Edom”) this must refer to the Dead Sea, which has been specified in the translation for clarity (cf. NEB, NLT).
Most Hebrew mss, the LXX, and Vulgate read “from Aram” (i.e., Syria), but this should be emended to “Edom,” which is the reading of one Hebrew ms and the Old Latin.

3.text: Jehoshaphat was afraid, so he decided to seek the Lord’s advice. He decreed that all Judah should observe a fast.

notes.text: Heb “and he set his face to seek the Lord.”

4.text: The people of Judah assembled to ask for the Lord’s help; they came from all the cities of Judah to ask for the Lord’s help.

notes.text: The words “the people of” are supplied in the translation for clarity. The Hebrew text uses the name “Judah” by metonymy for the people of Judah.
Heb “to seek from the Lord.” The verb here (‏בָּקַשׁ‎, baqash) is different from the one translated “seek” in v. 3 (‏דָּרַשׁ‎, darash).
Heb “to seek the Lord.” The verb here (‏בָּקַשׁ‎, baqash) is different from the one translated “seek” in v. 3 (‏דָּרַשׁ‎, darash).

5.text: Jehoshaphat stood before the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem at the Lord’s temple, in front of the new courtyard.

6.text: He prayed: “O Lord God of our ancestors, you are the God who lives in heaven and rules over all the kingdoms of the nations. You possess strength and power; no one can stand against you.

notes.text: Heb “fathers” (also in v. 33).
Heb “are you not God in heaven?” The rhetorical question expects the answer “yes,” resulting in the positive statement “you are the God who lives in heaven” employed in the translation.

7.text: Our God, you drove out the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel and gave it as a permanent possession to the descendants of your friend Abraham.

notes.text: Heb “did you not drive out . . . ?” This is another rhetorical question which expects a positive response; see the note on the word “heaven” in the previous verse.
Heb “permanently.”
Or perhaps “your covenantal partner.” See Isa 41:8.

8.text: They settled down in it and built in it a temple to honor you, saying,

notes.text: Or “sanctuary.”
Heb “for your name.” The word “name” sometimes refers to one’s reputation or honor (thus the translation here, “to honor you”).

9.text: ‘If disaster comes on us in the form of military attack, judgment, plague, or famine, we will stand in front of this temple before you, for you are present in this temple. We will cry out to you for help in our distress, so that you will hear and deliver us.’

notes.text: Heb “sword.”

Heb “for your name is in this house.” The “name” of the Lord sometimes designates the Lord himself, being indistinguishable from the proper name. In this case the temple is referred to as a “house” where the Lord himself can reside.
Or “so that you may.”

10.text: Now the Ammonites, Moabites, and men from Mount Seir are coming! When Israel came from the land of Egypt, you did not allow them to invade these lands. They bypassed them and did not destroy them.

notes.text: Heb “now, look, the sons of Ammon, Moab and Mount Seir.”
Heb “whom you did not allow Israel to enter when they came from the land of Egypt.”

11.text: Look how they are repaying us! They come to drive us out of our allotted land which you assigned to us!

12.text: Our God, will you not judge them? For we are powerless against this huge army that attacks us. We don’t know what we should do; we look to you for help.”

notes.text: Heb “for [or “indeed”] upon you are our eyes.”

13.text: All the men of Judah were standing before the Lord, along with their infants, wives, and children.

notes.text: Heb “Judah.” The words “the men of” are supplied in the translation for clarity. The Hebrew text uses the name “Judah” by metonymy for the men of Judah.

14.text: Then in the midst of the assembly, the Lord’s Spirit came upon Jachaziel son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah, a Levite and descendant of Asaph.

15.text: He said: “Pay attention, all you people of Judah, residents of Jerusalem, and King Jehoshaphat! This is what the Lord says to you: ‘Don’t be afraid and don’t panic because of this huge army! For the battle is not yours, but God’s.

notes.text: Heb “all Judah.” The words “you people of” are supplied in the translation for clarity. The Hebrew text uses the name “Judah” by metonymy for the people of Judah. Unlike the previous instance in v. 13 where infants, wives, and children are mentioned separately, this reference appears to include them all.
Or perhaps “don’t get discouraged.”

16.text: Tomorrow march down against them as they come up the Ascent of Ziz. You will find them at the end of the ravine in front of the wilderness of Jeruel.

notes.text: Heb “look.”

17.text: You will not fight in this battle. Take your positions, stand, and watch the Lord deliver you, O Judah and Jerusalem. Don’t be afraid and don’t panic! Tomorrow march out toward them; the Lord is with you!’”

notes.text: Heb “the deliverance of the Lord with you.”
Or perhaps “don’t get discouraged.”

18.text: Jehoshaphat bowed down with his face toward the ground, and all the people of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem fell down before the Lord and worshiped him.

notes.text: Heb “all Judah.” The words “you people of” are supplied in the translation for clarity. See the note on the word “Judah” in v. 15.
Heb “to worship the Lord.”

19.text: Then some Levites, from the Kohathites and Korahites, got up and loudly praised the Lord God of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “arose to praise the Lord God of Israel with a very loud voice.”

20.text: Early the next morning they marched out to the wilderness of Tekoa. When they were ready to march, Jehoshaphat stood up and said: “Listen to me, you people of Judah and residents of Jerusalem! Trust in the Lord your God and you will be safe! Trust in the message of his prophets and you will win.”

notes.text: Heb “O Judah.” The words “you people of” are supplied in the translation for clarity. See the note on the word “Judah” in v. 15.

There is a wordplay in the Hebrew text. The Hiphil verb form ‏הַאֲמִינוּ‎ (haʾaminu, “trust”) and the Niphal form ‏תֵאָמֵנוּ‎ (teʾamenu, “you will be safe”) come from the same verbal root (‏אָמַן‎, ʾaman).

21.text: He met with the people and appointed musicians to play before the Lord and praise his majestic splendor. As they marched ahead of the warriors they said: “Give thanks to the Lord, for his loyal love endures.”

notes.text: Or “consulted.”
Or “is eternal.”

22.text: When they began to shout and praise, the Lord suddenly attacked the Ammonites, Moabites, and men from Mount Seir who were invading Judah, and they were defeated.

notes.text: Heb “set ambushers against.” This is probably idiomatic here for launching a surprise attack.
Heb “the sons of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir.”

23.text: The Ammonites and Moabites attacked the men from Mount Seir and annihilated them. When they had finished off the men of Seir, they attacked and destroyed one another.

notes.text: Heb “the sons of Ammon and Moab stood against the residents of Mount Seir.”
Heb “to annihilate and to destroy.”
Heb “residents.”

Heb “they helped, each one his fellow, for destruction.” The verb ‏עָזַר‎ (ʿazar), traditionally understood as the well-attested verb meaning “to help,” is an odd fit in this context. It is possible that it is from a homonymic root, perhaps meaning to “attack.” This root is attested in Ugaritic in a nominal form meaning “young man, warrior, hero.” For a discussion of the proposed root, see HALOT 811 s.v. II ‏עזר‎.

24.text: When the men of Judah arrived at the observation post overlooking the wilderness and looked at the huge army, they saw dead bodies on the ground; there were no survivors.

notes.text: Heb “Judah.” The words “the men of” are supplied in the translation for clarity. The Hebrew text uses the name “Judah” by metonymy for the men of Judah.
Heb “turned toward.”

25.text: Jehoshaphat and his men went to gather the plunder; they found a huge amount of supplies, clothing, and valuable items. They carried away everything they could. There was so much plunder, it took them three days to haul it off.

notes.text: Or “army.”

The MT reads ‏פְגָרִים‎ (fegarim, “corpses”), but this seems odd among a list of plunder. A few medieval Hebrew mss and the Vulgate read ‏בְגָדִים‎ (vegadim, “clothing”), which fits the context much better.
Heb “and they snatched away for themselves so that there was no carrying away.”
Heb “and they were three days looting the plunder for it was great.”

26.text: On the fourth day they assembled in the Valley of Berachah, where they praised the Lord. So that place is called the Valley of Berachah to this very day.

notes.text: Heb “for there.”
The name Berachah, which means “blessing” in Hebrew, is derived from the verbal root “to praise [or “to bless”],” which appears earlier in the verse.

27.text: Then all the men of Judah and Jerusalem returned joyfully to Jerusalem with Jehoshaphat leading them; the Lord had given them reason to rejoice over their enemies.

28.text: They entered Jerusalem to the sound of stringed instruments and trumpets and proceeded to the temple of the Lord.

29.text: All the kingdoms of the surrounding lands were afraid of God when they heard how the Lord had fought against Israel’s enemies.

notes.text: Heb “and the terror of God [or “a great terror”] was upon all the kingdoms of the lands.” It is uncertain if ‏אֱלֹהִים‎ (ʾelohim) should be understood as a proper name here (“God”), or taken in an idiomatic superlative sense.

30.text: Jehoshaphat’s kingdom enjoyed peace; his God made him secure on every side.

notes.text: Heb “and his God gave him rest all around.”

31.text: Jehoshaphat reigned over Judah. He was thirty-five years old when he became king and he reigned for twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother was Azubah, the daughter of Shilhi.

notes.text: Heb “The name of his mother.”

32.text: He followed in his father Asa’s footsteps and was careful to do what the Lord approved.

notes.text: Heb “he walked in the way of his father Asa and did not turn from it, doing what is right in the eyes of the Lord.”

33.text: However, the high places were not eliminated; the people were still not devoted to the God of their ancestors.

notes.text: Heb “and still the people did not set their heart[s] on the God of their fathers.”

34.text: The rest of the events of Jehoshaphat’s reign, from start to finish, are recorded in the Annals of Jehu son of Hanani, which are included in the Scroll of the Kings of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “the rest of the events of Jehoshaphat, the former and the latter, look, they are written in the records of Jehu son of Hanani, which are taken up in the scroll of the kings of Israel.”

35.text: Later King Jehoshaphat of Judah made an alliance with King Ahaziah of Israel, who did evil.

notes.text: Heb “he.” The pronoun has been translated as a relative pronoun for stylistic reasons.

36.text: They agreed to make large seagoing merchant ships; they built the ships in Ezion Geber.

notes.text: Heb “he made an alliance with him.”

Heb “make ships to go to Tarshish.” This probably refers to large ships either made in or capable of traveling to the distant western port of Tarshish; a “Tarshish-ship” was essentially a large seagoing merchant ship.

37.text: Eliezer son of Dodavahu from Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, “Because you made an alliance with Ahaziah, the Lord will shatter what you have made.” The ships were wrecked and unable to go to sea.

notes.text: Heb “when.”
Heb “to go to Tarshish.”

1.text: Jehoshaphat passed away and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His son Jehoram replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”
Heb “fathers” (also in vv. 10, 12, 19).
The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.
The parallel account in 2 Kgs 8:20-24 has the variant spelling “Joram” for the son of Jehoshaphat.

2.text: His brothers, Jehoshaphat’s sons, were Azariah, Jechiel, Zechariah, Azariahu, Michael, and Shephatiah. All these were sons of King Jehoshaphat of Israel.

notes.text: A number of times in 2 Chronicles “Israel” is used instead of the more specific “Judah”; see 2 Chr 12:6; 23:2). In the interest of consistency some translations (e.g., NAB, NRSV) substitute “Judah” for “Israel” here.

3.text: Their father gave them many presents, including silver, gold, and other precious items, along with fortified cities in Judah. But he gave the kingdom to Jehoram because he was the firstborn.

4.text: Jehoram took control of his father’s kingdom and became powerful. Then he killed all his brothers, as well as some of the officials of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “and Jehoram arose over the kingdom of his father and strengthened himself.”
Heb “and he killed all his brothers with the sword.”

5.text: Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned for eight years in Jerusalem.

6.text: He followed in the footsteps of the kings of Israel, just as Ahab’s dynasty had done, for he married Ahab’s daughter. He did evil in the sight of the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, just as the house of Ahab did, for the daughter of Ahab was his wife.”
Heb “in the eyes of.”

7.text: But the Lord was unwilling to destroy David’s dynasty because of the promise he had made to give David a perpetual dynasty.

notes.text: Heb “house.”
Or “covenant.”
Heb “which he made to David, just as he had promised to give him and his sons a lamp all the days.” Here “lamp” is metaphorical, symbolizing the Davidic dynasty.

8.text: During Jehoram’s reign Edom freed themselves from Judah’s control and set up their own king.

notes.text: Heb “his”; the referent (Jehoram) has been specified in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.
Heb “in his days Edom rebelled from under the hand of Judah and enthroned a king over them.”

9.text: Jehoram crossed over with his officers and all his chariots. The Edomites, who had surrounded him, attacked at night and defeated him and his chariot officers.

notes.text: Heb “and he arose at night and defeated Edom, who had surrounded him, and the chariot officers.” The Hebrew text as it stands gives the impression that Jehoram was surrounded and launched a victorious nighttime counterattack. Yet v. 10 goes on to state that the Edomite revolt was successful. The translation above assumes an emendation of the Hebrew text. Adding a third masculine singular pronominal suffix to the accusative sign before Edom (reading ‏אֹתוֹ‎ [ʾoto, “him”] instead of just ‏אֶת‎ [ʾet]) and taking Edom as the subject of verbs allows one to translate the verse in a way that is more consistent with the context, which depicts an Israelite defeat, not victory. See also 2 Kgs 8:21.

10.text: So Edom has remained free from Judah’s control to this very day. At that same time Libnah also rebelled and freed themselves from Judah’s control because Jehoram rejected the Lord God of his ancestors.

notes.text: Heb “and Edom rebelled from under the hand of Judah until this day.”
Or “from Jehoram’s control”; Heb “from under his hand.” The pronominal suffix may refer to Judah in general or, more specifically, to Jehoram.
Heb “he.” This pronoun could refer to Judah, but the context focuses on Jehoram’s misdeeds. See especially v. 11.

11.text: He also built high places on the hills of Judah; he encouraged the residents of Jerusalem to be unfaithful to the Lord and led Judah away from the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “and he caused the residents of Jerusalem to commit adultery.” In this context spiritual unfaithfulness to the Lord is in view rather than physical adultery.
Heb “and drove Judah away.”

12.text: Jehoram received this letter from Elijah the prophet: “This is what the Lord God of your ancestor David says: ‘You have not followed in the footsteps of your father Jehoshaphat and of King Asa of Judah,

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Jehoram) has been specified in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

Heb “Because you…” In the Hebrew text this lengthy sentence is completed in vv. 14-15. Because of its length and complexity (and the tendency of contemporary English to use shorter sentences), the translation has divided it up into several English sentences.
Heb “walked in the ways.”
Heb “in the ways of.”

13.text: but have instead followed in the footsteps of the kings of Israel. You encouraged the people of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem to be unfaithful to the Lord, just as the family of Ahab does in Israel. You also killed your brothers, members of your father’s family, who were better than you.

notes.text: Heb “and you walked in the way of the kings of Israel and caused Judah and the residents of Jerusalem to commit adultery, like the house of Ahab causes to commit adultery.”
Heb “the house of your father.”

14.text: So look, the Lord is about to severely afflict your people, your sons, your wives, and all you own.

notes.text: Heb “to strike with a great striking.”

15.text: And you will get a serious, chronic intestinal disease which will cause your intestines to come out.’”

notes.text: Heb “and you [will have] a serious illness, an illness of the intestines until your intestines come out because of the illness days upon days.”

16.text: The Lord stirred up against Jehoram the Philistines and the Arabs who lived beside the Cushites.

notes.text: Heb “the spirit of the Philistines.”

17.text: They attacked Judah and swept through it. They carried off everything they found in the royal palace, including his sons and wives. None of his sons was left, except for his youngest, Ahaziah.

notes.text: Heb “broke it up.”
Heb “all the property which was found in the house of the king.”

18.text: After all this happened, the Lord afflicted him with an incurable intestinal disease.

notes.text: Heb “in his intestines with an illness [for which] there was no healing.”

19.text: After about two years his intestines came out because of the disease, so that he died a very painful death. His people did not make a bonfire to honor him, as they had done for his ancestors.

notes.text: Heb “and it was to days from days, and about the time of the going out of the end for the days, two, his intestines came out with his illness and he died in severe illness.”
Heb “and his people did not make for him a fire, like the fire of his fathers.”

20.text: Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. No one regretted his death; he was buried in the City of David, but not in the royal tombs.

notes.text: Heb “and he went without desire.”
The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

1.text: The residents of Jerusalem made his youngest son Ahaziah king in his place, for the raiding party that invaded the camp with the Arabs had killed all the older sons. So Ahaziah son of Jehoram became king of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “for all the older [ones] the raiding party that came with the Arabs to the camp had killed.”

2.text: Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned for one year in Jerusalem. His mother was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri.

notes.text: Heb “forty-two,” but some mss of the LXX and the Syriac along with the parallel passage in 2 Kgs 8:26 read “twenty-two.”
Heb “The name of his mother.”
The Hebrew term ‏בַּת‎ (bat, “daughter”) can refer, as here, to a granddaughter. See HALOT 165-66 s.v. I ‏בַּת‎ 1.

3.text: He followed in the footsteps of Ahab’s dynasty, for his mother gave him evil advice.

notes.text: Heb “and also he walked in the ways of the house of Ahab.”
Heb “for his mother was his adviser to do evil.”

4.text: He did evil in the sight of the Lord like Ahab’s dynasty because, after his father’s death, they gave him advice that led to his destruction.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”
That is, the members of Ahab’s royal house.

5.text: He followed their advice and joined Ahab’s son King Joram of Israel in a battle against King Hazael of Syria at Ramoth Gilead in which the Syrians defeated Joram.

notes.text: Heb “Jehoram.”Jehoram and Joram are alternate spellings of the Israelite king’s name (also in vv. 6-7). The shorter form is used in these verses to avoid confusion with King Jehoram of Judah, father of Azariah.
Heb “Aram” (also in v. 6).

6.text: Joram returned to Jezreel to recover from the wounds he received from the Syrians in Ramah when he fought against King Hazael of Syria. Ahaziah son of King Jehoram of Judah went down to visit Joram son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he had been wounded.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Joram) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “which they inflicted [on] him.”
Most Hebrew mss read “Azariah.” A few Hebrew mss, the LXX, Vulgate, and Syriac read “Ahaziah” (cf. 2 Kgs 8:29).
Heb “because he was sick,” presumably referring to the wounds he received in the battle with the Syrians.

7.text: God brought about Ahaziah’s downfall through his visit to Joram. When Ahaziah arrived, he went out with Joram to meet Jehu son of Nimshi, whom the Lord had commissioned to wipe out Ahab’s family.

notes.text: Heb “From God was the downfall of Ahaziah by going to Joram.”
Heb “he”; the referent (Ahaziah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “anointed.”
Heb “to cut off the house of Ahab.”

8.text: While Jehu was dishing out punishment to Ahab’s family, he discovered the officials of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah’s relatives who were serving Ahaziah and killed them.

9.text: He looked for Ahaziah, who was captured while hiding in Samaria. They brought him to Jehu and then executed him. They did give him a burial, for they reasoned, “He is the son of Jehoshaphat, who sought the Lord with his whole heart.” There was no one in Ahaziah’s family strong enough to rule in his place.

notes.text: Heb “they said.”
Heb “and there was no one belonging to the house of Ahaziah to retain strength for kingship.”

10.text: When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she was determined to destroy the entire royal line of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “she arose and she destroyed all the royal offspring.” The verb ‏קוּם‎ (qum, “arise”) is here used in an auxiliary sense to indicate that she embarked on a campaign to destroy the royal offspring. See M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 125.
Heb “house of Judah.”

11.text: So Jehoshabeath, the daughter of King Jehoram, took Ahaziah’s son Joash and stole him away from the rest of the royal descendants who were to be executed. She hid him and his nurse in the room where the bed covers were stored. So Jehoshabeath the daughter of King Jehoram, wife of Jehoiada the priest and sister of Ahaziah, hid him from Athaliah so she could not execute him.

notes.text: Jehoshabeath is a variant spelling of the name Jehosheba (2 Kgs 11:2).
Heb “the king”; the referent (King Jehoram, see later in this verse) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

12.text: He remained in hiding in God’s temple for six years while Athaliah was ruling over the land.

notes.text: Heb “and he was with them in the house of God hiding.”

1.text: In the seventh year Jehoiada made a bold move. He made a pact with the officers of the units of hundreds: Azariah son of Jehoram, Ishmael son of Jehochanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zikri.

notes.text: Or “covenant.”

2.text: They traveled throughout Judah and assembled the Levites from all the cities of Judah, as well as the Israelite family leaders. They came to Jerusalem,

3.text: and the whole assembly made a covenant with the king in the temple of God. Jehoiada said to them, “The king’s son will rule, just as the Lord promised David’s descendants.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Jehoiada the priest, cf. v. 8) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

4.text: This is what you must do. One-third of you priests and Levites who are on duty during the Sabbath will guard the doors.

5.text: Another third of you will be stationed at the royal palace and still another third at the Foundation Gate. All the others will stand in the courtyards of the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: Heb “all the people.”

6.text: No one must enter the Lord’s temple except the priests and Levites who are on duty. They may enter because they are ceremonially pure. All the others should carry out their assigned service to the Lord.

7.text: The Levites must surround the king. Each of you must hold his weapon in his hand. Whoever tries to enter the temple must be killed. You must accompany the king wherever he goes.”

notes.text: Heb “house.”
Heb “and be with the king when he goes in/enters and when he goes out/exits.”

8.text: The Levites and all the men of Judah did just as Jehoiada the priest ordered. Each of them took his men, those who were on duty during the Sabbath as well as those who were off duty on the Sabbath. Jehoiada the priest did not release his divisions from their duties.

notes.text: Heb “all Judah.” The words “the men of” are supplied in the translation for clarity. The Hebrew text uses the name “Judah” by metonymy for the men of Judah.

9.text: Jehoiada the priest gave to the officers of the units of hundreds King David’s spears and shields that were kept in God’s temple.

notes.text: The Hebrew text lists two different types of shields here. Most translations render “the large and small shields” (so NASB, NIV, NRSV; NEB “King David’s spears, shields, and bucklers”).

10.text: He placed the men at their posts, each holding his weapon in his hand. They lined up from the south side of the temple to the north side and stood near the altar and the temple, surrounding the king.

notes.text: Heb “and he stationed all the people, each with his weapon in his hand, from the south shoulder of the house to the north shoulder of the house, at the altar and at the house, near the king all around.”

11.text: Jehoiada and his sons led out the king’s son and placed on him the crown and the royal insignia. They proclaimed him king and poured olive oil on his head. They declared, “Long live the king!”

notes.text: The Hebrew word ‏עֵדוּת‎ (ʿedut) normally means “witness” or “testimony.” Here it probably refers to some tangible symbol of kingship, perhaps a piece of jewelry such as an amulet or neck chain (see the discussion in M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings [AB], 128). Some suggest that a document is in view, perhaps a copy of the royal protocol or of the stipulations of the Davidic covenant (see HALOT 790-91 s.v.).
Or “they made him king and anointed him.”

12.text: When Athaliah heard the royal guard shouting and praising the king, she joined the crowd at the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: Heb “and Athaliah heard the sound of the people, the runners.”
Heb “she came to the people.”

13.text: Then she saw the king standing by his pillar at the entrance. The officers and trumpeters stood beside the king and all the people of the land were celebrating and blowing trumpets, and the musicians with various instruments were leading the celebration. Athaliah tore her clothes and yelled, “Treason! Treason!”

notes.text: Heb “and she saw, and behold.”
Or “Conspiracy! Conspiracy!”

14.text: Jehoiada the priest sent out the officers of the units of hundreds, who were in charge of the army, and ordered them, “Bring her outside the temple to the guards. Put the sword to anyone who follows her.” The priest gave this order because he had decided she should not be executed in the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: Heb “ranks.”
Heb “for the priest had said, ‘Do not put her to death in the house of the Lord.’”

15.text: They seized her and took her into the precincts of the royal palace through the horses’ entrance. There they executed her.

notes.text: Heb “and they placed hands on her, and she went through the entrance of the gate of the horses [into] the house of the king.” Some English versions treat the phrase “gate of the horses” as the name of the gate (“the Horse Gate”; e.g., NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV).

16.text: Jehoiada then drew up a covenant stipulating that he, all the people, and the king should be loyal to the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “and Jehoiada made a covenant between himself and [between] all the people and [between] the king, to become a people for the Lord.”

17.text: All the people went and demolished the temple of Baal. They smashed its altars and idols. They killed Mattan the priest of Baal in front of the altars.

notes.text: Or “tore down.”
Or “images.”

18.text: Jehoiada then assigned the duties of the Lord’s temple to the priests, the Levites whom David had assigned to the Lord’s temple. They were responsible for offering burnt sacrifices to the Lord with joy and music, according to the law of Moses and the edict of David.

notes.text: Heb “as it is written in.”

19.text: He posted guards at the gates of the Lord’s temple, so no one who was ceremonially unclean in any way could enter.

20.text: He summoned the officers of the units of hundreds, the nobles, the rulers of the people, and all the people of the land, and he then led the king down from the Lord’s temple. They entered the royal palace through the Upper Gate and seated the king on the royal throne.

notes.text: Heb “took.”

21.text: All the people of the land celebrated, for the city had rest now that they had killed Athaliah.

notes.text: Heb “killed Athaliah with the sword.”

1.text: Joash was seven years old when he began to reign. He reigned for forty years in Jerusalem. His mother was Zibiah, who was from Beer Sheba.

notes.text: Heb “the name of his mother.”

2.text: Joash did what the Lord approved throughout the lifetime of Jehoiada the priest.

notes.text: Heb “and Joash did what was proper in the eyes of the Lord.”
Heb “all the days of.”

3.text: Jehoiada chose two wives for him who gave him sons and daughters.

4.text: Later, Joash was determined to repair the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: Heb “and it was, later, there was with the heart of Joash to repair the house of the Lord.”

5.text: He assembled the priests and Levites and ordered them, “Go out to the cities of Judah and collect the annual quota of silver from all Israel for repairs on the temple of your God. Be quick about it!” But the Levites delayed.

6.text: So the king summoned Jehoiada the chief priest, and said to him, “Why have you not made the Levites collect from Judah and Jerusalem the tax authorized by Moses the Lord’s servant and by the assembly of Israel at the tent containing the tablets of the law?”

notes.text: Heb “Jehoiada the head”; the word “priest” not in the Hebrew text but is implied.
Heb “demanded of.”
Heb “to bring.”
Heb “the tent of testimony.”

7.text: (Wicked Athaliah and her sons had broken into God’s temple and used all the holy items of the Lord’s temple in their worship of the Baals.)

8.text: The king ordered a chest to be made and placed outside the gate of the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: Heb “and the king said [it] and they made a chest and placed it in the gate of the house of the Lord outside.”

9.text: An edict was sent throughout Judah and Jerusalem requiring the people to bring to the Lord the tax that Moses, God’s servant, imposed on Israel in the wilderness.

notes.text: Heb “and they gave voice in Judah and Jerusalem to bring to the Lord the tax of Moses the servant of God upon Israel in the wilderness.”

10.text: All the officials and all the people gladly brought their silver and threw it into the chest until it was full.

11.text: Whenever the Levites brought the chest to the royal accountant and they saw there was a lot of silver, the royal scribe and the accountant of the high priest emptied the chest and then took it back to its place. They went through this routine every day and collected a large amount of silver.

12.text: The king and Jehoiada gave it to the construction foremen assigned to the Lord’s temple. They hired carpenters and craftsmen to repair the Lord’s temple, as well as those skilled in working with iron and bronze to restore the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: Heb “doers of the work.”

13.text: They worked hard and made the repairs. They followed the measurements specified for God’s temple and restored it.

notes.text: Heb “and the doers of the work worked, and the repairs went up for the work by their hand.”
Heb “and they caused the house of God to stand according to its measurements and they strengthened it.”

14.text: When they were finished, they brought the rest of the silver to the king and Jehoiada. They used it to make items for the Lord’s temple, including items used in the temple service and for burnt sacrifices, pans, and various other gold and silver items. Throughout Jehoiada’s lifetime, burnt sacrifices were offered regularly in the Lord’s temple.

15.text: Jehoiada grew old and died at the age of 130.

16.text: He was buried in the City of David with the kings, because he had accomplished good in Israel and for God and his temple.

notes.text: The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

17.text: After Jehoiada died, the officials of Judah visited the king and declared their loyalty to him. The king listened to their advice.

notes.text: Heb “came and bowed down to the king.”
Heb “to them.”

18.text: They abandoned the temple of the Lord God of their ancestors and worshiped the Asherah poles and idols. Because of this sinful activity, God was angry with Judah and Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “fathers” (also in v. 24).
Heb “served.”

19.text: The Lord sent prophets among them to lead them back to him. They warned the people, but they would not pay attention.

notes.text: Heb “and he sent among them prophets to bring them back to the Lord.”
Heb “testified among.”

20.text: God’s Spirit energized Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest. He stood up before the people and said to them, “This is what God says: ‘Why are you violating the commands of the Lord? You will not be prosperous. Because you have rejected the Lord, he has rejected you!’”

notes.text: Heb “clothed.”

21.text: They plotted against him and by royal decree stoned him to death in the courtyard of the Lord’s temple.

22.text: King Joash disregarded the loyalty Zechariah’s father Jehoiada had shown him and killed Jehoiada’s son. As Zechariah was dying, he said, “May the Lord take notice and seek vengeance!”

notes.text: Heb “did not remember.”
Heb “his”; the referent (Jehoiada) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “he”; the referent (Zechariah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “and seek [—].” The direct object of “seek” is omitted in the Hebrew text but implied; “vengeance” is supplied for clarification.

23.text: At the beginning of the year the Syrian army attacked Joash and invaded Judah and Jerusalem. They wiped out all the leaders of the people and sent all the plunder they gathered to the king of Damascus.

notes.text: Heb “turning.”
Heb “went up against.”
Heb “him”; the referent (Joash) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

24.text: Even though the invading Syrian army was relatively weak, the Lord handed over to them Judah’s very large army, for the people of Judah had abandoned the Lord God of their ancestors. The Syrians gave Joash what he deserved.

notes.text: Heb “though with a small amount of men the army of Aram came, the Lord gave into their hand an army [that was] very large.”
Heb “they”; the referent (the people of Judah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “they”; the referent (the Syrians) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “executed judgments on Joash.”

25.text: When they withdrew, they left Joash badly wounded. His servants plotted against him because of what he had done to the son of Jehoiada the priest. They murdered him on his bed. Thus he died and was buried in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.

notes.text: Heb “him”; the referent (Joash) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “because of the shed blood of.”
The MT has the plural ‏בְּנֵי‎ (bene, “sons”), but the final yod is dittographic. Note the yod that immediately follows.
Heb “and he died.”
The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

26.text: The conspirators were Zabad son of Shimeath (an Ammonite woman) and Jehozabad son of Shimrith (a Moabite woman).

27.text: The list of Joash’s sons, the many prophetic oracles about him, and the account of his building project on God’s temple are included in the record of the Scroll of the Kings. His son Amaziah replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “his”; the referent (Joash) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “and the founding of the house of God, look, they are written on the writing of the scroll of the kings?”

1.text: Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jehoaddan, who was from Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “the name of his mother.”

2.text: He did what the Lord approved, but not with wholehearted devotion.

notes.text: Heb “he did what was proper in the eyes of the Lord.”
Heb “a complete heart.”

3.text: When he had secured control of the kingdom, he executed the servants who had assassinated his father the king.

notes.text: Heb “when the kingdom was secure upon him.”

4.text: However, he did not execute their sons. He obeyed the Lord’s commandment as recorded in the law scroll of Moses, “Fathers must not be executed for what their sons do, and sons must not be executed for what their fathers do. A man must be executed only for his own sin.”

notes.text: Heb “as it is written in the scroll of the law of Moses which the Lord commanded, saying.”
Heb “on account of sons.”
Heb “on account of fathers.”
This law is recorded in Deut 24:16.

5.text: Amaziah assembled the people of Judah and assigned them by families to the commanders of units of 1,000 and the commanders of units of 100 for all Judah and Benjamin. He counted those twenty years old and up and discovered there were 300,000 young men of fighting age equipped with spears and shields.

notes.text: Heb “Judah.” The words “the people of” are supplied in the translation for clarity. The Hebrew text uses the name “Judah” by metonymy here for the people of Judah.
Heb “young men going out to war.”
Heb “holding a spear and a shield.”

6.text: He hired 100,000 Israelite warriors for 100 talents of silver.

notes.text: The Hebrew word ‏כִּכַּר‎ (kikkar, “circle”) refers generally to something that is round. When used of metals it can refer to a disk-shaped weight made of the metal or, by extension, to a standard unit of weight. According to the older (Babylonian) standard the “talent” weighed 130 lbs. (58.9 kg), but later this was lowered to 108.3 lbs. (49.1 kg). More recent research suggests the “light” standard talent was 67.3 lbs. (30.6 kg). Using this as the standard for calculation, the weight of the silver was 6,730 lbs. (3,060 kg).

7.text: But a prophet visited him and said: “O king, the Israelite troops must not go with you, for the Lord is not with Israel or any of the Ephraimites.

notes.text: Heb “man of God.”
Heb “Israel, all the sons of Ephraim.”

8.text: Even if you go and fight bravely in battle, God will defeat you before the enemy. God is capable of helping or defeating.”

notes.text: Heb “cause you to stumble.”
Heb “to cause to stumble.”

9.text: Amaziah asked the prophet: “But what should I do about the 100 talents of silver I paid the Israelite troops?” The prophet replied, “The Lord is capable of giving you more than that.”

notes.text: Heb “said to the man of God.”
Heb “man of God.”

10.text: So Amaziah dismissed the troops that had come to him from Ephraim and sent them home. They were very angry at Judah and returned home incensed.

notes.text: Heb “and Amaziah separated them, the troops who came to him from Ephraim, to go to their place.”

11.text: Amaziah boldly led his army to the Valley of Salt, where he defeated 10,000 Edomites.

notes.text: Heb “and Amaziah strengthened himself and led his people and went to the Valley of Salt.”
Or “struck down.”
Heb “sons of Seir.”

12.text: The men of Judah captured 10,000 men alive. They took them to the top of a cliff and threw them over. All the captives fell to their death.

notes.text: Heb “sons.”
Heb “and threw them from the top of the cliff.”
Heb “all of them.”
Heb “smashed in pieces.”

13.text: Now the troops Amaziah had dismissed and had not allowed to fight in the battle raided the cities of Judah from Samaria to Beth Horon. They killed 3,000 people and carried off a large amount of plunder.

notes.text: Heb “had sent back from going with him to the battle.”
Heb “stripped.”
Heb “struck down.”

14.text: When Amaziah returned from defeating the Edomites, he brought back the gods of the people of Seir and made them his personal gods. He bowed down before them and offered them sacrifices.

notes.text: Heb “sons.”
Heb “caused them to stand for him as gods.”

15.text: The Lord was angry at Amaziah and sent a prophet to him, who said, “Why are you following these gods that could not deliver their own people from your power?”

notes.text: Heb “seeking,” perhaps in the sense of “consulting [an oracle from].”
Heb “the gods of the people.”
Heb “hand.”

16.text: While he was speaking, Amaziah said to him, “Did we appoint you to be a royal counselor? Stop prophesying or else you will be killed!” So the prophet stopped, but added, “I know that God has decided to destroy you, because you have done this thing and refused to listen to my advice.”

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Amaziah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “Stop yourself! Why should they strike you down?”

The verb ‏יָעַץ‎ (yaʿats, “has decided”) is from the same root as ‏יוֹעֵץ‎ (yoʿets, “counselor”) in v. 16 and ‏עֵצָה‎ (ʿetsah, “advice”) later in v. 16. The wordplay highlights the appropriate nature of the divine punishment. Amaziah rejected the counsel of God’s prophet; now he would be the victim of God’s “counsel.”

17.text: After King Amaziah of Judah consulted with his advisers, he sent this message to the king of Israel, Joash son of Jehoahaz, the son of Jehu, “Come, face me on the battlefield.”

notes.text: The words “with his advisers” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “let us look at each other [in the] face.” The expression refers here not to a visit but to meeting in battle. See v. 21.

18.text: King Joash of Israel sent this message back to King Amaziah of Judah, “A thorn bush in Lebanon sent this message to a cedar in Lebanon, ‘Give your daughter to my son as a wife.’ Then a wild animal of Lebanon came by and trampled down the thorn bush.

notes.text: The thorn bush in the allegory is Judah. Amaziah’s success had deceived him into thinking he was on the same level as the major powers in the area (symbolized by the cedar). In reality he was not capable of withstanding an attack by a real military power such as Israel (symbolized by the wild animal).

19.text: You defeated Edom and it has gone to your head. Gloat over your success, but stay in your palace. Why bring calamity on yourself? Why bring down yourself and Judah along with you?”

notes.text: Heb “you say [to yourself], ‘look, you have defeated Edom.’”
Heb “and your heart is lifted up.”
Heb “to glorify.”
Heb “Why get involved in calamity and fall, you and Judah with you?”

20.text: But Amaziah did not heed the warning, for God wanted to hand them over to Joash because they followed the gods of Edom.

notes.text: Heb “did not listen.”
Heb “because it was from God in order to give them into the hand because they sought the gods of Edom.”

21.text: So King Joash of Israel attacked. He and King Amaziah of Judah faced each other on the battlefield in Beth Shemesh of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “looked at each other [in the] face.” See the note on the expression “Come on, face me on the battlefield” in v. 17.

22.text: Judah was defeated by Israel, and each man ran back home.

notes.text: Heb “and Judah was struck down before Israel and they fled, each to his tent.”

23.text: King Joash of Israel captured King Amaziah of Judah, son of Joash son of Jehoahaz, in Beth Shemesh and brought him to Jerusalem. He broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Gate of Ephraim to the Corner Gate—a distance of about 600 feet.

notes.text: Heb “400 cubits.” Assuming a cubit of 18 inches (45 cm), the distance would have been about 600 feet (180 m).

24.text: He took away all the gold and silver, all the items found in God’s temple that were in the care of Obed-Edom, the riches in the royal palace, and some hostages. Then he went back to Samaria.

25.text: King Amaziah son of Joash of Judah lived for fifteen years after the death of King Joash son of Jehoahaz of Israel.

26.text: The rest of the events of Amaziah’s reign, from start to finish, are recorded in the Scroll of the Kings of Judah and Israel.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Amaziah, the former and the latter, are they not—behold, they are written on the scroll of the kings of Judah and Israel.”

27.text: From the time Amaziah turned from following the Lord, conspirators plotted against him in Jerusalem, so he fled to Lachish. But they sent assassins after him and they killed him there.

notes.text: Heb “and they conspired against him [with] a conspiracy in Jerusalem.”
Heb “and they sent after him to Lachish.”

28.text: His body was carried back by horses, and he was buried with his ancestors in the City of David.

notes.text: Heb “and they carried him on horses.”
Heb “fathers.”
The Hebrew text has “Judah,” but some medieval mss read “David,” as does the parallel passage in 2 Kgs 14:20.
The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

1.text: All the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in his father Amaziah’s place.

notes.text: The parallel account in 2 Kgs 15:1-8 has the variant spelling “Azariah.”

2.text: Uzziah built up Elat and restored it to Judah after King Amaziah had passed away.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Uzziah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “after the king”; the referent (Amaziah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
“slept with his fathers.”

3.text: Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jecholiah, who was from Jerusalem.

4.text: He did what the Lord approved, just as his father Amaziah had done.

notes.text: Heb “he did what was proper in the eyes of the Lord, according to all which Amaziah his father had done.”

5.text: He followed God during the lifetime of Zechariah, who taught him how to honor God. As long as he followed the Lord, God caused him to succeed.

notes.text: Heb “sought.”
Heb “in the days of.”
Heb “in the days of his seeking.”
Or “prosper.”

6.text: Uzziah attacked the Philistines and broke down the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod. He built cities in the region of Ashdod and throughout Philistine territory.

notes.text: Heb “went out and fought.”
Heb “in Ashdod and among the Philistines.”

7.text: God helped him in his campaigns against the Philistines, the Arabs living in Gur Baal, and the Meunites.

notes.text: The words “in his campaigns” are supplied in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

8.text: The Ammonites paid tribute to Uzziah and his fame reached the border of Egypt, for he grew in power.

notes.text: Heb “and his name went to.”

9.text: Uzziah built and fortified towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, Valley Gate, and at the Angle.

notes.text: On the meaning of the Hebrew word ‏מִקְצוֹעַ‎ (miqtsoaʿ), see HALOT 628 s.v. ‏עַ‎(‏וֹ‎)‏מִקְצֹ‎. The term probably refers to an “angle” or “corner” somewhere on the eastern wall of Jerusalem.

10.text: He built towers in the wilderness and dug many cisterns, for he owned many herds in the foothills and on the plain. He had workers in the fields and vineyards in the hills and in Carmel, for he loved agriculture.

notes.text: The foothills (‏שְׁפֵלָה‎, shephelah) are the region between the Judean hill country and the Mediterranean coastal plain.
Heb “workers and vinedressers in the hills and in Carmel.” The words “he had” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “for a lover of the ground he [was].”

11.text: Uzziah had an army of skilled warriors trained for battle. They were organized by divisions according to the muster rolls made by Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the officer under the authority of Hananiah, a royal official.

12.text: The total number of family leaders who led warriors was 2,600.

13.text: They commanded an army of 307,500 skilled and able warriors who were ready to defend the king against his enemies.

notes.text: Heb “help.”

14.text: Uzziah supplied shields, spears, helmets, breastplates, bows, and slingstones for the entire army.

15.text: In Jerusalem he made war machines carefully designed to shoot arrows and large stones from the towers and corners of the walls. He became very famous, for he received tremendous support and became powerful.

notes.text: Heb “and his name went out to a distant place, for he did extraordinarily to be helped until he was strong.”

16.text: But once he became powerful, his pride destroyed him. He disobeyed the Lord his God. He entered the Lord’s temple to offer incense on the incense altar.

notes.text: Heb “his heart was high [i.e., proud] until to destroy.”
Or “was unfaithful to.”

17.text: Azariah the priest and eighty other brave priests of the Lord followed him in.

18.text: They confronted King Uzziah and said to him, “It is not proper for you, Uzziah, to offer incense to the Lord. That is the responsibility of the priests, the descendants of Aaron, who are consecrated to offer incense. Leave the sanctuary, for you have disobeyed and the Lord God will not honor you!”

notes.text: Heb “stood against.”
Or “been unfaithful.”

19.text: Uzziah, who had an incense censer in his hand, became angry. While he was ranting and raving at the priests, a skin disease appeared on his forehead right there in front of the priests in the Lord’s temple near the incense altar.

notes.text: Heb “angry.”
Traditionally “leprosy,” but this was probably a skin disorder of some type, not leprosy (technically known today as Hansen’s disease). See 2 Kgs 5:1.

20.text: When Azariah the high priest and the other priests looked at him, there was a skin disease on his forehead. They hurried him out of there; even the king himself wanted to leave quickly because the Lord had afflicted him.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (the king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

21.text: King Uzziah suffered from a skin disease until the day he died. He lived in separate quarters, afflicted by a skin disease and banned from the Lord’s temple. His son Jotham was in charge of the palace and ruled over the people of the land.

notes.text: The precise meaning of ‏בֵּית הַחָפְשִׁית‎ (bet hakhofshit, “house of [?]”) is uncertain. NASB, NIV, NRSV all have “in a separate house”; NEB has “in his own house…relieved of all duties.” For a discussion of various proposals, see M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 166-67.

22.text: The rest of the events of Uzziah’s reign, from start to finish, were recorded by the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Uzziah, the former and the latter, Isaiah son of Amoz, the prophet, recorded.”

23.text: Uzziah passed away and was buried near his ancestors in a cemetery belonging to the kings. (This was because he had a skin disease.) His son Jotham replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”
Heb “fathers.”
Heb “a field of burial.”
Heb “for they said, ‘He had a skin disease.’”

1.text: Jotham was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jerusha the daughter of Zadok.

notes.text: Heb “the name of his mother.”

2.text: He did what the Lord approved, just as his father Uzziah had done. (He did not, however, have the audacity to enter the temple.) Yet the people were still sinning.

notes.text: Heb “he did what was proper in the eyes of the Lord, according to all which Uzziah his father had done.”
Heb “except he did not enter the house of the Lord.”

3.text: He built the Upper Gate to the Lord’s temple and did a lot of work on the wall in the area known as Ophel.

notes.text: Heb “wall of Ophel.” See HALOT 861 s.v. II ‏עֹפֶל‎.

4.text: He built cities in the hill country of Judah and fortresses and towers in the forests.

5.text: He launched a military campaign against the king of the Ammonites and defeated them. That year the Ammonites paid him 100 talents of silver, 10,000 cors of wheat, and 10,000 cors of barley. The Ammonites also paid this same amount of annual tribute the next two years.

notes.text: Heb “he fought with.”

The Hebrew word ‏כִּכַּר‎ (kikkar, “circle”) refers generally to something that is round. When used of metals it can refer to a disk-shaped weight made of the metal or, by extension, to a standard unit of weight. According to the older (Babylonian) standard the “talent” weighed 130 lbs. (58.9 kg), but later this was lowered to 108.3 lbs. (49.1 kg). More recent research suggests the “light” standard talent was 67.3 lbs. (30.6 kg). Using this as the standard for calculation, the weight of the silver was 6,730 lbs. (3,060 kg).
As a unit of dry measure a cor was roughly equivalent to six bushels (about 220 liters).
Heb “10,000 cors of wheat and 10,000 of barley.” The unit of measure of the barley is omitted in the Hebrew text, but is understood to be “cors,” the same as the measures of wheat.
Heb “This the sons of Ammon brought to him, and in the second year and the third.”

6.text: Jotham grew powerful because he was determined to please the Lord his God.

notes.text: Heb “because he established his ways before the Lord his God.”

7.text: The rest of the events of Jotham’s reign, including all his military campaigns and his accomplishments, are recorded in the Scroll of the Kings of Israel and Judah.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Jotham, and his battles and his ways, look, they are written on the scroll of the kings of Israel and Judah.”

8.text: He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for sixteen years in Jerusalem.

9.text: Jotham passed away and was buried in the City of David. His son Ahaz replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”
The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

1.text: Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not do what pleased the Lord, in contrast to his ancestor David.

notes.text: Heb “and he did not do what was proper in the eyes of the Lord, like David his father.”
