2.text: He followed in the footsteps of the kings of Israel; he also made images of the Baals.

notes.text: Heb “he walked in the ways of.”

3.text: He offered sacrifices in the Valley of Ben Hinnom and passed his sons through the fire, a horrible sin practiced by the nations whom the Lord drove out before the Israelites.

notes.text: This may refer to child sacrifice, though some interpret it as a less drastic cultic practice (NEB “burnt his sons in the fire”; NASB “burned his sons in the fire”; NIV “sacrificed his sons in the fire”; NRSV “made his sons pass through fire”). For discussion see M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 266-67.
Heb “like the abominable practices of the nations.”

4.text: He offered sacrifices and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.

5.text: The Lord his God handed him over to the king of Syria. The Syrians defeated him and deported many captives to Damascus. He was also handed over to the king of Israel, who thoroughly defeated him.

notes.text: Heb “they”; the referent (the Syrians) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “and took captive from him a great captivity and brought [them] to Damascus.”
Heb “who struck him down with a great striking.”

6.text: In one day Pekah son of Remaliah killed 120,000 warriors in Judah, because they had abandoned the Lord God of their ancestors.

notes.text: Heb “fathers” (also in vv. 9, 25).

7.text: Zikri, an Ephraimite warrior, killed the king’s son Maaseiah, Azrikam, the supervisor of the palace, and Elkanah, the king’s second-in-command.

8.text: The Israelites seized from their brothers 200,000 wives, sons, and daughters. They also carried off a huge amount of plunder and took it back to Samaria.

notes.text: Heb “the loot.” The pronoun (“it”) has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons, to avoid redundancy.

9.text: Oded, a prophet of the Lord, was there. He went to meet the army as they arrived in Samaria and said to them: “Look, because the Lord God of your ancestors was angry with Judah he handed them over to you. You have killed them so mercilessly that God has taken notice.

notes.text: Heb “and you killed them with anger [that] reaches as far as heaven.”

10.text: And now you are planning to enslave the people of Judah and Jerusalem. Yet are you not also guilty before the Lord your God?

notes.text: Heb “saying.”
Heb “to enslave as male servants and female servants.”
Heb “sons.”

11.text: Now listen to me! Send back those you have seized from your brothers, for the Lord is very angry at you!”

notes.text: Heb “for the rage of the anger of the Lord is upon you.”

12.text: So some of the Ephraimite family leaders, Azariah son of Jehochanan, Berechiah son of Meshillemoth, Jechizkiah son of Shallum, and Amasa son of Hadlai confronted those returning from the battle.

notes.text: Heb “men from.”
Heb “arose against.”

13.text: They said to them, “Don’t bring those captives here! Are you planning on making us even more sinful and guilty before the Lord? Our guilt is already great, and the Lord is very angry at Israel.”

notes.text: Heb “for to the guilt of the Lord upon us you are saying to add to our sins and our guilty deeds.”
Heb “for great is [the] guilt to us and rage of anger is upon Israel.”

14.text: So the soldiers released the captives and the plunder before the officials and the entire assembly.

15.text: Men were assigned to take the prisoners and find clothes among the plunder for those who were naked. So they clothed them, supplied them with sandals, gave them food and drink, and provided them with oil to rub on their skin. They put the ones who couldn’t walk on donkeys. They brought them back to their brothers at Jericho, the city of date palm trees, and then returned to Samaria.

notes.text: Heb “and the men who were designated by names arose and took the captives and all their naked ones they clothed from the loot.”
Heb “and poured oil on them.”
Heb “and they led them on donkeys, with respect to everyone stumbling.”

16.text: At that time King Ahaz asked the king of Assyria for help.

notes.text: Most Hebrew mss read the plural, “kings,” but one Hebrew ms, the LXX and Vulgate read the singular “king.” Note the singular in v. 20.

17.text: The Edomites had again invaded and defeated Judah and carried off captives.

18.text: The Philistines had raided the cities of Judah in the foothills and the Negev. They captured and settled in Beth Shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco and its surrounding villages, Timnah and its surrounding villages, and Gimzo and its surrounding villages.

notes.text: The foothills (‏שְׁפֵלָה‎, shephelah) are the region between the Judean hill country and the Mediterranean coastal plain.
The Negev is an area of central, southern Judah, south of the hill country and Beer Sheba and west of the rift valley.

19.text: The Lord humiliated Judah because of King Ahaz of Israel, for he encouraged Judah to sin and was very unfaithful to the Lord.

notes.text: Or “subdued.”
That is, “of Judah.” Frequently in 2 Chronicles “Israel” is substituted for “Judah.”
The infinitive absolute precedes the cognate nominal form to emphasize the degree of Ahaz’s unfaithfulness.

20.text: King Tiglath-Pileser of Assyria came, but he gave him more trouble than support.

notes.text: Heb “Tilgath-Pilneser,” a variant spelling of Tiglath-Pileser.
Heb “and he caused him distress and did not strengthen him.”

21.text: Ahaz gathered riches from the Lord’s temple, the royal palace, and the officials and gave them to the king of Assyria, but that did not help.

notes.text: Heb “divided up,” but some read ‏חִלֵּץ‎ (khillets, “despoiled”).

22.text: During his time of trouble King Ahaz was even more unfaithful to the Lord.

23.text: He offered sacrifices to the gods of Damascus whom he thought had defeated him. He reasoned, “Since the gods of the kings of Syria helped them, I will sacrifice to them so they will help me.” But they caused him and all Israel to stumble.

notes.text: Heb “the gods of Damascus, the ones who had defeated him.” The words “he thought” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The perspective is that of Ahaz, not the narrator! Another option is that “the kings” has been accidentally omitted after “gods of.” See v. 23b.
Heb “said.”

24.text: Ahaz gathered the items in God’s temple and removed them. He shut the doors of the Lord’s temple and erected altars on every street corner in Jerusalem.

25.text: In every city throughout Judah he set up high places to offer sacrifices to other gods. He angered the Lord God of his ancestors.

26.text: The rest of the events of Ahaz’s reign, including his accomplishments from start to finish, are recorded in the Scroll of the Kings of Judah and Israel.

notes.text: Heb “As for the rest of his events, and all his ways, the former and the latter, look, they are written on the scroll of the kings of Judah and Israel.”

27.text: Ahaz passed away and was buried in the city of Jerusalem; they did not bring him to the tombs of the kings of Israel. His son Hezekiah replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”

1.text: Hezekiah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother was Abijah, the daughter of Zechariah.

notes.text: Heb “the name of his mother.”
The parallel passage in 2 Kgs 18:2 has “Abi.”

2.text: He did what the Lord approved, just as his ancestor David had done.

notes.text: Heb “he did what was proper in the eyes of the Lord, according to all which David his father had done.”

3.text: In the first month of the first year of his reign, he opened the doors of the Lord’s temple and repaired them.

4.text: He brought in the priests and Levites and assembled them in the square on the east side.

5.text: He said to them: “Listen to me, you Levites! Now consecrate yourselves, so you can consecrate the temple of the Lord God of your ancestors. Remove from the sanctuary what is ceremonially unclean.

notes.text: Heb “fathers.”

6.text: For our fathers were unfaithful; they did what is evil in the sight of the Lord our God and abandoned him. They turned away from the Lord’s dwelling place and rejected him.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”
Heb “turned their faces.”
Heb “and turned the back.”

7.text: They closed the doors of the temple porch and put out the lamps; they did not offer incense or burnt sacrifices in the sanctuary of the God of Israel.

8.text: The Lord was angry at Judah and Jerusalem and made them an appalling object of horror at which people hiss out their scorn, as you can see with your own eyes.

notes.text: Heb “and he made them [an object] of dread and devastation and hissing.”

9.text: Look, our fathers died violently and our sons, daughters, and wives were carried off because of this.

notes.text: Heb “fell by the sword.”
Heb “are in captivity.”

10.text: Now I intend to make a covenant with the Lord God of Israel, so that he may relent from his raging anger.

notes.text: Heb “now it is with my heart.”
Heb “so that the rage of his anger might turn from us.” The jussive with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding statement of intention.

11.text: My sons, do not be negligent now, for the Lord has chosen you to stand in his presence, to minister to him, to be his ministers, and offer sacrifices.”

notes.text: That is, to conduct the religious rituals directed to the Lord.
That is, to be his ministers for the nation.

Heb “ones who cause [sacrifices] to go up in smoke.” The Hiphil form of ‏קָטַר‎ (qatar) can refer specifically to offering incense (e.g. 2 Chr 26:19; 32:12), but it may also be a general word for making sacrifices (e.g. 1 Chr 6:49). If it refers to burning incense, then the altar of incense in the Holy place of the tabernacle may be in view. Otherwise it is more general (they sacrifice animals later in this chapter, 2 Chr 29:21-24) and includes making sacrifices as well as offering incense.

12.text: The following Levites prepared to carry out the king’s orders: From the Kohathites: Mahath son of Amasai and Joel son of Azariah; from the Merarites: Kish son of Abdi and Azariah son of Jehallelel; from the Gershonites: Joah son of Zimmah and Eden son of Joah;

notes.text: Heb “and the Levites arose.”

13.text: from the descendants of Elizaphan: Shimri and Jeiel; from the descendants of Asaph: Zechariah and Mattaniah;

14.text: from the descendants of Heman: Jehiel and Shimei; from the descendants of Jeduthun: Shemaiah and Uzziel.

15.text: They assembled their brothers and consecrated themselves. Then they went in to purify the Lord’s temple, just as the king had ordered, in accordance with the word of the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “words” (plural).

16.text: The priests then entered the Lord’s temple to purify it; they brought out to the courtyard of the Lord’s temple every ceremonially unclean thing they discovered inside. The Levites took them out to the Kidron Valley.

notes.text: Heb “in the temple of the Lord.”

17.text: On the first day of the first month they began consecrating; by the eighth day of the month they reached the porch of the Lord’s temple. For eight more days they consecrated the Lord’s temple. On the sixteenth day of the first month they were finished.

notes.text: Heb “porch of the Lord.”

18.text: They went to King Hezekiah and said: “We have purified the entire temple of the Lord, including the altar of burnt sacrifice and all its equipment, and the table for the Bread of the Presence and all its equipment.

19.text: We have prepared and consecrated all the items that King Ahaz removed during his reign when he acted unfaithfully. They are in front of the altar of the Lord.”

20.text: Early the next morning King Hezekiah assembled the city officials and went up to the Lord’s temple.

21.text: They brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven goats as a sin offering for the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah. The king told the priests, the descendants of Aaron, to offer burnt sacrifices on the altar of the Lord.

notes.text: Perhaps these terms refer metonymically to the royal court, the priests and Levites, and the people, respectively.
Heb “he”; the referent (the king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

22.text: They slaughtered the bulls, and the priests took the blood and splashed it on the altar. Then they slaughtered the rams and splashed the blood on the altar; next they slaughtered the lambs and splashed the blood on the altar.

23.text: Finally they brought the goats for the sin offering before the king and the assembly, and they placed their hands on them.

24.text: Then the priests slaughtered them. They offered their blood as a sin offering on the altar to make atonement for all Israel, because the king had decreed that the burnt sacrifice and sin offering were for all Israel.

notes.text: Heb “said.”

25.text: Hezekiah stationed the Levites in the Lord’s temple with cymbals and stringed instruments just as David, Gad the king’s prophet, and Nathan the prophet had ordered. (The Lord had actually given these orders through his prophets.)

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Hezekiah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “seer.”

26.text: The Levites had David’s musical instruments and the priests had trumpets.

notes.text: Heb “stood with” (i.e., stood holding).

27.text: Hezekiah ordered the burnt sacrifice to be offered on the altar. As they began to offer the sacrifice, they also began to sing to the Lord, accompanied by the trumpets and the musical instruments of King David of Israel.

28.text: The entire assembly worshiped, as the singers sang and the trumpeters played. They continued until the burnt sacrifice was completed.

29.text: When the sacrifices were completed, the king and all who were with him bowed down and worshiped.

30.text: King Hezekiah and the officials told the Levites to praise the Lord, using the psalms of David and Asaph the prophet. So they joyfully offered praise and bowed down and worshiped.

notes.text: Heb “with the words.”
Or “seer.”

31.text: Hezekiah said, “Now you have consecrated yourselves to the Lord. Come and bring sacrifices and thank offerings to the Lord’s temple.” So the assembly brought sacrifices and thank offerings, and whoever desired to do so brought burnt sacrifices.

notes.text: Heb “filled your hand.”
Or “tokens of thanks.”
Heb “and all who were willing of heart.”

32.text: The assembly brought a total of 70 bulls, 100 rams, and 200 lambs as burnt sacrifices to the Lord,

notes.text: Heb “and the number of burnt sacrifices which the assembly brought was seventy bulls, one hundred rams, two hundred lambs; for a burnt sacrifice to the Lord were all these.”

33.text: and 600 bulls and 3,000 sheep were consecrated.

notes.text: The Hebrew term ‏צֹאן‎ (tsoʾn) denotes smaller livestock in general; depending on context it can refer to sheep only or goats only, but there is nothing in the immediate context here to specify one or the other.

34.text: But there were not enough priests to skin all the animals, so their brothers, the Levites, helped them until the work was finished and the priests could consecrate themselves. (The Levites had been more conscientious about consecrating themselves than the priests.)

notes.text: Heb “the burnt sacrifices.”
Heb “for the Levites were more pure of heart to consecrate themselves than the priests.”

35.text: There was a large number of burnt sacrifices, as well as fat from the peace offerings and drink offerings that accompanied the burnt sacrifices. So the service of the Lord’s temple was reinstituted.

notes.text: Or “established.”

36.text: Hezekiah and all the people were happy about what God had done for them, for it had been done quickly.

notes.text: Heb “prepared.”
Heb “the people.” The pronoun “them” has been used here for stylistic reasons, to avoid redundancy.
Heb “for quickly was the matter.”

1.text: Hezekiah sent messages throughout Israel and Judah; he even wrote letters to Ephraim and Manasseh, summoning them to come to the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem and observe a Passover celebration for the Lord God of Israel.

2.text: The king, his officials, and the entire assembly in Jerusalem decided to observe the Passover in the second month.

3.text: They were unable to observe it at the regular time because not enough priests had consecrated themselves and the people had not assembled in Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “at that time.”

4.text: The proposal seemed appropriate to the king and the entire assembly.

notes.text: Heb “and the thing was proper in the eyes of.”

5.text: So they sent an edict throughout Israel from Beer Sheba to Dan, summoning the people to come and observe a Passover for the Lord God of Israel in Jerusalem, for they had not observed it on a nationwide scale as prescribed in the law.

notes.text: Heb “and they caused to stand a word to cause a voice to pass through.”
The words “summoning the people” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons, with the summons being the "voice" that passed throughout Israel.
Heb “because not for abundance had they done as written.”

6.text: Messengers delivered the letters from the king and his officials throughout Israel and Judah. This royal edict read: “O Israelites, return to the Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, so he may return to you who have been spared from the kings of Assyria.

notes.text: Heb “the runners.”
Heb “and according to the command of the king, saying.”
The jussive with vav conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.
Heb “to the survivors who are left to you from the palm of the kings of Assyria.”

7.text: Don’t be like your fathers and brothers who were unfaithful to the Lord God of their ancestors, provoking him to destroy them, as you can see.

notes.text: Heb “fathers” (also in vv. 19, 22).
Heb “and he made them a devastation” (or, perhaps, “an object of horror”).

8.text: Now, don’t be stubborn like your fathers. Submit to the Lord and come to his sanctuary which he has permanently consecrated. Serve the Lord your God so that he might relent from his raging anger.

notes.text: Heb “don’t stiffen your neck” (a Hebrew idiom for being stubborn).
Heb “give a hand.” On the meaning of the idiom here, see HALOT 387 s.v. I ‏יָד‎ 2.
Heb “so that the rage of his anger might turn from you.” The jussive with vav conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.

9.text: For if you return to the Lord, your brothers and sons will be shown mercy by their captors and return to this land. The Lord your God is merciful and compassionate; he will not reject you if you return to him.”

notes.text: Heb “turn [his] face from you.”

10.text: The messengers journeyed from city to city through the land of Ephraim and Manasseh as far as Zebulun, but people mocked and ridiculed them.

notes.text: Heb “and they were mocking them and ridiculing them.”

11.text: But some men from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.

12.text: In Judah God moved the people to unite and carry out the edict of the king and the officers in keeping with the Lord’s message.

notes.text: Heb “the hand of God was [such as] to give them one heart.”

13.text: A huge crowd assembled in Jerusalem to observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month.

notes.text: The Hebrew text adds here, “a very large assembly.” This has not been translated to avoid redundancy with the expression “a huge crowd” at the beginning of the verse.

14.text: They removed the altars in Jerusalem; they also removed all the incense altars and threw them into the Kidron Valley.

notes.text: Heb “and they arose and removed the altars which were in Jerusalem, and all the incense altars they removed and threw into the Kidron Valley.”

15.text: They slaughtered the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the second month. The priests and Levites were ashamed, so they consecrated themselves and brought burnt sacrifices to the Lord’s temple.

16.text: They stood at their posts according to the regulations outlined in the law of Moses, the man of God. The priests were splashing the blood as the Levites handed it to them.

notes.text: Heb “from the hand of the Levites.”

17.text: Because many in the assembly had not consecrated themselves, the Levites slaughtered the Passover lambs of all who were ceremonially unclean and could not consecrate their sacrifice to the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “were over the slaughter of.”
Heb “of everyone not pure to consecrate to the Lord.”

18.text: The majority of the many people from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun were ceremonially unclean, yet they ate the Passover in violation of what is prescribed in the law. For Hezekiah prayed for them, saying: “May the Lord, who is good, forgive

notes.text: Heb “without what is written.”
Heb “make atonement for.”

19.text: everyone who has determined to follow God, the Lord God of his ancestors, even if he is not ceremonially clean according to the standards of the temple.”

notes.text: Heb “everyone [who] has prepared his heart to seek God.”
Heb “and not according to the purification of the holy place.”

20.text: The Lord responded favorably to Hezekiah and forgave the people.

notes.text: Heb “listened.”
Heb “healed.”

21.text: The Israelites who were in Jerusalem observed the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with great joy. The Levites and priests were praising the Lord every day with all their might.

notes.text: Heb “and they were praising the Lord day by day, the Levites and the priests with instruments of strength to the Lord.” The phrase ‏בִּכְלֵי־עֹז‎ (bikhle ʿoz, “with instruments of strength”) might refer to loud sounding musical instruments (NASB “with loud instruments”; NEB “with unrestrained fervour”). The present translation assumes an emendation to ‏בְּכָל־עֹז‎ (bekhol ʿoz, “with all strength”); see 1 Chr 13:8, as well as HALOT 805 s.v. I ‏עֹז‎ and BDB 739 s.v. ‏עֹז‎).

22.text: Hezekiah expressed his appreciation to all the Levites, who demonstrated great skill in serving the Lord. They feasted for the seven days of the festival, and were making peace offerings and giving thanks to the Lord God of their ancestors.

notes.text: Heb “and Hezekiah spoke to the heart of all the Levites.” On the meaning of the idiom “speak to the heart of” here, see HALOT 210 s.v. II ‏דבר‎ 8.d.
Heb “who demonstrated skill [with] good skill for the Lord.”

Heb “and they ate [during] the appointed time [for] seven days.” ‏מוֹעֵד‎ (moʿed, “appointed time”) is probably an adverbial accusative of time referring to the festival. However, some understand it as metonymically referring to the food eaten during the festival. See BDB 417 s.v.

23.text: The entire assembly then decided to celebrate for seven more days; so they joyfully celebrated for seven more days.

24.text: King Hezekiah of Judah supplied 1,000 bulls and 7,000 sheep for the assembly, while the officials supplied them with 1,000 bulls and 10,000 sheep. Many priests consecrated themselves.

notes.text: The Hebrew term ‏צֹאן‎ (tsoʾn, translated “sheep” twice in this verse) denotes smaller livestock in general; depending on context it can refer to sheep only or goats only, but there is nothing in the immediate context here to specify one or the other.
Heb “the assembly.” The pronoun “them” has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons, to avoid redundancy.

25.text: The celebration included the entire assembly of Judah, the priests, the Levites, the entire assembly of those who came from Israel, the resident foreigners who came from the land of Israel, and those who were residents of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “they rejoiced.”

The term ‏גֵּר‎ (ger) refers to a foreign resident, but with different social implications in different settings. In Mosaic Law the resident foreigner was essentially a naturalized citizen and convert to worshiping the God of Israel (see Exod 12:19, 48; Deut 29:10-13). Here the term refers to those who had immigrated (or fled as refugees) from the conquered northern kingdom as well as those already residents of the southern kingdom of Judah.

26.text: There was a great celebration in Jerusalem, unlike anything that had occurred in Jerusalem since the time of King Solomon son of David of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “and there was great joy in Jerusalem, for from the days of Solomon son of David, king of Israel, there was nothing like this in Jerusalem.”

27.text: The priests and Levites got up and pronounced blessings on the people. The Lord responded favorably to them as their prayers reached his holy dwelling place in heaven.

notes.text: Heb “and it was heard with their voice.” BDB 1034 s.v. ‏שָׁמַע‎ Niph.4 interprets this to mean “hearing was granted to their voice.” It is possible that the name ‏יְהוָה‎ (yehvah, “the Lord”) has been accidentally omitted.

1.text: When all this was over, the Israelites who were in the cities of Judah went out and smashed the sacred pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and demolished all the high places and altars throughout Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. Then all the Israelites returned to their own homes in their cities.

notes.text: Heb “all Israel.”
Or “tore down.”
Heb “the high places and the altars from all Judah and Benjamin and in Ephraim and in Manasseh until finished.”
Heb “and the sons of Israel returned, each to his possession to their cities.”

2.text: Hezekiah appointed the divisions of the priests and Levites to do their assigned tasks —to offer burnt sacrifices and present offerings and to serve, give thanks, and offer praise in the gates of the Lord’s sanctuary.

notes.text: Heb “and Hezekiah appointed the divisions of the priests and the Levites according to their divisions, each in accordance with his service for the priests and for the Levites.”
Heb “in the gates of the encampments of the Lord.”

3.text: The king contributed some of what he owned for burnt sacrifices, including the morning and evening burnt sacrifices and the burnt sacrifices made on Sabbaths, new moon festivals, and at other appointed times prescribed in the law of the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “the portion of the king [was].”
Heb “festivals, as written.”

4.text: He ordered the people living in Jerusalem to contribute the portion prescribed for the priests and Levites so they might be obedient to the law of the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “said to.”
Heb “might hold firmly.”

5.text: When the edict was issued, the Israelites freely contributed the initial portion of their grain, wine, olive oil, honey, and all the produce of their fields. They brought a tenth of everything, which added up to a huge amount.

notes.text: Heb “and when the word spread out.”
Heb “the sons of Israel multiplied.”

6.text: The Israelites and people of Judah who lived in the cities of Judah also contributed a tenth of their cattle and sheep, as well as a tenth of the holy items consecrated to the Lord their God. They brought them and placed them in many heaps.

notes.text: Heb “and the sons of Israel and Judah.”
Heb “heaps, heaps.” Repetition of the noun draws attention to the large number of heaps.

7.text: In the third month they began piling their contributions in heaps and finished in the seventh month.

notes.text: Heb “they began the heaps to establish.”

8.text: When Hezekiah and the officials came and saw the heaps, they praised the Lord and pronounced blessings on his people Israel.

notes.text: Heb “they blessed the Lord and his people Israel.”

9.text: When Hezekiah asked the priests and Levites about the heaps,

10.text: Azariah, the head priest from the family of Zadok, said to him, “Since the contributions began arriving in the Lord’s temple, we have had plenty to eat and have a large quantity left over. For the Lord has blessed his people, and this large amount remains.”

11.text: Hezekiah ordered that storerooms be prepared in the Lord’s temple. When this was done,

notes.text: Heb “and they prepared.”

12.text: they brought in the contributions, tithes, and consecrated items that had been offered. Konaniah, a Levite, was in charge of all this, assisted by his brother Shimei.

notes.text: Heb “tenth.”
Heb “and holy things in faithfulness.”

13.text: Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismakiah, Mahath, and Benaiah worked under the supervision of Konaniah and his brother Shimei, as directed by King Hezekiah and Azariah, the supervisor of God’s temple.

14.text: Kore son of Imnah, a Levite and the guard on the east side, was in charge of the voluntary offerings made to God and disbursed the contributions made to the Lord and the consecrated items.

15.text: In the cities of the priests, Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah faithfully assisted him in making disbursements to their fellow priests according to their divisions, regardless of age.

notes.text: Heb “to their brothers.”
Heb “like great, like small” (i.e., old and young alike).

16.text: They made disbursements to all the males three years old and up who were listed in the genealogical records—to all who would enter the Lord’s temple to serve on a daily basis and fulfill their duties as assigned to their divisions.

notes.text: Heb “in addition enrolling them by males from a son of three years and upwards, to everyone who enters the house of the Lord for a matter of a day in its day, for their service by their duties according to their divisions.”

17.text: They made disbursements to the priests listed in the genealogical records by their families, and to the Levites twenty years old and up, according to their duties as assigned to their divisions,

18.text: and to all the infants, wives, sons, and daughters of the entire assembly listed in the genealogical records, for they faithfully consecrated themselves.

19.text: As for the descendants of Aaron, the priests who lived in the outskirts of all their cities, men were assigned to disburse portions to every male among the priests and to every Levite listed in the genealogical records.

notes.text: Heb “the priests in the fields of the pastureland of their cities in every city and city.”
Heb “designated by names.”

20.text: This is what Hezekiah did throughout Judah. He did what the Lord his God considered good and right and faithful.

21.text: He wholeheartedly and successfully reinstituted service in God’s temple and obedience to the law, in order to follow his God.

notes.text: Heb “and in all the work which he began with regard to the service of the house of God and with respect to the law and with respect to the commandment, to seek his God; with all his heart he acted and he succeeded.”

1.text: After these faithful deeds were accomplished, King Sennacherib of Assyria invaded Judah. He besieged the fortified cities, intending to seize them.

notes.text: Heb “and he said to break into them for himself.”

2.text: When Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had invaded and intended to attack Jerusalem,

notes.text: Heb “and his face was for war against Jerusalem.”

3.text: he consulted with his advisers and military officers about stopping up the springs outside the city, and they supported him.

notes.text: Heb “the waters of the springs.”

4.text: A large number of people gathered together and stopped up all the springs and the stream that flowed through the district. They reasoned, “Why should the kings of Assyria come and find plenty of water?”

notes.text: Heb “and they closed up all the springs and the stream that flows in the midst of the land.” Here ‏אָרֶץ‎ (ʾarets, “land”) does not refer to the entire land, but to a smaller region like a district.
Heb “land, saying.”

5.text: Hezekiah energetically rebuilt every broken wall. He erected towers and an outer wall and fortified the terrace of the City of David. He made many weapons and shields.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Hezekiah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “strengthened himself and built.”
Heb “and outside the wall another one.”
The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

6.text: He appointed military officers over the army and assembled them in the square at the city gate. He encouraged them, saying,

notes.text: Heb “and he placed officers of war over the people.”
Heb “he spoke to their heart[s].”

7.text: “Be strong and brave! Don’t be afraid and don’t panic because of the king of Assyria and this huge army that is with him. We have with us one who is stronger than those who are with him.

notes.text: Or perhaps, “and don’t be discouraged.”
Heb “for with us [is] a greater [one] than with him.”

8.text: He has with him mere human strength, but the Lord our God is with us to help us and fight our battles!” The army was encouraged by the words of King Hezekiah of Judah.

notes.text: Heb “With him is an arm of flesh.”
Or “people.”

9.text: Afterward King Sennacherib of Assyria, while attacking Lachish with all his military might, sent his messengers to Jerusalem. The message was for King Hezekiah of Judah and all the people of Judah who were in Jerusalem. It read:

notes.text: Heb “servants.”
Heb “all Judah.” The words “the people of” are supplied in the translation for clarity. The Hebrew text uses the name “Judah” here by metonymy for the people of Judah.

10.text: “This is what King Sennacherib of Assyria says: ‘Why are you so confident that you remain in Jerusalem while it is under siege?

notes.text: Heb “On what are you trusting that [you] are living during the siege in Jerusalem.”

11.text: Hezekiah says, “The Lord our God will rescue us from the power of the king of Assyria.” But he is misleading you, and you will die of hunger and thirst!

notes.text: Heb “hand.”
Heb “Is not Hezekiah misleading you to give you over to die by hunger and thirst, saying, ‘The Lord our God will rescue us from the hand of the king of Assyria’?’

12.text: Hezekiah is the one who eliminated the Lord’s high places and altars and then told Judah and Jerusalem, “At one altar you must worship and offer sacrifices.”

notes.text: Heb “Did not he, Hezekiah, eliminate…?” This rhetorical question presupposes a positive reply (“yes, he did”) and so has been translated here as a positive statement.
Heb “his”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

13.text: Are you not aware of what I and my predecessors have done to all the nations of the surrounding lands? Have the gods of the surrounding lands actually been able to rescue their lands from my power?

notes.text: Heb “fathers” (also in vv. 14, 15), but in this context the term does not necessarily refer to Sennacherib’s ancestors, but to his predecessors on the Assyrian throne.
Heb “hand.”

14.text: Who among all the gods of these nations whom my predecessors annihilated was able to rescue his people from my power, that your God would be able to rescue you from my power?

notes.text: Heb “hand.”

15.text: Now don’t let Hezekiah deceive you or mislead you like this. Don’t believe him, for no god of any nation or kingdom has been able to rescue his people from my power or the power of my predecessors. So how can your gods rescue you from my power?’”

notes.text: Heb “how much less.”
The verb is plural, suggesting that the preceding ‏אֱלֹהֵיכֶם‎ (ʾelohekhem) be translated “your gods,” rather than “your God.”

16.text: Sennacherib’s servants further insulted the Lord God and his servant Hezekiah.

notes.text: Heb “his”; the referent (Sennacherib) has been specified in the translation for clarity and for stylistic reasons.
Heb “spoke against.”

17.text: He wrote letters mocking the Lord God of Israel and insulting him with these words: “The gods of the surrounding nations could not rescue their people from my power. Neither can Hezekiah’s god rescue his people from my power.”

notes.text: Heb “and speaking against him, saying.”
Heb “Like the gods of the nations of the lands who did not rescue their people from my hand, so the god of Hezekiah will not rescue his people from my hand.”

18.text: They called out loudly in the Judahite dialect to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall, trying to scare and terrify them so they could seize the city.

19.text: They talked about the God of Jerusalem as if he were one of the man-made gods of the nations of the earth.

20.text: King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz prayed about this and cried out to heaven.

21.text: The Lord sent a messenger and he wiped out all the soldiers, princes, and officers in the army of the king of Assyria. So Sennacherib returned home humiliated. When he entered the temple of his god, some of his own sons struck him down with the sword.

notes.text: Or “an angel.”
Heb “he”; the referent (Sennacherib) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “and he returned with shame of face to his land.”
Heb “and some from those who went out from him, from his inward parts.”

22.text: The Lord delivered Hezekiah and the residents of Jerusalem from the power of King Sennacherib of Assyria and from all the other nations. He made them secure on every side.

notes.text: Heb “and from the hand of all.”

The Hebrew text reads literally, “and he led him from all around.” However, the present translation prefers the Septuagint and Vulgate reading, which suggests an original text of ‏וַיָּנַח לָהֶם מִסָּבִיב‎ (vayyanakh lahem missaviv, “and he gave rest to them from all around”). See 2 Chr 15:15 and 20:30.

23.text: Many were bringing presents to the Lord in Jerusalem and precious gifts to King Hezekiah of Judah. From that time on he was respected by all the nations.

notes.text: Or perhaps, “offerings.”
Heb “lifted up in the eyes of.”

24.text: In those days Hezekiah was stricken with a terminal illness. He prayed to the Lord, who answered him and gave him a sign confirming that he would be healed.

notes.text: Heb “was sick to the point of dying.”
Heb “and he spoke to him and a sign he gave to him.”

25.text: But Hezekiah was ungrateful; he had a proud attitude, provoking God to be angry at him, as well as Judah and Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “but not according to the benefit [given] to him did Hezekiah repay, for his heart was high, and there was anger against him and against Judah and Jerusalem.”

26.text: But then Hezekiah and the residents of Jerusalem humbled themselves and abandoned their pride, and the Lord was not angry with them for the rest of Hezekiah’s reign.

notes.text: Heb “and Hezekiah humbled himself in the height of his heart, he and the residents of Jerusalem, and the anger of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.”

27.text: Hezekiah was very wealthy and greatly respected. He made storehouses for his silver, gold, precious stones, spices, shields, and all his other valuable possessions.

28.text: He made storerooms for the harvest of grain, wine, and olive oil, and stalls for all his various kinds of livestock and his flocks.

notes.text: Heb “and stalls for all beasts and beasts, and flocks for the stalls.” The repetition of ‏בְּהֵמָה‎ (behemah, “beast”) here indicates various kinds of livestock.

29.text: He built royal cities and owned a large number of sheep and cattle, for God gave him a huge amount of possessions.

notes.text: Heb “and cities he made for himself.”

30.text: Hezekiah dammed up the source of the waters of the Upper Gihon and directed them down to the west side of the City of David. Hezekiah succeeded in all that he did.

notes.text: The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

31.text: So when the envoys arrived from the Babylonian officials to visit him and inquire about the sign that occurred in the land, God left him alone to test him, in order to know his true motives.

notes.text: Heb “and when the envoys of the officials of Babylon, who sent to him to inquire concerning the sign which was in the land, [arrived].”
Heb “to know all [that was] in his heart.”

32.text: The rest of the events of Hezekiah’s reign, including his faithful deeds, are recorded in the vision of the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz, included in the Scroll of the Kings of Judah and Israel.

notes.text: Heb “and the rest of the deeds of Hezekiah and his faithful acts, behold, they are written in the vision of Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet upon the scroll of the kings of Judah and Israel.”

33.text: Hezekiah passed away and was buried on the ascent of the tombs of the descendants of David. All the people of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem buried him with great honor. His son Manasseh replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”
Heb “and honor they did to him in his death, all Judah and the residents of Jerusalem.”

1.text: Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he reigned for fifty-five years in Jerusalem.

2.text: He did evil in the sight of the Lord and committed the same horrible sins practiced by the nations whom the Lord drove out ahead of the Israelites.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”
Heb “like the abominable practices of the nations.”

3.text: He rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had destroyed; he set up altars for the Baals and made Asherah poles. He bowed down to all the stars in the sky and worshiped them.

notes.text: The phrase ‏כָל צְבָא הֲַשָּׁמַיִם‎ (khol tsevaʾ hashamayim), traditionally translated “all the host of heaven,” refers to the heavenly lights, including stars and planets. In 1 Kgs 22:19 these heavenly bodies are pictured as members of the Lord’s royal court or assembly, but many other texts view them as the illegitimate objects of pagan and Israelite worship.
Or “served.”

4.text: He built altars in the Lord’s temple, about which the Lord had said, “Jerusalem will be my permanent home.”

notes.text: Heb “In Jerusalem my name will be permanently.”

5.text: In the two courtyards of the Lord’s temple he built altars for all the stars in the sky.

6.text: He passed his sons through the fire in the Valley of Ben Hinnom and practiced divination, omen reading, and sorcery. He set up a ritual pit to conjure up underworld spirits and appointed magicians to supervise it. He did a great amount of evil in the sight of the Lord and angered him.

notes.text: Or “he sacrificed his sons in the fire.” This may refer to child sacrifice, though some interpret it as a less drastic cultic practice (NEB, NASB “made his sons pass through the fire”; NIV “sacrificed his sons in the fire”; NRSV “made his sons pass through fire”). For discussion see M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 266-67.

Heb “and he set up a ritual pit, along with a conjurer.” Hebrew ‏אוֹב‎ (ʾov, “ritual pit”) refers to a pit used by a magician to conjure up underworld spirits. In 1 Sam 28:7 the witch of Endor is called a ‏בַּעֲלַת אוֹב‎ (baʿalat ʾov, “owner of a ritual pit”). See H. Hoffner, “Second Millennium Antecedents to the Hebrew ʾÔḆ,” JBL 86 (1967): 385-401.
Heb “and he multiplied doing what is evil in the eyes of the Lord, angering him.”

7.text: He put an idolatrous image he had made in God’s temple, about which God had said to David and to his son Solomon, “This temple in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, will be my permanent home.

notes.text: Heb “In this house and in Jerusalem, which I chose from all the tribes of Israel, I will place my name permanently” (or perhaps “forever”).

8.text: I will not make Israel again leave the land I gave to their ancestors, provided that they carefully obey all I commanded them, the whole law, the rules and regulations given through Moses.”

notes.text: Heb “I will not again make the feet of Israel wander from the land which I established for their fathers.”

9.text: But Manasseh misled the people of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem so that they sinned more than the nations whom the Lord had destroyed ahead of the Israelites.

notes.text: Heb “misled Judah.” The words “the people of” are supplied in the translation for clarity. The Hebrew text uses the name “Judah” here by metonymy for the people of Judah.

10.text: The Lord confronted Manasseh and his people, but they paid no attention.

notes.text: Heb “spoke to.”

11.text: So the Lord brought against them the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria. They seized Manasseh, put hooks in his nose, bound him with bronze chains, and carried him away to Babylon.

notes.text: Heb “and they seized him with hooks.”

12.text: In his pain Manasseh asked the Lord his God for mercy and truly humbled himself before the God of his ancestors.

notes.text: Or “distress.”
Heb “he”; the referent (Manasseh) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “appeased the face of the Lord his God.”
Or “greatly.”
Heb “fathers.”

13.text: When he prayed to the Lord, the Lord responded to him and answered favorably his cry for mercy. The Lord brought him back to Jerusalem to his kingdom. Then Manasseh realized that the Lord is the true God.

notes.text: Heb “him”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “was entreated by him,” or “allowed himself to be entreated by him.”
Heb “heard.”
Heb “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

14.text: After this Manasseh built up the outer wall of the City of David on the west side of the Gihon in the valley to the entrance of the Fish Gate and all around the terrace; he made it much higher. He placed army officers in all the fortified cities in Judah.

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Manasseh) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The phrase the City of David refers here to the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem, not to Bethlehem. See 2 Sam 5:7.

15.text: He removed the foreign gods and images from the Lord’s temple and all the altars he had built on the hill of the Lord’s temple and in Jerusalem; he threw them outside the city.

16.text: He erected the altar of the Lord and offered on it peace offerings and thank offerings. He told the people of Judah to serve the Lord God of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “told Judah.” The words “the people of” are supplied in the translation for clarity. The Hebrew text uses the name “Judah” here by metonymy for the people of Judah.

17.text: However, the people continued to offer sacrifices at the high places, but only to the Lord their God.

18.text: The rest of the events of Manasseh’s reign, including his prayer to his God and the words the prophets spoke to him in the name of the Lord God of Israel, are recorded in the Annals of the Kings of Israel.

notes.text: Or “seers.”
Heb “look, they are.”

19.text: The Annals of the Prophets include his prayer, give an account of how the Lord responded to it, record all his sins and unfaithful acts, and identify the sites where he built high places and erected Asherah poles and idols before he humbled himself.

notes.text: Heb “and his prayer and being entreated by him, and all his sin and his unfaithfulness and the places where he built high places and set up Asherah poles and idols before he humbled himself—behold, they are written on the words of his seers.”

20.text: Manasseh passed away and was buried in his palace. His son Amon replaced him as king.

notes.text: Heb “lay down with his fathers.”

21.text: Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned for two years in Jerusalem.

22.text: He did evil in the sight of the Lord, just as his father Manasseh had done. Amon offered sacrifices to all the idols his father Manasseh had made, and worshiped them.

notes.text: Heb “in the eyes of.”
Or “served.”

23.text: He did not humble himself before the Lord as his father Manasseh had done. Amon was guilty of great sin.

notes.text: Heb “as Manasseh his father had humbled himself.”
Heb “for he, Amon, multiplied guilt.”

24.text: His servants conspired against him and killed him in his palace.

25.text: The people of the land executed all who had conspired against King Amon, and they made his son Josiah king in his place.

notes.text: Heb “and the people of the land.”

1.text: Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned for thirty-one years in Jerusalem.

2.text: He did what the Lord approved and followed in his ancestor David’s footsteps; he did not deviate to the right or the left.

notes.text: Heb “he did what was proper in the eyes of the Lord.”
Heb “and walked in the ways of David his father.”

3.text: In the eighth year of his reign, while he was still young, he began to seek the God of his ancestor David. In his twelfth year he began ridding Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, Asherah poles, idols, and images.

notes.text: Heb “father.”
Heb “purifying.”

4.text: He ordered the altars of the Baals to be torn down, and broke the incense altars that were above them. He smashed the Asherah poles, idols, and images, crushed them, and sprinkled the dust over the tombs of those who had sacrificed to them.

notes.text: Heb “and they tore down before him the altars of the Baals.”

5.text: He burned the bones of the pagan priests on their altars; he purified Judah and Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “the priests”; the qualifying adjective “pagan” has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

6.text: In the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, as far as Naphtali, and in the ruins around them,

notes.text: “In their ruins” is the marginal reading (Qere) of the Hebrew text.

7.text: he tore down the altars and Asherah poles, demolished the idols, and smashed all the incense altars throughout the land of Israel. Then he returned to Jerusalem.

8.text: In the eighteenth year of his reign, he continued his policy of purifying the land and the temple. He sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the city official, and Joah son of Joahaz the secretary to repair the temple of the Lord his God.

notes.text: Heb “to purify the land and the house.”

9.text: They went to Hilkiah the high priest and gave him the silver that had been brought to God’s temple. The Levites who guarded the door had collected it from the people of Manasseh and Ephraim and from all who were left in Israel, as well as from all the people of Judah and Benjamin and the residents of Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “from Manasseh and Ephraim.” The words “the people of” are supplied in the translation for clarity. The Hebrew text uses the names “Manasseh and Ephraim” here by metonymy for the people of Manasseh and Ephraim.

Heb “all Judah and Benjamin.” The words “the people of” are supplied in the translation for clarity. The Hebrew text uses the names “Judah and Benjamin” here by metonymy for the people of Judah and Benjamin.
The Hebrew consonantal text (Kethib) assumes the reading, “and the residents of.” The marginal reading (Qere) is “and they returned.”

10.text: They handed it over to the construction foremen assigned to the Lord’s temple. They in turn paid the temple workers to restore and repair it.

notes.text: Heb “doer[s] of the work.”
Heb “and they gave it to the doers of the work who were working in the house of the Lord to restore and to repair the house.”

11.text: They gave money to the craftsmen and builders to buy chiseled stone and wood for the braces and rafters of the buildings that the kings of Judah had allowed to fall into disrepair.

notes.text: Heb “of the houses that the kings of Judah had destroyed.”

12.text: The men worked faithfully. Their supervisors were Jahath and Obadiah (Levites descended from Merari), as well as Zechariah and Meshullam (descendants of Kohath). The Levites, all of whom were skilled musicians,

13.text: supervised the laborers and all the foremen on their various jobs. Some of the Levites were scribes, officials, and guards.

notes.text: Heb “[were] over the laborers and were directing every doer of work for work assignment and work assignment.”

14.text: When they took out the silver that had been brought to the Lord’s temple, Hilkiah the priest found the law scroll the Lord had given to Moses.

15.text: Hilkiah informed Shaphan the scribe, “I found the law scroll in the Lord’s temple.” Hilkiah gave the scroll to Shaphan.

16.text: Shaphan brought the scroll to the king and reported, “Your servants are doing everything assigned to them.

notes.text: Heb “returned still the king a word, saying.”

17.text: They melted down the silver in the Lord’s temple and handed it over to the supervisors and the construction foremen.”

notes.text: Heb “that was found in the house of the Lord.”

18.text: Then Shaphan the scribe told the king, “Hilkiah the priest has given me a scroll.” Shaphan read it out loud before the king.

19.text: When the king heard the words of the law, he tore his clothes.

20.text: The king ordered Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Abdon son of Micah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant,

notes.text: The parallel account in 2 Kgs 22:12 has the variant spelling “Achbor son of Micaiah.”

21.text: “Go, ask the Lord for me and for those who remain in Israel and Judah about the words of this scroll that has been discovered. For the Lord’s great fury has been ignited against us, because our ancestors did not obey the word of the Lord by living according to all that is written in this scroll.”

notes.text: The implication is to seek a prophetic oracle.
The MT reads ‏נִתְּכָה‎ (nittekah, “has gushed forth”) but the LXX implies ‏נִצְתָה‎ (nitsetah, “has been ignited”).
Heb “doing.”

22.text: So Hilkiah and the others sent by the king went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum son of Tokhath, the son of Hasrah, the supervisor of the wardrobe. (She lived in Jerusalem in the Mishneh district.) They stated their business,

notes.text: Heb “and those who [were sent by] the king.”
The parallel account in 2 Kgs 22:14 has the variant spelling “son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas.”
Heb “the keeper of the clothes.”
Or “second.” For a discussion of the possible location of this district, see M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 283.
Heb “and they spoke to her like this.”

23.text: and she said to them: “This is what the Lord God of Israel says: ‘Say this to the man who sent you to me:

notes.text: Or “burned incense.”

Heb “angering me with all the work of their hands.” The present translation assumes this refers to idols they have manufactured (note the preceding reference to “other gods”). However, it is possible that this is a general reference to their sinful practices, in which case one might translate, “angering me by all the things they do.”

26.text: Say this to the king of Judah, who sent you to seek an oracle from the Lord: “This is what the Lord God of Israel says concerning the words you have heard:

27.text: ‘You displayed a sensitive spirit and humbled yourself before God when you heard his words concerning this place and its residents. You humbled yourself before me, tore your clothes and wept before me, and I have heard you,’ says the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “Because your heart was tender.”

notes.text: Heb “Therefore, behold, I am gathering you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your tomb in peace.”

29.text: The king summoned all the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem.

notes.text: Heb “and the king sent and gathered all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.”

All the people were there, from the oldest to the youngest. He read aloud all the words of the scroll of the covenant that had been discovered in the Lord’s temple.

31.text: The king stood by his pillar and renewed the covenant before the Lord, agreeing to follow the Lord and to obey his commandments, laws, and rules with all his heart and being, by carrying out the terms of this covenant recorded on this scroll.

notes.text: This assumes an emendation to ‏עַמּוּדוֹ‎ (ʿammudo), see 23:13. The MT reads “at his place.”
Heb “cut,” that is, “made” or “agreed to.”
