If one follows this emendation, then the text reads literally, “and to my neighbors [I am one who experiences] calamity.” The noun ‏פַחַד‎ (fakhad, “[object of] horror”) occurs in the next line; ‏אֵיד‎ and ‏פַחַד‎ appear in parallelism elsewhere (see Prov 1:26-27).
Heb “and [an object of ] horror to those known by me.”

12.text: I am forgotten, like a dead man no one thinks about; I am regarded as worthless, like a broken jar.

notes.text: Heb “I am forgotten, like a dead man, from [the] heart.” The “heart” is here viewed as the center of one’s thoughts.
Heb “I am like a broken jar.” One throws away a broken jar without a second thought because it is considered worthless and useless.

13.text: For I hear what so many are saying, the terrifying news that comes from every direction. When they plot together against me, they figure out how they can take my life.

notes.text: Heb “the report of many.”
Heb “the terror from all around.”

14.text: But I trust in you, O Lord! I declare, “You are my God!”

15.text: You determine my destiny. Rescue me from the power of my enemies and those who chase me.

notes.text: Heb “in your hand [are] my times.”

16.text: Smile on your servant. Deliver me because of your faithfulness.

notes.text: Heb “cause your face to shine.”

17.text: O Lord, do not let me be humiliated, for I call out to you. May evil men be humiliated. May they go wailing to the grave.

notes.text: The verb ‏יִדְּמוּ‎ (yiddemu) is understood as a form of ‏דָּמַם‎ (damam, “wail, lament”). Another option is to take the verb from ‏דָּמַם‎ (“be quiet”; see BDB 198-99 s.v. I ‏דָּמַם‎), in which case one might translate, “May they lie silent in the grave.”

18.text: May lying lips be silenced— lips that speak defiantly against the innocent with arrogance and contempt.

notes.text: Heb “the [ones which].”
Or “godly.”

19.text: How great is your favor, which you store up for your loyal followers. In plain sight of everyone you bestow it on those who take shelter in you.

notes.text: Or “How abundant are your blessings!”
Heb “for those who fear you.”

“Taking shelter” in the Lord is an idiom for seeking his protection. Seeking his protection presupposes and even demonstrates the subject’s loyalty to the Lord. In the psalms those who “take shelter” in the Lord are contrasted with the wicked and equated with those who love, fear, and serve the Lord (Pss 2:12; 5:11-12; 34:21-22).
Heb “you work [your favor] for the ones seeking shelter in you before the sons of men.”

20.text: You hide them with you, where they are safe from the attacks of men; you conceal them in a shelter, where they are safe from slanderous attacks.

notes.text: The noun ‏רֹכֶס‎ (rokhes) occurs only here. Its meaning is debated; some suggest “snare,” while others propose “slander” or “conspiracy.”
Heb “you hide them in the hiding place of your face from the attacks of man.” The imperfect verbal forms in this verse draw attention to God’s typical treatment of the faithful.
Heb “you conceal them in a shelter from the strife of tongues.”

21.text: The Lord deserves praise for he demonstrated his amazing faithfulness to me when I was besieged by enemies.

notes.text: Heb “blessed [be] the Lord.”

Heb “for he caused his faithfulness to be amazing to me in a besieged city.” The psalmist probably speaks figuratively here. He compares his crisis to being trapped in a besieged city, but the Lord answered his prayer for help. Verses 19-24 were apparently written after the Lord answered the prayer of vv. 1-18.

22.text: I jumped to conclusions and said, “I am cut off from your presence!” But you heard my plea for mercy when I cried out to you for help.

notes.text: Heb “and I, I said in my haste.”
Heb “from before your eyes.”

23.text: Love the Lord, all you faithful followers of his! The Lord protects those who have integrity, but he pays back in full the one who acts arrogantly.

notes.text: A “faithful follower” (‏חָסִיד‎, khasid) is one who does what is right in God’s eyes and remains faithful to God (see Pss 4:3; 12:1; 16:10; 31:23; 37:28; 86:2; 97:10).
The participial forms in the second and third lines characterize the Lord as one who typically protects the faithful and judges the proud.

24.text: Be strong and confident, all you who wait on the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “be strong and let your heart[s] be confident.”

1.text: How blessed is the one whose rebellious acts are forgiven, whose sin is pardoned.

notes.text: The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see Pss 1:1, 3; 2:12; 34:9; 41:1; 65:4; 84:12; 89:15; 106:3; 112:1; 127:5; 128:1; 144:15). Here it refers to the relief that one experiences when one’s sins are forgiven.
Heb “lifted up.”
Heb “covered over.”

2.text: How blessed is the one whose wrongdoing the Lord does not punish, in whose spirit there is no deceit.

notes.text: Heb “man.” The word choice reflects the perspective of the psalmist, who is male. The principle of the psalm is certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender or age. To facilitate modern application, the gender and age specific “man” has been translated with the more neutral “one.”
Heb “blessed [is] the man to whom the Lord does not impute wrongdoing.”

In whose spirit there is no deceit. The point is not that the individual is sinless and pure. In this context, which focuses on confession and forgiveness of sin, the psalmist refers to one who refuses to deny or hide his sin, but instead honestly confesses it to God.

3.text: When I refused to confess my sin, my whole body wasted away, while I groaned in pain all day long.

notes.text: Heb “when I was silent.”
Heb “my bones became brittle.” The psalmist pictures himself as aging and growing physically weak. Trying to cover up his sin brought severe physical consequences.

4.text: For day and night you tormented me; you tried to destroy me in the intense heat of summer. (Selah)

notes.text: Heb “your hand was heavy upon me.”

Heb “my [?] was turned.” The meaning of the Hebrew term ‏לְשַׁד‎ (leshad) is uncertain. A noun ‏לָשָׁד‎ (lashad, “cake”) is attested in Num 11:8, but it would make no sense to understand that word in this context. It is better to emend the form to ‏לְשֻׁדִּי‎ (leshuddi, “to my destruction”) and understand “your hand” as the subject of the verb “was turned.” In this case the text reads, “[your hand] was turned to my destruction.” In Lam 3:3 the author laments that God’s “hand” was “turned” (‏הָפַךְ‎, hafakh) against him in a hostile sense.
You tried to destroy me. The psalmist’s statement reflects his perspective. As far as he was concerned, it seemed as if the Lord was trying to kill him.
The translation assumes that the plural form indicates degree. If one understands the form as a true plural, then one might translate, “in the times of drought.”

Summer. Perhaps the psalmist suffered during the hot season and perceived the very weather as being an instrument of divine judgment. Another option is that he compares his time of suffering to the uncomfortable and oppressive heat of summer.

5.text: Then I confessed my sin; I no longer covered up my wrongdoing. I said, “I will confess my rebellious acts to the Lord.” And then you forgave my sins. (Selah)

notes.text: The Hiphil of ‏ידה‎ normally means “give thanks, praise,” but here, as in Prov 28:13, it means “confess.”
Heb “the wrongdoing of my sin.” By joining synonyms for “sin” in this way, the psalmist may be emphasizing the degree of his wrongdoing.

6.text: For this reason every one of your faithful followers should pray to you while there is a window of opportunity. Certainly when the surging water rises, it will not reach them.

notes.text: A “faithful follower” (‏חָסִיד‎, khasid) is one who does what is right in God’s eyes and remains faithful to God (see Pss 4:3; 12:1; 18:25; 31:23; 37:28; 86:2; 97:10).

Heb “at a time of finding.” This may mean, “while there is time to ‘find’ [the Lord]” and seek his forgiveness (cf. NIV). Some emend the text by combining ‏מְצֹא‎ (metsoʾ, “finding”) with the following term ‏רַק‎ (raq, “only, surely”) and read either ‏ר‎[‏וֹ‎]‏מָצ‎ (matsor, “distress”; see Ps 31:22) or ‏ק‎[‏וֹ‎]‏מָצ‎ (matsoq, “hardship”; see Ps 119:143). In this case, one may translate “in a time of distress/hardship” (cf. NEB, NRSV).
The Hebrew term ‏רַק‎ (raq) occasionally has an asseverative force.
The surging water is here a metaphor for trouble that endangers one’s life.
Heb “him.” The translation uses the plural “them” to agree with the plural “every one of your faithful followers” in the first line of v. 6.

7.text: You are my hiding place; you protect me from distress. You surround me with shouts of joy from those celebrating deliverance. (Selah)

notes.text: Heb “[with] shouts of joy of deliverance you surround me.”

8.text: I will instruct and teach you about how you should live. I will advise you as I look you in the eye.

notes.text: The second person pronominal forms in this verse are singular. The psalmist addresses each member of his audience individually (see also the note on the word “eye” in the next line). A less likely option (but one which is commonly understood) is that the Lord addresses the psalmist in vv. 8-9 (cf. NASB “I will instruct you and teach you…I will counsel you with My eye upon you”).
Heb “I will instruct you and I will teach you in the way [in] which you should walk.”

Heb “I will advise, upon you my eye,” that is, “I will offer advice [with] my eye upon you.” In 2 Chr 20:12 the statement “our eye is upon you” means that the speakers are looking to the Lord for intervention. Here the expression “my eye upon you” may simply mean that the psalmist will teach his pupils directly and personally.

9.text: Do not be like an unintelligent horse or mule, which will not obey you unless they are controlled by a bridle and bit.

notes.text: The verb form is plural (i.e., “do not all of you be”); the psalmist addresses the whole group.
Heb “like a horse, like a mule without understanding.”

Heb “with a bridle and bit, its [?] to hold, not to come near to you.” The meaning of the Hebrew noun ‏עֲדִי‎ (ʿadiy) is uncertain. Normally the word refers to “jewelry,” so some suggest the meaning “trappings” here (cf. NASB). Some emend the form to ‏לְחֵיהֶם‎ (lekhehem, “their jawbones”) but it is difficult to see how the present Hebrew text, even if defective, could have derived from this proposed original reading. P. C. Craigie (Psalms 1-50 [WBC], 265) takes the form from an Arabic root and translates “whose gallop.” Cf. also NRSV “whose temper must be curbed.”

10.text: An evil person suffers much pain, but the Lord’s faithfulness overwhelms the one who trusts in him.

notes.text: Heb “many [are the] pains of evil [one].” The singular form is representative here; the typical evildoer, representative of the larger group of wicked people, is in view.
Heb “but the one who trusts in the Lord, faithfulness surrounds him.”

11.text: Rejoice in the Lord and be happy, you who are godly! Shout for joy, all you who are morally upright!

notes.text: Heb “all [you] pure of heart.” The “heart” is here viewed as the seat of one’s moral character and motives. The “pure of heart” are God’s faithful followers who trust in and love the Lord and, as a result, experience his deliverance (see Pss 7:10; 11:2; 36:10; 64:10; 94:15; 97:11).

1.text: You godly ones, shout for joy because of the Lord! It is appropriate for the morally upright to offer him praise.

2.text: Give thanks to the Lord with the harp. Sing to him to the accompaniment of a ten-stringed instrument.

3.text: Sing to him a new song. Play skillfully as you shout out your praises to him.

notes.text: A new song is appropriate because the Lord is constantly intervening in the lives of his people in fresh and exciting ways.
Heb “play skillfully with a loud shout.”

4.text: For the Lord’s decrees are just, and everything he does is fair.

notes.text: Heb “word.” In this context, which depicts the Lord as the sovereign creator and ruler of the world, the Lord’s “word” refers to the decrees whereby he governs his dominion.
Or “upright.”
Heb “and all his work [is done] with faithfulness.”

5.text: He promotes equity and justice; the Lord’s faithfulness extends throughout the earth.

notes.text: Heb “loves.” The verb “loves” is here metonymic; the Lord’s commitment to principles of equity and justice causes him to actively promote these principles as he governs the world.
Heb “fills the earth.”

6.text: By the Lord’s decree the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all the starry hosts.

notes.text: Heb “word.”

The word ‏רוּחַ‎ (ruakh, “spirit, wind, breath”) is used in the creation account in Gen 1:2 “the Spirit of God was moving.” Here parallel to “decree/word,” it recalls the account of God speaking in order to create (cf. Gen 1:14).

7.text: He piles up the water of the sea; he puts the oceans in storehouses.

notes.text: Heb “[he] gathers like a pile the waters of the sea.” Some prefer to emend ‏נֵד‎ (ned, “heap, pile”; cf. NASB) to ‏נֹד‎ (nod, “bottle”; cf. NRSV; NIV “into jars”), but “pile” is used elsewhere to describe water that the Lord confines to one place (Exod 15:8; Josh 3:13, 16; Ps 78:13). This verse appears to refer to Gen 1:9, where God decrees that the watery deep be gathered to one place so that dry land might appear. If so, the participles in this and the following line depict this action with special vividness, as if the reader were present on the occasion. Another option is that the participles picture the confinement of the sea to one place as an ongoing divine activity.
Or “watery depths.” The form ‏תְּהוֹמוֹת‎ (tehomot, “watery depths”) is the plural form of ‏תְּהוֹם‎ (tehom, “great deep”; see Gen 1:2).

8.text: Let the whole earth fear the Lord. Let all who live in the world stand in awe of him.

notes.text: In this context “fear” probably means “to demonstrate respect for the Lord’s power and authority by worshiping him and obeying his commandments.”

9.text: For he spoke, and it came into existence. He issued the decree, and it stood firm.

notes.text: That is, “all the earth” in the first line of v. 8. The apparent antecedent of the masculine subject of the verbs in v. 9 (note ‏וַיֶּהִי‎ [vayyehiy] and ‏וַיַּעֲמֹד‎ [vayyaʿamod]) is “earth” or “world,” both of which are feminine nouns. However, ‏כָּל‎ (kol, “all”) may be the antecedent, or the apparent lack of agreement may be explained by the collective nature of the nouns involved here (see GKC 463 §145.e).
Heb “he commanded.”

10.text: The Lord frustrates the decisions of the nations; he nullifies the plans of the peoples.

notes.text: Heb “breaks” or “destroys.” The Hebrew perfect verbal forms here and in the next line generalize about the Lord’s activity.
Heb “thoughts.”

11.text: The Lord’s decisions stand forever; his plans abide throughout the ages.

notes.text: Heb “the thoughts of his heart for generation to generation.” The verb “abides” is supplied in the translation. The Lord’s “decisions” and “plans” here refer to his decrees and purposes.

12.text: How blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he has chosen to be his special possession.

notes.text: The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see Pss 1:1; 2:12; 34:9; 41:1; 65:4; 84:12; 89:15; 106:3; 112:1; 127:5; 128:1; 144:15).
Heb “inheritance.”

13.text: The Lord watches from heaven; he sees all people.

notes.text: The Hebrew perfect verbal forms in v. 13 state general facts.
Heb “all the sons of men.”

14.text: From the place where he lives he looks carefully at all the earth’s inhabitants.

15.text: He is the one who forms every human heart, and takes note of all their actions.

notes.text: Heb “the one who forms together their heart[s].” “Heart” here refers to human nature, composed of intellect, emotions and will. The precise force of ‏יָחַד‎ (yakhad, “together”) is unclear here. The point seems to be that the Lord is the creator of every human being.

16.text: No king is delivered by his vast army; a warrior is not saved by his great might.

17.text: A horse disappoints those who trust in it for victory; despite its great strength, it cannot deliver.

notes.text: Heb “a lie [is] the horse for victory.”

18.text: Look, the Lord takes notice of his loyal followers, those who wait for him to demonstrate his faithfulness

notes.text: Heb “look, the eye of the Lord [is] toward the ones who fear him.” The expression “the eye…[is] toward” here indicates recognition and the bestowing of favor. See Ps 34:15. The one who fears the Lord respects his sovereignty and obeys his commandments. See Ps 128:1; Prov 14:2.
Heb “for the ones who wait for his faithfulness.”

19.text: by saving their lives from death and sustaining them during times of famine.

notes.text: Heb “to save from death their live[s].”
Heb “and to keep them alive in famine.”

20.text: We wait for the Lord; he is our deliverer and shield.

notes.text: Or “our lives.” The suffixed form of ‏נֶפֶשׁ‎ (nefesh, “being, life”) is often equivalent to a pronoun in poetic texts.
Or “[source of] help.”
Or “protector.”

21.text: For our hearts rejoice in him, for we trust in his holy name.

22.text: May we experience your faithfulness, O Lord, for we wait for you.

notes.text: Heb “let your faithfulness, O Lord, be on us.”
Or “just as.”

1.text: I will praise the Lord at all times; my mouth will continually praise him.

notes.text: Heb “bless.”
Heb “continually [will] his praise [be] in my mouth.”

2.text: I will boast in the Lord; let the oppressed hear and rejoice.

notes.text: Heb “my soul will boast”; or better, “let my soul boast.” Following the cohortative form in v. 1, it is likely that the prefixed verbal form here is jussive.
The two prefixed verbal forms in this verse are best taken as jussives, for the psalmist is calling his audience to worship (see v. 3).

3.text: Magnify the Lord with me. Let us praise his name together.

notes.text: Or “exalt.”

4.text: I sought the Lord’s help and he answered me; he delivered me from all my fears.

notes.text: Heb “I sought the Lord.”

5.text: Look to him and be radiant; do not let your faces be ashamed.

notes.text: The translation follows the LXX. The MT reads “they looked to him and were radiant; let their faces not be ashamed.” The MT reads the first verb as a perfect (‏הִבִּיטוּ‎, hibbitu), which would be past time, while the LXX (supported by Aquila, the Syriac, Jerome, and some medieval Hebrew mss) reads an imperative (‏הַבִּיטוּ‎, habbitu). The MT reads the second verb as a vav plus perfect, while the LXX reads it as an imperative, again a difference of the initial vowel. The third verb is a jussive preceded by ‏אַל‎ (ʾal), which supports reading the first two as imperatives. The second masculine plural pronoun (“your faces”) of the LXX and the Syriac, matches this understanding of the preceding verbs. The MT reading (“their faces”) is consistent with its view of the previous verbs. The reading adopted here interprets the verse as interrupting a testimony given to the congregation with an admonition based on that testimony.

6.text: This oppressed man cried out and the Lord heard; he saved him from all his troubles.

notes.text: The pronoun refers back to “this oppressed man,” namely, the psalmist.

7.text: The angel of the Lord camps around the Lord’s loyal followers and delivers them.

notes.text: Heb “his”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “those who fear him.”
The prefixed verb with vav (‏ו‎) consecutive here carries the same generalizing force as the active participle in the first line. See GKC 329 §111.u.

8.text: Taste and see that the Lord is good. How blessed is the one who takes shelter in him.

notes.text: This verb is normally used of tasting food, as in eating a little bit of food (1 Sam 14:43; Jonah 3:7) or evaluating it (Job 12:11; 34:3). The two references to the physical senses stand for invitation and realization. Even a small or beginning experience of God reveals that he is good.

The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see Pss 1:1, 3; 2:12; 41:1; 65:4; 84:12; 89:15; 106:3; 112:1; 127:5; 128:1; 144:15).

Heb “man.” The principle of the psalm is certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender or age. To facilitate modern application, we translate the gender and age specific “man” with the more neutral “one.”

“Taking shelter” in the Lord is an idiom for seeking his protection. Seeking his protection presupposes and even demonstrates the subject’s loyalty to the Lord. In the psalms those who “take shelter” in the Lord are contrasted with the wicked and equated with those who love, fear, and serve the Lord (Pss 2:12; 5:11-12; 31:17-20; 34:21-22).

9.text: Fear the Lord, you chosen people of his, for those who fear him lack nothing.

notes.text: Heb “O holy ones of his.”

10.text: Even young lions sometimes lack food and are hungry, but those who seek the Lord lack no good thing.

11.text: Come children. Listen to me. I will teach you what it means to fear the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “the fear of the Lord I will teach you.” In vv. 13-14 the psalmist explains to his audience what it means to “fear” the Lord.

12.text: Do you want to really live? Would you love to live a long, happy life?

notes.text: Heb “Who is the man who desires life?” The rhetorical question is used to grab the audience’s attention. “Life” probably refers here to quality of life, not just physical existence or even duration of life. See the following line.
Heb “[Who] loves days to see good?”

13.text: Then make sure you don’t speak evil words or use deceptive speech.

notes.text: Heb “guard your tongue from evil.”
Heb “and your lips from speaking deception.”

14.text: Turn away from evil and do what is right. Strive for peace and promote it.

notes.text: Or “do good.”
Heb “seek peace and pursue it.”

15.text: The Lord pays attention to the godly and hears their cry for help.

notes.text: Heb “the eyes of the Lord [are] toward the godly, and his ears [are] toward their cry for help.”

16.text: But the Lord opposes evildoers and wipes out all memory of them from the earth.

notes.text: Heb “the face of the Lord [is] against the doers of evil to cut off from the earth memory of them.”

17.text: The godly cry out and the Lord hears; he saves them from all their troubles.

notes.text: Heb “they” (i.e., the godly mentioned in v. 15).
The three perfect verbal forms are taken in a generalizing sense in v. 17 and translated with the present tense (note the generalizing mood of vv. 18-22).

18.text: The Lord is near the brokenhearted; he delivers those who are discouraged.

notes.text: The Hebrew imperfect verbal form highlights the generalizing statement and draws attention to the fact that the Lord typically delivers the oppressed and needy.
Heb “the crushed in spirit.”

19.text: The godly face many dangers, but the Lord saves them from each one of them.

notes.text: The Hebrew text uses the singular form; the representative or typical godly person is envisioned.
Or “trials.”
The Hebrew imperfect verbal form highlights the generalizing statement and draws attention to the fact that the Lord typically delivers the godly.
Heb “him,” agreeing with the singular form in the preceding line.

20.text: He protects all his bones; not one of them is broken.

notes.text: The Hebrew participial form suggests such protection is characteristic.
That is, he protects the godly from physical harm.

Not one of them is broken. The author of the Gospel of John saw a fulfillment of these words in Jesus’ experience on the cross (see John 19:31-37), for the Roman soldiers, when they saw that Jesus was already dead, did not break his legs as was customarily done to speed the death of crucified individuals. John’s use of the psalm seems strange, for the statement in its original context suggests that the Lord protects the godly from physical harm. Jesus’ legs may have remained unbroken, but he was brutally and unjustly executed by his enemies. John seems to give the statement a literal sense that is foreign to its original literary context by applying a promise of divine protection to a man who was seemingly not saved by God. However, John saw in this incident a foreshadowing of Jesus’ ultimate deliverance and vindication. His unbroken bones were a reminder of God’s commitment to the godly and a sign of things to come. Jesus’ death on the cross was not the end of the story; God vindicated him, as John goes on to explain in the following context (John 19:38-20:18).

21.text: Evil people self-destruct; those who hate the godly are punished.

notes.text: Heb “evil kills the wicked [one].” The singular form is representative; the typical evil person is envisioned. The Hebrew imperfect verbal form draws attention to the typical nature of the action.
Heb “are guilty,” but the verb is sometimes used metonymically with the meaning “to suffer the consequences of guilt,” the effect being substituted for the cause.

22.text: The Lord rescues his servants; all who take shelter in him escape punishment.

notes.text: Heb “redeems the life of his servants.” The Hebrew participial form suggests such deliverance is characteristic.

“Taking shelter” in the Lord is an idiom for seeking his protection. Seeking his protection presupposes and even demonstrates the subject’s loyalty to the Lord. In the psalms those who “take shelter” in the Lord are contrasted with the wicked and equated with those who love, fear, and serve the Lord (Pss 2:12; 5:11-12; 31:19).

1.text: O Lord, fight those who fight with me. Attack those who attack me.

notes.text: Or “contend.”

2.text: Grab your small shield and large shield, and rise up to help me.

notes.text: Two different types of shields are mentioned here. See also Ezek 38:4. Many modern translations render the first term (translated here “small shield”) as “buckler” (cf. NASB “buckler and shield”; the order is often reversed in the translation, apparently for stylistic reasons: cf. NEB, NIV, NRSV “shield and buckler”). The English term “buckler,” referring to a small round shield held on the arm to protect the upper body, is unfamiliar to many modern readers, so the term “small shield” was used in the present translation for clarity.

3.text: Use your spear and lance against those who chase me. Assure me with these words: “I am your deliverer.”

notes.text: Or “javelin.” On the meaning of this word, which occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible, see M. Dahood, Psalms (AB), 1:210-11.
Heb “draw out spear and lance to meet.”
Heb “say to me,” or “say to my soul.”

4.text: May those who seek my life be embarrassed and humiliated. May those who plan to harm me be turned back and ashamed.

notes.text: The four prefixed verbal forms in this verse are understood as jussives. The psalmist is calling judgment down on his enemies. See also the distinct jussive form in v. 6.

5.text: May they be like wind-driven chaff, as the angel of the Lord attacks them.

notes.text: The prefixed verbal form is taken as a jussive. See v. 4.
See the mention of the angel of the Lord in Ps 34:7.
Heb “as the angel of the Lord pushes [them].”

6.text: May their path be dark and slippery, as the angel of the Lord chases them.

notes.text: The prefixed verbal form is distinctly jussive, indicating this is a prayer.

7.text: I did not harm them, but they hid a net to catch me and dug a pit to trap me.

notes.text: Heb “for without cause they hid for me a pit of their net, without cause they dug for my life.” It appears that the words “pit” and “net” have been transposed. “Net” goes with the verb “hid” in the first line (see v. 8, as well as Pss 9:15; 31:4), while “pit” goes with the verb “dug” in the second line (see Ps 7:15).

8.text: Let destruction take them by surprise. Let the net they hid catch them. Let them fall into destruction.

notes.text: Heb “let destruction [which] he does not know come to him.” The singular is used of the enemy in v. 8, probably in a representative or collective sense. The psalmist has more than one enemy, as vv. 1-7 make clear.
The psalmist’s prayer for his enemies’ demise continues. See vv. 4-6.

9.text: Then I will rejoice in the Lord and be happy because of his deliverance.

notes.text: Heb “then my soul will rejoice in the Lord and be happy in his deliverance.”

10.text: With all my strength I will say, “O Lord, who can compare to you? You rescue the oppressed from those who try to overpower them, the oppressed and needy from those who try to rob them.”

notes.text: Heb “all my bones will say.”
Heb “[the one who] rescues.” The substantival participle in the Hebrew text characterizes God as one who typically rescues the oppressed.
Heb “from [the one who is] too strong for him.” The singular forms are used in a representative sense. The typical oppressed individual and typical oppressor are in view.
Heb “the oppressed [one] and needy [one] from [the one who] robs him.” As in the previous line, the singular forms are used in a representative sense.

11.text: Violent men perjure themselves, and falsely accuse me.

notes.text: Heb “witnesses of violence rise up.”
Heb “[that] which I do not know they ask me.”

12.text: They repay me evil for the good I have done; I am overwhelmed with sorrow.

notes.text: Heb “they repay me evil instead of good.”
Heb “[there is] bereavement to my soul.”

13.text: When they were sick, I wore sackcloth, and refrained from eating food. (If I am lying, may my prayers go unanswered.)

notes.text: Heb “as for me, when they were sick, my clothing was sackcloth.” Sackcloth was worn by mourners. When the psalmist’s enemies were sick, he was sorry for their misfortune and mourned for them.
Fasting was also a practice of mourners. By refraining from normal activities, such as eating food, the mourner demonstrated the sincerity of his sorrow.

Heb “and my prayer upon my chest will return.” One could translate, “but my prayer was returning upon my chest,” but the use of the imperfect verbal form sets this line apart from the preceding and following lines (vv. 13a, 14), which use the perfect to describe the psalmist’s past actions.

14.text: I mourned for them as I would for a friend or my brother. I bowed down in sorrow as if I were mourning for my mother.

notes.text: Heb “like a friend, like a brother to me I walked about.”
I bowed down. Bowing down was a posture for mourning. See Ps 38:6.
Heb “like mourning for a mother [in] sorrow I bowed down.”

15.text: But when I stumbled, they rejoiced and gathered together; they gathered together to ambush me. They tore at me without stopping to rest.

notes.text: Heb “they gathered together against me, stricken [ones], and I did not know.” The Hebrew form ‏נֵכִים‎ (nekhim, “stricken ones” ?) is problematic. Some suggest an emendation to ‏נָכְרִים‎[‏כְ‎] (kenokherim, “foreigners”) or “like foreigners,” which would fit with what follows, “[like] foreigners that I do not recognize.” Perhaps the form should be read as a Qal active participle, ‏נֹכִים‎ (nokhim, “ones who strike”) from the verbal root ‏נָכָה‎ (nakhah, “to strike”). The Qal of this verb is unattested in biblical Hebrew, but the peal (basic) stem appears in Old Aramaic (J. Fitzmyer, The Aramaic Inscriptions of Sefire [BibOr], 114; DNWSI 1:730.) In this case one might translate, “attackers gathered together against me though I was not aware of it” (cf. NASB “smiters”; NEB, NRSV “ruffians”; NIV “attackers”).
Heb “they tore and did not keep quiet.” By using the verb “tear,” the psalmist likens his enemies to a wild animal (see Hos 13:8). In v. 17 he compares them to hungry young lions.

16.text: When I tripped, they taunted me relentlessly, and tried to bite me.

notes.text: The MT reads “as profane [ones] of mockers of food,” which is difficult. The present translation assumes (1) an emendation of ‏בְּחַנְפֵי‎ (bekhanfe, “as profane men”) to ‏בְּחַנְפִי‎ (bekhanfi, “when I tripped”; preposition + Qal infinitive construct from II ‏חָנַף‎ [“limp”] + first common singular pronominal suffix) and (2) an emendation of ‏לַעֲגֵי מָעוֹג‎ (laʿage maʿog, “mockers of food”) to ‏ עָגוּ‎ [‏ם‎]‏לַעְגָּ‎ (laʿgam ʿagu, “[with] taunting they taunted”; masculine plural noun with enclitic mem + Qal perfect third common plural from ‏לַּעַג‎ [laʿag, “taunt”]).
Heb “gnashing at me with their teeth.” The infinitive absolute adds a complementary action—they gnashed with their teeth as they taunted.

17.text: O Lord, how long are you going to watch this? Rescue me from their destructive attacks; guard my life from the young lions.

notes.text: Heb “bring back, restore.”
Or “my life.”

Heb “my only one.” The psalmist may mean that his life is precious, or that he feels isolated and alone (see Ps 22:20). The verb “guard” is supplied in the translation, because the verb “rescue” is understood by ellipsis (see the previous line).

18.text: Then I will give you thanks in the great assembly; I will praise you before a large crowd of people.

notes.text: The great assembly is also mentioned in Ps 22:25.
Heb “among numerous people.”

19.text: Do not let those who are my enemies for no reason gloat over me. Do not let those who hate me without cause carry out their wicked schemes.

notes.text: Heb “[with] a lie.” The Hebrew noun ‏שֶׁקֶר‎ (sheqer, “lie”) is used here as an adverb, “falsely, wrongfully” (see Ps 38:19).
Heb “rejoice.”

Heb “[do not let] those who hate me without cause pinch [i.e., wink] an eye.” The negative particle is understood in the second line by ellipsis (see the preceding line). In the Book of Proverbs “winking an eye” is associated with deceit and trickery (see 6:13; 10:10; 16:30).

20.text: For they do not try to make peace with others, but plan ways to deceive those who live peacefully in the land.

notes.text: Heb “for they do not speak peace.”
Heb “but against the quiet ones of the land words of deceit they plan.” The imperfect verbal forms in v. 20 highlight their characteristic behavior.

21.text: They are ready to devour me; they say, “Aha! Aha! We’ve got you!”

notes.text: Heb “and they cause their mouth to be wide against me.” The prefixed verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) consecutive here carries on the generalizing mood of the previous verse. For other examples of this use of the prefixed verbal form with vav consecutive, see GKC 329 §111.t.
Heb “our eye sees.” Apparently this is an idiom meaning to “look in triumph” or “gloat over” (see Ps 54:7).

22.text: But you take notice, Lord; do not be silent! O Lord, do not remain far away from me.

notes.text: Heb “you see, O Lord.” There is a deliberate play on words. In v. 21 the enemies say, “our eye sees,” but the psalmist is confident that the Lord “sees” as well, so he appeals to him for help (see also v. 17).

23.text: Rouse yourself, wake up and vindicate me. My God and Lord, defend my just cause.

notes.text: Though he is confident that the Lord is aware of his situation (see v. 22a), the psalmist compares the Lord’s inactivity to sleep and urges him to wake up.
Heb “for my justice.”
Heb “for my cause.”

24.text: Vindicate me by your justice, O Lord my God. Do not let them gloat over me.

notes.text: Heb “rejoice.”

25.text: Do not let them say to themselves, “Aha! We have what we wanted!” Do not let them say, “We have devoured him.”

notes.text: Heb “in their heart[s].”
Heb “Aha! Our desire!” The “desire” of the psalmist’s enemies is to triumph over him.

26.text: May those who rejoice in my troubles be totally embarrassed and ashamed. May those who arrogantly taunt me be covered with shame and humiliation.

notes.text: Heb “may they be embarrassed and ashamed together, the ones who rejoice over my harm.”

Heb “may they be clothed with shame and humiliation, the ones who magnify [themselves] against me.” The prefixed verbal forms in v. 26 are understood as jussives (see vv. 24b-25, where the negative particle ‏אַל‎ (ʾal) appears before the prefixed verbal forms, indicating they are jussives). The psalmist is calling down judgment on his enemies.

27.text: May those who desire my vindication shout for joy and rejoice. May they continually say, “May the Lord be praised, for he wants his servant to be secure.”

notes.text: The prefixed verbal forms in v. 27a are understood as jussives (see vv. 24b-26).
The prefixed verbal form is taken as a jussive, “may the Lord be magnified [in praise].” Another option is to take the verb as an imperfect, “the Lord is great.”
Heb “the one who desires the peace of his servant.”

28.text: Then I will tell others about your justice, and praise you all day long.

notes.text: Heb “and my tongue will proclaim your justice.”
Heb “all the day your praise.” The verb “proclaim” is understood by ellipsis in the second line (see the previous line).

1.text: An evil man is rebellious to the core. He does not fear God,

notes.text: Heb “[the] rebellion of an evil man [is] in the midst of my heart.” The translation assumes a reading “in the midst of his heart” (i.e., “to the core”) instead of “in the midst of my heart,” a change which finds support in a few medieval Hebrew mss, the Hebrew text of Origen’s Hexapla, and the Syriac.
Heb “there is no dread of God before his eyes.” The phrase “dread of God” refers here to a healthy respect for God which recognizes that he will punish evil behavior.

2.text: for he is too proud to recognize and give up his sin.

notes.text: Heb “for it causes to be smooth to him in his eyes to find his sin to hate.” The meaning of the Hebrew text is unclear. Perhaps the point is this: His rebellious attitude makes him reject any notion that God will hold him accountable. His attitude also prevents him from recognizing and repudiating his sinful ways.

3.text: The words he speaks are sinful and deceitful; he does not care about doing what is wise and right.

notes.text: Heb “he ceases to exhibit wisdom to do good.” The Hiphil forms are exhibitive, indicating the outward expression of an inner attitude.

4.text: While he lies in bed he plans ways to sin. He is committed to a sinful lifestyle; he does not reject what is evil.

notes.text: Heb “he takes a stand in a way [that is] not good.” The word “way” here refers metaphorically to behavior or life style.
The three imperfect verbal forms in v. 4 highlight the characteristic behavior of the typical evildoer.

5.text: O Lord, your loyal love reaches to the sky, your faithfulness to the clouds.

notes.text: Heb “[is] in the heavens.”
The Lord’s loyal love/faithfulness is almost limitless. He is loyal and faithful to his creation and blesses mankind and the animal kingdom with physical life and sustenance (vv. 6-9).

6.text: Your justice is like the highest mountains, your fairness like the deepest sea; you, Lord, preserve mankind and the animal kingdom.

notes.text: Heb “mountains of God.” The divine name ‏אֵל‎ (ʾel, “God”) is here used in an idiomatic manner to indicate the superlative.
Or “deliver.”

God’s justice/fairness is firm and reliable like the highest mountains and as abundant as the water in the deepest sea. The psalmist uses a legal metaphor to describe God’s preservation of his creation. Like a just judge who vindicates the innocent, God protects his creation from destructive forces.

7.text: How precious is your loyal love, O God! The human race finds shelter under your wings.

notes.text: Or “valuable.”
Heb “and the sons of man in the shadow of your wings find shelter.” The preservation of physical life is in view, as the next verse makes clear.

8.text: They are filled with food from your house, and you allow them to drink from the river of your delicacies.

9.text: For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we see light.

notes.text: Water (note “fountain”) and light are here metaphors for life.

10.text: Extend your loyal love to your faithful followers, and vindicate the morally upright.

notes.text: Heb “draw out to full length.”
Heb “to those who know you.” The Hebrew verb ‏יָדַע‎ (yadaʿ, “know”) is used here of those who “know” the Lord in the sense that they recognize his royal authority and obey his will (see Jer 22:16).
Heb “and your justice to.” The verb “extend” is understood by ellipsis in the second line (see the previous line).

Heb “the pure of heart.” The “heart” is here viewed as the seat of one’s moral character and motives. The “pure of heart” are God’s faithful followers who trust in and love the Lord and, as a result, experience his deliverance (see Pss 7:10; 11:2; 32:11; 64:10; 94:15; 97:11).

11.text: Do not let arrogant men overtake me, or let evil men make me homeless.

notes.text: Heb “let not a foot of pride come to me, and let not the hand of the evil ones cause me to wander as a fugitive.”

12.text: I can see the evildoers! They have fallen. They have been knocked down and are unable to get up.

notes.text: Heb “there the workers of wickedness have fallen.” The adverb ‏שָׁם‎ (sham, “there”) is used here for dramatic effect, as the psalmist envisions the evildoers lying fallen at a spot that is vivid in his imagination (BDB 1027 s.v.).
The psalmist uses perfect verbal forms in v. 12 to describe the demise of the wicked as if it has already taken place.

1.text: Do not fret when wicked men seem to succeed. Do not envy evildoers.

notes.text: The verb form is singular (see vv. 3-10 as well, where the second person verbs and pronouns are also singular). The psalmist’s exhortation has a wisdom flavor to it; it is personalized for each member of his audience.
Heb “over sinners.” The context indicates that the psalmist has in mind the apparent power and success of sinners. See v. 7b.

2.text: For they will quickly dry up like grass, and wither away like plants.

notes.text: Heb “like green vegetation.”

3.text: Trust in the Lord and do what is right. Settle in the land and maintain your integrity.

notes.text: Heb “tend integrity.” The verb ‏רָעָה‎ (raʿah, “tend, shepherd”) is probably used here in the sense of “watch over, guard.” The noun ‏אֱמוּנָה‎ (ʾemunah, “faithfulness, honesty, integrity”) is understood as the direct object of the verb, though it could be taken as an adverbial accusative, “[feed] securely,” if the audience is likened to a flock of sheep.

4.text: Then you will take delight in the Lord, and he will answer your prayers.

notes.text: Following the imperatives of v. 3 the prefixed verbal forms with vav (‏ו‎) in v. 4 indicate result. Faith and obedience (v. 3) will bring divine blessing (v. 4).
Or “and he will give you what you desire most.” Heb “and he will grant to you the requests of your heart.”

5.text: Commit your future to the Lord. Trust in him, and he will act on your behalf.

notes.text: Heb “roll your way upon the Lord.” The noun “way” may refer here to one’s activities or course of life.
Heb “he will act.” Verse 6 explains what is meant; the Lord will vindicate those who trust in him.

6.text: He will vindicate you in broad daylight, and publicly defend your just cause.

notes.text: Heb “and he will bring out like light your vindication, and your just cause like noonday.”

7.text: Wait patiently for the Lord! Wait confidently for him! Do not fret over the apparent success of a sinner, a man who carries out wicked schemes.

notes.text: Heb “Be quiet before the Lord!”

The Hebrew text has ‏וְהִתְחוֹלֵל‎ (vehitkholel, Hitpolel of ‏חִיל‎, khil, “writhe with fear, suffer”) but this idea fits awkwardly here. The text should be changed to ‏וְתוֹחֵל‎ (vetokhel; Hiphil of ‏יָחַל‎, yakhal, “wait”). It appears that the Hebrew text is the product of dittography: (1) the initial ‏וה‎ (vav-he) is accidentally repeated from the preceding word (‏יְהוָה‎, yehvah) and (2) the final ‏ל‎ (lamed) is accidentally repeated (note the preceding lamed and the initial lamed on the following form, ‏לו‎).
Heb “over one who causes his way to be successful.”

8.text: Do not be angry and frustrated. Do not fret. That only leads to trouble.

notes.text: Heb “Refrain from anger! Abandon rage!”

9.text: Wicked men will be wiped out, but those who rely on the Lord are the ones who will possess the land.

notes.text: Heb “for evil men.” The conjunction ‏כִּי‎ (ki, “for”) relates to the exhortations in v. 8; there is no reason to be frustrated, for the evildoers will be punished in due time.
Or “cut off, removed.”
Heb “and those who wait on the Lord, they will possess the land.”

10.text: Evil men will soon disappear; you will stare at the spot where they once were, but they will be gone.

notes.text: Heb “and yet, a little, there will be no wicked [one].”
Heb “and you will carefully look upon his place, but he will not be [there].” The singular is used here in a representative sense; the typical evildoer is in view.

11.text: But the oppressed will possess the land and enjoy great prosperity.

notes.text: Heb “and they will take delight in (see v. 4) abundance of peace.”

12.text: Evil men plot against the godly and viciously attack them.

notes.text: Or “innocent.” The singular is used here in a representative sense; the typical evildoer and the typical godly individual are in view.
Heb “and gnashes at him with his teeth” (see Ps 35:16). The language may picture the evil men as wild animals. The active participles in v. 12 are used for purposes of dramatic description.

13.text: The Lord laughs in disgust at them, for he knows that their day is coming.

notes.text: Heb “laughs.” As the next line indicates, this refers to derisive laughter (see 2:4). The Hebrew imperfect verbal form describes the action from the perspective of an eye-witness who is watching the divine response as it unfolds before his eyes.
Heb “for he sees that his day is coming.” As the following context makes clear (vv. 15, 17, 19-20), “his day” refers to the time when God will destroy evildoers.

14.text: Evil men draw their swords and prepare their bows, to bring down the oppressed and needy, and to slaughter those who are godly.

notes.text: Heb “to cause to fall.”
Heb “the upright in way,” i.e., those who lead godly lives.

15.text: Their swords will pierce their own hearts, and their bows will be broken.

notes.text: Heb “enter into.”

16.text: The little bit that a godly man owns is better than the wealth of many evil men,

notes.text: Heb “Better [is] a little to the godly one than the wealth of many evil ones.” The following verses explain why this is true. Though a godly individual may seem to have only meager possessions, he always has what he needs and will eventually possess the land. The wicked may prosper for a brief time, but will eventually be destroyed by divine judgment and lose everything.

17.text: for evil men will lose their power, but the Lord sustains the godly.

notes.text: Heb “for the arms of the evil ones will be broken.”
The active participle here indicates this is characteristically true.

18.text: The Lord watches over the innocent day by day, and they possess a permanent inheritance.

notes.text: Heb “the Lord knows the days of the innocent ones.” He “knows” their days in the sense that he is intimately aware of and involved in their daily struggles. He meets their needs and sustains them.
Heb “and their inheritance is forever.”

19.text: They will not be ashamed when hard times come; when famine comes they will have enough to eat.

notes.text: Heb “in a time of trouble.”
Heb “in days of famine they will be satisfied.”

20.text: But evil men will die; the Lord’s enemies will be incinerated — they will go up in smoke.

notes.text: Or “for,” but Hebrew ‏כִּי‎ (ki) in this case would have to extend all the way back to v. 17a. Another option is to understand the particle as asseverative, “surely” (see v. 22).

The meaning of the MT (‏כִּיקַר כָּרִים‎ [kiqar karim], “like what is precious among the pastures/rams”) is uncertain. One possibility is to take the noun ‏כָּרִים‎ as “pastures” and interpret “what is precious” as referring to flowers that blossom but then quickly disappear (see v. 2 and BDB 430 s.v. ‏יָקָר‎ 3). If ‏כָּרִים‎ is taken as “rams,” then “what is precious” might refer to the choicest portions of rams. The present translation follows a reading in the Dead Sea Scrolls (4QpPs37), ‏כיקוד כורם‎ (“like the burning of an oven”). The next line, which pictures the Lord’s enemies being consumed in smoke, supports this reading, which assumes confusion of the Hebrew letters ‏ר‎ (resh) and ‏ד‎ (dalet) at the end of the first word in the sequence.

Heb “they perish in smoke, they perish.” In addition to repeating the verb for emphasis, the psalmist uses the perfect form of the verb to picture the enemies’ demise as if it had already taken place. In this way he draws attention to the certitude of their judgment.

21.text: Evil men borrow, but do not repay their debt, but the godly show compassion and are generous.

notes.text: Heb “an evil [man] borrows and does not repay, but a godly [man] is gracious and gives.” The singular forms are used in a representative sense; the typical evildoer and godly individual are in view. The three active participles and one imperfect (“repay”) draw attention to the characteristic behavior of the two types.

22.text: Surely those favored by the Lord will possess the land, but those rejected by him will be wiped out.

notes.text: The particle ‏כִּי‎ (ki) is best understood as asseverative or emphatic here.
Heb “those blessed by him.” The pronoun “him” must refer to the Lord (see vv. 20, 23), so the referent has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “cursed.”
Or “cut off”; or “removed” (see v. 9).

23.text: The Lord grants success to the one whose behavior he finds commendable.

notes.text: Heb “from the Lord the steps of a man are established, and in his way he delights.” The second line qualifies the first. The man whose behavior is commendable in God’s sight is the one whose ways are established by God. Another option is that the second line refers to the godly man delighting in God’s “way,” namely the lifestyle which he prescribes for men. In this case one might translate, “The Lord grants success to the one who desires to obey his commands.”

24.text: Even if he trips, he will not fall headlong, for the Lord holds his hand.

notes.text: Other translation options for ‏כִּי‎ (ki) in this context are “when” (so NASB) or “though” (so NEB, NIV, NRSV).
Heb “be hurled down.”
The active participle indicates this is characteristically true. See v. 17.

25.text: I was once young, now I am old. I have never seen the godly abandoned, or their children forced to search for food.

notes.text: Or “offspring”; Heb “seed.”

Heb “or his offspring searching for food.” The expression “search for food” also appears in Lam 1:11, where Jerusalem’s refugees are forced to search for food and to trade their valuable possessions for something to eat.

26.text: All day long they show compassion and lend to others, and their children are blessed.

notes.text: The active participles describe characteristic behavior.
Or “offspring”; Heb “seed.”

27.text: Turn away from evil. Do what is right. Then you will enjoy lasting security.

notes.text: Or “Do good!” The imperatives are singular (see v. 1).
Heb “and dwell permanently.” The imperative with vav (‏ו‎) is best taken here as a result clause after the preceding imperatives.

28.text: For the Lord promotes justice, and never abandons his faithful followers. They are permanently secure, but the children of the wicked are wiped out.

notes.text: Heb “loves.” The verb “loves” is here metonymic; the Lord’s commitment to principles of justice causes him to actively promote these principles as he governs the world. The active participle describes characteristic behavior.
The imperfect verbal form draws attention to this generalizing statement.
Or “protected forever.”
Or “offspring”; Heb “seed.”
Or “cut off”; or “removed.” The perfect verbal forms in v. 28b state general truths.

29.text: The godly will possess the land and will dwell in it permanently.

30.text: The godly speak wise words and promote justice.

notes.text: Heb “The mouth of the godly [one] utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice.” The singular form is used in a representative sense; the typical godly individual is in view. The imperfect verbal forms draw attention to the characteristic behavior of the godly.

31.text: The law of their God controls their thinking; their feet do not slip.

notes.text: Heb “the law of his God [is] in his heart.” The “heart” is here the seat of one’s thoughts and motives.
Heb “his.” The pronoun has been translated as plural to agree with the representative or typical “godly” in v. 30.

32.text: The wicked set an ambush for the godly and try to kill them.

notes.text: Heb “an evil [one] watches the godly [one] and seeks to kill him.” The singular forms are used in a representative sense; the typical evildoer and godly individual are in view. The active participles describe characteristic behavior.

33.text: But the Lord does not surrender the godly, or allow them to be condemned in a court of law.

notes.text: Heb “the Lord does not abandon him into his hand or condemn him when he is judged.” The imperfects draw attention to the Lord’s characteristic behavior in this regard.

34.text: Rely on the Lord. Obey his commands. Then he will permit you to possess the land; you will see the demise of the wicked.

notes.text: Or “wait.”

Heb “keep his way.” The Lord’s “way” refers here to the “conduct required” by the Lord. In Ps 25 the Lord’s “ways” are associated with his covenantal demands (see vv. 4, 9-10). See also Ps 119:3 (cf. vv. 1, 4), as well as Deut 8:6; 10:12; 11:22; 19:9; 26:17; 28:9; 30:16.
Heb “and he will lift you up.” The prefixed verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) is best taken here as a result clause following the imperatives in the preceding lines.
Heb “when evil men are cut off you will see.”

35.text: I have seen ruthless, wicked people growing in influence, like a green tree grows in its native soil.

notes.text: The Hebrew uses the representative singular again here.

Heb “being exposed [?] like a native, luxuriant.” The Hebrew form ‏מִתְעָרֶה‎ (mitʿareh) appears to be a Hitpael participle from ‏עָרָה‎ (ʿarah, “be exposed”), but this makes no sense in this context. Perhaps the form is a dialectal variant of ‏מִתְעָלָה‎ (“giving oneself an air of importance”; see Jer 51:3), from ‏עָלָה‎ (ʿalah, “go up”; see P. C. Craigie, Psalms 1-50 [WBC], 296). The noun ‏אֶזְרָח‎ (ʾezrakh, “native, full citizen”) refers elsewhere to people, but here, where it is collocated with “luxuriant, green,” it probably refers to a tree growing in native soil.

36.text: But then one passes by, and suddenly they have disappeared. I looked for them, but they could not be found.

notes.text: Heb “and he passes by and, look, he is not [there].” The subject of the verb “passes by” is probably indefinite, referring to any passerby. Some prefer to change the form to first person, “and I passed by” (cf. NEB; note the first person verbal forms in preceding verse and in the following line).

37.text: Take note of the one who has integrity. Observe the upright. For the one who promotes peace has a future.

notes.text: Heb “for [there is] an end for a man of peace.” Some interpret ‏אַחֲרִית‎ (ʾakharit, “end”) as referring to offspring (see the next verse and Ps 109:13; cf. NEB, NRSV).

38.text: Sinful rebels are totally destroyed; the wicked have no future.

notes.text: Or “destroyed together.” In this case the psalmist pictures judgment sweeping them away as a group.

Heb “the end of evil men is cut off.” As in v. 37, some interpret ‏אַחֲרִית‎ (ʾakharit, “end”) as referring to offspring (see Ps 109:13). The perfect verbal forms in v. 38 probably express general truths. Another option is that they are used emphatically to state with certitude that the demise of the wicked is as good as done.

39.text: But the Lord delivers the godly; he protects them in times of trouble.

notes.text: Heb “and the deliverance of the godly [ones] [is] from the Lord.”
Heb “[he is] their place of refuge in a time of trouble.”

40.text: The Lord helps them and rescues them; he rescues them from the wicked and delivers them, for they seek his protection.

notes.text: The prefixed verbal forms with vav (‏ו‎) consecutive carry on the generalizing tone of the preceding verse.

1.text: O Lord, do not continue to rebuke me in your anger. Do not continue to punish me in your raging fury.

notes.text: The words “continue to” are supplied in the translation of both lines. The following verses make it clear that the psalmist is already experiencing divine rebuke/punishment. He asks that it might cease.
Cf. Ps 38:1 with Ps 6:1, which has similar wording.

2.text: For your arrows pierce me, and your hand presses me down.

notes.text: The verb Hebrew ‏נָחַת‎ (nakhat) apparently here means “penetrate, pierce” (note the use of the Qal in Prov 17:10). The psalmist pictures the Lord as a warrior who shoots arrows at him (see Ps 7:12-13).

Heb “and your hand [?] upon me.” The meaning of the verb ‏נָחַת‎ (nakhat) is unclear in this context. It could mean “your hand comes down on me.” It may be preferable to emend the form to ‏וַתָּנַח‎ (vattanakh) from the verb ‏נוּחַ‎ (nuakh, “rest”). In this case the text would read literally, “and your hand rests upon me” (see Isa 25:10, though the phrase is used in a positive sense there, unlike Ps 38:2).

3.text: My whole body is sick because of your judgment; I am deprived of health because of my sin.

notes.text: Heb “there is no soundness in my flesh from before your anger.” “Anger” here refers metonymically to divine judgment, which is the practical effect of God’s anger at the psalmist’s sin.
Heb “there is no health in my bones from before my sin.”

4.text: For my sins overwhelm me; like a heavy load, they are too much for me to bear.

notes.text: Heb “pass over my head.”

5.text: My wounds are infected and starting to smell, because of my foolish sins.

notes.text: The reference to wounds may be an extension of the metaphorical language of v. 2. The psalmist pictures himself as one whose flesh is ripped and torn by arrows.
Heb “my wounds stink, they are festering” (cf. NEB).
Heb “from before my foolishness.”

6.text: I am dazed and completely humiliated; all day long I walk around mourning.

notes.text: The verb’s precise shade of meaning in this context is not entirely clear. The verb, which literally means “to bend,” may refer to the psalmist’s posture. In Isa 21:3 it seems to mean “be confused, dazed.”
Heb “I am bowed down to excess.”

7.text: For I am overcome with shame, and my whole body is sick.

notes.text: Heb “for my loins are filled with shame.” The “loins” are viewed here as the seat of the psalmist’s emotions. The present translation assumes that ‏נִקְלֶה‎ (niqleh) is derived from ‏קָלָה‎ (qalah, “be dishonored”). Some derive it instead from a homonymic root ‏קָלָה‎ (qalah), meaning “to roast.” In this case one might translate “fever” (cf. NEB “my loins burn with fever”).
Heb “there is no soundness in my flesh” (see v. 3).

8.text: I am numb with pain and severely battered; I groan loudly because of the anxiety I feel.

notes.text: Heb “I am numb and crushed to excess.”
Heb “I roar because of the moaning of my heart.”

9.text: O Lord, you understand my heart’s desire; my groaning is not hidden from you.

notes.text: Heb “O Lord, before you [is] all my desire.”

10.text: My heart beats quickly; my strength leaves me. I can hardly see.

notes.text: Heb “and the light of my eyes, even they, there is not with me.” The “light of the eyes” may refer to physical energy (see 1 Sam 14:27, 29), life itself (Ps 13:3), or the ability to see (Prov 29:23).

11.text: Because of my condition, even my friends and acquaintances keep their distance; my neighbors stand far away.

notes.text: Or “wound,” or “illness.”
Heb “stand [aloof].”
Heb “and the ones near me off at a distance stand.”

12.text: Those who seek my life try to entrap me; those who want to harm me speak destructive words. All day long they say deceitful things.

notes.text: Heb “lay snares.”

13.text: But I am like a deaf man—I hear nothing; I am like a mute who cannot speak.

notes.text: I am like a deaf man…like a mute. The psalmist is like a deaf mute; he is incapable of defending himself and is vulnerable to his enemies’ deception (see v. 14).

14.text: I am like a man who cannot hear and is incapable of arguing his defense.

notes.text: Heb “and there is not in his mouth arguments.”

15.text: Yet I wait for you, O Lord! You will respond, O Lord, my God!

notes.text: Or perhaps “surely.”

16.text: I have prayed for deliverance, because otherwise they will gloat over me; when my foot slips they will arrogantly taunt me.

notes.text: Heb “For I said, ‘Lest they rejoice over me.’” The psalmist recalls the motivating argument of his petition. He probably prefaced this statement with a prayer for deliverance (see Pss 7:1-2; 13:3-4; 28:1).
Heb “they will magnify against me.” See Pss 35:26; 55:13.

17.text: For I am about to stumble, and I am in constant pain.

notes.text: Heb “and my pain [is] before me continually.”

18.text: Yes, I confess my wrongdoing, and I am concerned about my sins.

notes.text: Or “for.” The translation assumes that ‏כִּי‎ (ki) is asseverative here.

19.text: But those who are my enemies for no reason are numerous; those who hate me without cause outnumber me.

notes.text: Heb “and my enemies, life, are many.” The noun ‏חַיִּים‎ (khayyim, “life”) fits very awkwardly here. The translation assumes an emendation to ‏חִנָּם‎ (khinnam, “without reason”; note the parallelism with ‏שֶׁקֶר‎ [sheqer, “falsely”] and see Pss 35:19; 69:4; Lam 3:52). The verb ‏עָצַם‎ (ʿatsam) can sometimes mean “are strong,” but here it probably focuses on numerical superiority (note the parallel verb ‏רָבַב‎, ravav, “be many”).
Heb “are many.”

20.text: They repay me evil for the good I have done; though I have tried to do good to them, they hurl accusations at me.

notes.text: Heb “the ones who repay evil instead of good accuse me, instead of my pursuing good.”

21.text: Do not abandon me, O Lord. My God, do not remain far away from me.

22.text: Hurry and help me, O Lord, my deliverer.

notes.text: Heb “hurry to my help.” See Ps 22:19.

1.text: I decided, “I will watch what I say and make sure I do not sin with my tongue. I will put a muzzle over my mouth while in the presence of an evil person.”

notes.text: Heb “I said.”
Heb “I will watch my ways, from sinning with my tongue.”

The psalmist wanted to voice a lament to the Lord (see vv. 4-6), but he hesitated to do so in the presence of evil people, for such words might be sinful if they gave the wicked an occasion to insult God. See C. A. Briggs and E. G. Briggs, Psalms (ICC), 1:345.

2.text: I was stone silent; I held back the urge to speak. My frustration grew;

notes.text: Heb “I was mute [with] silence.”
Heb “I was quiet from good.” He kept quiet, resisting the urge to find emotional release and satisfaction by voicing his lament.

I held back the urge to speak. For a helpful discussion of the relationship (and tension) between silence and complaint in ancient Israelite lamentation, see E. S. Gerstenberger, Psalms, Part I (FOTL), 166-67.
Heb “and my pain was stirred up.” Emotional pain is in view here.

3.text: my anxiety intensified. As I thought about it, I became impatient. Finally I spoke these words:

notes.text: Heb “my heart was hot within me.”
Heb “In my reflection fire burned.” The prefixed verbal form is either a preterite (past tense) or an imperfect being used in a past progressive or customary sense (“fire was burning”).
Heb “I spoke with my tongue.” The phrase “these words” is supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.

4.text: “O Lord, help me understand my mortality and the brevity of life. Let me realize how quickly my life will pass.

notes.text: Heb “Cause me to know, O Lord, my end; and the measure of my days, what it is!”
Heb “Let me know how transient I am.”

5.text: Look, you make my days short-lived, and my life span is nothing from your perspective. Surely all people, even those who seem secure, are nothing but vapor. (Selah)

notes.text: Heb “Look, handbreadths you make my days.” The “handbreadth” (equivalent to the width of four fingers) was one of the smallest measures used by ancient Israelites. See P. C. Craigie, Psalms 1-50 (WBC), 309.
Heb “is like nothing before you.”
Heb “surely, all vapor [is] all mankind, standing firm.” Another option is to translate, “Surely, all mankind, though seemingly secure, is nothing but a vapor.”

6.text: Surely people go through life as mere ghosts. Surely they accumulate worthless wealth without knowing who will eventually haul it away.”

notes.text: Heb “surely, as an image man walks about.” The preposition prefixed to “image” indicates identity here.

People go through life (Heb “man walks about”). “Walking” is here used as a metaphor for living. The point is that human beings are here today, gone tomorrow. They have no lasting substance and are comparable to mere images or ghosts.

Heb “Surely [in] vain they strive, he accumulates and does not know who gathers them.” The MT as it stands is syntactically awkward. The verb forms switch from singular (“walks about”) to plural (“they strive”) and then back to singular (“accumulates and does not know”), even though the subject (generic “man”) remains the same. Furthermore there is no object for the verb “accumulates” and no plural antecedent for the plural pronoun (“them”) attached to “gathers.” These problems can be removed if one emends the text from ‏הֶבֶל יֶהֱמָיוּן‎ (hevel yehemayun, “[in] vain they strive”) to ‏הֶבְלֵי הָמוֹן‎ (hevle hamon, “vain things of wealth”). The present translation follows this emendation.

7.text: But now, O Lord, upon what am I relying? You are my only hope!

notes.text: Heb “my hope, for you it [is].”

8.text: Deliver me from all my sins of rebellion. Do not make me the object of fools’ insults.

9.text: I am silent and cannot open my mouth because of what you have done.

notes.text: Heb “because you acted.” The psalmist has in mind God’s disciplinary measures (see vv. 10-13).

10.text: Please stop wounding me. You have almost beaten me to death.

notes.text: Heb “remove from upon me your wound.”
Heb “from the hostility of your hand I have come to an end.”

11.text: You severely discipline people for their sins; like a moth you slowly devour their strength. Surely all people are a mere vapor. (Selah)

notes.text: “with punishments on account of sin you discipline a man.”

Heb “you cause to dissolve, like a moth, his desired [thing].” The translation assumes an emendation of ‏חֲמוּדוֹ‎ (khamudo, “his desirable [thing]”) to ‏חֶמְדוֹ‎ (khemdo, “his loveliness” [or “beauty”]), a reading that is supported by a few medieval Hebrew mss.

12.text: Hear my prayer, O Lord. Listen to my cry for help. Do not ignore my sobbing. For I am a resident foreigner with you, a temporary settler, just as all my ancestors were.

notes.text: Heb “do not be deaf to my tears.”

The Hebrew terms ‏גֵּר‎ (ger, “resident foreigner”) and ‏תּוֹשָׁב‎ (toshav, “resident/dweller”) have similar meanings. They are not used here with the technical distinctions of most references in Mosaic Law. Ps 39:12 takes up this language from Lev 25:23 where the terms emphasize that Israel would be a guest on God’s land. They were attached to the Lord’s household; they did not own the land. The Psalmist identifies himself with this privileged yet dependent position. Abraham also refers to himself by these terms in Gen 23:4.

13.text: Turn your angry gaze away from me, so I can be happy before I pass away.

notes.text: Heb “Gaze away from me and I will smile before I go and am not.” The precise identification of the initial verb form (‏הָשַׁע‎, hashaʿ) is uncertain. It could be from the root ‏שָׁעָע‎ (shaʿaʿ, “smear over”), but “your eyes” would be the expected object in this case (see Isa 6:10). The verb may be an otherwise unattested Hiphil form of ‏שָׁעָה‎ (shaʿah, “to gaze”) meaning “cause your gaze to be.” Some prefer to emend the form to the Qal ‏שְׁעֵה‎ (sheʿeh, “gaze”; see Job 14:6). If one does read a form of the verb “to gaze,” the angry divine “gaze” of discipline would seem to be in view (see vv. 10-11). For a similar expression of this sentiment see Job 10:20-21.

1.text: I relied completely on the Lord, and he turned toward me and heard my cry for help.

notes.text: Heb “relying, I relied.” The infinitive absolute precedes the finite verbal form to emphasize the verbal idea. The emphasis is reflected in the translation through the adverb “completely.” Another option is to translate, “I waited patiently” (cf. NASB, NIV, NRSV).

2.text: He lifted me out of the watery pit, out of the slimy mud. He placed my feet on a rock and gave me secure footing.

notes.text: Heb “cistern of roaring.” The Hebrew noun ‏בּוֹר‎ (bor, “cistern, pit”) is used metaphorically here of Sheol, the place of death, which is sometimes depicted as a raging sea (see Ps 18:4, 15-16). The noun ‏שָׁאוֹן‎ (shaʾon, “roaring”) refers elsewhere to the crashing sound of the sea’s waves (see Ps 65:7).

Heb “from the mud of mud.” The Hebrew phrase translated “slimy mud” employs an appositional genitive. Two synonyms are joined in a construct relationship to emphasize the single idea. For a detailed discussion of the grammatical point with numerous examples, see Y. Avishur, “Pairs of Synonymous Words in the Construct State (and in Appositional Hendiadys) in Biblical Hebrew,” Semitics 2 (1971): 17-81.
Heb “he established my footsteps.”

3.text: He gave me reason to sing a new song, praising our God. May many see what God has done, so that they might swear allegiance to him and trust in the Lord.

notes.text: A new song was appropriate because the Lord had intervened in the psalmist’s experience in a fresh and exciting way.
Heb “and he placed in my mouth a new song, praise to our God.”

Heb “may many see and fear and trust in the Lord.” The translation assumes that the initial prefixed verbal form is a jussive (“may many see”), rather than an imperfect (“many will see”). The following prefixed verbal forms with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive are taken as indicating purpose or result (“so that they might swear allegiance…and trust”) after the introductory jussive.

4.text: How blessed is the one who trusts in the Lord and does not seek help from the proud or from liars.

notes.text: The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see Pss 1:1, 3; 2:12; 34:9; 41:1; 65:4; 84:12; 89:15; 106:3; 112:1; 127:5; 128:1; 144:15).
Heb “man.” See the note on the word “one” in Ps 1:1.
Heb “who has made the Lord his [object of] trust.”
Heb “and does not turn toward.”
Heb “those falling away toward a lie.”

5.text: O Lord, my God, you have accomplished many things; you have done amazing things and carried out your purposes for us. No one can thwart you. I want to declare your deeds and talk about them, but they are too numerous to recount.

notes.text: Heb “many things you have done, you, O Lord my God, your amazing deeds and your thoughts toward us.” The precise meaning of the text is not clear, but the psalmist seems to be recalling the Lord’s miraculous deeds on Israel’s behalf (see Pss 9:1; 26:7), as well as his covenantal decrees and promises (see Ps 33:11).

Heb “there is none arrayed against you.” The precise meaning of the text is unclear, but the collocation ‏עָרַךְ אֶל‎ (ʿarakh ʾel, “array against”) is used elsewhere of military (Judg 20:30; 1 Chr 19:17) or verbal opposition (Job 32:14).

Heb “I will declare and I will speak, they are too numerous to recount.” The present translation assumes that the cohortatives are used in a hypothetical manner in a formally unmarked conditional sentence, “Should I try to declare [them] and speak [of them]…” (cf. NEB, NIV, NRSV). For other examples of cohortatives in the protasis (“if” clause) of a conditional sentence, see GKC 320 §108.e. (It should be noted, however, that GKC understands this particular verse in a different manner. See GKC 320 §108.f, where it is suggested that the cohortatives are part of an apodosis with the protasis being suppressed.) Another option is to take the cohortatives as a declaration of the psalmist’s resolve to announce the truth expressed in the next line. In this case one might translate: “I will declare and speak [the truth]: They are too numerous to recount.”

6.text: Receiving sacrifices and offerings are not your primary concern. You make that quite clear to me. You do not ask for burnt sacrifices and sin offerings.

notes.text: Heb “sacrifice and offering you do not desire.” The statement is exaggerated for the sake of emphasis (see Ps 51:16 as well). God is pleased with sacrifices, but his first priority is obedience and loyalty (see 1 Sam 15:22). Sacrifices and offerings apart from genuine allegiance are meaningless (see Isa 1:11-20).

Heb “ears you hollowed out for me.” The meaning of this odd expression is debated (this is the only collocation of “hollowed out” and “ears” in the OT). It may have been an idiomatic expression referring to making a point clear to a listener. The LXX has “but a body you have prepared for me,” a reading which is followed in Heb 10:5.

7.text: Then I say, “Look, I come! What is written in the scroll pertains to me.

notes.text: Heb “in the roll of the scroll it is written concerning me.” Apparently the psalmist refers to the law of God (see v. 8), which contains the commandments God desires him to obey. If this is a distinctly royal psalm, then the psalmist/king may be referring specifically to the regulations of kingship prescribed in Deut 17:14-20. See P. C. Craigie, Psalms 1-50 (WBC), 315.

8.text: I want to do what pleases you, my God. Your law dominates my thoughts.”

notes.text: Or “your will.”
Heb “your law [is] in the midst of my inner parts.” The “inner parts” are viewed here as the seat of the psalmist’s thought life and moral decision making.

9.text: I have told the great assembly about your justice. Look, I spare no words. O Lord, you know this is true.

notes.text: The great assembly is also mentioned in Pss 22:25 and 35:18.

Heb “I proclaim justice in the great assembly.” Though “justice” appears without a pronoun here, the Lord’s just acts are in view (see v. 10). His “justice” (‏צֶדֶק‎, tsedeq) is here the deliverance that originates in his justice; he protects and vindicates the one whose cause is just.
Heb “Look! My lips I do not restrain.”

10.text: I have not failed to tell about your justice; I spoke about your reliability and deliverance. I have not neglected to tell the great assembly about your loyal love and faithfulness.

notes.text: Heb “your justice I have not hidden in the midst of my heart.”
Heb “I have not hidden your loyal love and reliability.”

11.text: O Lord, you do not withhold your compassion from me. May your loyal love and faithfulness continually protect me!

notes.text: Some (cf. NIV, NRSV) translate the verb as a request (“do not withhold”), but elsewhere in the psalms the second masculine singular prefixed form, when addressed to God and preceded by ‏לֹא‎ (loʾ), is always indicative in mood and never has the force of a prayer (see Pss 16:10; 22:2; 44:9 51:16-17; 60:10; 108:11; cf. NEB, NASB).

In this line the psalmist makes the transition from confidence to petition (see v. 13). Since the prefixed verbal form in the preceding line is imperfect/indicative, one could take the verb in this line as imperfect as well and translate, “your loyal love and faithfulness continually protect me” (cf. NEB). However, the ‏כִּי‎ (ki) at the beginning of the next verse, if causal (“because”), is best understood as introducing a motivating argument in support of a petition. For this reason v. 11b is best taken as a prayer with the prefixed form being understood as jussive (cf. NIV, NRSV). For parallels to the proposed construction (jussive followed by ‏כִּי‎ + perfect introducing motivating argument), see Ps 25:21, as well as Pss 10:2-3; 22:8.

12.text: For innumerable dangers surround me. My sins overtake me so I am unable to see; they outnumber the hairs of my head so my strength fails me.

notes.text: Or “sinful deeds.” The Hebrew term used here can have a nonmoral nuance (“dangers”) or a moral one (“sinful deeds”) depending on the context. The next line (see “my sins”) seems to favor the moral sense, but the psalmist also speaks of enemies shortly after this (v. 14).
Heb “and my heart abandons me.” The “heart” is here viewed as the seat of emotional strength and courage. For a similar idea see Ps 38:10.

13.text: Please be willing, O Lord, to rescue me! O Lord, hurry and help me!

notes.text: Heb “hurry to my help.” See Pss 22:19; 38:22.

14.text: May those who are trying to snatch away my life be totally embarrassed and ashamed. May those who want to harm me be turned back and ashamed.

notes.text: Heb “may they be embarrassed and ashamed together, the ones seeking my life to snatch it away.”

The four prefixed verbal forms in this verse (“may those…be…embarrassed and ashamed…may those…be turned back and ashamed”) are understood as jussives. The psalmist is calling judgment down on his enemies.
See Ps 35:4 for a similar prayer.

15.text: May those who say to me, “Aha! Aha!” be humiliated and disgraced.

notes.text: The prefixed verbal form is understood as a jussive in this imprecation.
Heb “May they be humiliated according to their shame, those who say to me, ‘Aha! Aha!’”

16.text: May all those who seek you be happy and rejoice in you. May those who love to experience your deliverance say continually, “May the Lord be praised!”

notes.text: Heb “those who love,” which stands metonymically for its cause, the experience of being delivered by the Lord.
The three prefixed verbal forms prior to the quotation are understood as jussives. The psalmist balances out his imprecation against his enemies with a prayer of blessing upon the godly.
The prefixed verbal form is taken as a jussive, “may the Lord be magnified [in praise].” Another option is to take the verb as an imperfect, “the Lord is great” (cf. NRSV). See Ps 35:27.

17.text: I am oppressed and needy. May the Lord pay attention to me. You are my helper and my deliverer. O my God, do not delay.

notes.text: The prefixed verbal form may be taken as a jussive of prayer (as in the present translation; cf. NIV) or as an imperfect, “The Lord will pay attention to me” (cf. NRSV). The parallel in Ps 70:5 has, “O God, hurry to me!” For this reason some prefer to emend ‏יַחֲשָׁב‎ (yakhashav, “may he pay attention”) to ‏חוּשָׁה‎ (khushah, “hurry!”). The syntax of the Hebrew text is awkward; elsewhere when the Qal of ‏חָשַׁב‎ (khashav, “reckon; consider”) is collocated with the preposition ‏ל‎ (lamed) and a pronominal suffix there is an accompanying direct object or additional prepositional phrase/adverbial accusative (see Gen 15:6; 2 Sam 19:19; Job 13:24; 19:11; 33:10; Pss 32:2; 41:7; Amos 6:5).

1.text: How blessed is the one who treats the poor properly. When trouble comes, may the Lord deliver him.

notes.text: The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see Pss 1:1, 3; 2:12; 34:9; 65:4; 84:12; 89:15; 106:3; 112:1; 127:5; 128:1; 144:15).
