notes.text: This probably alludes to a sneak attack by enemies in the darkness of night (see Song 3:8).

6.text: the plague that stalks in the darkness, or the disease that ravages at noon.

notes.text: As in Deut 32:23-24, vv. 5-6 closely associate military attack and deadly disease. Perhaps the latter alludes to one of the effects of siege warfare on the population of an entrapped city, which was especially vulnerable to the outbreak of epidemics.

7.text: Though a thousand may fall beside you, and a multitude on your right side, it will not reach you.

notes.text: Apparently the deadly disease mentioned in v. 6b is the understood subject here.

8.text: Certainly you will see it with your very own eyes— you will see the wicked paid back.

notes.text: Heb “retribution on the wicked.”

9.text: For you have taken refuge in the Lord, my shelter, the Most High.

10.text: No harm will overtake you; no illness will come near your home.

notes.text: Or “confront.”
For this sense of the Hebrew term ‏נגע‎ see Ps 38:11.
Heb “your tent.”

11.text: For he will order his angels to protect you in all you do.

notes.text: Heb “for his angels he will command concerning you.”
Heb “in all your ways.”

12.text: They will lift you up in their hands, so you will not slip and fall on a stone.

notes.text: Heb “so your foot will not strike a stone.”

13.text: You will subdue a lion and a snake; you will trample underfoot a young lion and a serpent.

notes.text: Heb “walk upon.”
Or perhaps “cobra” (see Ps 58:4).

14.text: The Lord says, “Because he is devoted to me, I will deliver him; I will protect him because he is loyal to me.

notes.text: The words “the Lord says” are supplied in the translation to clarify that the words which follow are the Lord’s oracle of assurance.
Or “make him secure” (Heb “set him on high”).
Heb “because he knows my name” (see Ps 9:10).

15.text: When he calls out to me, I will answer him. I will be with him when he is in trouble; I will rescue him and bring him honor.

16.text: I will satisfy him with long life, and will let him see my salvation.”

notes.text: Heb “length of days.”

1.text: It is fitting to thank the Lord, and to sing praises to your name, O Most High.

notes.text: Or “good.”
The divine title “Most High” (‏עֶלְיוֹן‎ ʿelyon) pictures God as the exalted ruler of the universe who vindicates the innocent and judges the wicked. See especially Pss 7:17; 9:2; 18:13; 21:7; 47:2.

2.text: It is fitting to proclaim your loyal love in the morning, and your faithfulness during the night,

notes.text: The words “it is fitting” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons. Verses 1-3 are actually one long sentence in the Hebrew text, but this has been divided up into two shorter sentences in the translation in keeping with contemporary English style.

3.text: to the accompaniment of a ten-stringed instrument and a lyre, to the accompaniment of the meditative tone of the harp.

4.text: For you, O Lord, have made me happy by your work. I will sing for joy because of what you have done.

notes.text: Heb “the works of your hands.”

5.text: How great are your works, O Lord! Your plans are very intricate!

notes.text: Heb “very deep [are] your thoughts.” God’s “thoughts” refer here to his moral design of the world, as outlined in vv. 6-15.

6.text: The spiritually insensitive do not recognize this; the fool does not understand this.

notes.text: Heb “the brutish man does not know, and the fool does not understand this.” The adjective ‏בַּעַר‎ (baʿar, “brutish”) refers to spiritual insensitivity, not mere lack of intelligence or reasoning ability (see Pss 49:10; 73:22; Prov 12:1; 30:2, as well as the use of the related verb in Ps 94:8).

7.text: When the wicked sprout up like grass, and all the evildoers glisten, it is so that they may be annihilated.

notes.text: Or “flourish.”
Heb “in order that they might be destroyed permanently.”
God allows the wicked to prosper temporarily so that he might reveal his justice. When the wicked are annihilated, God demonstrates that wickedness does not pay off.

8.text: But you, O Lord, reign forever.

notes.text: Heb “[are elevated] on high.”

9.text: Indeed, look at your enemies, O Lord. Indeed, look at how your enemies perish. All the evildoers are scattered.

notes.text: Or “for.”
Or “for.”

10.text: You exalt my horn like that of a wild ox. I am covered with fresh oil.

notes.text: The horn of the wild ox is frequently a metaphor for military strength; the idiom “to exalt/lift up the horn” signifies military victory (see 1 Sam 2:10; Pss 75:10; 89:24; Lam 2:17).

The Hebrew verb ‏בָּלַל‎ (balal) usually has the nuance “to mix.” Here it seems to mean “to smear” or “to anoint.” Some emend the form to ‏בַּלֹּתַנִי‎ (ballotani; a second person form of the verb with a first person suffix) and read, “you anoint me.”

11.text: I gloat in triumph over those who tried to ambush me; I hear the defeated cries of the evil foes who attacked me.

notes.text: Heb “my eye gazes upon my walls.” See also Pss 5:8; 27:11; 56:2. The form ‏שׁוּרָי‎ shuray, “my walls”) should be emended to ‏שׁוֹרְרָי‎ (shoreray, “my foes” or perhaps “those who rebel against me” or “those who malign me”). See HALOT 1454 s.v. ‏שׁוֹרֵר‎ and also Pss 5:8; 27:11; 56:2.
Heb “those who rise up against me, evil [foes], my ears hear.”

12.text: The godly grow like a palm tree; they grow high like a cedar in Lebanon.

notes.text: The singular is used in a representative sense, with the typical godly person being in view.
The cedars of the Lebanon forest were well-known in ancient Israel for their immense size.

13.text: Planted in the Lord’s house, they grow in the courts of our God.

14.text: They bear fruit even when they are old; they are filled with vitality and have many leaves.

notes.text: Heb “they are juicy and fresh.”

15.text: So they proclaim that the Lord, my Protector, is just and never unfair.

notes.text: Heb “so that [they] proclaim that upright [is] the Lord, my rocky summit, and there is no injustice in him.”

1.text: The Lord reigns. He is robed in majesty. The Lord is robed; he wears strength around his waist. Indeed, the world is established; it cannot be moved.

notes.text: Strength is compared here to a belt that one wears for support. The Lord’s power undergirds his rule.

2.text: Your throne has been secure from ancient times; you have always been king.

notes.text: Heb “from antiquity [are] you.” As the context suggests, this refers specifically to God’s royal position, not his personal existence.

3.text: The waves roar, O Lord, the waves roar, the waves roar and crash.

notes.text: The Hebrew noun translated “waves” often refers to rivers or streams, but here it appears to refer to the surging waves of the sea (see v. 4, Ps 24:2).
Heb “the waves lift up, O Lord, the waves lift up their voice, the waves lift up their crashing.”

4.text: Above the sound of the surging water, and the mighty waves of the sea, the Lord sits enthroned in majesty.

notes.text: Heb “mighty waters.”

The surging waters here symbolizes the hostile enemies of God who seek to destroy the order he has established in the world (see Pss 18:17; 29:3; 32:6; 77:20; 144:7; Isa 17:13; Jer 51:55; Ezek 26:19; Hab 3:15). But the Lord is depicted as elevated above and sovereign over these raging waters.
Heb “mighty on high [is] the Lord.”

5.text: The rules you set down are completely reliable. Holiness aptly adorns your house, O Lord, forever.

notes.text: Traditionally “your testimonies.” The Hebrew noun ‏עֵדוּת‎ (ʿedut) refers here to the demands of God’s covenant law. See Ps 19:7.
The rules you set down. God’s covenant contains a clear, reliable witness to his moral character and demands.
Holiness refers here to God’s royal transcendence (see vv. 1-4), as well as his moral authority and perfection (see v. 5a).
Heb “for your house holiness is fitting, O Lord, for length of days.”

1.text: O Lord, the God who avenges! O God who avenges, reveal your splendor.

notes.text: Heb “shine forth” (see Pss 50:2; 80:1).

2.text: Rise up, O judge of the earth. Pay back the proud.

3.text: O Lord, how long will the wicked, how long will the wicked celebrate?

notes.text: Or “exult.”

4.text: They spew out threats and speak defiantly; all the evildoers boast.

notes.text: Heb “they gush forth [words].”
The Hitpael of ‏אָמַר‎ (ʾamar) occurs only here (and perhaps in Isa 61:6).

5.text: O Lord, they crush your people; they oppress the nation that belongs to you.

notes.text: Or “your inheritance.”

6.text: They kill the widow and the resident foreigner, and they murder the fatherless.

notes.text: The Hebrew noun ‏יָתוֹם‎ (yatom) refers to one who has lost his father (not necessarily his mother, see Ps 109:9). Because they were so vulnerable and were frequently exploited, fatherless children are often mentioned as epitomizing the oppressed (see Pss 10:14; 68:5; 82:3; 146:9; as well as Job 6:27; 22:9; 24:3, 9; 29:12; 31:17, 21).

7.text: Then they say, “The Lord does not see this; the God of Jacob does not take notice of it.”

notes.text: Heb “does not understand.”

8.text: Take notice of this, you ignorant people. You fools, when will you ever understand?

notes.text: Heb “understand.” The verb used in v. 7 is repeated here for rhetorical effect. The people referred to here claim God is ignorant of their actions, but the psalmist corrects their faulty viewpoint.
Heb “[you] brutish among the people.”

9.text: Does the one who makes the human ear not hear? Does the one who forms the human eye not see?

notes.text: Heb “The one who plants an ear, does he not hear? The one who forms an eye, does he not see?”

10.text: Does the one who disciplines the nations not punish? He is the one who imparts knowledge to human beings!

11.text: The Lord knows that peoples’ thoughts are morally bankrupt.

notes.text: Heb “the Lord knows the thoughts of man, that they are emptiness.” The psalmist thinks specifically of the “thoughts” expressed in v. 7.

12.text: How blessed is the one whom you instruct, O Lord, the one whom you teach from your law,

notes.text: Heb “[Oh] the happiness [of] the man.” Hebrew wisdom literature often assumes and reflects the male-oriented perspective of ancient Israelite society. The principle of the psalm is certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender or age. To facilitate modern application, we translate the gender and age specific “man” with the more neutral “one.” The generic masculine pronoun is used in v. 2.

13.text: in order to protect him from times of trouble, until the wicked are destroyed.

notes.text: Heb “to give him rest from the days of trouble.”
Heb “until a pit is dug for the wicked.”

14.text: Certainly the Lord does not forsake his people; he does not abandon the nation that belongs to him.

notes.text: Or “for.”
Or “his inheritance.”

15.text: For justice will prevail, and all the morally upright will be vindicated.

notes.text: Heb “for judgment will return to justice.”

Heb “all the pure of heart.” The “heart” is here viewed as the seat of one’s moral character and motives. The “pure of heart” are God’s faithful followers who trust in and love the Lord and, as a result, experience his deliverance (see Pss 7:10; 11:2; 32:11; 36:10; 64:10; 97:11).
Heb “and after it [are] the pure of heart.”

16.text: Who will rise up to defend me against the wicked? Who will stand up for me against the evildoers?

notes.text: Heb “for me.”
Who will stand up for me…? The questions anticipate the answer, “No one except God” (see v. 17).

17.text: If the Lord had not helped me, I would soon have dwelt in the silence of death.

notes.text: Heb “If the Lord [were] not my help, quickly my life would have dwelt in silence.” The psalmist, perhaps speaking as the nation’s representative, recalls God’s past intervention. For other examples of conditional sentences with the term ‏לוּלֵי‎ (lule, “if not”) in the protasis and a perfect verbal form in the apodosis, see Pss 119:92 and 124:2-5.

18.text: If I say, “My foot is slipping,” your loyal love, O Lord, supports me.

19.text: When worries threaten to overwhelm me, your soothing touch makes me happy.

notes.text: Heb “when my worries are many within me.”
Heb “your comforts cause my soul to delight.”

20.text: Cruel rulers are not your allies, those who make oppressive laws.

notes.text: Heb “a throne of destruction.” “Throne” stands here by metonymy for rulers who occupy thrones.

Heb “Is a throne of destruction united to you, one that forms trouble upon a statute?” The rhetorical question anticipates the answer, “Of course not!” The translation, while not preserving the interrogative form of the statement, reflects its rhetorical force.

21.text: They conspire against the blameless, and condemn to death the innocent.

notes.text: Or “attack.”
Heb “the life of the blameless.”
Heb “and the blood of the innocent they declare guilty.”

22.text: But the Lord will protect me, and my God will shelter me.

notes.text: Heb “and the Lord has become my elevated place.” The prefixed verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) consecutive is used in a rhetorical sense, describing an anticipated development as if it were already reality.
Heb “and my God [has become] a rocky summit of my safety.”

23.text: He will pay them back for their sin. He will destroy them because of their evil; the Lord our God will destroy them.

notes.text: The prefixed verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) consecutive is used in a rhetorical sense, describing an anticipated development as if it were already reality.
Or “in.”

1.text: Come, let us sing for joy to the Lord. Let us shout out praises to our Protector who delivers us.

notes.text: Heb “to the rocky summit of our deliverance.”

2.text: Let us enter his presence with thanksgiving. Let us shout out to him in celebration.

notes.text: Heb “meet his face.”
Heb “with songs of joy.”

3.text: For the Lord is a great God, a great king who is superior to all gods.

notes.text: Heb “above.”

4.text: The depths of the earth are in his hand, and the mountain peaks belong to him.

notes.text: The phrase “in his hand” means within the sphere of his authority.

5.text: The sea is his, for he made it. His hands formed the dry land.

6.text: Come, let us bow down and worship. Let us kneel before the Lord, our Creator.

notes.text: Heb “kneel down.”

7.text: For he is our God; we are the people of his pasture, the sheep he owns. Today, if only you would obey him.

notes.text: Heb “of his hand.”

Heb “if only you would listen to his voice.” The Hebrew particle ‏אִם‎ (ʾim, “if”) and following prefixed verbal form here express a wish (cf. Ps 81:8). Note that the apodosis (the “then” clause of the conditional sentence) is suppressed.

8.text: He says, “Do not be stubborn like they were at Meribah, like they were that day at Massah in the wilderness,

notes.text: The words “he says” are supplied in the translation to clarify that the following words are spoken by the Lord (see vv. 9-11).

The name Meribah means “strife.” Two separate but similar incidents at Meribah are recorded in the Pentateuch (Exod 17:1-7; Num 20:1-13, see also Pss 81:7; 106:32). In both cases the Israelites complained about lack of water and the Lord miraculously provided for them.

The name Massah means “testing.” This was another name (along with Meribah) given to the place where Israel complained following the Red Sea Crossing (see Exod 17:1-7, as well as Deut 6:16; 9:22; 33:8).
Heb “do not harden your heart[s] as [at] Meribah, as [in] the day of Massah in the wilderness.”

9.text: where your ancestors challenged my authority, and tried my patience, even though they had seen my work.

notes.text: Heb “where your fathers tested me.”

10.text: For forty years I was continually disgusted with that generation, and I said, ‘These people desire to go astray; they do not obey my commands.’

notes.text: The prefixed verbal form is either a preterite or an imperfect. If the latter, it emphasizes the ongoing nature of the condition in the past. The translation reflects this interpretation of the verbal form.
Heb “a people, wanderers of heart [are] they.”
Heb “and they do not know my ways.” In this context the Lord’s “ways” are his commands, viewed as a pathway from which his people, likened to wayward sheep (see v. 7), wander.

11.text: So I made a vow in my anger, ‘They will never enter into the resting place I had set aside for them.’”

notes.text: Heb “my resting place.” The promised land of Canaan is here viewed metaphorically as a place of rest for God’s people, who are compared to sheep (see v. 7).

1.text: Sing to the Lord a new song. Sing to the Lord, all the earth.

notes.text: A new song is appropriate because the Lord is constantly intervening in the world as its just king. See also Pss 33:3; 40:3; 98:1.

2.text: Sing to the Lord. Praise his name. Announce every day how he delivers.

notes.text: Heb “announce from day to day his deliverance.”

3.text: Tell the nations about his splendor. Tell all the nations about his amazing deeds.

notes.text: The verb “tell” is understood by ellipsis (note the preceding line).

4.text: For the Lord is great and certainly worthy of praise; he is more awesome than all gods.

notes.text: Or perhaps “and feared by all gods.” See Ps 89:7.

5.text: For all the gods of the nations are worthless, but the Lord made the sky.

notes.text: The Hebrew term ‏אֱלִילִים‎ (ʾelilim, “worthless”) sounds like ‏אֱלֹהִים‎ (ʾelohim, “gods”). The sound play draws attention to the statement.

6.text: Majestic splendor emanates from him; his sanctuary is firmly established and beautiful.

notes.text: Heb “majesty and splendor [are] before him.”
Heb “strength and beauty [are] in his sanctuary.”

7.text: Ascribe to the Lord, O families of the nations, ascribe to the Lord splendor and strength.

8.text: Ascribe to the Lord the splendor he deserves. Bring an offering and enter his courts.

notes.text: Heb “the splendor of [i.e., “due”] his name.”

9.text: Worship the Lord in holy attire. Tremble before him, all the earth.

notes.text: Or “in holy splendor.”

10.text: Say among the nations, “The Lord reigns! The world is established; it cannot be moved. He judges the nations fairly.”

11.text: Let the sky rejoice, and the earth be happy. Let the sea and everything in it shout.

12.text: Let the fields and everything in them celebrate. Then let the trees of the forest shout with joy

13.text: before the Lord, for he comes. For he comes to judge the earth. He judges the world fairly, and the nations in accordance with his justice.

notes.text: The verbal forms in v. 13 probably describe God’s typical, characteristic behavior, though they may depict in dramatic fashion the outworking of divine judgment or anticipate a future judgment of worldwide proportions, in which case they could be translated “will judge the world.”
Heb “and the nations with his integrity.”

1.text: The Lord reigns. Let the earth be happy. Let the many coastlands rejoice.

2.text: Dark clouds surround him; equity and justice are the foundation of his throne.

notes.text: The Lord’s throne symbolizes his kingship.

3.text: Fire goes before him; on every side it burns up his enemies.

notes.text: Heb “all around.”

4.text: His lightning bolts light up the world; the earth sees and trembles.

5.text: The mountains melt like wax before the Lord, before the Lord of the whole earth.

6.text: The sky declares his justice, and all the nations see his splendor.

7.text: All who worship idols are ashamed, those who boast about worthless idols. All the gods bow down before him.

notes.text: The translation assumes that the prefixed verbal form in the first line is an imperfect (“are ashamed”) and that the ambiguous form in the third line is a perfect (“bow down”) because the psalmist appears to be describing the effect of the Lord’s mighty theophany on those who witness it (see vv. 5, 8). Another option is to take the prefixed form in the first line as a jussive (“let all who worship idols be ashamed”) and the ambiguous form in the third line as an imperative (“All you gods, bow down before him!”; cf. NIV).

8.text: Zion hears and rejoices, the towns of Judah are happy, because of your judgments, O Lord.

notes.text: Heb “daughters.” The term “daughters” refers to the cities of Judah surrounding Zion (see Ps 48:11 and H. Haag, TDOT 2:336).

9.text: For you, O Lord, are the Most High over the whole earth; you are elevated high above all gods.

notes.text: The divine title “Most High” (‏עֶלְיוֹן‎ ʿelyon) pictures God as the exalted ruler of the universe who vindicates the innocent and judges the wicked. See especially Pss 7:17; 9:2; 18:13; 21:7; 47:2.

10.text: You who love the Lord, hate evil! He protects the lives of his faithful followers; he delivers them from the power of the wicked.

notes.text: The participle may be verbal, though it might also be understood as substantival and appositional to “the Lord.” In this case one could translate, “Hate evil, you who love the Lord, the one who protects the lives…and delivers them.”
Heb “hand.”

11.text: The godly bask in the light; the morally upright experience joy.

notes.text: Heb “Light is planted for the godly, and for the upright of heart joy.” The translation assumes an emendation of ‏זָרַע‎ (zaraʿ, “planted”) to ‏זָרַח‎ (zarakh, “shines”) which collocates more naturally with “light.” “Light” here symbolizes the joy (note the following line) that accompanies deliverance and the outpouring of divine favor.

12.text: You godly ones, rejoice in the Lord. Give thanks to his holy name.

notes.text: Heb “to his holy remembrance.” The Hebrew noun ‏זָכַר‎ (zakhar, “remembrance”) here refers to the name of the Lord as invoked in liturgy and praise. Cf. Pss 6:5; 30:4. The Lord’s “name” is “holy” in the sense that it is a reminder of his uniqueness and greatness.

1.text: Sing to the Lord a new song, for he performs amazing deeds. His right hand and his mighty arm accomplish deliverance.

notes.text: A new song is appropriate because the Lord is constantly intervening in the world as its just king. See Ps 96:1.

The perfect verbal forms in vv. 1-3 are understood here as describing characteristic divine activities. Another option is to translate them as present perfects, “has performed…has accomplished deliverance, etc.” referring to completed actions that have continuing results.

Heb “his right hand delivers for him and his holy arm.” The right hand and arm symbolize his power as a warrior-king (see Isa 52:10). His arm is “holy” in the sense that it is in a category of its own; God’s power is incomparable.

2.text: The Lord demonstrates his power to deliver; in the sight of the nations he reveals his justice.

notes.text: Heb “makes known his deliverance.”

3.text: He remains loyal and faithful to the family of Israel. All the ends of the earth see our God deliver us.

notes.text: Heb “he remembers his loyal love and his faithfulness to the house of Israel.”
Heb “the deliverance of our God,” with “God” being a subjective genitive (= God delivers).

4.text: Shout out praises to the Lord, all the earth. Break out in a joyful shout and sing!

5.text: Sing to the Lord accompanied by a harp, accompanied by a harp and the sound of music.

6.text: With trumpets and the blaring of the ram’s horn, shout out praises before the king, the Lord.

7.text: Let the sea and everything in it shout, along with the world and those who live in it.

8.text: Let the rivers clap their hands! Let the mountains sing in unison

9.text: before the Lord. For he comes to judge the earth. He judges the world fairly, and the nations in a just manner.

notes.text: The verbal forms in v. 9 probably describe God’s typical, characteristic behavior, though they may depict in dramatic fashion the outworking of divine judgment or anticipate a future judgment of worldwide proportions (“will judge…”).

1.text: The Lord reigns! The nations tremble. He sits enthroned above the cherubim; the earth shakes.

notes.text: The prefixed verbal forms in v. 1 are understood here as indicating the nations’ characteristic response to the reality of the Lord’s kingship. Another option is to take them as jussives: “let the nations tremble…let the earth shake!”

Cherubim are winged angels. As depicted in the OT, they possess both human and animal (lion, ox, and eagle) characteristics (see Ezek 1:10; 10:14, 21; 41:18). They are pictured as winged creatures (Exod 25:20; 37:9; 1 Kgs 6:24-27; Ezek 10:8, 19) and serve as the very throne of God when the ark of the covenant is in view (Ps 99:1; see Num 7:89; 1 Sam 4:4; 2 Sam 6:2; 2 Kgs 19:15). The picture of the Lord seated on the cherubim suggests they might be used by him as a vehicle, a function they carry out in Ezek 1:22-28 (the “living creatures” mentioned here are identified as cherubim in Ezek 10:20). In Ps 18:10 the image of a cherub serves to personify the wind.

The Hebrew verb ‏נוּט‎ (nut) occurs only here in the OT, but the meaning can be determined on the basis of the parallelism with ‏רָגַז‎ (ragaz, “tremble”) and evidence from the cognate languages (see H. R. Cohen, Biblical Hapax Legomena [SBLDS], 121).

2.text: The Lord is elevated in Zion; he is exalted over all the nations.

notes.text: Heb “great.”

3.text: Let them praise your great and awesome name. He is holy!

notes.text: The pronoun refers to the Lord himself (see vv. 5, 9).

4.text: The king is strong; he loves justice. You ensure that legal decisions will be made fairly; you promote justice and equity in Jacob.

notes.text: Heb “and strength, a king, justice he loves.” The syntax of the Hebrew text is difficult here. The translation assumes that two affirmations are made about the king, the Lord (see v. 1, and Ps 98:6). The noun ‏עֹז‎ (ʿoz, “strength”) should probably be revocalized as the adjective ‏עַז‎ (ʿaz, “strong”).
Heb “you establish fairness.”

5.text: Praise the Lord our God. Worship before his footstool. He is holy!

notes.text: Or “exalt.”
Or “bow down.”

6.text: Moses and Aaron were among his priests; Samuel was one of those who prayed to him. They prayed to the Lord and he answered them.

notes.text: Heb “among those who called on his name.”
Heb “those who.” The participle is in apposition to the phrase “those who called on his name” in the preceding line.

7.text: He spoke to them from a pillar of cloud; they obeyed his regulations and the ordinance he gave them.

notes.text: A pillar of cloud. The psalmist refers to the reality described in Exod 33:9-10; Num 12:5; and Deut 31:15.

8.text: O Lord our God, you answered them. They found you to be a forgiving God, but also one who punished their sinful deeds.

notes.text: Heb “a God of lifting up [i.e., forgiveness] you were to them, and an avenger concerning their deeds.” The present translation reflects the traditional interpretation, which understands the last line as qualifying the preceding one. God forgave Moses and Aaron, but he also disciplined them when they sinned (cf. NIV, NRSV). Another option is to take “their deeds” as referring to harmful deeds directed against Moses and Aaron. In this case the verse may be translated, “and one who avenged attacks against them.” Still another option is to emend the participial form ‏נֹקֵם‎ (noqem, “an avenger”) to ‏נֹקָם‎ (noqam), a rare Qal participial form of ‏נָקַה‎ (naqah, “purify”) with a suffixed pronoun. In this case one could translate, “and one who purified them from their [sinful] deeds” (cf. NEB “and held them innocent”).

9.text: Praise the Lord our God! Worship on his holy hill, for the Lord our God is holy.

notes.text: Or “exalt.”

1.text: Shout out praises to the Lord, all the earth!

2.text: Worship the Lord with joy. Enter his presence with joyful singing.

notes.text: Or “serve.”

3.text: Acknowledge that the Lord is God. He made us and we belong to him, we are his people, the sheep of his pasture.

notes.text: The present translation (like most modern translations) follows the Qere (marginal reading), which reads literally, “and to him [are] we.” The Kethib (consonantal text) has “and not we.” The suffixed preposition ‏לוֹ‎ (lo, “to him”) was confused aurally with the negative particle ‏לֹא‎ (loʾ, “not”) because the two sound identical.

4.text: Enter his gates with thanksgiving, and his courts with praise. Give him thanks. Praise his name.

5.text: For the Lord is good. His loyal love endures, and he is faithful through all generations.

notes.text: Or “is forever.”
Heb “and to a generation and a generation [is] his faithfulness.”

1.text: I will sing about loyalty and justice. To you, O Lord, I will sing praises.

2.text: I will walk in the way of integrity. When will you come to me? I will conduct my business with integrity in the midst of my palace.

notes.text: Heb “take notice of.”
Heb “I will walk about in the integrity of my heart in the midst of my house.”

3.text: I will not even consider doing what is dishonest. I hate doing evil; I will have no part of it.

notes.text: Heb “I will not set before my eyes a thing of worthlessness.”

Heb “the doing of swerving [deeds] I hate.” The Hebrew term ‏סֵטִים‎ (setim) is probably an alternate spelling of ‏שֵׂטִים‎ (setim), which appears in many medieval Hebrew mss. The form appears to be derived from a verbal root ‏שׂוּט‎ (sut, “to fall away; to swerve”; see Ps 40:4).
Heb “it [i.e., the doing of evil deeds] does not cling to me.”

4.text: I will have nothing to do with a perverse person; I will not permit evil.

notes.text: Heb “a perverse heart will turn aside from me.” The adjective ‏עִקֵּשׁ‎ (ʿiqqesh) has the basic nuance “twisted; crooked” and by extension refers to someone or something that is morally perverse (see Ps 18:26). It appears frequently in the Book of Proverbs, where it is used of evil people (22:5), speech (8:8; 19:1), thoughts (11:20; 17:20), and life styles (2:15; 28:6).
Heb “know.” The king will not willingly allow perverse individuals to remain in his royal court.

5.text: I will destroy anyone who slanders his neighbor in secret. I will not tolerate anyone who has a haughty demeanor and an arrogant attitude.

notes.text: Heb “[one who has] pride of eyes and wideness [i.e., arrogance] of heart, him I will not endure.”

6.text: I will favor the honest people of the land, and allow them to live with me. Those who walk in the way of integrity will attend me.

notes.text: Heb “my eyes [are] on the faithful of the land.”
The Hebrew text simply reads, “in order to live with me.”
Heb “one who walks in the way of integrity, he will minister to me.”

7.text: Deceitful people will not live in my palace. Liars will not be welcome in my presence.

notes.text: Heb “he will not live in the midst of my house, one who does deceit.”
Heb “one who speaks lies will not be established before my eyes.”

8.text: Each morning I will destroy all the wicked people in the land, and remove all evildoers from the city of the Lord.

1.text: O Lord, hear my prayer. Pay attention to my cry for help.

notes.text: Heb “and may my cry for help come to you.”

2.text: Do not ignore me in my time of trouble. Listen to me. When I call out to you, quickly answer me.

notes.text: Heb “do not hide your face from me in the day of my trouble.” The idiom “to hide the face” can mean “to ignore” (see Pss 10:11; 13:1; 51:9) or carry the stronger idea of “to reject” (see Pss 29:7; 30:7; 88:14).
Heb “turn toward me your ear.”

3.text: For my days go up in smoke, and my bones are charred as in a fireplace.

notes.text: Heb “for my days come to an end in smoke.”
The Hebrew noun ‏קֵד‎ (qed, “fireplace”) occurs only here, in Isa 33:14 (where it refers to the fire itself), and perhaps in Lev 6:2.

4.text: My heart is parched and withered like grass, for I am unable to eat food.

notes.text: Heb “struck, attacked.”
Heb “I forget.”
I am unable to eat food. During his time of mourning, the psalmist refrained from eating. In the following verse he describes metaphorically the physical effects of fasting.

5.text: Because of the anxiety that makes me groan, my bones protrude from my skin.

notes.text: Heb “from the sound of my groaning my bone[s] stick to my flesh.” The preposition at the beginning of the verse is causal; the phrase “sound of my groaning” is metonymic for the anxiety that causes the groaning. The point seems to be this: Anxiety (which causes the psalmist to groan) keeps him from eating (v. 4). This physical deprivation in turn makes him emaciated—he is turned to “skin and bones,” so to speak.

6.text: I am like an owl in the wilderness; I am like a screech owl among the ruins.

notes.text: The Hebrew term ‏קָאַת‎ (qaʾat) refers to some type of bird (see Lev 11:18; Deut 14:17) that was typically found near ruins (see Zeph 2:14). Modern translations have frequently rendered this as some type of owl (NIV, REB “desert owl”; NRSV “owl”).
The Hebrew term ‏כוֹס‎ (khos) refers to a bird (see Lev 11:17; Deut 14:16), probably a type of owl (cf. NIV, REB “owl”; NRSV “little owl”).
By comparing himself to a screech owl among the ruins, the psalmist may be highlighting his loneliness (see v. 7), though he may also be comparing his cries for help to the owl’s screech.

7.text: I stay awake; I am like a solitary bird on a roof.

notes.text: This probably refers to the psalmist’s inability to sleep. Another option is to translate, “I keep watch,” in which case it might refer to watching for a response from the Lord (see vv. 1-2).

8.text: All day long my enemies taunt me; those who mock me use my name in their curses.

notes.text: Heb “by me they swear.” When the psalmist’s enemies call judgment down on others, they hold the psalmist up as a prime example of what they desire their enemies to become.

9.text: For I eat ashes as if they were bread, and mix my drink with my tears,

notes.text: Mourners would sometimes put ashes on their head or roll in ashes as a sign of mourning (see 2 Sam 13:19; Job 2:8; Isa 58:5).
Heb “weeping.”

10.text: because of your anger and raging fury. Indeed, you pick me up and throw me away.

notes.text: Or “for.”

11.text: My days are coming to an end, and I am withered like grass.

notes.text: Heb “my days [are] like an extended [or “lengthening”] shadow,” that is, like a late afternoon shadow made by the descending sun that will soon be swallowed up by complete darkness.

12.text: But you, O Lord, rule forever, and your reputation endures.

notes.text: Heb “sit” (i.e., sit enthroned, see Ps 9:7). The imperfect verbal form highlights the generalization.
Heb “and your remembrance [is] for a generation and a generation.”

13.text: You will rise up and have compassion on Zion. For it is time to have mercy on her, for the appointed time has come.

notes.text: The imperfect verbal forms are understood as expressing the psalmist’s confidence in God’s intervention. Another option is to take them as expressing the psalmist’s request or wish, “You, rise up and have compassion!”

14.text: Indeed, your servants take delight in her stones, and feel compassion for the dust of her ruins.

notes.text: Or “for.”
The Poel of ‏חָנַן‎ (khanan) occurs only here and in Prov 14:21, where it refers to having compassion on the poor.
Heb “her dust,” probably referring to the dust of the city’s rubble.

15.text: The nations will respect the reputation of the Lord, and all the kings of the earth will respect his splendor,

notes.text: Heb “will fear the name of the Lord.” To “fear” God’s name means to have a healthy respect for his revealed reputation which in turn motivates one to obey God’s commands (see Ps 86:11).
The verb “will fear” is understood by ellipsis in the second line (see the preceding line).

16.text: when the Lord rebuilds Zion, and reveals his splendor,

17.text: when he responds to the prayer of the destitute, and does not reject their request.

notes.text: The Hebrew adjective ‏עַרְעָר‎ (ʿarar, “destitute”) occurs only here in the OT. It is derived from the verbal root ‏ערר‎ (“to strip oneself”).
Heb “despise.”
The perfect verbal forms in vv. 16-17 are functioning as future perfects, indicating future actions that will precede the future developments described in v. 15.

18.text: The account of his intervention will be recorded for future generations; people yet to be born will praise the Lord.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has simply “this,” referring to the anticipated divine intervention on behalf of Zion (vv. 13, 16-17). The referent has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “created.”

19.text: For he will look down from his sanctuary above; from heaven the Lord will look toward earth,

notes.text: Heb “from the height of his sanctuary.”
The perfect verbal forms in v. 19 are functioning as future perfects, indicating future actions that will precede the future developments described in v. 18.

20.text: in order to hear the painful cries of the prisoners, and to set free those condemned to die,

notes.text: Heb “the sons of death.” The phrase “sons of death” (see also Ps 79:11) is idiomatic for those condemned to die.

21.text: so they may proclaim the name of the Lord in Zion, and praise him in Jerusalem,

notes.text: Heb “his praise.”

22.text: when the nations gather together, and the kingdoms pay tribute to the Lord.

notes.text: “and the kingdoms to serve the Lord.”

23.text: He has taken away my strength in the middle of life; he has cut short my days.

notes.text: Heb “he has afflicted my strength in the way.” The term “way” refers here to the course of the psalmist’s life, which appears to be ending prematurely (vv. 23b-24).

24.text: I say, “O my God, please do not take me away in the middle of my life. You endure through all generations.

notes.text: Heb “do not lift me up in the middle of my days.”
Heb “in a generation of generations [are] your years.”

25.text: In earlier times you established the earth; the skies are your handiwork.

26.text: They will perish, but you will endure. They will wear out like a garment; like clothes you will remove them and they will disappear.

notes.text: Heb “stand.”
The Hebrew verb ‏חָלַף‎ (khalaf) occurs twice in this line, once in the Hiphil (“you will remove them”) and once in the Qal (“they will disappear”). The repetition draws attention to the statement.

27.text: But you remain; your years do not come to an end.

notes.text: Heb “you [are] he,” or “you [are] the one.” The statement may echo the Lord’s affirmation “I am he” in Isa 41:4; 43:10, 13; 46:10; 48:12. In each of these passages the affirmation emphasizes the fact that the Lord transcends time limitations, the very point being made in Ps 102:27.

28.text: The children of your servants will settle down here, and their descendants will live securely in your presence.”

notes.text: Or “offspring”; Heb “seed.”
Heb “before you will be established.”

1.text: Praise the Lord, O my soul. With all that is within me, praise his holy name.

notes.text: The verb “praise” is understood by ellipsis in the second line (see the preceding line).

2.text: Praise the Lord, O my soul. Do not forget all his kind deeds.

notes.text: Or “his benefits” (see 2 Chr 32:25, where the noun is also used of kind deeds performed by the Lord).

3.text: He is the one who forgives all your sins, who heals all your diseases,

notes.text: This relatively rare noun refers to deadly diseases (see Deut 29:22; Jer 14:18; 16:4; 2 Chr 21:19).

4.text: who delivers your life from the Pit, who crowns you with his loyal love and compassion,

notes.text: Or “redeems.”
The Hebrew term ‏שַׁחַת‎ (shakhat, “pit”) is often used as a title for Sheol (see Pss 16:10; 30:9; 49:9; 55:24 HT [55:23 ET]).

5.text: who satisfies your life with good things, so your youth is renewed like an eagle’s.

notes.text: Heb “who satisfies with the good of your ornaments.” The text as it stands makes little, if any, sense. The translation assumes an emendation of ‏עֶדְיֵךְ‎ (ʿedyekh, “your ornaments”) to ‏עֹדֵכִי‎ (ʿodekhi, “your duration; your continuance”), that is, “your life” (see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 18).
The expression your youth is renewed like an eagle’s may allude to the phenomenon of molting, whereby the eagle grows new feathers.

6.text: The Lord does what is fair, and executes justice for all the oppressed.

notes.text: Heb “the Lord does fairness, and [acts of] justice for all the oppressed.”

7.text: The Lord revealed his faithful acts to Moses, his deeds to the Israelites.

notes.text: Heb “made known his ways.” God’s “ways” in this context are his protective and salvific acts in fulfillment of his promise (see also Deut 32:4; Pss 18:30; 67:2; 77:13 [note vv. 11-12, 14]; 138:5; 145:17).

8.text: The Lord is compassionate and merciful; he is patient and demonstrates great loyal love.

notes.text: Heb “slow to anger” (see Ps 86:15).
Heb “and great of loyal love” (see Ps 86:15).

9.text: He does not always accuse, and does not stay angry.

notes.text: The Hebrew verb ‏נָטַר‎ (natar) is usually taken to mean “to keep; to guard,” with “anger” being understood by ellipsis. The idiom “to guard anger” is then understood to mean “to remain angry” (see Lev 19:18; Jer 3:5, 12; Nah 1:2). However, it is possible that this is a homonymic root meaning “to be angry” (see HALOT 695 s.v. ‏נטר‎).

10.text: He does not deal with us as our sins deserve; he does not repay us as our misdeeds deserve.

notes.text: Heb “not according to our sins does he do to us.”
Heb “and not according to our misdeeds does he repay us.”

11.text: For as the skies are high above the earth, so his loyal love towers over his faithful followers.

notes.text: For this sense of the verb ‏גָבַר‎ (gavar), see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 17, 19.
Heb “those who fear him.”

12.text: As far as the eastern horizon is from the west, so he removes the guilt of our rebellious actions from us.

notes.text: Heb “sunrise.”
Or “sunset.”
The Hebrew term ‏פֶּשַׁע‎ (peshaʿ, rebellious act”) is here used metonymically for the guilt such actions produce.

13.text: As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on his faithful followers.

notes.text: Or “sons,” but the Hebrew term sometimes refers to children in general.
Heb “those who fear him.”

14.text: For he knows what we are made of; he realizes we are made of clay.

notes.text: Heb “our form.”
Heb “remembers.”
Heb “we [are] clay.”

15.text: A person’s life is like grass. Like a flower in the field it flourishes,

notes.text: Heb “[as for] mankind, like grass [are] his days.” The Hebrew noun ‏אֱנוֹשׁ‎ (ʾenosh) is used here generically of human beings. What is said is true of all mankind.

16.text: but when the hot wind blows, it disappears, and one can no longer even spot the place where it once grew.

notes.text: Heb “[the] wind.” The word “hot” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

17.text: But the Lord continually shows loyal love to his faithful followers, and is faithful to their descendants,

notes.text: Heb “but the loyal love of the Lord [is] from everlasting to everlasting over those who fear him.”
Heb “and his righteousness to sons of sons.”

18.text: to those who keep his covenant, who are careful to obey his commands.

notes.text: Heb “to those who remember his precepts to do them.”

19.text: The Lord has established his throne in heaven; his kingdom extends over everything.

notes.text: Heb “his kingdom rules over all.”

20.text: Praise the Lord, you angels of his, you powerful warriors who carry out his decrees and obey his orders.

notes.text: Heb “[you] mighty ones of strength, doers of his word, by listening to the voice of his word.”

21.text: Praise the Lord, all you warriors of his, you servants of his who carry out his desires.

notes.text: Heb “all his hosts.”
Heb “his attendants, doers of his desire.”

22.text: Praise the Lord, all that he has made, in all the regions of his kingdom. Praise the Lord, O my soul.

notes.text: Heb “all his works,” which includes mankind.
Heb “places.”

1.text: Praise the Lord, O my soul! O Lord my God, you are magnificent. You are robed in splendor and majesty.

notes.text: Heb “very great.”

2.text: He covers himself with light as if it were a garment. He stretches out the skies like a tent curtain,

3.text: and lays the beams of the upper rooms of his palace on the rain clouds. He makes the clouds his chariot, and travels on the wings of the wind.

notes.text: Heb “one who lays the beams on water [in] his upper rooms.” The “water” mentioned here corresponds to the “waters above” mentioned in Gen 1:7. For a discussion of the picture envisioned by the psalmist, see L. I. J. Stadelmann, The Hebrew Conception of the World, 44-45.

Verse 3 may depict the Lord riding a cherub, which is in turn propelled by the wind current. Another option is that the wind is personified as a cherub. See Ps 18:10 and the discussion of ancient Near Eastern parallels to the imagery in M. Weinfeld, “‘Rider of the Clouds’ and ‘Gatherer of the Clouds’,” JANESCU 5 (1973): 422-24.

4.text: He makes the winds his messengers, and the flaming fire his attendant.

notes.text: Heb “and his attendants a flaming fire.” The lack of agreement between the singular “fire” and plural “attendants” has prompted various emendations. Some read “fire and flame.” The present translation assumes an emendation from ‏מְשָׁרְתָיו‎ (mesharetayv, “his attendants”) to ‏מְשָׁרְתוֹ‎ (meshareto, “his attendant”), a reading supported by one of the Dead Sea Scrolls, 4Q93.
In Ugaritic mythology Yam’s messengers appear as flaming fire before the assembly of the gods. See G. R. Driver, Canaanite Myths and Legends, 42.

5.text: He established the earth on its foundations; it will never be moved.

6.text: The watery deep covered it like a garment; the waters reached above the mountains.

notes.text: Heb “you covered it.” The masculine suffix is problematic if the grammatically feminine noun “earth” is the antecedent. For this reason some emend the form from ‏כִּסִּיתוֹ‎ (kissito) to a feminine verb with feminine suffix, ‏כִּסַּתָּה‎ (kissattah, “[the watery deep] covered it [i.e., the earth]”), a reading assumed by the present translation.
Heb “stood.”
Verse 6 refers to the condition described in Gen 1:2 (note the use of the Hebrew term ‏תְּהוֹם‎ [tehom, “watery deep”] in both texts).

7.text: Your shout made the waters retreat; at the sound of your thunderous voice they hurried off—

8.text: as the mountains rose up, and the valleys went down— to the place you appointed for them.

notes.text: Heb “from your shout they fled, from the sound of your thunder they hurried off.”
Verses 7-8 poetically depict Gen 1:9-10.

9.text: You set up a boundary for them that they could not cross, so that they would not cover the earth again.

notes.text: Heb “a boundary you set up, they will not cross, they will not return to cover the earth.”

10.text: He turns springs into streams; they flow between the mountains.

notes.text: Heb “[the] one who sends springs into streams.” Another option is to translate, “he sends streams [i.e., streams that originate from springs] into the valleys” (cf. NIV).

11.text: They provide water for all the animals in the field; the wild donkeys quench their thirst.

12.text: The birds of the sky live beside them; they chirp among the bushes.

notes.text: Heb “among the thick foliage they give a sound.”

13.text: He waters the mountains from the upper rooms of his palace; the earth is full of the fruit you cause to grow.

notes.text: Heb “from his upper rooms.”

Heb “from the fruit of your works the earth is full.” The translation assumes that “fruit” is literal here. If “fruit” is understood more abstractly as “product; result,” then one could translate, “the earth flourishes as a result of your deeds” (cf. NIV, NRSV, REB).

14.text: He provides grass for the cattle, and crops for people to cultivate, so they can produce food from the ground,

notes.text: Heb “causes the grass to sprout up.”
Heb “for the service of man” (see Gen 2:5).
Heb “to cause food to come out from the earth.”

15.text: as well as wine that makes people glad, and olive oil to make their faces shine, as well as bread that sustains them.

notes.text: Heb “and wine [that] makes the heart of man happy.”

Heb “to make [the] face shine from oil.” The Hebrew verb ‏צָהַל‎ (tsahal, “to shine”) occurs only here in the OT. It appears to be an alternate form of ‏צָהַר‎ (tsahar), a derivative from ‏צָהָרִים‎ (tsaharim, “noon”).
Heb “and food [that] sustains the heart of man.”

16.text: The trees of the Lord receive all the rain they need, the cedars of Lebanon that he planted,

notes.text: The trees of the Lord are the cedars of Lebanon (see the next line), which are viewed as special because of their great size and grandeur. The Lebanon forest was viewed elsewhere in the OT as the “garden of God” (see Ezek 31:8).
Heb “are satisfied,” which means here that they receive abundant rain (see v. 13).

17.text: where the birds make nests, near the evergreens in which the herons live.

notes.text: Heb “[the] heron [in the] evergreens [is] its home.”
The cedars and evergreens of the Lebanon forest are frequently associated (see, for example, 2 Chr 2:8; Isa 14:8; 37:24; Ezek 31:8).

18.text: The wild goats live in the high mountains; the rock badgers find safety in the cliffs.

notes.text: Heb “the high mountains [are] for the goats.”

19.text: He made the moon to mark the months, and the sun sets according to a regular schedule.

notes.text: Heb “he made [the] moon for appointed times.” The phrase “appointed times” probably refers to the months of the Hebrew lunar calendar.
Heb more metaphorically, “knows its setting.”

20.text: You make it dark and night comes, during which all the beasts of the forest prowl around.

notes.text: Heb “you make darkness, so that it might be night.”

21.text: The lions roar for prey, seeking their food from God.

notes.text: The lions’ roaring is viewed as a request for food from God.

22.text: When the sun rises, they withdraw and sleep in their dens.

notes.text: Heb “lie down.”

23.text: People then go out to do their work, and they labor until evening.

notes.text: Heb “man goes out to his work, and to his labor until evening.”

24.text: How many living things you have made, O Lord! You have exhibited great skill in making all of them; the earth is full of the living things you have made.

notes.text: Heb “How many [are] your works, O Lord.” In this case the Lord’s “works” are the creatures he has made, as the preceding and following contexts make clear.
Heb “all of them with wisdom you have made.”

25.text: Over here is the deep, wide sea, which teems with innumerable swimming creatures, living things both small and large.

notes.text: Heb “this [is] the sea, great and broad of hands [i.e., “sides” or “shores”].”
Heb “where [there are] swimming things, and without number.”

26.text: The ships travel there, and over here swims the whale you made to play in it.

notes.text: Heb “[and] this Leviathan, [which] you formed to play in it.” Elsewhere Leviathan is a multiheaded sea monster that symbolizes forces hostile to God (see Ps 74:14; Isa 27:1), but here it appears to be an actual marine creature created by God, probably some type of whale.

27.text: All your creatures wait for you to provide them with food on a regular basis.

notes.text: Heb “All of them.” The pronoun “them” refers not just to the sea creatures mentioned in vv. 25-26, but to all living things (see v. 24). This has been specified in the translation as “all of your creatures” for clarity.
Heb “to give their food in its time.”

28.text: You give food to them and they receive it; you open your hand and they are filled with food.

notes.text: Heb “they are satisfied [with] good.”

29.text: When you ignore them, they panic. When you take away their life’s breath, they die and return to dust.

notes.text: Heb “you hide your face, they are terrified.”

30.text: When you send your life-giving breath, they are created, and you replenish the surface of the ground.

31.text: May the splendor of the Lord endure. May the Lord find pleasure in the living things he has made.

notes.text: Heb “be forever.”
Or “rejoice in his works.”

32.text: He looks down on the earth and it shakes; he touches the mountains and they start to smolder.

33.text: I will sing to the Lord as long as I live; I will sing praise to my God as long as I exist.

notes.text: Heb “in my duration.”

34.text: May my thoughts be pleasing to him. I will rejoice in the Lord.

notes.text: That is, the psalmist’s thoughts as expressed in his songs of praise.

35.text: May sinners disappear from the earth, and the wicked vanish. Praise the Lord, O my soul. Praise the Lord.

notes.text: Or “be destroyed.”

1.text: Give thanks to the Lord. Call on his name. Make known his accomplishments among the nations.

2.text: Sing to him. Make music to him. Tell about all his miraculous deeds.

3.text: Boast about his holy name. Let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice.

4.text: Seek the Lord and the strength he gives. Seek his presence continually.

5.text: Recall the miraculous deeds he performed, his mighty acts and the judgments he decreed,

notes.text: Heb “and the judgments of his mouth.”

6.text: O children of Abraham, God’s servant, you descendants of Jacob, God’s chosen ones.

notes.text: Or “offspring”; Heb “seed.”
Some mss have “Israel,” which appears in the parallel version of this psalm in 1 Chr 16:13.
Heb “his”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “sons.”
Heb “his”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

7.text: He is the Lord our God; he carries out judgment throughout the earth.

notes.text: Heb “in all the earth [are] his judgments.”

8.text: He always remembers his covenantal decree, the promise he made to a thousand generations—

notes.text: Heb “[the] word he commanded.” The text refers here to God’s unconditional covenantal promise to Abraham and the patriarchs, as vv. 10-12 make clear.

9.text: the promise he made to Abraham, the promise he made by oath to Isaac.

notes.text: Heb “which.”

10.text: He gave it to Jacob as a decree, to Israel as a lasting promise,

notes.text: Or “eternal covenant.”

11.text: saying, “To you I will give the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance.”

12.text: When they were few in number, just a very few, and resident foreigners within it,

13.text: they wandered from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another.

notes.text: Heb “and from a kingdom to another nation.”

14.text: He let no one oppress them; he disciplined kings for their sake,

15.text: saying, “Don’t touch my chosen ones. Don’t harm my prophets.”

notes.text: The word “saying” is supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.
Heb “anointed.”

16.text: He called down a famine upon the earth; he cut off all the food supply.

notes.text: Heb “and every staff of food he broke.” The psalmist refers to the famine that occurred in Joseph’s time (see v. 17 and Gen 41:53-57).

17.text: He sent a man ahead of them — Joseph was sold as a servant.

notes.text: After the reference to the famine in v. 16, v. 17 flashes back to events that preceded the famine (see Gen 37).

18.text: The shackles hurt his feet; his neck was placed in an iron collar,

notes.text: Heb “they afflicted his feet with shackles.”

Heb “his neck came [into] iron.” The Hebrew term ‏נֶפֶשׁ‎ (nefesh) with the suffix could mean simply “he” or “his life.” But the nuance “neck” makes good sense here (note the reference to his “feet” in the preceding line). See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 38.

19.text: until the time when his prediction came true. The Lord’s word proved him right.

notes.text: Heb “word,” probably referring to Joseph’s prediction about the fate of Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker (see Gen 41:9-14).

This line may refer to Joseph’s prediction of the famine in response to Pharaoh’s dream. Joseph emphasized to Pharaoh that the interpretation of the dream came from God (see Gen 41:16, 25, 28, 32, 39).
Heb “refined him.”

20.text: The king authorized his release; the ruler of nations set him free.

notes.text: Heb “[the] king sent and set him free.”

21.text: He put him in charge of his palace, and made him manager of all his property,

notes.text: Heb “he made him master of his house.”

22.text: giving him authority to imprison his officials and to teach his advisers.

notes.text: Heb “to bind his officials by his will.”
Heb “and his elders he taught wisdom.”

23.text: Israel moved to Egypt; Jacob lived for a time in the land of Ham.

notes.text: Heb “entered.”
Heb “lived as a resident foreigner.”

24.text: The Lord made his people very fruitful, and made them more numerous than their enemies.

notes.text: Heb “and he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “him,” referring to “his people.”
Heb “his,” referring to “his people.”

25.text: He caused the Egyptians to hate his people, and to mistreat his servants.

notes.text: Heb “their heart.”
Or “to deal deceptively.” The Hitpael of ‏נָכַל‎ (nakhal) occurs only here and in Gen 37:18, where it is used of Joseph’s brothers “plotting” to kill him.

26.text: He sent his servant Moses, and Aaron, whom he had chosen.

27.text: They executed his miraculous signs among them, and his amazing deeds in the land of Ham.

notes.text: Apparently the pronoun refers to “his servants” (i.e., the Israelites, see v. 25).

28.text: He made it dark; Moses and Aaron did not disobey his orders.

notes.text: Heb “he sent darkness and made it dark.”
He made it dark. The psalmist begins with the ninth plague (see Exod 10:21-29).
Heb “they did not rebel against his words.” Apparently this refers to Moses and Aaron, who obediently carried out God’s orders.

29.text: He turned the Egyptians’ water into blood, and killed their fish.

30.text: Their land was overrun by frogs, which even got into the rooms of their kings.

31.text: He ordered flies to come; gnats invaded their whole territory.

notes.text: Heb “he spoke and flies came.”

32.text: He sent hail along with the rain; there was lightning in their land.

notes.text: Heb “he gave their rains hail.”
Heb “fire of flames [was] in their land.”

33.text: He destroyed their vines and fig trees, and broke the trees throughout their territory.

34.text: He ordered locusts to come, innumerable grasshoppers.

notes.text: Heb “he spoke and locusts came.”

35.text: They ate all the vegetation in their land, and devoured the crops of their fields.

notes.text: Heb “the fruit of their ground.”

36.text: He struck down all the firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of their reproductive power.

notes.text: Heb “the beginning of all their strength,” that is, reproductive power (see Ps 78:51).

Verses 28-36 recall the plagues in a different order than the one presented in Exodus: v. 28 (plague 9), v. 29 (plague 1), v. 30 (plague 2), v. 31a (plague 4), v. 31b (plague 3), vv. 32-33 (plague 7), vv. 34-35 (plague 8), v. 36 (plague 10). No reference is made in Ps 105 to plagues 5 and 6.

37.text: He brought his people out enriched with silver and gold; none of his tribes stumbled.

notes.text: Heb “them”; the referent (the Lord’s people) has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
The word “enriched” is supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.

38.text: Egypt was happy when they left, for they were afraid of them.

notes.text: Heb “for fear of them had fallen upon them.”

39.text: He spread out a cloud for a cover, and provided a fire to light up the night.

notes.text: Or “curtain.”

40.text: They asked for food, and he sent quail; he satisfied them with food from the sky.

notes.text: Heb “he [i.e., his people] asked.” The singular form should probably be emended to a plural ‏שָׁאֲלוּ‎ (shaʾalu, “they asked”), the ‏ו‎ (vav) having fallen off by haplography (note the vav at the beginning of the following form).
Or “bread of heaven.” The reference is to manna (see Exod 16:4, 13-15).

41.text: He opened up a rock and water flowed out; a river ran through dry regions.

42.text: Yes, he remembered the sacred promise he made to Abraham his servant.

notes.text: Or “for.”
Heb “his holy word.”

43.text: When he led his people out, they rejoiced; his chosen ones shouted with joy.

notes.text: Heb “and he led his people out with joy, with a ringing cry, his chosen ones.”

44.text: He handed the territory of nations over to them, and they took possession of what other peoples had produced,

notes.text: Heb “and the [product of the] work of peoples they possessed.”

45.text: so that they might keep his commands and obey his laws. Praise the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “guard.”

1.text: Praise the Lord. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, and his loyal love endures.

notes.text: Heb “for forever [is] his loyal love.”

2.text: Who can adequately recount the Lord’s mighty acts, or relate all his praiseworthy deeds?

notes.text: Heb “[or] cause to be heard all his praise.”

3.text: How blessed are those who promote justice, and do what is right all the time.

4.text: Remember me, O Lord, when you show favor to your people. Pay attention to me, when you deliver,

5.text: so I may see the prosperity of your chosen ones, rejoice along with your nation, and boast along with the people who belong to you.

notes.text: Heb “good.”
Heb “in order that [I may] rejoice with the rejoicing of your nation.”
Heb “with your inheritance.”

6.text: We have sinned like our ancestors; we have done wrong, we have done evil.

notes.text: Heb “with.”
Heb “fathers” (also in v. 7).

7.text: Our ancestors in Egypt failed to appreciate your miraculous deeds. They failed to remember your many acts of loyal love, and they rebelled at the sea, by the Red Sea.

notes.text: Heb “Reed Sea” (also in vv. 9, 22). “Reed Sea” (or “Sea of Reeds”) is a more accurate rendering of the Hebrew expression ‏יָם סוּף‎ (yam suf), traditionally translated “Red Sea.” See the note on the term “Red Sea” in Exod 13:18.
They rebelled. The psalmist recalls the people’s complaint recorded in Exod 14:12.

8.text: Yet he delivered them for the sake of his reputation, that he might reveal his power.

notes.text: Heb “his name,” which here stands metonymically for God’s reputation.

9.text: He shouted at the Red Sea and it dried up; he led them through the deep water as if it were a desert.

notes.text: Or “rebuked.”

10.text: He delivered them from the power of the one who hated them, and rescued them from the power of the enemy.

notes.text: Heb “hand.”
Or “redeemed.”
Heb “hand.”

11.text: The water covered their enemies; not even one of them survived.

notes.text: Heb “remained.”

12.text: They believed his promises; they sang praises to him.

notes.text: Heb “his words.”

13.text: They quickly forgot what he had done; they did not wait for his instructions.

notes.text: Heb “his works.”
Heb “his counsel.”

14.text: In the wilderness they had an insatiable craving for meat; they challenged God in the wastelands.

notes.text: They had an insatiable craving. This is described in Num 11:4-35.
Heb “they craved [with] a craving.”
Heb “they tested God.”

15.text: He granted their request, then struck them with a disease.

notes.text: Heb “and he sent leanness into their being.”
Disease. See Num 11:33-34, where this plague is described.

16.text: In the camp they resented Moses, and Aaron, the Lord’s holy priest.

notes.text: Or “envied.”
Heb “the holy one of the Lord.”

17.text: The earth opened up and swallowed Dathan; it engulfed the group led by Abiram.

notes.text: Or “covered.”
Or “the assembly of Abiram.”

18.text: Fire burned their group; the flames scorched the wicked.

notes.text: Verses 16-18 describe the events of Num 16:1-40.

19.text: They made an image of a calf at Horeb, and worshiped a metal idol.

20.text: They traded their majestic God for the image of an ox that eats grass.

notes.text: Heb “their glory.” According to an ancient Hebrew scribal tradition, the text originally read “his glory” or “my glory.” In Jer 2:11 the Lord states that his people (Israel) exchanged “their glory” (a reference to the Lord) for worthless idols.

21.text: They rejected the God who delivered them, the one who performed great deeds in Egypt,

notes.text: Heb “forgot.”

22.text: amazing feats in the land of Ham, mighty acts by the Red Sea.

notes.text: Or “awe-inspiring acts.”

23.text: He threatened to destroy them, but Moses, his chosen one, interceded with him and turned back his destructive anger.

notes.text: Heb “and he said.”
Heb “if not,” that is, “[and would have] if [Moses] had not.”
Heb “stood in the gap before him.”
Heb “to turn back his anger from destroying.”
Verses 19-23 describe the events of Exod 32:1-35.

24.text: They rejected the fruitful land; they did not believe his promise.

notes.text: Heb “a land of delight” (see also Jer 3:19; Zech 7:14).
Heb “his word.”

25.text: They grumbled in their tents; they did not obey the Lord.

notes.text: They grumbled in their tents. See Deut 1:27.
Heb “did not listen to the voice of.”

26.text: So he made a solemn vow that he would make them die in the wilderness,

notes.text: Heb “and he lifted his hand to [or “concerning”] them.” The idiom “to lift a hand” here refers to swearing an oath. One would sometimes solemnly lift one’s hand when making such a vow (see Ezek 20:5-6, 15).
Heb “to cause them to fall.”

27.text: make their descendants die among the nations, and scatter them among foreign lands.

notes.text: Or “offspring”; Heb “seed.”
Heb “and to cause their offspring to fall.” Some emend the verb to “scatter” to form tighter parallelism with the following line (cf. NRSV “disperse”).
Heb “among the lands.” The word “foreign” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

28.text: They worshiped Baal of Peor, and ate sacrifices offered to the dead.

notes.text: Heb “joined themselves to.”
They worshiped Baal of Peor. See Num 25:3, 5. Baal of Peor was a local manifestation of the Canaanite deity Baal located at Peor.

Here “the dead” may refer to deceased ancestors (see Deut 26:14). Another option is to understand the term as a derogatory reference to the various deities which the Israelites worshiped at Peor along with Baal (see Num 25:2 and L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 49).

29.text: They made the Lord angry by their actions, and a plague broke out among them.

notes.text: Heb “They made angry [him].” The pronominal suffix is omitted here, but does appear in a few medieval Hebrew mss. Perhaps it was accidentally left off, an original ‏וַיַּכְעִיסוּהוּ‎ (vayyakhʿisuhu) being misread as ‏וַיַּכְעִיסוּ‎ (vayyakhʿisu). In the translation the referent of the pronominal suffix (the Lord) has been specified for clarity to avoid confusion with Baal of Peor (mentioned in the previous verse).

30.text: Phinehas took a stand and intervened, and the plague subsided.

notes.text: The intervention of Phinehas is recounted in Num 25:7-8.

31.text: This was credited to Phinehas as a righteous act for all generations to come.

notes.text: Heb “and it was reckoned to him for righteousness, to a generation and a generation forever.” The verb ‏חָשַׁב‎ (khashav, “to reckon”) is collocated with ‏צְדָקָה‎ (tsedaqah, “righteousness”) only in Ps 106:31 and Gen 15:6, where God credits Abram’s faith as righteousness.

32.text: They made him angry by the waters of Meribah, and Moses suffered because of them,

notes.text: Heb “there was harm to Moses.”

33.text: for they aroused his temper, and he spoke rashly.

notes.text: The Hebrew text vocalizes the form as ‏הִמְרוּ‎ (himru), a Hiphil from ‏מָרָה‎ (marah, “to behave rebelliously”), but the verb fits better with the object (“his spirit”) if it is revocalized as ‏הֵמֵרוּ‎ (hemeru), a Hiphil from ‏מָרַר‎ (marar, “to be bitter”). The Israelites “embittered” Moses’ “spirit” in the sense that they aroused his temper with their complaints.
Heb “his spirit.”
The Hebrew text adds “with his lips,” but this has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Verses 32-33 allude to the events of Num 20:1-13.

34.text: They did not destroy the nations, as the Lord had commanded them to do.

notes.text: That is, the nations of Canaan.

35.text: They mixed in with the nations and learned their ways.

notes.text: Heb “their deeds.”

36.text: They worshiped their idols, which became a snare to them.

notes.text: Or “served.”
Became a snare. See Exod 23:33; Judg 2:3.

37.text: They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons.

notes.text: The Hebrew term ‏שֵׁדִים‎ (shedim, “demons”) occurs only here and in Deut 32:17. Some type of lesser deity is probably in view.

38.text: They shed innocent blood— the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan. The land was polluted by bloodshed.

notes.text: Num 35:33-34 explains that bloodshed defiles a land.

39.text: They were defiled by their deeds, and unfaithful in their actions.

notes.text: Heb “and they committed adultery in their actions.” This means that they were unfaithful to the Lord (see Ps 73:27).

40.text: So the Lord was angry with his people and despised the people who belonged to him.

notes.text: Heb “the anger of the Lord burned against his people.”
Heb “his inheritance.”

41.text: He handed them over to the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them.

notes.text: Heb “gave them into the hand of.”

42.text: Their enemies oppressed them; they were subject to their authority.

notes.text: Heb “they were subdued under their hand.”

43.text: Many times he delivered them, but they had a rebellious attitude, and degraded themselves by their sin.

notes.text: The prefixed verbal form is either preterite or imperfect, in which case it is customary, describing repeated action in past time (“he would deliver”).

Heb “but they rebelled in their counsel.” The prefixed verbal form is either preterite or imperfect, in which case it is customary, describing repeated action in past time (“they would have a rebellious attitude”).
Heb “they sank down.” The Hebrew verb ‏מָכַךְ‎ (makhakh, “to lower; to sink”) occurs only here in the Qal.

44.text: Yet he took notice of their distress, when he heard their cry for help.

45.text: He remembered his covenant with them, and relented because of his great loyal love.

notes.text: The Niphal of ‏נָחַם‎ (nakham) refers here to God relenting from a punishment already underway.

46.text: He caused all their conquerors to have pity on them.

notes.text: Or “captors.”

47.text: Deliver us, O Lord, our God. Gather us from among the nations. Then we will give thanks to your holy name, and boast about your praiseworthy deeds.

notes.text: Heb “to give thanks.” The infinitive construct indicates result after the imperative.
Heb “to boast in your praise.”

48.text: The Lord God of Israel deserves praise, in the future and forevermore. Let all the people say, “We agree! Praise the Lord!”

notes.text: Heb “[be] blessed.” See Pss 18:46; 28:6; 31:21.
Heb “from everlasting to everlasting.”
Heb “surely” (‏אָמֵן‎,ʾamen), traditionally transliterated “amen.”

The final verse (v. 48) is a conclusion to this fourth “book” (or major editorial division) of the Psalter. Similar statements appear at or near the end of each of the first, second and third “books” of the Psalter (see Pss 41:13; 72:18-19; 89:52, respectively).

1.text: Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, and his loyal love endures.

notes.text: Heb “for forever [is] his loyal love.”

2.text: Let those delivered by the Lord speak out, those whom he delivered from the power of the enemy,

notes.text: Or “let the redeemed of the Lord say [so].”
Or “redeemed.”
Heb “hand.”

3.text: and gathered from foreign lands, from east and west, from north and south.

notes.text: Heb “from lands.” The word “foreign” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

4.text: They wandered through the wilderness, in a wasteland; they found no road to a city in which to live.

notes.text: The MT divides the verse so the line ends “on a wasteland of a road.” The LXX divides the line before “road” as in the translation.

5.text: They were hungry and thirsty; they fainted from exhaustion.

notes.text: Heb “and their soul in them fainted.”

6.text: They cried out to the Lord in their distress; he delivered them from their troubles.

7.text: He led them on a level road, that they might find a city in which to live.

notes.text: A level road. See Jer 31:9.

8.text: Let them give thanks to the Lord for his loyal love, and for the amazing things he has done for people.

notes.text: Heb “and [for] his amazing deeds for the sons of man.”

9.text: For he has satisfied those who thirst, and those who hunger he has filled with food.

notes.text: Heb “[the] longing throat.” The noun ‏נֶפֶשׁ‎ (nefesh), which frequently refers to one’s very being or soul, here probably refers to one’s parched “throat” (note the parallelism with ‏נֶפֶשׁ רְעֵבָה‎, nefesh reʿevah, “hungry throat”).
Heb “and [the] hungry throat he has filled [with] good.”

10.text: They sat in utter darkness, bound in painful iron chains,

notes.text: Heb “those who sat in darkness and deep darkness.” Synonyms are joined here to emphasize the degree of “darkness” experienced by the exiles. The Hebrew term ‏צַלְמָוֶת‎ (tsalmavet, “deep darkness”) has traditionally been understood as a compound noun, meaning “shadow of death” (‏צֵל‎ + ‏מָוֶת‎ [tsel + mavet]; see BDB 853 s.v. ‏צַלְמָוֶת‎; cf. NASB). Other authorities prefer to vocalize the form ‏צַלְמוּת‎ (tsalmut) and understand it as an abstract noun (from the root ‏צלם‎) meaning “darkness.” An examination of the word’s usage favors the latter derivation. It is frequently associated with darkness/night and contrasted with light/morning (see Job 3:5; 10:21-22; 12:22; 24:17; 28:3; 34:22; Ps 107:10, 14; Isa 9:1; Jer 13:16; Amos 5:8). In some cases the darkness described is associated with the realm of death (Job 10:21-22; 38:17), but this is a metaphorical application of the word and does not reflect its inherent meaning. In Ps 107:10 the word refers metonymically to a dungeon, which in turn metaphorically depicts the place of Israel’s exile (see vv. 2-3).

Heb “those bound in suffering and iron.” “Suffering and iron” is a hendiadys (like English “good and angry”), where both words contribute to one idea. In this case the first word characterizes the second; the iron (chains) contribute to the prisoners’ pain and suffering.

11.text: because they had rebelled against God’s commands, and rejected the instructions of the Most High.

notes.text: Heb “the words of God.”
The divine title “Most High” (‏עֶלְיוֹן‎ ʿelyon) pictures God as the exalted ruler of the universe who vindicates the innocent and judges the wicked. See especially Pss 7:17; 9:2; 18:13; 21:7; 47:2.

12.text: So he used suffering to humble them; they stumbled and no one helped them up.

notes.text: Heb “and he subdued with suffering their heart.”

13.text: They cried out to the Lord in their distress; he delivered them from their troubles.

14.text: He brought them out of the utter darkness, and tore off their shackles.

notes.text: Heb “darkness and deep darkness.” See the note on the word “darkness” in v. 10.

15.text: Let them give thanks to the Lord for his loyal love, and for the amazing things he has done for people.

notes.text: Heb “and [for] his amazing deeds for the sons of man.” See v. 8.

16.text: For he shattered the bronze gates, and hacked through the iron bars.

notes.text: The language of v. 16 recalls Isa 45:2.

17.text: They acted like fools in their rebellious ways, and suffered because of their sins.

notes.text: Heb “fools [they were] because of the way of their rebellion.”

18.text: They lost their appetite for all food, and they drew near the gates of death.

notes.text: Heb “all food their appetite loathed.”

19.text: They cried out to the Lord in their distress; he delivered them from their troubles.

20.text: He sent them an assuring word and healed them; he rescued them from the pits where they were trapped.

notes.text: Heb “he sent his word.” This probably refers to an oracle of assurance which announced his intention to intervene (see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 59).

Heb “he rescued from their traps.” The Hebrew word ‏שְׁחִית‎ (shekhit, “trap”) occurs only here and in Lam 4:20, where it refers to a trap or pit in which one is captured. Because of the rarity of the term and the absence of an object with the verb “rescued,” some prefer to emend the text of Ps 107:20, reading ‏מִשַּׁחַת חַיָּתָם‎ (mishakhat khayyatam, “[he rescued] their lives from the pit”). Note also NIV “from the grave,” which interprets the “pit” as Sheol or the grave.

21.text: Let them give thanks to the Lord for his loyal love, and for the amazing things he has done for people.

notes.text: Heb “and [for] his amazing deeds for the sons of man.” See v. 8.

22.text: Let them present thank offerings, and loudly proclaim what he has done.

notes.text: Heb “and let them proclaim his works with a ringing cry.”

23.text: Some traveled on the sea in ships, and carried cargo over the vast waters.

notes.text: Verses 23-30, which depict the Lord rescuing sailors from a storm at sea, do not seem to describe the exiles’ situation, unless the word picture is metaphorical. Perhaps the psalmist here broadens his scope and offers an example of God’s kindness to the needy beyond the covenant community.
Heb “those going down [into].”
Heb “doers of work on the mighty waters.”

24.text: They witnessed the acts of the Lord, his amazing feats on the deep water.

25.text: He gave the order for a windstorm, and it stirred up the waves of the sea.

notes.text: Heb “he spoke and caused to stand a stormy wind.”
Heb “and it stirred up its [i.e., the sea’s, see v. 23] waves.”

26.text: They reached up to the sky, then dropped into the depths. The sailors’ strength left them because the danger was so great.

notes.text: That is, the waves (see v. 25).
Heb “their being”; traditionally “their soul” (referring to that of the sailors). This is sometimes translated “courage” (cf. NIV, NRSV).
Or “melted.”
Heb “from danger.”

27.text: They swayed and staggered like drunks, and all their skill proved ineffective.

notes.text: Only here does the Hebrew verb ‏חָגַג‎ (khagag; normally meaning “to celebrate”) carry the nuance “to sway.”

The Hitpael of ‏בָּלַע‎ (balaʿ) occurs only here in the OT. Traditionally the form is derived from the verbal root ‏בלע‎ (“to swallow”), but HALOT 135 s.v. III ‏בלע‎ understands a homonym here with the meaning “to be confused.”

28.text: They cried out to the Lord in their distress; he delivered them from their troubles.

29.text: He calmed the storm, and the waves grew silent.

notes.text: Heb “he raised [the] storm to calm.”
Heb “their waves.” The antecedent of the third masculine plural pronominal suffix is not readily apparent, unless it refers back to “waters” in v. 23.

30.text: The sailors rejoiced because the waves grew quiet, and he led them to the harbor they desired.

notes.text: Heb “they”; the referent (the sailors) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “they”; the referent (the waves) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The Hebrew noun occurs only here in the OT.

31.text: Let them give thanks to the Lord for his loyal love, and for the amazing things he has done for people.

notes.text: Heb “and [for] his amazing deeds for the sons of man.” See v. 8.

32.text: Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people. Let them praise him in the place where the leaders preside.

notes.text: Heb “in the seat of the elders.”

33.text: He turned streams into a desert, springs of water into arid land,
