notes.text: The verbal form appears to be a preterite, which is most naturally taken as narrational. (The use of prefixed forms with vav [‏ו‎] consecutive in vv. 36-37 favor this.) The psalmist may return to the theme of God’s intervention for the exiles (see vv. 4-22, especially vv. 4-9). However, many regard vv. 33-41 as a hymnic description which generalizes about God’s activities among men. In this case it would be preferable to use the English present tense throughout (cf. NEB, NRSV).

34.text: and a fruitful land into a barren place, because of the sin of its inhabitants.

notes.text: Heb “a salty land.”

35.text: As for his people, he turned a desert into a pool of water, and a dry land into springs of water.

notes.text: The words “As for his people” are not included in the Hebrew text, but have been supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity. The psalmist contrasts God’s judgment on his enemies with his blessing of his people. See the note on the word “enemies” in v. 39 for further discussion.
The verbal form appears to be a preterite, which is most naturally taken as narrational. See the note on the word “turned” in v. 33.

36.text: He allowed the hungry to settle there, and they established a city in which to live.

37.text: They cultivated fields, and planted vineyards, which yielded a harvest of fruit.

notes.text: Heb “sowed seed in.”
Heb “fruit [as] produce.”

38.text: He blessed them so that they became very numerous. He would not allow their cattle to decrease in number.

notes.text: “Bless” here carries the nuance “endue with sexual potency, make fertile.” See Gen 1:28, where the statement “he blessed them” directly precedes the command “be fruitful and populate the earth” (see also 1:22). The verb “bless” carries this same nuance in Gen 17:16 (where God’s blessing of Sarai imparts to her the capacity to bear a child); 48:16 (where God’s blessing of Joseph’s sons is closely associated with their having numerous descendants); and Deut 7:13 (where God’s blessing is associated with fertility in general, including numerous descendants). See also Gen 49:25 (where Jacob uses the noun derivative in referring to “blessings of the breast and womb,” an obvious reference to fertility) and Gen 27:27 (where the verb is used of a field to which God has given the capacity to produce vegetation).

The verbal form in this line appears to be an imperfect, which may be taken as customary (drawing attention to typical action in a past time frame) or as generalizing (in which case one should use the English present tense, understanding a move from narrative to present reality).

39.text: As for their enemies, they decreased in number and were beaten down, because of painful distress and suffering.

notes.text: The words “As for their enemies” are not included in the Hebrew text, but have been supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity. Without such clarification, one might think that v. 39 refers to those just mentioned in v. 38 as objects of divine blessing, which would contradict the point just emphasized by the psalmist. The structure of vv. 33-42 is paneled (A-B-A-B). In vv. 33-34 the psalmist describes God’s judgment upon his enemies (perhaps those who had enslaved his people). In vv. 35-38 he contrasts this judgment with the divine blessing poured out on God’s people. (See the note on the word “people” in v. 35.) In vv. 39-40 he contrasts this blessing with the judgment experienced by enemies, before returning in vv. 41-42 to the blessing experienced by God’s people.
Heb “from the oppression of calamity.”

40.text: He would pour contempt upon princes, and he made them wander in a wasteland with no road.

notes.text: The active participle is understood as past durative here, drawing attention to typical action in a past time frame. However, it could be taken as generalizing (in which case one should translate using the English present tense), in which case the psalmist moves from narrative to present reality. Perhaps the participial form appears because the statement is lifted from Job 12:21.

41.text: Yet he protected the needy from oppression, and cared for his families like a flock of sheep.

notes.text: Heb “set on high.”

42.text: When the godly see this, they rejoice, and every sinner shuts his mouth.

notes.text: Heb “all evil,” which stands metonymically for those who do evil.

43.text: Whoever is wise, let him take note of these things. Let them consider the Lord’s acts of loyal love.

1.text: I am determined, O God. I will sing and praise you with my whole heart.

notes.text: Or perhaps “confident”; Heb “my heart is steadfast.” The “heart” is viewed here as the seat of the psalmist’s volition and/or emotions.

Heb “also my glory,” but this makes little sense in the context. Some view the term ‏כָּבוֹד‎ (kavod, “glory”) here as a metonymy for man’s inner being (see BDB 459 s.v. II ‏כָּבוֹד‎ 5), but it is preferable to emend the form to ‏כְּבֵדִי‎ (kevedi, “my liver”). Like the heart, the liver is viewed as the seat of one’s emotions. See also Pss 16:9; 30:12; 57:9; as well as H. W. Wolff, Anthropology of the Old Testament, 64, and M. Dahood, Psalms (AB), 3:93. For an Ugaritic example of the heart/liver as the source of joy, see G. R. Driver, Canaanite Myths and Legends, 47-48: “her [Anat’s] liver swelled with laughter, her heart was filled with joy, the liver of Anat with triumph.”

2.text: Awake, O stringed instrument and harp. I will wake up at dawn.

notes.text: BDB 1007 s.v. ‏שַׁחַר‎ takes “dawn” as an adverbial accusative, though others understand it as a personified direct object. “Dawn” is used metaphorically for the time of deliverance and vindication the psalmist anticipates. When salvation “dawns,” the psalmist will “wake up” in praise.

3.text: I will give you thanks before the nations, O Lord. I will sing praises to you before foreigners.

notes.text: Or “the peoples.”

4.text: For your loyal love extends beyond the sky, and your faithfulness reaches the clouds.

notes.text: Heb “for great upon the sky [or “heavens”] [is] your loyal love.”

5.text: Rise up above the sky, O God. May your splendor cover the whole earth.

notes.text: Or “be exalted.”
Heb “over all the earth [be] your splendor.” Though no verb appears, the tone of the statement is a prayer or wish. (Note the imperative form in the preceding line.)

6.text: Deliver by your power and answer me, so that the ones you love may be safe.

notes.text: Heb “right hand.”
Or “may be rescued.” The lines are actually reversed in the Hebrew text: “So that the ones you love may be rescued, deliver by your power and answer me.”

7.text: God has spoken in his sanctuary: “I will triumph! I will parcel out Shechem; the Valley of Sukkoth I will measure off.

notes.text: Heb “in his holy place.”
Shechem stands for the territory west of the Jordan River; the Valley of Sukkoth represents the region east of the Jordan.

8.text: Gilead belongs to me, as does Manasseh. Ephraim is my helmet, Judah my royal scepter.

notes.text: Gilead was located east of the Jordan River. Half of the tribe of Manasseh lived east of the Jordan in the region of Bashan.
Heb “the protection of my head.”

Ephraim, one of Joseph’s sons, was one of two major tribes located west of the Jordan River. By comparing Ephraim to a helmet, the Lord suggests that the Ephraimites played a primary role in the defense of his land.
Judah, like Ephraim, was the other major tribe west of the Jordan River. The Davidic king, symbolized here by the royal scepter, came from this tribe.

9.text: Moab is my washbasin. I will make Edom serve me. I will shout in triumph over Philistia.”

notes.text: The metaphor of the washbasin, used to rinse one’s hands and feet, suggests that Moab, in contrast to Israel’s elevated position (vv. 7-8), would be reduced to the status of a servant.

Heb “over Edom I will throw my sandal.” The point of the metaphor is not entirely clear. Some interpret this as idiomatic for “taking possession of.” Others translate ‏עַל‎ (ʿal) as “to” and understand this as referring to a master throwing his dirty sandal to a servant so that the latter might dust it off.

10.text: Who will lead me into the fortified city? Who will bring me to Edom?

notes.text: The psalmist speaks again and acknowledges his need for help in battle. He hopes God will volunteer, based on the affirmation of sovereignty over Edom in v. 9, but he is also aware that God has seemingly rejected the nation of Israel (v. 11).

11.text: Have you not rejected us, O God? O God, you do not go into battle with our armies.

12.text: Give us help against the enemy, for any help men might offer is futile.

notes.text: Heb “and futile [is] the deliverance of man.”

13.text: By God’s power we will conquer; he will trample down our enemies.

notes.text: Heb “in God we will accomplish strength.” The statement refers here to military success (see Num 24:18; 1 Sam 14:48; Pss 60:12; 118:16).
On the expression trample down our enemies see Ps 44:5.

1.text: O God whom I praise, do not ignore me.

notes.text: Heb “do not be deaf.”

2.text: For they say cruel and deceptive things to me; they lie to me.

notes.text: Heb “for a mouth of evil and a mouth of deceit against me they open, they speak with me [with] a tongue of falsehood.”

3.text: They surround me and say hateful things; they attack me for no reason.

notes.text: Heb “and [with] words of hatred they surround me.”

4.text: They repay my love with accusations, but I continue to pray.

notes.text: Heb “in place of my love they oppose me.”
Heb “and I, prayer.”

5.text: They repay me evil for good, and hate for love.

notes.text: Heb “and they set upon me evil in place of good.”

6.text: Appoint an evil man to testify against him. May an accuser stand at his right side.

notes.text: In vv. 6-19 the psalmist calls on God to judge his enemies severely. Some attribute this curse-list to the psalmist’s enemies rather than the psalmist. In this case one should paraphrase v. 6: “They say about me, ‘Appoint an evil man, etc.’” Those supporting this line of interpretation point out that vv. 2-5 and 20 refer to the enemies’ attack on the psalmist being a verbal one. Furthermore in vv. 1-5, 20 the psalmist speaks of his enemies in the plural, while vv. 6-19 refer to an individual. This use of the singular in vv. 6-19 could be readily explained if this is the psalmist’s enemies’ curse on him. However, it is much more natural to understand vv. 6-19 as the psalmist’s prayer against his enemies. There is no introductory quotation formula in v. 6 to indicate that the psalmist is quoting anyone, and the statement “may the Lord repay my accusers in this way” in v. 20 most naturally appears to be a fitting conclusion to the prayer in vv. 6-19. But what about the use of the singular in vv. 6-19? Often in the psalms the psalmist will describe his enemies as a group, but then speak of them as an individual as well, as if viewing his adversaries collectively as one powerful foe. See, for example, Ps 7, where the psalmist uses both the plural (vv. 1, 6) and the singular (vv. 2, 4-5) in referring to enemies. Perhaps by using the singular in such cases, the psalmist wants to single out each enemy for individual attention, or perhaps he has one especially hostile enemy in mind who epitomizes the opposition of the whole group. This may well be the case in Ps 109. Perhaps we should understand the singular throughout vv. 6-19 in the sense of “each and every one.” For a lengthy and well-reasoned defense of the opposite view—that vv. 6-19 are a quotation of what the enemies said about the psalmist—see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 72-73.
Heb “appoint against him an evil [man].”
The prefixed verbal form is taken as a jussive here (note the imperative in the preceding line).

7.text: When he is judged, he will be found guilty. Then his prayer will be regarded as sinful.

notes.text: The prefixed verbal form could be taken as a jussive, but the use of the imperfect form in the following line suggests that v. 7 anticipates the outcome of the accusation envisioned in v. 6.
Heb “he will go out [as] a criminal” (that is, guilty).

8.text: May his days be few. May another take his job.

notes.text: The prefixed verbal forms (except those with vav [‏ו‎] consecutive) in vv. 8-20 are taken as jussives of prayer. Note the distinct jussive forms used in vv. 12-13, 15, 19.
The Hebrew noun ‏פְּקֻדָּה‎ (pequddah) can mean “charge” or “office,” though BDB 824 s.v. suggests that here it refers to his possessions.

9.text: May his children be fatherless, and his wife a widow.

notes.text: Or “sons.”

10.text: May his children roam around begging, asking for handouts as they leave their ruined home.

notes.text: Or “sons.”

Heb “and roaming, may his children roam and beg, and seek from their ruins.” Some, following the LXX, emend the term ‏וְדָרְשׁוּ‎ (vedareshu, “and seek”) to ‏יְגֹרְשׁוּ‎ (yegoreshu; a Pual jussive, “may they be driven away” [see Job 30:5; cf. NIV, NRSV]), but ‏דָּרַשׁ‎ (darash) nicely parallels ‏שִׁאֵלוּ‎ (shiʾelu, “and beg”) in the preceding line.

11.text: May the creditor seize all he owns. May strangers loot his property.

notes.text: Heb “lay snares for” (see Ps 38:12).
Heb “the product of his labor.”

12.text: May no one show him kindness. May no one have compassion on his fatherless children.

notes.text: Heb “may there not be for him one who extends loyal love.”
Perhaps this refers to being generous (see Ps 37:21).

13.text: May his descendants be cut off. May the memory of them be wiped out by the time the next generation arrives.

notes.text: Or “offspring.”
On the expression cut off see Ps 37:28.
Heb “in another generation may their name be wiped out.”

14.text: May his ancestors’ sins be remembered by the Lord. May his mother’s sin not be forgotten.

notes.text: Or “fathers’ sins.”
Heb “not be wiped out.”

According to ancient Israelite theology and its doctrine of corporate solidarity and responsibility, children could be and often were punished for the sins of their parents. For a discussion of this issue see J. Kaminsky, Corporate Responsibility in the Hebrew Bible (JSOTSup). (Kaminsky, however, does not deal with Ps 109.)

15.text: May the Lord be constantly aware of them, and cut off the memory of his children from the earth.

notes.text: Heb “may they [that is, the sins mentioned in v. 14] be before the Lord continually.”
Heb “their memory.” The plural pronominal suffix probably refers back to the children mentioned in v. 13, and for clarity this has been specified in the translation.

16.text: For he never bothered to show kindness; he harassed the oppressed and needy, and killed the disheartened.

notes.text: Heb “he did not remember to do loyal love.”
Heb “and he chased an oppressed and needy man, and one timid of heart to put [him] to death.”

17.text: He loved to curse others, so those curses have come upon him. He had no desire to bless anyone, so he has experienced no blessings.

notes.text: A curse in OT times consists of a formal appeal to God to bring judgment down upon another. Curses were sometimes justified (such as the one spoken by the psalmist here in vv. 6-19), but when they were not, the one pronouncing the curse was in danger of bringing the anticipated judgment down upon himself.

Heb “and he loved a curse and it came [upon] him.” A reference to the evil man experiencing a curse seems premature here, for the psalmist is asking God to bring judgment on his enemies. For this reason some (cf. NIV, NRSV) prefer to repoint the vav (‏ו‎) on “it came” as conjunctive and translate the verb as a jussive of prayer (“may it come upon him!”). The prefixed form with vav consecutive in the next line is emended in the same way and translated, “may it be far from him.” However, the psalmist may be indicating that the evil man’s lifestyle has already begun to yield its destructive fruit.
Heb “and he did not delight in a blessing and it is far from him.”

18.text: He made cursing a way of life, so curses poured into his stomach like water and seeped into his bones like oil.

notes.text: Heb “he put on a curse as [if it were] his garment.”

Heb “and it came like water into his inner being, and like oil into his bones.” This may refer to this individual’s appetite for cursing. For him cursing was as refreshing as drinking water or massaging oneself with oil. Another option is that the destructive effects of a curse are in view. In this case a destructive curse invades his very being, like water or oil. Some who interpret the verse this way prefer to repoint the verb from the preterite form ‏וַתָּבֹא‎ (vattavoʾ, “and it came”) to a jussive form ‏וְתָבֹא‎ (vetavoʾ, “and may it come!”).

19.text: May a curse attach itself to him, like a garment one puts on, or a belt one wears continually.

notes.text: Heb “may it be for him like a garment one puts on.”
The Hebrew noun ‏מֵזַח‎ (mezakh, “belt; waistband”) occurs only here in the OT. The form apparently occurs in Isa 23:10 as well, but an emendation is necessary there.

20.text: May the Lord repay my accusers in this way, those who say evil things about me.

notes.text: Heb “[may] this [be] the repayment to my accusers from the Lord.”
Or “against.”
The Hebrew term ‏נֶפֶשׁ‎ (nefesh, “being; soul”) with a pronominal suffix is often equivalent to a pronoun, especially in poetry (see BDB 660 s.v. ‏נֶפֶשׁ‎ 4.a).

21.text: O Sovereign Lord, intervene on my behalf for the sake of your reputation. Because your loyal love is good, deliver me.

notes.text: Heb “but you, Lord, Master, deal with me for the sake of your name” or “on account of your name.” Here “name” stands metonymically for God’s reputation. The Psalmist’s appeal is for God to act consistently with, and therefore maintain, his reputation (as a deliverer of the righteous and one who punishes evildoers). Note that “for your name’s sake” is paralleled by “because your loyal love is good.” The point is that the Psalmist is making an appeal not based on his own personal whim or vendetta but is calling for judicial penalties (or the fulfillment of prior prophetic indictment).

22.text: For I am oppressed and needy, and my heart beats violently within me.

notes.text: The verb in the Hebrew text (‏חָלַל‎, khalal) appears to be a Qal form from the root ‏חלל‎ meaning “pierced; wounded.” However, the Qal of this root is otherwise unattested. The translation assumes an emendation to ‏יָחִיל‎ (yakhil), a Qal imperfect from ‏חוּל‎ (khul, “tremble”) or to ‏חֹלַל‎ (kholal), a Polal perfect from ‏חוּל‎ (khul). See Ps 55:4, which reads ‏לִבִּי יָחִיל בְּקִרְבִּי‎ (libbi yakhil beqirbbi, “my heart trembles [i.e., “beats violently”] within me”).

23.text: I am fading away like a shadow at the end of the day; I am shaken off like a locust.

notes.text: Heb “like a shadow when it is extended I go.” He is like a late afternoon shadow made by the descending sun that will soon be swallowed up by complete darkness. See Ps 102:11.

24.text: I am so starved my knees shake; I have turned into skin and bones.

notes.text: Heb “my knees stagger from fasting.”
Heb “and my flesh is lean away from fatness [i.e., “lean so as not to be fat”].”

25.text: I am disdained by them. When they see me, they shake their heads.

notes.text: Heb “as for me, I am a reproach to them.”
They shake their heads. Apparently shaking the head was a taunting gesture. See also Job 16:4; Ps 22:7; Lam 2:15.

26.text: Help me, O Lord my God. Because you are faithful to me, deliver me.

notes.text: Heb “deliver me according to your faithfulness.”

27.text: Then they will realize this is your work, and that you, Lord, have accomplished it.

notes.text: After the preceding imperative, the prefixed verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose or result.
Heb “that your hand [is] this.”

28.text: They curse, but you will bless. When they attack, they will be humiliated, but your servant will rejoice.

notes.text: Another option is to translate the imperfect as a prayer/request (“may you bless”).

The verbal sequence is perfect + prefixed form with vav (‏ו‎) consecutive. Since the psalmist seems to be anticipating the demise of his enemies, he may be using these forms rhetorically to describe the enemies’ defeat as if it were already accomplished. Some emend the text to ‏קָמוּ יֵבֹשׁוּ‎ (qamu yevoshu, “may those who attack me be humiliated”). See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 75.

29.text: My accusers will be covered with shame, and draped in humiliation as if it were a robe.

notes.text: Heb “clothed.” Another option is to translate the prefixed verbal forms in this line and the next as jussives (“may my accusers be covered with shame”).

30.text: I will thank the Lord profusely. In the middle of a crowd I will praise him,

notes.text: Heb “I will thank the Lord very much with my mouth.”
Heb “many.”

31.text: because he stands at the right hand of the needy, to deliver him from those who threaten his life.

notes.text: Heb “judge.”

1.text: Here is the Lord’s proclamation to my lord: “Sit down at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.”

notes.text: The word ‏נְאֻם‎ (neʾum) is used frequently in the OT of a formal divine announcement through a prophet.

My lord. In the psalm’s original context the speaker is an unidentified prophetic voice in the royal court, likely addressing David, the head of the dynasty. In the course of time the psalm is applied to each successive king in the dynasty, and is likely understood as such by David (see 2 Sam 7:11-14, 19). Since the Psalm as a whole is attributed to David, it is appropriate to speak of any of its parts as coming from him, whether he composed them, reported them, or commissioned them. Ultimately these words come to apply to the ideal Davidic king, specifically Jesus Christ, the Son of David. Thus, in the irony of the incarnation, the lord who receives the promise is the Lord who made the promise. This creates some complexity in typographic convention, as NET chooses to use lower case here in the Psalm (“my lord”) due to its original context, even though we now know it to be ultimately fulfilled by our Lord. The Greek translation introduces more difficulty because it uses κύριος (kurios, “lord”) for both the Lord’s name, ‏יהוה‎ (YHWH, probably pronounced “Yahweh”) and the title ‏אֲדוֹנַי‎ (ʾadonay, “Lord”) (the word here is not the title, but simply “lord” [‏אָדוֺן‎, ʾadon] with the suffix “my”). This complexity and irony are the grounds for the riddle posed by Jesus in the gospels (Matt 22:43-45; Mark 12:36-37; Luke 20:42-44), which the Pharisees could not solve because they were not expecting the Davidic lord to be the Lord. Peter incorporates the answer “that God has made this Jesus whom you crucified both Lord and Christ” into his sermon at Pentecost (Acts 2:34-35).

To sit at the “right hand” of the king was an honor (see 1 Kgs 2:19). The Lord’s invitation to the Davidic king to sit down at his right hand reflects the king’s position as the Lord’s vice-regent. In Ugaritic myth (CTA 4 v. 108-10) the artisan god Kothar-wa-Khasis is described as sitting at the right hand of the storm god Baal. See G. R. Driver, Canaanite Myths and Legends, 61-62.
When the Lord made his covenant with David, he promised to subdue the king’s enemies (see 2 Sam 7:9-11; Ps 89:22-23).

2.text: The Lord extends your dominion from Zion. Rule in the midst of your enemies.

notes.text: Since the Lord is mentioned in the third person (note the use of the first person in v. 1), it is likely that these are the psalmist’s words to the king, not a continuation of the oracle per se.
The prefixed verbal form is understood here as descriptive-dramatic or as generalizing, though it could be taken as future.
Heb “your strong scepter,” symbolic of the king’s royal authority and dominion.

3.text: Your people willingly follow you when you go into battle. On the holy hills at sunrise the dew of your youth belongs to you.

notes.text: Heb “your people, free will offerings.” Perhaps the people, in their willingness to volunteer, are compared metaphorically to freewill offerings. Following the LXX, some revocalize the text and read “with you is nobility.”
Heb “in the day of your power.”

Heb “in splendor of holiness.” The plural construct form ‏הַדְרֵי‎ (hadre, from ‏הָדַר‎, hadar, “splendor”) occurs only here; it may indicate degree or perhaps refer by metonymy to garments (see Pss 29:2 and 96:9, where the phrase ‏הַדְרַת קֹדֶשׁ‎ [hadrat qodesh] refers to “holy attire”). If one retains the reading of the MT, this phrase should probably be taken with the preceding line. However, because of the subsequent references to “dawn” and to “dew,” it is better to emend the text to ‏הַרְרֵי קֹדֶשׁ‎ (harere qodesh, “mountains of holiness”), a reading found in many medieval Hebrew mss and in some other ancient witnesses (see Joel 2:2; Ps 133:3, as well as L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 80). The “mountains of holiness” are probably the hills surrounding Zion (see Pss 87:1; 125:2; 133:3).

Heb “from the womb of dawn.” The Hebrew noun ‏רֶחֶם‎ (rekhem, “womb”) is probably used here metonymically for “birth.” The form ‏מִשְׁחָר‎ (mishkhar) occurs only here and should be emended to ‏שַׁחַר‎ (shakhar, “dawn”) with the ‏מ‎ (mem) being understood as a duplication of the mem ending the preceding word. The phrase “womb [i.e., “birth”] of dawn” refers to sunrise.
The point of the metaphor is not entirely clear. The dew may symbolize the king’s youthful vitality or, more likely (note the parallelism), may refer to his army of strong, youthful warriors.
Heb “to you [is].”

4.text: The Lord makes this promise on oath and will not revoke it: “You are an eternal priest after the pattern of Melchizedek.”

notes.text: Or “swears, vows.”

Or “will not change his mind.” The negated Niphal imperfect of ‏נָחַם‎ (nakham) is a way of marking an announcement as an irrevocable decree. See 1 Sam 15:29; Ezek 24:14, as well as R. B. Chisholm, “Does God ‘Change His Mind’?” BSac 152 (1995): 387-99.

You are an eternal priest. The Davidic king exercised a non-Levitical priestly role. The king superintended Judah’s cultic ritual, had authority over the Levites, and sometimes led in formal worship. David himself instructed the Levites to bring the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:11-15), joined the procession, offered sacrifices, wore a priestly ephod, and blessed the people (2 Sam 6:12-19). At the dedication of the temple Solomon led the ceremony, offering sacrifices and praying on behalf of the people (1 Kgs 8).

The phrase ‏עַל־דִּבְרָתִי‎ (ʿal divrati) is a variant of ‏עַל־דִּבְרָת‎ (ʿal divrat; the final ‏י‎ [yod] being an archaic genitive ending), which in turn is a variant of ‏עַל דָּבַר‎ (ʿal davar). Both phrases can mean “concerning” or “because of,” but neither of these nuances fits the use of ‏עַל־דִּבְרָתִי‎ in Ps 110:4. Here the phrase probably carries the sense “according to the manner of.” See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 81.

The Davidic king’s priestly role is analogous to that of Melchizedek, who was both “king of Salem” (i.e., Jerusalem) and a “priest of God Most High” in the time of Abraham (Gen 14:18-20). Like Melchizedek, the Davidic king was a royal priest, distinct from the Aaronic line (see Heb 7). The analogy focuses on the king’s priestly role; the language need not imply that Melchizedek himself was “an eternal priest.”

5.text: O Lord, at your right hand he strikes down kings in the day he unleashes his anger.

notes.text: The MT reads ‏אֲדֹנָי‎ (ʾadonay, “Lord”), which in this form to God. Many medieval Hebrew mss read ‏יְהוָה‎ (Yehwah, “Lord”) here. The present translation assumes that the psalmist here addresses the Lord as he celebrates what the king is able to accomplish while positioned at God’s “right hand.” According to this view the king is the subject of the third person verb forms in vv. 5b-7. (2) Another option is to understand the king as the addressee (as in vv. 2-3). In this case “the Lord” is the subject of the third person verbs throughout vv. 5-7 and is depicted as a warrior in a very anthropomorphic manner. In this case the Lord is pictured as being at the psalmist’s right hand (just the opposite of v. 1). See Pss 16:8; 121:5. (3) A third option is to revocalize ‏אֲדֹנָי‎ (ʾadonay, “Lord” a reference to God) as ‏אֲדֹנִי‎ (ʾadoni, “my lord”; see v. 1). In this case one may translate, “My lord, at his [God’s] right hand, strikes down.” In this case the king is the subject of the third person verbs in vv. 5b-7.

The perfect verbal forms in vv. 5-6 are understood here as descriptive-dramatic or as generalizing. Another option is to take them as rhetorical. In this case the psalmist describes anticipated events as if they had already taken place.
Heb “in the day of his anger.”

6.text: He executes judgment against the nations. He fills the valleys with corpses; he shatters their heads over the vast battlefield.

notes.text: The imperfect verbal forms in vv. 6-7 are understood here as descriptive-dramatic or as generalizing, though they could be taken as future.
Or “among.”

Heb “he fills [with] corpses,” but one expects a double accusative here. The translation assumes an emendation to ‏גְוִיּוֹת גֵאָיוֹת‎(‏בִּ‎) ‏מִלֵּא‎ or ‏מִלֵּא גֵאָיוֹת גְּוִיוֹת‎ (for a similar construction see Ezek 32:5). In the former case ‏ גֵאָיוֹת‎ (geʾayot) has accidentally dropped from the text due to homoioteleuton; in the latter case it has dropped out due to homoioarcton.

Heb “he strikes [the verb is ‏מָחַץ‎ (makhats), translated “strikes down” in v. 5] head[s] over a great land.” The Hebrew term ‏רַבָּה‎ (rabbah, “great”) is here used of distance or spatial measurement (see 1 Sam 26:13).

7.text: From the stream along the road he drinks; then he lifts up his head.

notes.text: Here the expression “lifts up the head” refers to the renewed physical strength and emotional vigor (see Ps 3:3) provided by the refreshing water. For another example of a victorious warrior being energized by water in the aftermath of battle, see Judg 15:18-19 (see also 1 Sam 30:11-12, where the setting is different, however).

1.text: Praise the Lord! I will give thanks to the Lord with my whole heart, in the assembly of the godly and the congregation.

2.text: The Lord’s deeds are great, eagerly awaited by all who desire them.

notes.text: Heb “sought out.”

3.text: His work is majestic and glorious, and his faithfulness endures forever.

notes.text: For other uses of the Hebrew phrase ‏וְהָדָר‎‏הוֹד ‎ (hod vehadar, “majesty and splendor”) see 1 Chr 16:27; Job 40:10; Pss 21:5; 96:6; 104:1.
Or “stands.”

4.text: He does amazing things that will be remembered; the Lord is merciful and compassionate.

notes.text: Or “did,” if this refers primarily to the events of the exodus and conquest period (see vv. 6, 9).
Heb “a memorial he had made for his amazing deeds.”

5.text: He gives food to his faithful followers; he always remembers his covenant.

notes.text: Or “gave,” if the events of the exodus and conquest period (see v. 6, 9) are primarily in view.
Heb “those who fear him.”
Or “he remembers his covenant forever” (see Ps 105:8).

6.text: He announced that he would do mighty deeds for his people, giving them a land that belonged to other nations.

notes.text: Heb “the strength of his deeds he proclaimed to his people, to give to them an inheritance of nations.”

7.text: His acts are characterized by faithfulness and justice; all his precepts are reliable.

notes.text: Heb “the deeds of his hands [are].”
That is, fair and for man’s good.

8.text: They are forever firm, and should be faithfully and properly carried out.

notes.text: Heb “done in faithfulness and uprightness.” The passive participle probably has the force of a gerund. See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 89.

9.text: He delivered his people; he ordained that his covenant be observed forever. His name is holy and awesome.

notes.text: Heb “redemption he sent for his people.”
Heb “he commanded forever his covenant.”

10.text: To obey the Lord is the fundamental principle for wise living; all who carry out his precepts acquire good moral insight. He will receive praise forever.

notes.text: Heb “the beginning of wisdom [is] the fear of the Lord.”

Heb “good sense [is] to all who do them.” The third masculine plural pronominal suffix must refer back to the “precepts” mentioned in v. 7. In the translation the referent has been specified for clarity. The phrase ‏שֵׂכֶל טוֹב‎ (sekhel tov) also occurs in Prov 3:4; 13:15 and 2 Chr 30:22.
Heb “his praise stands forever.”

1.text: Praise the Lord! How blessed is the one who obeys the Lord, who takes great delight in keeping his commands.

notes.text: Heb “[Oh] the happiness [of] the man.” Hebrew wisdom literature often assumes and reflects the male-oriented perspective of ancient Israelite society. The individual is representative of a larger group, called the “godly” in vv. 3-4. The principle of the psalm is certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender. To facilitate modern application, we translate the gender specific “man” with the more neutral “one.” The generic masculine pronoun is used in the following verses.
Heb “fears.”

Heb “in his commands he delights very much.” The words “in keeping” are supplied in the translation for clarification. Taking delight in the law is metonymic here for obeying God’s moral will. See Ps 1:2.

2.text: His descendants will be powerful on the earth; the godly will be blessed.

notes.text: Or “offspring”; Heb “seed.”

Heb “His seed will be mighty on the earth, the generation of the godly.” The Hebrew term ‏דוֹר‎ (dor, “generation”) could be taken as parallel to “offspring” and translated “posterity,” but the singular more likely refers to the godly as a class. See BDB 189-90 s.v. for other examples where “generation” refers to a class of people.

3.text: His house contains wealth and riches; his integrity endures.

notes.text: Heb “stands forever.”

4.text: In the darkness a light shines for the godly, for each one who is merciful, compassionate, and just.

notes.text: In this context “light” symbolizes divine blessing in its various forms (see v. 2), including material prosperity and stability.

Heb “merciful and compassionate and just.” The Hebrew text has three singular adjectives, which are probably substantival and in apposition to the “godly” (which is plural, however). By switching to the singular, the psalmist focuses on each individual member of the group known as the “godly.” Note how vv. 5-9, like vv. 1-2a, use the singular to describe the representative godly individual who typifies the whole group.

5.text: It goes well for the one who generously lends money, and conducts his business honestly.

notes.text: Heb “man.”
Heb “he sustains his matters with justice.”

6.text: For he will never be shaken; others will always remember one who is just.

notes.text: Heb “for an eternal memorial a just [one] will be.”

7.text: He does not fear bad news. He is confident; he trusts in the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “his heart,” viewed here as the seat of the volition and emotions (see Ps 108:1).

8.text: His resolve is firm; he will not succumb to fear before he looks in triumph on his enemies.

notes.text: Heb “his heart,” viewed here as the seat of the volition.

9.text: He generously gives to the needy; his integrity endures. He will be vindicated and honored.

notes.text: Heb “he scatters, he gives.”
Heb “stands forever.”

Heb “his horn will be lifted up in honor.” The horn of an ox underlies the metaphor (see Deut 33:17; 1 Kgs 22:11; Ps 92:10). The horn of the wild ox is frequently a metaphor for military strength; the idiom “exalt/lift up the horn” signifies military victory (see 1 Sam 2:10; Pss 89:17, 24; 92:10; Lam 2:17).

10.text: When the wicked see this, they will worry; they will grind their teeth in frustration and melt away. The desire of the wicked will perish.

notes.text: The Hebrew text uses the singular; the representative wicked individual is in view as typifying the group (note the use of the plural form in v. 10).
Heb “his teeth he will gnash.” In Pss 35:16 and 37:12 this action is associated with a vicious attack.

This could mean that the desires of the wicked will go unfulfilled. Another possibility is that “desire” refers by metonymy to the object desired and acquired. In this case the point is that the wicked will lose what they desired so badly and acquired by evil means (see Ps 10:3).

1.text: Praise the Lord. Praise, you servants of the Lord, praise the name of the Lord.

2.text: May the Lord’s name be praised now and forevermore.

3.text: From east to west the Lord’s name is deserving of praise.

notes.text: Heb “from the rising of the sun to its setting.” The extent is not temporal (“from sunrise to sunset”) but spatial (“from the place where the sun rises [the east] to the place where it sets [the west].” In the phenomenological language of OT cosmology, the sun was described as rising in the east and setting in the west.

4.text: The Lord is exalted over all the nations; his splendor reaches beyond the sky.

notes.text: Heb “above the sky [is] his splendor.”

5.text: Who can compare to the Lord our God, who sits on a high throne?

notes.text: Heb “the one who makes high to sit.”

6.text: He bends down to look at the sky and the earth.

notes.text: Heb “the one who makes low to see.”

7.text: He raises the poor from the dirt, and lifts up the needy from the garbage pile,

notes.text: The language of v. 7 is almost identical to that of 1 Sam 2:8.

8.text: that he might seat him with princes, with the princes of his people.

9.text: He makes the barren woman of the family a happy mother of children. Praise the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “of the house.”
Heb “sons.”

1.text: When Israel left Egypt, when the family of Jacob left a foreign nation behind,

notes.text: Heb “the house of Jacob from a nation speaking a foreign language.”

2.text: Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his kingdom.

3.text: The sea looked and fled; the Jordan River turned back.

notes.text: The psalmist recalls the crossing of the Red Sea (Exod 14:21).
Heb “the Jordan” (also in v. 5). The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
The psalmist recalls the crossing of the Jordan River (Josh 3:13, 16).

4.text: The mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs.

notes.text: The mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs. This may recall the theophany at Sinai when the mountain shook before God’s presence (Exod 19:18).

5.text: Why do you flee, O sea? Why do you turn back, O Jordan River?

6.text: Why do you skip like rams, O mountains, like lambs, O hills?

7.text: Tremble, O earth, before the Lord— before the God of Jacob,

8.text: who turned a rock into a pool of water, a hard rock into springs of water.

notes.text: In v. 8 the psalmist recalls the event(s) recorded in Exod 17:6 and/or Num 20:11 (see also Deut 8:15 and Ps 78:15-16, 20).

1.text: Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name bring honor, for the sake of your loyal love and faithfulness.

notes.text: Or “give glory.”

The psalmist asks the Lord to demonstrate his loyal love and faithfulness, not simply so Israel may benefit, but primarily so that the Lord will receive honor among the nations, who will recognize, contrary to their present view (see v. 2), that Israel’s God is committed to his people.

2.text: Why should the nations say, “Where is their God?”

3.text: Our God is in heaven. He does whatever he pleases.

notes.text: He does whatever he pleases. Such sovereignty is characteristic of kings (see Eccl 8:3).

4.text: Their idols are made of silver and gold— they are man-made.

notes.text: The referent of the pronominal suffix is “the nations” (v. 2).
Heb “the work of the hands of man.”

5.text: They have mouths, but cannot speak, eyes, but cannot see,

6.text: ears, but cannot hear, noses, but cannot smell,

7.text: hands, but cannot touch, feet, but cannot walk. They cannot even clear their throats.

notes.text: Heb “they cannot mutter in their throats.” Verse 5a refers to speaking, v. 7c to inarticulate sounds made in the throat (see M. Dahood, Psalms [AB], 3:140-41).

8.text: Those who make them will end up like them, as will everyone who trusts in them.

notes.text: Heb “will be.” Another option is to take the prefixed verbal form as a prayer, “may those who make them end up like them.”
Because the idols are lifeless, they cannot help their worshipers in times of crisis. Consequently the worshipers end up as dead as the gods in which they trust.

9.text: O Israel, trust in the Lord. He is their deliverer and protector.

notes.text: Or “[source of] help.”
Heb “and their shield.”

10.text: O family of Aaron, trust in the Lord. He is their deliverer and protector.

notes.text: Heb “house.”
Or “[source of] help.”
Heb “and their shield.”

11.text: You loyal followers of the Lord, trust in the Lord. He is their deliverer and protector.

notes.text: Heb “[you] fearers of the Lord.” See Ps 15:4.
Or “[source of] help.”
Heb “and their shield.”

12.text: The Lord takes notice of us; he will bless — he will bless the family of Israel, he will bless the family of Aaron.

notes.text: Or “remembers us.”
Another option is to translate the prefixed form of the verb “bless” in vv. 12-13 as a jussive, “may he bless” (see v. 14).
Heb “house.”

13.text: He will bless his loyal followers, both young and old.

notes.text: Heb “the fearers of the Lord.”

Heb “the small along with the great.” The translation assumes that “small” and “great” here refer to age (see 2 Chr 15:13). Another option is to translate “both the insignificant and the prominent” (see Job 3:19; cf. NEB “high and low alike”).

14.text: May he increase your numbers, yours and your children’s.

notes.text: Heb “may he add to you, to you and your sons.” The prefixed verbal form is jussive, indicating this is a prayer.

15.text: May you be blessed by the Lord, the Creator of heaven and earth.

notes.text: Or “maker.”

16.text: The heavens belong to the Lord, but the earth he has given to mankind.

notes.text: Heb “the heavens [are] heavens to the Lord.”
Heb “to the sons of man.”

17.text: The dead do not praise the Lord, nor do any of those who descend into the silence of death.

notes.text: Heb “silence,” a metonymy here for death (see Ps 94:17).

18.text: But we will praise the Lord now and forevermore. Praise the Lord!

1.text: I love the Lord because he heard my plea for mercy,

notes.text: Heb “I love because the Lord heard my voice, my pleas.” It is possible that “the Lord” originally appeared directly after “I love” and was later accidentally misplaced. The translation assumes the prefixed verbal form is a preterite. The psalmist recalls that God heard his cry for help (note the perfect in v. 2a and the narrative in vv. 3-4).

2.text: and listened to me. As long as I live, I will call to him when I need help.

notes.text: Heb “because he turned his ear to me.”
Heb “and in my days I will cry out.”

3.text: The ropes of death tightened around me, the snares of Sheol confronted me. I was confronted with trouble and sorrow.

notes.text: Heb “surrounded me.”

The Hebrew noun ‏מֵצַר‎ (metsar, “straits; distress”) occurs only here, Ps 118:5 and Lam 1:3. If retained, it refers to Sheol as a place where one is confined or severely restricted (cf. BDB 865 s.v. ‏מֵצַר‎, “the straits of Sheol”; NIV “the anguish of the grave”; NRSV “the pangs of Sheol”). However, HALOT 624 s.v. ‏מֵצַר‎ suggests an emendation to ‏מְצָדֵי‎ (metsade, “snares of”), a rare noun attested in Job 19:6 and Eccl 7:26. This proposal, which is reflected in the translation, produces better parallelism with “ropes” in the preceding line.
The translation assumes the prefixed verbal form is a preterite. The psalmist recalls the crisis from which the Lord delivered him.

4.text: I called on the name of the Lord, “Please, Lord, rescue my life!”

5.text: The Lord is merciful and fair; our God is compassionate.

6.text: The Lord protects the untrained; I was in serious trouble and he delivered me.

notes.text: Heb “guards.” The active participle indicates this is a characteristic of the Lord.
Or “the [morally] naive,” that is, the one who is young and still in the process of learning right from wrong and distinguishing wisdom from folly. See Ps 19:7.
Heb “I was low.”

7.text: Rest once more, my soul, for the Lord has vindicated you.

notes.text: Heb “return, my soul, to your place of rest.”
The Hebrew idiom ‏גָּמַל עַל‎ (gamal ʿal) means “to repay,” here in a positive sense (cf. Ps 13:5).

8.text: Yes, Lord, you rescued my life from death, kept my eyes from tears and my feet from stumbling.

notes.text: Or “for.”
“Lord” is supplied here in the translation for clarification.

9.text: I will serve the Lord in the land of the living.

notes.text: Heb “walk before” (see Ps 56:13). On the meaning of the Hebrew idiom, see the notes at 2 Kgs 20:3/Isa 38:3.
Heb “lands, regions.”

10.text: I had faith when I said, “I am severely oppressed.”

11.text: I rashly declared, “All men are liars.”

notes.text: Heb “I said in my haste.”

12.text: How can I repay the Lord for all his acts of kindness to me?

13.text: I will celebrate my deliverance, and call on the name of the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “a cup of deliverance I will lift up.” Perhaps this alludes to a drink offering the psalmist will present as he thanks the Lord for his deliverance. See v. 17.

14.text: I will fulfill my vows to the Lord before all his people.

15.text: The Lord values the lives of his faithful followers.

notes.text: Heb “precious in the eyes of the Lord [is] the death of his godly ones.” The point is not that God delights in or finds satisfaction in the death of his followers! The psalmist, who has been delivered from death, affirms that the life-threatening experiences of God’s followers get God’s attention, just as a precious or rare object would attract someone’s eye. See Ps 72:14 for a similar expression of this belief.

16.text: Yes, Lord! I am indeed your servant; I am your servant, the son of your female servant. You saved me from death.

notes.text: Heb “I am your servant, the son of your female servant.” The phrase “son of a female servant” (see also Ps 86:16) is used of a son born to a secondary wife or concubine (Exod 23:12). In some cases the child’s father is the master of the house (see Gen 21:10, 13; Judg 9:18). It may used metaphorically and idiomatically to emphasize the psalmist’s humility before the Lord and his status as the Lord’s servant. Or it may be a reference to the psalmist’s own mother who also was a servant of the Lord.
Heb “you have loosed my bonds.” In this context the imagery refers to deliverance from death (see v. 3).

17.text: I will present a thank offering to you, and call on the name of the Lord.

18.text: I will fulfill my vows to the Lord before all his people,

19.text: in the courts of the Lord’s temple, in your midst, O Jerusalem. Praise the Lord!

1.text: Praise the Lord, all you nations. Applaud him, all you foreigners.

notes.text: Or “peoples” (see Ps 108:3).

2.text: For his loyal love towers over us, and the Lord’s faithfulness endures. Praise the Lord.

notes.text: For this sense of the Hebrew verb ‏גָּבַר‎ (gavar), see Ps 103:11 and L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 17, 19.

1.text: Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, and his loyal love endures.

notes.text: Or “is forever.”

2.text: Let Israel say, “Yes, his loyal love endures.”

3.text: Let the family of Aaron say, “Yes, his loyal love endures.”

notes.text: Heb “house.”

4.text: Let the loyal followers of the Lord say, “Yes, his loyal love endures.”

notes.text: Heb “fearers of the Lord.” See Ps 15:4.

5.text: In my distress I cried out to the Lord. The Lord answered me and put me in a wide open place.

notes.text: Heb “from the distress.” The noun ‏מֵצַר‎ (metsar, “straits; distress”) occurs only here and in Lam 1:3. In Ps 116:3 ‏מֵצַר‎ should probably be emended to ‏מְצָדֵי‎ (metsade, “snares of”).
Heb “the Lord answered me in a wide open place.”

6.text: The Lord is on my side; I am not afraid. What can people do to me?

notes.text: Heb “for me.”
The rhetorical question assumes the answer, “Nothing!” The imperfect is used in a modal sense here, indicating capability or potential. See Ps 56:11.

7.text: The Lord is on my side as my helper. I look in triumph on those who hate me.

notes.text: Heb “for me.”
Heb “among my helpers.” The preposition may indicate identity here, while the plural may be one of majesty or respect.

8.text: It is better to take shelter in the Lord than to trust in people.

notes.text: “Taking shelter” in the Lord is an idiom for seeking his protection. Seeking his protection presupposes and even demonstrates the subject’s loyalty to the Lord. In the psalms those who “take shelter” in the Lord are contrasted with the wicked and equated with those who love, fear, and serve the Lord (Pss 5:11-12; 31:17-20; 34:21-22).

9.text: It is better to take shelter in the Lord than to trust in princes.

10.text: All the nations surrounded me. Indeed, in the name of the Lord I pushed them away.

notes.text: The reference to an attack by the nations suggests the psalmist may have been a military leader.
In this context the phrase “in the name of the Lord” means “by the Lord’s power.”

Traditionally the verb has been derived from ‏מוּל‎ (mul, “to circumcise”) and translated “[I] cut [them] off” (see BDB 557-58 s.v. II ‏מוּל‎). However, it is likely that this is a homonym meaning “to fend off” (see HALOT 556 s.v. II ‏מול‎) or “to push away.” In this context, where the psalmist is reporting his past experience, the prefixed verbal form is best understood as a preterite. The phrase also occurs in vv. 11, 12.

11.text: They surrounded me, yes, they surrounded me. Indeed, in the name of the Lord I pushed them away.

12.text: They surrounded me like bees. But they disappeared as quickly as a fire among thorns. Indeed, in the name of the Lord I pushed them away.

notes.text: Heb “were extinguished.”

The point seems to be that the hostility of the nations (v. 10) is short-lived, like a fire that quickly devours thorns and then burns out. Some, attempting to create a better parallel with the preceding line, emend ‏דֹּעֲכוּ‎ (doʿakhu, “they were extinguished”) to ‏בָּעֲרוּ‎ (baʿaru, “they burned”). In that case the statement emphasizes their hostility.

13.text: “You aggressively attacked me and tried to knock me down, but the Lord helped me.

notes.text: Heb “pushing, you pushed me.” The infinitive absolute emphasizes the following verbal idea. The psalmist appears to address the nations as if they were an individual enemy. Some find this problematic and emend the verb form (which is a Qal perfect second masculine singular with a first person singular suffix) to ‏נִדְחֵיתִי‎ (nidkheti), a Niphal perfect first common singular, “I was pushed.”
Heb “to fall,” i.e., “that [I] might fall.”

14.text: The Lord gives me strength and protects me; he has become my deliverer.”

notes.text: Heb “my strength and protection [is] the Lord.” The Hebrew term ‏זִמְרָת‎ (zimrat) is traditionally understood as meaning “song” (“my strength and song [is] the Lord”) in which case one might translate, “for the Lord gives me strength and joy” (i.e., a reason to sing). However, many recent commentators have argued that the noun ‏זִמְרָת‎ is here a homonym, meaning “protection” or “strength.” See HALOT 274 s.v.; cf. NEB “The Lord is my refuge and defence”; NRSV “my strength and my might.”
Or “salvation.”

15.text: They celebrate deliverance in the tents of the godly. The Lord’s right hand conquers.

notes.text: Heb “the sound of a ringing shout and deliverance [is] in the tents of the godly.”
Heb “does valiantly.” The statement refers here to military success (see Num 24:18; 1 Sam 14:48; Pss 60:12; 108:13).

16.text: The Lord’s right hand gives victory; the Lord’s right hand conquers.

notes.text: Heb “exalts.”

17.text: I will not die, but live, and I will proclaim what the Lord has done.

notes.text: Heb “the works of the Lord.”

18.text: The Lord severely punished me, but he did not hand me over to death.

notes.text: The infinitive absolute emphasizes the following verbal idea.

19.text: Open for me the gates of the just king’s temple. I will enter through them and give thanks to the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “the gates of justice.” The gates of the Lord’s temple are referred to here, as v. 20 makes clear. They are called “gates of justice” because they are the entrance to the just king’s palace. This has been specified in the translation for clarity.

20.text: This is the Lord’s gate— the godly enter through it.

21.text: I will give you thanks, for you answered me, and have become my deliverer.

22.text: The stone that the builders discarded has become the cornerstone.

notes.text: Or “rejected.”
Heb “the head of the corner.”

The metaphor of the stone…the builders discarded describes the way in which God’s deliverance reversed the psalmist’s circumstances. When he was in distress, he was like a stone which was discarded by builders as useless, but now that he has been vindicated by God, all can see that he is of special importance to God, like the cornerstone of the building.

23.text: This is the Lord’s work. We consider it amazing!

notes.text: Heb “it is amazing in our eyes.” The use of the plural pronoun here and in vv. 24-27 suggests that the psalmist may be speaking for the entire nation. However, it is more likely that vv. 22-27 are the people’s response to the psalmist’s thanksgiving song (see especially v. 26). They rejoice with him because his deliverance on the battlefield (see vv. 10-12) had national repercussions.

24.text: This is the day the Lord has brought about. We will be happy and rejoice in it.

notes.text: Heb “this is the day the Lord has made.” Though sometimes applied in a general way, this statement in its context refers to the day of deliverance which the psalmist and people celebrate.

25.text: Please, Lord, deliver! Please, Lord, grant us success!

notes.text: A petition for deliverance and success seems odd in a psalm thanking God for deliverance, but it is not unique (see Ps 9:19-20). The people ask God to continue to intervene for them as he has for the psalmist.

26.text: May the one who comes in the name of the Lord be blessed. We will pronounce blessings on you in the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: The people refer here to the psalmist, who enters the Lord’s temple to thank him publicly (see vv. 19-21), as the one who comes in the name of the Lord.

The pronominal suffix is second masculine plural, but the final mem (‏ם‎) is probably dittographic (note the mem [‏מ‎] at the beginning of the following form) or enclitic, in which case the suffix may be taken as second masculine singular, referring to the psalmist.
Heb “from the house of the Lord.”

27.text: The Lord is God, and he has delivered us. Tie the offering with ropes to the horns of the altar.

notes.text: Heb “and he has given us light.” This may be an elliptical expression, with “his face” being implied as the object (see Num 6:25; Pss 31:16; 67:1; 80:3, 7, 19). In this case, “his face has given us light” = “he has smiled on us,” or “he has shown us his favor.” Another option (the one reflected in the translation) is that “light” here symbolizes divine blessing in the form of deliverance. “Light” is often used as a metaphor for deliverance and the life/blessings it brings. See Pss 37:6; 97:11; 112:4; Isa 49:6; 51:4; Mic 7:8. Some prefer to repoint the preterite form ‏וַיָּאֶר‎ (vayyaʾer, “he made light”) as a jussive ‏וְיָאֵר‎ (veyaʾer; “may he make light [for us]”).

The Hebrew noun ‏חַג‎ (khag) normally means “festival,” but here it apparently refers metonymically to an offering made at the festival. BDB 291 s.v. ‏חַג‎ 2 interprets the word in this way here, citing as comparable the use of later Hebrew ‏חֲגִיגָה‎, which can refer to both a festival and a festival offering (see Jastrow 424 s.v. ‏חֲגִיגָה‎).
The second half of v. 27 has been translated and interpreted in a variety of ways. For a survey of major views, see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 122.

28.text: You are my God, and I will give you thanks. You are my God and I will praise you.

notes.text: You are my God. The psalmist speaks again (see v. 21), responding to the words of the worshipers (vv. 22-27).

29.text: Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good and his loyal love endures.

notes.text: Or “is forever.”

1.text: How blessed are those whose actions are blameless, who obey the law of the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “[Oh] the happiness of those who are blameless of way.”
Heb “walk in.”

2.text: How blessed are those who observe his rules, and seek him with all their heart,

3.text: who, moreover, do no wrong, but follow in his footsteps.

notes.text: Heb “walk in his ways.”

4.text: You demand that your precepts be carefully kept.

notes.text: Heb “you, you commanded your precepts, to keep, very much.”

5.text: If only I were predisposed to keep your statutes.

notes.text: Heb “if only my ways were established.”

6.text: Then I would not be ashamed, if I were focused on all your commands.

notes.text: Or “when.”
Heb “I gaze at.”

7.text: I will give you sincere thanks, when I learn your just regulations.

notes.text: Heb “I will give you thanks with an upright heart.”

8.text: I will keep your statutes. Do not completely abandon me. ב (Bet)

notes.text: Heb “do not abandon me to excess.” For other uses of the phrase ‏עַד מְאֹד‎ (ʿad meʾod, “to excess”), see Ps 38:6, 8.

9.text: How can a young person maintain a pure life? By guarding it according to your instructions.

notes.text: Heb “young man.” Hebrew wisdom literature often assumes and reflects the male-oriented perspective of ancient Israelite society. The principle of the psalm is certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender or age. To facilitate modern application, the gender specific “young man” has been translated with the more neutral “young person.”
Heb “purify his path.”
Heb “by keeping according to your word.” Many medieval Hebrew mss as well as the LXX read the plural, “your words.”

10.text: With all my heart I seek you. Do not allow me to stray from your commands.

11.text: In my heart I store up your words, so I might not sin against you.

notes.text: Or “hide.”
Heb “your word.” Some medieval Hebrew mss as well as the LXX read the plural, “your words.”

12.text: You deserve praise, O Lord. Teach me your statutes.

notes.text: Heb “[are] blessed.”

13.text: With my lips I proclaim all the regulations you have revealed.

notes.text: Heb “of your mouth.”

14.text: I rejoice in the lifestyle prescribed by your rules as if they were riches of all kinds.

notes.text: Heb “in the way of your rules.”
Heb “as upon,” meaning “as if” (see 2 Chr 32:19).
Heb “all wealth.” The phrase refers to all kinds of wealth and riches. See Prov 1:13; 6:31; 24:4; Ezek 27:12, 18.

15.text: I will meditate on your precepts and focus on your behavior.

notes.text: The cohortative verbal forms in this verse express the psalmist’s resolve.
Heb “gaze [at].”
Heb “ways” (referring figuratively to God’s behavior here).

16.text: I find delight in your statutes; I do not forget your instructions. ג (Gimel)

notes.text: The imperfects in this verse emphasize the attitude the psalmist maintains toward God’s law. Another option is to translate with the future tense, “I will find delight…I will not forget.”
Heb “your word.” Many medieval Hebrew mss as well as the LXX read the plural here.

17.text: Be kind to your servant. Then I will live and keep your instructions.

notes.text: The prefixed verbal form is probably a cohortative indicating purpose/result after the preceding imperative.
The cohortative with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the imperative that begins the verse.
Heb “your word.” Many medieval Hebrew mss as well as several ancient versions read the plural here.

18.text: Open my eyes so I can truly see the marvelous things in your law.

notes.text: Heb “uncover.” The verb form ‏גַּל‎ (gal) is an apocopated Piel imperative from ‏גָּלָה‎ (galah, see GKC 214 §75.cc).
The cohortative with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.

19.text: I am a resident foreigner in this land. Do not hide your commands from me.

notes.text: Heb This metaphor probably derives from Lev 25:23, which uses the terms ‏גֵּר‎ (ger, “resident foreigner”) and ‏תּוֹשָׁב‎; (toshav, “resident/temporary settler”). Lev 25:23 emphasizes that Israel would be a guest on God’s land. They were attached to the Lord’s household; they did not own the land. Cf. also Ps 39:12 and Gen 23:4.

20.text: I desperately long to know your regulations at all times.

notes.text: Heb “my soul languishes for longing for.”

21.text: You reprimand arrogant people. Those who stray from your commands are doomed.

notes.text: Heb “accursed.” The traditional punctuation of the Hebrew text takes “accursed” with the previous line (“arrogant, accursed ones”), but it is preferable to take it with the second line as the predicate of the statement.

22.text: Spare me shame and humiliation, for I observe your rules.

notes.text: Heb “roll away from upon me.” Some derive the imperatival form ‏גַּל‎ (gal) from ‏גָּלָה‎ (galah, “uncover,” as in v. 18), but here the form is from ‏גָּלַל‎ (galal, “roll”; see Josh 5:9, where ‏חֶרְפָּה‎ [kherpah, “shame; reproach”] also appears as object of the verb). Some, following the lead of a Dead Sea scroll (11QPsa), emend the form to ‏גֹּל‎ (gol).

23.text: Though rulers plot and slander me, your servant meditates on your statutes.

notes.text: Heb “though rulers sit, about me they talk together.” (For another example of the Niphal of ‏דָּבַר‎ (davar) used with a suffixed form of the preposition ‏ב‎ (bet), see Ezek 33:30.)

24.text: Yes, I find delight in your rules; they give me guidance. ד (Dalet)

notes.text: Heb “men of my counsel.” That is, God’s rules are like advisers to the psalmist, for they teach him how to live in a godly manner that refutes the accusations of his enemies.

25.text: I collapse in the dirt. Revive me with your word.

notes.text: Heb “my soul clings to the dirt.” The Hebrew term ‏נֶפֶשׁ‎ (nefesh, “being; soul”) with a pronominal suffix is often equivalent to a pronoun, especially in poetry (see BDB 660 s.v. ‏נֶפֶשׁ‎ 4.a).
Heb “according to your word.” Many medieval Hebrew mss read the plural “your words.”

26.text: I told you about my ways and you answered me. Teach me your statutes.

notes.text: Heb “my ways I proclaimed.”

27.text: Help me to understand what your precepts mean. Then I can meditate on your marvelous teachings.

notes.text: Heb “the way of your precepts make me understand.”
The cohortative with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.
Heb “your amazing things,” which refers here to the teachings of the law (see v. 18).

28.text: I collapse from grief. Sustain me by your word.

notes.text: Some translate “my soul weeps,” taking the verb ‏דָלַף‎ (dalaf) from a root meaning “to drip; to drop” (BDB 196 s.v. ‏דֶּלַף‎). On the basis of cognate evidence from Arabic and Akkadian, HALOT 223 s.v. II ‏דלף‎ proposes a homonymic root here, meaning “be sleepless.” Following L. C. Allen (Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 127, 135) the translation assumes that the verb is cognate with Ugaritic dlp, “to collapse; to crumple” in CTA 2 iv. 17, 26. See G. R. Driver, Canaanite Myths and Legends, 44, 144.
Heb “according to your word.” Many medieval Hebrew mss read the plural “your words.”

29.text: Remove me from the path of deceit. Graciously give me your law.

notes.text: The “path of deceit” refers to a lifestyle characterized by deceit and disloyalty to God. It stands in contrast to the “way of faithfulness” in v. 30.
Heb “be gracious to me.” The verb is used metonymically here for “graciously giving” the law. (See Gen 33:5, where Jacob uses this verb in describing how God had graciously given him children.)

30.text: I choose the path of faithfulness; I am committed to your regulations.

notes.text: BDB 1000-1001 s.v. I ‏שָׁוָה‎ derives the verb from the first homonym listed, meaning “to agree with; to be like; to resemble.” It here means (in the Piel stem) “to be accounted suitable,” which in turn would mean by metonymy “to accept; to be committed to.” Some prefer to derive the verb from a homonym meaning “to place; to set,” but in this case an elliptical prepositional phrase must be understood, “I place your regulations [before me]” (see Ps 16:8).

31.text: I hold fast to your rules. O Lord, do not let me be ashamed.

notes.text: Or “cling to.”

32.text: I run along the path of your commands, for you enable me to do so. ה (He)

notes.text: Heb “for you make wide my heart.” The “heart” is viewed here as the seat of the psalmist’s volition and understanding. The Lord gives the psalmist the desire and moral understanding that are foundational to the willing obedience depicted metaphorically in the preceding line. In Isa 60:5 the expression “your heart will be wide” means “your heart will swell with pride,” but here the nuance appears to be different.

33.text: Teach me, O Lord, the lifestyle prescribed by your statutes, so that I might observe it continually.

notes.text: Heb “the way of your statutes.”

Heb “and I will keep it to the end.” The prefixed verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative. The Hebrew term ‏עֵקֶב‎ (ʿeqev) is understood to mean “end” here. Another option is to take ‏עֵקֶב‎ as meaning “reward” here (see Ps 19:11) and to translate, “so that I might observe it and be rewarded.”

34.text: Give me understanding so that I might observe your law, and keep it with all my heart.

notes.text: The two prefixed verbal forms with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicate purpose/result after the introductory imperative.

35.text: Guide me in the path of your commands, for I delight to walk in it.

notes.text: Or “make me walk.”
Heb “for in it I delight.”

36.text: Give me a desire for your rules, rather than for wealth gained unjustly.

notes.text: Heb “turn my heart to your rules.”
Heb “and not unjust gain.”

37.text: Turn my eyes away from what is worthless. Revive me with your word.

notes.text: Heb “Make my eyes pass by from looking at what is worthless.”
Heb “by your word.”

38.text: Confirm to your servant your promise, which you made to the one who honors you.

notes.text: Heb “word.”
Heb “which [is] for your fear,” that is, the promise made to those who exhibit fear of God.

39.text: Take away the insults that I dread. Indeed, your regulations are good.

notes.text: Heb “my reproach that I fear.”
Or “for.”

40.text: Look, I long for your precepts. Revive me with your deliverance. ו (Vav)

notes.text: Or “righteousness.”

41.text: May I experience your loyal love, O Lord, and your deliverance, as you promised.

notes.text: Heb “and may your loyal love come to me.”
Or “salvation” (so many English versions).
Heb “according to your word.”

42.text: Then I will have a reply for the one who insults me, for I trust in your word.

notes.text: Heb “and I will answer [the] one who insults me a word.” The prefixed verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the jussive (see v. 41).

43.text: Do not completely deprive me of a truthful testimony, for I await your justice.

notes.text: Heb “do not snatch from my mouth a word of truth to excess.” The psalmist wants to be able to give a reliable testimony about the Lord’s loyal love (vv. 41-42), but if God does not intervene, the psalmist will be deprived of doing so, for the evidence of such love (i.e., deliverance) will be lacking.

44.text: Then I will keep your law continually now and for all time.

notes.text: The cohortative verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the negated jussive (see v. 43).
Or “forever and ever.”

45.text: I will be secure, for I seek your precepts.

notes.text: Heb “and I will walk about in a wide place.” The cohortative with prefixed vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive gives a further consequence of the anticipated positive divine response (see vv. 43-44). Another option is to take the cohortative as expressing the psalmist’s request. In this case one could translate, “and please give me security.”

46.text: I will speak about your regulations before kings and not be ashamed.

notes.text: The series of four cohortatives with prefixed vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive in vv. 46-48 list further consequences of the anticipated positive divine response to the request made in v. 43.

47.text: I will find delight in your commands, which I love.

48.text: I will lift my hands to your commands, which I love, and I will meditate on your statutes. ז (Zayin)

notes.text: Lifting the hands is often associated with prayer (Pss 28:2; 63:4; Lam 2:19). (1) Because praying to God’s law borders on the extreme, some prefer to emend the text to “I lift up my hands to you,” eliminating “your commands, which I love” as dittographic. In this view these words were accidentally repeated from the previous verse. (2) However, it is possible that the psalmist closely associates the law with God himself because he views the law as the expression of the divine will. (3) Another option is that “lifting the hands” does not refer to prayer here, but to the psalmist’s desire to receive and appropriate the law. (4) Still others understand this to be an action praising God’s commands (so NCV; cf. TEV, CEV, NLT).

49.text: Remember your word to your servant, for you have given me hope.

50.text: This is what comforts me in my trouble, for your promise revives me.

notes.text: The demonstrative “this” refers back to the hope just mentioned or forward to the statement in the second line concerning the promise’s power to revive. See the note on the word “me” at the end of the verse for further discussion.

The hope generated by the promise (see v. 49b) brings comfort because (note “for” at the beginning of the line) the promise revives the psalmist’s spirits. Another option is to take ‏כִּי‎ (ki) at the beginning of the second line in the sense of “that,” in which case “this” refers to the promise’s power to revive.

51.text: Arrogant people do nothing but scoff at me. Yet I do not turn aside from your law.

notes.text: Heb “scoff at me to excess.”

52.text: I remember your ancient regulations, O Lord, and console myself.

notes.text: Heb “I remember your regulations from of old.” The prepositional phrase “from of old” apparently modifies “your regulations,” alluding to the fact that God revealed them to Israel in the distant past. Another option is to understand the prepositional phrase as modifying the verb, in which case one might translate, “I have long remembered your regulations.”
Or “find comfort.”

53.text: Rage takes hold of me because of the wicked, those who reject your law.

54.text: Your statutes have been my songs in the house where I live.

notes.text: Heb “songs were your statutes to me.”

Heb “in the house of my dwelling place.” Some take the Hebrew noun ‏מָגוֹר‎ (magor) in the sense of “temporary abode,” and see this as a reference to the psalmist’s status as a resident foreigner (see v. 19). But the noun can refer to a dwelling place in general (see Ps 55:15).

55.text: I remember your name during the night, O Lord, and I will keep your law.

notes.text: The cohortative verbal form expresses the psalmist’s resolve to obey the law.

56.text: This has been my practice, for I observe your precepts. ח (Khet)

notes.text: Heb “this has been to me.” The demonstrative “this” (1) refers back to the practices mentioned in vv. 54-55, or (2) looks forward to the statement in the second line, in which case the ‏כִּי‎ (ki) at the beginning of the second line should be translated “that.”

57.text: The Lord is my source of security. I have determined to follow your instructions.

notes.text: Heb “my portion [is] the Lord.” The psalmist compares the Lord to landed property, which was foundational to economic stability in ancient Israel (see Ps 16:5).
Heb “I said.”
Heb “to keep your words” (see v. 9).

58.text: I seek your favor with all my heart. Have mercy on me as you promised.

notes.text: Heb “I appease your face.”
Heb “according to your word.”

59.text: I consider my actions and follow your rules.

notes.text: Heb “my ways.”
Heb “and I turn my feet toward.”

60.text: I keep your commands eagerly and without delay.

notes.text: Heb “I hurry and I do not delay to keep your commands.”

61.text: The ropes of the wicked tighten around me, but I do not forget your law.

notes.text: Heb “surround.”

62.text: In the middle of the night I arise to thank you for your just regulations.

notes.text: The psalmist uses an imperfect verbal form to emphasize that this is his continuing practice.

63.text: I am a friend to all your loyal followers, and to those who keep your precepts.

notes.text: Heb “to all who fear you.”

64.text: O Lord, your loyal love fills the earth. Teach me your statutes! ט (Tet)

65.text: You are good to your servant, O Lord, just as you promised.

notes.text: Heb “do good.”
Heb “according to your word.”

66.text: Teach me proper discernment and understanding. For I consider your commands to be reliable.

notes.text: Heb “goodness of taste.” Here “taste” refers to moral and ethical discernment.
Heb “for I believe in your commands.”

67.text: Before I was afflicted I used to stray off, but now I keep your instructions.

notes.text: Heb “before I suffered, I was straying off.”
Heb “your word.”

68.text: You are good and you do good. Teach me your statutes.

69.text: Arrogant people smear my reputation with lies, but I observe your precepts with all my heart.

notes.text: Heb “smear over me a lie.”

70.text: Their hearts are calloused, but I find delight in your law.

notes.text: Heb “their heart is insensitive like fat.”

71.text: It was good for me to suffer, so that I might learn your statutes.

72.text: The law you have revealed is more important to me than thousands of pieces of gold and silver. י (Yod)

notes.text: Heb “better to me [is] the law of your mouth than thousands of gold and silver.”

73.text: Your hands made me and formed me. Give me understanding so that I might learn your commands.

notes.text: Heb “made me and established me.” The two verbs also appear together in Deut 32:6, where God, compared to a father, is said to have “made and established” Israel.
The cohortative verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.

74.text: Your loyal followers will be glad when they see me, for I find hope in your word.

notes.text: Heb “those who fear you will see me and rejoice.”

75.text: I know, Lord, that your regulations are just. You disciplined me because of your faithful devotion to me.

notes.text: In this context (note the second line) the Hebrew term ‏מִשְׁפָּטִים‎ (mishpatim), which so often refers to the regulations of God’s law elsewhere in this psalm, may refer instead to his decisions or disciplinary judgment.
Heb “and [in] faithfulness you afflicted me.”

76.text: May your loyal love console me, as you promised your servant.

notes.text: Heb “according to your word to your servant.”

77.text: May I experience your compassion, so I might live. For I find delight in your law.

notes.text: Heb “and may your compassion come to me.”

78.text: May the arrogant be humiliated, for they have slandered me. But I meditate on your precepts.

notes.text: Heb “for [with] falsehood they have denied me justice.”

79.text: May your loyal followers turn to me, those who know your rules.

notes.text: Heb “those who fear you.”

80.text: May I be fully committed to your statutes, so that I might not be ashamed. כ (Kaf)

notes.text: Heb “may my heart be complete in your statutes.”

81.text: I desperately long for your deliverance. I find hope in your word.

notes.text: Heb “my soul pines for.” See Ps 84:2.

82.text: My eyes grow tired as I wait for your promise to be fulfilled. I say, “When will you comfort me?”

notes.text: Heb “my eyes fail for your word.” The psalmist has intently kept his eyes open, looking for God to intervene, but now his eyes are watery and bloodshot, impairing his vision. See Ps 69:3.
Heb “saying.”

83.text: For I am like a wineskin dried up in smoke. I do not forget your statutes.

notes.text: Or “even though.”
The Hebrew word ‏נֹאד‎ (noʾd, “leather container”) refers to a container made from animal skin which is used to hold wine or milk (see Josh 9:4, 13; Judg 4:19; 1 Sam 16:20).
Heb “in the smoke.”

84.text: How long must your servant endure this? When will you judge those who pursue me?

notes.text: Heb “How long are the days of your servant?”

85.text: The arrogant dig pits to trap me, which violates your law.

notes.text: Heb “for me.”
Heb “which [is] not according to your law.”

86.text: All your commands are reliable. I am pursued without reason. Help me!

notes.text: God’s commands are a reliable guide to right and wrong. By keeping them the psalmist is doing what is right, yet he is still persecuted.

87.text: They have almost destroyed me here on the earth, but I do not reject your precepts.

88.text: Revive me with your loyal love, that I might keep the rules you have revealed. ל (Lamed)

notes.text: Heb “according to.”
The cohortative verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.
Heb “of your mouth.”

89.text: O Lord, your instructions endure; they stand secure in heaven.

notes.text: Heb “Forever, O Lord, your word stands firm in heaven,” or “Forever, O Lord, [is] your word; it stands firm in heaven.” The translation assumes that “your word” refers here to the body of divine instructions contained in the law (note the frequent references to the law in vv. 92-96). See vv. 9, 16-17, 57, 101, 105, 130, 139 and 160-61. The reference in v. 86 to God’s law being faithful favors this interpretation. Another option is that “your word” refers to God’s assuring word of promise, mentioned in vv. 25, 28, 42, 65, 74, 81, 107, 114, 147 and 169. In this case one might translate, “O Lord, your promise is reliable, it stands firm in heaven.”

90.text: You demonstrate your faithfulness to all generations. You established the earth and it stood firm.

notes.text: Heb “to a generation and a generation [is] your faithfulness.”

91.text: Today they stand firm by your decrees, for all things are your servants.

92.text: If I had not found encouragement in your law, I would have died in my sorrow.

notes.text: Heb “if your law had not been my delight.”
Or “my suffering.”

93.text: I will never forget your precepts, for by them you have revived me.

94.text: I belong to you. Deliver me! For I seek your precepts.

95.text: The wicked prepare to kill me, yet I concentrate on your rules.

notes.text: Heb “the wicked wait for me to kill me.”

96.text: I realize that everything has its limits, but your commands are beyond full comprehension. מ (Mem)

notes.text: Heb “to every perfection I have seen an end, your command is very wide.” God’s law is beyond full comprehension, which is why the psalmist continually studies it (vv. 95, 97).

97.text: O how I love your law! All day long I meditate on it.

98.text: Your commandments make me wiser than my enemies, for I am always aware of them.

notes.text: The plural form needs to be revocalized as a singular in order to agree with the preceding singular verb and the singular pronoun in the next line. The Lord’s “command” refers here to the law (see Ps 19:8).

99.text: I have more insight than all my teachers, for I meditate on your rules.
