100.text: I am more discerning than those older than I, for I observe your precepts.

101.text: I stay away from every evil path, so that I might keep your instructions.

notes.text: Heb “I hold back my feet.”
Heb “your word.” Many medieval Hebrew mss read the plural.

102.text: I do not turn aside from your regulations, for you teach me.

103.text: Your words are sweeter in my mouth than honey!

notes.text: Heb “How smooth they are to my palate, your word, more than honey to my mouth.” A few medieval Hebrew mss, as well as several other ancient witnesses, read the plural “your words,” which can then be understood as the subject of the plural verb “they are smooth.”

104.text: Your precepts give me discernment. Therefore I hate all deceitful actions. נ (Nun)

notes.text: Heb “every false path.”

105.text: Your word is a lamp to walk by, and a light to illumine my path.

notes.text: Many medieval Hebrew mss read the plural (“words”).
Heb “[is] a lamp for my foot and a light for my path.”

106.text: I have vowed and solemnly sworn to keep your just regulations.

107.text: I am suffering terribly. O Lord, revive me with your word.

notes.text: Heb “according to your word.”

108.text: O Lord, please accept the freewill offerings of my praise. Teach me your regulations.

notes.text: Heb “of my mouth.”

109.text: My life is in continual danger, but I do not forget your law.

notes.text: Heb “my life [is] in my hands continually.”

110.text: The wicked lay a trap for me, but I do not wander from your precepts.

111.text: I claim your rules as my permanent possession, for they give me joy.

notes.text: Heb “for the joy of my heart [are] they.”

112.text: I am determined to obey your statutes at all times, to the very end. ס (Samek)

notes.text: Heb “I turn my heart to do.”

113.text: I hate people with divided loyalties, but I love your law.

notes.text: Heb “divided ones.” The word occurs only here; it appears to be derived from a verbal root, attested in Arabic, meaning “to split” (see HALOT 762 s.v. *‏סֵעֵף‎). Since the psalmist is emphasizing his unswerving allegiance to God and his law, the term probably refers to those who lack such loyalty. The translation is similar to that suggested by L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 131.

114.text: You are my hiding place and my shield. I find hope in your word.

115.text: Turn away from me, you evil men, so that I can observe the commands of my God.

notes.text: The cohortative verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.
The psalmist has already declared that he observes God’s commands despite persecution, so here the idea must be “so that I might observe the commands of my God unhindered by threats.”

116.text: Sustain me as you promised, so that I will live. Do not disappoint me.

notes.text: Heb “according to your word.”
The prefixed verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.
Heb “do not make me ashamed of my hope.” After the Hebrew verb ‏בּוֹשׁ‎ (bosh, “to be ashamed”) the preposition ‏מִן‎ (min, “from”) often introduces the reason for shame.

117.text: Support me, so that I will be delivered. Then I will focus on your statutes continually.

notes.text: Or “and that I might focus.” The two cohortatives with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicate purpose/result after the imperative at the beginning of the verse.

118.text: You despise all who stray from your statutes, for such people are deceptive and unreliable.

notes.text: The Hebrew verb ‏סָלָה‎ (salah, “to disdain”) occurs only here and in Lam 1:15. Cognate usage in Aramaic and Akkadian, as well as Lam 1:15, suggest it may have a concrete nuance of “to throw away.”
Heb “for their deceit [is] falsehood.”

119.text: You remove all the wicked of the earth like slag. Therefore I love your rules.

notes.text: Traditionally “dross” (so KJV, ASV, NIV). The metaphor comes from metallurgy; “slag” is the substance left over after the metallic ore has been refined.
As he explains in the next verse, the psalmist’s fear of judgment motivates him to obey God’s rules.

120.text: My body trembles because I fear you; I am afraid of your judgments. ע (Ayin)

notes.text: Heb “my flesh.”
The Hebrew verb ‏סָמַר‎ (samar, “to tremble”) occurs only here and in Job 4:15.
Heb “from fear of you.” The pronominal suffix on the noun is an objective genitive.

121.text: I do what is fair and right. Do not abandon me to my oppressors.

notes.text: Heb “do justice and righteousness.”

122.text: Guarantee the welfare of your servant. Do not let the arrogant oppress me.

notes.text: Heb “be surety for your servant for good.”

123.text: My eyes grow tired as I wait for your deliverance, for your reliable promise to be fulfilled.

notes.text: Heb “my eyes fail for your deliverance.” The psalmist has intently kept his eyes open, looking for God to intervene, but now his eyes are watery and bloodshot, impairing his vision. See the similar phrase in v. 82.
Heb “and for the word of your faithfulness.”

124.text: Show your servant your loyal love. Teach me your statutes.

notes.text: Heb “do with your servant according to your loyal love.”

125.text: I am your servant. Give me insight, so that I can understand your rules.

notes.text: or “know.” The cohortative verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.

126.text: It is time for the Lord to act— they break your law.

127.text: For this reason I love your commands more than gold, even purest gold.

notes.text: “For this reason” connects logically with the statement made in v. 126. Because the judgment the psalmist fears (see vv. 119-120) is imminent, he remains loyal to God’s law.

128.text: For this reason I carefully follow all your precepts. I hate all deceitful actions. פ (Pe)

notes.text: Heb “for this reason all the precepts of everything I regard as right.” The phrase “precepts of everything” is odd. It is preferable to take the ‏כ‎ (kaf) on ‏כֹּל‎ (kol, “everything) with the preceding form as a pronominal suffix, “your precepts,” and the ‏ל‎ (lamed) with the following verb as an emphatic particle. See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 138.
Heb “every false path.”

129.text: Your rules are marvelous. Therefore I observe them.

130.text: Your instructions are a doorway through which light shines. They give insight to the untrained.

notes.text: Heb “the doorway of your words gives light.” God’s “words” refer here to the instructions in his law (see vv. 9, 57).
Heb “it [i.e., the doorway] gives.”
Or “the [morally] naive,” that is, the one who is young and still in the process of learning right from wrong and distinguishing wisdom from folly. See Pss 19:7; 116:6.

131.text: I open my mouth and pant, because I long for your commands.

notes.text: The verb occurs only here in the OT.

132.text: Turn toward me and extend mercy to me, as you typically do to your loyal followers.

notes.text: Heb “according to custom toward the lovers of your name.” The “lovers of” God’s “name” are the Lord’s loyal followers. See Pss 5:11; 69:36; Isa 56:6.

133.text: Direct my steps by your word. Do not let any sin dominate me.

notes.text: God’s “word” refers here to his law (see v. 11).

134.text: Deliver me from oppressive men, so that I can keep your precepts.

notes.text: Or “redeem me.”
The cohortative verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.

135.text: Smile on your servant. Teach me your statutes!

notes.text: Heb “cause your face to shine.”

136.text: Tears stream down from my eyes, because people do not keep your law. צ (Tsade)

notes.text: Heb “[with] flowing streams my eyes go down.”
Heb “they”; even though somewhat generic, the referent (people) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

137.text: You are just, O Lord, and your judgments are fair.

138.text: The rules you impose are just, and absolutely reliable.

notes.text: Heb “you commanded [in] justice your rules.”

139.text: My zeal consumes me, for my enemies forget your instructions.

notes.text: or “zeal.”
Heb “destroys,” in a hyperbolic sense.
Heb “your words.”

140.text: Your word is absolutely pure, and your servant loves it.

141.text: I am insignificant and despised, yet I do not forget your precepts.

142.text: Your justice endures, and your law is reliable.

notes.text: Heb “your justice [is] justice forever.”
Or “truth.”

143.text: Distress and hardship confront me, yet I find delight in your commands.

notes.text: Heb “find.”

144.text: Your rules remain just. Give me insight so that I can live. ק (Qof)

notes.text: Heb “just are your rules forever.”
The cohortative verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.

145.text: I cried out with all my heart, “Answer me, O Lord! I will observe your statutes.”

146.text: I cried out to you, “Deliver me, so that I can keep your rules.”

notes.text: The cohortative verbal form with vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.

147.text: I am up before dawn crying for help. I find hope in your word.

148.text: My eyes anticipate the nighttime hours, so that I can meditate on your word.

149.text: Listen to me because of your loyal love. O Lord, revive me, as you typically do.

notes.text: Heb “my voice.”
Heb “according to.”
Heb “according to your custom.”

150.text: Those who are eager to do wrong draw near; they are far from your law.

notes.text: Heb “those who pursue.”

151.text: You are near, O Lord, and all your commands are reliable.

notes.text: Or “truth.”

152.text: I learned long ago that you ordained your rules to last. ר (Resh)

notes.text: Heb “long ago I knew concerning your rules, that forever you established them.” See v. 89 for the same idea. The translation assumes that the preposition ‏מִן‎ (min) prefixed to “your rules” introduces the object of the verb ‏יָדַע‎ (yadaʿ), as in 1 Sam 23:23. Another option is that the preposition indicates source, in which case one might translate, “Long ago I realized from your rules that forever you established them” (cf. NIV, NRSV).

153.text: See my pain and rescue me. For I do not forget your law.

154.text: Fight for me and defend me. Revive me with your word.

notes.text: Or “argue my case.”
Heb “and redeem me.” The verb “redeem” casts the Lord in the role of a leader who protects members of his extended family in times of need and crisis (see Ps 19:14).

155.text: The wicked have no chance for deliverance, for they do not seek your statutes.

notes.text: Heb “far from the wicked [is] deliverance.”

156.text: Your compassion is great, O Lord. Revive me, as you typically do.

notes.text: Heb “according to your customs.”

157.text: The enemies who chase me are numerous. Yet I do not turn aside from your rules.

notes.text: Heb “many [are] those who chase me and my enemies.”

158.text: I take note of the treacherous and despise them, because they do not keep your instructions.

notes.text: Heb “your word.”

159.text: See how I love your precepts. O Lord, revive me with your loyal love.

160.text: Your instructions are totally reliable; all your just regulations endure. שׂ/שׁ (Sin/Shin)

notes.text: Heb “the head of your word is truth, and forever [is] all your just regulation.” The term “head” is used here of the “sum total” of God’s instructions.

161.text: Rulers pursue me for no reason, yet I am more afraid of disobeying your instructions.

notes.text: Heb “and because of your instructions my heart trembles.” The psalmist’s healthy “fear” of the consequences of violating God’s instructions motivates him to obey them. See v. 120.

162.text: I rejoice in your instructions, like one who finds much plunder.

notes.text: Heb “like one who finds great plunder.” See Judg 5:30. The image is that of a victorious warrior who finds a large amount of plunder on the field of battle.

163.text: I hate and despise deceit; I love your law.

164.text: Seven times a day I praise you because of your just regulations.

notes.text: The number “seven” is use rhetorically to suggest thoroughness.

165.text: Those who love your law are completely secure; nothing causes them to stumble.

notes.text: Heb “great peace [is] to the lovers of your law.”
Heb “and there is no stumbling to them.”

166.text: I hope for your deliverance, O Lord, and I obey your commands.

notes.text: Heb “do.”

167.text: I keep your rules; I love them greatly.

168.text: I keep your precepts and rules, for you are aware of everything I do. ת (Tav)

notes.text: Heb “for all my ways [are] before you.”

169.text: Listen to my cry for help, O Lord. Give me insight by your word.

notes.text: Heb “may my cry approach before you.”

170.text: Listen to my appeal for mercy. Deliver me, as you promised.

notes.text: Heb “may my appeal for mercy come before you.”
Heb “according to your speech.”

171.text: May praise flow freely from my lips, for you teach me your statutes.

172.text: May my tongue sing about your instructions, for all your commands are just.

notes.text: Heb “your word.”

173.text: May your hand help me, for I choose to obey your precepts.

notes.text: The words “to obey” are not in the Hebrew text, but have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons and for clarity.

174.text: I long for your deliverance, O Lord; I find delight in your law.

175.text: May I live and praise you. May your regulations help me.

notes.text: Heb “my life.”
God’s regulations will “help” the psalmist by giving him moral and ethical guidance.

176.text: I have wandered off like a lost sheep. Come looking for your servant, for I do not forget your commands.

notes.text: Heb “I stray like a lost sheep.” It is possible that the point of the metaphor is vulnerability: The psalmist, who is threatened by his enemies, feels as vulnerable as a straying, lost sheep. This would not suggest, however, that he has wandered from God’s path (see the second half of the verse, as well as v. 110).

1.text: In my distress I cried out to the Lord and he answered me.

2.text: I said, “O Lord, rescue me from those who lie with their lips and those who deceive with their tongues.

notes.text: The words “I said” are supplied in the translation for clarification. See the introductory note for this psalm.
Or “my life.”
Heb “from a lip of falsehood.”
Heb “from a tongue of deception.”

3.text: How will he severely punish you, you deceptive talker?

notes.text: Heb “What will he give to you, and what will he add to you, O tongue of deception?” The psalmist addresses his deceptive enemies. The Lord is the understood subject of the verbs “give” and “add.” The second part of the question echoes a standard curse formula, “thus the Lord/God will do…and thus he will add” (see Ruth 1:17; 1 Sam 3:17; 14:44; 20:13; 25:22; 2 Sam 3:9, 35; 19:13; 1 Kgs 2:23; 2 Kgs 6:31).

4.text: Here’s how! With the sharp arrows of warriors, with arrowheads forged over the hot coals.

notes.text: The words “here’s how” are supplied in the translation as a clarification. In v. 4 the psalmist answers the question he raises in v. 3.
Heb “with coals of the wood of the broom plant.” The wood of the broom plant was used to make charcoal, which in turn was used to fuel the fire used to forge the arrowheads.

5.text: How miserable I am. For I have lived temporarily in Meshech; I have resided among the tents of Kedar.

notes.text: Or “woe to me.” The Hebrew term ‏אוֹיָה‎ (ʾoyah, “woe”) which occurs only here, is an alternate form of ‏אוֹי‎ (ʾoy).
Heb “I live as a resident foreigner.”

Meshech was located in central Anatolia (modern Turkey). Kedar was located in the desert to east-southeast of Israel. Because of the reference to Kedar, it is possible that Ps 120:5 refers to a different Meshech, perhaps one associated with the individual mentioned as a descendant of Aram in 1 Chr 1:17. (However, the LXX in 1 Chr 1:17 follows the parallel text in Gen 10:23, which reads “Mash,” not Meshech.) It is, of course, impossible that the psalmist could have been living in both the far north and the east at the same time. For this reason one must assume that he is recalling his experience as a wanderer among the nations or that he is using the geographical terms metaphorically and sarcastically to suggest that the enemies who surround him are like the barbarians who live in these distant regions. For a discussion of the problem, see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 146.

6.text: For too long I have had to reside with those who hate peace.

notes.text: The singular participial form probably has a representative function here. The psalmist envisions the typical hater of peace who represents the entire category of such individuals.

7.text: I am committed to peace, but when I speak, they want to make war.

notes.text: Heb “I, peace.”
Heb “they [are] for war.”

1.text: I look up toward the hills. From where does my help come?

notes.text: Heb “I lift my eyes.”

The Hebrew term ‏מֵאַיִן‎ (meʾayin) is interrogative, not relative, in function. Rather than directly stating that his source of help descends from the hills, the psalmist is asking, “From where does my help come?” Nevertheless, the first line does indicate that he is looking toward the hills for help, probably indicating that he is looking up toward the sky, or up toward the temple, in anticipation of supernatural intervention. The psalmist assumes the dramatic role of one needing help. He answers his own question in v. 2.

2.text: My help comes from the Lord, the Creator of heaven and earth.

notes.text: Heb “my help [is] from with the Lord.”
Or “Maker.”

3.text: May he not allow your foot to slip. May your Protector not sleep.

notes.text: Heb “the one who guards you.”

The prefixed verbal forms following the negative particle ‏אַל‎ (ʾal) appear to be jussives. As noted above, if they are taken as true jussives of prayer, then the speaker in v. 3 would appear to be distinct from both the speaker in vv. 1-2 and the speaker in vv. 4-8. However, according to GKC 322 §109.e), the jussives are used rhetorically here “to express the conviction that something cannot or should not happen.” In this case one should probably translate, “he will not allow your foot to slip, your protector will not sleep,” and understand just one speaker in vv. 4-8. But none of the examples in GKC for this use of the jussive are compelling.

4.text: Look! Israel’s Protector does not sleep or slumber.

notes.text: Heb “the one who guards Israel.”

5.text: The Lord is your protector; the Lord is the shade at your right hand.

6.text: The sun will not harm you by day, or the moon by night.

notes.text: One hardly thinks of the moon’s rays as being physically harmful, like those of the sun. The reference to the moon may simply lend poetic balance to the verse, but it is likely that the verse reflects an ancient, primitive belief that the moon could have an adverse effect on the mind (note the English expression “moonstruck,” which reflects such a belief). Another possibility is that the sun and moon stand by metonymy for harmful forces characteristic of the day and night, respectively.

7.text: The Lord will protect you from all harm; he will protect your life.

8.text: The Lord will protect you in all you do, now and forevermore.

notes.text: Heb “your going out and your coming in.”

1.text: I was glad because they said to me, “We will go to the Lord’s temple.”

notes.text: Heb “in the ones saying to me.” After the verb ‏שָׂמַח‎ (samakh), the preposition ‏ב‎ (bet) usually introduces the reason for joy.

2.text: Our feet are standing inside your gates, O Jerusalem.

notes.text: Or “were.”

3.text: Jerusalem is a city designed to accommodate an assembly.

notes.text: Heb “Jerusalem, which is built like a city which is joined to her together.” The meaning of the Hebrew text is unclear. Many regard this as a description of the compact way in which the city was designed or constructed. The translation assumes an emendation of the verb ‏חֻבְּרָה‎ (khubberah, “is joined”) to a noun ‏חֶבְרָה‎ (khevrah, “association; company”). The text then reads literally, “Jerusalem, which is built like a city which has a company together.” This in turn can be taken as a reference to Jerusalem’s role as a city where people congregated for religious festivals and other civic occasions (see vv. 4-5).

4.text: The tribes go up there, the tribes of the Lord, where it is required that Israel give thanks to the name of the Lord.

notes.text: Or “went up.”
Heb “which is where the tribes go up.”
Heb “[it is] a statute for Israel to give thanks to the name of the Lord.”

5.text: Indeed, the leaders sit there on thrones and make legal decisions, on the thrones of the house of David.

notes.text: Or “for.”
Or “sat.”
Heb “Indeed, there they sit [on] thrones for judgment, [on] thrones [belonging] to the house of David.”

6.text: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem. May those who love her prosper.

notes.text: Heb “ask [for].”
Or “be secure.”

7.text: May there be peace inside your defenses, and prosperity inside your fortresses.

notes.text: or “security.”
The psalmist uses second feminine singular pronominal forms to address personified Jerusalem.

8.text: For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors I will say, “May there be peace in you.”

9.text: For the sake of the temple of the Lord our God I will pray for you to prosper.

notes.text: Heb “I will seek good for you.” The psalmist will seek Jerusalem’s “good” through prayer.

1.text: I look up toward you, the one enthroned in heaven.

notes.text: Heb “I lift my eyes.”
Heb “sitting.” The Hebrew verb ‏יָשַׁב‎ (yashav) is here used metonymically of “sitting enthroned” (see Pss 9:7; 29:10; 55:19; 102:12).

2.text: Look, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a female servant look to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes will look to the Lord, our God, until he shows us favor.

notes.text: Servants look to their master for food, shelter, and other basic needs.

3.text: Show us favor, O Lord, show us favor! For we have had our fill of humiliation, and then some.

notes.text: Heb “for greatly we are filled [with] humiliation.”

4.text: We have had our fill of the taunts of the self-assured, of the contempt of the proud.

notes.text: Heb “greatly our soul is full to it.”

1.text: “If the Lord had not been on our side”— let Israel say this.—

2.text: if the Lord had not been on our side, when men attacked us,

notes.text: Heb “rose up against us.”

3.text: they would have swallowed us alive, when their anger raged against us.

4.text: The water would have overpowered us; the current would have overwhelmed us.

notes.text: Or “stream.”
Heb “would have passed over.”
Heb “our being.” The Hebrew term ‏נֶפֶשׁ‎ (nefesh) with a pronominal suffix is often equivalent to a pronoun, especially in poetry (see BDB 660 s.v. ‏נֶפֶשׁ‎ 4.a).

5.text: The raging water would have overwhelmed us.

notes.text: Heb “then they would have passed over our being, the raging waters.”

6.text: The Lord deserves praise, for he did not hand us over as prey to their teeth.

notes.text: Heb “blessed [be] the Lord.”
Heb “[the one] who.”

7.text: We escaped with our lives, like a bird from a hunter’s snare. The snare broke, and we escaped.

notes.text: Heb “our life escaped.”

8.text: Our deliverer is the Lord, the Creator of heaven and earth.

notes.text: Heb “our help [is] in the name of the Lord.”
Or “Maker.”

1.text: Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved and will endure forever.

2.text: As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the Lord surrounds his people, now and forevermore.

3.text: Indeed, the scepter of a wicked king will not settle upon the allotted land of the godly. Otherwise the godly might do what is wrong.

notes.text: Or “for.”
Heb “a scepter of wickedness.” The “scepter” symbolizes royal authority; when collocated with “wickedness” the phrase refers to an oppressive foreign conqueror.
Or “rest.”
Heb “so that the godly might not stretch out their hands in wrongdoing.” A wicked king who sets a sinful example can have an adverse moral and ethical effect on the people he rules.

4.text: Do good, O Lord, to those who are good, to the morally upright.

notes.text: Heb “pure of heart.” The “heart” is here viewed as the seat of one’s moral character and motives. The “pure of heart” are God’s faithful followers who trust in and love the Lord and, as a result, experience his deliverance (see Pss 7:10; 11:2; 32:11; 36:10; 64:10; 94:15; 97:11).

5.text: As for those who are bent on traveling a sinful path, may the Lord remove them, along with those who behave wickedly. May Israel experience peace.

notes.text: Heb “and the ones making their paths twisted.” A sinful lifestyle is compared to a twisting, winding road.

Heb “lead them away.” The prefixed verbal form is understood as a jussive of prayer here (note the prayers directly before and after this). Another option is to translate, “the Lord will remove them” (cf. NIV, NRSV).
Heb “the workers of wickedness.”
Heb “peace [be] upon Israel.” The statement is understood as a prayer (see Ps 122:8 for a similar prayer for peace).

1.text: When the Lord restored the well-being of Zion, we thought we were dreaming.

notes.text: Heb “turns with a turning [toward] Zion.” The Hebrew noun ‏שִׁיבַת‎ (shivat) occurs only here in the OT. For this reason many prefer to emend the form to the more common ‏שְׁבִית‎ (shevit) or ‏שְׁבוּת‎ (shevut), both of which are used as a cognate accusative of ‏שׁוּב‎ (shuv; see Ps 14:7). However an Aramaic cognate of ‏שְׁבִית‎ appears in an eighth century b.c. Old Aramaic inscription with the verb ‏שׁוּב‎. This cognate noun appears to mean “return” (see J. Fitzmyer, The Aramaic Treaties of Sefire [BibOr], 119-20) or “restoration” (see DNWSI 2:1125). Therefore it appears that ‏שְׁבִית‎ should be retained and understood as a cognate accusative of ‏שׁוּב‎. In addition to Fitzmyer (119-20) see L. C. Allen, who offers the literal translation, “turn with a turning toward” (Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 170). Allen takes ‏שְׁבִית‎ as construct and understands “Zion” as an objective genitive.

Heb “we were like dreamers.” This could mean the speakers were so overcome with ecstatic joy (see v. 3b) that they were like those who fantasize about pleasurable experiences in their sleep (see Isa 29:7-8). Since dreams are more commonly associated in the OT with prophetic visions, the community may be comparing their experience of God’s renewed favor to a prophet’s receiving divine visions. Just as a prophetic dream sweeps the individual into a different dimension and sometimes brings one face-to-face with God himself (see Gen 28:11-15; 1 Kgs 3:5-15), so the community was aware of God’s presence in a special way in the day of Zion’s restoration. Though the MT as it stands makes good sense, some choose to understand a homonymic root here meaning “to be healthy; to be strong” (see BDB 321 s.v. I ‏חָלַם‎) and translate, “we were like those restored to health.” This reading appears to have the support of several ancient translations as well as 11QPsa. See L. C. Allen (Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 170-71) for a discussion of the viewpoints.

2.text: At that time we laughed loudly and shouted for joy. At that time the nations said, “The Lord has accomplished great things for these people.”

notes.text: Heb “then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with a shout.”
Heb “they said among the nations.”

3.text: The Lord did indeed accomplish great things for us. We were happy.

4.text: O Lord, restore our well-being, just as the streams in the arid south are replenished.

notes.text: Heb “like the streams in the Negev.”

The streams in the arid south. Y. Aharoni writes of the streams in the Negev: “These usually dry wadis collect water on rainy days from vast areas. The situation is also aggravated by floods from the desert mountains and southern Judah. For a day or two or, more frequently, for only a few hours they turn into dangerous torrents” (Y. Aharoni, The Land of the Bible, 26). God’s people were experiencing a “dry season” after a time of past blessing; they pray here for a “flash flood” of his renewed blessing. This does not imply that they are requesting only a brief display of God’s blessing. Rather the point of comparison is the suddenness with which the wadis swell during a rain, as well as the depth and power of these raging waters. The community desires a sudden display of divine favor in which God overwhelms them with blessings.

5.text: Those who shed tears as they plant will shout for joy when they reap the harvest.

notes.text: O. Borowski says regarding this passage: “The dependence on rain for watering plants, the uncertainty of the quantity and timing of the rains, and the possibility of crop failure due to pests and diseases appear to have kept the farmer in a gloomy mood during sowing” (Agriculture in Iron Age Israel, 54). Perhaps the people were experiencing a literal drought, the effects of which cause them to lament their plight as they plant their seed in hopes that the rain would come. However, most take the language as metaphorical. Like a farmer sowing his seed, the covenant community was enduring hardship as they waited for a new outpouring of divine blessing. Yet they are confident that a time of restoration will come and relieve their anxiety, just as the harvest brings relief and joy to the farmer.

6.text: The one who weeps as he walks along, carrying his bag of seed, will certainly come in with a shout of joy, carrying his sheaves of grain.

notes.text: The noun occurs only here and in Job 28:18 in the OT. See HALOT 646 s.v. I ‏מֶשֶׁךְ‎ which gives “leather pouch” as the meaning.
The Hebrew noun ‏אֲלֻמָּה‎ (ʾalummah, “sheaf”) occurs only here and in Gen 37:7 in the OT.
Verse 6 expands the image of v. 5. See the note on the word “harvest” there.

1.text: If the Lord does not build a house, then those who build it work in vain. If the Lord does not guard a city, then the watchman stands guard in vain.

notes.text: The expression build a house may have a double meaning here. It may refer on the surface level to a literal physical structure in which a family lives, but at a deeper, metaphorical level it refers to building, perpetuating, and maintaining a family line. See Deut 25:9; Ruth 4:11; 1 Sam 2:35; 2 Sam 7:27; 1 Kgs 11:38; 1 Chr 17:10, 25. Having a family line provided security in ancient Israel.
The city symbolizes community security, which is the necessary framework for family security.

2.text: It is vain for you to rise early, come home late, and work so hard for your food. Yes, he provides for those whom he loves even when they sleep.

notes.text: Heb “[it is] vain for you, you who are early to rise, who delay sitting, who eat the food of hard work.” The three substantival participles are parallel and stand in apposition to the pronominal suffix on the preposition. See ‏לָכֶם‎ (lakhem, “for you”).
Here the Hebrew particle ‏כֵּן‎ (ken) is used to stress the following affirmation (see Josh 2:4; Ps 63:2).

Heb “he gives to his beloved, sleep.” The translation assumes that the Hebrew term ‏שֵׁנָא‎ (shenaʾ, “sleep,” an alternate form of ‏שֵׁנָה‎, shenah) is an adverbial accusative. The point seems to be this: Hard work by itself is not what counts, but one’s relationship to God, for God is able to bless an individual even while he sleeps. (There may even be a subtle allusion to the miracle of conception following sexual intercourse; see the reference to the gift of sons in the following verse.) The statement is not advocating laziness, but utilizing hyperbole to give perspective and to remind the addressees that God must be one’s first priority. Another option is to take “sleep” as the direct object: “yes, he gives sleep to his beloved” (cf. NIV, NRSV). In this case the point is this: Hard work by itself is futile, for only God is able to bless one with sleep, which metonymically refers to having one’s needs met. He blesses on the basis of one’s relationship to him, not on the basis of physical energy expended.

3.text: Yes, sons are a gift from the Lord; the fruit of the womb is a reward.

notes.text: or “look.”

Some prefer to translate this term with the gender neutral “children,” but “sons” are plainly in view here, as the following verses make clear. Daughters are certainly wonderful additions to a family, but in ancient Israelite culture sons were the “arrows” that gave a man security in his old age, for they could defend the family interests at the city gate, where the legal and economic issues of the community were settled.

4.text: Sons born during one’s youth are like arrows in a warrior’s hand.

notes.text: Heb “like arrows in the hand of a warrior, so [are] sons of youth.” Arrows are used in combat to defend oneself against enemies; sons are viewed here as providing social security and protection (see v. 5). The phrase “sons of youth” is elliptical, meaning “sons [born during the father’s] youth.” Such sons will have grown up to be mature adults and will have children of their own by the time the father reaches old age and becomes vulnerable to enemies. Contrast the phrase “son of old age” in Gen 37:3 (see also 44:20), which refers to Jacob’s age when Joseph was born.

5.text: How blessed is the man who fills his quiver with them. They will not be put to shame when they confront enemies at the city gate.

notes.text: Being “put to shame” is here metonymic for being defeated, probably in a legal context, as the reference to the city gate suggests. One could be humiliated (Ps 69:12) or deprived of justice (Amos 5:12) at the gate, but with strong sons to defend the family interests this was less likely to happen.
Heb “speak with.”

1.text: How blessed is every one of the Lord’s loyal followers, each one who keeps his commands.

notes.text: Heb “every fearer of the Lord.”
Heb “the one who walks in his ways.”

2.text: You will eat what you worked so hard to grow. You will be blessed and secure.

notes.text: The psalmist addresses the representative God-fearing man, as indicated by the references to “your wife” (v. 3) and “the man” (v. 4), as well as the second masculine singular pronominal and verbal forms in vv. 2-6.
Heb “the work of your hands, indeed you will eat.”
Heb “how blessed you [will be] and it will be good for you.”

3.text: Your wife will be like a fruitful vine in the inner rooms of your house; your children will be like olive branches, as they sit all around your table.

notes.text: The metaphor of the fruitful vine pictures the wife as fertile; she will give her husband numerous children (see the next line).
One could translate “sons” (see Ps 127:3 and the note on the word “sons” there), but here the term seems to refer more generally to children of both genders.

4.text: Yes indeed, the man who fears the Lord will be blessed in this way.

notes.text: Heb “look, indeed thus will the man, the fearer of the Lord, be blessed.”

5.text: May the Lord bless you from Zion, that you might see Jerusalem prosper all the days of your life,

notes.text: The prefixed verbal form is understood as a jussive of prayer (note the imperatives that are subordinated to this clause in vv. 5b-6a). Having described the blessings that typically come to the godly, the psalmist concludes by praying that this ideal may become reality for the representative godly man being addressed.
The imperative with prefixed vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding jussive.

6.text: and that you might see your grandchildren. May Israel experience peace.

notes.text: The imperative with prefixed vav (‏ו‎) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the jussive in v. 5a.
Heb “sons to your sons.”
Heb “peace [be] upon Israel.” The statement is understood as a prayer (see Ps 125:5).

1.text: “Since my youth they have often attacked me,” let Israel say.

2.text: “Since my youth they have often attacked me, but they have not defeated me.

3.text: The plowers plowed my back; they made their furrows long.

4.text: The Lord is just; he cut the ropes of the wicked.”

notes.text: The background of the metaphor is not entirely clear. Perhaps the “ropes” are those used to harness the ox for plowing (see Job 39:10). Verse 3 pictures the wicked plowing God’s people as if they were a field. But when God “cut the ropes” of their ox, as it were, they could no longer plow. The point of the metaphor seems to be that God took away the enemies’ ability to oppress his people. See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 187.

5.text: May all who hate Zion be humiliated and turned back.

6.text: May they be like the grass on the rooftops, which withers before one can even pull it up,

notes.text: The Hebrew verb ‏שָׁלַף‎ (shalaf) normally means “to draw [a sword]” or “to pull.” BDB 1025 s.v. suggests the meaning “to shoot up” here, but it is more likely that the verb here means “to pluck; to pull up,” a nuance attested for this word in later Hebrew and Aramaic (see Jastrow 1587 s.v. ‏שָׁלַף‎).

7.text: which cannot fill the reaper’s hand, or the lap of the one who gathers the grain.

8.text: Those who pass by will not say, “May you experience the Lord’s blessing! We pronounce a blessing on you in the name of the Lord.”

notes.text: The perfect verbal form is used for rhetorical effect; it describes an anticipated development as if it were already reality.

1.text: From the deep water I cry out to you, O Lord.

notes.text: Heb “depths,” that is, deep waters (see Ps 69:2, 14; Isa 51:10), a metaphor for the life-threatening danger faced by the psalmist.

2.text: O Lord, listen to me. Pay attention to my plea for mercy.

notes.text: Heb “my voice.”
Heb “may your ears be attentive to the voice of.”

3.text: If you, O Lord, were to keep track of sins, O Lord, who could stand before you?

notes.text: Heb “observe.”
The words “before you” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The psalmist must be referring to standing before God’s judgment seat. The rhetorical question expects the answer, “No one.”

4.text: But you are willing to forgive, so that you might be honored.

notes.text: Or “surely.”
Heb “for with you [there is] forgiveness.”
Or “consequently you are.”
Heb “feared.”

5.text: I rely on the Lord. I rely on him with my whole being; I wait for his assuring word.

notes.text: Or “wait for.”
Heb “my soul waits.”
Heb “his word.”

6.text: I yearn for the Lord, more than watchmen do for the morning, yes, more than watchmen do for the morning.

notes.text: Heb “my soul for the master.”
Heb “more than watchmen for the morning, watchmen for the morning.” The words “yes, more” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

7.text: O Israel, hope in the Lord, for the Lord exhibits loyal love, and is more than willing to deliver.

notes.text: Heb “for with the Lord [is] loyal love.”
Heb “and abundantly with him [is] redemption.”

8.text: He will deliver Israel from all their sins.

notes.text: Or “redeem.”

Or “all the consequences of their sins.” The Hebrew noun ‏עָוֹן‎ (ʿavon) can refer to sin, the guilt sin produces, or the consequences of sin. Only here is the noun collocated with the verb ‏פָּדָה‎ (padah, “to redeem; to deliver”). The psalmist may refer to deliverance from the national consequences of sin or forgiveness per se (v. 4). See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 192.

1.text: O Lord, my heart is not proud, nor do I have a haughty look. I do not have great aspirations, or concern myself with things that are beyond me.

notes.text: Heb “and my eyes are not lifted up.”
Heb “I do not walk in great things, and in things too marvelous for me.”

2.text: Indeed, I have calmed and quieted myself like a weaned child with its mother; I am content like a young child.

notes.text: Or “but.”
Heb “I make level and make quiet my soul.”
Heb “like a weaned [one] upon his mother.”
Heb “like the weaned [one] upon me, my soul.”

3.text: O Israel, hope in the Lord now and forevermore!

1.text: O Lord, for David’s sake remember all his strenuous effort,

notes.text: Heb “all his affliction.” This may refer to David’s strenuous and tireless efforts to make provision for the building of the temple (see 1 Chr 22:14). Some prefer to revocalize the text as ‏עַנַוָתוֹ‎ (ʿanavato, “his humility”).

2.text: and how he made a vow to the Lord, and swore an oath to the Powerful One of Jacob.

3.text: He said, “I will not enter my own home, or get into my bed.

notes.text: The words “he said” are supplied in the translation to clarify that what follows is David’s vow.
Heb “the tent of my house.”
Heb “go up upon the bed of my couch.”

4.text: I will not allow my eyes to sleep, or my eyelids to slumber,

5.text: until I find a place for the Lord, a fine dwelling place for the Powerful One of Jacob.”

notes.text: The plural form of the noun may indicate degree or quality; David envisions a special dwelling place (see Pss 43:3; 46:4; 84:1).
Or “the Mighty One of Jacob.”

6.text: Look, we heard about it in Ephrathah; we found it in the territory of Jaar.

notes.text: Rather than having an antecedent, the third feminine singular pronominal suffix here (and in the next line) appears to refer to the ark of the covenant, mentioned in v. 8. (The Hebrew term ‏אָרוֹן‎ [ʾaron, “ark”] is sometimes construed as grammatically feminine. See 1 Sam 4:17; 2 Chr 8:11.)

Some understand Ephrathah as a reference to Kiriath Jearim because of the apparent allusion to this site in the next line (see the note on “Jaar”). The ark was kept in Kiriath Jearim after the Philistines released it (see 1 Sam 6:21-7:2). However, the switch in verbs from “heard about” to “found” suggests that Ephrathah not be equated with Jair. The group who is speaking heard about the ark while they were in Ephrath. They then went to retrieve it from Kiriath Jearim (“Jaar”). It is more likely that Ephrathah refers to a site near Bethel (Gen 35:16, 19; 48:7) or to Bethlehem (Ruth 4:11; Mic 5:2).

Heb “fields of the forest.” The Hebrew term ‏יָעַר‎ (yaʿar, “forest”) is apparently a shortened alternative name for ‏קִרְיַת יְעָרִים‎ (qiryat yeʿarim, “Kiriath Jearim”), the place where the ark was kept after it was released by the Philistines and from which David and his men retrieved it (see 1 Chr 13:6).

7.text: Let us go to his dwelling place. Let us worship before his footstool.

notes.text: Or “bow down.”

8.text: Ascend, O Lord, to your resting place, you and the ark of your strength.

9.text: May your priests be clothed with integrity. May your loyal followers shout for joy.

notes.text: Or “righteousness.”

10.text: For the sake of David, your servant, do not reject your chosen king.

notes.text: Heb “do not turn away the face of your anointed one.”

11.text: The Lord made a reliable promise to David; he will not go back on his word. He said, “I will place one of your descendants on your throne.

notes.text: Heb “the Lord swore an oath to David [in] truth.”
Heb “he will not turn back from it.”
The words “he said” are supplied in the translation to clarify that what follows are the Lord’s words.
Heb “the fruit of your body.”

12.text: If your sons keep my covenant and the rules I teach them, their sons will also sit on your throne forever.”

13.text: Certainly the Lord has chosen Zion; he decided to make it his home.

notes.text: Or “for.”
Heb “he desired it for his dwelling place.”

14.text: He said, “This will be my resting place forever; I will live here, for I have chosen it.

notes.text: The words “he said” are added in the translation to clarify that what follows are the Lord’s words.
Heb “for I desired it.”

15.text: I will abundantly supply what she needs; I will give her poor all the food they need.

notes.text: Heb “I will greatly bless her provision.” The infinitive absolute is used to emphasize the verb.
Heb “her poor I will satisfy [with] food.”

16.text: I will protect her priests, and her godly people will shout exuberantly.

notes.text: Heb “and her priests I will clothe [with] deliverance.”
Heb “[with] shouting they will shout.” The infinitive absolute is used to emphasize the verb.

17.text: There I will make David strong; I have determined that my chosen king’s dynasty will continue.

notes.text: Heb “there I will cause a horn to sprout for David.” The horn of an ox underlies the metaphor (cf. Deut 33:17; 1 Kgs 22:11; Pss 18:2; 92:10). The horn of the wild ox is frequently a metaphor for military strength; the idiom “exalt the horn” signifies military victory (see 1 Sam 2:10; Pss 89:17, 24; 92:10; Lam 2:17). In the ancient Near East powerful warrior-kings would sometimes compare themselves to a goring bull that used its horns to kill its enemies. For examples, see P. Miller, “El the Warrior,” HTR 60 (1967): 422-25, and R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of Psalm 18/2 Samuel 22” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 135-36.
Heb “I have arranged a lamp for my anointed one.” Here the “lamp” is a metaphor for the Davidic dynasty (see 1 Kgs 11:36).

18.text: I will humiliate his enemies, and his crown will shine.”

notes.text: Heb “his enemies I will clothe [with] shame.”

1.text: Look! How good and how pleasant it is when brothers truly live in unity.

notes.text: This statement refers to the extended family structure of ancient Israel, where brothers would often live in proximity to one another (Deut 25:5), giving the family greater social prominence and security. However, in its later application in the nation of Israel it probably envisions unity within the covenant community. See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 212-15.

2.text: It is like fine oil poured on the head, which flows down the beard — Aaron’s beard, and then flows down his garments.

notes.text: Heb “[it is] like the good oil on the head, going down on the beard.”

Heb “which goes down in accordance with his measured things.” The Hebrew phrase ‏מִדּוֹתָיו‎ (middotayv, “his measured things”) refers here to the robes worn by Aaron. HALOT 546 s.v. *‏מַד‎ derives the term from ‏מַד‎ (mad, “robe”) rather than ‏מִדָּה‎ (middah, “measured thing”). Ugaritic md means “robe” and is pluralized mdt.

3.text: It is like the dew of Hermon, which flows down upon the hills of Zion. Indeed, that is where the Lord has decreed a blessing will be available—eternal life.

notes.text: Hermon refers to Mount Hermon, located north of Israel.

The hills of Zion are those surrounding Zion (see Pss 87:1; 125:2). The psalmist does not intend to suggest that the dew from Mt. Hermon in the distant north actually flows down upon Zion. His point is that the same kind of heavy dew that replenishes Hermon may also be seen on Zion’s hills. See A. Cohen, Psalms (SoBB), 439. “Dew” here symbolizes divine blessing, as the next line suggests.
Or “for.”
Heb “there the Lord has commanded the blessing, life forever.”

1.text: Attention! Praise the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, who serve in the Lord’s temple during the night.

notes.text: Heb “Look!”
Heb “stand.”

2.text: Lift your hands toward the sanctuary and praise the Lord.

3.text: May the Lord, the Creator of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion.

notes.text: The pronominal suffix is second masculine singular, suggesting that the servants addressed in vv. 1-2 are responding to the psalmist.
Heb “may the Lord bless you from Zion, the maker of heaven and earth.”

1.text: Praise the Lord. Praise the name of the Lord. Offer praise, you servants of the Lord,

2.text: who serve in the Lord’s temple, in the courts of the temple of our God.

notes.text: Heb “stand.”

3.text: Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good. Sing praises to his name, for it is pleasant.

notes.text: Heb “for [it is] pleasant.” The translation assumes that it is the Lord’s “name” that is pleasant. Another option is to understand the referent of “it” as the act of praising (see Ps 147:1).

4.text: Indeed, the Lord has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel to be his special possession.

notes.text: Or “for.”
His special possession. The language echoes Exod 19:5; Deut 7:6; 14:2; 26:18. See also Mal 3:17.

5.text: Yes, I know the Lord is great, and our Lord is superior to all gods.

notes.text: Or “for.”

6.text: He does whatever he pleases in heaven and on earth, in the seas and all the ocean depths.

7.text: He causes the clouds to arise from the end of the earth, makes lightning bolts accompany the rain, and brings the wind out of his storehouses.

8.text: He struck down the firstborn of Egypt, including both men and animals.

9.text: He performed awesome deeds and acts of judgment in your midst, O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants.

notes.text: Or “signs” (see Ps 65:8).
Or “portents”; “omens” (see Ps 71:7). The Egyptian plagues are alluded to here.

10.text: He defeated many nations, and killed mighty kings—

11.text: Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan.

12.text: He gave their land as an inheritance, as an inheritance to Israel his people.

13.text: O Lord, your name endures, your reputation, O Lord, lasts.

notes.text: Or “is forever.”
Heb “O Lord, your remembrance [is] for a generation and a generation.” See Ps 102:12.

14.text: For the Lord vindicates his people, and has compassion on his servants.

notes.text: Heb “judges,” but here the idea is that the Lord “judges on behalf of” his people. The imperfect verbal forms here and in the next line draw attention to the Lord’s characteristic actions.
Verse 14 echoes Deut 32:36, where Moses affirms that God mercifully relents from fully judging his wayward people.

15.text: The nations’ idols are made of silver and gold; they are man-made.

notes.text: Heb “the work of the hands of man.”

16.text: They have mouths, but cannot speak, eyes, but cannot see,

17.text: and ears, but cannot hear. Indeed, they cannot breathe.

notes.text: Heb “indeed, there is not breath in their mouth.” For the collocation ‏אַף אֵין‎ (ʾaf ʾen, “indeed, there is not”) see Isa 41:26. Another option is to take ‏אַף‎ as “nose” (see Ps 115:6), in which case one might translate, “a nose, [but] they have no breath in their mouths.”

18.text: Those who make them will end up like them, as will everyone who trusts in them.

notes.text: Heb “will be.” Another option is to take the prefixed verbal form as a prayer, “may those who make them end up like them.”
Because the idols are lifeless, they cannot help their worshipers in times of crisis. Consequently the worshipers end up as dead as the gods in which they trust.

19.text: O family of Israel, praise the Lord. O family of Aaron, praise the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “house” (here and in the next two lines).

20.text: O family of Levi, praise the Lord. You loyal followers of the Lord, praise the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “fearers.”

21.text: The Lord deserves praise in Zion — he who dwells in Jerusalem. Praise the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “praised be the Lord from Zion.”

1.text: Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his loyal love endures.

notes.text: Or “is forever.”

2.text: Give thanks to the God of gods, for his loyal love endures.

3.text: Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his loyal love endures,

4.text: to the one who performs magnificent, amazing deeds all by himself, for his loyal love endures,

5.text: to the one who used wisdom to make the heavens, for his loyal love endures,

6.text: to the one who spread out the earth over the water, for his loyal love endures,

7.text: to the one who made the great lights, for his loyal love endures,

8.text: the sun to rule by day, for his loyal love endures,

9.text: the moon and stars to rule by night, for his loyal love endures,

10.text: to the one who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, for his loyal love endures,

11.text: and led Israel out from their midst, for his loyal love endures,

12.text: with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, for his loyal love endures,

13.text: to the one who divided the Red Sea in two, for his loyal love endures,

notes.text: Or “cut.”

Heb “Reed Sea” (also in v. 15). “Reed Sea” (or “Sea of Reeds”) is a more accurate rendering of the Hebrew expression ‏יָם סוּף‎ (yam suf), traditionally translated “Red Sea.” See the note on the term “Red Sea” in Exod 13:18.
Heb “into pieces.”

14.text: and led Israel through its midst, for his loyal love endures,

15.text: and tossed Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea, for his loyal love endures,

notes.text: Or “shook off.”

16.text: to the one who led his people through the wilderness, for his loyal love endures,

17.text: to the one who struck down great kings, for his loyal love endures,

18.text: and killed powerful kings, for his loyal love endures,

19.text: Sihon, king of the Amorites, for his loyal love endures,

20.text: Og, king of Bashan, for his loyal love endures,

21.text: and gave their land as an inheritance, for his loyal love endures,

22.text: as an inheritance to Israel his servant, for his loyal love endures,

23.text: to the one who remembered us when we were down, for his loyal love endures,

notes.text: Heb “who, in our low condition, remembered us.”

24.text: and snatched us away from our enemies, for his loyal love endures,

25.text: to the one who gives food to all living things, for his loyal love endures.

notes.text: Heb “to all flesh,” which can refer to all people (see Pss 65:2; 145:21) or more broadly to mankind and animals. Elsewhere the psalms view God as the provider for all living things (see Pss 104:27-28; 145:15).

26.text: Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his loyal love endures!

1.text: By the rivers of Babylon we sit down and weep when we remember Zion.

notes.text: Heb “there we sit down, also we weep.”

2.text: On the poplars in her midst we hang our harps,

3.text: for there our captors ask us to compose songs; those who mock us demand that we be happy, saying: “Sing for us a song about Zion!”

notes.text: Heb “ask us [for] the words of a song.”

Heb “our [?] joy.” The derivation and meaning of the Hebrew phrase ‏תוֹלָלֵינוּ‎ (tolalenu, “our [?]”) are uncertain. A derivation from ‏תָּלַל‎ (talal, “to mock”) fits contextually, but this root occurs only in the Hiphil stem. For a discussion of various proposals, see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 236.

Heb “from a song of Zion.” Most modern translations read, “one of the songs of Zion,” taking the preposition ‏מִן‎ (min, “from”) as partitive and “song” as collective. The present translation assumes the mem (‏ם‎) is enclitic, being misunderstood later as the prefixed preposition.

4.text: How can we sing a song to the Lord in a foreign land?

5.text: If I forget you, O Jerusalem, may my right hand be crippled.

notes.text: Heb “may my right hand forget.” In this case one must supply an object, such as “how to move” or “its skill.” The elliptical nature of the text has prompted emendations (see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 236). The translation assumes an emendation to ‏תִּכְשַׁח‎ (tikhshakh), from an otherwise unattested root ‏כָּשַׁח‎ (kashakh), meaning “to be crippled; to be lame.” See HALOT 502 s.v. ‏כשׁח‎, which cites Arabic cognate evidence in support of the proposal. The difficulty of the MT can be explained as an error of transposition facilitated by the use of ‏שָׁכַח‎ (shakhakh, “forget”) just before this.

6.text: May my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth, if I do not remember you, and do not give Jerusalem priority over whatever gives me the most joy.

notes.text: Heb “if I do not lift up Jerusalem over the top of my joy.”

7.text: Remember, O Lord, what the Edomites did on the day Jerusalem fell. They said, “Tear it down, tear it down, right to its very foundation!”

notes.text: Heb “remember, O Lord, against the sons of Edom, the day of Jerusalem.”
Heb “lay [it] bare, lay [it] bare.”

8.text: O daughter Babylon, soon to be devastated, how blessed will be the one who repays you for what you dished out to us.

notes.text: Heb “O devastated daughter of Babylon.” The psalmist dramatically anticipates Babylon’s demise.
Heb “O the happiness of the one who repays you your wage which you paid to us.”

9.text: How blessed will be the one who grabs your babies and smashes them on a rock.

notes.text: For other references to the wholesale slaughter of babies in the context of ancient Near Eastern warfare, see 2 Kgs 8:12; Isa 13:16; Hos 13:16; Nah 3:10.

1.text: I will give you thanks with all my heart; before the heavenly assembly I will sing praises to you.

notes.text: The referent of the Hebrew term ‏אֱלֹהִים‎ (ʾelohim) is unclear. It refers either to the angelic assembly (see Gen 3:5; Ps 8:5) or to the pagan gods (see Pss 82:1, 6; 86:8; 97:7), in which case the psalmist’s praise takes on a polemical tone.

2.text: I will bow down toward your holy temple, and give thanks to your name, because of your loyal love and faithfulness, for you have exalted your promise above the entire sky.

notes.text: The MT reads, “for you have made great over all your name your word.” If retained, this must mean that God’s mighty intervention, in fulfillment of his word of promise, surpassed anything he had done prior to this. However, the statement is odd and several emendations have been proposed. Some read, “for you have exalted over everything your name and your word,” while others suggest, “for you have exalted over all the heavens your name and your word.” The translation assumes an emendation of “your name” to “your heavens” (a construction that appears in Pss 8:3 and 144:5). The point is that God has been faithful to his promise and the reliability of that promise is apparent to all. For a fuller discussion of these options, see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 244.

3.text: When I cried out for help, you answered me. You made me bold and energized me.

notes.text: Heb “in the day.”
Heb “you made me bold in my soul [with] strength.”

4.text: Let all the kings of the earth give thanks to you, O Lord, when they hear the words you speak.

notes.text: The prefixed verbal forms here and in the following verse are understood as jussives, for the psalmist appears to be calling upon the kings to praise God. Another option is to take them as imperfects and translate, “the kings of the earth will give thanks…and will sing.” In this case the psalmist anticipates a universal response to his thanksgiving song.
Heb “the words of your mouth.”

5.text: Let them sing about the Lord’s deeds, for the Lord’s splendor is magnificent.

notes.text: Heb “ways.”
Heb “great.”

6.text: Though the Lord is exalted, he looks after the lowly, and from far away humbles the proud.

notes.text: The form of the verb is ‏יְיֵדָע‎ (yeyedaʿ) commonly understood to be Qal of ‏יָדַע‎ I (yadaʿ), although the Qal should not have two yod’s. Most likely one ‏י‎ (yod) should be deleted as dittography, or the second should be read as a ‏ו‎ (vav) and the form be understood as a Hifil.

The Hifil of ‏יָדַע‎ II (yadaʿ) means “to humiliate,” causative of the Qal “be submissive, humbled, quiet” (cf. Job 21:19; Prov 5:6; Isa 45:4; Jer 14:18; Hos 9:7). DCH supposes that the Qal can mean “to humiliate” in this verse. The more common homophonous root ‏יָדַע‎ means “to know,” sometimes with the nuance “to care for.” Alternatively the adjective ‏גָּבֹהַּ‎ (gavoah) can be understood as the subject, referring to God, “the exalted one cares for [the lowly] from a distance,” but the parallel thought in the next verse favors a contrast in this verse also.

7.text: Even when I must walk in the midst of danger, you revive me. You oppose my angry enemies, and your right hand delivers me.

notes.text: Or “distress.”
Heb “against the anger of my enemies you extend your hand.”

8.text: The Lord avenges me. O Lord, your loyal love endures. Do not abandon those whom you have made.

notes.text: Heb “avenges on my behalf.” For the meaning “to avenge” for the verb ‏גָּמַר‎ (gamar), see HALOT 197-98 s.v. ‏גמר‎.
Heb “the works of your hands.” Many medieval Hebrew mss read the singular, “work of your hands.”

1.text: O Lord, you examine me and know me.

notes.text: The statement is understood as generalizing—the psalmist describes what God typically does.

2.text: You know when I sit down and when I get up; even from far away you understand my motives.

3.text: You carefully observe me when I travel or when I lie down to rest; you are aware of everything I do.

notes.text: Heb “my traveling and my lying down you measure.” The verb ‏זָרָה‎ (zarah, “to measure”) is probably here a denominative from ‏זֶרֶת‎ (zeret, “a span; a measure”), though some derive it from ‏זָרָה‎ (zarat, “to winnow; to sift”; see BDB 279-80 s.v. ‏זָרָה‎).
Heb “all my ways.”

4.text: Certainly my tongue does not frame a word without you, O Lord, being thoroughly aware of it.

notes.text: Or “for.”
Heb “look, O Lord, you know all of it.”

5.text: You squeeze me in from behind and in front; you place your hand on me.

6.text: Your knowledge is beyond my comprehension; it is so far beyond me, I am unable to fathom it.

notes.text: Heb “too amazing [is this] knowledge for me, it is elevated, I cannot attain to it.”

7.text: Where can I go to escape your Spirit? Where can I flee to escape your presence?

notes.text: Heb “Where can I go from your spirit, and where from your face can I flee?” God’s “spirit” may refer here (1) to his presence (note the parallel term, “your face,” and see Ps 104:29-30, where God’s “face” is his presence and his “spirit” is the life-giving breath he imparts) or (2) to his personal Spirit (see Ps 51:10).

8.text: If I were to ascend to heaven, you would be there. If I were to sprawl out in Sheol, there you would be.

notes.text: The Hebrew verb ‏סָלַק‎ (salaq, “to ascend”) occurs only here in the OT, but the word is well-attested in Aramaic literature from different time periods and displays a wide semantic range (see DNWSI 2:788-90).

The verb ‏יָצַע‎ (yatzaʿ) is rare in the Bible (see Isa 58:5 also Hiphil, and Isa 1:14; Est 4:3 for Hophal examples). There are three main options for understanding this phrase. It may mean “to descend to Sheol,” as in the LXX. This takes the motion in the verb as very generic for this context and understands “Sheol” without a preposition as the default “to Sheol.” Many translations take it as spreading out [something] to act as a bed, couch, or area to lie down. It is uncertain that the idea of a bed has to be implied and this does not required to fit the other contexts. Or, as taken here, it may “to spread [oneself] out, to sprawl.” Each view has merits and it is difficult to decide because the are so few examples.
Heb “look, you.”

9.text: If I were to fly away on the wings of the dawn, and settle down on the other side of the sea,

notes.text: Heb “rise up.”

On the wings of the dawn. This personification of the “dawn” may find its roots in mythological traditions about the god Shachar, whose birth is described in an Ugaritic myth (see G. R. Driver, Canaanite Myths and Legends, 126) and who is mentioned in Isa 14:12 as the father of Helel.
Heb “at the end.”

10.text: even there your hand would guide me, your right hand would grab hold of me.

11.text: If I were to say, “Certainly the darkness will cover me, and the light will turn to night all around me,”

notes.text: The Hebrew verb ‏שׁוּף‎ (shuf), which means “to crush; to wound,” in Gen 3:15 and Job 9:17, is problematic here. For a discussion of attempts to relate the verb to Arabic roots, see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 251. Many emend the form to ‏יְשׂוּכֵּנִי‎ (yesukkeni), from the root ‏שָׂכַך‎ (sakhakh, “to cover,” an alternate form of ‏סָכַך‎ [sakhakh]), a reading assumed in the present translation.
Heb “and night, light, around me.”

12.text: even the darkness is not too dark for you to see, and the night is as bright as day; darkness and light are the same to you.

notes.text: The words “to see” are supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.
Heb “shines like.”
Heb “like darkness, like light.”

13.text: Certainly you made my mind and heart; you wove me together in my mother’s womb.

notes.text: Or “for.”

Heb “my kidneys.” The kidneys were sometimes viewed as the seat of one’s emotions and moral character (cf. Pss 7:9; 26:2). A number of translations, recognizing that “kidneys” does not communicate this idea to the modern reader, have generalized the concept: “inmost being” (NAB, NIV); “inward parts” (NASB, NRSV); “the delicate, inner parts of my body” (NLT). In the last instance, the focus is almost entirely on the physical body rather than the emotions or moral character. The present translation, by using a hendiadys (one concept expressed through two terms), links the concepts of emotion (heart) and moral character (mind).
The Hebrew verb ‏סָכַךְ‎ (sakhakh, “to weave together”) is an alternate form of ‏שָׂכַךְ‎ (sakhakh, “to weave”) used in Job 10:11.

14.text: I will give you thanks because your deeds are awesome and amazing. You knew me thoroughly;

notes.text: Heb “because awesome things, I am distinct, amazing [are] your works.” The text as it stands is syntactically problematic and makes little, if any, sense. The Niphal of ‏פָּלָה‎ (palah) occurs elsewhere only in Exod 33:16. Many take the form from ‏פָלָא‎ (palaʾ; see GKC 216 §75.qq), which in the Niphal perfect means “to be amazing” (see 2 Sam 1:26; Ps 118:23; Prov 30:18). Some, following the LXX and some other ancient witnesses, also prefer to emend the verb from first to second person, “you are amazing” (see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 249, 251). The present translation assumes the text conflates two variants: ‏נִפְלָאִים‎ (niflaʾim), the otherwise unattested masculine plural participle of ‏פָלָא‎, and ‏נִפְלָאוֹת‎ (niflaʾot), the usual (feminine) plural form of the Niphal participle. The latter has been changed to a verb by later scribes in an attempt to accommodate it syntactically. The original text likely read, ‏נוראות נפלאותים מעשׂיך‎ (“your works [are] awesome [and] amazing”).

Heb “and my being knows very much.” Better parallelism is achieved (see v. 15a) if one emends ‏יֹדַעַת‎ (yodaʿat), a Qal active participle, feminine singular form, to ‏יָדַעְתָּ‎ (yadaʿta), a Qal perfect second masculine singular perfect. See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 252.

15.text: my bones were not hidden from you, when I was made in secret and sewed together in the depths of the earth.

notes.text: The Hebrew term ‏אֲשֶׁר‎ (ʾasher, “which”) should probably be emended to ‏כֲּאַשֶׁר‎ (kaʾasher, “when”). The ‏כ‎ (kaf) may have been lost by haplography (note the kaf at the end of the preceding form).

The phrase depths of the earth may be metaphorical (euphemistic) or it may reflect a prescientific belief about the origins of the embryo deep beneath the earth’s surface (see H. W. Wolff, Anthropology of the Old Testament, 96-97). Job 1:21 also closely associates the mother’s womb with the earth.

16.text: Your eyes saw me when I was inside the womb. All the days ordained for me were recorded in your scroll before one of them came into existence.

notes.text: Heb “Your eyes saw my shapeless form.” The Hebrew noun ‏גֹּלֶם‎ (golem) occurs only here in the OT. In later Hebrew the word refers to “a lump, a shapeless or lifeless substance,” and to “unfinished matter, a vessel wanting finishing” (Jastrow 222 s.v. ‏גּוֹלֶם‎). The translation employs the dynamic rendering “when I was inside the womb” to clarify that the speaker was still in his mother’s womb at the time he was “seen” by God.

Heb “and on your scroll all of them were written, [the] days [which] were formed, and [there was] not one among them.” This “scroll” may be the “scroll of life” mentioned in Ps 69:28 (see the note on the word “living” there).

17.text: How difficult it is for me to fathom your thoughts about me, O God! How vast is their sum total.

notes.text: Heb “and to me how precious are your thoughts, O God.” The Hebrew verb ‏יָקַר‎ (yaqar) probably has the sense of “difficult [to comprehend]” here (see HALOT 432 s.v. ‏יקר‎ qal.1 and note the use of Aramaic ‏יַקִּר‎ in Dan 2:11). Elsewhere in the immediate context the psalmist expresses his amazement at the extent of God’s knowledge about him (see vv. 1-6, 17b-18).
Heb “how vast are their heads.” Here the Hebrew word “head” is used of the “sum total” of God’s knowledge of the psalmist.

18.text: If I tried to count them, they would outnumber the grains of sand. Even if I finished counting them, I would still have to contend with you.

notes.text: Heb “I awake and I [am] still with you.” A reference to the psalmist awaking from sleep makes little, if any, sense contextually. For this reason some propose an emendation to ‏הֲקִצּוֹתִי‎ (haqitsoti), a Hiphil perfect form from an otherwise unattested verb ‏קָצַץ‎ (qatsats) understood as a denominative of ‏קֵץ‎ (qets, “end”). See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 252-53.

19.text: If only you would kill the wicked, O God! Get away from me, you violent men!

notes.text: The Hebrew particle ‏אִם‎ (ʾim, “if”) and following prefixed verbal form here express a wish (see Pss 81:8; 95:7, as well as GKC 321 §109.b).
Heb “men of bloodshed.”

20.text: They rebel against you and act deceitfully; your enemies lie.

notes.text: Heb “who.”

Heb “they speak [of] you.” The suffixed form of the verb ‏אָמַר‎ (ʾamar, “to speak”) is peculiar. The translation assumes an emendation to ‏יַמְרֻךָ‎ (yamrukha), a Hiphil form from ‏מָרָה‎ (marah, “to rebel”; see Ps 78:40).
Heb “by deceit.”

Heb “lifted up for emptiness, your cities.” The form ‏נָשֻׂא‎ (nasuʾ; a Qal passive participle) should be emended to ‏נָשְׂאוּ‎ (naseʾu; a Qal perfect, third common plural, “[they] lift up”). Many emend ‏עָרֶיךָ‎ (ʿarekha, “your cities”) to ‏עָלֶיךָ‎ (ʿalekha, “against you”), but it is preferable to understand the noun as an Aramaism and translate “your enemies” (see Dan 4:16 and L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 253).

21.text: O Lord, do I not hate those who hate you, and despise those who oppose you?

notes.text: Heb “who raise themselves up against you.” The form ‏וּבִתְקוֹמְמֶיךָ‎ (uvitqomemekha) should be emended to ‏וּבְמִתְקוֹמְמֶיךָ‎ (uvemitqomemekha), a Hitpolel participle (the prefixed ‏מ‎ [mem] of the participle is accidentally omitted in the MT, though a few medieval Hebrew mss have it).

22.text: I absolutely hate them; they have become my enemies.

notes.text: Heb “[with] completeness of hatred I hate them.”

23.text: Examine me, O God, and probe my thoughts. Test me, and know my concerns.

notes.text: Heb “and know my heart.”
The Hebrew noun ‏שַׂרְעַפַּי‎ (sarʿappay, “concerns”) is used of “worries” in Ps 94:19.

24.text: See if there is any idolatrous way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.

notes.text: Many understand the Hebrew term ‏עֹצֶב‎ (ʿotsev) as a noun meaning “pain,” and translate the phrase ‏דֶּרֶךְ עֹצֶב‎ (derekh ʿotsev) as “of pain,” but this makes little sense here. (Some interpret it to refer to actions which bring pain to others.) It is preferable to take ‏עֹצֶב‎ as “idol” (see HALOT 865 s.v. I ‏עֹצֶב‎) and understand “way of an idol” to refer to idolatrous actions or tendency. See L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 253.
Or “in the ancient path.” This phrase may refer to the moral path prescribed by the Lord at the beginning of Israel’s history. See Jer 6:16; 18:15, as well as L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 (WBC), 253.

1.text: O Lord, rescue me from wicked men. Protect me from violent men,

notes.text: Heb “from a wicked man.” The Hebrew uses the singular in a representative or collective sense (note the plural verbs in v. 2).
Heb “a man of violent acts.” The Hebrew uses the singular in a representative or collective sense (note the plural verbs in v. 2).

2.text: who plan ways to harm me. All day long they stir up conflict.

notes.text: Heb “they devise wicked [plans] in [their] mind.”

Heb “they attack [for] war.” Some revocalize the verb (which is a Qal imperfect from ‏גּוּר‎, gur, “to attack”) as ‏יְגָרוּ‎ (yegaru), a Piel imperfect from ‏גָרָה‎ (garah, “stir up strife”). This is followed in the present translation.

3.text: Their tongues wound like a serpent; a viper’s venom is behind their lips. (Selah)

notes.text: Heb “they sharpen their tongue like a serpent.” Ps 64:3 reads, “they sharpen their tongues like sword.” Perhaps Ps 140:3 uses a mixed metaphor, the point being that “they sharpen their tongues [like a sword],” as it were, so that when they speak, their words wound like a serpent’s bite. Another option is that the language refers to the pointed or forked nature of a serpent’s tongue, which is viewed metaphorically as “sharpened.”
The Hebrew term is used only here in the OT.
Heb “under.”

4.text: O Lord, shelter me from the power of the wicked. Protect me from violent men, who plan to knock me over.

notes.text: Heb “hands.”
Heb “to push down my steps.”

5.text: Proud men hide a snare for me; evil men spread a net by the path. They set traps for me. (Selah)

notes.text: Heb “and ropes,” but many prefer to revocalize the noun as a participle (‏חֹבְלִים‎, khovelim) from the verb ‏חָבַל‎ (khaval, “act corruptly”).

6.text: I say to the Lord, “You are my God.” O Lord, pay attention to my plea for mercy.

7.text: O Sovereign Lord, my strong deliverer, you shield my head in the day of battle.

notes.text: Heb “the strength of my deliverance.”
Heb “cover.”

8.text: O Lord, do not let the wicked have their way. Do not allow their plan to succeed when they attack. (Selah)

notes.text: Heb “do not grant the desires of the wicked.”
Heb “his.” The singular is used in a representative sense (see v. 1).

Heb “his plot do not promote, they rise up.” The translation understands the final verb as being an unmarked temporal clause. Another option is to revocalize the verb as a Hiphil and take the verb with the next verse, “those who surround me lift up [their] head,” which could refer to their proud attitude as they anticipate victory (see Ps 27:6).

9.text: As for the heads of those who surround me— may the harm done by their lips overwhelm them.

notes.text: Heb “harm of their lips.” The genitive here indicates the source or agent of the harm.

10.text: May he rain down fiery coals upon them. May he throw them into the fire. From bottomless pits they will not escape.

notes.text: The verb form in the Kethib (consonantal Hebrew text) appears to be a Hiphil imperfect from the root ‏מוּט‎ (mut, “to sway”), but the Hiphil occurs only here and in Ps 55:3, where it is preferable to read ‏יַמְטִירוּ‎ (yamtiru, “they rain down”). In Ps 140:10 the form ‏יַמְטֵר‎ (yamter, “let him rain down”) should probably be read.

Heb “into bottomless pits, they will not arise.” The translation assumes that the preposition ‏ב‎ (bet) has the nuance “from” here. Another option is to connect the line with what precedes, take the final clause as an asyndetic relative clause, and translate, “into bottomless pits [from which] they cannot arise.” The Hebrew noun ‏מַהֲמֹרָה‎ (mahamorah, “bottomless pit”) occurs only here in the OT.

11.text: A slanderer will not endure on the earth; calamity will hunt down a violent man and strike him down.

notes.text: Heb “a man of a tongue.”
Heb “be established in.”
Heb “for blows.” The Hebrew noun ‏מַדְחֵפֹה‎ (madkhefoh, “blow”) occurs only here in the OT.

12.text: I know that the Lord defends the cause of the oppressed and vindicates the poor.

notes.text: The translation follows the Qere and many medieval Hebrew mss in reading a first person verb form here. The Kethib reads the second person.
Heb “and the just cause of the poor.”

13.text: Certainly the godly will give thanks to your name; the morally upright will live in your presence.

1.text: O Lord, I cry out to you. Come quickly to me. Pay attention to me when I cry out to you.

2.text: May you accept my prayer like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering.

notes.text: Heb “may my prayer be established [like] incense before you, the uplifting of my hands [like] an evening offering.”

3.text: O Lord, place a guard on my mouth. Protect the opening of my lips.

notes.text: Heb “door.” The Hebrew word occurs only here in the OT.
My mouth…my lips. The psalmist asks God to protect him from speaking inappropriately or sinfully.

4.text: Do not let me have evil desires, or participate in sinful activities with men who behave wickedly. I will not eat their delicacies.

notes.text: Heb “do not turn my heart toward an evil thing.”
Heb “to act sinfully in practices in wickedness with men, doers of evil.”
Their delicacies. This probably refers to the enjoyment that a sinful lifestyle appears to offer.

5.text: May the godly strike me in love and correct me. May my head not refuse choice oil. Indeed, my prayer is a witness against their evil deeds.

notes.text: The form ‏יָנִי‎ (yani) appears to be derived from the verbal root ‏נוּא‎ (nuʾ). Another option is to emend the form to ‏יְנָא‎ (yenaʾ), a Piel from ‏נָאָה‎ (naʾah), and translate “may choice oil not adorn my head” (see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 271). In this case, choice oil, like delicacies in v. 4, symbolize the pleasures of sin.
May my head not refuse choice oil. The psalmist compares the constructive criticism of the godly (see the previous line) to having refreshing olive oil poured over one’s head.

Heb “for still, and my prayer [is] against their evil deeds.” The syntax of the Hebrew text is difficult; the sequence -‏כִּי־עוֹד וּ‎ (ki ʿod u-, “for still and”) occurs only here. The translation assumes an emendation to ‏כִּי עֵד תְּפִלָּתִי‎ (ki ʿed tefillati, “indeed a witness [is] my prayer”). The psalmist’s lament about the evil actions of sinful men (see v. 4) testifies against the wicked in the divine court.

6.text: They will be thrown over the side of a cliff by their judges. They will listen to my words, for they are pleasant.

notes.text: Heb “they are thrown down by the hands of a cliff, their judges.” The syntax of the Hebrew text is difficult and the meaning uncertain. The perfect verbal form is understood as rhetorical; the psalmist describes the anticipated downfall of the wicked as if it had already occurred. “Their judges” could be taken as the subject of the verb, but this makes little, if any, sense. The translation assumes the judges are the agents and that the wicked, mentioned earlier in the psalm, are the subjects of the verb.

It is unclear how this statement relates to the preceding sentence. Perhaps the judges are the referent of the pronominal subject (“they”) of the verb “will listen,” and “my words” are the referent of the pronominal subject (“they”) of the phrase “are pleasant.” The psalmist may be affirming here his confidence that he will be vindicated when he presents his case before the judges, while the wicked will be punished.

7.text: As when one plows and breaks up the soil, so our bones are scattered at the mouth of Sheol.

notes.text: Heb “like splitting and breaking open in the earth.” The meaning of the statement and the point of the comparison are not entirely clear. Perhaps the psalmist is suggesting that he and other godly individuals are as good as dead; their bones are scattered about like dirt that is dug up and tossed aside.

8.text: Surely I am looking to you, O Sovereign Lord. In you I take shelter. Do not expose me to danger.

notes.text: Heb “my eyes [are] toward you.”

Heb “do not lay bare my life.” Only here is the Piel form of the verb collocated with the term ‏נֶפֶשׁ‎ (nefesh, “life”). In Isa 53:12 the Lord’s servant “lays bare (the Hiphil form of the verb is used) his life to death.”

9.text: Protect me from the snare they have laid for me, and the traps the evildoers have set.

notes.text: Heb “and the traps of the doers of evil.”

10.text: Let the wicked fall into their own nets, while I escape.
