10.text: Night and day it will burn; its smoke will ascend continually. Generation after generation it will be a wasteland, and no one will ever pass through it again.

notes.text: Heb “it will not be extinguished.”

11.text: Owls and wild animals will live there, all kinds of wild birds will settle in it. The Lord will stretch out over her the measuring line of ruin and the plumb line of destruction.

notes.text: ‏קָאַת‎ (qaʾat) refers to some type of bird (cf. Lev 11:18; Deut 14:17) that was typically found near ruins (see Zeph 2:14). ‏קִפּוֹד‎ (qippod) may also refer to a type of bird (NAB “hoot owl”; NIV “screech owl”; TEV “ravens”), but some have suggested a rodent may be in view (cf. NCV “small animals”; ASV “porcupine”; NASB, NRSV “hedgehog”).
Heb “will possess it” (so NIV).
The Hebrew text has ‏יַנְשׁוֹף וְעֹרֵב‎ (yanshof veʿorev). Both the ‏יַנְשׁוֹף‎ (“owl”; see Lev 11:17; Deut 14:16) and ‏עֹרֵב‎ (“raven”; Lev 11:15; Deut 14:14) were types of wild birds.
Heb “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “stones,” i.e., the stones used in a plumb bob.
The metaphor in v. 11b emphasizes that God has carefully planned Edom’s demise.

12.text: Her nobles will have nothing left to call a kingdom, and all her officials will disappear.

notes.text: Heb “will be nothing”; NCV, TEV, NLT “will all be gone.”

13.text: Her fortresses will be overgrown with thorns; thickets and weeds will grow in her fortified cities. Jackals will settle there; ostriches will live there.

notes.text: The words “will grow” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

Heb “and she will be a settlement for wild dogs, a dwelling place for ostriches.” The translation assumes an emendation of ‏חָצִיר‎ (khatsir, “grass”) to ‏חָצֵר‎ (khatser, “settlement”). One of the Qumran scrolls of Isaiah (1QIsaa) supports this emendation (cf. HALOT 344 s.v. II ‏חָצִיר‎)

14.text: Wild animals and wild dogs will congregate there; wild goats will bleat to one another. Yes, nocturnal animals will rest there and make for themselves a nest.

notes.text: Heb “will meet” (so NIV); NLT “will mingle there.”
Heb “and a goat will call to its neighbor.”

The precise meaning of ‏לִילִית‎ (lilit) is unclear, though in this context the word certainly refers to some type of wild animal or bird. The word appears to be related to ‏לַיְלָה‎ (laylah, “night”). Some interpret it as the name of a female night demon, on the basis of an apparent Akkadian cognate used as the name of a demon. Later Jewish legends also identified Lilith as a demon. Cf. NRSV “Lilith.”
Heb “and will find for themselves a resting place.”

15.text: Owls will make nests and lay eggs there; they will hatch them and protect them. Yes, hawks will gather there, each with its mate.

notes.text: Hebrew ‏קִפּוֹז‎ (qippoz) occurs only here; the precise meaning of the word is uncertain.
For this proposed meaning for Hebrew ‏מָלַט‎ (malat), see HALOT 589 s.v. I ‏מלט‎.
Heb “and brood [over them] in her shadow.”
The precise meaning of ‏דַּיָּה‎ (dayyah) is uncertain, though the term appears to refer to some type of bird of prey, perhaps a vulture.

16.text: Carefully read the scroll of the Lord! Not one of these creatures will be missing, none will lack a mate. For the Lord has issued the decree, and his own spirit gathers them.

notes.text: Heb “Seek from upon the scroll of the Lord and read.”
It is uncertain what particular scroll is referred to here. Perhaps the phrase simply refers to this prophecy and is an admonition to pay close attention to the details of the message.

Heb “one from these will not be missing.” ‏הֵנָּה‎ (hennah, “these”) is feminine plural in the Hebrew text. It may refer only to the birds mentioned in v. 15b or may include all of the creatures listed in vv. 14b-15 (all of which are identified with feminine nouns).
Heb “each its mate they will not lack.”

The Hebrew text reads literally, “for a mouth, it has commanded.” The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa and a few medieval mss have ‏פִּיהוּ‎ (pihu, “his mouth [has commanded]”), while a few other medieval mss read ‏פִּי יְהוָה‎ (pi yehvah, “the mouth of the Lord [has commanded]”).

Heb “and his spirit, he gathers them.” The pronominal suffix (“them”) is feminine plural, referring to the birds mentioned in v. 15b or to all of the creatures listed in vv. 14b-15 (all of which are identified with feminine nouns).

17.text: He assigns them their allotment; he measures out their assigned place. They will live there permanently; they will settle in it through successive generations.

notes.text: Heb “and he causes the lot to fall for them.” Once again the pronominal suffix (“them”) is feminine plural, referring to the birds mentioned in v. 15b or to all of the creatures listed in vv. 14b-15 (all of which are identified with feminine nouns).

Heb “and his hand divides for them with a measuring line.” The pronominal suffix (“them”) now switches to masculine plural, referring to all the animals and birds mentioned in vv. 11-15, some of which were identified with masculine nouns. This signals closure for this portion of the speech, which began in v. 11. The following couplet (v. 17b) forms an inclusio with v. 11a through verbal repetition.
Heb “will possess it” (so NIV); NCV “they will own that land forever.”

1.text: Let the wilderness and desert be happy; let the arid rift valley rejoice and bloom like a lily!

notes.text: The final mem (‏ם‎) on the verb ‏יְשֻׂשׂוּם‎ (yesusum) is dittographic (note the initial mem on the following noun ‏מִדְבָּר‎ [midbar]). The ambiguous verbal form is translated as a jussive because it is parallel to the jussive form ‏תָגֵל‎ (tagel). The jussive is used rhetorically here, not as a literal command or prayer.

This verse employs three terms for desolate paces: ‏מִדְבָּר‎ (midbar, “wilderness”), ‏צִיָּה‎ (tsiyyah, “dry place, desert”), and ‏עֲרָבָה‎ (ʿaravah, “rift valley”). A midbar is an area that receives less than twelve inches of rain per year. It may have some pasturage (if receiving six to twelve inches of rain), but often has desert-like qualities. A tsiyyah is not a sandy desert per se, but of the three terms most clearly indicates a dry, desert region. The rift valley includes the Jordan Valley, but it still has a reputation as a dry, desolate place from its conditions near the Dead Sea and southward.

2.text: Let it richly bloom; let it rejoice and shout with delight! It is given the grandeur of Lebanon, the splendor of Carmel and Sharon. They will see the grandeur of the Lord, the splendor of our God.

notes.text: The ambiguous verb form ‏תִּפְרַח‎ (tifrakh) is translated as a jussive because it is parallel to the jussive form ‏תָגֵל‎ (tagel).
Heb “and let it rejoice, yes [with] rejoicing and shouting.” ‏גִּילַת‎ (gilat) may be an archaic feminine nominal form (see GKC 421 §130.b).
Or “glory” (KJV, NIV, NRSV); also a second time later in this verse.

3.text: Strengthen the hands that have gone limp, steady the knees that shake.

notes.text: Heb “staggering knees”; KJV, ASV, NRSV “feeble knees”; NIV “knees that give way.”

4.text: Tell those who panic, “Be strong! Do not fear! Look, your God comes to avenge; with divine retribution he comes to deliver you.”

notes.text: Heb “Say to the hasty of heart,” i.e., those whose hearts beat quickly from fear.
The jussive form ‏וְיֹשַׁעֲכֶם‎ (veyoshaʿakhem), which is subordinated to the preceding imperfect with vav conjunctive, indicates purpose.

5.text: Then blind eyes will open, deaf ears will hear.

6.text: Then the lame will leap like a deer, the mute tongue will shout for joy; for water will burst forth in the wilderness, streams in the arid rift valley.

notes.text: The rift valley (‏עֲרָבָה‎, ʿaravah) extends from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba. Near the Dead Sea and southward its conditions are very dry and desolate. Other translations render it as “desert” (KJV, NIV, NRSV), “wastelands” (NLT), or by its Hebrew name, “the Arabah” (NASB).

7.text: The dry soil will become a pool of water, the parched ground springs of water. Where jackals once lived and sprawled out, grass, reeds, and papyrus will grow.

8.text: A thoroughfare will be there— it will be called the Way of Holiness. The unclean will not travel on it; it is reserved for those authorized to use it — fools will not stray into it.

notes.text: The Hebrew text reads literally, “and there will be there a road and a way, and the Way of Holiness it will be called.” ‏וְדֶרֶךְ‎ (vederekh, “and a/the way”) is accidentally duplicated; the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa does not reflect the repetition of the phrase.

The precise meaning of this line is uncertain. The text reads literally “and it is for them, the one who walks [on the] way.” In this context those authorized to use the Way of Holiness would be morally upright people who are the recipients of God’s deliverance, in contrast to the morally impure and foolish who are excluded from the new covenant community.
In this context “fools” are those who are morally corrupt, not those with limited intellectual capacity.

9.text: No lions will be there, no ferocious wild animals will be on it — they will not be found there. Those delivered from bondage will travel on it,

notes.text: Heb “will go up on it”; TEV “will pass that way.”

10.text: those whom the Lord has ransomed will return that way. They will enter Zion with a happy shout. Unending joy will crown them, happiness and joy will overwhelm them; grief and suffering will disappear.

notes.text: Heb “and the redeemed will walk, the ransomed of the Lord will return.”

Heb “[will be] on their head[s].” “Joy” may be likened here to a crown (cf. 2 Sam 1:10). The statement may also be an ironic twist on the idiom “earth/dust on the head” (cf. 2 Sam 1:2; 13:19; 15:32; Job 2:12), referring to a mourning practice.
Heb “will overtake” (NIV); NLT “they will be overcome with.”
Heb “grief and groaning will flee”; KJV “sorrow and sighing shall flee away.”

1.text: In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah’s reign, King Sennacherib of Assyria marched up against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them.

notes.text: The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.

2.text: The king of Assyria sent his chief adviser from Lachish to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem, along with a large army. The chief adviser stood at the conduit of the upper pool that is located on the road to the field where they wash and dry cloth.

notes.text: For a discussion of this title see M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 229-30.
Heb “he”; the referent (the chief adviser) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “the field of the washer”; traditionally “the fuller’s field” (so KJV, ASV, NAB, NASB, NRSV).

3.text: Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the palace supervisor, accompanied by Shebna the scribe and Joah son of Asaph, the secretary, went out to meet him.

4.text: The chief adviser said to them, “Tell Hezekiah: ‘This is what the great king, the king of Assyria, says: “What is your source of confidence?

notes.text: Heb “What is this object of trust in which you are trusting?”

5.text: Your claim to have a strategy and military strength is just empty talk. In whom are you trusting, that you would dare to rebel against me?

notes.text: Heb “you say only a word of lips, counsel and might for battle.” Sennacherib’s message appears to be in broken Hebrew at this point. The phrase “word of lips” refers to mere or empty talk in Prov 14:23.

6.text: Look, you must be trusting in Egypt, that splintered reed staff. If someone leans on it for support, it punctures his hand and wounds him. That is what Pharaoh king of Egypt does to all who trust in him!

7.text: Perhaps you will tell me, ‘We are trusting in the Lord our God.’ But Hezekiah is the one who eliminated his high places and altars and then told the people of Judah and Jerusalem, ‘You must worship at this altar.’

8.text: Now make a deal with my master the king of Assyria, and I will give you 2,000 horses, provided you can find enough riders for them.

9.text: Certainly you will not refuse one of my master’s minor officials and trust in Egypt for chariots and horsemen.

notes.text: Heb “How can you turn back the face of an official [from among] the least of my master’s servants and trust in Egypt for chariots and horsemen?” In vv. 8-9 the chief adviser develops further the argument begun in v. 6. His reasoning seems to be as follows: “In your weakened condition you obviously need military strength. Agree to the king’s terms, and I will personally give you more horses than you are capable of outfitting. If I, a mere minor official, am capable of giving you such military might, just think what power the king has. There is no way the Egyptians can match our strength. It makes much better sense to deal with us.”

10.text: Furthermore it was by the command of the Lord that I marched up against this land to destroy it. The Lord told me, ‘March up against this land and destroy it!’”’”

notes.text: In v. 10 the chief adviser develops further the argument begun in v. 7. He claims that Hezekiah has offended the Lord and that the Lord has commissioned Assyria as his instrument of discipline and judgment.

11.text: Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the chief adviser, “Speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Don’t speak with us in the Judahite dialect in the hearing of the people who are on the wall.”

notes.text: Aramaic was the diplomatic language of the Assyrian empire.
Or “in Hebrew” (NIV, NCV, NLT); NAB, NASB “in Judean.”

12.text: But the chief adviser said, “My master did not send me to speak these words only to your master and to you. His message is also for the men who sit on the wall, for they will eat their own excrement and drink their own urine along with you!”

notes.text: Heb “To your master and to you did my master send me to speak these words?” The rhetorical question expects a negative answer.
Heb “[Is it] not [also] to the men…?” The rhetorical question expects the answer, “Yes, it is.”
The chief adviser alludes to the horrible reality of siege warfare, when the starving people in the besieged city would resort to eating and drinking anything to stay alive.

13.text: The chief adviser then stood there and called out loudly in the Judahite dialect, “Listen to the message of the great king, the king of Assyria.

notes.text: The Hebrew text includes “and he said.”

14.text: This is what the king says: ‘Don’t let Hezekiah mislead you, for he is not able to rescue you!

15.text: Don’t let Hezekiah talk you into trusting in the Lord by saying, “The Lord will certainly rescue us; this city will not be handed over to the king of Assyria.”

16.text: Don’t listen to Hezekiah!’ For this is what the king of Assyria says, ‘Send me a token of your submission and surrender to me. Then each of you may eat from his own vine and fig tree and drink water from his own cistern,

notes.text: Heb “make with me a blessing and come out to me.”

17.text: until I come and take you to a land just like your own—a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards.

18.text: Hezekiah is misleading you when he says, “The Lord will rescue us.” Have any of the gods of the nations rescued their lands from the power of the king of Assyria?

notes.text: Heb “Have the gods of the nations rescued, each his land, from the hand of the king of Assyria?” The rhetorical question expects the answer, “Of course not!”

19.text: Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? Indeed, did any gods rescue Samaria from my power?

notes.text: The rhetorical questions suggest the answer, “Nowhere. They seem to have disappeared in the face of Assyria’s might.”

Heb “that they rescued Samaria from my hand?” But this gives the impression that the gods of Sepharvaim were responsible for protecting Samaria, which is obviously not the case. The implied subject of the plural verb “rescued” must be the generic “gods of the nations/lands” (vv. 18, 20).

20.text: Who among all the gods of these lands have rescued their lands from my power? So how can the Lord rescue Jerusalem from my power?’”

notes.text: Heb “that the Lord might rescue Jerusalem from my hand?” The logic runs as follows: Since no god has ever been able to withstand the Assyrian onslaught, how can the people of Jerusalem possibly think the Lord will rescue them?

21.text: They were silent and did not respond, for the king had ordered, “Don’t respond to him.”

22.text: Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the palace supervisor, accompanied by Shebna the scribe and Joah son of Asaph, the secretary, went to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported to him what the chief adviser had said.

notes.text: As a sign of grief and mourning.

1.text: When King Hezekiah heard this, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and went to the Lord’s temple.

notes.text: The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.

2.text: Eliakim the palace supervisor, Shebna the scribe, and the leading priests, clothed in sackcloth, sent this message to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz:

notes.text: Heb “elders of the priests” (so KJV, NAB, NASB); NCV “the older priests”; NRSV, TEV, CEV “the senior priests.”

3.text: “This is what Hezekiah says: ‘This is a day of distress, insults, and humiliation, as when a baby is ready to leave the birth canal, but the mother lacks the strength to push it through.

notes.text: In the Hebrew text this verse begins with “they said to him” (cf. NRSV).
Or “rebuke” (KJV, NAB, NIV, NRSV), or “correction.”
Or “contempt”; NAB, NIV, NRSV “disgrace.”
Heb “when sons come to the cervical opening and there is no strength to give birth.”

4.text: Perhaps the Lord your God will hear all these things the chief adviser has spoken on behalf of his master, the king of Assyria, who sent him to taunt the living God. When the Lord your God hears, perhaps he will punish him for the things he has said. So pray for this remnant that remains.’”

notes.text: Heb “all the words of the chief adviser whom his master, the king of Assyria, sent to taunt the living God.”
Heb “and rebuke the words which the Lord your God hears.”
Heb “and lift up a prayer on behalf of the remnant that is found.”

5.text: When King Hezekiah’s servants came to Isaiah,

6.text: Isaiah said to them, “Tell your master this: ‘This is what the Lord has said: “Don’t be afraid because of the things you have heard—these insults the king of Assyria’s servants have hurled against me.

notes.text: Heb “by which the servants of the king of Assyria have insulted me.”

7.text: Look, I will take control of his mind; he will receive a report and return to his own land. I will cut him down with a sword in his own land.”’”

notes.text: Heb “I will put in him a spirit.” The precise sense of ‏רוּחַ‎ (ruakh, “spirit”) is uncertain in this context. It may refer to a spiritual being who will take control of his mind (see 1 Kgs 22:19), or it could refer to a disposition of concern and fear. In either case the Lord’s sovereignty over the king is apparent.
Heb “cause him to fall” (so KJV, ASV, NAB), that is, “kill him.”

8.text: When the chief adviser heard the king of Assyria had departed from Lachish, he left and went to Libnah, where the king was campaigning.

notes.text: Heb “and the chief adviser returned and he found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he heard that he had departed from Lachish.”

9.text: The king heard that King Tirhakah of Ethiopia was marching out to fight him. He again sent messengers to Hezekiah, ordering them:

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (the king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “Cush” (so NASB); NIV, NCV “the Cushite king of Egypt.”
Heb “heard concerning Tirhakah king of Cush, ‘He has come out to fight with you.’”
The Hebrew text has, “and he heard and he sent,” but the parallel in 2 Kgs 19:9 has ‏וַיָּשָׁב וַיִּשְׁלַח‎ (vayyashav vayyishlakh, “and he returned and he sent”), i.e., “he again sent.”

10.text: “Tell King Hezekiah of Judah this: ‘Don’t let your God in whom you trust mislead you when he says, “Jerusalem will not be handed over to the king of Assyria.”

11.text: Certainly you have heard how the kings of Assyria have annihilated all lands. Do you really think you will be rescued?

notes.text: Heb “Look, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the lands, annihilating them.”
Heb “and will you be rescued?” The rhetorical question expects the answer, “No, of course not!”

12.text: Were the nations whom my predecessors destroyed—the nations of Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden in Telassar—rescued by their gods?

notes.text: Heb “fathers” (so KJV, NAB, NASB); NIV “forefathers”; NCV “ancestors.”
Heb “Did the gods of the nations whom my fathers destroyed rescue them—Gozan and Haran, and Rezeph and the sons of Eden who are in Telassar?”

13.text: Where is the king of Hamath or the king of Arpad or the kings of Lair, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?’”

notes.text: Lair was a city located in northeastern Babylon. See M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 235.

14.text: Hezekiah took the letter from the messengers and read it. Then Hezekiah went up to the Lord’s temple and spread it out before the Lord.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has the plural, “letters.” The final mem (‏ם‎) may be dittographic (note the initial mem on the form that immediately follows). Some Greek and Aramaic witnesses have the singular. If so, one still has to deal with the yod that is part of the plural ending. J. N. Oswalt refers to various commentators who have suggested ways to understand the plural form (Isaiah [NICOT], 1:652).
In the parallel text in 2 Kgs 19:14 the verb has the plural suffix, “them,” but this may reflect a later harmonization to the preceding textual reading of “letters.”

15.text: Hezekiah prayed before the Lord:

16.text: “O Lord of Heaven’s Armies, O God of Israel, who is enthroned on the cherubim! You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the sky and the earth.

notes.text: The cherubim (singular “cherub”) refer to the images of winged angelic creatures that were above the ark of the covenant.
Or “the heavens.” The Hebrew term ‏שָׁמַיִם‎ (shamayim) may be translated “heavens” or “sky” depending on the context.

17.text: Pay attention, Lord, and hear! Open your eyes, Lord, and observe! Listen to this entire message Sennacherib sent and how he taunts the living God!

notes.text: Heb “Hear all the words of Sennacherib which he sent to taunt the living God.”

18.text: It is true, Lord, that the kings of Assyria have destroyed all the nations and their lands.

notes.text: The Hebrew text here has “all the lands,” but the parallel text in 2 Kgs 19:17 has “the nations.”

19.text: They have burned the gods of the nations, for they are not really gods, but only the product of human hands manufactured from wood and stone. That is why the Assyrians could destroy them.

notes.text: Heb “and they put their gods in the fire.”
Heb “so they destroyed them” (NASB similar).

20.text: Now, O Lord our God, rescue us from his power, so all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the Lord.”

notes.text: The parallel text in 2 Kgs 19:19 reads, “that you, Lord, are the only God.”

21.text: Isaiah son of Amoz sent this message to Hezekiah: “This is what the Lord God of Israel has said: ‘As to what you have prayed to me concerning King Sennacherib of Assyria,

notes.text: The parallel text in 2 Kgs 19:20 includes a verb, “What you have prayed … I have heard.”

22.text: this is what the Lord says about him: “‘The virgin daughter Zion despises you—she makes fun of you; daughter Jerusalem shakes her head after you.

notes.text: Heb “this is the word which the Lord has spoken about him.”

Zion (Jerusalem) is pictured here as a young, vulnerable daughter whose purity is being threatened by the would-be Assyrian rapist. The personification hints at the reality which the young girls of the city would face if the Assyrians conquered it.
Shaking the head was a mocking gesture of derision.

23.text: Whom have you taunted and hurled insults at? At whom have you shouted and looked so arrogantly? At the Holy One of Israel!

notes.text: Heb “and lifted your eyes on high?” Cf. NIV “lifted your eyes in pride”; NRSV “haughtily lifted your eyes.”
See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in 1:4.

24.text: Through your messengers you taunted the Lord, “With my many chariots I climbed up the high mountains, the slopes of Lebanon. I cut down its tall cedars and its best evergreens. I invaded its remotest regions, its thickest woods.

notes.text: The Hebrew term translated “Lord” here is ‏אֲדֹנָי‎ (ʾadonay).
Heb “the height of its extremity”; ASV “its farthest height.”

25.text: I dug wells and drank water. With the soles of my feet I dried up all the rivers of Egypt.”’

notes.text: The Hebrew text has simply, “I dug and drank water.” But the parallel text in 2 Kgs 19:24 has “foreign waters.” ‏זָרִים‎ (zarim, “foreign”) may have accidentally dropped out of the Isaianic text by homoioteleuton (cf. NCV, NIV, NLT). Note that the preceding word, ‏מַיִם‎ (mayim, “water) also ends in mem (‏ם‎). The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has “foreign waters” for this line. However, in several other passages the 1QIsaa scroll harmonizes with 2 Kgs 19 against the MT (Isa 36:5; 37:9, 20). Since the addition of “foreign” to this text in Isaiah by a later scribe would be more likely than its deletion, the MT reading should be accepted.

26.text: Certainly you must have heard! Long ago I worked it out, in ancient times I planned it, and now I am bringing it to pass. The plan is this: Fortified cities will crash into heaps of ruins.

notes.text: Having quoted the Assyrian king’s arrogant words in vv. 23-24, the Lord now speaks to the king.
Heb “Have you not heard?” The rhetorical question expresses the Lord’s amazement that anyone might be ignorant of what he is about to say.
Heb “formed” (so KJV, ASV).

Heb “and it is to cause to crash into heaps of ruins fortified cities.” The subject of the third feminine singular verb ‏תְהִי‎ (tehi) is the implied plan, referred to in the preceding lines with third feminine singular pronominal suffixes.

27.text: Their residents are powerless; they are terrified and ashamed. They are as short-lived as plants in the field or green vegetation. They are as short-lived as grass on the rooftops when it is scorched by the east wind.

notes.text: Heb “short of hand”; KJV, ASV “of small power”; NASB “short of strength.”
Heb “they are plants in the field and green vegetation.” The metaphor emphasizes how short-lived these seemingly powerful cities really were. See Ps 90:5-6; Isa 40:6-8, 24.
Heb “[they are] grass on the rooftops.” See the preceding note.

The Hebrew text has “scorched before the standing grain” (perhaps meaning “before it reaches maturity”), but it is preferable to emend ‏קָמָה‎ (qamah, “standing grain”) to ‏קָדִים‎ (qadim, “east wind”) with the support of 1Q Isaa; cf. J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:657, n. 8.

28.text: I know where you live and everything you do and how you rage against me.

notes.text: Heb “your going out and your coming in and how you have raged against me.” Several scholars have suggested that this line is probably dittographic (note the beginning of the next line). However, most English translations include the statement in question at the end of v. 28 and the beginning of v. 29. Interestingly, the LXX does not have this clause at the end of v. 28 and the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa does not have it at the beginning of v. 29. In light of this ambiguous manuscript evidence, it appears best to retain the clause in both verses.

29.text: Because you rage against me and the uproar you create has reached my ears, I will put my hook in your nose, and my bit between your lips, and I will lead you back the way you came.’

notes.text: Heb “and your complacency comes up into my ears.” The parallelism is improved if ‏שַׁאֲנַנְךָ‎ (shaʾananekha, “your complacency”) is emended to ‏שְׁאוֹנְךָ‎ (sheʾonekha, “your uproar”). See M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 237-38. However, the LXX seems to support the MT, and Sennacherib’s cavalier dismissal of Yahweh depicts an arrogant complacency (J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah [NICOT], 1:658, n. 10).
The word-picture has a parallel in Assyrian sculpture. See M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 238.

30.text: “This will be your reminder that I have spoken the truth: This year you will eat what grows wild, and next year what grows on its own. But the year after that you will plant seed and harvest crops; you will plant vines and consume their produce.

notes.text: At this point the word concerning the king of Assyria (vv. 22-29) ends, and the Lord again addresses Hezekiah and the people directly (see v. 21).

Heb “and this is your sign.” In this case the ‏אוֹת‎ (ʾot, “sign”) is a future reminder of God’s intervention designated before the actual intervention takes place. For similar “signs” see Exod 3:12 and Isa 7:14-25.
This refers to crops that grew up on their own (that is, without cultivation) from the seed planted in past years.
Heb “and in the second year” (so ASV).
Heb “in the third year” (so KJV, NAB).
The four plural imperatival verb forms in v. 30b are used rhetorically. The Lord commands the people to plant, harvest, etc. to emphasize the certainty of restored peace and prosperity.

31.text: Those who remain in Judah will take root in the ground and bear fruit.

notes.text: Heb “The remnant of the house of Judah that is left will add roots below and produce fruit above.”

32.text: “For a remnant will leave Jerusalem; survivors will come out of Mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord of Heaven’s Armies will accomplish this.

notes.text: Traditionally, “the Lord of hosts.” In this context the Lord’s “zeal” refers to his intense devotion to and love for his people that prompts him to protect and restore them.

33.text: So this is what the Lord says about the king of Assyria: “‘He will not enter this city, nor will he shoot an arrow here. He will not attack it with his shielded warriors, nor will he build siege works against it.

notes.text: Heb “there” (so KJV, NASB, NRSV). In terms of English style “here” is expected in collocation with “this” in the previous line.
Heb “[with] a shield” (so ASV, NASB, NRSV).

34.text: He will go back the way he came— he will not enter this city,’ says the Lord.

35.text: I will shield this city and rescue it for the sake of my reputation and because of my promise to David my servant.”

notes.text: Heb “for my sake and for the sake of David my servant.”

36.text: The angel of the Lord went out and killed 185,000 troops in the Assyrian camp. When they got up early the next morning, there were all the corpses!

notes.text: The word “troops” is supplied in the translation for smoothness and clarity.
This refers to the Israelites and/or the rest of the Assyrian army.
Heb “look, all of them were dead bodies”; NLT “they found corpses everywhere.”

37.text: So King Sennacherib of Assyria broke camp and went on his way. He went home and stayed in Nineveh.

notes.text: Heb “and Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and went and returned and lived in Nineveh.”

38.text: One day, as he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him down with the sword. They ran away to the land of Ararat; his son Esarhaddon replaced him as king.

notes.text: The assassination of King Sennacherib probably took place in 681 b.c.
The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.

No such Mesopotamian god is presently known. Perhaps the name Nisroch is a textual variation of Nusku, the Mesopotamian god of light and fire. Other proposals have tried to relate the name to Ashur, the chief god of the Assyria, or to Ninurta, the Assyrian god of war.
Extra-biblical sources also mention the assassination of Sennacherib, though they refer to only one assassin. See M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 239-40.

1.text: In those days Hezekiah was stricken with a terminal illness. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz visited him and told him, “This is what the Lord says, ‘Give instructions to your household, for you are about to die; you will not get well.’”

notes.text: Heb “was sick to the point of dying”; NRSV “became sick and was at the point of death.”

2.text: Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the Lord,

3.text: “Please, Lord. Remember how I have served you faithfully and with wholehearted devotion, and how I have carried out your will.” Then Hezekiah wept bitterly.

notes.text: Heb “walked before you.” For a helpful discussion of the background and meaning of this Hebrew idiom, see M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 254.
Heb “and with a complete heart”; KJV, ASV “with a perfect heart.”
Heb “and that which is good in your eyes I have done.”
Heb “wept with great weeping”; NCV “cried loudly”; TEV “began to cry bitterly.”

4.text: The Lord’s message came to Isaiah,

5.text: “Go and tell Hezekiah: ‘This is what the Lord God of your ancestor David says: “I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Look, I will add fifteen years to your life.

notes.text: Heb “father” (so KJV, NAB, NIV).

6.text: I will also rescue you and this city from the king of Assyria. I will shield this city.”’”

7.text: Isaiah replied, “This is your sign from the Lord confirming that the Lord will do what he has said:

notes.text: The words “Isaiah replied” are supplied in the translation for clarification. In the present form of the Hebrew text v. 7 is joined directly to v. 6, but vv. 21-22, if original to Isaiah 38, must be inserted here. See 2 Kgs 20:7-8.

8.text: Look, I will make the shadow go back ten steps on the stairs of Ahaz.” And then the shadow went back ten steps.

notes.text: Heb “the shadow on the steps which it [the sun] had gone down, on the steps of Ahaz, with the sun, back ten steps.”
These steps probably functioned as a type of sundial. See HALOT 614 s.v. ‏מַעֲלָה‎ and M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, II Kings (AB), 256.
Heb “and the sun returned ten steps on the steps which it had gone down.”

9.text: This is the prayer of King Hezekiah of Judah when he was sick and then recovered from his illness:

10.text: “I thought, ‘In the middle of my life I must walk through the gates of Sheol, I am deprived of the rest of my years.’

notes.text: Or “I said” (KJV, NIV, NRSV, NLT).

The precise meaning of the phrase ‏בִּדְמִי יָמַי‎ (bidmi yamay, “in the [?] of my days”) is uncertain. According to HALOT 226 s.v. ‏דְּמִי‎ this word is a hapax legomenon meaning “half.” Others derive the form from ‏דַּמִי‎ (dami, “quiet, rest, peacefulness”).

The precise meaning of the verb is uncertain. The Pual of of ‏פָּקַד‎ (paqad) occurs only here and in Exod 38:21, where it appears to mean “passed in review” or “mustered.” Perhaps the idea is, “I have been called away for the remainder of my years.” To bring out the sense more clearly, one can translate, “I am deprived of the rest of my years.”

11.text: “I thought, ‘I will no longer see the Lord in the land of the living, I will no longer look on humankind with the inhabitants of the world.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has ‏יָהּ יָהּ‎ (yah yah, the abbreviated form of ‏יְהוָה‎ [yehvah] repeated), but this probably should be emended to ‏יְהוָה‎.

The Hebrew text has ‏חָדֶל‎ (khadel), which appears to be derived from a verbal root meaning “to cease, refrain.” But the form has probably suffered an error of transmission; the original form (attested in a few medieval Hebrew mss) was likely ‏חֶלֶד‎ (kheled, “world”).

12.text: My dwelling place is removed and taken away from me as a shepherd’s tent. I rolled up my life like a weaver rolls cloth; from the loom he cuts me off. You turn day into night and end my life.

notes.text: According to HALOT 217 s.v. ‏דּוֹר‎ this noun is a hapax legomenon meaning “dwelling place,” derived from a verbal root meaning “live” (see Ps 84:10). For an interpretation that understands the form as the well-attested noun meaning “generation,” see J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:679, n. 4.

The verb form appears to be a Niphal from ‏גָּלָה‎ (galah), which normally means “uncovered, revealed” in the Niphal. Because of the following reference to a shepherd’s tent, some prefer to emend the form to ‏וְנָגַל‎, a Niphal from ‏גָלָל‎ (galal, “roll”) and translate “is rolled [or “folded”] up.”
Heb “I rolled up, like a weaver, my life” (so ASV).
For a discussion of the imagery employed here, see J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:684.
Heb “from day to night you bring me to an end.”

13.text: I cry out until morning; like a lion he shatters all my bones; you turn day into night and end my life.

notes.text: The verb form in the Hebrew text is a Piel from ‏שָׁוַה‎ (shavah). There are two homonyms ‏שָׁוַה‎, one meaning in the Piel “level, smooth out,” the other “set, place.” Neither fits in v. 13. It is likely that the original reading was ‏שִׁוַּעְתִּי‎ (shivvaʿti, “I cry out”) from the verbal root ‏שָׁוַע‎ (shavaʿ), which occurs exclusively in the Piel.
Heb “from day to night you bring me to an end.”

14.text: Like a swallow or a thrush I chirp, I coo like a dove; my eyes grow tired from looking up to the sky. O Lord, I am oppressed; help me!

notes.text: Or “moan” (ASV, NAB, NASB, NRSV); KJV, CEV “mourn.”
Heb “my eyes become weak, toward the height.”
The Hebrew term translated “Lord” here and in v. 16 is ‏אֲדֹנָי‎ (ʾadonay).
Heb “stand surety for me.” Hezekiah seems to be picturing himself as a debtor who is being exploited; he asks that the Lord might relieve his debt and deliver him from the oppressive creditor.

15.text: What can I say? He has decreed and acted. I will walk slowly all my years because I am overcome with grief.

notes.text: Heb “and he has spoken and he has acted.”
Heb “because of the bitterness of my soul.”

16.text: O Lord, your decrees can give men life; may years of life be restored to me. Restore my health and preserve my life.’

notes.text: The translation offered here is purely speculative. The text as it stands is difficult and obscure. It reads literally, “O Lord, on account of them [the suffix is masculine plural], they live, and to all in them [the suffix is feminine plural], life of my spirit.”
The prefixed verbal form could be taken as indicative, “you restore my health,” but the following imperatival form suggests it be understood as an imperfect of request.

17.text: “Look, the grief I experienced was for my benefit. You delivered me from the Pit of oblivion. For you removed all my sins from your sight.

notes.text: Heb “Look, for peace bitterness was to me bitter”; NAB “thus is my bitterness transformed into peace.”

The Hebrew text reads, “you loved my soul,” but this does not fit syntactically with the following prepositional phrase. ‏חָשַׁקְתָּ‎ (khashaqta, “you loved”), may reflect an aural error; most emend the form to ‏חָשַׂכְת‎, (khasakht, “you held back”).
‏בְּלִי‎ (beli) most often appears as a negation, meaning “without,” suggesting the meaning “nothingness, oblivion,” here. Some translate “decay” or “destruction.”
Heb “for you threw behind your back all my sins.”

18.text: Indeed Sheol does not give you thanks; death does not praise you. Those who descend into the Pit do not anticipate your faithfulness.

notes.text: Or “For” (KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).
The negative particle is understood by ellipsis in this line. See GKC 483 §152.z.

19.text: The living person, the living person, he gives you thanks, as I do today. A father tells his sons about your faithfulness.

20.text: The Lord is about to deliver me, and we will celebrate with music for the rest of our lives in the Lord’s temple.”

notes.text: The infinitive construct is used here to indicate that an action is imminent. See GKC 348-49 §114.i, and IBHS 610 §36.2.3g.
Heb “and music [or perhaps, “stringed instruments”] we will play.”
Heb “all the days of our lives in the house of the Lord.”
Note that vv. 21-22 have been placed between vv. 6-7, where they logically belong. See 2 Kgs 20:7-8.

21.text: (Isaiah ordered, “Let them take a fig cake and apply it to the ulcerated sore and he will get well.”

notes.text: If original to Isaiah 38, vv. 21-22 have obviously been misplaced in the course of the text’s transmission, and would most naturally be placed here, between Isa 38:6 and 38:7. See 2 Kgs 20:7-8, where these verses are placed at this point in the narrative, not at the end. Another possibility is that these verses were not in the original account, and a scribe, familiar with the 2 Kgs version of the story, appended vv. 21-22 to the end of the account in Isaiah 38.

22.text: Hezekiah said, “What is the confirming sign that I will go up to the Lord’s temple?”)

1.text: At that time Merodach Baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he heard that Hezekiah had been ill and had recovered.

2.text: Hezekiah welcomed them and showed them his storehouse with its silver, gold, spices, and high-quality olive oil, as well as his whole armory and everything in his treasuries. Hezekiah showed them everything in his palace and in his whole kingdom.

notes.text: Heb “was happy with”; NAB, NASB “was pleased”; NIV “received the envoys gladly.”
Heb “there was nothing which Hezekiah did not show them in his house and in all his kingdom.”

3.text: Isaiah the prophet visited King Hezekiah and asked him, “What did these men say? Where do they come from?” Hezekiah replied, “They come from the distant land of Babylon.”

4.text: Isaiah asked, “What have they seen in your palace?” Hezekiah replied, “They have seen everything in my palace. I showed them everything in my treasuries.”

notes.text: Heb “he”; the referent (Isaiah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

5.text: Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Listen to the message of the Lord of Heaven’s Armies:

6.text: ‘Look, a time is coming when everything in your palace and the things your ancestors have accumulated to this day will be carried away to Babylon; nothing will be left,’ says the Lord.

notes.text: Heb “fathers” (so KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV).

7.text: ‘Some of your very own descendants whom you father will be taken away and will be made eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.’”

notes.text: Heb “Some of your sons, who go out from you, whom you father.”

8.text: Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The Lord’s message that you have announced is appropriate.” Then he thought, “For there will be peace and stability during my lifetime.”

notes.text: Heb “good” (so KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT); NAB “favorable.”
Heb “and he said.” The verb ‏אָמַר‎ (ʾamar, “say”) is sometimes used of what one thinks (that is, says to oneself).
Or “surely”; cf. CEV “At least.”

1.text: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God.

notes.text: The pronominal suffix is second masculine plural. The identity of the addressee is uncertain: (1) God’s people may be addressed, or (2) the unidentified heralds commanded to comfort Jerusalem.

2.text: “Speak kindly to Jerusalem and tell her that her time of warfare is over, that her punishment is completed. For the Lord has made her pay double for all her sins.”

notes.text: Heb “speak to the heart of Jerusalem.” Jerusalem is personified as a woman.
Heb “that she is filled [with] her warfare.” Some understand ‏צָבָא‎ (tsavah, “warfare”) as meaning “hard service” or “compulsory labor” in this context.
Heb “that her punishment is accepted [as satisfactory].”

Heb “for she has received from the hand of the Lord double.” The principle of the double portion in punishment is also seen in Jer 16:18; 17:18 and Rev 18:6. For examples of the double portion in Israelite law, see Exod 22:4, 7, 9 (double restitution by a thief) and Deut 21:17 (double inheritance portion for the firstborn).

3.text: A voice cries out, “In the wilderness clear a way for the Lord; build a level road through the rift valley for our God.

notes.text: Heb “make level a built road.” The verb ‏יָשַׁר‎ (yashar) in the Piel means “to make smooth, or straight.” The noun ‏מְסִלָּה‎ (mesillah) typically refers to a main road, possibly paved with stones or made level with fill (see HALOT 606 s.v. and The Concise DCH 230 s.v.).

Most translations render this as “desert” (KJV, NASB, ESV, NRSV, NIV 2011, Holman), “wilderness” (NIV 1984), or “wasteland” (NLV). The rift valley (‏עֲרָבָה‎, ʿaravah), which extends from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba, is quite arid and desert-like in the areas near the Dead Sea and southward (see the note at Num 22:1). But the point here has more to do with preparation for a royal visit. To come to Jerusalem from the east requires coming through the rift valley (or Jordan Valley). Thematically, God is typically portrayed as coming to Israel from the east. Similarly in the Gospel accounts Jesus approaches Jerusalem from the east.

4.text: Every valley must be elevated, and every mountain and hill leveled. The rough terrain will become a level plain, the rugged landscape a wide valley.

5.text: The splendor of the Lord will be revealed, and all people will see it at the same time. For the Lord has decreed it.”

notes.text: Or “glory.” The Lord’s “glory” is his theophanic radiance and royal splendor (see Isa 6:3; 24:23; 35:2; 60:1; 66:18-19).
Heb “flesh” (so KJV, ASV, NASB); NAB, NIV “mankind”; TEV “the whole human race.”
Or “indeed.”
Heb “the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (so NASB, NIV, NRSV).

6.text: A voice says, “Cry out!” Another asks, “What should I cry out?” The first voice responds: “All people are like grass, and all their promises are like the flowers in the field.

notes.text: Heb “and he says.” Apparently a second “voice” responds to the command of the first “voice.”
The words “the first voice responds” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The first voice tells the second one what to declare.
Heb “all flesh is grass.” The point of the metaphor is explained in v. 7.

Heb “and all his loyalty.” The antecedent of the third masculine suffix is ‏בָּשָׂר‎ (basar, “flesh”), which refers collectively to mankind. The LXX, apparently understanding the antecedent as “grass,” reads “glory,” but ‏חֶסֶד‎ (khesed) rarely, if ever, has this nuance. The normal meaning of ‏חֶסֶד‎ (“faithfulness, loyalty, devotion”) fits very well in the argument. Human beings and their faithfulness (verbal expressions of faithfulness are specifically in view; cf. NRSV “constancy”) are short-lived and unreliable, in stark contrast to the decrees and promises of the eternal God.

7.text: The grass dries up, the flowers wither, when the wind sent by the Lord blows on them. Surely humanity is like grass.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has ‏רוּחַ יְהוָה‎ (ruakh yehvah), which in this context probably does not refer to the Lord’s personal Spirit. The phrase is better translated “the breath of the Lord,” or “the wind of [i.e., sent by] the Lord.” The Lord’s sovereign control over nature, including the hot desert winds that dry up vegetation, is in view here (cf. Ps 147:18; Isa 59:19).
Heb “the people” (so KJV, ASV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV).

8.text: The grass dries up, the flowers wither, but the decree of our God is forever reliable.”

notes.text: Heb “but the word of our God stands forever.” In this context the divine “word” specifically refers to his decreed promise assuring Jerusalem that her suffering is over and his glorious return imminent (vv. 1-5).

9.text: Go up on a high mountain, O herald Zion. Shout out loudly, O herald Jerusalem! Shout, don’t be afraid! Say to the towns of Judah, “Here is your God!”

notes.text: The second feminine singular imperatives are addressed to personified Zion/Jerusalem, who is here told to ascend a high hill and proclaim the good news of the Lord’s return to the other towns of Judah. Isa 41:27 and 52:7 speak of a herald sent to Zion, but the masculine singular form ‏מְבַשֵּׂר‎ (mevasser) is used in these verses, in contrast to the feminine singular form ‏מְבַשֶּׂרֶת‎ (mevasseret) employed in 40:9, where Zion is addressed as a herald.

10.text: Look, the Sovereign Lord comes as a victorious warrior; his military power establishes his rule. Look, his reward is with him; his prize goes before him.

notes.text: Heb “comes as a strong one”; ASV “will come as a mighty one.” The preposition ‏בְּ‎ (bet) here carries the nuance “in the capacity of.” It indicates that the Lord possesses the quality expressed by the noun. See GKC 379 §119.i and HALOT 104 s.v. ‏בְּ‎.
Heb “his arm rules for him” (so NIV, NRSV). The Lord’s “arm” symbolizes his military power (see Isa 51:9-10; 63:5).

As the Lord returns to Jerusalem as a victorious warrior, he brings with him the spoils of victory, called here his “reward” and “prize.” These terms might also be translated “wages” and “recompense.” Verse 11 indicates that his rescued people, likened to a flock of sheep, are his reward.

11.text: Like a shepherd he tends his flock; he gathers up the lambs with his arm; he carries them close to his heart; he leads the ewes along.

notes.text: Heb “in his bosom” (so KJV, NAB, NASB, NRSV), an expression which reflects closeness and protective care.

12.text: Who has measured out the waters in the hollow of his hand, or carefully measured the sky, or carefully weighed the soil of the earth, or weighed the mountains in a balance, or the hills on scales?

notes.text: The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has ‏מי ים‎ (“waters of the sea”), a reading followed by NAB.
Heb “with a span.” A “span” was the distance between the ends of the thumb and the little finger of the spread hand” (BDB 285 s.v. ‏זֶרֶת‎).
Or “the heavens.” The Hebrew term ‏שָׁמַיִם‎ (shamayim) may be translated “heavens” or “sky” depending on the context.
Heb “or weighed by a third part [of a measure].”

The implied answer to the rhetorical questions of v. 12 is, “No one but the Lord.” The Lord, and no other, created the world. Like a merchant weighing out silver or commodities on a scale, the Lord established the various components of the physical universe in precise proportions.

13.text: Who comprehends the mind of the Lord, or gives him instruction as his counselor?

notes.text: Perhaps the verb is used metonymically here in the sense of “advises” (note the following line).
In this context ‏רוּחַ‎ (ruakh) likely refers to the Lord’s “mind,” or mental faculties, rather than his personal Spirit (see BDB 925 s.v. 6).
Heb “or [as] the man of his counsel causes him to know?”

14.text: From whom does he receive directions? Who teaches him the correct way to do things, or imparts knowledge to him, or instructs him in skillful design?

notes.text: Heb “With whom did he consult, so that he gave discernment to him?”
Heb “and taught him.” The vav (‏ו‎) consecutive with prefixed verbal form continues the previous line. The translation employs an interrogative pronoun for stylistic reasons.

The phrase ‏אֹרַח מִשְׁפָּט‎ (ʾorakh mishpat) could be translated “path of justice” (so NASB, NRSV), but in this context, where creative ability and skill is in view, the phrase is better understood in the sense of “the way that is proper or fitting” (see BDB 1049 s.v. ‏מִשְׁפָּט‎ 6); cf. NIV, NCV “the right way.”
Heb “or the way of understanding causes him to know?”

The implied answer to the rhetorical questions in vv. 13-14 is, “No one.” In contrast to Marduk, the creator-god of Mesopotamian myths who receives help from the god of wisdom, the Lord neither needs nor receives any such advice or help. See R. Whybray, Heavenly Counsellor (SOTSMS), 64-77.

15.text: Look, the nations are like a drop in a bucket; they are regarded as dust on the scales. He lifts the coastlands as if they were dust.

notes.text: Or “weighs” (NIV); NLT “picks up.”
Or “islands” (NASB, NIV, NLT).

16.text: Not even Lebanon could supply enough firewood for a sacrifice; its wild animals would not provide enough burnt offerings.

notes.text: The words “for a sacrifice” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
The point is that not even the Lebanon forest could supply enough wood and animals for an adequate sacrifice to the Lord.

17.text: All the nations are insignificant before him; they are regarded as absolutely nothing.

notes.text: Heb “[as derived] from nothing and unformed.”

18.text: To whom can you compare God? To what image can you liken him?

19.text: A craftsman casts an idol; a metalsmith overlays it with gold and forges silver chains for it.

notes.text: Heb “pours out”; KJV “melteth.”

20.text: To make a contribution one selects wood that will not rot; he then seeks a skilled craftsman to make an idol that will not fall over.

notes.text: The first two words of the verse (‏הַמְסֻכָּן תְּרוּמָה‎, hamesukkan terumah) are problematic. Some take ‏מְסֻכָּן‎ as an otherwise unattested Pual participle from ‏סָכַן‎ (sakhan, “be poor”) and translate “the one who is impoverished.” ‏תְּרוּמָה‎ (terumah, “contribution”) can then be taken as an adverbial accusative, “with respect to a contribution,” and the entire line translated, “the one who is too impoverished for such a contribution [i.e., the metal idol of v. 19?] selects wood that will not rot.” However, ‏מְסֻכָּן‎ is probably the name of a tree used in idol manufacturing (cognate with Akkadian musukkanu, cf. H. R. Cohen, Biblical Hapax Legomena [SBLDS], 133). ‏מְסֻכָּן‎ may be a scribal interpretive addition attempting to specify ‏עֵץ‎ (ʿets) or ‏עֵץ‎ may be a scribal attempt to categorize ‏מְסֻכָּן‎. How an idol constitutes a ‏תְּרוּמָה‎ (“contribution”) is not entirely clear.
Or “set up” (ASV, NAB, NIV, NRSV); KJV, NASB “to prepare.”

21.text: Do you not know? Do you not hear? Has it not been told to you since the very beginning? Have you not understood from the time the earth’s foundations were made?

22.text: He is the one who sits on the earth’s horizon; its inhabitants are like grasshoppers before him. He is the one who stretches out the sky like a thin curtain, and spreads it out like a pitched tent.

notes.text: Heb “the circle of the earth” (so KJV, NIV, NRSV, NLT).
The words “before him” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

The otherwise unattested noun ‏דֹּק‎ (doq), translated here “thin curtain,” is apparently derived from the verbal root ‏דקק‎ (“crush”) from which is derived the adjective ‏דַּק‎ (daq, “thin”; see HALOT 229 s.v. ‏דקק‎). The nuance “curtain” is implied from the parallelism (see “tent” in the next line).

The meaning of the otherwise unattested verb ‏מָתַח‎ (matakh, “spread out”) is determined from the parallelism (note the corresponding verb “stretch out” in the previous line) and supported by later Hebrew and Aramaic cognates. See HALOT 654 s.v. *‏מתה‎.
Heb “like a tent [in which] to live”; NAB, NASB “like a tent to dwell (live NIV, NRSV) in.”

23.text: He is the one who reduces rulers to nothing; he makes the earth’s leaders insignificant.

24.text: Indeed, they are barely planted; yes, they are barely sown; yes, they barely take root in the earth, and then he blows on them, causing them to dry up, and the wind carries them away like straw.

25.text: “To whom can you compare me? Whom do I resemble?” says the Holy One.

notes.text: See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in 1:4.

26.text: Look up at the sky! Who created all these heavenly lights? He is the one who leads out their ranks; he calls them all by name. Because of his absolute power and awesome strength, not one of them is missing.

notes.text: Heb “Lift on high your eyes and see.”
The words “heavenly lights” are supplied in the translation for clarification. See the following lines.

Heb “the one who brings out by number their host.” The stars are here likened to a huge army that the Lord leads out. Perhaps the next line pictures God calling roll. If so, the final line may be indicating that none of them dares “go AWOL.” (“AWOL” is a military acronym for “absent without leave.”)

27.text: Why do you say, Jacob, Why do you say, Israel, “The Lord is not aware of what is happening to me; My God is not concerned with my vindication”?

notes.text: Heb “my way is hidden from the Lord” (so NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV).
Heb “and from my God my justice passes away”; NRSV “my right is disregarded by my God.”

28.text: Do you not know? Have you not heard? The Lord is an eternal God, the Creator of the whole earth. He does not get tired or weary; there is no limit to his wisdom.

notes.text: Heb “the ends of the earth,” but this is a merism, where the earth’s extremities stand for its entirety, i.e., the extremities and everything in between them.

Exiled Israel’s complaint (v. 27) implies that God might be limited in some way. Perhaps he, like so many of the pagan gods, has died. Or perhaps his jurisdiction is limited to Judah and does not include Babylon. Maybe he is unable to devise an adequate plan to rescue his people, or is unable to execute it. But v. 28 affirms that he is not limited temporally or spatially nor are his power and wisdom restricted in any way. He can and will deliver his people, if they respond in hopeful faith (v. 31a).

29.text: He gives strength to those who are tired; to the ones who lack power, he gives renewed energy.

30.text: Even youths get tired and weary; even strong young men clumsily stumble.

notes.text: Heb “stumbling they stumble.” The verbal idea is emphasized by the infinitive absolute.

31.text: But those who wait for the Lord’s help find renewed strength; they rise up as if they had eagles’ wings, they run without growing weary, they walk without getting tired.

notes.text: The word “help” in the phrase “for the Lord’s help” is supplied in the translation for clarification, as is the possessive on “Lord.”
Heb “they rise up [on] wings like eagles” (TEV similar).

1.text: “Listen to me in silence, you coastlands! Let the nations find renewed strength! Let them approach and then speak; let us come together for debate.

notes.text: Or “islands” (KJV, NIV, CEV); TEV “distant lands”; NLT “lands beyond the sea.”
The Hebrew term ‏מִשְׁפָּט‎ (mishpat) could be translated “judgment,” but here it seems to refer to the dispute or debate between the Lord and the nations.

2.text: Who stirs up this one from the east? Who officially commissions him for service? He hands nations over to him, and enables him to subdue kings. He makes them like dust with his sword, like windblown straw with his bow.

notes.text: The expression this one from the east refers to the Persian conqueror Cyrus, as later texts indicate (see 44:28-45:6; 46:11; 48:14-16).
The interrogative particle is understood by ellipsis.
Heb “[in] righteousness called him to his foot.”
Heb “he [the Lord] places before him [Cyrus] nations.”

The verb ‏יַרְדְּ‎ (yard) is an otherwise unattested Hiphil form from ‏רָדָה‎ (radah, “rule”). But the Hiphil makes no sense with “kings” as object; one must understand an ellipsis and supply “him” (Cyrus) as the object. The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has ‏יוֹרִיד‎ (yorid), which appears to be a Hiphil form from ‏יָרַד‎ (yarad, “go down”). Others suggest reading ‏יָרֹד‎ (yarod), a Qal form from ‏רָדַד‎ (radad, “beat down”).
The point is that they are powerless before Cyrus’ military power and scatter before him.

3.text: He pursues them and passes by unharmed; he advances with great speed.

notes.text: Heb “[in] peace”; KJV, ASV “safely”; NASB “in safety”; NIV “unscathed.”

Heb “a way with his feet he does not come [or “enter”].” One could translate, “by a way he was not [previously] entering with his feet.” This would mean that he is advancing into new territory and expanding his conquests. The present translation assumes this is a hyperbolic description of his speedy advance. He moves so quickly he does not enter the way with his feet, i.e., his feet don’t even touch the ground. See C. R. North, Second Isaiah, 94.

4.text: Who acts and carries out decrees? Who summons the successive generations from the beginning? I, the Lord, am present at the very beginning, and at the very end—I am the one.

notes.text: Heb “Who acts and accomplishes?”; NASB “Who has performed and accomplished it.”
The interrogative particle is understood by ellipsis (note the preceding line).
Heb “I, the Lord, [am with] the first, and with the last ones I [am] he.”

5.text: The coastlands see and are afraid; the whole earth trembles; they approach and come.

notes.text: Or “islands” (NIV, CEV); NCV “faraway places”; NLT “lands beyond the sea.”
Heb “the ends of the earth,” but this is a merism, where the earth’s extremities stand for its entirety, i.e., the extremities and everything in between them.

6.text: They help one another; one says to the other, ‘Be strong!’

notes.text: Heb “each his neighbor helps”; NCV “The workers help each other.”

7.text: The craftsman encourages the metalsmith, the one who wields the hammer encourages the one who pounds on the anvil. He approves the quality of the welding, and nails it down so it won’t fall over.

notes.text: The verb “encourages” is understood by ellipsis (note the preceding line).
Heb “saying of the welding, ‘It is good.’”

8.text: “You, my servant Israel, Jacob, whom I have chosen, offspring of Abraham my friend,

notes.text: Or perhaps, “covenantal partner” (see 1 Kgs 5:15 HT [5:1 ET]; 2 Chr 20:7).

9.text: you whom I am bringing back from the earth’s extremities, and have summoned from the remote regions— I told you, ‘You are my servant.’ I have chosen you and not rejected you.

notes.text: Heb “whom I have taken hold of [i.e., to lead back].”

10.text: Don’t be afraid, for I am with you! Don’t be frightened, for I am your God! I strengthen you— yes, I help you— yes, I uphold you with my victorious right hand!

notes.text: According to BDB (1043 s.v. ‏שָׁעָה‎), the verb ‏תִּשְׁתָּע‎ (tishtaʿ) in the second line of the poetic couplet is a Hitpael form from the root ‏שָׁעָה‎ (shaʿah, “gaze,” with metathesis of the stem prefix and the first root letter). Taking the Hitpael as iterative, one may then translate “do not anxiously look about.” However, the alleged Hitpael form of ‏שָׁעָה‎ (shaʿah) only occurs here and in verse 23. HALOT 1671 s.v. ‏שׁתע‎ proposes that the verb is instead a Qal form from the root ‏שׁתע‎ (“fear”). Its attestation in cognate Semitic languages, including Ugaritic (discovered after the publishing of BDB), suggests the existence of this root. The poetic structure of v. 10 also supports the proposal, for the form in question is in synonymous parallelism to ‏יָרֵא‎ (yareʾ, “fear”).

The “right hand” is a symbol of the Lord’s power to deliver (Exod 15:6, 12) and protect (Ps 63:9 HT [63:8 ET]). Here ‏צֶדֶק‎ (tsedeq) has its well-attested nuance of “vindicated righteousness,” i.e., “victory, deliverance” (see 45:8; 51:5, and BDB 841-42 s.v.).

11.text: Look, all who were angry at you will be ashamed and humiliated; your adversaries will be reduced to nothing and perish.

notes.text: Heb “the men of your strife”; NASB “those who contend with you.”
Heb “like nothing”; NAB “come to nought.”

12.text: When you will look for your opponents, you will not find them; your enemies will be reduced to absolutely nothing.

notes.text: Heb “the men of your struggle”; NASB “those who quarrel with you.”
Heb “the men of your battle”; NAB “who do battle with you.”

13.text: For I am the Lord your God, the one who takes hold of your right hand, who says to you, ‘Don’t be afraid, I am helping you.’

14.text: Don’t be afraid, despised insignificant Jacob, men of Israel. I am helping you,” says the Lord, your Protector, the Holy One of Israel.

notes.text: Heb “O worm Jacob” (NAB, NIV). The worm metaphor suggests that Jacob is insignificant and despised.
On the basis of the parallelism (note “worm”) and an alleged Akkadian cognate, some read “louse” or “weevil.” Cf. NAB “O maggot Israel”; NRSV “you insect Israel.”
Heb “your kinsman redeemer.” A ‏גֹּאֵל‎ (goʾel, “kinsman redeemer”) was a protector of the extended family’s interests.
See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in 1:4.

15.text: “Look, I am making you like a sharp threshing sledge, new and double-edged. You will thresh the mountains and crush them; you will make the hills like straw.

notes.text: Heb “into” (so NIV); ASV “have made thee to be.”
Heb “owner of two-mouths,” i.e., double-edged.
The mountains and hills symbolize hostile nations that are obstacles to Israel’s restoration.

16.text: You will winnow them and the wind will blow them away; the wind will scatter them. You will rejoice in the Lord; you will boast in the Holy One of Israel.

17.text: The oppressed and the poor look for water, but there is none; their tongues are parched from thirst. I, the Lord, will respond to their prayers; I, the God of Israel, will not abandon them.

notes.text: Heb “will answer them” (so ASV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).

18.text: I will make streams flow down the slopes and produce springs in the middle of the valleys. I will turn the wilderness into a pool of water and the arid land into springs.

19.text: I will make cedars, acacias, myrtles, and olive trees grow in the wilderness; I will make evergreens, firs, and cypresses grow together in the arid rift valley.

notes.text: The rift valley (‏עֲרָבָה‎, ʿaravah) is known for its arid, desert-like conditions in the area of the Dead Sea and southward (although it also includes the Jordan Valley, extending from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba). The point here is the contrast from its normal arid conditions to being productive with trees, which implies being watered. Similarly, the wilderness (‏מִדְבָּר‎, midbar) in the first line is an area that receives less than twelve inches of rainfall annually and so cannot support trees.

20.text: I will do this so people will observe and recognize, so they will pay attention and understand that the Lord’s power has accomplished this, and that the Holy One of Israel has brought it into being.

notes.text: The words “I will do this” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The Hebrew text has here simply, “in order that.”
Heb “they”; NAB, NRSV “that all may see”; CEV, NLT “Everyone will see.”
Heb “hand” (so KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV).
Or “created it” (KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV); TEV “has made it happen.”

21.text: “Present your argument,” says the Lord. “Produce your evidence,” says Jacob’s king.

notes.text: Heb “strong [words],” see HALOT 870 s.v. *‏עֲצֻמוֹת‎.
Apparently this challenge is addressed to the pagan idol gods, see vv. 23-24.

22.text: “Let them produce evidence! Let them tell us what will happen! Tell us about your earlier predictive oracles, so we may examine them and see how they were fulfilled. Or decree for us some future events!

notes.text: Heb “As for the former things, tell us what they are!”
Heb “so we might set [them to] our heart.”
Heb “and might know their outcome.”

23.text: Predict how future events will turn out, so we might know you are gods. Yes, do something good or something bad, so we might be frightened and in awe.

notes.text: Heb “Declare the coming things, with respect to the end.”
The translation assumes the Qere (‏וְנִרְאֶה‎ [venirʾeh], from ‏יָרֵא‎ [yareʾ], “be afraid”).
Heb “so we might be frightened and afraid together.” On the meaning of the verb ‏שָׁתָע‎ (shataʿ), see the note at v. 10.

24.text: Look, you are nothing, and your accomplishments are nonexistent; the one who chooses to worship you is disgusting.

notes.text: Heb “an object of disgust [is he who] chooses you.”

25.text: I have stirred up one out of the north and he advances, one from the eastern horizon who prays in my name. He steps on rulers as if they were clay, like a potter treading the clay.

notes.text: That is, Cyrus the Persian. See the note at v. 2.
Heb “[one] from the rising of the sun [who] calls in my name.”
The Hebrew text has ‏וְיָבֹא‎ (veyavoʾ, “and he comes”), but this likely needs to be emended to an original ‏וַיָּבָס‎ (vayyavas), from ‏בּוּס‎ (bus, “step on”).

26.text: Who decreed this from the beginning, so we could know? Who announced it ahead of time, so we could say, ‘He’s correct’? Indeed, none of them decreed it. Indeed, none of them announced it. Indeed, no one heard you say anything!

notes.text: The words “who announced it” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The interrogative particle and verb are understood by ellipsis (see the preceding line).

27.text: I first decreed to Zion, ‘Look, here’s what will happen!’ I sent a herald to Jerusalem.

notes.text: The Hebrew text reads simply, “First to Zion, ‘Look here they are!’” The words “I decreed” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

28.text: I look, but there is no one, among them there is no one who serves as an adviser, that I might ask questions and receive answers.

29.text: Look, all of them are nothing, their accomplishments are nonexistent; their metal images lack any real substance.

notes.text: The Hebrew text has ‏אָוֶן‎ (ʾaven, “deception,” i.e., “false”), but the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has ‏אין‎ (“nothing”), which forms a better parallel with ‏אֶפֶס‎ (ʾefes, “nothing”) in the next line. See also 40:17 and 41:12.
Heb “their statues are wind and nothing”; NASB “wind and emptiness”; NIV “wind and confusion.”

1.text: “Here is my servant whom I support, my chosen one in whom I take pleasure. I have placed my Spirit on him; he will make just decrees for the nations.

notes.text: Verses 1-7 contain the first of Isaiah’s “servant songs,” which describe the ministry of a special, ideal servant who accomplishes God’s purposes for Israel and the nations. This song depicts the servant as a just king who brings justice to the earth and relief for the oppressed. The other songs appear in 49:1-13; 50:4-11; and 52:13-53:12.
Heb “he will bring out justice” (cf. ASV, NASB, NRSV).
Like the ideal king portrayed in Isa 11:1-9, the servant is energized by the divine spirit and establishes justice on the earth.

2.text: He will not cry out or shout; he will not publicize himself in the streets.

notes.text: Heb “he will not cause his voice to be heard in the street.”

3.text: A crushed reed he will not break, a dim wick he will not extinguish; he will faithfully make just decrees.

notes.text: The “crushed reed” and “dim wick” symbolize the weak and oppressed who are on the verge of extinction.
Heb “faithfully he will bring out justice” (cf. NASB, NRSV).

4.text: He will not grow dim or be crushed before establishing justice on the earth; the coastlands will wait in anticipation for his decrees.”

notes.text: For rhetorical effect the terms used to describe the “crushed (‏רָצַץ‎, ratsats) reed” and “dim (‏כָּהָה‎, kahah) wick” in v. 3 are repeated here.
Or “islands” (NIV); NLT “distant lands beyond the sea.”
Or “his law” (KJV, ASV, NASB, NIV) or “his instruction” (NLT).

5.text: This is what the true God, the Lord, says— the one who created the sky and stretched it out, the one who fashioned the earth and everything that lives on it, the one who gives breath to the people on it, and life to those who live on it:

notes.text: Heb “the God.” The definite article here indicates distinctiveness or uniqueness.
Heb “and its offspring” (so NASB); NIV “all that comes out of it.”
Heb “and spirit [i.e., “breath”] to the ones walking in it” (NAB, NASB, and NRSV all similar).

6.text: “I, the Lord, officially commission you; I take hold of your hand. I protect you and make you a covenant mediator for people, and a light to the nations,

notes.text: Heb “call you in righteousness.” The pronoun “you” is masculine singular, referring to the servant. See the note at 41:2.
The translation assumes the verb is derived from the root ‏נָצַר‎ (natsar, “protect”). Some prefer to derive it from the root ‏יָצַר‎ (yatsar, “form”).

Heb “a covenant of people.” A person cannot literally be a covenant; ‏בְּרִית‎ (berit) is probably metonymic here, indicating a covenant mediator. The precise identity of ‏עָם‎ (ʿam, “people”) is uncertain. In v. 5 ‏עָם‎ refers to mankind, and the following reference to “nations” also favors this. But in 49:8, where the phrase ‏בְּרִית עָם‎ occurs again, Israel seems to be in view.
Light here symbolizes deliverance from bondage and oppression; note the parallelism in 49:6b and in 51:4-6.
Or “the Gentiles” (so KJV, ASV, NIV); the same Hebrew word can be translated “nations” or “Gentiles” depending on the context.

7.text: to open blind eyes, to release prisoners from dungeons, those who live in darkness from prisons.

notes.text: This does not refer to literal physical healing of the blind. As the next two lines suggest, this refers metonymically to freeing captives from their dark prisons where their eyes have grown unaccustomed to light.

This does not refer to hardened, dangerous criminals, who would have been executed for their crimes in ancient Near Eastern society. This verse refers to political prisoners or victims of social injustice.

8.text: “I am the Lord! That is my name! I will not share my glory with anyone else, or the praise due me with idols.

9.text: Look, my earlier predictive oracles have come to pass; now I announce new events. Before they begin to occur, I reveal them to you.”

notes.text: Heb “the former things, look, they have come.”

Heb “before they sprout up, I cause you to hear.” The pronoun “you” is plural, referring to the people of Israel. In this verse “the former things” are the Lord’s earlier predictive oracles which have come to pass, while “the new things” are predicted events that have not yet begun to take place. “The former things” are earlier events in Israel’s history which God announced beforehand, such as the Exodus (see 43:16-18). “The new things” are the predictions about the servant (42:1-7). and may also include Cyrus’ conquests (41:25-27).

10.text: Sing to the Lord a brand new song! Praise him from the horizon of the earth, you who go down to the sea, and everything that lives in it, you coastlands and those who live there.

notes.text: Heb “his praise.” The phrase stands parallel to “new song” in the previous line.
Heb “and its fullness”; NASB, NIV “and all that is in it.”
Or “islands” (NASB, NIV); NLT “distant coastlands.”

11.text: Let the wilderness and its cities shout out, the towns where the nomads of Kedar live. Let the residents of Sela shout joyfully; let them shout loudly from the mountaintops.

12.text: Let them give the Lord the honor he deserves; let them praise his deeds in the coastlands.

notes.text: Heb “Let them ascribe to the Lord glory.”
Heb “and his praise in the coastlands [or “islands”] let them declare.”

13.text: The Lord emerges like a hero, like a warrior he inspires himself for battle; he shouts, yes, he yells, he shows his enemies his power.

notes.text: Heb “like a man of war he stirs up zeal” (NIV similar).
Or perhaps, “he triumphs over his enemies” (cf. NIV); NLT “will crush all his enemies.”

14.text: “I have been inactive for a long time; I kept quiet and held back. Like a woman in labor I groan; I pant and gasp.

notes.text: Heb “silent” (so NASB, NIV, TEV, NLT); CEV “have held my temper.”
The imagery depicts the Lord as a warrior who is eager to fight and can no longer hold himself back from the attack.

15.text: I will make the trees on the mountains and hills wither up; I will dry up all their vegetation. I will turn streams into islands, and dry up pools of water.

notes.text: Heb “I will dry up the mountains and hills.” The “mountains and hills” stand by synecdoche for the trees that grow on them. Some prefer to derive the verb from a homonymic root and translate, “I will lay waste.”

The Hebrew text reads, “I will turn streams into coastlands [or “islands”].” Scholars who believe that this reading makes little sense have proposed an emendation of ‏אִיִּים‎ (ʾiyyim, “islands”) to ‏צִיּוֹת‎ (tsiyyot, “dry places”; cf. NCV, NLT, TEV). However, since all the versions support the MT reading, there is insufficient grounds for an emendation here. Although the imagery of changing rivers into islands is somewhat strange, J. N. Oswalt describes this imagery against the backdrop of rivers of the Near East. The receding of these rivers at times occasioned the appearance of previously submerged islands (Isaiah [NICOT], 2:126).
The imagery of this verse, which depicts the Lord bringing a curse of infertility to the earth, metaphorically describes how the Lord will destroy his enemies.

16.text: I will lead the blind along an unfamiliar way; I will guide them down paths they have never traveled. I will turn the darkness in front of them into light, and level out the rough ground. This is what I will do for them. I will not abandon them.

notes.text: Heb “a way they do not know” (so NASB); NRSV “a road they do not know.”
Heb “in paths they do not know I will make them walk.”
Heb “and the rough ground into a level place.”

17.text: Those who trust in idols will turn back and be utterly humiliated, those who say to metal images, ‘You are our gods.’

notes.text: Heb “be ashamed with shame”; ASV, NASB “be utterly put to shame.”

18.text: “Listen, you deaf ones! Take notice, you blind ones!

notes.text: Heb “look to see”; NAB, NCV “look and see”; NRSV “look up and see.”

19.text: My servant is truly blind, my messenger is truly deaf. My covenant partner, the servant of the Lord, is truly blind.

notes.text: The precise meaning of ‏מְשֻׁלָּם‎ (meshullam) in this context is uncertain. In later biblical Hebrew the form (which appears to be a Pual participle from the root ‏שָׁלַם‎, shalam) occurs as a proper name, Meshullam. The Pual of ‏שָׁלַם‎ (“be complete”) is attested with the meaning “repaid, requited,” but that makes little sense here. BDB 1023 s.v. ‏שָׁלַם‎ relates the form to the denominative verb ‏שָׁלַם‎ (“be at peace”) and paraphrases “one in a covenant of peace” (J. N. Oswalt suggests “the covenanted one”; Isaiah [NICOT], 2:128, n. 59) Some emend the form to ‏מֹשְׁלָם‎ (moshelam, “their ruler”) or to ‏מְשֻׁלָּחִי‎ (meshullakhi, “my sent [or “commissioned”] one”), which fits nicely in the parallelism (note “my messenger” in the previous line). The translation above assumes an emendation to ‏כְּמוֹ שֹׁלְמִי‎ (kemo sholemi, “like my ally”). Isaiah uses ‏כְּמוֹ‎ in 30:22 and perhaps 51:5; for ‏שֹׁלְמי‎ (“my ally”) see Ps 7:5 HT (7:4 ET).

Heb “Who is blind but my servant, and deaf like my messenger I send? Who is blind like my commissioned one, blind like the servant of the Lord?” The point of the rhetorical questions is that no one is as blind/deaf as this servant. In this context the Lord’s “servant” is exiled Israel (cf. 41:8-9), which is spiritually blind and deaf and has failed to fulfill God’s purpose for it. This servant stands in contrast to the ideal “Israel” of the servant songs.

20.text: You see many things, but don’t comprehend; their ears are open, but do not hear.”

notes.text: The consonantal text (Kethib) has a perfect, second person masculine singular; the marginal reading (Qere) has an infinitive absolute, which functions here as a finite verb.
Heb “but you do not guard [i.e., retain in your memory]”; NIV “but have paid no attention.”

21.text: The Lord wanted to exhibit his justice by magnifying his law and displaying it.

notes.text: Heb “The Lord was pleased for the sake of his righteousness [or “justice”], he was magnifying [the] law and was making [it] glorious.” The Lord contrasts his good intentions for the people with their present crisis (v. 22). To demonstrate his just character and attract the nations, the Lord wanted to showcase his law among and through Israel (Deut 4:5-8). But Israel disobeyed (v. 24) and failed to carry out their commission.
