notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative
This is one of the few uses of the specific term salvation in Luke (1:69, 71, 77), though the concept runs throughout the Gospel.
The household is not a reference to the building, but to the people who lived within it (L&N 10.8).
Zacchaeus was personally affirmed by Jesus as a descendant (son) of Abraham and a member of God’s family.

10.text: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”

notes.text: The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost is Jesus’ mission succinctly defined. See Luke 15:1-32.

11.text: While the people were listening to these things, Jesus proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they thought that the kingdom of God was going to appear immediately.

notes.text: Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The present active infinitive δοκεῖν (dokein) has been translated as causal.
Luke means here the appearance of the full kingdom of God in power with the Son of Man as judge as Luke 17:22-37 describes.
Or perhaps, “the kingdom of God must appear immediately (see L&N 71.36).

12.text: Therefore he said, “A nobleman went to a distant country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return.

notes.text: Grk “a man of noble birth” or “a man of noble status” (L&N 87.27).

Note that the receiving of the kingdom takes place in the far country. This suggests that those in the far country recognize and acknowledge the king when his own citizens did not want him as king (v. 14; cf. John 1:11-12).

The background to this story about the nobleman who went…to receive for himself a kingdom had some parallels in the area’s recent history: Archelaus was appointed ethnarch of Judea, Samaria, and Idumea in 4 b.c., but the people did not like him. Herod the Great also made a similar journey to Rome where he was crowned King of Judea in 40 b.c., although he was not able to claim his kingdom until 37 b.c.

13.text: And he summoned ten of his slaves, gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Do business with these until I come back.’

notes.text: See the note on the word “slave” in 7:2.
That is, one for each. A mina was a Greek monetary unit worth 100 denarii or about four months’ wages for an average worker based on a six-day work week.

14.text: But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to be king over us!’

notes.text: Or “subjects.” Technically these people were not his subjects yet, but would be upon his return. They were citizens of his country who opposed his appointment as their king; later the newly-appointed king will refer to them as his “enemies” (v. 27).
The imperfect is intense in this context, suggesting an ongoing attitude.
Grk “this one” (somewhat derogatory in this context).
Or “to rule.”

15.text: When he returned after receiving the kingdom, he summoned these slaves to whom he had given the money. He wanted to know how much they had earned by trading.

notes.text: Grk “And it happened that when.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
Grk “he said for these slaves to be called to him.” The passive construction has been translated as an active one and simplified to “he summoned.”

Grk “in order that he might know” (a continuation of the preceding sentence). Due to the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was started here in the translation by supplying the pronoun “he” as subject and the verb “wanted” to convey the idea of purpose.
The Greek verb earned refers to profit from engaging in commerce and trade (L&N 57.195). This is an examination of stewardship.

16.text: So the first one came before him and said, ‘Sir, your mina has made ten minas more.’

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of the royal summons.
Or “Lord”; or “Master.” (and so throughout this paragraph).
See the note on the word “minas” in v. 13.

17.text: And the king said to him, ‘Well done, good slave! Because you have been faithful in a very small matter, you will have authority over ten cities.’

notes.text: Grk “he”; the referent (the nobleman of v. 12, now a king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
See Luke 16:10.
The faithful slave received expanded responsibility (authority over ten cities) as a result of his faithfulness; this in turn is an exhortation to faithfulness for the reader.

18.text: Then the second one came and said, ‘Sir, your mina has made five minas.’

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.

19.text: So the king said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of the second slave’s report.
Grk “he”; the referent (the nobleman of v. 12, now a king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

20.text: Then another slave came and said, ‘Sir, here is your mina that I put away for safekeeping in a piece of cloth.

notes.text: Though ten were given minas, the story stops to focus on the one who did nothing with the opportunity given to him. Here is the parable’s warning about the one who does not trust the master. This figure is called “another,” marking him out as different than the first two.
The word “slave” is not in the Greek text, but has been supplied for stylistic reasons.
Grk “behold.”
Or “that I stored away.” L&N 85.53 defines ἀπόκειμαι (apokeimai) here as “to put something away for safekeeping—‘to store, to put away in a safe place.’”
The piece of cloth, called a σουδάριον (soudarion), could have been a towel, napkin, handkerchief, or face cloth (L&N 6.159).

21.text: For I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You withdraw what you did not deposit and reap what you did not sow.’

notes.text: Or “exacting,” “harsh,” “hard.”

Grk “man, taking out.” The Greek word can refer to withdrawing money from a bank (L&N 57.218), and in this context of financial accountability that is the most probable meaning. Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was started here in the translation by supplying the pronoun “you” as subject and translating the participle αἴρεις (aireis) as a finite verb.
The Greek verb τίθημι (tithēmi) can be used of depositing money with a banker to earn interest (L&N 57.217). In effect the slave charges that the master takes what he has not earned.

22.text: The king said to him, ‘I will judge you by your own words, you wicked slave! So you knew, did you, that I was a severe man, withdrawing what I didn’t deposit and reaping what I didn’t sow?

notes.text: Grk “He”; the referent (the nobleman of v. 12, now a king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “out of your own mouth” (an idiom).
Note the contrast between this slave, described as “wicked,” and the slave in v. 17, described as “good.”
Or “exacting,” “harsh,” “hard.”

23.text: Why then didn’t you put my money in the bank, so that when I returned I could have collected it with interest?’

notes.text: That is, “If you really feared me why did you not do a minimum to get what I asked for?”
Grk “on the table”; the idiom refers to a place where money is kept or managed, or credit is established, thus “bank” (L&N 57.215).

24.text: And he said to his attendants, ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has ten.’

notes.text: Grk “to those standing by,” but in this context involving an audience before the king to give an accounting, these would not be casual bystanders but courtiers or attendants.
Grk “the ten minas.”

25.text: But they said to him, ‘Sir, he has ten minas already!’

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast present in this context. Those watching the evaluation are shocked, as the one with the most gets even more. The word “already” is supplied at the end of the statement to indicate this surprise and shock.
A few mss (D W 69 and a few versional witnesses) omit this verse either to harmonize it with Matt 25:28-29 or to keep the king’s speech seamless.

26.text: ‘I tell you that everyone who has will be given more, but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.

notes.text: Grk “to everyone who has, he will be given more.”
Everyone who has will be given more. Again, faithfulness yields great reward (see Luke 8:18; also Matt 13:12; Mark 4:25).

The one who has nothing has even what he seems to have taken away from him, ending up with no reward at all (see also Luke 8:18). The exact force of this is left ambiguous, but there is no comfort here for those who are pictured by the third slave as being totally unmoved by the master. Though not an outright enemy, there is no relationship to the master either. Three groups are represented in the parable: the faithful of various sorts (vv. 16, 18); the unfaithful who associate with Jesus but do not trust him (v. 21); and the enemies (v. 27).

27.text: But as for these enemies of mine who did not want me to be their king, bring them here and slaughter them in front of me!’”

notes.text: Grk “to rule over them.”
This term, when used of people rather than animals, has some connotations of violence and mercilessness (L&N 20.72).
Slaughter them. To reject the king is to face certain judgment from him.

28.text: After Jesus had said this, he continued on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.

notes.text: Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
This could mean “before [his disciples],” but that is slightly more awkward, requiring an elided element (the disciples) to be supplied.
This is yet another travel note on the journey to Jerusalem. See also Luke 18:31; 19:11. Jesus does not actually enter Jerusalem until 19:45.

29.text: Now when he approached Bethphage and Bethany, at the place called the Mount of Olives, he sent two of the disciples,

notes.text: Grk “And it happened that when.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated. Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the transition to a new topic.
The exact location of the village of Bethphage is not known. Most locate it on the southeast side of the Mount of Olives and northwest of Bethany, about 1.5 miles (3 km) east of Jerusalem.
Grk “at the mountain called ‘of Olives.’” This form of reference is awkward in contemporary English, so the more familiar “Mount of Olives” has been used in the translation.

“Mountain” in English generally denotes a higher elevation than it often does in reference to places in Palestine. The Mount of Olives is really a ridge running north to south about 1.8 mi (3 km) long, east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley. Its central elevation is about 100 ft (30 m) higher than Jerusalem. It was named for the large number of olive trees which grew on it.

30.text: telling them, “Go to the village ahead of you. When you enter it, you will find a colt tied there that has never been ridden. Untie it and bring it here.

notes.text: Grk “saying.”
Grk “the village lying before [you]” (BDAG 530 s.v. κατέναντι 2.a).
Grk “in which entering.” This is a continuation of the previous sentence in Greek, but because of the length and complexity of the construction a new sentence was started here in the translation.
Grk “a colt tied there on which no one of men has ever sat.”

31.text: If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ just say, ‘The Lord needs it.’”

notes.text: The custom called angaria allowed the impressment of animals for service to a significant figure.

32.text: So those who were sent ahead found it exactly as he had told them.

notes.text: Grk “sent ahead and went and found.”
Exactly as he had told them. Nothing in Luke 19-23 catches Jesus by surprise. Often he directs the action.

33.text: As they were untying the colt, its owners asked them, “Why are you untying that colt?”

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “said to them.”

34.text: They replied, “The Lord needs it.”

35.text: Then they brought it to Jesus, threw their cloaks on the colt, and had Jesus get on it.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “garments,” but this refers in context to their outer cloaks. The action is like 2 Kgs 9:13.
See Zech 9:9.

Although ἐπεβίβασαν (epebibasan) is frequently translated “set [Jesus] on it” or “put [Jesus] on it,” when used of a riding animal the verb can mean “to cause to mount” (L&N 15.98); thus here “had Jesus get on it.” The degree of assistance is not specified.

36.text: As he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.

The disciples initiated this action (since in 19:35 and 37 they are the subject) but the other gospels indicate the crowds also became involved. Thus it is difficult to specify the referent here as “the disciples” or “people.”

37.text: As he approached the road leading down from the Mount of Olives, the whole crowd of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works they had seen:

notes.text: Grk “the descent of”; this could refer to either the slope of the hillside itself or the path leading down from it (the second option has been adopted for the translation, see L&N 15.109).
See the note on the name Mount of Olives in v. 29.
Grk “the”; the Greek article has been translated here as a possessive pronoun (ExSyn 215).
Here the participle χαίροντες (chairontes) has been translated as a finite verb in English; it could also be translated adverbially as a participle of manner: “began to praise God joyfully.”
Or “works of power,” “miracles.” Jesus’ ministry of miracles is what has drawn attention. See Luke 7:22.
Grk “they had seen, saying.” The participle λέγοντες (legontes) is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.

38.text: “Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!”

notes.text: Luke adds the title king to the citation from Ps 118:26 to make clear who was meant (see Luke 18:38). The psalm was used in looking for the deliverance of the end, thus leading to the Pharisees’ reaction.
A quotation from Ps 118:26.

39.text: But some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.”

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast present in this context. Not all present are willing to join in the acclamation.
See the note on Pharisees in 5:17.
Teacher, rebuke your disciples. The Pharisees were complaining that the claims were too great.

40.text: He answered, “I tell you, if they keep silent, the very stones will cry out!”

notes.text: Grk “and answering, he said.” This has been simplified in the translation to “He answered.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “these.”
This statement amounts to a rebuke. The idiom of creation speaking means that even creation knows what is taking place, yet the Pharisees miss it. On this idiom, see Gen 4:10 and Hab 2:11.

41.text: Now when Jesus approached and saw the city, he wept over it,

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the transition to a new topic.
Grk “he.”
When Jesus approached and saw the city. This is the last travel note in Luke’s account (the so-called Jerusalem journey), as Jesus approached and saw the city before entering it.

42.text: saying, “If you had only known on this day, even you, the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.

notes.text: On this day. They had missed the time of Messiah’s coming; see v. 44.
Grk “the things toward peace.” This expression seems to mean “the things that would ‘lead to,’ ‘bring about,’ or ‘make for’ peace.”

But now they are hidden from your eyes. This becomes an oracle of doom in the classic OT sense; see Luke 13:31-35; 11:49-51; Jer 9:2; 13:7; 14:7. They are now blind and under judgment (Jer 15:5; Ps 122:6).

43.text: For the days will come upon you when your enemies will build an embankment against you and surround you and close in on you from every side.

notes.text: Jesus now predicted the events that would be fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem in a.d. 70. The details of the siege have led some to see Luke writing this after Jerusalem’s fall, but the language of the verse is like God’s exilic judgment for covenant unfaithfulness (Hab 2:8; Jer 6:6, 14; 8:13-22; 9:1; Ezek 4:2; 26:8; Isa 29:1-4). Specific details are lacking and the procedures described (build an embankment against you) were standard Roman military tactics.
An embankment refers to either wooden barricades or earthworks, or a combination of the two.

44.text: They will demolish you —you and your children within your walls —and they will not leave within you one stone on top of another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God.”

notes.text: Grk “They will raze you to the ground.”
The singular pronoun you refers to the city of Jerusalem personified.
Grk “your children within you.” The phrase “[your] walls” has been supplied in the translation to clarify that the city of Jerusalem, metaphorically pictured as an individual, is spoken of here.
(Not) one stone on top of another is an idiom for total destruction.
Grk “leave stone on stone.”
Grk “the time of your visitation.” To clarify what this refers to, the words “from God” are supplied at the end of the verse, although they do not occur in the Greek text.
You did not recognize the time of your visitation refers to the time God came to visit them. They had missed the Messiah; see Luke 1:68-79.

45.text: Then Jesus entered the temple courts and began to drive out those who were selling things there,

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “he.”
Grk “the temple” (also in v. 47).
The merchants (those who were selling things there) would have been located in the Court of the Gentiles.

Matthew (21:12-27), Mark (11:15-19) and Luke (here, 19:45-46) record this incident of the temple cleansing at the end of Jesus’ ministry. John (2:13-16) records a cleansing of the temple at the beginning of Jesus’ ministry. See the note on the word temple courts in John 2:14 for a discussion of the relationship of these accounts to one another.

46.text: saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house will be a house of prayer,’ but you have turned it into a den of robbers!”

notes.text: A quotation from Isa 56:7.
Or “a hideout” (see L&N 1.57).

A quotation from Jer 7:11. The meaning of Jesus’ statement about making the temple courts a den of robbers probably operates here at two levels. Not only were the religious leaders robbing the people financially, but because of this they had also robbed them spiritually by stealing from them the opportunity to come to know God genuinely. It is possible that these merchants had recently been moved to this location for convenience.

47.text: Jesus was teaching daily in the temple courts. The chief priests and the experts in the law and the prominent leaders among the people were seeking to assassinate him,

notes.text: Grk “And he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity. Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “and the scribes.” See the note on the phrase “experts in the law” in 5:21.
Grk “to destroy.”
The action at the temple was the last straw. In their view, if Jesus could cause trouble in the holy place, then he must be stopped, so the leaders were seeking to assassinate him.

48.text: but they could not find a way to do it, for all the people hung on his words.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast present in this context.
Grk “they did not find the thing that they might do.”
All the people hung on his words is an idiom for intent, eager listening. Jesus’ popularity and support made it unwise for the leadership to seize him.

1.text: Now one day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple courts and proclaiming the gospel, the chief priests and the experts in the law with the elders came up

notes.text: Grk “Now it happened that one.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated. Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the transition to a new topic.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “the temple.”
Or “preaching.”
Or “and the scribes.” See the note on the phrase “experts in the law” in 5:21.
The chief priests and the experts in the law with the elders came up. The description is similar to Luke 19:47. The leaders are really watching Jesus at this point.

2.text: and said to him, “Tell us: By what authority are you doing these things? Or who is it who gave you this authority?”

notes.text: Grk “and said, saying to him.” This is redundant in English and has been simplified in the translation.
On this phrase, see BDAG 844 s.v. ποῖος 2.a.γ.
The leadership is looking back to acts like the temple cleansing (19:45-48). How could a Galilean preacher do these things?

3.text: He answered them, “I will also ask you a question, and you tell me:

notes.text: Grk “answering, he said to them.” This is redundant in English and has been simplified in the translation.

4.text: John’s baptism —was it from heaven or from people?”

notes.text: John, like Jesus, was not a part of the official rabbinic order. So the question “John’s baptism—was it from heaven or from men?” draws an analogy between John the Baptist and Jesus. See Luke 3:1-20; 7:24-27. The phrase John’s baptism refers to the baptism practiced by John.

The plural Greek term ἀνθρώπων (anthrōpōn) is used here (and in v. 6) in a generic sense, referring to both men and women (cf. NAB, NRSV, “of human origin”; TEV, “from human beings”; NLT, “merely human”).
The question is whether John’s ministry was of divine or human origin.

5.text: So they discussed it with one another, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of Jesus’ question.

6.text: But if we say, ‘From people,’ all the people will stone us, because they are convinced that John was a prophet.”

7.text: So they replied that they did not know where it came from.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of the dilemma Jesus’ opponents faced.

Very few questions could have so completely revealed the wicked intentions of the religious leaders. Jesus’ question revealed the motivation of the religious leaders and exposed them for what they really were—hypocrites. They indicted themselves when they cited only two options and chose neither of them. The point of Luke 20:1-8 is that no matter what Jesus said in response to their question they were not going to believe it and would in the end use it against him.

8.text: Then Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by whose authority I do these things.”

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Neither will I tell you. Though Jesus gave no answer, the analogy he used to their own question makes his view clear. His authority came from heaven.
On this phrase, see BDAG 844 s.v. ποῖος 2.a.γ. This is exactly the same phrase as in v. 2.

9.text: Then he began to tell the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard, leased it to tenant farmers, and went on a journey for a long time.

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative. The parable Jesus tells here actually addresses the question put to him by the leaders.

‡ There are several variants here, most of which involve variations in word order that do not affect translation. However, the presence or absence of τις (tis) after ἄνθρωπος (anthrōpos), which would be translated “a certain man,” does affect translation. The witnesses that have τις include A W Θ ƒ13 1241 2542 al sy. Those that lack it include ‏א‎ B C D L Ψ ƒ1 33 M it. Externally, the evidence is significantly stronger for the omission. Internally, however, there is some pause. A feature unique to Luke-Acts in the NT is to use the construction ἄνθρωπος τις (cf. 10:30; 12:16; 14:2, 16; 15:11; 16:1; 19:12; Acts 9:33). However, scribes who were familiar with this idiom may have inserted it here. In light of the overwhelming external support for the omission of τις, the shorter reading is preferred. NA28 places τις in brackets, indicating some doubts as to its authenticity.

The vineyard is a figure for Israel in the OT (Isa 5:1-7). The nation and its leaders are the tenants, so the vineyard here may well refer to the promise that resides within the nation. The imagery is like that in Rom 11:11-24.
The leasing of land to tenant farmers was common in this period.

10.text: When harvest time came, he sent a slave to the tenants so that they would give him his portion of the crop. However, the tenants beat his slave and sent him away empty-handed.

notes.text: This slave (along with the next two) represent the prophets God sent to the nation, who were mistreated and rejected.

Instead of the future indicative δώσουσιν (dōsousin, “they will give”), most witnesses (C D W Θ Ψ ƒ1 M) have the aorist subjunctive δῶσιν (dōsin, “they might give”). The aorist subjunctive is expected following ἵνα (hina, “so that”), so it is almost surely a motivated reading. Further, early and excellent witnesses, as well as a few others (‏א‎ A B ƒ13 33 579 1241 2542 al), have δώσουσιν. It is thus more likely that the future indicative is authentic. For a discussion of this construction, see BDF §369.2.
Grk “from the fruit of the vineyard.”
Grk “him”; the referent (the slave sent by the owner) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The image of the tenants beating up the owner’s slave pictures the nation’s rejection of the prophets and their message.

11.text: So he sent another slave. They beat this one too, treated him outrageously, and sent him away empty-handed.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of the tenants’ mistreatment of the first slave.
The slaves being sent empty-handed suggests that the vineyard was not producing any fruit—and thus neither was the nation of Israel.

12.text: So he sent still a third. They even wounded this one, and threw him out.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of the tenants’ mistreatment of the first two slaves.

13.text: Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What should I do? I will send my one dear son; perhaps they will respect him.’

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “my beloved son.” See comment at Luke 3:22.
The owner’s decision to send his one dear son represents God sending Jesus.

14.text: But when the tenants saw him, they said to one another, ‘This is the heir; let’s kill him so the inheritance will be ours!’

15.text: So they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them?

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of the tenants’ decision to kill the son.
Throwing the heir out of the vineyard pictures Jesus’ death outside of Jerusalem.

16.text: He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” When the people heard this, they said, “May this never happen!”

notes.text: The statement that the owner will come and destroy those tenants is a promise of judgment; see Luke 13:34-35; 19:41-44.

The warning that the owner would give the vineyard to others suggests that the care of the promise and the nation’s hope would be passed to others. This eventually looks to Gentile inclusion; see Eph 2:11-22.
Grk “they”; the referent (the people addressed in v. 9) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
May this never happen! Jesus’ audience got the point and did not want to consider a story where the nation would suffer judgment.

17.text: But Jesus looked straight at them and said, “Then what is the meaning of that which is written: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’?

notes.text: Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Or “capstone,” “keystone.” Although these meanings are lexically possible, the imagery in Eph 2:20-22 and 1 Cor 3:11 indicates that the term κεφαλὴ γωνίας (kephalē gōnias) refers to a cornerstone, not a capstone.

The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The use of Ps 118:22-23 and the “stone imagery” as a reference to Christ and his suffering and exaltation is common in the NT (see also Matt 21:42; Mark 12:10; Acts 4:11; 1 Pet 2:6-8; cf. also Eph 2:20). The irony in the use of Ps 118:22-23 here is that in the OT, Israel was the one rejected (or perhaps her king) by the Gentiles, but in the NT it is Jesus who is rejected by Israel.

18.text: Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, and the one on whom it falls will be crushed.”

notes.text: On this term, see BDAG 972 s.v. συνθλάω.
Grk “on whomever it falls, it will crush him.”
This proverb basically means that the stone crushes, without regard to whether it falls on someone or someone falls on it. On the stone as a messianic image, see Isa 28:16 and Dan 2:44-45.

19.text: Then the experts in the law and the chief priests wanted to arrest him that very hour, because they realized he had told this parable against them. But they were afraid of the people.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Or “The scribes” See the note on the phrase “experts in the law” in 5:21.
Grk “tried to lay hands on him.”
Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast present in this context.

20.text: Then they watched him carefully and sent spies who pretended to be sincere. They wanted to take advantage of what he might say so that they could deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “righteous,” but in this context the point is their false sincerity.
Grk “so that they might catch him in some word.”
This word is often translated “authority” in other contexts, but here, in combination with ἀρχή (archē), it refers to the domain or sphere of the governor’s rule (L&N 37.36).

21.text: Thus they asked him, “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach correctly, and show no partiality, but teach the way of God in accordance with the truth.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “thus” to indicate the implied result of the plans by the spies.
Or “precisely”; Grk “rightly.” Jesus teaches exactly, the straight and narrow.
Teach the way of God in accordance with the truth. Very few comments are as deceitful as this one; they did not really believe this at all. The question was specifically designed to trap Jesus.

22.text: Is it right for us to pay the tribute tax to Caesar or not?”

notes.text: Or “lawful,” that is, in accordance with God’s divine law. On the syntax of ἔξεστιν (exestin) with an infinitive and accusative, see BDF §409.3.
This was a “poll tax.” L&N 57.182 states this was “a payment made by the people of one nation to another, with the implication that this is a symbol of submission and dependence—‘tribute tax.’”
Or “to the emperor” (“Caesar” is a title for the Roman emperor).

23.text: But Jesus perceived their deceit and said to them,

notes.text: Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “craftiness.” The term always has negative connotations in the NT (1 Cor 3:19; 2 Cor 4:2; 11:3; Eph 4:14).

24.text: “Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription are on it?” They said, “Caesar’s.”

notes.text: Here the specific name of the coin was retained in the translation, because not all coins in circulation in Palestine at the time carried the image of Caesar. In other places δηνάριον (dēnarion) has been translated simply as “silver coin” with an explanatory note.

A denarius was a silver coin worth approximately one day’s wage for a laborer. The fact that the leaders had such a coin showed that they already operated in the economic world of Rome. The denarius would have had a picture of Tiberius Caesar, the Roman emperor, on it.
Or “whose likeness.”

In this passage Jesus points to the image (Grk εἰκών, eikōn) of Caesar on the coin. This same Greek word is used in Gen 1:26 (LXX) to state that humanity is made in the “image” of God. Jesus is making a subtle yet powerful contrast: Caesar’s image is on the denarius, so he can lay claim to money through taxation, but God’s image is on humanity, so he can lay claim to each individual life.
Grk “whose likeness and inscription does it have?”

25.text: So he said to them, “Then give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate that Jesus’ pronouncement results from the opponents’ answer to his question.
Jesus’ answer to give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and to God the things that are God’s was a both/and, not the questioners’ either/or. So he slipped out of their trap.

26.text: Thus they were unable in the presence of the people to trap him with his own words. And stunned by his answer, they fell silent.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “thus” to indicate the implied result of Jesus’ unexpected answer.
On this term, see BDAG 374 s.v. ἐπιλαμβάνομαι 3.
Grk “to trap him in a saying.”
Or “amazed.”

27.text: Now some Sadducees (who contend that there is no resurrection) came to him.

notes.text: The Sadducees controlled the official political structures of Judaism at this time, being the majority members of the Sanhedrin. They were known as extremely strict on law and order issues (Josephus, J. W. 2.8.2 [2.119], 2.8.14 [2.164-166]; Ant. 13.5.9 [13.171-173], 13.10.6 [13.293-298], 18.1.2 [18.11], 18.1.4 [18.16-17], 20.9.1 [20.199]; Life 2 [10-11]). They also did not believe in resurrection or in angels, an important detail in v. 36. See also Matt 3:7; 16:1-12; 22:23-34; Mark 12:18-27; Acts 4:1; 5:17; 23:6-8.
This remark is best regarded as a parenthetical note by the author.

28.text: They asked him, “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies leaving a wife but no children, that man must marry the widow and father children for his brother.

notes.text: Grk “asked him, saying.” The participle λέγοντες (legontes) is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
Grk “his brother,” but this would be redundant in English with the same phrase “his brother” at the end of the verse, so most modern translations render this phrase “the man” (so NIV, NRSV).
The use of ἵνα (hina) with imperatival force is unusual (BDF §470.1).
Grk “and raise up seed,” an idiom for procreating children (L&N 23.59).

A quotation from Deut 25:5. Because the OT quotation does not include “a wife” as the object of the verb, it has been left as normal type. This practice is called levirate marriage (see also Ruth 4:1-12; Mishnah, m. Yevamot; Josephus, Ant. 4.8.23 [4.254-256]). The levirate law is described in Deut 25:5-10. The brother of a man who died without a son had an obligation to marry his brother’s widow. This served several purposes: It provided for the widow in a society where a widow with no children to care for her would be reduced to begging, and it preserved the name of the deceased, who would be regarded as the legal father of the first son produced from that marriage.

29.text: Now there were seven brothers. The first one married a woman and died without children.

notes.text: Grk “took a wife” (an idiom for marrying a woman).

30.text: The second

notes.text: Most mss (A W Θ Ψ ƒ1,13 33 M lat) have the words, “took the wife and this one died childless” after “the second.” But this looks like a clarifying addition, assimilating the text to Mark 12:21. In light of the early and diverse witnesses that lack the expression (‏א‎ B D L 0266 892 1241 co), the shorter reading should be considered authentic.

31.text: and then the third married her, and in this same way all seven died, leaving no children.

32.text: Finally the woman died too.

33.text: In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For all seven had married her.”

notes.text: The point is a dilemma. In a world arguing a person should have one spouse, whose wife will she be in the afterlife? The question was designed to show that (in the opinion of the Sadducees) resurrection leads to a major problem.
Grk “For the seven had her as wife.”

34.text: So Jesus said to them, “The people of this age marry and are given in marriage.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate that Jesus’ response is a result of their framing of the question.
Grk “sons of this age” (an idiom, see L&N 11.16). The following clause which refers to being “given in marriage” suggests both men and women are included in this phrase.

35.text: But those who are regarded as worthy to share in that age and in the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage.

notes.text: Grk “to attain to.”

Life in the age to come is different than life here (they neither marry nor are given in marriage). This means Jesus’ questioners had made a false assumption that life was the same both now and in the age to come.

36.text: In fact, they can no longer die, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, since they are sons of the resurrection.

notes.text: Angels do not die, nor do they eat according to Jewish tradition (1 En. 15:6; 51:4; Wis 5:5; 2 Bar. 51:10; 1QH 3.21-23).
Grk “sons of God, being.” The participle ὄντες (ontes) has been translated as a causal adverbial participle here.

Or “people.” The noun υἱός (huios) followed by the genitive of class or kind (“sons of…”) denotes a person of a class or kind, specified by the following genitive construction. This Semitic idiom is frequent in the NT (L&N 9.4).

37.text: But even Moses revealed that the dead are raised in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.

notes.text: Grk “But that the dead are raised even Moses revealed.”
See Exod 3:6. Jesus used a common form of rabbinic citation here to refer to the passage in question.
A quotation from Exod 3:6.

38.text: Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live before him.”

notes.text: He is not God of the dead but of the living. Jesus’ point was that if God could identify himself as God of the three old patriarchs, then they must still be alive when God spoke to Moses; and so they must be raised.
On this syntax, see BDF §192. The point is that all live “to” God or “before” God.

39.text: Then some of the experts in the law answered, “Teacher, you have spoken well!”

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Or “some of the scribes.” See the note on the phrase “experts in the law” in 5:21.
Teacher, you have spoken well! The scribes, being Pharisees, were happy for the defense of resurrection and angels, which they (unlike the Sadducees) believed in.

40.text: For they did not dare any longer to ask him anything.

notes.text: The attempt to show Jesus as ignorant had left the experts silenced. At this point they did not dare any longer to ask him anything.

41.text: But he said to them, “How is it that they say that the Christ is David’s son?

notes.text: If the religious leaders will not dare to question Jesus any longer, then he will question them.
Or “Messiah”; both “Christ” (Greek) and “Messiah” (Hebrew and Aramaic) mean “one who has been anointed.”
See the note on Christ in 2:11.

It was a common belief in Judaism that Messiah would be David’s son in that he would come from the lineage of David. On this point the Pharisees agreed and were correct. But their understanding was nonetheless incomplete, for Messiah is also David’s Lord. With this statement Jesus was affirming that, as the Messiah, he is both God and man.

42.text: For David himself says in the book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my lord, “Sit at my right hand,

notes.text: The Lord said to my lord. With David being the speaker, this indicates his respect for his descendant (referred to as my lord). Jesus was arguing, as the ancient exposition assumed, that the passage is about the Lord’s anointed. The passage looks at an enthronement of this figure and a declaration of honor for him as he takes his place at the side of God. In Jerusalem, the king’s palace was located to the right of the temple to indicate this kind of relationship. Jesus was pressing the language here to get his opponents to reflect on how great Messiah is.

43.text: until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’

notes.text: A quotation from Ps 110:1.

44.text: If David then calls him ‘Lord,’ how can he be his son?”

notes.text: Grk “David thus calls him ‘Lord.’ So how is he his son?” The conditional nuance, implicit in Greek, has been made explicit in the translation (cf. Matt 22:45).

45.text: As all the people were listening, Jesus said to his disciples,

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has not been translated.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

46.text: “Beware of the experts in the law. They like walking around in long robes, and they love elaborate greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets.

notes.text: Or “Be on guard against.” This is a present imperative and indicates that pride is something to constantly be on the watch against.
Or “of the scribes.” See the note on the phrase “experts in the law” in 5:21.
Grk “who,” continuing the sentence begun by the prior phrase.
There is later Jewish material in the Talmud that spells out such greetings in detail. See D. L. Bock, Luke (BECNT), 2:1642; H. Windisch, TDNT 1:498.
See the note on marketplace in Luke 7:32.
See Luke 14:7-14.
See the note on synagogues in 4:15.

47.text: They devour widows’ property, and as a show make long prayers. They will receive a more severe punishment.”

notes.text: Grk “who,” continuing the sentence begun in v. 46.

How they were able to devour widows’ houses is debated. Did they seek too much for contributions, or take too high a commission for their work, or take homes after debts failed to be paid? There is too little said here to be sure.
Grk “houses,” “households”; however, the term can have the force of “property” or “possessions” as well (O. Michel, TDNT 5:131; BDAG 695 s.v. οἶκια 1.a).

1.text: Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box.

notes.text: Grk “He”; the referent has been specified in the translation for clarity. Here δέ (de) has not been translated.
Grk “looking up, he saw.” The participle ἀναβλέψας (anablepsas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

On the term γαζοφυλάκιον (gazophulakion), often translated “treasury,” see BDAG 186 s.v., which states, “For Mk 12:41, 43; Lk 21:1 the mng. contribution box or receptacle is attractive. Acc. to Mishnah, Shekalim 6, 5 there were in the temple 13 such receptacles in the form of trumpets. But even in these passages the general sense of ‘treasury’ is prob., for the contributions would go [into] the treasury via the receptacles.” Based upon the extra-biblical evidence (see sn following), however, the translation opts to refer to the actual receptacles and not the treasury itself.

The offering box probably refers to the receptacles in the temple forecourt by the Court of Women used to collect freewill offerings. These are mentioned by Josephus, J. W. 5.5.2 (5.200), 6.5.2 (6.282); Ant. 19.6.1 (19.294); and in 1 Macc 14:49 and 2 Macc 3:6, 24, 28, 40 (see also Mark 12:41; John 8:20).

2.text: He also saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins.

notes.text: These two small copper coins were lepta (sing. “lepton”), the smallest and least valuable coins in circulation in Palestine, worth one-half of a quadrans or 1/128 of a denarius, or about six minutes of an average daily wage. This was next to nothing in value.

3.text: He said, “I tell you the truth, this poor widow has put in more than all of them.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “Truly, I say to you.”
Has put in more than all of them. With God, giving is weighed evaluatively, not counted. The widow was praised because she gave sincerely and at some considerable cost to herself.

4.text: For they all offered their gifts out of their wealth. But she, out of her poverty, put in everything she had to live on.”

notes.text: Grk “out of what abounded to them.”
Or “put in her entire livelihood.”

5.text: Now while some were speaking about the temple, how it was adorned with beautiful stones and offerings, Jesus said,

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the transition to a new topic.

The Jerusalem temple was widely admired around the world. See Josephus, Ant. 15.11 (15.380-425); J. W. 5.5 (5.184-227) and Tacitus, History 5.8, who called it “immensely opulent.” Josephus compared it to a beautiful snowcapped mountain.
For the translation of ἀνάθημα (anathēma) as “offering” see L&N 53.18.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

6.text: “As for these things that you are gazing at, the days will come when not one stone will be left on another. All will be torn down!”

notes.text: With the statement days will come when not one stone will be left on another Jesus predicted the total destruction of the temple, something that did occur in a.d. 70.
Grk “the days will come when not one stone will be left on another that will not be thrown down.”

7.text: So they asked him, “Teacher, when will these things happen? And what will be the sign that these things are about to take place?”

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of Jesus’ comments about the temple’s future destruction.
Grk “asked him, saying.” The participle λέγοντες (legontes) is redundant in English and has not been translated.
Both references to these things are plural, so more than the temple’s destruction is in view. The question may presuppose that such a catastrophe signals the end.
Grk “when.”

8.text: He said, “Watch out that you are not misled. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and, ‘The time is near.’ Do not follow them!

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has not been translated.
Or “Be on guard.”
That is, “I am the Messiah.”

9.text: And when you hear of wars and rebellions, do not be afraid. For these things must happen first, but the end will not come at once.”

notes.text: Social and political chaos also precedes the end. This term refers to revolutions (L&N 39.34).
This is not the usual term for fear, but refers to a deep sense of terror and emotional distress (Luke 24:37; BDAG 895 s.v. πτοέω).
The end will not come at once. This remark about timing not only indicates that there will be events before the end, but that some time will also pass before it comes.

10.text: Then he said to them, “Nation will rise up in arms against nation, and kingdom against kingdom.

notes.text: For the translation “rise up in arms” see L&N 55.2.

11.text: There will be great earthquakes, and famines and plagues in various places, and there will be terrifying sights and great signs from heaven.

notes.text: This term, φόβητρον (phobētron), occurs only here in the NT. It could refer to an object, event, or condition that causes fear, but in the context it is linked with great signs from heaven, so the translation “sights” was preferred.

12.text: But before all this, they will seize you and persecute you, handing you over to the synagogues and prisons. You will be brought before kings and governors because of my name.

notes.text: But before all this. Another note of timing is present, this one especially important in understanding the sequence in the discourse. Before the things noted in vv. 8-11 are the events of vv. 12-19.
Grk “will lay their hands on you.”
Some of the persecution is of Jewish origin (the synagogues). Some fulfillment of this can be seen in Acts. See the note on synagogues in 4:15.
Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was started here in the translation.

13.text: This will be a time for you to serve as witnesses.

notes.text: Grk “This will turn out to you for [a] testimony.”

14.text: Therefore be resolved not to rehearse ahead of time how to make your defense.

notes.text: Grk “determine in your hearts.”
This term could refer to rehearsing a speech or a dance. On its syntax, see BDF §392.2.

15.text: For I will give you the words along with the wisdom that none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict.

notes.text: Grk “a mouth.” It is a metonymy and refers to the reply the Lord will give to them.
Grk “and wisdom.”

16.text: You will be betrayed even by parents, brothers, relatives, and friends, and they will have some of you put to death.

notes.text: To confess Christ might well mean rejection by one’s own family, even by parents.

Grk “and brothers and relatives,” but καί (kai) has not been translated twice here since English normally uses a coordinating conjunction only between the last two elements in a series of three or more.

17.text: You will be hated by everyone because of my name.

18.text: Yet not a hair of your head will perish.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “yet” to indicate the contrast present in this context.
Given v. 16, the expression not a hair of your head will perish must be taken figuratively and refer to living ultimately in the presence of God.

19.text: By your endurance you will gain your lives.

notes.text: By your endurance is a call to remain faithful, because trusting in Jesus is the means to life.

Some significant Greek witnesses plus the majority of mss (‏א‎ D L W Ψ ƒ1 M) read the aorist imperative κτήσασθε (ktēsasthe) here, though some mss (A B Θ ƒ13 33 lat sa) read the future indicative κτήσεσθε (ktēsesthe). A decision is difficult because the evidence is so evenly balanced, but the aorist imperative is the harder reading and better explains the rise of the other. J. A. Fitzmyer assesses the translation options this way: “In English one has to use something similar [i.e., a future indicative], even if one follows the [aorist imperative]” (Luke [AB], 2:1341); in the same vein, although this translation follows the aorist imperative, because of English requirements it has been translated as though it were a future indicative.

Grk “your souls,” but ψυχή (psuchē) is frequently used of one’s physical life. In light of v. 16 that does not seem to be the case here. The entire phrase could be taken as an idiom meaning “you will save yourselves” (L&N 21.20), or (as in v. 18) this could refer to living ultimately in the presence of God.

20.text: “But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near.

notes.text: See Luke 19:41-44. This passage refers to the events associated with the fall of Jerusalem, when the city is surrounded by armies.
Grk “her,” referring to the city of Jerusalem (the name “Jerusalem” in Greek is a feminine noun).

The phrase its desolation is a reference to the fall of the city, which is the only antecedent present in Luke’s account. The parallels to this in Matt 24:15 and Mark 13:14 refer to the temple’s desolation, though Matthew’s allusion is clearer. They focus on the parallel events of the end, not on the short term realization in a.d. 70. The entire passage has a prophetic “two events in one” typology, where the near term destruction (a.d. 70) is like the end. So the evangelists could choose to focus on the near time realization (Luke) or on its long term fulfillment, which mirrors it (Matthew, Mark).

21.text: Then those who are in Judea must flee to the mountains. Those who are inside the city must depart. Those who are out in the country must not enter it,

notes.text: Fleeing to the mountains is a key OT image: Gen 19:17; Judg 6:2; Isa 15:5; Jer 16:16; Zech 14:5.
Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.

22.text: because these are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written.

notes.text: Or “of punishment.” This is a time of judgment.
The passive construction with the infinitive πλησθῆναι (plēsthēnai) has been translated as an active construction for simplicity, in keeping with contemporary English style.

23.text: Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing their babies in those days! For there will be great distress on the earth and wrath against this people.

notes.text: Great distress means that this is a period of great judgment.

24.text: They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led away as captives among all nations. Jerusalem will be trampled down by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “by the mouth of the sword” (an idiom for the edge of a sword).
Here is the predicted judgment against the nation until the time of Gentile rule has passed: Its people will be led away as captives.
Grk “And Jerusalem.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled implies a time when Israel again has a central role in God’s plan.

25.text: “And there will be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and on the earth nations will be in distress, anxious over the roaring of the sea and the surging waves.

notes.text: Signs in the sun and moon and stars are cosmic signs that turn our attention to the end and the Son of Man’s return for the righteous. OT imagery is present: See Isa 13:9-10; 24:18-20; 34:4; Ezek 32:7-8; Joel 2:1, 30-31; 3:15.
Grk “distress of nations.”
Or “in consternation” (L&N 32.9).

26.text: People will be fainting from fear and from the expectation of what is coming on the world, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

notes.text: According to L&N 23.184 this could be mainly a psychological experience rather than actual loss of consciousness. It could also refer to complete discouragement because of fear, leading people to give up hope (L&N 25.293).

An allusion to Isa 34:4. The heavens were seen as the abode of heavenly forces, so their shaking indicates distress in the spiritual realm. Although some take the powers as a reference to bodies in the heavens (like stars and planets, “the heavenly bodies,” NIV) this is not as likely.

27.text: Then they will see the Son of Man arriving in a cloud with power and great glory.

notes.text: Grk “And then” (καὶ τότε, kai tote). Here καί has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
An allusion to Dan 7:13. Here is Jesus returning with full judging authority.

28.text: But when these things begin to happen, stand up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”

notes.text: These things are all the events of vv. 8-27. Disciples represent the righteous here. The events surrounding the fall of the nation are a down payment on a fuller judgment to come on all humanity. The presence of one guarantees the other.
With Jesus’ return comes the manifestation of judgment and final salvation (redemption).

29.text: Then he told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree and all the other trees.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “all the trees.”

30.text: When they sprout leaves, you see for yourselves and know that summer is now near.

notes.text: Grk “seeing for yourselves, you know.” The participle βλέποντες (blepontes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

31.text: So also you, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.

notes.text: The verb γινώσκετε (ginōskete, “know”) can be parsed as either present indicative or present imperative. In this context the imperative fits better, since the movement is from analogy (trees and seasons) to the future (the signs of the coming of the kingdom) and since the emphasis is on preparation for this event.
The kingdom of God refers here to the kingdom in all its power. See Luke 17:20-37.

32.text: I tell you the truth, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.

notes.text: Grk “Truly (ἀμήν, amēn), I say to you.”

This is one of the hardest verses in the gospels to interpret. Various views exist for what generation means. (1) Some take it as meaning “race” and thus as an assurance that the Jewish race (nation) will not pass away. But it is very questionable that the Greek term γενεά (genea) can have this meaning. Two other options are possible. (2) Generation might mean “this type of generation” and refer to the generation of wicked humanity. Then the point is that humanity will not perish, because God will redeem it. Or (3) generation may refer to “the generation that sees the signs of the end” (vv. 25-26), who will also see the end itself. In other words, once the movement to the return of Christ starts, all the events connected with it happen very quickly, in rapid succession.

33.text: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.

notes.text: The words that Jesus predicts here will never pass away. They are more stable and lasting than creation itself. For this kind of image, see Isa 40:8; 55:10-11.

34.text: “But be on your guard so that your hearts are not weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and the worries of this life, and that day close down upon you suddenly like a trap.

notes.text: Grk “watch out for yourselves.”
Disciples are to watch out. If they are too absorbed into everyday life, they will stop watching and living faithfully.

Or like a thief, see Luke 12:39-40. The metaphor of a trap is a vivid one. Most modern English translations traditionally place the words “like a trap” at the end of v. 34, completing the metaphor. In the Greek text (and in the NRSV and REB) the words “like a trap” are placed at the beginning of v. 35. This does not affect the meaning.

35.text: For it will overtake all who live on the face of the whole earth.

notes.text: There is debate in the textual tradition about the position of γάρ (gar) and whether v. 35 looks back to v. 34 or is independent. The textual evidence does slightly favor placing γάρ after the verb and thus linking it back to v. 34. The other reading looks like Isa 24:17. However, the construction is harsh and the translation prefers for stylistic reasons to start a new English sentence here.
Or “come upon.”
This judgment involves everyone: all who live on the face of the whole earth. No one will escape this evaluation.

36.text: But stay alert at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that must happen, and to stand before the Son of Man.”

notes.text: The call to be alert at all times is a call to remain faithful in looking for the Lord’s return.
For the translation of μέλλω (mellō) as “must,” see L&N 71.36.

37.text: So every day Jesus was teaching in the temple courts, but at night he went and stayed on the Mount of Olives.

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” since vv. 37-38 serve as something of a summary or transition from the discourse preceding to the passion narrative that follows.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “in the temple.”
Grk “and spent the night,” but this is redundant because of the previous use of the word “night.”
Grk “at the mountain called ‘of Olives.’”
See the note on the phrase Mount of Olives in 19:29.

38.text: And all the people came to him early in the morning to listen to him in the temple courts.

notes.text: Jesus’ teaching was still quite popular with all the people at this point despite the leaders’ opposition.
Some mss (those of ƒ13) place John 7:53-8:11 here after v. 38, no doubt because it was felt that this was a better setting for the pericope.
Grk “in the temple.”

1.text: Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called the Passover, was approaching.

notes.text: The Feast of Unleavened Bread was a week long celebration that followed the day of Passover, so one name was used for both feasts (Exod 12:1-20; 23:15; 34:18; Deut 16:1-8).

2.text: The chief priests and the experts in the law were trying to find some way to execute Jesus, for they were afraid of the people.

notes.text: Grk “And the.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Or “and the scribes.” See the note on the phrase “experts in the law” in 5:21.
Grk “were seeking how.”
The Greek verb here means “to get rid of by execution” (BDAG 64 s.v. ἀναιρέω 2; cf. also L&N 20.71, which states, “to get rid of someone by execution, often with legal or quasi-legal procedures”).
Grk “him”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The suggestion here is that Jesus was too popular to openly arrest him. The verb were trying is imperfect. It suggests, in this context, that they were always considering the opportunities.

3.text: Then Satan entered Judas, the one called Iscariot, who was one of the twelve.

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
The cross is portrayed as part of the cosmic battle between Satan and God; see Luke 4:1-13; 11:14-23.
Grk “Iscariot, being of the number of the twelve.”

4.text: He went away and discussed with the chief priests and officers of the temple guard how he might betray Jesus, handing him over to them.

notes.text: The full title στρατηγὸς τοῦ ἱεροῦ (stratēgos tou hierou; “officer of the temple” or “captain of the temple guard”) is sometimes shortened to στρατηγός as here (L&N 37.91).
Luke uses this frequent indirect question to make his point (BDF §267.2).
Grk “him”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “how he might hand him over to them,” in the sense of “betray him.”

5.text: They were delighted and arranged to give him money.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.

The leaders were delighted when Judas contacted them about betraying Jesus, because it gave them the opportunity they had been looking for, and they could later claim that Jesus had been betrayed by one of his own disciples.
Matt 26:15 states the amount of money they gave Judas was thirty pieces of silver (see also Matt 27:3-4; Zech 11:12-13).

6.text: So Judas agreed and began looking for an opportunity to betray Jesus when no crowd was present.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of the arrangement worked out in the preceding verse.
Grk “he”; the referent (Judas) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “betray him to them”; the referent of the first pronoun (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “apart from the crowd.”
The leaders wanted to do this quietly, when no crowd was present, so no public uproar would result (cf. v. 21:38; 22:2).

7.text: Then the day for the feast of Unleavened Bread came, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed.

notes.text: The words “for the feast” are not in the Greek text, but have been supplied for clarity.

Generally the feast of Unleavened Bread would refer to Nisan 15 (Friday), but the following reference to the sacrifice of the Passover lamb indicates that Nisan 14 (Thursday) was what Luke had in mind (Nisan = March 27 to April 25). The celebration of the Feast of Unleavened Bread lasted eight days, beginning with the Passover meal. The celebrations were so close together that at times the names of both were used interchangeably.

8.text: Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and prepare the Passover for us to eat.”

notes.text: Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

This required getting a suitable lamb and finding lodging in Jerusalem where the meal could be eaten. The population of the city swelled during the feast, so lodging could be difficult to find. The Passover was celebrated each year in commemoration of the Israelites’ deliverance from Egypt; thus it was a feast celebrating redemption (see Exod 12). The Passover lamb was roasted and eaten after sunset in a family group of at least ten people (m. Pesahim 7.13). People ate the meal while reclining (see the note on table in 22:14). It included, besides the lamb, unleavened bread and bitter herbs as a reminder of Israel’s bitter affliction at the hands of the Egyptians. Four cups of wine mixed with water were also used for the meal. For a further description of the meal and the significance of the wine cups, see E. Ferguson, Backgrounds of Early Christianity, 523-24.
Grk “for us, so that we may eat.”

9.text: They said to him, “Where do you want us to prepare it?”

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has not been translated.
In the Greek text this a deliberative subjunctive.

10.text: He said to them, “Listen, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters,

notes.text: Grk “behold.”
Since women usually carried these jars, it would have been no problem for Peter and John to recognize the man Jesus was referring to.
Jesus is portrayed throughout Luke 22-23 as very aware of what will happen, almost directing events. Here this is indicated by his prediction that a man carrying a jar of water will meet you.

11.text: and tell the owner of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, “Where is the guest room where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?”’

notes.text: Grk “to the master of the household,” referring to one who owns and manages the household, including family, servants, and slaves (L&N 57.14).

12.text: Then he will show you a large furnished room upstairs. Make preparations there.”

13.text: So they went and found things just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of Jesus’ instructions.
The word “things” is not in the Greek text, but is implied. Direct objects were frequently omitted in Greek when clear from the context.
The author’s note that the disciples found things just as he had told them shows that Jesus’ word could be trusted.

14.text: Now when the hour came, Jesus took his place at the table and the apostles joined him.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the transition to a new topic.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Grk “reclined at table,” as 1st century middle eastern meals were not eaten while sitting at a table, but while reclining on one’s side on the floor with the head closest to the low table and the feet farthest away.
Grk “the apostles with him.”

15.text: And he said to them, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.

notes.text: This phrase parallels a Hebrew infinitive absolute and serves to underline Jesus’ enthusiasm for holding this meal (BDF §198.6).

16.text: For I tell you, I will not eat it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.”

notes.text: Although the word “again” is not in the Greek text, it is supplied to indicate that Jesus did indeed partake of this Passover meal, as statements in v. 18 suggest (“from now on”). For more complete discussion see D. L. Bock, Luke (BECNT), 2:1720.

Jesus looked to a celebration in the kingdom to come when the Passover is fulfilled. This reference could well suggest that some type of commemorative sacrifice and meal will be celebrated then, as the antecedent is the Passover sacrifice. The reference is not to the Lord’s supper as some argue, but the Passover.
The kingdom of God here refers to the kingdom in all its power. See Luke 17:20-37.

17.text: Then he took a cup, and after giving thanks he said, “Take this and divide it among yourselves.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.

Then he took a cup. Only Luke mentions two cups at this meal; the other synoptic gospels (Matt, Mark) mention only one. This is the first of the two. It probably refers to the first cup in the traditional Passover meal, which today has four cups (although it is debated whether the fourth cup was used in the 1st century).

18.text: For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.”

notes.text: Grk “the produce” (“the produce of the vine” is a figurative expression for wine).
Until the kingdom of God comes is a reference to the kingdom in all its power. See Luke 17:20-37. Jesus awaits celebration with the arrival of full kingdom blessing.

19.text: Then he took bread, and after giving thanks he broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.

Some significant Western witnesses (D it) lack the words from this point to the end of v. 20. However, the authenticity of these verses is very likely. It is found in a variety of witnesses that represent a broad geographical base (P75 ‏א‎ A B C L Tvid W Δ Θ Ψ ƒ1,13 M al co), rendering the rise of the shorter reading much easier of explanation than the reverse. Further, the inclusion of the second cup is the harder reading, since it differs from Matt 26:26-29 and Mark 14:22-25. Further discussion of this complicated problem (the most difficult in Luke) can be found in TCGNT 148-50.
The language of the phrase given for you alludes to Christ’s death in our place. It is a powerful substitutionary image of what he did for us.

20.text: And in the same way he took the cup after they had eaten, saying, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.

notes.text: The words “he took” are not in the Greek text at this point, but are an understood repetition from v. 19.
The phrase “after they had eaten” translates the temporal infinitive construction μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι (meta to deipnēsai), where the verb δειπνέω (deipneō) means “to eat a meal” or “to have a meal.”
Jesus’ death established the forgiveness promised in the new covenant of Jer 31:31. Jesus is reinterpreting the symbolism of the Passover meal, indicating the presence of a new era.

21.text: “But look, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me on the table.

notes.text: The one who betrays me. Jesus knows about Judas and what he has done.

The point of Jesus’ comment here is not to identify the specific individual per se, but to indicate that it is one who was close to him—somebody whom no one would suspect. His comment serves to heighten the treachery of Judas’ betrayal.

22.text: For the Son of Man is to go just as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!”

notes.text: Jesus’ death has been determined as a part of God’s plan (Acts 2:22-24).

23.text: So they began to question one another as to which of them it could possibly be who would do this.

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of Jesus’ comments: The disciples begin wondering who would betray him.

24.text: A dispute also started among them over which of them was to be regarded as the greatest.

notes.text: Or “happened.”
Though the term μείζων (meizōn) here is comparative in form, it is superlative in sense (BDF §244).

25.text: So Jesus said to them, “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those in authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’

notes.text: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of the dispute among the apostles.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The title ‘benefactor,’ highlighting grace and meaning something like “helper of the people,” was even given to tyrants (2 Macc 4:2; 3 Macc 3:19; Josephus, J. W. 3.9.8 [3.459]).

26.text: Not so with you; instead the one who is greatest among you must become like the youngest, and the leader like the one who serves.

notes.text: Grk “But you are not thus.”
Or “the ruler.”

And the leader like the one who serves. Leadership was not to be a matter of privilege and special status, but of service. All social status is leveled out by these remarks. Jesus himself is the prime example of the servant-leader.

27.text: For who is greater, the one who is seated at the table, or the one who serves? Is it not the one who is seated at the table? But I am among you as one who serves.

notes.text: Grk “who reclines at table,” as 1st century middle eastern meals were not eaten while sitting at a table, but while reclining on one’s side on the floor with the head closest to the low table and the feet farthest away.
The interrogative particle used here in the Greek text (οὐχί, ouchi) expects a positive reply.
Jesus’ example of humble service, as one who serves, shows that the standard for a disciple is different from that of the world. For an example see John 13:1-17.

28.text: “You are the ones who have remained with me in my trials.

notes.text: Or “continued” (L&N 34.3). Jesus acknowledges the disciples’ faithfulness.

29.text: Thus I grant to you a kingdom, just as my Father granted to me,

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “thus” to indicate the implied result of the disciples’ perseverance with Jesus.

With the statement “I grant to you a kingdom” Jesus gave the disciples authority over the kingdom, as God had given him such authority. The present tense looks at authority given presently, though the major manifestation of its presence is yet to come as the next verse shows.
Or “I give you the right to rule” (cf. CEV). For this translation of διατίθεμαι βασιλείαν (diatithemai basileian) see L&N 37.105.

30.text: that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and you will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

notes.text: This verb is future indicative, and thus not subordinate to “grant” (διατίθεμαι, diatithemai) as part of the result clause beginning with ἵνα ἔσθητε (hina esthēte) at the beginning of v. 30. It is better understood as a predictive future.
The statement you will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel looks at the future authority the Twelve will have when Jesus returns. They will share in Israel’s judgment.

31.text: “Simon, Simon, pay attention! Satan has demanded to have you all, to sift you like wheat,

notes.text: The majority of mss (‏א‎ A D W Θ Ψ ƒ1,13 M as well as several versional witnesses) begin this verse with an introductory comment, “and the Lord said,” indicating a change in the subject of discussion. But this is apparently a reading motivated by the need for clarity. Some of the best witnesses, along with a few others (P75 B L T 1241 2542c sys co), do not contain these words. The abrupt shift is the more difficult reading and thus more likely to be autographic.
Grk “behold” (for “pay attention” see L&N 91.13).
This pronoun is plural in the Greek text, so it refers to all the disciples of which Peter is the representative.
Satan has demanded permission to put them to the test. The idiom “sift (someone) like wheat” is similar to the English idiom “to pick (someone) apart.” The pronoun you is implied.

32.text: but I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith may not fail. When you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.”

notes.text: Here and in the remainder of the verse the second person pronouns are singular, so only Peter is in view. The name “Simon” has been supplied as a form of direct address to make this clear in English.
That your faith may not fail. Note that Peter’s denials are pictured here as lapses, not as a total absence of faith.
Grk “And when.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Or “turned around.”
Strengthen your brothers refers to Peter helping to strengthen their faith. Jesus quite graciously restores Peter “in advance,” even with the knowledge of his approaching denials.

33.text: But Peter said to him, “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death!”

notes.text: Grk “he”; the referent (Peter) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The confidence Peter has in private (Lord, I am ready…) will wilt under the pressure of the public eye.

34.text: Jesus replied, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know me.”

notes.text: Grk “he said”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
That is, Peter’s denials will happen before the sun rises.
Once again, Jesus is quite aware that Peter will deny him. Peter, however, is too nonchalant about the possibility of stumbling.

35.text: Then Jesus said to them, “When I sent you out with no money bag, or traveler’s bag, or sandals, you didn’t lack anything, did you?” They replied, “Nothing.”

notes.text: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Traditionally, “purse” (likewise in v. 36).
Or possibly “beggar’s bag” (L&N 6.145).
This refers back to 9:3 and 10:3-4. The Greek construction anticipates a negative reply which is indicated in the translation by the ‘tag’ at the end, “did you?” Nothing was lacking.
Grk “said.”

36.text: He said to them, “But now, the one who has a money bag must take it, and likewise a traveler’s bag too. And the one who has no sword must sell his cloak and buy one.

notes.text: The syntax of this verse is disputed, resulting in various translations. The major options are either (1) that reflected in the translation or (2) that those who have a money bag and traveler’s bag should get a sword, just as those who do not have these items should sell their cloak to buy a sword.
